- Notes: - Penetration declined from 4.2% (2021–22) to 3.7% (2023–24), below global average (7%). - Density increased from $11 (2001–02) to $95 (2023–24), but remains low compared to developing countries like Malaysia. - ULIP Savings-Linked Policies and Insurance Gap: - Insurance gap: - Inadequate insurance coverage, leaving households vulnerable. - Unit Linked Insurance Plans (ULIPs): - Combine life insurance with savings/investment components. - Issue: - ULIPs have minimal protection components, exposing households to significant financing gaps upon premature death of the primary breadwinner. - Implication: - Metrics like insurance density don’t fully reflect coverage adequacy due to savings-focused products. - Recent Trends (2025): - Insurance penetration stabilized at 3.8% in 2024–25, with density reaching $100, driven by rural-focused schemes like Bima Vahak and increased health insurance uptake (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). - Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Insurance Sector - Definition of FDI: - FDI = Foreign Direct Investment. - Occurs when a foreign entity invests in an Indian company’s equity. - Ownership >10% typically qualifies as FDI (as per global standards). - Investor gets ownership + management control. - Example: - Walmart (USA) bought 77% stake in Flipkart (India) in 2018 for $16 billion. - FDI Limits (Before vs After) -
Category Before After Year
LIC (State-owned) No provision 20% 2022
Insurance Companies (non-LIC) 49% 74% 2021
Insurance Companies (non-LIC) - 100% (if all funds invested in India) 2025
Insurance Intermediaries (agents, brokers etc.) 49% 100% 2020
- Budget 2021 Safeguards for 74% FDI: - Majority of Board and Key Management Persons (KMP) must be Resident Indians. - At least 50% of directors must be Independent Directors. - A certain percentage of profits must be kept in general reserve. - Budget 2025 Provision: - 100% FDI allowed only if entire insurance premium collections are invested in India. - Notes: - Intermediaries = Insurance agents, surveyors, third-party administrators (TPAs). - All under IRDAI regulation. - FDI Debates: - Political: - Concerns over loss of sovereignty in policy-making. - Opposition by political parties and farmer/trader lobbies to sectors like retail FDI. - Debate over foreign influence on domestic policymaking. - Social: - Impact on small retailers, employment, and traditional businesses. - FDI in retail and pharma can disrupt livelihoods in informal sectors. - Consumer benefits via better quality and lower prices. - Economic: - Brings in capital, technology, and global best practices. - Helps bridge the current account deficit. - May lead to profit repatriation and domination by foreign players. - Can crowd out local startups or MSMEs. - Recommendations by Parliamentary Committee (2023): - FDI in LIC should be raised to 74% or 100% to improve capital inflow. - Raise 49% limit for Indian promoters in foreign reinsurers (like Lloyd’s). - IRDAI should clarify whether reinsurers need Indian partner or not. - Recommend 100% FDI in insurance brokers to attract global talent. - Insurance Intermediaries: Bankers, Agents, Brokers - Definition: - Insurance intermediaries act as the middlemen between the insurer (company) and the insured (customer). - Regulated by IRDAI. - Insurance Agent vs Insurance Broker -
Insurance Agent Insurance Broker
- Sells policies of a single insurance company.
- Works as a representative of the insurer.
- Example: LIC life insurance agent. 		- Sells policies of multiple insurance companies.
- Works in the interest of the customer.
- Example: Policybazaar.com.
- Types of Brokers & Bancassurance - 1. Direct Broker: - Sells life, general, or health insurance policies of multiple companies. - Services: - advice, claims assistance, risk assessment. - 2. Reinsurance Broker: - Specializes in selling reinsurance contracts of multiple companies. - Works between insurance company and reinsurer. - 3. Composite Broker: - Performs functions of both Direct + Reinsurance Broker. - 4. Bancassurance: - Derived from French term meaning “bank + insurance.” - Refers to banks selling insurance products to their customers. - Benefits: - Banks earn commission. - Insurance companies access a large customer base. - Customers get one-stop access to banking + insurance. - Notes: - All brokers must register with IRDAI. - Composite brokers must fulfill stricter capital & compliance norms. - Bancassurance allowed under RBI & IRDAI frameworks. - Micro Insurance: - Low-sum (≤ ₹50,000) insurance (life/general) for rural poor, farmers, labourers. - Designed to reduce vulnerability to death, illness, crop failure, etc. - Delivered through SHGs, NGOs, MFIs in vernacular languages. - Examples: - LIC’s Jeevan Madhur, Jeevan Mangal. - Pillar 1D2: Pension - Definition: - Pension: - A pension is a fixed monthly payment provided to an individual after retirement, typically starting at the age of 58 or 60. It continues until the person's death, and in most cases, a reduced amount is paid to the surviving spouse thereafter. - Unlike insurance, which offers a lump-sum compensation for specific events like death or damage (e.g., ₹2 lakh under Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana), a pension is a long-term income stream meant for sustenance in old age. - Financial Inclusion: - Financial inclusion refers to efforts aimed at ensuring that vulnerable and unorganized sections of society have access to essential financial services such as pensions, insurance, and banking. - It aligns with the objectives of the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), which seeks to bring the poor into the formal financial system by offering them zero-balance bank accounts, credit, and security. - Significance: - Social Security: - Pensions act as a safety net for the elderly by providing a regular income after retirement, helping them maintain a minimum standard of living and preventing old-age poverty. - Economic Impact: - Pension funds mobilize long-term household savings and channel them into productive investments such as government securities and bonds. - This not only deepens the domestic financial markets but also contributes to the overall capital formation and infrastructure development of the country. - Employee Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) - Establishment: - Formed in 1951–52 through an ordinance, and formalized under the Employees’ Provident Fund & Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952. - It functions under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, with headquarters located in New Delhi. - Governance Structure: - Managed by the Central Board of Trustees, a tripartite body comprising: - 15 members nominated by the Central and State Governments, - 10 members representing employers, and - 10 members representing employees. - The Board decides how EPFO funds are to be invested (e.g., allocation in government securities, corporate bonds, and equities within limits) and also recommends annual interest rates for subscribers. - Coverage and Applicability: - Mandatory for establishments employing 20 or more workers. - Certain exceptions apply, such as cooperatives with fewer than 50 workers not using electricity (e.g., handloom, beedi). - Employee Identification: - Universal Account Number (UAN): - A unique, portable account number allotted to each EPFO subscriber. - Remains constant even if the employee switches jobs, ensuring continuity in EPF contributions. - 2019 Reform: - Employees can now self-generate their UAN using Aadhaar and mobile number, removing the earlier dependency on employers for UAN issuance. - Employer Identification: - Labour Identification Number (LIN): - A unique code issued to employers for accessing EPFO and other labour law compliance systems via the Shram Suvidha Portal (maintained by the Labour Ministry). - Transaction & Access Platforms: - Financial transactions can be managed through partnered public and private sector banks. - The UMANG App (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance), developed by the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY), allows users to check balances, track claims, and file grievances from mobile devices. - EPFO Schemes - Employee Provident Fund (EPF, 1952): - A compulsory retirement savings scheme in which both employer and employee contribute a fixed percentage of the employee’s salary every month. Upon retirement at age 58 or earlier in case of death, the employee or nominee receives a lump sum consisting of principal plus accumulated interest. - Interest Rates: - The interest is declared annually by EPFO. It was 8.5% in 2020–21, dipped to a 40-year low of 8.1% in 2022–23, and slightly improved to 8.25% in both 2023–24 and 2024–25. - Partial Withdrawals: - Allowed under specific conditions such as for higher education, marriage, medical emergencies, or house purchase/construction. The withdrawal limit varies based on the purpose and service tenure. - Employees Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme (EDLI, 1976): - Offers life insurance coverage to EPF subscribers without the need for individual premium contributions by employees. The employer pays the premium. If the employee dies during service, the nominee/family receives a lump-sum insurance payout. - 2020 Reform: - The scheme was extended to cover COVID-related deaths with enhanced insurance benefits, increasing coverage between ₹2.5 lakh and ₹7 lakh depending on salary and service conditions. - Employee Pension Scheme (EPS, 1995): - Provides a fixed monthly pension to employees after retirement (age 58) or in case of permanent disability. It is not linked to stock market performance, unlike the National Pension System (NPS). - If the employee dies before retirement, the spouse becomes eligible for a minimum monthly pension of ₹1,000. The actual pension depends on pensionable salary and years of service. - EPF Commutation (2020): - Allows employees to withdraw a portion of their pension corpus before reaching age 58. However, this reduces the monthly pension amount they would receive after retirement. - Centralized Pension Payments System (CITES-CPPS): - An IT modernization initiative that centralizes the pension disbursal mechanism under EPFO. - Pre-CITES: - Pensioners had to physically visit banks for verification. Zonal EPFO offices were linked with only 3–4 banks, causing issues for retirees without accounts in those banks. - Post-CITES: - All banks are digitally integrated with EPFO, enabling seamless pension processing. Retirees no longer need to visit banks or EPFO offices for PPO (Pension Payment Order) updates or verification. - EPFO 3.0 (2025): - A major upgrade to the EPFO’s digital interface, designed to resemble modern e-banking platforms. - Key Features: - Enables ATM withdrawals from EPF accounts, online updates such as address change, and lodging complaints or service requests without physically visiting EPFO offices. - Government Schemes for EPFO Contribution - Pradhan Mantri Rojgar Protsahan Yojana (PMRPY, 2016): - Aimed at incentivizing employers to generate new employment by reimbursing EPF contributions for new employees. - Applicable to employees earning ≤ ₹15,000/month and registered with EPFO. - Government paid 8.33% (Employer’s EPS share), later extended to cover 12% (full employer share). - Valid for new employees added on or after April 1, 2016. - Discontinued and deleted from the 2023 PIB handbook due to overlap with newer schemes. - Atmanirbhar Bharat Rozgar Yojana (ABRY, 2020): - Launched as part of Atmanirbhar Bharat Package 3.0 in November 2020. - Nodal Ministry: - Ministry of Labour and Employment. - Objective: - Promote job creation during post-pandemic recovery. - Eligibility: - Employees earning less than ₹15,000/month. - Either newly registered with EPFO or those who lost jobs during Mar–Sep 2020 and rejoined after Oct 1, 2020. - Applicable for establishments registered with EPFO and having up to 1,000 employees. - Government Contribution: -
Firm Size Worker Contribution Employer Contribution
Up to 1,000 employees 12% of wages (Govt pays to EPFO) 12% of wages (Govt pays to EPFO)
More than 1,000 employees 12% of wages (Govt pays to EPFO) 12% of wages (Paid by Employer)
- Benefits Duration: - Two years from the date of registration under the scheme. - Outcomes: - Promoted formal job creation. - Helped boost disposable income and social security during COVID-19 recovery. - Reduced compliance burden on MSMEs. - Registration Deadline: - Extended till June 30, 2021. - Employment Linked Incentive Scheme (ELI, Budget 2024): - Announced in Union Budget 2024–25. - Nodal Ministry: - Ministry of Labour and Employment. - Target: - Generate over 2 crore formal jobs in two years. - ELI-Scheme A (First-Time Employees): - Direct Benefit Transfer of ₹15,000 to first-time EPFO-registered employees. - Paid in 3 equal installments. - Exclusion: Employees earning more than ₹1 lakh/month not eligible. - ELI-Scheme B (Manufacturing Sector Boost): - Government to contribute both worker and employer shares to EPFO. - Applicable for 4 years to new jobs created in the manufacturing sector. - Estimated 30 lakh jobs targeted. - Implementation details pending. - ELI-Scheme C (Wage Subsidy to Employers): - Applies to jobs paying up to ₹1 lakh/month. - Government will contribute up to ₹3,000/month per employee to EPFO for 2 years. - Estimated to support creation of 50 lakh jobs. - Coal Miners’ Pension (CMPFO): - Governed by the Coal Mines Provident Fund & Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1948. - Nodal Ministry: - Ministry of Coal. - Coal Mines Provident Fund Organisation (CMPFO): - A statutory body distinct from EPFO. - Administers provident fund, pension, and deposit-linked insurance for coal sector employees. - C-CARES Portal: - Digital platform to simplify pension application, grievance redressal, and status tracking for retired coal miners and their families. - FAQ: Why Not Merge EPFO with ESIC? - EPFO and ESIC are governed by distinct legislations: - EPFO: - Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952. - ESIC: - Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948. - Merging requires complex legal and structural changes. - Functional domains are different: - EPFO: - Provident fund, pension, insurance. - ESIC: - Healthcare and cash benefits for sickness, maternity, disability. - Pension for Government Employees - Types: - Old Pension Scheme (OPS): - A defined benefit scheme offering a fixed pension post-retirement, applicable to employees who joined before 01/01/2004. Discontinued for new entrants due to long-term fiscal burden. - National Pension System (NPS): - Introduced in 2004 as a defined contribution and market-linked scheme for central government employees joining after 01/01/2004 (excluding armed forces). Later extended to all citizens aged 18–55 in 2009. - Unified Pension Scheme (UPS): - Introduced in 2024 as a hybrid scheme aiming to balance fiscal sustainability with adequate retirement benefits. Applicable from 01/04/2025. - National Pension System (NPS): - Employee contributes 10% of basic salary; Government contributes 14% (raised from 10% in 2019 Interim Budget). - Investments are made in a mix of government securities, corporate bonds, and equities as per subscriber's choice under: - Tier 1 (mandatory; has withdrawal restrictions), - Tier 2 (voluntary; flexible withdrawals). - Each subscriber receives a PRAN (Permanent Retirement Account Number), similar to EPFO’s UAN. - Regulated by PFRDA (Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority); managed through NPS Trust. - In 2023, the T V Somanathan Committee was constituted to review NPS and suggest improvements, leading to the recommendation of the Unified Pension Scheme (UPS). - Unified Pension Scheme (UPS): - Officially notified in August 2024; effective from 01/04/2025. - Government employees may opt to stay with NPS or shift to UPS. - Contribution comparison: -
Contributor NPS UPS
Government 14% 18.5%
Employee 10% 10%
- UPS provides: - Fixed pension of ₹10,000/month after minimum 10 years of service. - 50% of average last 12-month salary as pension after 25 years of service. - Family pension of 60% in case of pensioner's death (to spouse). - Pension indexed to inflation via CPI-IW. - Lump sum benefit at retirement (not relevant for UPSC exams). - OPS Revival in Non-BJP States: - States like Rajasthan have revived OPS, citing demands from employee unions. - Union Government opposes OPS revival, warning of fiscal unsustainability. - Centre advocates targeted welfare schemes over universal pension promises like OPS. - Andhra Pradesh’s Guaranteed Pension Scheme (GPS): - AP introduced GPS as a hybrid between OPS and NPS to address concerns of state employees. - Contributions and pension under GPS: -
Contributor Contribution Pension
Employee 10% 33% of last salary
State Government 14% 40% of last salary
- Penny Drop Verification (2023): - Introduced in NPS pension disbursal to ensure account validity. - A token amount of ₹1 is credited to verify correct bank account and IFSC before full pension transfer. - Aimed at reducing transaction errors and preventing fraud. - NPS for Non-Government Employees: - NPS-Lite (Swavalamban Scheme, 2010): - Aimed at economically vulnerable individuals in the unorganized sector who were excluded from formal pension coverage. - Under this scheme, the government contributed ₹1,000 per year to each eligible account holder for a period of 5 years to incentivize pension savings. - Managed by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA), this scheme laid the groundwork for future inclusive pension models. - NPS-Vatsalya (Announced in Union Budget 2024): - Introduced as a child-focused pension savings mechanism allowing minors (under 18 years) to have NPS accounts. - Parents or legal guardians are responsible for making the contributions on behalf of the minor. - The minimum annual contribution is ₹1,000, with no upper cap, making it flexible for different income groups. - Once the minor turns 18, the account is seamlessly converted into a regular NPS account under their name. - Minimum Assured Return Scheme (MARS): - Proposed by PFRDA to offer a guaranteed minimum return (e.g., 8%) for NPS subscribers from the private or unorganized sector. - If the actual market-based returns fall below the assured threshold, the shortfall would be covered by PFRDA or a designated financial institution. - This is intended to reduce the perceived risk of market-linked pension instruments and boost voluntary NPS enrollment among non-government workers. - Jeevan Pramaan (Launched in 2014): - An Aadhaar-enabled Digital Life Certificate developed by the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY), eliminating the need for physical submission of life certificates by pensioners. - The pensioner authenticates their identity using Aadhaar and biometric inputs like fingerprint or iris scan. In 2022, facial recognition was added to ease access for the elderly. - This digital certification is then automatically transmitted to the Pension Disbursing Agency, ensuring uninterrupted pension payments. - In 2020, the scope of Jeevan Pramaan was expanded to include EPFO pensioners as well. - Pension for Senior Citizens with Capacity to Invest: - Pradhan Mantri Vaya Vandana Yojana (PMVVY, 2017): - A pension scheme designed for senior citizens aged 60 years and above, aimed at providing them with a fixed and secure return on investment to ensure financial stability during retirement. - Nodal Authority: - Department of Financial Services, Ministry of Finance. - Implemented and managed exclusively by the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC). - The scheme offered a guaranteed pension at a specified rate (initially 8%, then revised periodically) for a policy term of 10 years. - Senior citizens could invest a lump sum (up to ₹15 lakh limit per individual) and receive regular monthly, quarterly, half-yearly, or annual pension payments. - The scheme was closed for new subscriptions after 31 March 2023. - Related / Similar Schemes: - Senior Citizen Savings Scheme (SCSS): - A government-backed savings option offered via banks and post offices. - Meant for individuals aged 60 years and above, with investment capped at ₹30 lakh (as per recent Budget revisions). - Offers higher interest rates than typical savings instruments, with quarterly interest payout. - Tenure is 5 years, extendable by 3 years. - LIC Varistha Pension Bima Yojana (VPBY): - Launched in 2003 and relaunched in 2014 (short-term window). - Also targeted at 60+ citizens with lump-sum investment and fixed pension benefits. - Now discontinued; holds minimal current relevance for UPSC except historical reference. - Pension for Poor with Capacity to Invest - Maan Dhan Yojanas: -

- ES25 Observations on pension sector - Pension sector challenges as per ES25: - Globally, the elderly population has surpassed children. - Growing elderly population and increasing life expectancy → pension companies must pay for more years. - Pensioners save less than active workers, leading to lower national savings in countries with a larger elderly population. - Countries like Japan, France, and China raised retirement ages, causing worker resentment. - Rising inflation increases the need for higher pension amounts. - Pension market not yet fully developed in India says ES25: -
Nation Pension assets as a % of GDP
OECD Nations 80%
India EPFO (17%) & NPS (4.5%)
- OECD = Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development - Out of the total number of pensioners in India: 80% are Atal Pension Yojana (APY) subscribers. - APY gives hardly ₹1,000–₹5,000 pension. - Micro pension scheme problems as per ES25: - Micro-pension schemes like Atal Pension and Shram Yogi Maan-Dhan provide small pensions to poor families. - Poor people often prioritize immediate consumption over saving for pensions or insurance. - Consequently, 93% of Atal Pension subscribers joined the ₹1,000 plan because the ₹5,000 plan requires more contributions. - Behavioral interventions needed: - Simplifying enrollment - Timely reminders for renewal - To increase active subscribers in micro-pensions - Britain’s PAYGO schemes & demographic changes - ES25: - Pay-As-You-Go (PAYGO) schemes: - Young salaried employees bear the cost of pensions for the older generation. - Worker’s money is NOT invested in shares/bonds (unlike EPFO/NPS). - Current worker’s money is directly paid to the pensioners. - Britain and several OECD nations follow PAYGO. - For such schemes to be sustainable: (i) Outflows must be adequately linked to the inflows → more young workers must keep joining to pay for retiring workers. (ii) Inflows must increase with rising inflation index → Indexation = formula to increase salary & pension with inflation. - Otherwise: - Asset-liability mismatch occurs. - Government ends up borrowing to pay pensions (as seen in Greece & Italy). - Britain may face similar issues in the next 2 decades. - Globally, the number of pensioners exceeds children → reduces active workers → increases pensioners in future. - Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) - Establishment: - Initially set up in 2003 through an executive order by the Government of India. - Later granted statutory status via the PFRDA Act, 2013 (came into effect from 1st February 2014). - Headquarters: - New Delhi. - Composition & Tenure: - 1 Chairperson: - 5 years or until age 65 (whichever is earlier); eligible for reappointment. - 5 Whole-time Members: - 5 years or until age 62 (whichever is earlier); re-appointable. - Appointed by: - Government of India. - Functions & Powers: - Administers and oversees the National Pension System (NPS) for government and non-government sectors. - Selects and licenses Pension Fund Managers (PFMs) who manage subscriber investments. - Regulates various types of pension schemes and intermediaries (e.g., CRA, POP, Annuity Service Providers). - Exclusions: - Does not regulate pension funds under: - EPFO (Employees' Provident Fund Organisation). - Seamen’s Provident Fund (under Merchant Shipping Act). - Coal Miners’ Provident Fund (CMPF Act). - Assam Tea Plantation Workers' Provident Fund (specific Act). - Investor Protection: - Ensures transparency, fair practices, grievance redressal for pension subscribers. - Prescribes rules for asset allocation, minimum returns (like MARS), fund liquidity, and auditing standards. - Quasi-judicial Powers: - Empowered to conduct inquiries, summon witnesses, and enforce penalties similar to a civil court under the PFRDA Act. - Promotional Activities: - Conducts outreach and pension literacy via: - Official site - Public portal - FDI Norms: - Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Pension Sector: - Capped at 49% (same as Insurance Sector). - FDI policy is governed by Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), not PFRDA itself. - Social Security for Overseas Indians - Pravasi Bharatiya Bima Yojana (PBBY, 2017) - Nodal Ministry: - Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Government of India. - Applicability: - Mandatory insurance scheme for Indian workers going to Emigration Check Required (ECR) countries. - ECR countries include Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) nations like: - Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates (UAE), Qatar, Oman, Kuwait, Bahrain, and others. - Purpose: - To provide social security cover to vulnerable Indian emigrant workers working abroad, especially in blue-collar jobs. - Key Benefits (Insurance Coverage): - ₹10 lakh in case of accidental death or permanent disability. - Maternity benefits for female workers. - Hospitalization expenses for family members in India (coverage subject to limits). - Repatriation costs in case of death or serious injury. - Legal expenses for litigation related to employment abroad. - Funding: - Premium is paid by the emigrant worker (mandatory before departure). - Implementation: - Carried out through empanelled insurance companies in India. - Validity of insurance is typically linked with the employment contract period (usually up to 2 or 3 years). - Totalisation Pact (India–USA) - Concept: - A bilateral agreement intended to prevent dual payment of social security taxes by expatriates. - Especially important for Indian professionals working in the US on H-1B and L-1 visas. - Issue: - Indian workers temporarily employed in the US pay into the US Social Security system but are not eligible for benefits unless they stay for 10 years. - Upon returning to India, they forfeit their contributions, leading to financial loss. - Purpose of the Pact: - To enable portability of pension/social security benefits. - To allow short-term workers to be exempted from contributing to host country's social security if already covered in home country. - Current Status: - India has signed totalisation agreements with countries like Germany, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, etc. - However, negotiations with the United States are ongoing. - No agreement has been finalized as of now. - Relevance: - Important for safeguarding financial rights of NRIs and improving cross-border social protection. - Although not finalised, the issue is relevant for policy and international labour rights. - Pillar 1D3: Financial Inclusion - Definition: - Financial Inclusion (FI): - Refers to the process of ensuring access to useful and affordable financial products and services—such as banking, savings, credit, insurance, and pension—delivered in a responsible and sustainable way to every individual, particularly the marginalized and unorganized sectors. - Aims to provide S-E-T security: - Social security - Economic security - Transactional security - Enablers: - PM Jan Dhan Yojana, RuPay cards, Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT), mobile banking, etc. - Social Security (SS): - Refers to state-sponsored protection against economic and social distress, ensuring financial support for citizens in cases such as illness, disability, unemployment, old age, or maternity. - Constitutional roots in: - Article 41: - Right to work, education, and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, and disablement. - Article 42: - Provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. - Examples: - PM Atmanirbhar Bharat Rozgar Yojana - Employees’ State Insurance Scheme (ESI) - National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) - Social Justice (SJ): - A political and legal philosophy aiming at the fair and equitable distribution of wealth, opportunities, and privileges within a society. - Ensures protection and empowerment of vulnerable groups through: - Affirmative action (reservations in jobs, education) - Legal safeguards (e.g., SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act) - Welfare schemes (e.g., Stand Up India, SC/ST sub-plan) - Fundamental to achieving equality and dignity as enshrined in the Preamble of the Constitution. - Significance: - Together, FI, SS, and SJ form the triad for equitable development and democratic deepening. - Foster human development by ensuring economic access and social dignity. - Enhance financial literacy and reduce dependence on informal financial systems. - Empower marginalized communities, especially women, SCs, STs, minorities, and rural poor. - Support efficient targeting of government subsidies and entitlements via: - JAM Trinity (Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile) - DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) architecture - Promote inclusive growth in line with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially: - Goal 1 (No Poverty) - Goal 5 (Gender Equality) - Goal 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) - Goal 10 (Reduced Inequalities) - Reduces leakages, corruption, and cash-based shadow economy. - Contributes to social cohesion, nation-building, and trust in governance. - Example Use Case: - A woman in a rural village opens a Jan Dhan account → receives maternity assistance via DBT → uses RuPay card at a local kirana shop → also covered under PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana and Atal Pension Yojana → this integration ensures FI, SS, and contributes toward SJ. - Bank Accounts for Everyone - Historical Context: -
Year Milestone in Financial Inclusion
1955 Establishment of State Bank of India to extend banking to rural areas.
1961 Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) Act enacted to protect small depositors.
1966 Bringing Cooperative Banks under RBI regulation for unified oversight.
1969 & 1980 Nationalization of 14 (1969) and 6 (1980) major banks to enhance outreach in underserved regions.
1969 Launch of Lead Bank Scheme:
  • Each district assigned to a lead commercial bank.
  • Banks to prepare district credit plans using the Service Area Approach.
  • Coordinated planning with Government, NBFCs, and cooperative institutions.
1971 Formation of State-Level Bankers’ Committees (SLBCs) to monitor state-level FI implementation.
1976 Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) established under RRB Act to bridge rural credit gaps.
2005 RBI allows 'No-frills accounts' (zero-balance) to bring the unbanked population into the formal system.
2006 Business Correspondent (BC) model permitted to deliver banking services in remote areas through intermediaries.
2011 Launch of Swabhiman Scheme to promote banking penetration in rural India using BCAs and mobile technology.
2013 Introduction of e-KYC using Aadhaar and biometrics—no need for paper documents for identity verification.
2014
  • Launch of Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) for universal banking access.
  • Approval of two new private sector banks—Bandhan and IDFC First Bank.
2015 Launch of Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks to target underserved segments and enhance last-mile delivery.
2017–18 India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) launched, leveraging postal network for financial inclusion (see Pillar#1B1).
- RBI Norms: - Commercial banks must open 25% of branches in unbanked rural areas. - Similar norms for White Label ATM companies. - Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY, 2014) - Nodal: - Finance Ministry, Dept. of Financial Services (DFS) - Motto: - “Mera Khaata, Bhagya Vidhaata.” - Phases and Objectives: - Phase I (2014–15): - Financial literacy programs. - Banking access within 5 km radius. - One account per family: - Overdraft facility. - RuPay ATM-cum-debit card. - Phase II (2015–18): - Creation of Credit Guarantee Fund for overdraft risks. - Seamless Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) of subsidies, scholarships. - Promotion of micro-insurance and pension products via banking channel. - Features: - Account Eligibility and Nature: - Accounts opened in Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) and Cooperative Banks. - Banks must be on Core Banking System (CBS) and use RuPay Payment Gateway. - Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account (BSBDA): - For individuals aged 10 and above. - Zero-balance account; no penalties for non-maintenance. - Chequebook optional but requires minimum balance. - Overdraft Facility: - Up to ₹10,000 (earlier ₹5,000). - Conditions: - Based on satisfactory operation for 6 months. - One account per household (preferably woman). - Repayable with interest over 3 years. - Interest rate set by the bank. - Insurance Benefits: -
Type Amount Conditions
Accidental Insurance ₹1 lakh
  • Funded by NPCI
  • Regular RuPay card usage (e.g., balance inquiry)
  • Not available for income taxpayers or Union Govt employees
- Withdrawal Limits: - Monthly withdrawal limits imposed to ensure account discipline and curb misuse. - Significance: - Forms the JAM Trinity (Jan Dhan – Aadhaar – Mobile) for financial inclusion. - Enables leakage-free delivery of welfare via DBT. - Emergency Relief Examples: - 2020: PM Garib Kalyan Yojana: - ₹500/month for 3 months transferred to 20 crore women’s PMJDY accounts. - 2023: - PMJDY deposits crossed ₹2 lakh crore (₹2 trillion) mark. - Criticism: - Many dormant or zero-balance accounts. - Used as money mules during demonetization (2016). - Jan Dhan Darshak App (2018): - Developed by Department of Financial Services and NIC. - Purpose: - Geo-location of nearest financial touchpoints: - Bank branches - ATMs - Post Offices - Business Correspondents (BCs) - Investments Other Than Bank - Overview: - Small savings schemes offer higher returns than bank deposits, especially for poor/lower-middle-class individuals. - Funds are routed to National Small Savings Fund (NSSF), which is used for: - Lending to Union Government. - Lending to select state governments. - Interest rates are set quarterly by the Finance Ministry’s Department of Economic Affairs (DEA). - Schemes: -

- Mahila Samman Bachat Patra (2023) - Purpose: - To promote savings and financial inclusion among women and girls. - Announced In: - Budget 2023; available till 31 Mar 2025. - Eligibility: - Women and girl children; guardian can open account for minor. - Tenure: - Fixed for 2 years from date of deposit. - Deposit Limit: - Minimum ₹1,000; maximum ₹2 lakh (only one account allowed per eligible individual). - Interest Rate: - 7.5% per annum, compounded quarterly. - Withdrawal: - 40% of eligible balance can be withdrawn after 1 year. - Taxation: - Interest taxable; no deduction under Section 80C. - Operated By: - Department of Posts; available at post offices and select banks. - Senior Citizen Savings Scheme (SCSS) - Purpose: - To provide regular income to senior citizens post-retirement. - Introduced In: - 2004; revised via Budget 2023. - Eligibility: - Citizens aged 60+; or 55–60 if retired under VRS/superannuation with proof. - Tenure: - 5 years, extendable by 3 years once. - Deposit Limit: - ₹30 lakh (raised from ₹15 lakh in Budget 2023); in multiples of ₹1,000. - Interest Rate: - 8.2% per annum for Q1 FY25; paid quarterly. - Premature Withdrawal: - Allowed with penalty (1%–1.5% depending on tenure completed). - Taxation: - Interest fully taxable; principal eligible under Section 80C (within ₹1.5 lakh limit). - Operated By: - Banks and post offices; one of the most preferred schemes for seniors. - Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (2015): - Fixed deposit scheme for girl child (0–10 years age). - Annual Deposit: - Minimum: - ₹250 - Maximum: - ₹1.5 lakh - Until girl turns 14. - Interest: - Originally 9.1%, now ~8.5%. - Set by DEA quarterly. - Withdrawal: - Allowed at age 18–21. - Based on marriage status. - Purpose: - Prevent child marriage, promote girl’s education/business. - Limits: - One account per daughter. - Maximum: - 2 daughters per family. - Five Star Village Scheme (2020): - Nodal Ministry: - Ministry of Communications, Department of Posts. - Purpose: - Post offices to promote: - Small Savings Schemes: - PPF, NSC, Sukanya Samriddhi. - Insurance Schemes: - RPLI, PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY), PM Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY). - Focus: - Rural outreach. - Sampoorna Bima Gram Yojana (2017): - Nodal Agency: - Department of Posts. - Aim: - Cover at least one RPLI (Rural Postal Life Insurance) policy for every household in one village per district. - Model Insurance Villages (MIV, 2021): - Proposed by: - Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI). - Objective: - Ensure full insurance coverage in villages: - Life insurance - Health insurance - Crop insurance - Livestock insurance - Vehicle insurance - Funding: - Sources: - Union Government - State Governments - Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) - NABARD - Other All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) - Chit Funds: - Description: - Collective investment scheme. - Members contribute monthly; one member gets loan from the pooled fund. - Legal Status: - Item in Concurrent List (both Union & States can make laws). - Regulators: - RBI - SEBI - State Governments - Issues: - Scam-prone due to weak/lax regulation. - Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act, 2019: - Purpose: - Prohibits unregistered entities from soliciting deposits or investments from public. - Example: - Builders, jewelers, chit-fund scams. - Regulators: - RBI → Banks, NBFCs - SEBI → Mutual Funds, REITs - IRDAI → Insurance - PFRDA → Pensions - MCA → NIDHI companies - State Govts → Chit Funds - EPFO - Penalties: - Fine up to ₹50 crore. - Imprisonment up to 10 years. - Power to attach properties for refunding investors. - Online Database: - Union Government to build an online database of all legal deposit-taking activities. - Credit (Loans) - Context: - Links to Pillar#1A2 (Priority Sector Lending) and Pillar#1B1 (Microfinance). - Refinance: - AIFIs (e.g., NABARD, SIDBI) or MUDRA provide new finance to banks/NBFCs based on loans already given to end-borrowers, often via securitization. - Credit Guarantee: - Covers bank/NBFC losses if borrowers default, enabling collateral-free lending. - Earlier by DICGC; now by specialized organizations (e.g., CGTMSE, NCGTC). - Credit Guarantee Organizations: -

- Credit Guarantee for MSMEs in Manufacturing: - Details pending; enhances collateral-free loans for manufacturing MSMEs. - Interest Equalisation Scheme: - Nodal: - Commerce Ministry (DGFT); 2–3% interest subsidy for MSME exporters, disbursed via RBI to banks. - Various government initiatives - MUDRA (2015) - Full Form: - Micro Units Development & Refinance Agency Ltd. - Status: - 100% subsidiary of SIDBI. - Objectives: - Promote micro-entrepreneurship via indirect lending. - Refinance support to: - SCBs, RRBs, Cooperative Banks, MFIs, NBFCs. - Funding Sources: - PSL shortfalls (directed by RBI). - Budgetary allocations from Department of Financial Services (DFS). - Target Beneficiaries: - Non-corporate, non-farm small enterprises (manufacturing, trading, service, allied agri). - Product Segments: -

- Key Features: - Collateral-free loans. - Credit risk covered by CGFMU (operated by NCGTC). - MUDRA RuPay Card: ATM/debit card linked to loan account for working capital usage. - Challenges: - High interest rates by intermediaries. - Growing risk of NPAs. - Stand Up India (2016) - Nodal Ministry: - Department of Financial Services (DFS). - Timeline: - Extended till 31 March 2025 (via Budget 2019). - Objective: - Promote SC/ST and women entrepreneurship. - Each SCB branch to provide ₹10 lakh – ₹1 crore loan to at least: - 1 SC/ST borrower and 1 woman borrower. - Loan Tenure: - Up to 7 years; moratorium up to 18 months. - Collateral: - Optional; covered by CGFSI (Credit Guarantee Fund for Stand-Up India). - Budget 2021 Update: - Margin money reduced from 25% to 15%. - Agri-allied activities made eligible. - Self Help Groups (SHGs) – Credit Linkage - Informal groups (10–20 members); women-dominated. - Activities: - Cottage industries, agarbatti making, weaving, food processing. - Formation: - Under schemes like NRLM (see Pillar#6). - SHG–Bank Linkage Programme (1992): - Launched by NABARD. - Provides collateral-free credit via formal banking. - India: - Largest microfinance movement. - PM SVANidhi (PM Street Vendor’s AtmaNirbhar Nidhi, 2020) - Nodal Ministry: - Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs (MoHUA). - Objective: - Empower street vendors affected by COVID-19 through micro-credit. - Loan Amounts: - 1st cycle: - ₹10,000 | 2nd: ₹20,000 | 3rd: ₹50,000. - Tenure: - 1 year, monthly EMI basis. - Interest Rate: - Market-linked (~7.25%); 7% interest subsidy for timely repayments. - Budget 2025 Update: - ₹30,000 credit card facility announced (integration with loan cycles pending clarity). - SVANidhi – Main Bhi Digital (2021) - MoHUA-led digital literacy initiative under SVANidhi. - ULBs (Urban Local Bodies) funded to train vendors in: - UPI, BHIM, NetBanking, QR Payments. - Vendor Onboarding: - Food vendors connected to Swiggy, Zomato, etc. - SVANidhi – Rashtriya Udyamita Vikas Pariyojana (2024) - Nodal Ministry: - Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. - Aim: - Entrepreneurship training for street vendors. - Format: - 22-week blended training (offline/online/hybrid). - Support: - Stipend and official certification. - Key Partners: - Flipkart, IIE (Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship), NIESBUD. - PM Vishwakarma Scheme (2023) - Nodal: - MSME Ministry; Targets 18 trades (e.g., carpenter, blacksmith, tailor). - Entitlements: - Recognition: - PM Vishwakarma certificate, ID card; registration on Udyam Assist Portal. - Skill Upgradation: - 5–7 days basic training, 15+ days advanced training; ₹500/day stipend. - Toolkit: - ₹15,000 e-voucher for purchase. - Digital Incentive: - ₹1 per digital transaction (max ₹100/month). - Marketing and loan support (see below). - PM Vishwakarma Loans: - Collateral-free Enterprise Development Loans up to ₹3 lakh. - Interest: - 5% paid by beneficiary, 8% subsidized by government (total 13% for banker). - Rationale: - Subsidies ensure banks lend without losses, given typical 13–16% rates. - Agricultural Credit - Kisan Credit Card (KCC, 1998) - Launched by RBI & NABARD; issued by PSBs, RRBs, Coop. - Farm Loan Waivers - Economic Survey 2024-25 (ES25) opposes blanket waivers: - Waivers incentivize willful default, especially during elections. - Lead to fiscal burden & stress on state finances. - Disrupt credit culture and hurt punctual borrowers. - Suggested alternatives: - Expand credit guarantee schemes. - Encourage crop insurance and targeted income support (e.g., PM-KISAN). - Social Security Code, 2020: Coverage of Gig and Platform Workers: - Categories: - Informal Workers: - No formal contract (e.g., domestic help, construction). - Gig Workers: - Temporary, task-based (e.g., Uber, Zomato). - Platform Workers: - Use online platforms for jobs (e.g., Swiggy, Ola). - Social Security Code Provisions: - Coverage under life, disability, health insurance. - Maternity benefits, old age pensions, education support for children. - Funding through Central/State + aggregator contributions. - e-Shram Portal: - National database of unorganised workers. - Registration mandatory to claim benefits. - Aadhaar-linked, portable benefits. - Budget 2025: Focused Measures for Financial Inclusion & Social Security: -

- Notes: - Many older schemes now merged or obsolete. - Social Security Code 2020 intended to replace the 2008 Act, pending full implementation. - Customer Protection - Purpose: - Ensures grievance redressal across various financial sectors (banking, insurance, securities, pensions). - Protects consumers from mis-selling, service deficiencies, fraud, delays, and unethical practices. - Promotes transparency, trust, and financial inclusion. - Redressal Mechanisms by Sector: -
Sector Mechanism Handled By Notes
Bank / NBFC / Payment Systems RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (2021) RBI “One Nation, One Ombudsman” — merged banking, NBFC, and digital transaction ombudsmen
Insurance Insurance Ombudsman for claims ≤ ₹30 lakh IRDAI Above ₹30 lakh → appeal to SAT
Securities / Commodities SCORES Portal + Appellate Tribunal SEBI SCORES = SEBI Complaints Redress System
Pensions Internal: EPFO; External: PFRDA, NSDL EPFO / PFRDA NPS grievances → NSDL & PFRDA; Private pensions → PFRDA
- RBI’s Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (2021): - Launched under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act. - Replaces 3 earlier schemes: - Banking Ombudsman Scheme (2006) - NBFC Ombudsman Scheme (2018) - Digital Transaction Ombudsman Scheme (2019) - Key Features: - Single portal - No need to identify the correct scheme/authority. - No fee for filing complaints. - “Deficiency in Service” replaced with broad “Grounds for Complaint”. - Covers Scheduled Commercial Banks, NBFCs, and non-bank payment system providers. - Exception: - Cooperative banks not covered (unless brought under scheduled list). - SEBI SCORES Portal: - Online grievance mechanism for securities investors. - Mandatory for all listed companies and SEBI-registered intermediaries to be registered on SCORES. - Timeline: - 30 days for companies to respond. - After escalation: - SEBI intervenes if unsatisfied. - IRDAI Grievance Redress: - 17 Insurance Ombudsman Offices across India. - Handles: - Delays in claim settlement, partial or total denial, misrepresentation, non-issuance of policy documents. - Above ₹30 lakh: - Appeals go to SAT. - Pension Sector Grievance Handling: - EPFO (for EPF-related grievances): - via internal officers & CPGRAMS. - NPS (for government/private subscribers): - CRA (NSDL), then escalation to PFRDA. - Private Pensions: - Regulated by PFRDA, with SAT as appellate body. - Cross-Cutting Initiatives: - CPGRAMS: - Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System by Govt of India — available across sectors. - Financial Literacy Programs by RBI and other regulators aim to empower consumers to file complaints confidently. - Web Portals - PaiSA Portal (2018): - "Portal for Affordable Credit and Interest Subvention Access". - Initially launched by Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) to provide centralized tracking of interest subvention to SHG & PM SVANidhi beneficiaries. - Status: - Discontinued in 2024–25 due to low relevance and integration with newer platforms. - psbloansin59minutes.com (2018): - Developed by SIDBI in collaboration with 5 Public Sector Banks. - Objective: - Provide MSMEs quick access to working capital/term loans within 59 minutes. - Eligibility: - GST-registered MSMEs, income tax return filed. - Features: - Loan amount: - ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore. - Collateral-free under CGTMSE scheme. - Integrated checks via Aadhaar, GSTN, IT data, and CIBIL score. - Fee: - ₹1,000 charged only if loan is sanctioned. - Jan Samarth Portal (2022): - Nodal Ministry: - Ministry of Finance. - Objective: - Unified national digital platform for providing access to various credit-linked government schemes. - Coverage: - Sectors: - Education, Agriculture, Business, Livelihood. - Banks: - Connects with 125+ banks and NBFCs. - Features: - Auto-verification of Aadhaar, GST, UDYAM Registration, CIBIL. - Scheme suggestion engine based on borrower profile and needs. - Tracks application and disbursement status. - SARTHI Portal (2024): - Full Form: - Smart Agriculture Resource & Technology Hub for Insurance. - Nodal Ministry: - Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers’ Welfare, with technical support from UNDP India. - Target Users: - Farmers and rural households. - Objective: Facilitate access to multiple types of insurance: - Crop insurance (PMFBY), life, health, tractor, livestock, shop, and dwelling insurance. - Features: - Integrated claims tracking. - Premium subsidy calculators. - KYC through Aadhaar and land record linkage. - PM-SURAJ Portal (2024): - Full Form: - PM Social Upliftment through Rationalised Assistance and Justice. - Nodal Ministry: - Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. - Target: - SC, ST, OBC, de-notified, semi-nomadic, and nomadic tribe entrepreneurs. - Features: - Facilitates enterprise loans up to ₹15 lakh. - Integrated interest subsidy and credit guarantee modules. - Initially targets 1 lakh beneficiaries in FY2024–25. - Status: - Detailed operational guidelines pending. - Financial Inclusion Reports - Global Microscope Report: - Published by Economist Intelligence Unit in collaboration with Accion and Gates Foundation. - Assesses financial inclusion enabling environment across 50+ countries. - India ranked high due to digitization, regulatory frameworks, and inclusive policies. - Global Findex Database: - Released by World Bank & Gates Foundation every 3 years. - Tracks financial account ownership, savings, borrowings, digital payments. - India’s 2021 edition showed 78% adults had bank accounts (up from 53% in 2014). - Global Pension Index: - Prepared by Mercer CFA Institute. - Measures pension systems across adequacy, sustainability, and integrity. - India’s score declined from 45.9 (2023) to 44.0 (2024, per Economic Survey 2024–25). - India’s FI Index (by DFS): - Released by Department of Financial Services. - Measures progress on three dimensions: access, usage, and quality of financial services. - RBI’s FI Index (launched 2021): - Scored on scale of 0 to 100 (higher = better financial inclusion). - Index rose from 60.1 (Mar 2023) to 64.2 (Mar 2024). - Sub-components include banking penetration, insurance coverage, digital usage, grievance redress. - National Strategy for Financial Inclusion (NSFI): - Published by RBI in 2020 (vision: 2020–2024). - Goals: - Provide universal access to financial services, strengthen digital infrastructure, promote financial literacy, and protect consumers. - Pillar 2A1-i: Budget - Fiscal Policy - Definition: - Fiscal policy involves government decisions on taxation, expenditure, subsidies, and other financial operations to influence savings, investment, and consumption, achieving national goals like income redistribution, socio-economic welfare, economic development, and inclusive growth. - Etymology: - Derived from Greek “fiscus” (basket), symbolizing the public purse. - Significance: - Employment: - Funds welfare schemes (e.g., MGNREGA, Pillar#6) to create jobs. - Inflation Control: - Higher income taxes reduce disposable income, curbing demand; lower taxes during deflation boost demand (Pillar#4). - Economic Growth: - Tax benefits on savings (e.g., LIC, Mutual Funds) provide capital for industries, leading to factory expansion, jobs, and GDP growth (Pillar#4). - Inclusive Growth: - Higher taxes on the rich fund health, education, and poverty alleviation (Pillar#6). - Regional Balance: - Tax incentives for industries in backward areas (e.g., North East, Naxal-affected regions). - Exchange Rate Stability: - Tax benefits for exporters and higher import duties reduce Current Account Deficit (CAD), stabilizing INR:USD rates (Pillar#3). - Budget - Definition: - Annual financial statement detailing estimated revenues and expenditures for the next financial year, serving as the primary tool for implementing fiscal policy. - Constitutional Basis: - Article 112 mandates the Annual Financial Statement (AFS). - Funds - Three Constitutional Funds related to Budget - 1. Article 266: Consolidated Fund of India (CFI) - Contains: - All incoming tax revenues (both direct and indirect), - All money raised via borrowings (internal and external loans), - Recoveries of loans previously given by the government. - Withdrawal requires Parliamentary approval. - Exception: - Charged Expenditure (e.g. salaries of President, Judges, CAG) – automatic withdrawal without vote. - This is the largest and most important fund for the Government of India. - 2. Article 266: Public Account of India - Includes: - Transactions where the government acts as a banker or trustee. - Examples: - Provident Fund, Postal Savings, Small Savings, Income Tax Refunds, etc. - Since the money does not belong to the government, Parliamentary approval is not required for withdrawal. - However, if a new fund is being created (e.g., Central Road Fund via Act of 2000), Parliament’s approval is needed to create it. - Government only manages this account, transfers in and out as needed. - 3. Article 267: Contingency Fund of India - Purpose: - To meet unforeseen and urgent expenditure (natural disasters, emergencies, pandemics, etc.). - Held by: - Finance Secretary (Dept of Economic Affairs) on behalf of the President. - Process: - Government spends first → then takes ex post-facto approval from Parliament. - The amount is later refilled from the Consolidated Fund of India (CFI). - Budget 2021 Reforms: - Corpus raised from ₹500 crore to ₹30,000 crore. - Distribution: - 40% kept with Department of Expenditure, - 60% with Department of Economic Affairs (DEA). - Non-budgetary / Extra-budgetary / Donation funds - Definition - Funds that operate outside the Consolidated Fund of India. - Not voted or discussed in Parliament; hence, not part of the Union Budget. - Typically formed as public charitable trusts under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. - Mainly used for emergency relief, public welfare, or disaster assistance. - Financed via voluntary donations from individuals, corporates, and institutions. - No direct budgetary allocation or disbursement from government expenditure. - Some enjoy income tax exemption benefits and CSR eligibility. - Features - Operate outside Government accounts like Consolidated/Contingency Fund. - Administered directly by the PM or designated committees. - Not audited by the CAG by default unless voluntarily submitted. - Transparent reporting may be voluntary or court-directed, not mandatory. - No parliamentary oversight unless judicially compelled. - Examples - Prime Minister’s National Relief Fund (PMNRF) - Set up in 1948 by PM Nehru, initially to aid Partition refugees. - Now used for assistance to victims of: - Natural disasters (floods, earthquakes) - Accidents - Acid attacks - Major illnesses (e.g., cancer, kidney failure) - Accepts individual and corporate donations. - Donations eligible for 100% Income Tax deduction under Section 80G. - Does not receive funds from Consolidated Fund of India. - PM CARES Fund (Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations): - Set up in 2020 to deal with COVID-19 pandemic. - For disaster management and research funding (e.g., ventilators, vaccines). - Donations: - 100% tax-deductible under Section 80G. - Eligible under CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) norms. - Audit: - Not audited by CAG; audited by private Chartered Accountants appointed by trustees. - Criticism: - Lack of transparency. - Overlap with existing funds like PMNRF. - Not subject to RTI as per PMO’s response. - CM Relief Funds (e.g., Maharashtra CM’s Relief Fund, Tamil Nadu CM Relief Fund): - State-level counterparts to PMNRF. - Accept public donations for natural calamities, accidents, medical emergencies. - Eligibility for tax deduction and CSR support varies by state and notification. - Notes - These funds are not extra-budgetary resources (EBRs) used for capital expenditure. - Should not be confused with statutory non-lapsable funds like NDRF (which are part of Public Account of India). - Courts (e.g., SC in 2020) have recognized PM CARES as a separate public charitable trust distinct from state accountability mechanisms. - A separate National Defence Fund (created in 1962) also exists under PM’s office for welfare of armed forces and paramilitary forces. - Both PMNRF and PM CARES are considered private charitable trusts under Indian Trust Act, 1882, but there is debate over whether they should be treated as public accounts for transparency. - RTI Controversy: - PM CARES is not currently subject to Right to Information (RTI) disclosures; this has led to criticism and ongoing legal debate regarding public accountability. – Three Documents Related to Budget (Constitutional and Legal Basis) - Definition: - The Indian Constitution mandates the Union Government to present a set of financial documents before Parliament every financial year. These are not just formalities but are required for legal authorization of revenue collection and expenditure. - Origin: - The term "Budget" comes from the French word *bougette*, meaning a leather bag or small pouch. - Traditionally, the Finance Minister would carry the budget documents in a suitcase. - In 2019, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman replaced the suitcase with a traditional red cloth (called 'Bahi-Khata') to shed colonial symbolism. - Key Budget-Related Documents: - 1. Annual Financial Statement (AFS) – Article 112 - Constitutionally mandated budget document. - Contains: - Actual receipts and expenditures of the previous financial year. - Estimated receipts and expenditures for the current financial year. - Revenue expenditure must be shown separately from other expenditures (like capital expenditure). - There is no requirement to: - Present a separate Railway Budget. - Show plan vs. non-plan expenditure (a practice now obsolete). - 2. Finance Bill – Articles 110 & 117 - Required to give legal effect to the government’s taxation proposals. - Parliament's approval is necessary to impose, modify, or remove taxes. - Parliament can: - Reduce or abolish a proposed tax. - Parliament cannot: - Increase a tax beyond what is proposed in the Finance Bill. - E.g., If government proposes 35% import duty on shoes, MPs can vote to reduce or retain it, not raise it to 45%. - Finance Bill is a Money Bill: - Passed only by Lok Sabha. - Rajya Sabha can only suggest changes within 14 days—Lok Sabha is not bound to accept them. - 3. Appropriation Bill – Article 114 - Authorizes the government to withdraw funds from the Consolidated Fund of India (CFI). - Covers all government spending. - Two types of expenditures: - a. Charged Expenditures (non-votable): - Automatically approved without voting. - E.g., salaries of Supreme Court Judges, CAG, President. - b. Votable Expenditures: - Government schemes, departmental spending, etc. - Subject to discussion and vote in Lok Sabha. - Appropriation Bill is also a Money Bill (Art. 110), so same Rajya Sabha limitations apply. - Special Notes: - Sometimes, to bypass Rajya Sabha, the ruling party may include non-financial provisions (like regulatory changes) inside the Finance Bill. - Whether a Bill is classified as a Money Bill is solely decided by the Lok Sabha Speaker. - [Art. 110(3)] — Speaker's decision is final. - [Art. 122] — Courts cannot question this decision. - Six Stages of Passing the Budget in Parliament - Stages: - 1. Presentation of Budget. - 2. General Discussion. - 3. Scrutiny by Departmental Committees. - 4. Voting on Demands for Grants, Cut Motions, Guillotine. - 5. Passing of Appropriation Bill. - 6. Passing of Finance Bill. - Reference: - Self-study from Indian Polity by M. Laxmikanth (Parliament chapter). - Financial Year (FY) - The concept of Financial Year in India dates back to 1867 when the British Indian Government adopted the 1st April to 31st March cycle to align with the financial year followed in Britain. - Although the Constitution of India does not prescribe any specific dates or months for the Financial Year, we have continued the colonial-era legacy of April–March. - In 2016-17, the Ministry of Finance constituted the Shankar Acharya Committee to evaluate whether India should shift the financial year to alternatives like: - January to December (calendar year), or - Cropping seasons such as Rabi–Kharif cycle, with the goal of improving estimation and management of tax revenues and expenditures. - In 2017, the proposal for change was dropped because most states opposed it. The change would have required major overhauls in accounting systems, reporting software, training, and budget cycles — and the anticipated benefits were not substantial enough to justify this transition. - In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, there were widespread rumors that the Government had shifted the financial year to a different period — however, these were confirmed to be false. The financial year remains unchanged: 1st April to 31st March. - Vote on Account - Definition: - A temporary legislative authorization for the government to withdraw money from the Consolidated Fund of India (CFI) to meet essential expenses until the full Budget is passed. - Required when the Appropriation Bill for the new financial year is not enacted before 31st March. - Background: - The Constitution does not fix a mandatory date for presenting the Union Budget. - Before 2017, the Budget was presented on the last working day of February. - But the entire Budget process (6 stages) took until May to complete. - Meanwhile, the financial year would end on 31st March. - After 31st March, the previous year’s Appropriation Act expires. - Hence, government would not have legal authority to withdraw funds, even for routine expenses like salaries, pensions, electricity bills, etc. - Purpose: - To avoid a financial vacuum or shutdown of routine government operations. - Parliament (practically Lok Sabha) grants temporary permission through a Vote on Account to withdraw funds from the CFI. - It typically authorizes spending for two months, usually one-sixth of the estimated annual expenditure. - Duration and Limit: - Usually valid for two months. - Amount approved is generally around one-sixth of the total budgeted expenditure. - Can be extended in case of extraordinary situations like elections or emergencies. - Not a substitute for the full budget: - Vote on Account only allows withdrawal for essential services. - It does not include provisions for major policy changes or new schemes. - Post-2017 Developments: - From 2017 onwards, the government began presenting the Budget on the 1st working day of February. - This ensured that the entire process — including Appropriation Bill — is completed before 31st March. - Hence, Vote on Account became unnecessary in regular years. - Exceptions: - In 2019 and 2024, interim budgets were presented before general elections. - Government sought a Vote on Account instead of full budget, as the new government post-election might want to make significant changes or present a fresh budget. - This also gave the incumbent government flexibility to introduce a large Appropriation Bill if re-elected. - FAQ / Counterpoints: - Why did Modi Govt use Vote on Account in 2019 and 2024 even after early Budget timing reform? - No detailed justification was publicly given. - No PILs were filed in Supreme Court challenging this. - Neither NITI Aayog nor Economic Survey commented on it. - Columnists and experts also did not raise major issues. - Practically, it was seen as a politically strategic and legally permissible move. - Interim Budget - Our Constitution does not define or mandate the concept of an Interim Budget. - However, during an election year or in extreme situations (e.g. when a coalition government collapses prematurely), it is considered unethical for the outgoing government to make drastic or populist changes in the budget, like announcing "free gold for BPL girls' marriages". - Hence, while such governments still present a budget in the regular format (3 documents: Annual Financial Statement, Finance Bill, Appropriation Bill; and undergo 6 stages of passing), they generally avoid grand populist announcements. - Such budgets are called Interim Budgets. - Examples of Interim Budgets: - 2004 - Yashwant Sinha - 2009 - Pranab Mukherjee - 2014 - P. Chidambaram - 2019 - Piyush Goyal - 2024 - Nirmala Sitharaman - Just like a regular General Budget, an Interim Budget is also valid for the whole financial year. - However, if a new government is formed in between, it may present another (full/general) budget to change provisions. - Example: - In February 2014, FM Chidambaram presented the Interim Budget in the 15th Lok Sabha. After the elections, the BJP-led government presented the full General Budget in July 2014 (16th Lok Sabha) via FM Arun Jaitley. - Similarly, in both 2019 and 2024, Interim Budgets were presented in February, followed by full budgets in July after elections. - Note: - For easier revision and visualization, the term "Full Budget" is used here to distinguish it from "Interim Budget". But in UPSC Mains, use the correct term: General Budget. - Budget Theme - Although the Constitution doesn’t require it, sometimes Finance Ministers include a specific "theme" in their Budget speech to create media attention. -
Budget Year Theme Mentioned Details
2021 Paperless - No specific theme was mentioned in the FM speech.
- Focus was on AtmaNirbhar Bharat.
- Introduced paperless/digital budget using a Samsung tablet (Made in India), wrapped in a red cover.
2024-Feb Interim, Paperless - Due to the general election, only an Interim Budget was presented.
- No changes in taxes, very few new schemes announced.
- Finance Minister also released a 'White Paper' comparing UPA vs 10 years of Modi Govt.
2024-July General, Paperless - A full General Budget was presented after elections.
- Continued the paperless/digital format.
- Economic Survey - The Economic Survey is usually prepared by the Chief Economic Adviser (CEA) in the Ministry of Finance. - It is not mandated by the Constitution, but is typically tabled in Parliament a day before the Union Budget. - 2019-Feb: - No Economic Survey was presented before the Interim Budget. - 2019-July: - Economic Survey presented before the Full General Budget. - 2024: - Similar to 2019, no survey in Feb; survey presented before July General Budget. - Note 1: - While the Budget is labelled for the upcoming financial year (e.g. Budget 2019-20), the Economic Survey is labelled for the previous year (e.g. Survey 2018-19). - Note 2: - For easier revision, the following short labels are used: - "ES22" = Economic Survey 2021-22 (presented on 31/01/2022) - "ES21" = Economic Survey 2020-21 (presented on 31/01/2021), and so on. -

- Chief Economic Adviser (CEA) - Works under the Department of Economic Affairs in the Ministry of Finance. - Usual tenure is 3 years (renewable). It is not a constitutional or statutory position. - The CEA oversees officers of the Indian Economic Service (IES). - Notable former CEAs include: - Dr. Manmohan Singh - Dr. Raghuram Rajan - Arvind Subramanian (2014–2018) - Krishnamurthy Subramanian (2018–2021) - In January 2022, Dr. V. Anantha Nageswaran was appointed as CEA. He holds an MBA from IIM-Ahmedabad. - Author of books: - "Can India Grow?" - "The Rise of Finance: Causes, Consequences and Cures" - His current tenure is valid until 31st March 2027. - Finance Ministry and Its Departments - Overview: - The Finance Ministry, through its six departments, shapes fiscal and monetary policy, oversees budget preparation, taxation, financial inclusion, disinvestment, and public enterprises, ensuring economic stability and growth. It coordinates with regulatory bodies and manages public assets, aligning with monetary policy objectives of financial governance and inclusion. - 1. Department of Economic Affairs (DEA): - Functions: - Formulates fiscal policy and prepares/presents the Union Budget, including the Railway component, budgets for Union Territories without legislatures, and states under President’s Rule. - Announces interest rates for small savings schemes (details in Pillar#1D). - Maintains www.pppinindia.gov.in for Public-Private Partnership (PPP) information (details in Pillar#5: Infrastructure). - Organizations Under/Related to DEA: -

- Finance Secretary: - The senior-most Secretary among the six departments (usually from DEA) is designated Finance Secretary, authorized to sign ₹1 notes. - National Land Monetization Corporation (NLMC, 2022): - Announced in Budget 2021, established in March 2022 under DPE. - 100% government-owned with ₹150 crore paid-up capital. - Functions: - Rents/sells surplus or non-core land assets of government departments/CPSEs. - Employs private sector professionals for efficient management. - Related to PM Gati Shakti, National Monetization Pipeline, National Infra Pipeline (details in Pillar#5: PPP). - Recent Trends (2025): - NLMC monetized 1,000 acres of surplus CPSE land in 2024–25, generating ₹5,000 crore for infrastructure projects (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). - Indian Audit and Accounts Department (IAAD): - Overview: - The Indian Audit and Accounts Department (IAAD), led by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), ensures financial accountability, complementing the Finance Ministry’s taxation framework. Direct taxes like corporation tax, managed under the Department of Revenue, fund the Consolidated Fund of India (CFI), supporting fiscal policy and economic stability within the monetary policy framework. - Not part of MoF - Establishment: - A lesser-known department under the Finance Ministry, headed by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), a constitutional body under Article 148. - Functions: - Oversees audit and accounts of Union and State Governments, ensuring transparency and accountability. - Implements One Indian Audit & Accounts Department One System (OIOS) for paperless administration. - Recent Trends (2025): - OIOS digitized 90% of CAG audit processes by 2024–25, reducing processing time by 30% (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). - Tax Receipts: - Direct vs. Indirect: -
Parameter Direct Tax (e.g., 5% Income Tax) Indirect Tax (e.g., 18% GST on Biscuits)
Definition Tax levied directly on an individual's or entity's income or wealth Tax levied on goods and services, collected by intermediaries
Impact (Collection Point) On the individual/entity earning the income On seller/supplier at the time of transaction
Incidence (Burden Point) Same as impact — taxpayer bears the burden Shifted to the final consumer (buyer pays the tax)
Taxpayer Visibility Clearly visible — deducted from salary/income Less visible — embedded in product price
Examples Income Tax, Wealth Tax, Corporate Tax GST, Customs Duty, Excise Duty
Administrative Authority Primarily handled by CBDT Primarily handled by CBIC
- Note: - Indirect tax burden can be regressive in nature. Concepts like "burden shifting" and "tax incidence" are part of microeconomics but not deeply tested in UPSC Prelims. - Progressive vs. Regressive: -
Type Description Impact on Income Inequality Example
Progressive Tax Tax rate increases with income level Reduces inequality (more tax from the rich) Income Tax slabs (5%, 20%, 30%)
Regressive Tax Flat tax rate affects poor more in relative terms Worsens inequality (same tax affects poor more) 18% GST on biscuits: ₹18 for both rich and poor
- Note: - GST is not intentionally regressive, but its effects can be regressive depending on the commodity. Essential goods are taxed at lower rates to counter this. - Proportional vs. Degressive: -
Type Description Tax Rate Structure Example
Proportional Tax Flat tax rate for all income levels Same percentage irrespective of income Single 10% income tax on all incomes
Progressive Tax Higher income → higher tax rate Increasing slabs (5%, 20%, 30%) Indian Income Tax
Degressive Tax Initially progressive, then becomes flat beyond a threshold 5%, 10%, 10% (flattens after a point) Hypothetical tax models
- Note: - Indian income tax is typically classified as progressive for UPSC. Degressive taxes are theoretical, rarely implemented as standalone policies. - Non-Tax Receipts - Definition: - Non-tax receipts are government revenues from sources other than taxes, contributing to fiscal resources without direct taxation. - Notable Components: - Interest Receipts: - Earned on loans to states, railways, CPSEs, and foreign countries. Loan principal repayments are capital receipts. - Dividends and Profits: - From CPSEs, public sector banks, and RBI. Share sales (disinvestment) are capital receipts. - Goods and Services Income: - From railways, postal services, publication sales (e.g., India Yearbook), CISF fees for private airport security, spectrum/mining auctions, and commemorative coins. - Grants-in-Aid and Donations: - Contributions received by the Union (loans are capital receipts). - Non-Tax Revenue from Union Territories: - From UTs without legislatures (e.g., Chandigarh, Lakshadweep). - Budget 2025 Estimate: - Gross Tax Revenue (Union’s direct/indirect taxes + cess/surcharge): - Rs. 42 lakh crore. - UT Taxes: - Rs. 10,133 crore. - Net Tax Revenue (after devolution to states and disaster fund contributions): - ~Rs. 28 lakh crore. - Adam Smith’s Four Canons of Taxation: -
CanonDescription
EqualityTax proportionate to income; rich pay more
CertaintyClear dates, slabs, and rates announced in advance
ConvenienceSimple payment process, minimal paperwork
EconomyLow administrative cost relative to revenue

They are taxed based on the applicable income slabs, just like anyone else. - Taxable income: - "Taxable income" refers to the portion of income that remains after deducting all exemptions and deductions allowed under the Income Tax Act. - Types: -

- Union Tax, Cess, and Surcharge: -
Type Description Distribution Examples
Union Tax
  • Levied by Union Govt. on income, profits, goods/services, etc.
  • Forms part of Consolidated Fund of India (CFI).
  • Shared with States as per Finance Commission.
 CFI → Shared between Union & States Income Tax, Corporation Tax, CGST, IGST (Union share)
Surcharge
  • Additional tax levied on the base tax amount (not on income directly).
  • Not shared with States.
  • Used for general revenue enhancement.
 CFI (not shared with States) Surcharge on High-Income Individuals or Corporates, Social Welfare Surcharge on customs
Cess
  • Additional charge on tax amount (or transaction), levied for a specific purpose.
  • Not shared with States.
  • Usually transferred from CFI to designated funds in Public Account.
 CFI → earmarked fund in Public Account (not shared) Health & Education Cess, Road & Infrastructure Cess, GST Compensation Cess
- Cess FAQs: - Why levy cess/surcharge? - Allows Union to fund schemes without sharing with states. - Mandatory? - Not compulsory, depends on government discretion. - Applicable on? - Both direct (e.g., Health & Education Cess on Income Tax) and indirect taxes (e.g., Health Cess on customs, GST Compensation Cess). - Health vs. Health & Education Cess? - Different; Health Cess on customs, Health & Education Cess on direct taxes. -

- Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) & Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT): - Purpose: - Introduced in Budget 1996 (FM: P. Chidambaram) to ensure companies showing zero taxable income due to deductions, exemptions, or accounting adjustments still pay tax. - MAT: - 18.5% on book profits of “zero tax” companies, reduced to 15% by Modi government. - AMT: - 15% on cooperative societies (e.g., Amul, IFFCO). - Mechanism: - Uses a different formula for book profits (details not critical for UPSC). - FAQ: How tax on zero taxable income? - Problem: - Many entities show zero taxable income by using exemptions, deductions (like SEZ benefits, depreciation, etc.). - But their financial books show large profits. - Solution: - MAT/AMT mandates tax even on book profits or adjusted income. - This prevents “zero-tax” outcomes in high-profit entities. - Example: - Company A: - Book profit = ₹100 crore - Taxable income after deductions = ₹0 - Normal tax = ₹0 - MAT = 15% of ₹100 crore = ₹15 crore payable - Conclusion: - Even if taxable income is legally brought to zero, MAT/AMT ensures companies or entities still contribute to tax revenue. - Prevents abuse of loopholes and maintains revenue neutrality. - Recent Trends (2025): - MAT compliance simplified, with 20% increase in digital filings by 2024–25 (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). -

- Corporation Tax on Startups: - Definition: - Startups: - Companies ≤10 years old, turnover ≤₹100 crore, focused on innovation in goods/services, supported by Startup India Scheme (details in Pillar#4B). - Tax Benefits: - 100% tax holiday (deduction) on profits for 3 years within the first 10 years of incorporation. - Angel Tax (2012–2024): - Introduced in 2012 (UPA Govt) under DPIIT (Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, Commerce Ministry). - 30% tax + penalty on investments from angel investors for “suspicious” startups. - Controversy: - Discouraged startup growth. - Abolished in Budget 2024 (July). - Recent Trends (2025): - Post-Angel Tax abolition, startup investments grew by 25% in 2024–25, with 5,000 new DPIIT-recognized startups (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). -

Not critical for UPSC, covered in IRS training. - Recent Trends (2025): - Post-abolition, digital MNC compliance costs reduced by 15%, boosting foreign investment in India’s tech sector (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). - Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT): - Introduction: - Introduced in 1997 (FM: P. Chidambaram) on shareholders’ dividend income. - Rate: - 15% + cess + surcharge = 20.56%. - Shareholders exempt from separate income tax on dividends. - Abolition: - Budget 2020 abolished DDT; dividends now taxable as income (0–5% for lower/middle-class shareholders). - Benefits: - Lower tax burden for middle-class shareholders. - Increased disposable income boosts consumption, demand, and economic growth. - Recent Trends (2025): - Post-DDT abolition, dividend payouts rose by 10% in 2024–25, enhancing retail investor participation (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). -

- Buyback Tax: - Background: - Earlier, companies could avoid DDT by buying back their shares instead of paying dividends. - Is paying dividends optional? - Paying dividends is optional, not mandatory. A company’s board of directors decides whether to declare and distribute dividends to shareholders. - If they choose to not declare dividends, no Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT) was triggered under the old regime. - Instead, companies could use their profits to buy back their own shares from shareholders. - This reduced the number of shares in the market, potentially increasing share value and indirectly rewarding shareholders without formally paying dividends. - Even though dividends are optional, the share holders primary way of earning is capital appreciation on bought shares, dividends are just optional bonuses - Share buyback results in capital gains tax for shareholders (which may be lower), whereas dividends attract higher taxation. - Purpose: - To discourage companies from avoiding Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT) by repurchasing shares instead of declaring dividends. - Prevents companies from using buybacks as a tax avoidance tool. - Applicability: - Imposed on companies (mainly listed and unlisted) that buy back their own shares from shareholders. - Introduced in 2013 for unlisted companies; extended to listed companies from July 2019. - Who Pays: - Company pays the tax, not the shareholder. - Shareholder receives buyback proceeds tax-free in most cases. - Capital Gains Tax (CGT): - Definition: - Levied on profits from selling capital assets (e.g., non-agricultural land, property, jewellery, paintings, vehicles, machinery, patents, trademarks, shares, bonds, securities). - Types: - Short-Term Capital Gains Tax (SCGT): - Assets sold within 12 months (financial assets) or 24 months (other assets like property). - Long-Term Capital Gains Tax (LCGT): - Assets sold after 12/24 months. - Rates (Budget 2024): -
