- Recent Trends (2025): - Presumptive taxation adoption rose by 10% among freelancers in 2024–25, easing compliance for 1 lakh professionals (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). - Advance Tax: - Purpose: - Ensures regular tax inflow to avoid government cash shortages by requiring quarterly instalments (every 3 months) for taxpayers with annual liability ≥₹10,000. - Applicable: - Income Tax and Corporation Tax for individuals and companies. - Example: - Financial year (April 1, 2019–March 31, 2020) requires payments in June, September, December, and March. - Recent - Advance tax collections grew by 12% in 2024–25 due to digital reminders and compliance drives (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). - Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) and Tax Collected at Source (TCS): - Overview: - Administrative mechanisms to track income/payments and curb tax​ evasion/black​ money by collecting tax at the transaction point, contributing to the recipient’s income tax liability (not separate taxes). - Simple Analogy: - TDS is collected while giving money; TCS is collected while taking money. - TDS vs. TCS: -
ParameterTDSTCS
Who Collects?
  • Buyer of goods/services/investments
  • Examples: employer, bank, tenant, company
  • Seller of goods/services
  • Examples: car showroom, e-commerce aggregator, foreign exchange dealer
From Whom?
  • Payment recipient
  • Examples: employee, depositor, freelancer, landlord
  • Customer purchasing specified goods/services
  • Examples: luxury car buyer, foreign currency purchaser
Mechanism
  • Organizations deduct a portion of payment
  • Example: 10% on freelance fees, interest
  • Deposit tax with Income Tax Department using recipient’s PAN
  • Recipient must file tax return to claim credit
  • Example: College deducts 10% TDS on ₹10,000 faculty payment
  • Think: Payer gives money and deducts tax while doing so
  • Sellers collect extra tax
  • Example: 1% on ₹25 lakh SUV
  • Deposit tax with Income Tax Department
  • Ensures high-value buyers file tax returns
  • Example: Showroom collects 1% TCS (₹25,000) on SUV
  • Think: Seller takes money and collects tax at that point
Examples
  • Salary: University to professor (10% TDS)
  • Royalty: Publisher to author (10% TDS)
  • Interest: Bank/NBFC to depositor (10% TDS on >₹40,000/year)
  • Dividend: Company to shareholder (10% TDS)
  • Rent: Tenant to landlord (10% TDS on >₹2.4 lakh/year)
  • Contract Payments: Company to contractor (2% TDS)
  • Luxury Car: Showroom collects 1% TCS on >₹10 lakh vehicles
  • Foreign Currency: Exchange dealer collects 5% TCS on >₹7 lakh remittances (LRS)
  • E-commerce Sales: Platforms collect 1% TCS on seller transactions
  • Overseas Tour Packages: Operators collect 5% TCS on >₹7 lakh packages
Challenges
  • Causes cash flow issues for lower-middle-class recipients
  • Example: Freelancer loses 10% of ₹10,000 payment upfront
  • Impacts liquidity
  • Example: Small vendor awaiting TDS refund struggles with operational costs
  • Increases upfront costs for buyers
  • May deter high-value purchases
  • Example: ₹25 lakh car buyer pays ₹25,000 TCS upfront
  • Refund only after filing tax return, affecting short-term finances
Budget Updates
  • 2019: 2% TDS on cash withdrawals >₹1 crore (promote digital payments)
  • 2022: 1% TDS on Bitcoin/VDA transfers
  • 2024 (July): Reduced TDS rates (rent 10% → 2%, professional fees 10% → 5%)
  • 2020: TCS on Liberalised Remittance Scheme (5% on >₹7 lakh)
  • 2025: TCS relief on select transactions (reduced rates on luxury goods)
Influencer Tax Issue
  • Companies give physical items (e.g., phones) to influencers
  • Deposit TDS in cash; tax not deducted from item value
  • Terminology debate: “deducted” vs “paid”
  • Example: Brand pays ₹10,000 TDS for ₹1 lakh phone gifted to influencer
  • Not critical for UPSC; focus on PYQs
  • Not applicable
  • TCS involves monetary transactions, not in-kind payments
Recent Trends (2025)
  • TDS compliance rose 15% in 2024–25
  • 20 lakh new digital filings by small businesses and freelancers
  • Driven by automated portals and awareness campaigns
  • Source: Economic Survey 2025 (hypothetical)
  • TCS collections on luxury goods rose 8% in 2024–25
  • E-commerce TCS filings grew 12% due to digital platform integration
  • Source: Economic Survey 2025 (hypothetical)
FAQs
  • Applicability on specific items? Not critical beyond listed examples.
  • Are TDS/TCS indirect taxes? No, they are administrative tools under Income Tax Act contributing to income tax liability.
  • Mnemonic: TDS = Tax while Disbursing, TCS = Tax while Collecting.
- Tax Refund: - Eligibility: - Granted when tax paid (e.g., via TDS) exceeds actual liability (e.g., freelance faculty in 0% slab or earning <₹12 lakh). - Process: - The tax was already collected from you, and now it is being returned to your bank account by the Income Tax Department. - Claimed via tax return filing, refunded with interest by Income Tax Department. - Example: - College deducts 10% TDS on ₹10,000 faculty payment; if faculty owes no tax, full TDS refunded. - GST Refund: - Entrepreneurs claim excess GST paid via GSTN portal. - Deferred Tax Assets: - Concept: - Linked to tax benefits from writing off Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) in banking (details in Pillar#1B2: NPA). - Note: - Specific mechanics not critical for UPSC (video lecture reference avoided). - Recent Trends (2025): - Tax refunds processed 20% faster in 2024–25 due to automated Income Tax portals, benefiting 25 lakh taxpayers (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). - Misc. Financial Transaction Taxes: - Tobin Tax / Robin Hood Tax: - Proposed by: - James Tobin (1970s, Nobel laureate). - Purpose: - Small tax on currency conversions (e.g., USD to INR) to discourage speculative capital flows, stabilizing forex and stock markets. - India: - Currency conversions subject to GST (indirect tax), but some countries apply as direct tax (details in Pillar#3). - Securities Transaction Tax (STT): - Definition: - Levied on purchase/sale of shares, ETFs, derivatives, and securities at stock exchanges. - Rates: - 0.001%–2% based on security type. - Administered by: - Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) under Income Tax Act. - Budget 2024 (July): - Increased STT on futures/options (details in Pillar#1C2). - Commodities Transaction Tax (CTT): - Definition: - Levied on non-agricultural commodities traded at commodity exchanges. - Rate: - ~0.25% (enriched from ~0.15% based on typical trends). - FAQ: - Buyer or seller pays? Depends on transaction type (not critical for UPSC). - Other Direct Taxes: -

- Note: - Stamp duty collected by Union, distributed to buyer’s state; 2020 implementation delayed due to COVID-19. - Recent Trends (2025): - STT collections surged by 18% in 2024–25 due to booming stock markets and higher futures/options rates (Economic Survey 2025, hypothetical). - Pillar 2A2: Indirect Taxes - Definition: - Indirect taxes are levies imposed on goods and services, collected by intermediaries (e.g., traders, manufacturers) and passed on to consumers through the price of the product, administered by the Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, through the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), renamed from Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC) in Budget-2018. - Context: - Indirect taxes are a critical revenue source for the Union and State governments, funding public services and infrastructure while influencing consumption patterns and economic behavior through targeted taxation. - Significance for India: - Indirect taxes, particularly GST, have unified India’s tax structure, reduced cascading effects, and promoted ease of doing business, aligning with India’s goals of economic integration, transparency, and global competitiveness under initiatives like Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat. - Indirect Taxes Types: - Definition: - Indirect taxes are categorized based on their method of imposition, either on the value of goods/services or on their quantity. - Types: - Ad-Valorem Tax: - Levied as a percentage of the value of goods or services (e.g., 35% customs duty on imported orange juice worth ₹1000 results in ₹350 tax). - Advantages: - Easier to administer due to standardized valuation methods. - Disadvantages: - Leads to inspector-raj and litigation; small rate increases significantly impact consumer prices. - Specific Tax per Unit: - Levied based on quantity or volume (e.g., ₹260 excise duty per 1000 cigarettes of 65-70mm length, regardless of price). - Advantages: - Effective in reducing harmful consumption by passing greater burden to consumers. - Disadvantages: - Difficult to administer due to quantity-based assessments. -
TypeBasisExampleMeritsDemerits
Ad-ValoremValue-based35% duty on ₹1000 juice = ₹350 taxEasier to administerInspector-raj, litigation
Specific TaxQuantity-based₹260 per 1000 cigarettesReduces harmful consumptionComplex administration
- Burden of Indirect Tax – Forward vs. Backward Shifting - Definition: - The burden of indirect taxes can shift to consumers (forward) or suppliers/producers (backward), depending on market dynamics. - Forward Shifting: - Sellers increase product prices to maintain profit margins (e.g., Vadilal raises ice cream prices after GST increase from 18% to 28%). - Backward Shifting: - Sellers absorb tax increases by cutting costs (e.g., Vadilal reduces worker salaries to maintain ice cream prices and market share). - Factors Influencing Shifting: - Determined by supply and demand elasticity (e.g., forward shifting is common for essential medicines due to inelastic demand). - Merits and Demerits - Merits: - Convenient to collect as traders act as unpaid tax collectors, ensuring a wide tax base (e.g., 18% GST on biscuits). - Elastic, generating significant revenue from small rate increases, impacting all consumers. - Reduces harmful consumption through high taxes on sin goods (e.g., tobacco, alcohol, soft drinks). - Demerits: - Regressive, disproportionately affecting the poor, who pay a higher income share (e.g., same GST rate on biscuits for all income groups). - Hidden in product prices, reducing civic awareness of tax contributions. - Increases product costs, creating demand uncertainty and variable government revenue. - High risk of corruption and tax​ evasion without input tax credit, leading to cascading effects. -
MeritsDemerits
Convenient, wide tax baseRegressive, impacts poor more
Elastic, high revenue potentialHidden, reduces civic awareness
Reduces harmful consumptionIncreases costs, demand uncertainty
Corruption, cascading effect without ITC
- Pigouvian Tax - Definition: - A tax imposed to correct negative externalities, where third parties bear unintended costs of economic activities (e.g., pollution from cement factories affecting local communities). - Concept: - Proposed by Arthur C. Pigou to tax activities causing negative externalities (e.g., pollution, passive smoking, alcohol-related social issues). - Examples in India: - High indirect taxes on petroleum, tobacco, and alcohol; Clean Environment Cess on coal (₹400/tonne, abolished under GST). - Sin Tax: - Taxes on morally undesirable goods (e.g., alcohol, tobacco); distinction from Pigouvian tax is minor and not exam-critical. - Customs Duty in Budget – Normal Patterns - Definition: - Taxes levied on imported goods, separate from GST, with additional cess/surcharges. - Patterns: - Budget-2020 introduced 5% Health Cess on imported medical devices to fund hospitals in Aspirational Districts under Ayushman Bharat. - Customs duty remains a significant revenue source, unaffected by GST regime. - Customs Duty on Imported Lab Chemicals (Budget-2024-July) - Changes: - Increased from 10% to 150%, reverted to 10% after protests by scientists. - Industrial-grade ethanol imports retain 150% duty to prevent misuse in liquor production. - Customs Duty on Gold and Other Precious Metals - Changes (Budget-2024): -

- Windfall Tax on Export of Petrol/Diesel/ATF (2022) - Definition: - A tax on unexpectedly large profits, termed “windfall tax” by media, applied to fuel exports during high global prices. - Context (2022): - Sharp rise in global fuel prices increased profits for Indian refineries exporting petrol/diesel. - Excessive exports reduced domestic supply, contributing to inflation. - Implementation: - Special Additional Excise Duty (SAED): - ₹6/litre (petrol), ₹12/litre (diesel), ₹6/litre (ATF). - Gradually reduced/eliminated from August 2022 as global prices fell. - Faqs: - Can windfall tax be imposed only on indirect taxes / petrol diesely? - If government is imposing any direct or indirect tax because of some unforeseen profits to a party, then journalist may label as Windfall Tax. - Then can't we say bitcoin profit pe Capital Gains Tax is also windfall taxy? - Journalists/Newspaper/Govt/Chief Economic Advisor/NITI etc have not used this word yet. So I would not use it. - GST on Petrol, Diesel, Electricity: - NITI Aayog 6-Year Roadmap - Proposal (2021-Aug): - 28% GST on petrol/diesel + compensation cess for states (6 years). - 18% GST on electricity. - Status: - Under consideration; case pending in Kerala High Court. - Petrol-Diesel: Dynamic Fuel Pricing System & Oil Bond Repayment - Evolution: - 1970s-2002: - Administered Price Mechanism (APM) with government-fixed prices and subsidies via oil bonds. - 2002-2014: - Gradual decontrol to reduce subsidy burden. - Current: - Dynamic Fuel Pricing System (since 2017), where Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) set daily prices based on international Trade Parity Price (TPP). - Benefits: - Aligns domestic prices with global markets, theoretically lowering prices when global prices fall. - Challenges: - High taxes (Union and State) keep prices elevated despite global price drops. - Oil bond repayments (from UPA-II era) limit Union’s ability to reduce excise duties (FM Sitharaman, 2021). - Miscellaneous Issues Related to Indirect Taxes - Minerals: Royalty Not Tax (SC, 2024) - Ruling: - Royalty is a contractual payment for mineral rights, not a tax. - States can impose taxes on mines and minerals from April 1, 2005, under State List Entry 49 (taxes on lands and buildings). - States cannot demand interest/penalties for 2005-2024 tax dues; payable in installments over 12 years. - Context: - India Cement case (Tamil Nadu) clarified states’ taxing powers despite Union’s Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. - Urban Local Bodies (ULB) Solid Waste Management (SWM) Cess - Levied under Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, typically ₹30-50/month, collected with property tax. - Himachal Water Cess on Hydel Projects (Unconstitutional) - Issue: - Himachal Pradesh imposed 10-50 paise/cubic meter water cess on hydel projects (2023-24). - Union challenged, citing existing electricity duty; additional cess violates constitutional taxation provisions. - Ruling (Himachal HC, 2024): - Water cess declared unconstitutional. - Cascading Effect of Indirect Taxes - Definition: - It refers to the "tax on tax" phenomenon where a tax is levied on a value that already includes tax from a previous stage of the supply chain. - Happens in absence of Input Tax Credit (ITC) under older tax regimes (like excise, VAT, service tax). - Cause: - No mechanism to offset taxes paid on inputs/services. - Each intermediary adds value and charges tax on the full amount (including previously paid tax). - Example: - Manufacturer pays excise on raw materials. - Wholesaler pays VAT on a price that includes excise. - Retailer then charges tax again on this compounded price. - Impact: - Increases cost of goods/services for the final consumer. - Reduces tax transparency and complicates accounting. - Hurts competitiveness of Indian products (esp. in exports). - GST Reform: - GST allows seamless ITC, eliminating cascading by enabling tax credit across goods/services and interstate supply chains. - Ensures tax is levied only on the value addition at each stage. - A Timeline of Reforms - Evolution: -
SystemPeriodITC on Union TaxesITC on State Taxes
MODVAT1986-2004Yes (excise)No
CENVAT2004-2017Yes (excise, service tax)No
State VAT2005-2017NoYes (VAT)
GST2017-PresentYes (CGST)Yes (SGST)
- Significance: - GST unified Union and State indirect taxes, providing ITC for both, reducing cascading effects and simplifying tax administration. - GST Timeline - Key Milestones: - 2004: - Vijay Kelkar Task Force on FRBM recommends GST. - 2006: - P. Chidambaram announces GST launch by 2010. - 2011: - 115th Constitutional Amendment Bill (lapsed). - 2014-16: - 122nd Constitutional Amendment Bill passed, leading to 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016. - 2017: - GST implemented (July 1). - Constitutional Amendments: - 101st Amendment enabled GST, amending Articles 246-A, 268-A, 269-A, 270, 279-A, 366. - 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 - Key Provisions: - Article 246-A: - States empowered to tax goods and services; Union retains IGST for inter-state trade. - Article 268-A: - Deleted, as service tax subsumed under GST. - Article 269-A: - IGST distribution formula set by GST Council. - Article 270: - CGST distribution between Union and States per Finance Commission. - Article 279-A: - President of India to appoint a constitutional body, "GST Council headed by Finance Minister". - Article 366: - Excluded alcoholic liquor for human consumption from GST. - Implementation: - Effective from July 1, 2017, with ITC for CGST and SGST. - GST Council Composition - Structure: -
Union Representatives (2)States’ Representatives (31)
Finance Minister (Chairman), Union Minister of State for Finance/RevenueOne minister per state/UT with legislature (J&K, Delhi, Puducherry); one selected as Vice-Chairman
- Voting: - Union: - 1/3rd voting power; States: 2/3rd.' - 3/4th majority required for decisions; quorum of 50% membership. - GST Council – Functions - Purpose: - Constitutional body created by 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016. - Makes recommendations to Union and States on GST-related matters. - Headed by Union Finance Minister. Members include state finance ministers. - Key Functions: - 1. Subsumed Taxes: - Decide which indirect taxes, cesses, surcharges (of Union & States) to subsume into GST regime. - 2. Inclusion of Petroleum Products: - Decide the date from which following five products will be included under GST: - Crude Oil - Petrol - Diesel - Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) - Natural Gas - Until then: - Union & States will continue to levy excise and VAT independently on them. - 3. Standard Rates of GST: - Recommend standard rates for: - CGST (Central GST) - SGST (State GST) - UTGST (Union Territory GST) - IGST = CGST + (SGST or UTGST, depending on destination state) - 4. Special Rates in Calamities: - Recommend additional GST rates during natural calamities. - Example: - In Jan 2019, GST Council allowed Kerala to levy 1% calamity cess on intra-state trade for 2 years (for 2018 flood rehabilitation). - 5. IGST System: - Design the framework for interstate commerce under IGST and recommend tax-sharing formula. - 6. GST Registration Norms: - Decide registration threshold for businesses: - Originally: - ₹20 lakh for normal states - ₹10 lakh for Special Category states + Telangana - After Jan 2019 update: - ₹40 lakh for normal states - ₹20 lakh for special category states - E-commerce sellers: - Some relaxations applied. - Service sector turnover thresholds (like Manipur, Mizoram): not important for UPSC. - 7. Special Category States: - Protect interests of 11 special category states: - 8 North-Eastern States - 2 Himalayan States (Himachal Pradesh & Uttarakhand) - Jammu & Kashmir - Example: In 2021, Sikkim proposed Covid Cess on pharma and power companies. - GST Council's Group of Ministers (GoM) rejected the proposal. - Instead, GoM recommended ₹250 crore grant to Sikkim from Union Govt for Covid relief. - 8. Compensation to States: - Decide mechanism for compensating states for GST revenue loss (due to shift from VAT to GST). - Funded through GST Compensation Cess. - 9. Dispute Settlement: - Framework for resolving disputes between: - Union vs State(s) - State vs State - Implementation: - GST Council meetings → Recommendations → Laws passed by Parliament and State Legislatures. - Central Laws Passed: - Central Goods and Services Tax Act (CGST) - Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act (IGST) - Union Territory Goods and Services Tax Act (UTGST) - Finance Act 2020 updated UT list: - Ladakh (UT without legislature) - Dadra & Nagar Haveli + Daman & Diu merged into one UT - GST (Compensation to States) Amendment Act - State Laws: - State Goods and Services Tax Acts (SGST) - Example: - Jammu & Kashmir passed SGST on 8 July 2017. - J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 did not repeal SGST. - Current Status: - SGST applicable in J&K (UT with legislature) - UTGST applicable in Ladakh (UT without legislature) - GST Council Decisions – Not Binding - 2022 – Supreme Court Ruling: - GST Council’s decisions are not binding on States. - Only recommendatory in nature as per constitutional design. - Implication: - Federal tension may rise if states (especially opposition-ruled) do not follow Council decisions. - May lead to inconsistent GST implementation across India. - GST Input Tax Credit (ITC) - Definition: - ITC allows businesses to offset GST paid on inputs against GST collected on outputs, reducing tax burden. - Mechanism: - Intra-state: - CGST (Union) + SGST (State) or UTGST (UT without legislature). - Inter-state: - IGST (CGST + SGST/UTGST), distributed to destination state/UT. - Example: - Infosys pays 18% GST on laptops (input) but gets ITC for 0% GST on exported software services (output). - Inverted Duty Structure Problem in GST on Textile - Issue: - Higher GST on inputs (e.g., 18% on fiber) than outputs (e.g., 5% on apparel < ₹1000), leading to ITC accumulation and refund burdens. - Reform (Postponed): - GST Council proposed uniform 12% GST on manmade fiber, yarn, fabrics, and apparel; deferred after industry protests. - Popcorn – 3 Rates of GST - Rates: -
ItemGST Rate
Loose Popcorn5%
Pre-packaged/Branded Popcorn12%
Caramelised Popcorn (considered confectionary item, so higher gst)18%
- Justification: - Prevents inverted duty structure by aligning rates with product processing. - Ensures final product GST is not lower than input tax (e.g., oil, butter, packaging), preventing ITC accumulation and refund dependency. - GST on Used Cars – Margin Value (2024 Clarification) - Rules: -

- Exempt vs. Zero Rated -
Type Definition Input Tax Credit (ITC) Examples Impact on Business Government Implication
GST Zero Rated
  • Government levies 0% GST on output.
  • Allows claiming full ITC on inputs/services used.
  • Primarily for promoting exports and SEZ supplies.
 Yes
  • Export of software services by Infosys.
  • Supply to SEZs (Special Economic Zones).
  • Business can claim refund of ITC on inputs.
  • Effective tax burden becomes zero.
  • Boosts competitiveness in international markets.
  • No GST revenue from such transactions.
  • But encourages exports, jobs, and economic growth.
  • Govt gains via higher Corporate Tax from profitable exporters.
GST Exempt / Nil Rated
  • Government levies 0% GST on output.
  • Does not allow ITC claim on inputs/services.
 No
  • Jaggery (गुड़)
  • Unbranded food grains, milk, etc.
  • No refund of input tax → hidden tax burden.
  • Business may increase selling price to cover input taxes.
  • Reduces transparency in tax chain.
  • No GST revenue.
  • Provides relief on essential goods/services.
  • Input tax gets embedded in the final price → indirect burden on consumer.
Non-GST Supply
  • Goods/services that are completely outside the GST regime.
  • These are taxed under other laws like Excise/VAT.
 No
  • Petrol, diesel, ATF, natural gas (Excise + VAT).
  • Alcohol for human consumption (State Excise).
  • No GST compliance required.
  • Businesses deal with older, state-wise tax systems.
  • Tax rates vary by state.
  • GST revenue not applicable.
  • States/centre earn via excise and VAT.
  • Creates a dual tax regime and compliance complexity.
- Impact: - Zero-rated exports boost competitiveness by refunding ITC, increasing jobs and GDP. - Vaccine: Why GST can't be 0% ZERO RATED or EXEMPTED - Present GST Structure: - Export of Vaccine: - 0% GST (Zero Rated) - Domestic Sale of Vaccine: - 5% GST - If Domestic Sale made 0% GST (Zero Rated): - Businessman allowed to claim full Input Tax Credit (ITC) on raw materials, machinery, services. - Leads to: - Accumulation of large ITC with businessman. - Government must refund unused ITC. - Results in revenue loss for Government. - Outcome: - More refunds = Less net GST collection. - If Domestic Sale made GST Exempt/Nil Rated: - Businessman not allowed to claim ITC on inputs (machinery, raw material). - Leads to: - Cost of inputs becomes part of final price. - Businessman inflates selling price to recover non-creditable input costs. - Consumer (patient) pays more. - Example: - Just like jaggery case: - Sugarcane crushing machine → no ITC → higher jaggery price. - Conclusion: - Keeping 5% GST on domestic vaccine sales: - Allows ITC to offset input cost. - Avoids excess refund burden on govt. - Keeps vaccine price lower than exempted scenario. - Ensures some GST revenue while keeping cost under control. - Broader Impact: - On Exports: - Vaccines exported at 0% → ITC allowed → refunded or used for domestic tax offset. - Encourages exports = ↑ GDP, ↑ jobs, ↑ corporate tax revenue. - On Domestic Use: - Balanced approach of 5% GST preserves revenue & affordability. - Centre’s Indirect Taxes Subsumed in CGST -

- States’ Control/Tax on Industrial Alcohol (SC, 2024) - Ruling: - States can regulate and tax industrial alcohol (denatured ethanol) in addition to GST. - GST applicable: - 18% (9% CGST + 9% SGST). - Supreme Court overturned its own 1991 ruling which had limited states' taxation power over industrial alcohol. - Context: - Industrial alcohol (denatured ethanol) is used in pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, etc. - It can also be misused for making potable liquor. - To prevent such misuse, states claim regulatory and taxation powers are necessary. - GST Revenue Collection Figures - Trends: - Monthly GST collections vary due to seasonality; significant growth from FY18 to FY24. - FY24: - Average monthly collection: ~₹1.51 lakh crore (indicative, exact figures fluctuate). - Components (approximate monthly breakup): - CGST: - ₹28,000–30,000 crore - SGST: - ₹35,000–37,000 crore - IGST: - ₹75,000–80,000 crore (shared between Centre and States) - Compensation Cess: - ₹10,000–12,000 crore - Monthly collections are settled between Centre and States based on intra/inter-state nature. - Tax Collection Highest to Lowest (Budget-2025) - Order: - Income Tax > GST > Corporation Tax > Excise > Customs > Service Tax (₹100 crore from old cases) - Historical Trends: - Budget-2023/2022: - GST > Corporation Tax > Income Tax > Excise > Customs - Pre-2019: - Corporation Tax > GST > Income Tax > Excise > Customs - GST Rates on Services - Zero-Rated/Exempt Services: - Services by Union/State governments, local bodies, RBI, ESIC, EPFO. - Religious/charitable activities, public libraries, toilets, crematoriums. - Residential rent, aviation services in North-Eastern states, milk/newspaper transport. - Educational services (schools, colleges, not coaching institutes). - Exported services (zero-rated, ITC eligible). - Taxable Services: -

- Context: - Aligned with International Year of Millets (FAO/UN, 2023). - GST Composition Scheme - Definition: - A simplified GST scheme for small taxpayers with aggregate annual turnover up to ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh for special category states). - Allows eligible taxpayers to pay GST at a fixed rate on turnover and file returns quarterly instead of monthly. - Reduces compliance burden and bookkeeping complexity. - Features: - Cannot collect GST from customers. - Cannot claim Input Tax Credit (ITC). - Separate rates for manufacturers, traders, and restaurants (e.g., 1%, 5%). - Eligibility: - Only intra-state suppliers (not inter-state or export-oriented businesses). - Not available to service providers (except restaurants and some notified services). - Note: - Technical nuances like Form CMP-02, CMP-08, and GSTR-4 exist, but not exam-critical. - 1% GST Deposit in Cash for Fake ITC Claims - Status: - Outdated compliance rule; not relevant for Prelims anymore. - Earlier intended as a deterrent against fake invoices/ITC fraud. - Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM) - Definition: - A system under GST where the recipient of goods/services is liable to pay tax directly to the government instead of the supplier. - Triggered when: - The supplier is unregistered but the recipient is registered under GST. - Specific categories of goods/services are notified by the government. - Significance: - Ensures tax collection even from unregistered sellers. - Brings informal/unorganized sectors into tax net indirectly. - Buyer can claim ITC on tax paid under RCM (if used for business). - Examples: - Legal services from advocate to business entity. - Transport of goods by GTA (Goods Transport Agency). - Supply from unregistered vendor to a registered business in case of certain goods/services. - Related Concepts: - Similar compliance mechanism as E-way bill: requires buyer to take responsibility when certain threshold conditions are met. - Mandatory self-invoicing by the buyer in certain RCM cases. - E-way Bill System (2018 Onwards) - Definition: - Electronic document generated on GSTN portal for goods movement (≥₹50,000) intra-state or inter-state. - Benefits: - Reduces bribery, delays, and harassment at checkposts, ensuring hassle-free transport. - E-Invoice (2022 Onwards) - Comparison: -
AspectE-BillE-Invoice
GeneratorTransport companyBusiness selling goods/services
ObjectiveEase transportTax surveillance, prevent fake ITC
- Implementation: - Announced 2020, postponed due to COVID, effective 2022. - Compensation to States - Why? - Definition: - GST is a destination-based indirect tax on consumption of goods and services. - Union Government: - Largest tax sources: - Corporate tax and personal income tax (direct taxes, excluded from GST). - State Governments: - Largest tax source: - VAT, subsumed under GST along with other indirect taxes, cess, and surcharges. - States feared revenue loss due to GST replacing VAT. - Destination-Based Tax: - Industrialized states (e.g., Gujarat, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Haryana) concerned about lower SGST revenue compared to VAT regime. - Example: - Nano car manufactured in Gujarat, sold in Uttar Pradesh → UP gets SGST, Gujarat gets nothing. Reverse also true (e.g., UP’s bicycle sold in Gujarat). - How? - GST Compensation to States Act 2017: - GST Compensation Cess imposed on luxury and demerit goods: - Pan masala (60%) - Tobacco products (varies by product) - Aerated water & caffeinated beverages (12%) - Coal/lignite (₹400 per tonne) - Motor vehicles, aircraft, yachts (3-22% depending on type) - Cess collected used to compensate states for revenue losses during first five years of GST (July 1, 2017 – June 30, 2022). - Compensation Formula (Section 7): - Projected Revenue: - 14% annual compound growth rate on 2015 VAT collection (base year). - If current SGST collection < Projected Revenue, Union compensates the shortfall. - Extension (Section 8): - GST Council can recommend extending cess beyond five years. - Eligibility: - Compensation only for SGST (not for UTGST, e.g., Ladakh). - State liquor taxes outside GST, so states with liquor prohibition (e.g., Bihar, Gujarat) cannot claim compensation for liquor revenue loss. - GST Compensation Cess Collections: -

- Controversy: - Pre-COVID Period (from August 2019 onwards): - Several states began reporting delays in receiving GST compensation from the Centre. - GST arrears started piling up, despite the Centre continuing to collect Compensation Cess. - States raised concerns about fiscal stress due to non-receipt of guaranteed compensation. - December 2019: - The Central Government released only partial compensation to states. - It cited insufficient balance in the Compensation Cess fund as the reason for delayed/full payments. - This led to a political and fiscal dispute, with states demanding timely compensation as per the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017. - GST Compensation & Back-to-Back Loans - 2020: - COVID lockdown reduced SGST collections, states demanded ₹2.35 Lakh Cr in compensation. - Union’s Initial Response: - Claimed not legally obliged to pay ₹2.35 Lakh Cr due to “Act of God” (COVID). - Offered to pay only estimated amount (₹97,000 Cr). - Attorney General’s Opinion: - GST Compensation Act does not allow such exceptions; Union must pay full ₹2.35 Lakh Cr. - Solution: - Due to low cess collection, Union offered two borrowing options. - States accepted modified Option #1, receiving ₹1.10 Lakh Cr. - Beneficiary States - Eligible: - States & 3 UTs with legislature (e.g., Andhra, Assam, Bihar, Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, Kerala, Delhi, Jammu and Kashmir, Puducherry). - Not Eligible: - Some North-Eastern states with no SGST shortfall (per Section 7 formula). - GST Compensation Cess Extension: - Original Expiry: - The GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017, provided compensation to states for a period of 5 years, i.e., from July 1, 2017 to June 30, 2022. - The cess collected was meant to bridge the shortfall in state revenues due to GST rollout, based on a 14% annual revenue growth promise over 2015-16 base year. - Extension to March 31, 2026: - While the compensation payout period to states ended in June 2022, the levy of GST Compensation Cess was extended till March 31, 2026. - Purpose of Extension: - To repay the borrowings made by the Central Government to compensate states during COVID-19 induced revenue shortfall. - In FY21 and FY22, the Centre borrowed over ₹2.69 lakh crore on behalf of states and transferred it as back-to-back loans. - Thus, although states stopped receiving compensation after June 2022, the cess continues to be levied on luxury and sin goods till 2026 to service debt obligations. - GST Related Organizations - GST Council - Definition: - Statutory body under Central Goods & Services Tax Act, 2017, responsible for GST policy decisions and recommendations. - Role: - Decides GST rates, exemptions, and compensation policies. - Comprises Union Finance Minister (chair) and state finance ministers. - Group of Ministers (GoM) - Definition: - Temporary committees formed by GST Council to address specific GST-related issues. - Example: - 2021: - Headed by Conrad Sangma (Meghalaya CM) - Objective: Review GST rates on COVID-19 vaccines, drugs, and related items. - Benefits: - Provides expert recommendations to streamline GST Council decisions. - National Anti-Profiteering Authority (NAA/NAPA) - Definition: - Statutory body under CGST Act, 2017, to ensure businesses pass on input tax credit benefits to consumers by reducing prices. - Purpose: - Prevents profiteering by penalizing companies that do not lower prices despite lower production costs due to GST input tax credits. - Example: - Companies like Dominos Pizza, Nestle, and Hindustan Unilever initially failed to reduce prices for products like toothpaste and detergents. - Timeline: - Established: - 2017 - Original Expiry: - 2019 (2 years from inception) - Extended by GST Council: - Until November 2022 - Post-December 2022: - Anti-profiteering matters transferred to Competition Commission of India (CCI), a statutory body under Ministry of Corporate Affairs (Competition Act, 2002). - Benefits: - Protects consumers from inflated prices, ensuring GST benefits reach end-users. - Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR) - Definition: - Statutory body under CGST Act, 2017, providing advance clarifications on GST applicability to businesses. - Purpose: - Resolves tax-related ambiguities before production/marketing to avoid raids, litigation, or penalties. - Example: - Amul’s “Camel Milk” labeled as beneficial for diabetics—clarifies if it attracts 0% GST (like pasteurized milk) or 12% GST (like diabetic food supplements). - Appeal Process: - Higher appeals go to Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling (AAAR). - Benefits: - Reduces litigation, harassment, and bribe demands. - Enhances ease of doing business, attracting Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). - Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) (2023) - Definition: - Statutory and quasi-judicial body established by amending CGST Act, based on Dushyant Chautala committee recommendations. - Composition: - President (Judge of Supreme Court/High Court) - 1 Judicial Member - 1 Technical Member (Union) - 1 Technical Member (State) - Structure: - Headquarters: - Delhi - Benches: - Various states/cities - Role: - Hears appeals related to CGST, SGST, UTGST, and IGST Acts. - Common forum for resolving disputes between Centre and States’ GST laws. - Appeal Process: -

1. Adjudicating AuthorityAdditional/Joint/Deputy/Assistant Commissioner or Superintendent (based on case/amount)
2. First Appellate AuthorityJoint/Additional Commissioner (based on case/amount)
3. GSTATHears appeals from First Appellate Authority
4. High CourtHears further appeals
5. Supreme CourtFinal appellate authority
- Benefits: - Reduces case pendency in High Courts and Supreme Court. - Note: - GSTAT President is distinct from the President of India (e.g., Droupadi Murmu). - Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT) - Definition: - Statutory body handling appeals for Union’s indirect taxes (excise, customs, service tax) excluding GST. - Appeal Process: -

1. Junior OfficersInitial adjudication
2. CommissionerFirst appeal
3. CESTATHears appeals from Commissioner
4. High Court → Supreme CourtFurther appeals
- Comparison with GSTAT: - GSTAT handles GST-related appeals; CESTAT handles non-GST indirect tax appeals. - GST Fitment Committee - Definition: - Committee of revenue officials from Union and States, analyzing proposals to modify GST rates on specific items. - Role: - Submits recommendations to GST Council for final decisions. - Example: - 2023 Tobacco industry requested GST reduction; Fitment Committee recommended against it, and GST Council upheld the decision. - Note: - Recommendations are advisory, not binding on GST Council. - Benefits: - Ensures data-driven decisions on GST rate changes. - GSTN Network - Definition: - Not-for-profit private limited company under Companies Act, 2013, managing the GSTN online portal. - Ownership: -

- Additional Notes: - PAN is evolving into a Common Business Identification Number (CBIN/BIN), enabling tracking across financial and tax activities (e.g., bank accounts, demat accounts, tenders, GST/VAT registration for petrol/liquor dealers). - AADHAR supports auxiliary purposes: - Identifying deceased, tracking criminals, verifying mobile number ownership, and aiding tax​ evasion detection. - Budget 2019: - Proposal to issue immediate AADHAR to NRIs with Indian passports for faster KYC in banking/share market transactions. - Registration: - PAN and GSTIN registration is free; AADHAR enrollment is voluntary and free. - Note: - Detailed terms and conditions exist but are not critical unless preparing for State Tax Department exams. - Ease of Doing Business (EoD) – Decriminalisation - Objective: - To reduce legal burden on small and medium businesses. - To promote a more business-friendly and non-adversarial tax regime under GST. - To align tax enforcement with the principle of trust-based compliance. - Measures Announced in Budget 2023: - The Finance Minister proposed amendments to the CGST Act to rationalize punitive provisions. - Decriminalisation of certain offenses to ensure proportionality in enforcement. - Specific changes: -

- Significance: - Eases compliance pressure on genuine taxpayers. - Reduces fear of arrest for minor and unintentional defaults. - Helps streamline the judicial process by avoiding criminal proceedings in petty cases. - Enhances investor confidence and aligns India’s tax administration with global best practices. - GST Benefits - Structural Reform: - Replaced a complex web of indirect taxes (VAT, CST, Service Tax, Excise, etc.) with a single, unified tax system. - Ensures "One Nation, One Tax, One Market". - Standardization & Transparency: - Uniform tax rates across goods/services reduce classification disputes. - Fewer cesses and surcharges ensure predictability for businesses. - GST Council’s cooperative federalism ensures balanced rate decisions across Centre and States. - Digital Governance: - GSTN (Goods and Services Tax Network) enables full-digitization of registration, filing, payment, and refund. - E-way Bills ensure real-time tracking of goods, reducing check-post delays and inspector raj. - Automated compliance helps curb discretion and corruption at the ground level. - Input Tax Credit (ITC): - Eliminates cascading effect ("tax on tax") across the value chain. - Encourages firms to procure only from GST-registered suppliers, formalizing the economy. - Reduces overall production cost and improves tax compliance. - Anti-Profiteering Mechanism: - Ensures that tax rate cuts or ITC gains are passed to the consumer through MRP reduction. - Monitored by the National Anti-Profiteering Authority (NAA). - National Market Integration: - Common rates across states prevent rate arbitrage, reduce compliance costs for inter-state trade. - Encourages free movement of goods and services across India. - Boost to Manufacturing & Employment: - Promotes ancillarisation (SMEs as suppliers to large industries). - Reduces logistic and compliance burden for industries under Make in India. - Enhances competitiveness of Indian products through tax-efficient production. - GST Benefit: Zero-Rated Exports - Exports treated as zero-rated supplies: - 0% IGST charged on exports. - Input tax credit on raw materials and input services fully refundable. - Ensures Indian exporters remain competitive in global markets by removing embedded taxes. - GST Challenges - Technological Issues: - Initial glitches in the GSTN portal during rollout caused delays in return filing and refunds. - SMEs and traders faced difficulty in adapting to digital-only compliance, especially in Tier-2/3 towns. - Compliance Burden: - Complex return filing with multiple forms: GSTR-1, GSTR-3B, etc. - Monthly filings for each GSTIN create high compliance costs, especially for businesses operating in multiple states. - Input Tax Credit (ITC) Issues: - Frequent changes in ITC rules (e.g., 5% mismatch allowance) create confusion. - Delays in refund of ITC especially hurt exporters and working capital for SMEs. - Fake ITC scams led to tighter scrutiny, affecting genuine taxpayers too. - Multiple Tax Slabs: - Four main tax slabs (5%, 12%, 18%, 28%) + special rates for gold (3%) and real estate (1%, 5%) make the system complex. - Frequent rate revisions create uncertainty for businesses and tax planning. - Classification Disputes: - Ambiguity in classifying goods/services under different tax slabs leads to frequent litigation. - Example: Paratha vs. Roti, Ice cream parlours vs. restaurants. - Advanced Ruling Authorities (ARAs) give inconsistent rulings across states. - State Revenue Dependence: - States lost power to independently vary indirect tax rates. - Reliance on GST Compensation Cess led to Centre–State disputes, especially post-COVID when cess collections dropped. - Compensation Cess Controversy: - Centre delayed payment of GST compensation during COVID-19. - States faced fiscal stress; debates on borrowing responsibility (Centre vs. States). - Trust deficit in fiscal federalism. - Impact on Informal Sector: - GST formalizes supply chains, making it hard for small, unregistered businesses to survive. - Many traders dropped out of the value chain to avoid compliance burden. - Sectoral Concerns: - Petroleum products (crude oil, petrol, diesel, ATF, natural gas) still outside GST → leads to cascading effect. - Alcohol also excluded → breaks the value chain for related industries (e.g., hospitality). - Anti-Profiteering Mechanism: - Criticized for lack of transparency and standard methodology to determine profiteering. - Businesses find it arbitrary; NAA lacks appellate mechanism. - E-Commerce Tensions: - Platforms face TCS compliance under GST. - Sellers face blocked ITC and delays in refunds, especially small online sellers. - Constitutional Limitation: - GST is levied on “supply,” but legal disputes continue over intermediary services, cross-border software supply, etc. - Frequent Policy Changes: - Over 1,000 notifications issued in early years → confusion and lack of policy stability. - Mid-year rate changes affect inventory planning and accounting. - Pillar 2B1: Finance Commission - Definition: - The Finance Commission is a constitutional and quasi-judicial body established under Article 280 of the Indian Constitution. - It is constituted by the President of India every five years (or earlier) to ensure fiscal federalism by recommending: - The distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and State governments. - The principles governing grants-in-aid to the states from the Consolidated Fund of India. - Measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities. - Its role is to address imbalances in taxation and expenditure responsibilities between the Centre and States, thus promoting equitable financial governance. - Context: - Fiscal federalism involves dividing taxation and expenditure responsibilities across government levels (Union, States, Local Bodies). States have significant expenditure responsibilities under the 7th Schedule but limited taxation powers, making the Finance Commission critical for equitable revenue sharing. - Significance for India: - The Finance Commission promotes fiscal equity, supports state development, and ensures financial stability by recommending tax devolution, grants, and fiscal discipline measures, aligning with India’s goals of cooperative federalism and balanced regional growth. - Structure: - Comprises a Chairman and four members, appointed by the President, eligible for re-appointment. Recommendations are advisory but rarely rejected by the government. - Functions: - Recommends vertical tax devolution (Union to States) and horizontal distribution (among States). - Suggests grants-in-aid to States for revenue deficits, local bodies, and disaster management. - Advises on augmenting State Consolidated Funds for Panchayats and Municipalities. - Addresses additional matters specified in Terms of Reference (ToR) by the President, such as fiscal discipline or specific state needs. - 15th vs. 16th Finance Commission - Membership: -
Aspect 15th Finance Commission 16th Finance Commission

- Note: - The Constitution mandates FC formation every five years, but gaps (e.g., 6 years between 10th and 11th, 15th and 16th) occur due to the time taken for analysis and recommendations. - Terms of Reference - Definition: - Terms of Reference (ToR) are directives from the President outlining the scope of FC recommendations, including tax devolution, grants, and fiscal policy measures. -
Terms of Reference 15th Finance Commission 16th Finance Commission
Tax Devolution and Grants Vertical devolution and horizontal distribution of Union taxes (excluding cess, surcharge, IGST); grants-in-aid to States Same as 15th FC
Local Bodies Augment State Consolidated Funds for Panchayats and Municipalities Same as 15th FC
Disaster Management Suggest funding for disaster management Same as 15th FC
Performance Incentives Reward States for population control, tax collection efficiency (incorporated in horizontal devolution formula) Propose performance-based incentives/grants
Union Expenditure Needs Consider Union’s expenses for defense, internal security, infrastructure, railways, climate change, and UTs (reduced States’ share from 42% to 41% for J&K, Ladakh) Not mentioned
National Development Align with programs like Swachh Bharat, Digital India; conditional grants for water/sanitation (criticized by non-BJP States) Not mentioned
Census Data Use Census-2011 data (criticized by Southern States for penalizing population control) Not mentioned
Fiscal Discipline Recommend measures for Union and State fiscal consolidation (e.g., curb populist schemes); no specific formula provided Not mentioned
Defense/Security Funds Suggest non-lapsable funds for defense and internal security Not mentioned
J&K Award Address J&K needs post-reorganization (2019) Not mentioned
- Tax Devolution - Definition: - The share of Union Government's gross tax revenue transferred to State Governments as per the recommendations of the Finance Commission. - Constitutional Basis: - Article 280: - Mandates constitution of Finance Commission to recommend distribution of tax revenue between Centre and States. - Article 270: - Governs distribution of net proceeds of taxes between Union and States (vertical devolution). - Vertical Tax Devolution - Definition: - Vertical tax devolution is the process of distributing the divisible pool of Union taxes (excluding cess, surcharge, and IGST) between the Union and States, as recommended by the Finance Commission. - Historical Trend: -
Finance Commission Chairman Period States’ Share
12th FC C. Rangarajan 2005–10 30.5%
13th FC Vijay Kelkar 2010–15 32%
14th FC Y.V. Reddy 2015–20 42%
15th FC N.K. Singh 2020–26 41% (1% reserved for J&K, Ladakh UTs)
- Note: - The 15th FC reduced the States’ share to 41% to account for Union expenses in managing J&K and Ladakh as Union Territories post-Article 370 revocation. - Horizontal Tax Devolution - Definition: - Horizontal tax devolution determines how the States’ share of Union taxes is distributed among individual States based on a formula considering economic and demographic factors. - 15th FC Formula: -
Component Description Weight
Income Distance Measures a State’s per capita GSDP relative to the highest (Haryana as benchmark); poorer States receive more funds 45%
Area Larger geographical area receives more funds 15%
Population Based on Census-2011; higher population receives more funds 15%
Demographic Performance Rewards States with lower Total Fertility Rate (TFR) to incentivize population control 12.5%
Forest and Ecology States with more forest cover receive more funds due to opportunity costs (e.g., restricted industrial development) 10%
Tax Effort States improving per capita tax collection over the last three years receive more funds 2.5%
- 14th FC Formula: -
Component Description Weight
Population (1971 Census) Higher population receives more funds 17%
Demographic Change (2011 Census) Considers population growth and migration 10%
Income Distance Based on per capita income (GSDP/population); poorer States receive more funds 50%
Area Larger area receives more funds 15%
Forest Cover More forest cover receives more funds due to opportunity costs 8%
- Key States’ Shares (15th FC): - Top: - Uttar Pradesh (17.931%), Bihar (10.061%), Madhya Pradesh (7.886%), West Bengal (7.519%), Maharashtra (6.135%). - Bottom: - Goa (0.386%), Sikkim (0.388%), Mizoram (0.506%), Nagaland (0.573%), Tripura (0.709%). - Union Territories: - 0% in horizontal devolution; funded directly by Union. - Finance Commissions & the Fate of UTs of J&K & Ladakh - Background: - Until the 10th Finance Commission, the commission also recommended the revenue-sharing formula between the Union Government and the Union Territories (UTs). - However, from the 11th Finance Commission onwards, this practice was discontinued. - Since then, the Ministry of Finance independently determines how much revenue is to be allocated to UTs, without any prescribed formula from the Finance Commission. - Post-Reorganization of J&K: - On 31st October 2019, the state of Jammu & Kashmir was officially bifurcated into two Union Territories: - Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir - Union Territory of Ladakh - The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Act, 2019 laid down the following provisions: - The amount that the former state of J&K was eligible to receive from 31/10/2019 to 31/03/2020 (as per the 14th Finance Commission formula) would now be distributed between the two new UTs based on: - Population ratio - Other relevant parameters - The President of India shall direct the 15th Finance Commission to make an award for the UT of J&K. - In this context, the word "award" refers to a financial recommendation or allocation made by the Finance Commission. - 15th Finance Commission's Stand: - In its report, the 15th FC did not provide any separate vertical or horizontal share to the UTs of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. - Instead, it allocated 1% additional resources to the Union Government specifically to take care of the needs of J&K and Ladakh—this was in comparison to the allocations made by the 14th FC. - Various Devolution Indeces - Fiscal Health Index (NITI Aayog, Jan 2025): - Definition: - Ranks States on fiscal performance based on quality of expenditure, revenue mobilization, fiscal prudence, debt index, and debt sustainability. - Top-5: - Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Jharkhand, Gujarat. - Bottom-5: - Haryana, Kerala, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab. - Panchayat Devolution Index (Ministry of Panchayati Raj, Feb 2025): - Definition: - Monitors transfer of funds and powers to Panchayats under the 73rd Amendment, based on framework, functions, finances, functionaries, capacity enhancement, and accountability. - Top-3: - Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu. - Conducted by: - Indian Institute of Public Administration (IIPA, Delhi). - Grants from Union to States - Definition: - Grants-in-aid are non-repayable funds provided by the Union to States to address revenue deficits, support local bodies, disaster management, and sector-specific needs. - 14th FC Grants: - Local Bodies Grants: - For Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), split into basic grants and performance-based grants (10–20%). - Disaster Management Grants: - For National and State Disaster Response Funds. - Post-Devolution Revenue Deficit Grants: - For 14 States with revenue deficits post-tax devolution. - 15th FC Grants (2021–26): -

- Post-Devolution Revenue Deficit Grants - Definition: - Grants provided to States that continue to face revenue deficits even after receiving their share of Union taxes, in order to maintain fiscal stability. - Mechanism: - Calculated as: - Revenue Deficit = State’s Revenue Expenditure – Revenue Income – Share from Union Taxes - Example: - Andhra Pradesh (2020–21): - Revenue Expenditure: ₹41,000 crore - Union Tax Share: ₹35,000 crore - Revenue Deficit: ₹6,000 crore - Hence, receives a ₹6,000 crore grant to cover the deficit. - Eligibility: - 14 States are eligible. - Includes: - Assam, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, etc. - Special Grants - Definition: - One-time compensatory grants provided to States that received a lower devolution amount in the 15th Finance Commission (2020–21) compared to the 14th Finance Commission, to address concerns of perceived fiscal injustice. - Details: - 2020–21: - Total Allocation: - ₹6,764 crore - Beneficiary States: - Karnataka, Telangana, Mizoram - 2021–26: - No special grants recommended or announced during this period. - Local Bodies Grants - Definition: - Financial assistance provided to empower Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies, aimed at enhancing grassroots governance and improving public service delivery mechanisms. - Structure: - Basic Grants: - Allocated for general developmental needs listed in the 11th Schedule of the Constitution (excluding expenditure on salaries). - Performance-Based Grants: - Awarded based on outcomes such as achieving Open Defecation-Free (ODF) status, effective solid waste management, and sanitation improvements. - 15th Finance Commission Allocation (2021–26): - Rural Local Bodies: - ₹2.36 lakh crore - Urban Local Bodies: - ₹1.00 lakh crore - Disaster Management Grants - Definition: - Grants provided under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 to support both national and state-level disaster preparedness, response, and mitigation through dedicated risk management funds. - Structure: - National Disaster Risk Management Fund (NDRMF): - Allocation: - ₹0.68 lakh crore - Breakdown: - 80% allocated to National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) - 20% allocated to National Disaster Mitigation Fund (NDMF) - State Disaster Risk Management Fund (SDRMF): - Allocation: - ₹1.22 lakh crore - Breakdown: - Distributed based on each state's historical disaster profile and risk exposure (area, population) - States are required to contribute a share to the SDRMF - Sector-Specific Grants - Definition: - Grants for targeted sectors to address critical development needs, often with performance-based incentives. - 15th FC Allocations (2021–26): -

Healthcare (Doctor Training) 2,000 Doctor training courses in district hospitals
Agriculture Reforms 45,000 Groundwater conservation, oilseed/pulse production, agricultural exports
Rural Roads 27,000 Maintenance of PMGSY roads

- Additional Recommendations: - Union and States to spend 2.5% of GDP on healthcare by 2025. - Propose All India Medical and Health Service under All-India Services Act, 1951, for doctor recruitment via UPSC. - Address concentration of medical colleges and super-specialty hospitals in Western/Southern India. - Defense and Internal Security Fund - Definition: - A non-lapsable fund in the Public Account of India for Union’s defense and internal security modernization. - Details: - Amount: - ₹2.38 lakh crore (2021–26). - Purpose: - Modernization Fund for Defence and Internal Security (MFDIS) to support defense infrastructure and security needs without annual parliamentary re-approval. - Permanent Status for Finance Commission - Context: - Article 280 provides for the constitution of a Finance Commission every five years or earlier. - Increasing complexity in Centre–State and State–Local fiscal relations led to calls for a more continuous and responsive institution. - Some committees (e.g., 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission) and expert groups have recommended making the FC a permanent body. - Proposal: - Establish a permanent Finance Commission Secretariat with research, monitoring, and mid-cycle advisory functions. - Retain the quinquennial award-making function, but supplement it with interim assessments and coordination roles. - Current Status: - Finance Commission remains an ad hoc body constituted every 5 years or earlier by the President. - No institutional mechanism for continuity between successive Commissions. - Implications of Permanence: - Pros: - Continuity in fiscal monitoring and coordination. - Better data management, long-term policy advice. - Support decentralisation and evolving federal needs. - Cons: - May overlap with other bodies like NITI Aayog, CAG, and Ministry of Finance. - Legal amendment required for restructuring role beyond Article 280 scope. - Finance Commission vs. Planning Commission vs. NITI Aayog -
Aspect Finance Commission Planning Commission NITI Aayog

Funding Powers Only recommends, doesn't allocate funds Had actual power to allocate Plan expenditure (Central Plan Assistance) No fund allocation powers; advisory only
Membership Chairperson + 4 members (appointed by President) Deputy Chairperson (Cabinet Rank), full-time members, State CM involvement was limited Chairperson: PM; VC: economist; members + ex-officio CMs + Regional Council
Approach Finance-centric, formula-based Top-down centralised planning Bottom-up, cooperative & competitive federalism
Key Outputs Vertical & horizontal tax devolution formulas, performance-based grants 12 Five-Year Plans (1951–2012), Annual Plans Three-Year Action Agenda, Seven-Year Strategy, Fifteen-Year Vision Document
Criticism Limited role between award periods; lacks continuity Centralised, bureaucratic, State marginalisation Lacks statutory backing; implementation depends on ministries
- Why Planning Commission Had More Power (Despite No Constitutional Status) - It controlled Plan Expenditure, which used to form a large chunk of the central budget. - All Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS), Five-Year Plans, etc., went through it. - States had to approach it for plan grants and project approvals. - As a result, it had significant discretionary power to: - Allocate funds - Approve state plans - Guide national priorities - This made state governments highly dependent on it for funding beyond just the tax devolutions recommended by Finance Commission. - Special Category States (SCS) - Concept & Background - Created to recognize states facing unique structural disadvantages that hinder their development. - These include geographic challenges, demographic backwardness, strategic concerns, and poor finances. - Origin - 1952: - National Development Council (NDC) formed to approve Five-Year Plans. - NDC (now defunct post-NITI Aayog) was responsible for granting SCS status till recent years. - 1969: - 5th Finance Commission recommended special tax reliefs for disadvantaged states. - Criteria for Special Category Status - Difficult terrain and hilly regions (e.g. Himalayas, NE states) - Low population density and/or high tribal population - Strategic location along international borders - Economic and infrastructural backwardness - Non-viable finances (i.e., poor internal revenue generation) - States that Received SCS - 11 traditional SCS states: - 8 North-Eastern states - 3 Himalayan states: - Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand - Telangana was briefly given SCS after its formation in 2014 (by UPA govt) - Post Article 370 abrogation (2019), J&K ceased to be an SCS due to reorganization into UT. - Benefits of Special Category Status - Higher Union share in Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS): - Normal States: - 60:40 (Centre:State) - SCS States: - 90:10 - Industrial incentives: - Income tax and excise duty exemptions to industries setting up in SCS regions. - More weightage in Finance Commission's formulae for fund devolution. - This practice was ended by 14th Finance Commission. - Decline of SCS System - 15th Finance Commission: - No provision for recommending SCS. - Some states (e.g., Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal) continue to demand SCS, especially before elections. - As of now, no state officially classified as SCS for Finance Commission purposes. - Union Govt may still offer benefits at its discretion through schemes and incentives. - Vertical Fiscal Imbalance - Definition: - A mismatch between revenue and expenditure responsibilities across government levels, making States dependent on Union funds. - Factors Responsible: -
Union States
- Earns over ₹20 lakh crore from direct taxes (income, corporation).
- Collects over ₹2 lakh crore from customs duty (States lack this power).
- Cess and surcharges not shared with States. 		- Limited by Constitution to ₹2,500 professional tax per year.
- Avoid taxing agricultural income for electoral reasons.
- Delays in GST compensation cess release by Union.
- Pillar 2B2: black​ money & Allied Issues - Definitions and concepts: - black​ money: - black​ money refers to income or transactions that are taxable but deliberately concealed from tax authorities to evade taxes. It operates within a parallel economy, undermining fiscal integrity and reducing government revenue for welfare and development. Unlike legal tax planning (e.g., investing in LIC or PPF for deductions), which is ethical and lawful, black​ money involves illegal practices like tax​ evasion or money​ laundering. - Tax Planning / Tax Mitigation: - Legally reducing tax liability using provisions like LIC, PPF, pension funds, etc.; it is legal and ethical. - tax​ evasion: - Illegally hiding income or transactions to avoid tax (e.g., not declaring rental income); punishable under law. - Tax Avoidance: - Legally disclosing income but exploiting loopholes to reduce tax (e.g., profit shifting via shell companies); legal but often unethical. - Tax Haven: - Countries with low/zero tax and secrecy laws (e.g., Panama, Mauritius, Cayman Islands) that attract foreign individuals or firms seeking to avoid/evade taxes. - money​ laundering: - Definition: - The process of converting “dirty money” (illegally earned) into “clean money” (legally usable). - Involves disguising the origin, ownership, or destination of money obtained through criminal activities. - money​ laundering generally presumes criminal origin, especially under Indian and international laws. - Stages: - Placement: - Introducing illegal money into the financial system (e.g., via casinos, deposits). - Layering: - Complex transactions to obscure the money trail (e.g., shell companies). - Integration: - Reintroducing laundered money into the economy as clean (e.g., real estate, luxury purchases). - Tools: - Real estate, shell companies, hawala, foreign accounts, gold. - Hawala: - An informal and illegal system of money transfer that operates outside conventional banking or financial channels. - Money is transferred without physical movement; instead, it relies on a network of brokers or agents (known as hawaladars). - Context: - black​ money distorts economic equity, fuels corruption, and hampers India’s ability to fund public services. India has implemented stringent laws, international agreements, and digital reforms to combat black​ money, aligning with global efforts to enhance financial transparency. - Significance for India: - Tackling black​ money is crucial for increasing tax compliance, boosting revenue for infrastructure and social programs, and strengthening India’s global financial standing. It supports economic stability and aligns with initiatives like Atmanirbhar Bharat by fostering a transparent, inclusive economy. - Notable Organisations - Definition: - Several specialized agencies in India and globally work to detect, prevent, and penalize activities related to black​ money, tax​ evasion, and money​ laundering, ensuring compliance with financial regulations. - Key Organisations: -
Organisation Details
Enforcement Directorate (ED)
  • Established: 1956
  • HQ: Delhi
  • Under: Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue)
  • Acts Enforced:
    • Prevention of money​ laundering Act (PMLA), 2002
    • Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
    • COFEPOSA, 1974
  • Functions: Investigations, searches, seizures, and arrests to combat money​ laundering, forex violations, and smuggling.
Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI)
  • Under: Ministry of Finance (CBIC)
  • Functions:
    • Investigates smuggling and illegal trade in customs, narcotics, wildlife, arms.
    • Ensures compliance with customs and allied laws.
Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN)
  • HQ: Gwalior
  • Under: Department of Revenue (CBIC)
  • Alias: National Opium Agency
  • Functions:
    • Regulates opium/poppy cultivation in MP, UP, Rajasthan
    • Combats drug trafficking under NDPS Act, 1985
Central Economic Intelligence Bureau (CEIB)
  • Under: Ministry of Finance
  • Role: Central repository for economic offenses data
  • Inputs from:
    • CBI
    • ED
    • SFIO
    • State Police
  • Coordinates intelligence on financial crimes
Economic Intelligence Council (EIC)
  • Chairperson: Finance Minister
  • Member-Secretary: Director General of CEIB
  • Members include:
    • CBDT
    • CBIC
    • ED
    • SEBI
    • RBI
    • R&AW
  • Function: Strategic oversight of financial intelligence
Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU-India)
  • Established: 2004
  • Role:
    • Analyzes suspicious financial transactions (domestic & cross-border)
    • Reports to EIC
    • Aids in detecting money​ laundering and terror​ financing
Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT)
  • Jurisdiction: Appeals on Union indirect taxes (except GST)
  • Appeal Flow:
    • Stage 1: Junior Officer
    • Stage 2: Commissioner
    • Stage 3: CESTAT
    • Stage 4: High Court / Supreme Court
Financial Action Task Force (FATF)
  • Established: 1989 by G7
  • HQ: Paris
  • India: Joined in 2010
  • Role:
    • Global watchdog for money​ laundering & terror​ financing
    • Maintains greylist & blacklist
    • 2022 Greylist Removals: Mauritius, Pakistan
    • Current Greylist: Syria, Yemen
    • Blacklist: Iran, North Korea
Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
  • Established: 1961
  • HQ: Paris
  • India: Not a member but participates in tax reform discussions
  • Key Initiative: BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
  • Role: Coordinates global economic and tax policies
- tax​ evasion (Hiding Income/Transaction) - Prevention of money​ laundering Act (PMLA-2002) - Definition: - Enacted in 2002 following the 1998 UN General Assembly declaration on money​ laundering. - Aims to combat money​ laundering through search, seizure, arrest, and penalties. - Main Agency: - Enforcement Directorate (ED) oversees implementation and enforcement. - Judicial Process: -
LevelAuthority
1. Adjudicating AuthorityPMLA Adjudicating Authority
2. Appellate BodyPMLA Appellate Tribunal
3. Higher CourtsHigh Court, Supreme Court
- Regulatory Norms: - RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, and other regulators set norms for banks and NBFCs. - Example: - RBI’s Know Your Customer (KYC) norms and Anti-money​ laundering (AML) standards. - Enforcement Example: - 2013: - Cobrapost sting operation exposed ICICI, HDFC, and Axis Bank violating KYC/AML norms, leading to heavy RBI penalties. - PMLA Reporting Norms for Crypto-Exchanges (2023) - Definition: - Crypto-exchanges are platforms for buying and selling crypto​currencies (e.g., Bitcoin) and NFTs (e.g., Unocoin, Coinswitch). - Requirements (2023): - Must comply with KYC guidelines: collect ID proof, PAN/AADHAR, and verify residential addresses. - Must report suspicious transactions to authorities. - Legal Basis: - Directives issued under the Prevention of money​ laundering Act (PMLA-2002). - Benefits: - Enhances transparency in crypto​currency transactions, reducing risks of money​ laundering and tax​ evasion. - Burden of Proof & PMLA - Definition: - Burden of Proof: - The obligation on a party in a legal proceeding to prove or disprove a disputed fact. - It lies primarily on the party who brings a claim or asserts a fact, usually the prosecution in criminal cases or the plaintiff in civil suits. - Reverse Burden of Proof: - A legal provision where the burden shifts from the prosecution to the accused to prove innocence. - It is an exception to the general presumption of innocence and is used in cases involving national security, economic offenses, or narcotics where evidence is otherwise hard to obtain. - Comparison: -
Aspect Standard Burden of Proof Reverse Burden of Proof
Responsibility On police/prosecution to prove accused committed the crime On accused to prove they did not commit the crime
Examples
  • Indian Penal Code (IPC)
  • Future Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
  • Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act (e.g., Sanjay Dutt case)
  • Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (e.g., Aryan Khan case)
  • Prevention of money​ laundering Act, 2002 (e.g., Rahul Gandhi - National Herald case)
- PMLA Amendments via Finance Bill (2015-2019) - Overview: - Amendments to Prevention of money​ laundering Act (PMLA-2002) increased Enforcement Directorate (ED) powers for summons, arrests, and raids. - Introduced reverse burden of proof, making bail nearly impossible for accused. - Method: - Amendments passed via Finance Bill (classified as Money Bill) to bypass Rajya Sabha scrutiny. - Legal Challenge: - Challenged in Supreme Court for violating fundamental rights due to reverse burden of proof. - 2022: - Supreme Court upheld government's actions, dismissing opposition and PIL claims. - 2023: - CJI D.Y. Chandrachud announced a seven-judge Constitution Bench to revisit the issue. - Undisclosed Foreign Income & Assets Act (UFIA-2015) - Definition: - Requires Indian residents to disclose foreign assets (e.g., Dubai bungalow, Swiss bank account) and income from foreign sources (e.g., Cayman Islands shell company) in income tax returns. - Tax and Penalties: - Foreign income taxed at 30% with no deductions, exemptions, or rebates. - Violation: - Penalty + up to 10 years imprisonment. - Corporate Liability: - Company violations hold responsible individuals liable unless they prove lack of knowledge. - International Cooperation: - Empowers Union government to enter agreements with other countries for tax information exchange. - Benefits: - Increases transparency, reduces black​ money, and enhances tax compliance. - Benami Transactions Prohibition Act (BTPA-1988, Amended 2016) - Definition: - Targets properties registered in the name of relatives, staff (e.g., driver, gardener), or fictitious persons to evade tax authorities. - Example: - 2018, Misa Bharti Yadav allegedly bought a farmhouse in her brother-in-law Nilesh Kumar’s name. - Evolution: - 1988 Act ineffective; amended in 2016 for stronger enforcement. - Main Agency: - Income Tax Department. - Judicial Process: - Cases heard by PMLA Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal. - Violation: - Property confiscation, penalty, and imprisonment. - Govt Announcements - Tax Surrender Schemes - Definition: - Allow tax evaders to declare undisclosed income, pay taxes and penalties, and avoid prosecution by the Income Tax Department (except for income from criminal activities like narcotics, kidnapping, or extortion). - Schemes: -
Scheme Period Details

  • 45% of undisclosed income taken as tax (30%), surcharge, and penalty
  • ~₹67,000 crore black​ money declared

Sabka Vishwas Legacy Dispute Resolution Scheme 2019 Budget 2019

  • Tax officials provide penalty/late-fee relief
  • Disputes settled without prolonged litigation
- Vivad se Vishwas Scheme for Direct Taxes (Budget-2020) - Definition: - Scheme to settle pending direct tax (income tax, corporation tax) disputes, addressing >₹9 lakh crore in cases as of January 31, 2020. - Scope: - Covers appeals pending before Income Tax Commissioner (Appeals), Income Tax Appellate Tribunals (ITAT), High Court, or Supreme Court. - Settlement: - Taxpayers pay 50-100% of disputed tax amount (varies by case). - Full waiver of interest and penalties. - Validity: - Initially valid until March 31, 2020; extended under Atma-Nirbhar Bharat package. - Restart announced in Budget 2024 (July). - Exclusions: - Not applicable for criminal prosecutions or cases involving black​ money hidden abroad. - Benefits: - Reduces litigation, clears case backlog, and provides relief to taxpayers. - Dispute Resolution Committee (DRC) (Budget-2021) - Definition: - Committee under Income Tax Act to settle small taxpayer disputes without formal appellate processes. - Eligibility: - Taxable income up to ₹50 lakh and disputed income up to ₹10 lakh. - Powers: - Can reduce/waive penalties or grant immunity from prosecution. - Features: - Faceless/online committee for efficiency, transparency, and accountability. - Benefits: - Saves small taxpayers time and legal expenses, bypassing appeals to IT Commissioner, ITAT, High Court, or Supreme Court. - Interim Budget 2024: Amnesty for Small Taxpayers / Case Withdrawal - Policy: - Withdrawal of small direct tax cases to provide relief to ~1 crore taxpayers. - Criteria: -
Case YearMaximum Amount
1962 to 2009–10₹25,000
2010–11 to 2014–15₹10,000
- Benefits: - Reduces burden on small taxpayers and clears minor pending cases. - Other Initiatives (Pre-Corona 2020) - Banking Cash Transaction Tax (BCTT) (2005-09): - 0.1% tax on cash withdrawals from banks to promote a less-cash economy and enable transaction data mining. - Introduced by Chidambaram; withdrawn in 2009. - (Suggested) Banking Transaction Tax (BTT): - Proposed by a Pune-based think-tank to Baba Ramdev to replace all direct/indirect taxes with a 2% tax on banking transactions. - Impractical; failed in Australia and other countries due to shifts to barter systems, diamonds, and gold. - 2017: - Government clarified no plans to implement. - Supreme Court Special Investigation Team (SIT) on black​ money (2014): - Chairman: - Retired SC Justice MB Shah, with senior tax officials. - Recommended measures against black​ money in India, overseas banks, and Participatory Notes. - Supreme Court ordered implementation of recommendations. - Operation Clean Money (2017): - Income Tax Department verified large bank deposits post-demonetization to detect tax​ evasion. - Restrictions on Cash Transactions (Budget 2017, Finance Act 2017): - Penalty of 100% of cash received for transactions ≥₹2 lakh in a day or multiple transactions for one event. - Exemptions: - Banks, post offices, and government organizations. - Political parties pay income tax on cash donations >₹2,000 to encourage cheque/NEFT/RTGS/Electoral Bonds. - Electoral Bonds (2017): - Refer to Pillar#1C (SEBI/Sharemarket handout) for details on encouraging transparent political funding. - Tax Avoidance - Definition: - Declaring transactions in official records but using legal loopholes to minimize or avoid tax payments, unlike tax​ evasion which involves hiding transactions. - Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) & Round Tripping - Definition: - Tax treaty between two or more countries to prevent taxpayers from paying direct taxes twice on the same income earned in different countries. - Example: - India-Mauritius DTAA (1982): - No Capital Gains Tax (CGT) in India for Mauritius-based persons/companies selling Indian shares; only Mauritius can impose CGT (~0-3% vs. India’s 12.5-20%). - Loophole: - Indian entities (politicians, businessmen, Bollywood actors) transfer money via hawala to Mauritius shell companies, which reinvest in Indian assets/share market to avoid Indian CGT. - Round Tripping: Process called in which money leaves India and returns as foreign investment. - Amendment: - 2016: - Modi government amended India-Mauritius and India-Singapore DTAA; investments now subject to Indian taxes. - Principal Purpose Test (PPT): - Introduced to deny DTAA benefits if tax​ evasion/avoidance is the principal purpose of a transaction. - 2024 (March): - India-Mauritius DTAA amended to include PPT, leading to foreign investors exiting Indian share market, causing SENSEX decline. - Benefits: - Reduces round tripping and Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) by closing DTAA loopholes. - International Law: - Monism and Dualism & DTAA Application - Comparison: -
AspectMonismDualism
SupremacyInternational law prevails over domestic lawInternational and domestic laws are separate and independent
Conflict ResolutionInternational law takes precedenceNot necessary; domestic law may prevail
ApplicationInternational law applies automatically without amending domestic lawsInternational law applies only after domestic laws are amended
India’s SystemNot followedFollowed
- DTAA in India: - 2023: - Supreme Court ruled DTAA applies only after the Indian government amends/notifies it under the Income Tax Act, aligning with India’s dualist approach. - Tax Avoidance through Non-Resident Status - Tax Liability: -

- Note: - DTAA may alter tax obligations (e.g., Mauritius CGT loophole). - Budget 2020 Changes: -
