- Implication: - Longer stay outside India required to claim non-resident status, reducing tax avoidance on global income. - Place of Effective Management (POEM) - Definition: - Determines tax residency based on where key management and commercial decisions are made, preventing companies from claiming non-resident status to avoid taxes. - Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) - Definition: - MNCs shift profits from high-tax countries to tax havens to reduce tax liability. - India’s Response: - Signed OECD’s Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent BEPS (MLI), enhancing anti-BEPS measures in tax treaties. - Transfer Pricing & Authority for Advance Rulings (AAR) - Definition: - Transfer Pricing: - Pricing of transactions between related entities (e.g., parent and subsidiary) to shift profits and avoid taxes. - AAR: - Provides advance rulings to clarify tax implications of transactions, reducing disputes. - General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR) - Definition: - Introduced by UPA/Congress via Parthasarathi Shome panel; added to Income Tax Act. - Empowers tax officials to issue notices for suspected tax avoidance (distinct from tax​ evasion laws like PMLA, UFIA, BTPA). - Implementation: - Delayed due to concerns of tax terrorism and business harassment; implemented April 1, 2017. - Criticism: - Critics argued GAAR could lead to excessive scrutiny, hindering ease of doing business. - Safe Harbour Rules - Definition: - Provide legal immunity for specific transactions to reduce tax disputes. - Examples: -
ContextSafe Harbour Rule
Social MediaNo action against platforms (e.g., Facebook) for user-uploaded illegal content (e.g., pirated movies) if removed; action against user only
Direct TaxesNo action against foreign investors in certain transfer pricing transactions
- Benefits: - Reduces litigation and provides clarity for taxpayers and businesses. - Retrospective Tax - Introduction: - Foreign companies create shell companies to indirectly transfer Indian assets, avoiding capital gains tax (CGT) in India. - Definition: - Demanding tax on past transactions that were not taxable at the time they occurred (e.g., 2012 demand for tax on a 2007 transaction not taxable in 2007). - Vodafone Case: - Context: - Vodafone acquired Hutchison’s Indian assets in 2007 via an offshore transaction; Income Tax Department demanded CGT. - Outcome: - Case litigated; highlighted issues with retrospective tax demands. - Cairn Energy Case: - Context: - Cairn Energy, a UK-based oil and gas exploration company, entered India in the 1990s through its Indian subsidiary Cairn India. - Similar to Vodafone; Income Tax Department demanded CGT on Cairn’s 2006-07 transactions. - Cairn challenged via Netherlands Arbitration Court under India-Britain Bilateral Investment Treaty. - Arbitration Ruling (2020-21): - Court ordered India to pay $1.2 billion to Cairn for tax harassment. - Cairn sought to seize Indian assets abroad (e.g., Air India planes in the USA, Indian embassy properties in Paris) to recover compensation. - Legislative Response (2021): - August 2021: - Finance Ministry introduced Taxation Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2021 to end retrospective tax. - Rule: - No tax demands on indirect transfers of Indian assets before May 28, 2012. - Condition: - Companies (e.g., Cairn, Vodafone) must drop all related cases in Indian and foreign courts. - Resolution: - September 2021: - Cairn agreed to drop cases in France, Netherlands, USA, etc.; India dropped retrospective tax demands. - Vodafone planned similar resolution. - Global Minimum Tax - Introduction: - Tax Havens: - Low-tax nations (e.g., Luxembourg: 1.39% corporation tax, British Virgin Islands: 0.07%, Cayman Islands: 0.2%) attract foreign investors/tourists due to their small size and limited viable economies. - Issue: - Multinational corporations (MNCs) register in tax havens to transfer profits, avoiding taxes in operating countries; India loses ~$100 crore annually, USA ~$500 crore. - Context: - USA’s Trump reduced corporation tax from 35% to 21%; Biden pushed for higher taxes for welfare and urged G20 for a global minimum corporation tax. - G7 Framework (2021): - Summit: - Cornwall, England; theme: "Build Back Better"; members: USA, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Canada, Japan. - Outcomes: - Companies must pay taxes in countries where they conduct business. - Global minimum tax framework set at 15% for corporations. - Discourages tax-reduction races to attract FDI. - Enables sanctions/lawsuits to pressure tax havens to increase taxes, reducing tax avoidance. - Developments: - 2021 (July): - India supported the framework. - 2025 (January): - USA (Trump) withdrew, citing economic sovereignty and competitiveness concerns. - G7-OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) Two-Pillar Solution: - Purpose: - Address tax challenges from digital economy under the 15% global minimum tax framework. - Details: -
AspectPillar #1Pillar #2
Applies to~100 largest, most profitable MNCsCompanies with >€750 million annual revenue
ImplicationsReallocate a portion of profits to countries where goods/services are sold for local taxation; member nations remove Digital Services Taxes (e.g., India’s Equalisation Levy/Google Tax)Subject to minimum 15% tax on profits; includes Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Taxes (QDMTT)
- USA/Trump Withdrawal (2025): - Trump declared the global minimum tax deal invalid in the USA, rejecting Biden’s commitments. - Reason: - Taxes paid abroad (e.g., to India) harm USA’s economic sovereignty and competitiveness. - Reforms to Reduce Tax Terrorism/Harassment - Context: - Income Tax Department balances strict measures against tax​ evasion (e.g., cash transaction bans, Operation Clean Money) with taxpayer-friendly reforms to reduce harassment. - Pre-filled Online Forms for Taxpayers: - Mechanism: - Income Tax Department extracts data from banks, NBFCs, stock exchanges, mutual funds, EPFO, and employers’ TDS submissions to provide pre-filled tax returns (salary, capital gains, bank interest). - Benefits: - Saves time/energy; reduces need for chartered accountants. - Improves accuracy in income reporting and tax payments. - Updated Return Form (Budget-2022): - Purpose: - Allows taxpayers to correct errors in income tax returns within two years of filing. - Benefit: - Reduces penalties and stress from unintentional mistakes. - Faceless Interaction: - Mechanism: - Random computerized case allocation to IT officials without disclosing their name, designation, or location. - Faceless assessment and appeals via email, Zoom, or video-conference. - Benefit: - Minimizes personal interaction, reducing harassment and bribery risks. - Document Identification Number (DIN): - Implementation: - Since 2019, CBDT and CBIC assign computer-generated DIN to documents (e.g., search authorizations, summons, arrest memos, inspection notices). - Benefits: - Creates a digital directory for transparency, accountability, and efficient case clearance. - Invalidates documents without DIN, preventing fake notices and harassment by corrupt officials. - Note: - Distinct from Director Identification Number (DIN) under the Companies Act, which monitors company directors. - Taxpayers’ Charter (Budget-2020): - Definition: - A document outlining government commitments to citizens for service delivery. - Context: - Historically, tax administrations focused less on taxpayer services; modern global trend includes charters/rights for taxpayers (e.g., UK 1986/2009, USA 1988/1991, Canada 2007). - Indian Charter (August 2020): - Promises to Taxpayers: - Impartial, courteous, professional treatment. - Presumption of honesty unless proven otherwise. - Timely, accurate information on rules and complaint mechanisms. - Collection of only the correct tax amount. - Respect for privacy and confidentiality. - Accountability for officials’ wrongful actions. - Option to appoint a representative/tax lawyer. - Reduced compliance costs (e.g., fewer forms, photocopies). - Expectations from Taxpayers: - Be honest, pay taxes on time, maintain accurate records, stay informed, respond to notices promptly. - Tax Ombudsman: - Definition: - An independent representative addressing citizen grievances; originated in Sweden (1809). - Indian Experience: -

- Direct Tax Code (DTC) Task Force (2017-2019) - Overview: - 2017: - Finance Ministry established task force under CBDT member Arbind Modi; later chaired by Akhilesh Ranjan after Modi’s retirement. - Members: - IRS officers, chartered accountants, tax lawyers, corporate consultants. - Report: - Not fully public, but media reports highlight key suggestions. - Suggestions: - Replace Income Tax Act, 1961 with a simpler Direct Tax Code. - Reduce corporation tax rates further to enhance competitiveness. - Uniform tax rates for domestic and foreign companies to promote ease of doing business. - Additional tax relief for startups (details in Pillar4B). - Increase income tax slabs from three (5%, 20%, 30%) to four (10%, 20%, 30%, 35% for super-rich earning >₹2 crore). - Abolish Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT); implemented in Budget 2020. - Establish Litigation Management Unit for efficient handling of tax-related court cases. - Other reforms noted, but limited cost-benefit value for further pursuit. - Tax Harassment Measures (Budget 2024, July): - Reduced TDS rates for certain transactions (refer to Pillar#2A1 for TDS theory). - Policy to avoid reopening very old tax cases, reducing taxpayer harassment. - Vivad se Vishwas Scheme: - Restarted in Budget 2024 for out-of-court settlements of tax disputes. - Income Tax Bill 2025 - Objective: - Simplify and compress the Income Tax Act, 1961. - Comparison: -
AspectIncome Tax Act, 1961New Bill 2025
Words5.12 lakh2.60 lakh
- Simplification: - Compressed paragraphs into tables, reducing chapters, sections, and pages. - Criticism: - Limited substantive reforms; primarily focuses on word compression. - Notable Changes: -

Property: Land, buildings, shares, gold, jewellery, paintings, sculpturesProperty includes virtual digital assets (e.g., Bitcoin, crypto​currencies, NFTs) subject to 30% capital gains tax on profit
- Note: - Bill not yet passed; changes may occur before final version. - Taxation Related Global Treaties, Agreements & Indexes - Tax Information Exchange Agreement (TIEA): - India signed TIEAs with multiple countries to share information, detect tax avoidance/evasion. - Example: - 2019 TIEA with Marshall Islands. - Nodal Agency: Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT). - USA’s Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA-2010): - Requires foreign financial institutions (e.g., Indian banks, Pakistani insurance, Chinese mutual funds) to report American-held assets. - Helps US tax authorities detect tax avoidance/evasion by Americans. - Tax Inspectors Without Borders (TIWB): - Joint initiative by UNDP and OECD for training tax inspectors. - India participates, training tax officers in Eswatini (formerly Swaziland). - Global Financial Secrecy Index: - Prepared by: - Tax Justice Network (TJN), London-based think tank. - Measures: - Financial secrecy, tax avoidance, and BEPS using 20 indicators. - 2022 Ranking: - 1st: USA, 2nd: Switzerland, 3rd: Singapore, India: 36th. - Finding: - India loses >$10 billion annually due to MNC tax abuse. - Demonetisation - Definition: - Wholesale withdrawal of currency notes from circulation under RBI Act, 1934. - Process: - RBI Central Board recommends; Finance Ministry’s Department of Economic Affairs issues gazette notification. - History: - 1946: - ₹500 notes demonetised. - 1978: - ₹1,000, ₹5,000, ₹10,000 notes demonetised. - 2016 (Nov 8): - ₹500 and ₹1,000 Mahatma Gandhi series notes (Specified Bank Notes, SBN) ordered to be deposited in banks/post offices by Dec 30, 2016. - Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Ordinance/Act (2017): - From Dec 31, 2016: - RBI not obligated to honor/exchange SBN (except for NRIs with relaxed deadlines). - Public prohibited from holding SBN, except for research/numismatics/museums in limited amounts. - Global Context: - Demonetisation also occurred in Sweden (2013), European Union (2016), Pakistan (2015). - Purpose (2016): - Combat corruption, black​ money, counterfeiting, terror​ financing. - Context: - India’s cash-to-GDP ratio (12.04%) was high; currency printing/transportation cost 1.7% of GDP. - Cash-to-GDP ratio of 12.04% means that the total value of currency in circulation was about 12.04% of India's GDP. - Currency printing + transportation cost = 1.7% of GDP implies the cost of managing physical currency (including printing, transporting, securing it) amounts to 1.7% of the GDP, not of the currency value. - Low soil rate (damage rate) of ₹500/₹1,000 notes suggested use for storing black​ money, not transactions. - Estimate: - ₹3 lakh crore (~2% GDP) of black​ money stored in SBN. - Expected Outcome: - black​ money holders would avoid depositing SBN, fearing IT raids, destroying black​ money. - Actual Outcome: - ~99.3% SBN returned to banks; only ~₹10,720 crore black​ money destroyed. - Supreme Court Verdict (2023): - Challenge: - Filed by Congress leader P. Chidambaram and others in 2016. - Ruling: - Upheld demonetisation in a 4:1 verdict. - Tax-to-GDP Ratio: Why Low in India? - Lack of civic sense regarding tax payment as a duty. - Informal sector, parallel/cash-based economy enables income hiding. - Low per capita income, high poverty, income concentration among few who evade/avoid taxes. - Election funding fuels corruption and black​ money; politician-builder nexus. - State/local governments avoid levying taxes (e.g., agricultural income) due to political considerations, narrowing the tax base. - Loopholes in tax laws encourage avoidance; wealth tax, gift tax, estate duty (paper taxes) yielded low revenue and were abolished due to evasion and lax monitoring. - Economic Survey 2019: - Use Behavioural Economics to Improve Tax Compliance: - Shifted to Mains-QEP (refer to Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah for context). - Revenue Shortfall - Definition: - Occurs when government earns less tax than projected. - Data: -

- Laffer Curve: - Concept: - By Arthur Laffer; high tax rates reduce revenue by discouraging work or encouraging evasion; tax cuts can increase revenue. - Applications: - Modi Budgets (2017+): - Lowest income tax slab cut from 10% to 5%; corporation tax for small companies reduced from 30% to 25% (phased). - Budget 2020: - Optional income tax slabs introduced. - USA Budget 2017: - Corporation tax cut from 35% to 15%. - Tax Buoyancy & Elasticity: - Tax Elasticity: - Measures absolute increase in tax revenue from a tax rate change (e.g., 5% to 15% income tax slab). - Tax Buoyancy: - Measures tax collection growth relative to GDP growth. - Example (ES23): - GST buoyancy = 1.12 (high; grows faster than GDP); pre-GST indirect taxes = 0.99 (low). - Net Tax Revenue of Union: -
ComponentBudget 2025 (₹ Crore)
A. Gross Tax Revenue (Union’s direct/indirect taxes, cess, surcharge)42 lakh
B. Union Territories without Legislature Taxes10,133
C. Gross Tax Revenue (A+B)~42 lakh
D. Minus Tax Devolution to States (per Finance Commission)(-) 14 lakh
E. Minus Contributions to National Disaster Response Fund(-) 10,380
Net Tax Revenue (C-D-E)~28 lakh
- Note: - National Disaster Response Fund (statutory under Disaster Management Act, 2005; formerly National Calamity Contingency Fund). - Pillar 2B3: Revenue Expenditure - Definition: - Revenue expenditure refers to government spending on the day-to-day operations and maintenance of state functions, which does not create long-term income-generating or permanent assets. It includes expenses like salaries, pensions, subsidies, and interest payments on loans, critical for sustaining administrative, social, and economic services. - Context: - Revenue expenditure forms a significant portion of India’s Union Budget, ensuring the smooth functioning of executive, judiciary, legislature, and statutory bodies while supporting welfare schemes through subsidies and grants. Efficient management is vital to balance fiscal health and public welfare. - Significance for India: - Revenue expenditure supports essential services like defense, education, and healthcare, and funds welfare programs like subsidies for food, fuel, and fertilizers. It is crucial for maintaining governance and social equity but must be controlled to prevent fiscal deficits and ensure sustainable economic growth. - Overview - Definition: - Revenue expenditure encompasses routine expenses that maintain government operations without creating capital assets, such as salaries, pensions, utilities (e.g., electricity, stationery), and interest payments on loans. - Characteristics: - Does not result in income-generating or permanent assets (unlike capital expenditure, which creates assets like roads or buildings). - Funds the operational costs of executive, judiciary, legislature, constitutional bodies (e.g., Election Commission), and statutory bodies (e.g., SEBI). - Includes payments for social services (health, education), economic services (agriculture, transport), and administrative functions (police, external affairs). - Key Components: - Interest Payments: - Payments on interest for loans (principal repayment is capital expenditure). This is the largest revenue expenditure, reflecting India’s debt servicing obligations. - Subsidies: - Financial assistance to reduce the burden on citizens or industries (e.g., food, fertilizer, fuel subsidies). - Salaries and Pensions: - Compensation for government employees and retirees, including dearness allowances to offset inflation. - Grants-in-Aid: - Funds provided to states, local bodies, or institutions (e.g., disaster management, Panchayati Raj) without repayment obligations. - Defense Expenditure: - Salaries, fuel, and maintenance for armed forces (e.g., fuel for tanks, soldier salaries). - Union Territories without Legislature: - Operational expenses for UTs like Chandigarh and Lakshadweep. -
Component Details
Interest Payments Highest revenue expenditure; e.g., Budget 2024–25 allocated ~Rs. 10.5 lakh crore for interest payments.
Subsidies Includes food (~Rs. 2 lakh crore), fertilizer (~Rs. 1.6 lakh crore), and fuel subsidies as per Budget 2024–25.
Salaries & Pensions Covers central government employees and retirees; e.g., ~Rs. 5 lakh crore in Budget 2024–25.
Grants-in-Aid Finance Commission-recommended grants for states and local bodies; e.g., ~Rs. 2 lakh crore for disaster management and rural development.
Defense Revenue component includes salaries and maintenance; e.g., ~Rs. 3 lakh crore in Budget 2024–25.
- Subsidies - Definition: - Subsidies are financial benefits provided by the government to individuals, farmers, or industries to reduce costs, promote welfare, or support economic activities. Unlike taxes, subsidies are voluntary and not punishable if refused. - Comparison with Taxes: -
Aspect Tax Subsidy
Nature Compulsory contribution to the state; non-payment is punishable. Voluntary benefit to reduce burden; refusal is not penalized.
Benefit No direct or specific goods/services guaranteed (e.g., Mukesh Ambani’s taxes don’t ensure pothole-free roads). Provides specific benefits (e.g., Rs. 6,000 under PM-KISAN, subsidized LPG).
- Types of Subsidies - Definition: - Subsidies are categorized based on their delivery mechanism and purpose, aimed at promoting affordability, equity, or economic growth. - Types and Examples: - Direct Cash Subsidies: - Transferred directly to beneficiaries’ bank accounts (e.g., PM-KISAN: Rs. 6,000 annually for farmers; DBT-PAHAL: ~Rs. 200 per LPG cylinder). - In-Kind Subsidies: - Non-monetary benefits like free school bags, uniforms, books for poor students, free medicines in public hospitals, or free insurance schemes (e.g., Ayushman Bharat). - Indirect Subsidies: - Government pays organizations to offer goods/services at reduced rates (e.g., low fees in government colleges, subsidized kerosene, urea, or crop insurance premiums). - Implicit Subsidies: - Government policies suppress supply to raise prices for a sector’s benefit (e.g., banning American poultry imports creates a shortage, allowing Indian poultry farmers to charge higher prices, indirectly subsidizing them). - Cross-Subsidization: - One group’s higher payments offset another’s lower costs (e.g., Indian Railways charges higher freight rates to keep passenger fares affordable for the poor). - Regulatory Subsidies: - Mandated price caps by regulators (e.g., State Electricity Regulatory Commission limits electricity rates for farmers to Rs. 2–4 per unit). - Procurement Subsidies: - Government purchases at above-market prices (e.g., Food Corporation of India buys food grains at Minimum Support Price to support farmers). - Interest Subsidies (Subvention): - Government pays part of the interest on loans for farmers, MSMEs, or affordable housing (e.g., LIC’s Vaya Vandana Yojana for senior citizens). -
Type Example
Direct Cash PM-KISAN (Rs. 6,000/year), DBT-PAHAL (LPG subsidy).
In-Kind Free school supplies, Ayushman Bharat insurance.
Indirect Subsidized urea, low-cost government college fees.
Implicit Ban on poultry imports to support local farmers.
Cross-Subsidization Railways’ high freight rates to subsidize passenger fares.
Regulatory Electricity rate caps for farmers.
Procurement FCI’s MSP-based food grain purchases.
Interest Subvention Subsidized loans for farmers, MSMEs, housing.
- Impact of Subsidies - Positive Impacts: - Merit Goods: - Subsidies on healthcare, education, LPG, solar panels, and windmills increase access and generate positive externalities (e.g., LPG subsidies reduce firewood use, preserving trees and reducing indoor air pollution). - Economic Support: - Subsidies like PM-KISAN and fertilizer subsidies stabilize farmers’ incomes, enhancing agricultural productivity and rural welfare. - Social Equity: - In-kind subsidies (e.g., free school supplies) and indirect subsidies (e.g., cheap college fees) promote access to education and healthcare for the poor. - Negative Impacts: - Environmental Harm: - Subsidies on diesel, kerosene, and urea lead to negative externalities like air pollution, soil degradation, water pollution, and algae blooms due to overuse. - Subsidy Leakage: - Inefficiencies like ghost beneficiaries (non-existent recipients created by corrupt officials) and ineligible beneficiaries (e.g., wealthy individuals receiving subsidies) waste resources. - Fiscal Burden: - High subsidy costs strain government budgets, potentially increasing fiscal deficits (e.g., food subsidies alone cost ~Rs. 2 lakh crore in Budget 2024–25). - Market Distortion: - Implicit subsidies (e.g., poultry import bans) and procurement subsidies (e.g., MSP) can distort market prices, affecting economic efficiency. -
Impact Positive Negative
Merit Goods Promotes healthcare, education, clean energy. Limited impact if poorly targeted.
Environment LPG reduces deforestation, pollution. Diesel, urea subsidies harm soil, air, water.
Fiscal Supports welfare and economic stability. High costs increase fiscal deficits.
Leakage Targeted delivery benefits the poor. Ghost/ineligible beneficiaries waste funds.
- Subsidy Delivery → JAM and DBT - Definition: - JAM (Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile) and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) are mechanisms to deliver subsidies efficiently by linking bank accounts, Aadhaar, and mobile numbers to reduce leakage and ensure benefits reach intended recipients. - Economic Survey Observations (2015–23): - 2015–16: - JAM introduced to streamline subsidy delivery, reducing middlemen and ghost beneficiaries. - 2016–17: - DBT saved ~Rs. 36,000 crore by eliminating fake LPG connections. - 2018–19: - Highlighted DBT’s role in food subsidies (e.g., PDS) and MGNREGA payments, ensuring transparency. - 2022–23: - DBT expanded to 300+ schemes, transferring ~Rs. 6.3 lakh crore annually, with Aadhaar-based authentication minimizing fraud. - Process: - Beneficiaries’ bank accounts are linked to Aadhaar and mobile numbers. - Subsidies (e.g., PM-KISAN, LPG) are transferred directly to accounts, bypassing intermediaries. - Example: - PAHAL scheme transfers LPG subsidies to consumers’ accounts, reducing black-market sales of cylinders. - Challenges: - Digital divide in rural areas limits access to mobile/internet for DBT. - Aadhaar authentication failures due to biometric mismatches exclude genuine beneficiaries. - High administrative costs for maintaining DBT infrastructure. - National Recruitment Agency (NRA) - Definition: - Established in 2020 under Budget 2020, NRA conducts a Common Eligibility Test (CET) to shortlist candidates for non-gazetted Group B and C posts in central government and public sector banks (PSBs). - Objectives: - Streamline recruitment by replacing multiple agency exams with a single CET, reducing time and cost for candidates and recruiters. - SSC and IBPS conduct subsequent mains exams for specific posts. - Features: - Computerized test centers in every district for accessibility. - CET scores valid for multiple agencies, simplifying the application process. - Focus on aspirational districts (117) to enhance employment opportunities. - Significance: - Reduces duplication of exams (e.g., SSC, IBPS, Railways) and lowers financial burden on candidates. - Enhances transparency and efficiency in government recruitment. - Note: - NRA is not a constitutional body and was not established in 2014, nor does it facilitate private-sector jobs. - Revenue Expenditure → Salaries - Definition: - Salaries and related allowances for central government employees and retirees form a significant portion of revenue expenditure, ensuring workforce compensation and inflation protection. - 7th Pay Commission (2014–16): - Overview: - Constituted by the Ministry of Finance (Department of Expenditure) under Justice A.K. Mathur, effective from 1 January 2016. The first commission was led by Srinivasa Varadachariar (1946). - Key Recommendations: - Introduced Pay Matrix, replacing pay bands and grade pay for simplified salary structures. - Increased minimum salary to Rs. 18,000/month (Group D) and maximum to Rs. 2.25 lakh/month (Apex scale, e.g., Department Secretary) and Rs. 2.5 lakh/month (Cabinet Secretary). - Regulatory body salaries raised (e.g., Chairman: Rs. 4.5 lakh/month). - Adopted Dr. Aykroyd’s formula to adjust wages based on commodity price changes, potentially eliminating the need for future pay commissions. - Strengthened Modified Assured Career Progression (MACP) to ensure merit-based promotions, curbing automatic promotions for underperforming officials. - Reforms for defense and Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF), including better allowances and service conditions. -
Aspect Details
Pay Matrix Replaces pay bands; simplifies salary structure.
Salary Range Rs. 18,000 (Group D) to Rs. 2.5 lakh (Cabinet Secretary).
Aykroyd Formula Adjusts wages based on commodity price changes.
MACP Ensures merit-based promotions.
- 8th Pay Commission (Budget 2025) - Overview: - Announced in Budget 2025, but chairman details were unavailable as of 1 February 2025. Aims to further refine salary structures and address inflation and employee welfare. - Context: - Likely to build on the 7th Pay Commission’s Pay Matrix and Aykroyd formula, ensuring dynamic salary adjustments. - Expected to address concerns like rising living costs and pension disparities. - Dearness Allowance (DA) and Dearness Relief (DR) - Definition: - Dearness Allowance (DA) is a cost-of-living adjustment for serving central government employees to offset inflation. Dearness Relief (DR) is a similar allowance for retired employees. - Mechanism: - Calculated as a percentage of basic salary/pension, based on the All India Consumer Price Index (AICPI). - Revised biannually (January and July) by the Department of Expenditure. - Key Developments: - 2020: - DA/DR frozen due to COVID-19 fiscal constraints. - 2021 (July): - Resumed at 28% (from 17%), with arrears paid to employees and pensioners. - 2024: - DA increased to 50% of basic salary for ~1 crore employees and pensioners, reflecting inflation adjustments. -
Aspect DA DR
Beneficiaries Serving employees Retired employees
Purpose Protect against inflation Protect against inflation
2021 Update Resumed at 28% Resumed at 28%
- Bonus to Government Employees - Definition: - Bonuses are additional payments beyond regular salaries, given occasionally to boost morale or reward performance. - Types: - Productivity-Linked Bonus (PLB): - Tied to measurable output (e.g., files cleared, trees planted, or sales improved in postal/railways departments). - Non-Productivity-Linked (Ad-Hoc) Bonus: - Given regardless of performance, e.g., Diwali bonus (up to Rs. 7,000 for non-gazetted employees in 2024). - Example: - 2024: - Productivity-linked bonuses for railway employees based on train operation efficiency; ad-hoc Diwali bonuses for Group C and D staff. - Miscellaneous Terms - House Rent Allowance (HRA): - Provided to cover accommodation costs, varying by city classification (e.g., 27% of basic salary in metro cities like Delhi, 9% in smaller towns under 7th Pay Commission). - Gratuity: - Lump-sum payment for employees with continuous service (typically 5+ years), governed by the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. Maximum limit: Rs. 20 lakh (2024). - One Rank One Pension (OROP): - Introduced in 2015 for military personnel to ensure equal pensions for the same rank and service length, regardless of retirement date. Criticisms include disputes over base year and calculation formulas, with ex-servicemen seeking revisions. -
Term Details
HRA 9–27% of basic salary based on city type.
Gratuity Up to Rs. 20 lakh for 5+ years of service.
OROP Equal pensions for same rank/service; implemented 2015.
- Pillar 2D1: Capital Receipts & Expenditure - Definition: - Capital receipts and expenditure in the Union Budget involve funds that affect the government’s assets or liabilities, distinct from revenue receipts/expenditure, which support day-to-day operations. Capital receipts include borrowings and disinvestment proceeds, while capital expenditure creates long-term assets or reduces liabilities. - Context: - Capital receipts provide funds for infrastructure, debt repayment, and investments, crucial for economic growth and fiscal stability. Capital expenditure drives development through asset creation (e.g., highways, hospitals) and financial investments, aligning with initiatives like Atmanirbhar Bharat and Gati Shakti. - Significance for India: - Effective management of capital receipts and expenditure enhances infrastructure, boosts economic productivity, and reduces fiscal deficits. Strategic disinvestment and monetization policies under Modi’s regime optimize public sector resources, fostering private sector participation and economic efficiency. - Capital Receipts - Definition: - Capital receipts are funds that increase the government’s liabilities (e.g., borrowings) or reduce its assets (e.g., disinvestment). They are categorized into debt and non-debt receipts. - Types of Capital Receipts: - Capital Debt Receipts: - Internal Borrowing: - Funds raised from domestic sources like RBI, banks, NBFCs, small savings schemes (e.g., Post Office Savings Accounts, Kisan Vikas Patra), and Provident Funds (e.g., EPFO, PPF). - External Borrowing: - Loans from foreign countries and institutions like IMF, World Bank, and BRICS Bank, typically in foreign currencies (e.g., USD, Euro). - Loan Principal Recovered: - Repayments of principal (not interest) from loans given by the Union to states, foreign countries, or public sector companies. - Capital Non-Debt Receipts: - Disinvestment: - Proceeds from selling government shares in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) or Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs). -
Type Examples
Internal Borrowing RBI, banks, NBFCs, Post Office Savings, PPF.
External Borrowing IMF, World Bank, BRICS Bank loans.
Loan Principal Recovered Repayments from states, CPSEs, foreign nations.
Disinvestment Sale of shares in CPSEs like ONGC, SAIL.
- Foreign Borrowing in Foreign Currency - Introduction: - In Budget 2019, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced that India’s sovereign external debt-to-GDP ratio is low (~5%), allowing the government to raise part of its borrowing from external markets in foreign currencies (e.g., USD, Euro). - Arguments in Favor: - Reduces Crowding Out: - Domestic borrowing reduces funds available for private corporates. External borrowing frees up domestic capital for private sector growth, enabling factory expansion, job creation, and GDP growth. - Lower Interest Rates: - Advanced economies (e.g., USA, EU) offer lower interest rates, making foreign loans cheaper than domestic ones. - Manageable Debt Levels: - India’s low external debt ratio suggests that moderate foreign borrowing is unlikely to cause significant fiscal strain. - Arguments Against: - Exchange Rate Risk: - A weakening rupee (e.g., $1 = Rs. 60 to Rs. 70) increases the repayment burden in rupees, making loans more expensive than anticipated. - Risk of Over-Borrowing: - Future governments may excessively borrow abroad to fund populist schemes, risking a debt crisis if the rupee depreciates significantly. - Alternative Approach: - Increasing foreign investment limits in Government Securities (G-Secs) in INR attracts foreign capital without currency risk, preferable to borrowing in foreign currency. - Conclusion: - While foreign borrowing can reduce domestic crowding out and leverage low global interest rates, the exchange rate risk and potential for over-borrowing outweigh benefits. Economists like Raghuram Rajan advocate caution, suggesting more deliberation before expanding foreign currency borrowing. -
Arguments In Favor Against
Economic Impact Reduces crowding out, boosts private sector growth. Exchange rate risk increases repayment costs.
Interest Rates Lower rates in advanced economies. Future over-borrowing risks debt crisis.
Alternative - Increase G-Sec investment limits in INR.
- Foreign/External Borrowing Data - Economic Survey 2023: - Most of India’s external debt is in INR, minimizing currency risk. - Data (in Rs. Crore): -
Year External Debt
2022–23 37,124
2023–24 24,832
2024–25 32,000
2025–26 23,500
- Significance: - India’s external borrowing remains low relative to GDP, reducing fiscal vulnerability. The decline in 2025–26 reflects cautious borrowing strategies. - Disinvestment - Definition: - Disinvestment involves the government selling its shareholding in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) or Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) to raise funds, typically retaining at least 51% ownership to maintain control. - Types of Government-Owned Entities: - Departmental Undertakings: - Directly managed by ministries (e.g., Railways, Postal Services). No separate legal entity, high ministerial interference, audited by CAG. - Statutory Corporations: - Created by specific Acts (e.g., RBI, LIC, SBI, EPFO). Some have internal audits, excluding CAG. Moderate operational flexibility. - Government Companies (CPSEs): - Registered under the Companies Act with ≥51% government shareholding (e.g., Coal India, NTPC). Audited by CAG-empaneled private auditors, higher operational flexibility. -
Type Examples Features
Departmental Undertakings Railways, Postal High interference, CAG audit.
Statutory Corporations RBI, LIC, SBI Moderate flexibility, some exclude CAG.
Government Companies Coal India, NTPC High flexibility, private auditors.
- Objectives: - Promote public welfare through affordable services, develop infrastructure, ensure regional balance, and prevent economic concentration in private hands. - Challenges: - Political interference, lack of innovation, employee union resistance, and loss-making operations hinder efficiency. - CPSE vs. PSU vs. PSB - Public Sector Banks (PSBs): - Banks with majority government shareholding (e.g., SBI, PNB). - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Government companies under the Companies Act with ≥51% Union shareholding, excluding PSBs, public sector insurance companies, and NBFCs (e.g., ONGC, SAIL). - Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs): - Collective term for all government-owned entities, including CPSEs, PSBs, and state/local government companies. -
Entity Definition Examples
PSB Banks with ≥51% government shareholding. SBI, PNB.
CPSE Government companies excluding PSBs, insurance, NBFCs. ONGC, SAIL.
PSU All government-owned entities (Union, state, local). CPSEs, PSBs, state companies.
- Ratna Companies - Definition: - Ratna status, granted by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE, shifted to Finance Ministry in 2021), provides operational autonomy to high-performing CPSEs (not PSBs, statutory corporations, or private companies). - Categories and Conditions: - Miniratna (Category I & II): - CPSEs with continuous profits for three years, subdivided based on profit levels (e.g., NHPC, Mazagaon Dock). - Navratna: - Miniratna or other CPSEs meeting criteria like manpower cost ratios (e.g., Hindustan Aeronautics, Bharat Electronics). - Maharatna: - Navratna CPSEs with ≥Rs. 5,000 crore annual profit for three years, listed on stock exchanges, and significant global presence (e.g., Coal India, NTPC). - Benefits: - Autonomy in hiring, acquisitions, and decision-making without government approval for minor decisions. - Examples (as of 1/1/2020): - Miniratna: - National Film Development Corporation, WAPCOS. - Navratna: - Oil India, Container Corporation. - Maharatna: - Bharat Petroleum, GAIL, ONGC. -
Category Conditions Examples
Miniratna Profits for 3 years. NHPC, Mazagaon Dock.
Navratna Miniratna or specific criteria. Bharat Electronics, Oil India.
Maharatna Navratna, ≥Rs. 5,000 crore profit, global presence. Coal India, NTPC.
- Government Policy Towards Disinvestment (Pre-2021) - Disinvestment: - Reducing government shareholding in CPSEs while retaining ≥51% to maintain control. - Privatization/Strategic Disinvestment: - Selling ≥50% shareholding with management control transfer, as defined by DIPAM. - Historical Developments: - 1951: - First Constitution Amendment Act allowed nationalization by imposing restrictions on private industries for public interest. - 1953: - Air Corporations Act nationalized nine private airlines into Indian Airlines and Air India International. - 1991: - Interim Budget introduced disinvestment, with PM Narasimha Rao announcing shareholding reduction in government companies. - 1998–99 (Vajpayee Era): - No disinvestment in strategic sectors (e.g., railways, defense, atomic energy). - Phased disinvestment in non-strategic sectors; established Department of Disinvestment (1999), privatizing Maruti Udyog, VSNL, etc. - UPA-1 (2004–09): - No disinvestment due to Leftist coalition pressure; focus on reviving sick government companies. - UPA-2 (2009–14): - Allowed disinvestment up to 49%, retaining 51% control. Proceeds went to National Investment Fund (NIF) for bank recapitalization, metro rail, etc. - Launched CPSE-Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs). - Arguments for Disinvestment: - Private investors enhance efficiency, innovation, and autonomy. - Proceeds fund welfare schemes and reduce fiscal deficits. - Arguments Against: - Risks MNC monopolies, worker exploitation, and job losses. -
Year Policy
1951 First Amendment enabled nationalization.
1991 Disinvestment introduced in Interim Budget.
1998–99 No disinvestment in strategic sectors; phased disinvestment elsewhere.
2004–09 No disinvestment; revive sick companies.
2009–14 Up to 49% disinvestment; NIF and CPSE-ETFs.
- Disinvestment & Privatization in Modi Raj (2014–) - Methods of Disinvestment: - Initial Public Offerings (IPOs): - Converting private limited CPSEs to public companies (e.g., IRCTC, RVNL). - Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs): - CPSE-ETF, Bharat-22-ETF for diversified share sales. - Institutional Placement Programme (IPP): - Shares offered to non-retail investors (e.g., institutions). - Offer for Sale (OFS): - Shares sold to both retail and non-retail investors. - Share Buyback: - CPSEs buy back government-held shares, reducing government shareholding. - Key Actions: - Closed loss-making CPSEs (e.g., HMT Watches, Hindustan Photo Film). - 2016: - Renamed Department of Disinvestment to Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM). - Privatization Examples: - Budget 2022: - Neelanchal Ispat Nigam Limited (NINL) privatized. - Economic Survey 2023: - 10 CPSEs privatized, including HPCL, REC, Air India. - 2024: - Ferro Scrap Nigam Limited (FSNL) sold to a Japanese company for Rs. 320 crore. -
Method Example
IPO IRCTC, RVNL.
ETF CPSE-ETF, Bharat-22-ETF.
IPP Shares to institutional investors.
OFS Shares to retail/non-retail investors.
Share Buyback CPSEs buy government shares.
- New Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) Policy (2021) - Strategic Sectors: - Atomic energy, space, defense, transport, telecom, power, petroleum, coal, minerals, banking, insurance, financial services. - Policy: - Retain at least one government company; others may be merged, privatized, or closed. - Non-Strategic Sectors: - All other sectors (e.g., manufacturing, hospitality). - Policy: - All government companies to be privatized or closed. - Terminology: - NITI Aayog prefers “strategic disinvestment” or “strategic sale” over “privatization” to avoid political backlash. -
Sector Policy Examples
Strategic Retain ≥1 company; merge/privatize others. Defense, telecom, banking.
Non-Strategic Privatize/close all companies. Manufacturing, hospitality.

- Analysis: - Consistent underachievement reflects challenges like market conditions, political opposition, and valuation disputes. - National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP, 2021) - Definition: - A government initiative to monetize assets of CPSEs, National Highways, and Railways by selling, renting, or leasing land, buildings, or machinery to raise Rs. 6 lakh crore by 2025. - Objectives: - Mobilize funds for infrastructure development, reduce fiscal burden, and enhance asset efficiency. - Examples: - Leasing railway stations, toll roads, or CPSE land to private entities. - Related Topics: - National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF). - National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP) and Gati Shakti initiative (refer to Pillar 5). - National Land Monetization Corporation (NLMC, 2022) - Definition: - Established under the Finance Ministry to monetize surplus land and non-core assets of CPSEs and government departments. - Objectives: - Optimize land use, generate revenue, and support NMP goals. - Functions: - Identify, value, and monetize (sell/lease) surplus land (e.g., unused PSU land for commercial development). - Note: - Refer to Pillar 2A1 for details on Finance Ministry departments. - Minimum Dividend Rule (2024–Nov) - Policy: - Finance Ministry mandates CPSEs (e.g., ONGC) and government NBFCs (e.g., LIC, Power Finance Corp) to pay ≥30% of profits as dividends to shareholders, including the government. - Exclusions: - Public Sector Banks (e.g., SBI, PNB) not explicitly covered, as per available data. - Significance: - Ensures steady revenue for the government, supporting fiscal consolidation. - Note: - Additional conditions related to net worth apply but are not critical for memorization due to low cost-benefit for UPSC. - Capital Expenditure - Definition: - Capital expenditure involves government spending to create long-term assets or reduce liabilities, such as infrastructure projects, loan repayments, or investments in PSUs. - Notable Components: - Capital Assets: - Expenditure on buildings, vehicles, and equipment for schemes, ministries, and departments. - Debt/Equity Financing: - Investments in PSUs, foreign institutions, or loans to state/foreign governments. - Loan Principal Repayments: - Repaying principal for internal and external debts (interest payments are revenue expenditure). - Indian Development and Economic Assistance Scheme (IDEAS): - Managed by the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), provides loans to foreign nations for development projects. -
Component Details
Capital Assets Buildings, highways, hospitals, vehicles.
Debt/Equity Financing Loans to states, PSUs, foreign nations.
Loan Repayments Principal for internal/external debts.
IDEAS Loans for foreign development projects.
- State CAPEX Loans - Special Assistance to States for Capital Expenditure (CAPEX Scheme): - Introduced in 2020, provides interest-free, 50-year loans to states for capital projects (e.g., health, rural development, water supply, irrigation, power, transport, education, urban development). - Budget 2020: - Allocated ~Rs. 12,000 crore. - Budget 2025: - Increased to Rs. 1.5 lakh crore. - Linked Reforms (Budget 2023): - Scrapping old government vehicles to reduce emissions. - Urban planning reforms to improve city infrastructure. - Strengthening urban local bodies to issue municipal bonds. - Housing for policemen to enhance security infrastructure. - Constructing Unity Malls to promote regional products (refer to Pillar 3A). - Libraries and digital infrastructure for children and adolescents. - Significance: - Enhances state-level infrastructure, promotes fiscal federalism, and aligns with national development goals. - Effective Capital Expenditure - Definition: - Effective capital expenditure includes direct Union capital expenditure and grants-in-aid to states for capital projects, reflecting the total capital investment impact. - Significance: - Measures the government’s contribution to asset creation and economic growth, critical for infrastructure development and job creation. - Note: - Detailed explanation available in referenced video lectures, focusing on budget allocations and economic impact. - Capital Expenditure for a Company - Definition: - Capital expenditure by a company involves investments in income-generating assets, categorized as tangible or intangible. - Types of Assets: - Tangible Assets: - Land, buildings, vehicles, equipment, raw materials, unsold inventory. - Intangible Assets: - Patents, copyrights, brand logos, trade secrets (e.g., KFC recipe), licenses (e.g., telecom spectrum), investments in shares/bonds, client databases, accounts receivable, goodwill, website domains. - Subcategories: - Current Assets: - Short-term assets like cash, inventory. - Financial Assets: - Investments in shares, bonds. - Fixed Assets: - Long-term assets like buildings, equipment. -
Asset Type Examples
Tangible Land, buildings, vehicles, inventory.
Intangible Patents, copyrights, goodwill, licenses.
- Significance: - Capital expenditure drives company growth, innovation, and competitiveness, contributing to economic development. - Pillar 2D2: Deficits and Fiscal Policy - Introduction: - Deficits occur when government expenditure exceeds its receipts, impacting fiscal stability and economic growth. Understanding types of deficits, their financing, and related policies is crucial for assessing India’s fiscal health and compliance with the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003. - Types of Budget - Surplus Budget: - Occurs when government receipts (revenue and capital) exceed expenditure, allowing debt repayment or reserve creation. - Balanced Budget: - Receipts equal expenditure, ensuring no borrowing is required. - Deficit Budget: - Expenditure exceeds receipts, necessitating borrowing to bridge the gap. -
Budget Type Definition
Surplus Receipts > Expenditure
Balanced Receipts = Expenditure
Deficit Expenditure > Receipts
- Budget Deficit - Definition: - Excess of total expenditure (revenue and capital) over total receipts (revenue and capital). Since 1997–98, the Union Budget has ceased reporting budget deficit, focusing instead on fiscal deficit. - Example Data (Budget 2025): - Not explicitly reported due to discontinuation; fiscal deficit is now the primary metric. - Fiscal Deficit - Definition: - Excess of total expenditure over total receipts, excluding borrowings. It represents the amount the government must borrow to meet its financial obligations. - Formulas: - Tamilnadu Textbook: - Fiscal Deficit = Budget Deficit + Borrowings (internal, RBI, external). - NCERT Textbook: - Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure – (Revenue Receipts + Non-Debt Creating Capital Receipts). - Alternatively: - Difference between total expenditure and total receipts, excluding borrowings. - Note: - Sukhmoy Chakravarti Committee (1997–98) emphasized fiscal deficit as a key indicator. - Example Data (Budget 2025): - Fiscal Deficit Target: - 4.5% of GDP (as per 15th Finance Commission recommendation). -
Source Formula
Tamilnadu Textbook Budget Deficit + Borrowings
NCERT Total Expenditure – (Revenue Receipts + Non-Debt Capital Receipts)
- Gross Fiscal Deficit (GFD) vs. Net Fiscal Deficit - Gross Fiscal Deficit (GFD): - Total borrowings (internal, RBI, external). - Net Fiscal Deficit: - GFD minus net lending by the central government (e.g., loans to states or PSUs). - Note: - RBI is listed separately in formulas per NCERT, despite being domestic, for clarity in source differentiation. -
Type Definition
Gross Fiscal Deficit Total Borrowings (Internal + RBI + External)
Net Fiscal Deficit GFD – Net Lending
- Primary Deficit - Definition: - Fiscal Deficit minus interest payments on previous loans, indicating borrowing for new programs rather than servicing past debt. - Significance: - High interest payments from accumulated debt increase borrowing needs, creating a vicious cycle. Primary deficit isolates borrowing for current expenditures. - Introduced: - 1993 Budget Speech by Finance Minister Manmohan Singh. - Example Data (Budget 2025): - Primary Deficit Target: - Shifted to 0% by 2022–23, not achieved due to COVID-19. - Gross Primary Deficit (GPD) - Definition: - Gross Fiscal Deficit minus net interest liabilities. - Net Primary Deficit: - Net Fiscal Deficit minus net interest liabilities. - Note: - Formulas vary by context (A-B or B-A), but the focus is on isolating non-interest borrowing. - Revenue Deficit - Definition: - Excess of revenue expenditure (e.g., salaries, subsidies, interest payments) over revenue receipts (e.g., taxes, non-tax revenue). - Formula: - Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure – Revenue Receipts. - Significance: - High revenue deficit forces borrowing for operational expenses, reducing funds for capital expenditure (e.g., schools, hospitals), hindering human development and economic growth. -
Deficit Formula
Revenue Deficit Revenue Expenditure – Revenue Receipts
- Effective Revenue Deficit - Definition: - Revenue Deficit minus grants-in-aid to states/local bodies used for capital asset creation (e.g., panchayat buildings, disaster management infrastructure). - Introduced: - Budget 2011 by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram. - Significance: - Adjusts revenue deficit to account for productive expenditure, providing a clearer picture of non-productive borrowing. - Formula: - Effective Revenue Deficit = Revenue Deficit – Grants for Capital Assets. -
Deficit Formula
Effective Revenue Deficit Revenue Deficit – Grants for Capital Assets
- Fiscal Glide - Definition: - Gradual reduction in fiscal deficit over time to achieve economic stability without abrupt cuts. - Example: - Budget 2018: - Finance Minister Arun Jaitley aimed for a 3% fiscal deficit by 2020–21, likened to a glider descending smoothly. Temporarily relaxed in 2020 due to structural reforms (FRBM trigger). - Extra-Budgetary Resources (EBR) - Definition: - Loans raised by public sector undertakings (PSUs) or government entities, repaid from the Union Budget, often bypassing immediate fiscal deficit calculations. - Examples: - Food Corporation of India (FCI) borrowing from National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) for food subsidies (discontinued in Budget 2021). - Data (in Rs. Crore): -

2021–22 121,000
2022–23 & 2023–24 0
- Criticism: - 15th Finance Commission and Economic Survey 2020 criticized EBR for reducing transparency, as they escape media scrutiny, parliamentary debate, and audits. - Debt Composition - Amount-Wise (Economic Survey 2022, in Rs. Lakh Crore): -

- Type-Wise: - Union vs. State Debt: - Economic Survey: - States (70%), Union (30%). - Kerala Petition (Supreme Court): - States (40%), Union (60%). - Union Debt Breakdown: - Internal (94%), External (6%). - Repayment Currency: - Mostly Rupee, minimal foreign currency. - Interest Type: - Fixed (95%), Floating (5%, e.g., tied to LIBOR). - Tenure: - Mostly long-term. - Debt-to-GDP Ratio: - External Debt: - <3% of GDP. - Total Public Debt: - Declined since 2003, stable since 2011, among the lowest in G20, OECD, and BRICS. - Note: - Marketable debt - Government's dated securities (G-Sec) and Treasury Bills, issued through auctions. Investor can be easily resell it in secondary market - Majority of Govts internal debt is marketable debt. - Non-marketable debt - Special types of securities/bonds issued by Union Govt to EXIM Bank and other All India Financial Institutions (AIFI), State Govts etc. It's diOcult/sometimes not possible to re-sell such securities/bonds in the secondary market. - External Debt - Borrowed from other nations and multilateral institutions such as IMF, World Bank, ADB etc. - At present Govt of India doesn't borrow directly from the International Capital Market. - Negative Consequences Of Financing the Deficit: - Methods and Issues: -
Method Issues
Increasing Taxes May lead to tax​ evasion or reduced work motivation (Laffer Curve).
Borrowing Ricardian Equivalence, crowding out, lower sovereign ratings.
Printing Money (Monetization) Hyperinflation, reduced purchasing power.
- Ricardian Equivalence: - Theory: - High fiscal deficit → Government borrows more → At maturity (G-Sec redemption), government must repay principal + interest → This may lead to future tax hikes. - Anticipating this, rational citizens may increase savings and reduce consumption → Lower demand → Inventory buildup → Slows economic growth. - Economist David Ricardo proposed this theory: called Ricardian Equivalence Proposition (REP). - Invalid for India (Economic Survey 2021): - REP assumes people are rational, forward-looking, and understand future liabilities → Not always true in India. - Reasons for invalidity: - Citizens are not perfectly rational; decisions often influenced by emotional/personal needs (e.g., weddings, iPhones, foreign trips). - High prevalence of tax​ evasion, black​ money, and a parallel economy → Not all citizens bear the tax burden equally. - Large informal sector and financial illiteracy weaken the theoretical assumptions of REP in the Indian context. - Crowding Out Effect: - Concept: - When the government borrows heavily from households and financial institutions (LIC, EPFO, banks via SLR), less money is left for private corporate borrowers → Crowds out private investment → Slows factory expansion and job creation. - Financial Repression: - Forcing public institutions (e.g., SBI, LIC, EPFO) to buy G-Secs using depositors’ money → deprives households of optimal returns. - Example: Govt forced NABARD to buy ₹15,000 crore Swachh Bharat Mission (Gramin) bonds (10-year maturity). - Govt pressures RBI and others to pay higher dividends → reduces their operational freedom. - ES21 Observations (1950s–1990s): - Found some evidence of crowding out due to: - Very high CRR and SLR → PSBs had limited loanable funds. - Absence of large private banks. - Low earnings and savings among public. - Underdeveloped capital markets. - ES21 Findings (Post-1990): - No evidence of crowding out (1990–2019) due to structural changes: - Economic growth ↑ → household income ↑ → savings ↑ → more money available to both govt and private borrowers. - Rise in banking habits, NBFCs, mutual funds, and capital market participation. - Demographic dividend → more working population → improved financial behavior. - Implication: - If govt borrowing is for productive infrastructure (health, education, transport, etc.), it raises GDP and incomes → boosts overall savings → the 'size of the dish' increases, so both govt and private sectors get enough funds. - Thus, "crowding out" is less likely when savings are not fixed but expand with growth. - Monetization of Deficit: - When central bank prints more money to pay for government's loans → Monetizing the Deficit. - It can result in hyperinflation and ↓↓ purchasing power of currency (if supply of goods like onion, tomato is not increased sufficiently). Example: Germany after Treaty of Versailles (1919). - Therefore, Monetizing the Deficit is also called "inflating away of debt". - FRBM Act prevents monetization of deficit with following provisions: - RBI must not subscribe to G-Sec in primary market from 2006-07 onwards. - Govt shall not borrow from RBI, except for Ways and Means Advances (WMA). [Refer: Pillar#1C] - Fiscal Deficit ↑↑ = India Sovereign Rating ↓↓ -

Aaa Prime, highest quality e.g. US Treasury Bonds
Aa1 to Aa3 High grade Investment-grade upper medium
A1 Upper medium grade Investment-grade
Baa1 to Baa3 Lower medium grade India's rating in June 2020 reduced to Baa3 due to weak fiscal position and rising deficit
BA1 and lower Non-investment grade (junk) Junk status if downgraded further
- Implications of junk status for India: - Govt will need to offer higher interest on new G-Sec to attract investors. - Foreign capital may flee India. - Foreign investors may fear default by Indian govt → will sell G-Secs → capital flight. - Capital flight → Dollar strengthens, Rupee weakens. (Refer: Pillar 3) - However, ES21 said not to worry too much about it. - Countercyclical Fiscal Policy - Introduction and Historical Context: - Historically, governments have used public spending during times of economic distress to provide employment and stimulate growth. - In ancient economies, rulers invested in infrastructure like roads, canals, and public buildings during famines to create jobs. - In modern macroeconomics, this principle is institutionalized as countercyclical fiscal policy. - Definition: - A countercyclical fiscal policy involves increasing public expenditure and/or reducing taxes during economic slowdowns, and reducing spending and/or increasing taxes during economic booms. - The objective is to smoothen economic fluctuations, support aggregate demand, and maintain macroeconomic stability. - How it Works: - During Economic Slowdown (Recessionary Phase): - Government increases capital and revenue expenditure. - Objectives: - Stimulate demand through infrastructure projects. - Generate employment and raise household income. - Boost private sector confidence and investment. - Effect: Crowding-In - Increased government investment leads to complementary private sector activity. - Example: - Government constructs national highways → private sector builds logistics parks, fuel stations, hotels → more jobs and tax revenue. - During Economic Boom (Expansionary Phase): - Government reduces expenditure and increases savings. - Objectives: - Control inflationary pressures. - Accumulate fiscal buffers (surpluses) to deploy during future downturns. - Avoid overheating of the economy. - Overheating of an economy refers to a situation where economic growth is unsustainably high, leading to inflationary pressures, resource shortages, and imbalances. - Strategic Benefits: - Ensures long-term fiscal sustainability. - Enhances economic resilience to external shocks (e.g., global financial crises, pandemics). - Improves sovereign credit ratings and investor confidence. - Pro-cyclical Fiscal Policy: - Opposite of countercyclical approach. - Government increases expenditure during booms and cuts spending during slowdowns. - Consequences: - Amplifies economic volatility. - Worsens inflation during booms and unemployment during recessions. - Example: - India’s historical fiscal stance has often been pro-cyclical, as highlighted by Economic Surveys. - Real-World Examples: - Chile: - Uses a structural fiscal rule based on long-term copper prices to avoid pro-cyclicality. - United States: - Large fiscal stimulus packages during the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and COVID-19 pandemic. - India: - National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP) and PM Gati Shakti are attempts to institutionalize countercyclical investment. - Key Terminology: - Crowding-In: - When public investment encourages private sector investment. - Fiscal Multipliers: - The ratio of change in output to the change in government spending. - IRGD (Interest Rate – Growth Rate Differential) and Debt Sustainability - Concept: - IRGD measures the difference between the interest rate on government borrowing and the nominal GDP growth rate. - Indicator of whether public debt is sustainable over the medium to long term. - Formula: - Version 1: IRGD = Interest Rate – GDP Growth Rate - If IRGD is negative (e.g., 6% – 9% = –3%), it indicates strong debt sustainability. - Version 2: IRGD = GDP Growth Rate – Interest Rate - If IRGD is positive (e.g., 9% – 6% = +3%), it implies faster growth than borrowing cost → sustainable. -
IndicatorFormulaInterpretation
IRGD (Interest Rate – Growth Rate) 6% – 9% = –3% Negative IRGD is favourable; debt burden reduces over time.
GRID (Growth Rate – Interest Rate) 9% – 6% = +3% Positive GRID also indicates sustainability.
- Domar Condition of Debt Sustainability - Concept Origin: - Proposed by economist Evsey Domar in 1944. - Provides a theoretical foundation for assessing long-term debt sustainability. - Domar's Rule: - If the growth rate of nominal GDP is higher than the interest rate on public debt, then public debt as a percentage of GDP will decline over time. - Formula: - If g > r → debt-to-GDP ratio stabilizes or declines. - Where g = GDP growth rate, r = interest rate on debt. - Implications: - Countries with high GDP growth can afford higher deficits without increasing their debt burden. - Countries with low growth need to either raise taxes or cut spending to maintain fiscal stability. - Indian Scenario: - India’s nominal GDP growth post-COVID recovery has remained higher than the average cost of borrowing. - Indicates that fiscal expansion (within limits) can be sustainable if accompanied by growth-enhancing reforms. - Automatic Stabilizers - Definition: - Mechanisms in the government budget that automatically increase spending or decrease tax liability during economic slowdowns without requiring changes in tax laws or parliamentary approval. - Examples: - Income tax, corporation tax, unemployment allowance, food subsidies, and government schemes targeting the poor/lower-middle class. - Note: - Countercyclical fiscal policy/fiscal stimulus requires new budgets/laws/parliamentary approval, making them discretionary stabilizers, not automatic. - Disposable Income & Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC): - Disposable Income: - Personal income minus personal income taxes; available for consumption and saving. - MPC: - Fraction of additional disposable income spent on consumption. - Tax Multiplier: - Negative multiplier: - Increase in taxes reduces disposable income, decreasing consumption and GDP. - Autonomous Expenditure Multiplier (AEM) & Government Expenditure Multiplier: -
MultiplierMeaning
Autonomous Expenditure Multiplier (AEM)Measures change in GDP/income/output due to change in autonomous spending (e.g., food, shelter, medicine, regardless of income level)
Government Expenditure MultiplierMeasures change in GDP/income/output due to change in government expenditure
Balanced Budget MultiplierMeasures change in GDP/income/output due to equal changes in taxes and government expenditure
- Balanced Budget Multiplier (BBM): - Value: - Equals 1. - Explanation (Simplified): - GDP = Consumption (C) + Investment (I) + Government Expenditure (G) + Exports (X) - Imports (M). - If I = 0, X = 0, M = 0, then GDP = C + G. - Example: -
StageConsumption (C, ₹)Govt Expenditure (G, ₹)GDP (C+G, ₹)
Before200100300
After100 (reduced due to negative tax multiplier)200 (increased by govt expenditure)300 (unchanged)
- Reason: In a balanced budget, increased taxes reduce consumption (via negative tax multiplier), offsetting increased government spending, resulting in no net GDP change (multiplier = 1). - Effects of Budget/Fiscal Policy: - Impacts demand (consumption) and savings through changes in taxes and government spending. - Three Functions of Government Budget: -
FunctionMeaning/Example
AllocationProvides public goods not supplied by markets (e.g., national defense, police, roads, railways)
RedistributionCollects taxes from the rich to fund welfare for the poor
StabilisationIncreases spending during economic slowdowns to stabilize the economy (see counter-cyclical fiscal policy)
- Methods for Repaying Public Debt: - Redemption (Terminal Annuity): - Meaning: - Refers to the repayment of both principal and interest at regular intervals. - It concludes the debt obligation over time. - Notes: - Common in long-term borrowing arrangements. - Ensures gradual reduction in outstanding liabilities. - Sinking Fund: - Meaning: - A special fund created by the government wherein money is deposited regularly. - At the time of maturity of Government Securities (G-secs), this fund is used to repay the debt. - Significance: - Reduces pressure on budget at the time of redemption. - Enhances creditworthiness of the government. - History: - First introduced in England as a fiscal prudence measure. - Conversion / Restructuring: - Meaning: - Old debt is replaced with new debt having modified terms such as lower interest rate or longer tenure. - Example: - Lowering the interest burden by converting old high-interest debt into new low-interest debt. - Context: - 2020: - Zambia became the first African nation to default on Eurobond payments during the COVID-19 pandemic. - Experts recommended restructuring for debt sustainability. - Evergreening of Loans: - Meaning: - Taking a new loan to repay the old one. - Risks: - Creates a debt trap situation if repeated frequently. - May hide the true fiscal health of the government. - Repudiation: - Meaning: - Government refuses to acknowledge and repay its debt obligations. - Example: - After the Russian Revolution (1917), Lenin's regime repudiated the loans taken by the previous Czarist regime from Britain and France. - Implication: - Considered a poor strategy in modern economics. - Leads to loss of investor confidence and denial of future credit. - Fiscal Consolidation / Prudence - Definition: - Fiscal Consolidation refers to policies aimed at reducing government deficits and debt accumulation. - It is primarily achieved by rationalizing expenditures and improving efficiency in revenue collection. - Objectives: - Reduce fiscal deficit. - Improve macroeconomic stability. - Control inflation. - Maintain investor confidence. - Prevent sovereign credit downgrade. - Measures for Fiscal Consolidation: - Reduction in Leakages: - Targeted delivery of subsidies and welfare schemes via DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer). - Implementation through the JAM Trinity: - Jan Dhan Yojana - Aadhaar - Mobile connectivity - Reduces pilferage and corruption in welfare distribution. - Reduction in Subsidy Burden: - Deregulation of Fuel Prices: - Petrol deregulated in 2010. - Diesel deregulated in 2013. - Targeting LPG Subsidy: - Since 2016, LPG-Pahal subsidy blocked for individuals with taxable income above ₹10 lakh. - Phasing Out Kerosene Subsidy: - In 2017, Oil Ministry instructed PSU oil companies to increase subsidised kerosene price by ₹0.25 every fortnight to eventually eliminate the subsidy. - Closure of Loss-Making PSUs: - Government shut down several consistently loss-making public sector units including: - Hindustan Photo Films - HMT Bearings - HMT Chinar Watches - Tungabhadra Steel - Hindustan Cable - HMT Watches - Action began around 2014. - Privatization of Loss-Making PSUs: - Examples: - Air India (disinvestment completed in 2022). - IDBI Bank (stake sale ongoing). - Expenditure Management Commission (2014–16): - Headed by Bimal Jalan. - Mandated to recommend institutional reforms for reducing non-essential expenditure. - Suggested rationalizing subsidies and restructuring centrally sponsored schemes. - Austerity Measures: - Reduce non-essential government expenses to promote fiscal discipline. - Examples: - 2018: - West Bengal Government issued austerity directives: - Ban on flower bouquets, mementoes in public functions. - Banned official meetings in private hotels. - Restricted purchase of new cars, office renovations, air conditioning installations. - Promoted use of video conferencing over travel. - 2019: - PM’s Cabinet Committee on Investment and Growth (CCIG) directed: - 20% cut in non-essential expenses (travel, food, conferences) for Union ministries. - 2021: - Parliament canteen subsidy discontinued: - Example: - Masala dosa, earlier sold at ₹6, now sold at full market price. - Estimated savings of ₹8 crore annually. - Types of Government Actions Toward Fiscal Consolidation -

- Fiscal Stimulus - Definition: - Fiscal Stimulus refers to a government’s use of reduced taxes and/or increased public expenditure to boost economic demand and revive growth, especially during a slowdown or crisis. - It involves direct intervention by the government to increase disposable income, create employment, and restore investor and consumer confidence. - Key Mechanisms: - Tax cuts to increase consumer and business spending. - Increased government expenditure (capital and revenue). - Direct cash transfers or subsidies. - Credit guarantees and support to MSMEs. - Fiscal Stimulus by Dr. Manmohan Singh (2008) - Context: - Triggered by the Global Financial Crisis (2007–08) originating in the US subprime lending market. - India’s exports and industrial growth were adversely impacted. - Key Measures: - Reduction in excise duty and customs duty on exports. - Tax concessions to industries purchasing new commercial vehicles (to support auto sector). - Hike in Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for key crops to boost rural demand. - Outcome: - Provided short-term relief to industry and rural sector. - However, led to widened fiscal deficit in the following years. - Raised concerns in Economic Surveys regarding sustainability and efficiency of blanket stimulus. - Atma-Nirbhar Bharat Economic Stimulus Package (2020) - Context: - 2020: - COVID-19 pandemic-induced nationwide lockdown. - Economic disruption affected all sectors — from corporates to daily wage earners. - Objective: - Revive demand and supply chains. - Provide liquidity and credit access. - Promote self-reliance and structural reforms. - Launch: - Announced in May 2020 by the Prime Minister of India. - Built on 5 pillars: - Economy, Infrastructure, System, Demand, Vibrant Demography. - Components and Allocations: -

Total Stimulus (as per Govt) ₹20 lakh crore (~10% of GDP)

- Criticism and Evaluation: - Claimed 10–15% of GDP as stimulus, but much of it was in form of credit guarantees and liquidity measures (not direct fiscal spending). - Questions raised about actual fiscal push vs. accounting overlaps. - Mixed reviews on how much it revived actual demand or accelerated recovery. - Risks of Fiscal Stimulus - Overheating of the Economy: - Overheating of an economy refers to a situation where economic growth is unsustainably high, leading to inflationary pressures, resource shortages, and imbalances. - Excess stimulus in low-supply environments can trigger inflationary pressures. - Rising Fiscal Deficit: - Short-term revival may come at the cost of long-term fiscal stability. - Crowding Out: - High government borrowing can reduce availability of credit to private sector. - Global Investor Reaction: - Ratings agencies may view rising deficit negatively, impacting India’s sovereign credit rating. - Fiscal Responsibility & Budget Management Act, 2003 (FRBM Act) - Overview: - Enacted to control Union and State fiscal deficits with specific targets. - Original Targets (by 2008): - Fiscal Deficit: - 3% of GDP (Union) or GSDP (States). - Revenue Deficit: - 0% of GDP/GSDP. - Compliance: - Some states achieved targets; Union governments struggled, leading to repeated amendments to extend deadlines. - 2012 Amendment: - Replaced 0% Revenue Deficit target with 0% Effective Revenue Deficit by 2015; deadlines further extended. - Trigger Mechanism (Section 4(2)): - Allows government to exceed deficit targets by up to 0.5% of GDP/GSDP under specific conditions (per NK Singh’s FRBM Review Committee): - National security/act of war. - National calamity. - Collapse in agriculture output/farm incomes. - Significant fall in real output/GDP growth rate. - Structural reforms with unanticipated fiscal implications. - State Application: - States can exceed targets similarly but must amend their state FRBM Acts. - Example: - Budget 2020 cited structural reforms to escape FRBM targets for 2019-20 and 2020-21. - Deficit Targets and Outcomes: -
YearFiscal Deficit Target (% of GDP)Actual/Overcrossed (% of GDP)
2019-203.33.8
2020-213.03.5
- Primary Deficit Target (0% for 2020-21): - Shifted to 2022-23. - Revenue Deficit/Effective Revenue Deficit: - Abandoned as targets since 2018 amendment. - 2020 Corona Crisis: - Reduced government income and increased expenses led to unprecedented deficits. - Budget 2021 Amendment: - Fiscal Deficit: - 6.8% (2021-22), 4.5% (2025-26, per 15th Finance Commission recommendation). - Miscellaneous Concepts: - Fiscal Glide Path: - 2018: - FM Jaitley promised gradual reduction of fiscal deficit to 3% by 2020-21. - Continued by subsequent FMs; temporarily escaped in Budget 2020 via trigger mechanism. - Fiscal Profligacy: - Refers to reckless/wasteful public expenditure. - Fiscal Slippage: - Exceeding targeted fiscal deficit (e.g., crossing 3.3% of GDP). - Miscellaneous Bodies - Expenditure Management Commission (2014): - Chaired by Dr. Bimal Jalan; suggested ways to reduce fiscal deficit and subsidy bill. - Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA): - Proposed but not established; shifted to Mains handout. - Fiscal Council: - Proposed but not established; shifted to Mains handout. - Corona Ex-Gratia Yojana: - Disaster Management Act, 2005 (Section 12): - National Disaster Management Authority (chaired by PM) sets relief standards for disaster victims. - Corona Notified as Disaster: - PIL in Supreme Court demanded compensation for families of deceased. - 2021 (Oct): - SC ordered ₹50,000 per Corona death, straining government fiscal capacity. - Required Documents: - FRBM Act mandates Union Government to present with annual budget: - Macroeconomic Framework Statement: - Details GDP, growth rate, imports/exports, receipts, expenditure. - Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement: - Outlines deficit control strategies and potential deviations. - Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement: - Explains deficit management (combined with Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement in practice). - Medium-Term Expenditure Framework: - Not presented from Budget 2021-2025, citing Corona crisis. - Fiscal Indicators (Budget 2025): - Central government debt at 56% of GDP does not imply state debt is 44% (100-56); no direct linkage, and FRBM documents do not specify latest state debt as % of GDP. - NK Singh FRBM Review Panel - Background: - Budget 2016: - FM Jaitley found FRBM Act targets too rigid, limiting crisis response (e.g., farm loan waivers, unemployment allowances). - Panel formed under NK Singh to review FRBM Act. - Note: - Recommendations outdated post-Corona; not followed, hence omitted. - UPSC PYQs on NK Singh Report skipped for same reason. - Fiscal Federalism - Helping the States in Atmanirbhar - Tax Devolution and Grants: - Despite reduced tax income during Corona, Union provided tax devolution and grants to states as per Budget and Finance Commission reports. - States’ Fiscal Deficit Limits: - Constitution Article 293: - States require Union permission to borrow. - Pre-Atmanirbhar: - Net borrowing ceiling at 3% of Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP). - Post-Atmanirbhar (2020-21): - Increased to 5% of GSDP, with additional borrowing tied to reforms: -

- Notes: - GSDP: - Gross State Domestic Product. - Power Sector Reforms: - Refer to Pillar#5 (Energy Infrastructure). - 2024-25 Targets: - Not disclosed in Budget speech. - Kerala State Deficit Issue: - Context: - Union restricted Kerala from further borrowing due to high deficits; matter under Supreme Court review. - Challenges to Fiscal Federalism and Public Finance: - 1. Vertical Imbalance: - Tax powers are concentrated with the Centre, but spending responsibilities are higher at the state level. - Creates dependence of states on central transfers (Finance Commission, GST compensation, grants). - Example: - States have limited access to income tax or customs, but must fund health, education, etc. - 2. Horizontal Imbalance: - Fiscal capacity varies widely among states due to differences in resource endowment, development level. - Richer states like Maharashtra generate more revenue, while poorer states depend more on transfers. - 3. Delayed and Unpredictable Transfers: - States face uncertainty in fund flows from Centre (e.g. GST compensation delays). - Hinders planning and execution of welfare schemes and infrastructure projects. - 4. GST-related Issues: - States surrendered significant tax autonomy for GST. - Delay in GST compensation and disputes on rate-setting dilute cooperative federalism. - Centre has more control via GST Council decisions, reducing states’ fiscal flexibility. - 5. Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS): - Majority of CSS are designed and controlled by Centre. - States bear part of the cost but have limited say in design/implementation. - Reduces state autonomy and imposes strain on state finances. - 6. Borrowing Constraints: - FRBM Act limits fiscal deficit and borrowing of states. - Centre also controls external borrowing by states. - States’ ability to raise resources for development is curtailed. - 7. Non-Devolution of Cesses and Surcharges: - Cesses and surcharges collected by Centre are not shared with states. - Their rising share in gross tax revenue reduces the divisible pool for states. - Erodes the spirit of fiscal federalism. - 8. Asymmetric Federalism: - Special category status or special packages for some states leads to perceived inequities. - Creates friction among states and raises questions on fairness and uniformity. - 9. Institutional Weaknesses: - Limited role of Inter-State Council or other cooperative bodies. - Finance Commission recommendations are only advisory; implementation depends on Centre. - Need for stronger fiscal federal institutions for dispute resolution and coordination. - 10. Pandemic & Crisis-Induced Strain: - COVID-19 exposed limits of states in mobilizing resources independently. - States sought more borrowing space and timely GST dues. - Widened Centre-state fiscal gap and trust deficit. - 11. Climate Financing and New Mandates: - New responsibilities on states (climate adaptation, SDGs) without matching fiscal support. - Risk of fiscal stress and unmet development needs. - 12. Politicization of Fund Allocation: - Perception of bias in release of funds based on ruling party alignment with Centre. - Undermines federal neutrality and fiscal accountability. - Fiscal Responsibility: Freebies/Revdi Culture - Definition: - PM Modi’s term for political parties’ unsustainable freebie promises to win elections. - Criticism: - Supreme Court criticized; urged Union to act. - Note: - Developing topic; to be revisited in Mains Course. - Budget Marksmanship - Definition: - Ability to keep income and expenditure within budget targets. - Performance (2019-20): -
