- Ad-hoc Expenditure Management: - Excessive reliance on extra-budgetary resources. - Random cuts in scheme expenditure. - Delayed contractor payments, leading to substandard construction quality. - Pillar 2D3: Budget → Types of Budget and Schemes - Introduction: - Budgets in India are classified based on their purpose, funding, and expenditure types, guiding resource allocation and fiscal policy. Understanding these classifications and their management is critical for assessing government efficiency and economic impact. - Revenue vs. Capital Budget - Revenue Budget: - Covers short-term (1 year or less), non-asset-creating income and expenditure. - Includes: - Taxes, non-tax revenue (e.g., fees, dividends), and revenue expenditure (e.g., salaries, pensions, subsidies, interest payments). - Capital Budget: - Covers long-term, asset-creating income and expenditure. - Includes: - Borrowings, disinvestment proceeds, and capital expenditure (e.g., infrastructure, machinery, financial assets like bonds). -
Budget Type Nature Examples
Revenue Budget Short-term, non-asset-creating Taxes, salaries, subsidies
Capital Budget Long-term, asset-creating Borrowings, infrastructure, disinvestment
- General Budget vs. Railway Budget - Historical Context: - 1920–21: - Acworth Committee recommended a separate Railway Budget due to railways’ significant revenue contribution during British rule. - 1924: - Separation Convention formalized this practice. - Post-independence, the Railway Budget was presented before the General Budget. - Merger (2017): - Modi government merged the Railway Budget with the General Budget, based on NITI Aayog’s Bibek Debroy Committee recommendations: - No constitutional requirement for a separate budget. - Populist measures (e.g., low fares) during coalition governments eroded railway profitability. - Railway revenue became a small fraction of the General Budget, not justifying separate presentation. - Impact: - Streamlined budgeting, reduced populism, and aligned railway finances with national fiscal goals. - Plan vs. Non-Plan Expenditure Budget - Definition: - Plan Expenditure: - Linked to Five-Year Plans (e.g., development projects). - Non-Plan Expenditure: - Routine expenses (e.g., salaries, maintenance). - Discontinuation (Budget 2017): - Modi government ended the distinction due to: - No constitutional mandate. - Dissolution of the Planning Commission (2014–15). - End of the 12th Five-Year Plan (2012–17). - Impact: - Simplified budget presentation, focusing on revenue and capital classifications. - Budgeting Methods - Traditional/Line-Item Budgeting: - Focuses on listing income and expenditure without evaluating benefits (e.g., Rs. 10,000 for hospital beds). - Lacks performance measurement. - Performance Budgeting: - Ties expenditure to measurable outcomes (e.g., Rs. 50,000 for computers to achieve 30% faster RTI processing). - Enhances cost-benefit analysis and efficiency. - Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB): - Requires departments to justify all expenditure from scratch, not incrementally (e.g., reviewing education schemes’ effectiveness before reallocation). - Prevents automatic budget increases. - Sunset Budgeting: - Schemes have predefined deadlines (e.g., a subsidy for two years), ensuring automatic termination unless renewed. -
Method Description Advantage
Traditional Lists income/expenditure without outcomes Simple but lacks efficiency
Performance Ties expenditure to outcomes Improves efficiency
Zero-Based Justifies all expenditure from zero Eliminates wasteful spending
Sunset Schemes with fixed deadlines Ensures timely review
- Gender Budget - Definition: - A statement within the General Budget (since 2005) highlighting allocations for women-centric schemes, though not constitutionally mandated. - Structure (Budget 2025): - Part A: - 100% women-focused schemes (e.g., SAMBAL, SAMARTHYA under Women and Child Development Ministry) – >Rs. 1 lakh crore. - Part B: - Schemes with at least 30% allocation for women (e.g., school education) – >Rs. 3 lakh crore. - Part C (since Budget 2024–July): - Schemes with less than 30% for women (e.g., PM-KISAN, Rs. 6,000 to farmers) – >Rs. 16,000 crore. - Total: - >Rs. 4 lakh crore. - Criticism: - Three-part system (introduced in 2024) accused of data manipulation to exaggerate women-focused spending. -
Part Allocation Examples Amount (Rs. Crore)
Part A 100% for women SAMBAL, SAMARTHYA >1,00,000
Part B Min. 30% for women School education >3,00,000
Part C <30% for women PM-KISAN >16,000
- Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP) and Scheduled Castes Sub-Plan (SCSP) - Definition: - Since the 1970s, ministries must earmark funds for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) within their budgets. - Monitoring: - SCSP: - Social Justice Ministry via e-utthaan.gov.in. - TSP: - Tribal Affairs Ministry via stcmis.gov.in. - Additional Allocations: - Budget documents also include allocations for children and North Eastern Areas (not constitutionally required). - Output-Outcome Framework for Schemes - Introduced: - Budget 2017. - Purpose: - Tracks scheme outlays, outputs (deliverables), and outcomes (impact), monitored by NITI Aayog. - Example: -
Ministry/Scheme Outlay Output Outcome
MEITY/PMGDISHA Rs. 400 crore Computer training for 5 crore rural persons Increased digital literacy in rural areas
- Cash vs. Accrual Budgeting - Note: - Outdated topic, removed from recent handouts. Cash budgeting records transactions when cash changes hands; accrual budgeting records when obligations are incurred. Not relevant for Prelims. - Lapsable Funds and March Rush - Definition: - Appropriation Act allows spending from the Consolidated Fund of India within one financial year (ending March 31). Unspent funds lapse and require fresh parliamentary approval. - March Rush: - Departments rush to spend funds in March to avoid lapse, often leading to inefficient or reckless expenditure. - Mitigation (2017–18): - Finance Ministry capped fourth-quarter spending at 33% and March spending at 15% of annual budget to curb wasteful spending. - Non-Lapsable Funds - Definition: - Funds that do not lapse on March 31, usable without fresh parliamentary approval (e.g., Nirbhaya Fund for women’s safety). - Criticism: - Lax utilization; e.g., Nirbhaya Fund (2013) had ~Rs. 3,000 crore by 2018, with less than 50% utilized. - 2018: - Defence Ministry’s request for a non-lapsable modernization fund rejected due to utilization concerns. - 15th Finance Commission: - Recommended Modernisation Fund for Defence and Internal Security (MFDIS) of Rs. 2.38 lakh crore (2021–26). -
Fund Purpose Issue
Nirbhaya Fund Women’s safety Underutilization
MFDIS Defence modernization Recommended by 15th FC
- Types of Schemes - Classification: - Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS): - Shared funding between Union and States. - Central Sector Schemes: - Fully funded by the Union. - Union Territory Schemes (without legislature): - 100% Union-funded. - Management: - Disbursed and monitored via Public Financial Management System (PFMS) by Controller General of Accounts (CGA), Department of Expenditure. - Budget 2022 CSS Rationalization: - Reduced CSS from 130 to 65 to eliminate duplication and improve efficiency. - Examples: - Stopped: - National Dairy Plan-II, Dairying Through Cooperatives. - Merged: - Women and Child Development Ministry: - 19 schemes merged into Mission Shakti, Mission Vatsalya, Saksham Anganwadi, and POSHAN 2.0. - Agriculture Ministry: - 20 CSS merged into Krishionati Yojana, Integrated Scheme on Agricultural Cooperative, Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana. - Impact: - Reduced subsidy burden and fiscal deficit through better monitoring. - Ministry-Wise Highest Allocation (Budget 2025) - Note: - Specific data not provided in the prompt; typically, ministries like Defence, Agriculture, and Education receive the highest allocations (in Rs. crore). Refer to Budget 2025 documents for exact figures. - Result-Based Financing - Definition: - Shifts from input-based financing (funding inputs like materials) to result-based financing (funding tied to outcomes, e.g., 15 km road constructed daily or 80% skill trainees employed). - Budget 2023: - Adopted for select schemes to ensure accountability, with penalties for unmet targets. -
Financing Type Description Impact
Input-Based Funds inputs (e.g., materials) Lacks outcome focus
Result-Based Funds tied to outcomes Enhances accountability
- Pillar 3A: Balance of Payment (BoP) - Definition and overview: - Definition: - The Balance of Payments (BoP) is a systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world over a specific period, typically a year. - It reflects the inflow and outflow of money, influencing exchange rates and economic stability. - Currency exchange involves the conversion of one currency into another, determined by exchange rates, which are critical for international trade and financial stability. - Context: - BoP and currency exchange are pivotal for India’s economic policy, affecting trade, investment, and monetary stability. - Managed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), these elements ensure India can meet external obligations, stabilize the rupee, and foster economic growth. - Compiled by: - Reserve Bank of India (RBI), following IMF’s Balance of Payments Manual-6 (BPM6). - Reporting Currency: - US Dollars (USD) - Why US Dollar? - USD is the dominant international reserve currency. - Most global trade (especially oil, gold, etc.) is invoiced in USD. - Using a common benchmark ensures global comparability and consistency. - Principle: - Globally, BoP is always balanced (double-entry system) - one country's debit is another's credit. - Significance: - Indicates a country's economic position vis-à-vis the rest of the world. - Persistent BoP deficit can impact exchange rate, reserves, and investor confidence. - A stable BoP supports India’s economic resilience, enhances global creditworthiness, and mitigates external shocks (e.g., oil price volatility, global financial crises). - Robust foreign exchange reserves and remittances strengthen India’s position in the global economy. - India BoP Example (2018–19): - Current Account Deficit: - Amount: - -$57 billion - Meaning: - India imported more goods/services/income than it exported. - Indicates a net outflow of $57 billion from the country. - Capital Account Surplus: - Amount: - +$54 billion - Meaning: - India received net inflows of capital through: - FDI (Foreign Direct Investment) - FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investment) - ECBs (External Commercial Borrowings) - NRI deposits and other capital receipts - Indicates $54 billion came into the country. - Balanced using: - Drawdown of forex reserves - Amount covered: - $3 billion (approx.) - Nature: - Accommodating transaction - Meaning: - RBI used part of its foreign currency reserves to finance the remaining BoP gap. - Types of Transactions: - Autonomous Transactions (also called "Above the Line"): - Definition: - Transactions done for economic considerations or commercial motives. - These occur regardless of BoP condition. - Examples: - Exports, imports, FDI inflow/outflow, remittances, tourism spending, etc. - Impact: - These affect the BoP position directly, causing surplus or deficit. - Accommodating Transactions (also called "Below the Line"): - Definition: - Transactions done specifically to bridge the BoP deficit/surplus caused by autonomous flows. - Managed by: - Primarily the Central Bank (RBI in India). - Examples: - RBI selling forex reserves to bridge a current account deficit. - Borrowing from IMF to manage BoP crisis. - Purpose: - To ensure BoP always balances as per accounting rule. - RBI Classification of BoP (IMF BPM6-Aligned): - Current Account: - Goods (BoT - Balance of Trade): - Export and import of physical goods. - Services: - Software exports, tourism, shipping, consulting, etc. - Primary Income: - Wages, interest, dividends received from abroad. - Secondary Income: - Remittances from NRIs, grants, donations. - Capital & Financial Account: - FDI (Foreign Direct Investment): - Long-term investment involving management/ownership control (≥10% equity stake). - FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investment): - Investment in financial assets (stocks, bonds) without management control (<10% equity). - ECBs (External Commercial Borrowings): - Loans from foreign lenders to Indian corporates or government. - NRI Deposits: - Non-Resident Indian savings in Indian banks: - FCNR (Foreign Currency Non-Resident) - NRE (Non-Resident External) - NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) - Reserve Assets: - Foreign exchange reserves managed by RBI (includes gold, SDRs, foreign securities). - Errors and Omissions: - Balancing entry to account for discrepancies due to data gaps, lags, or unreported flows. -

- Terms of Trade (ToT): - Net Terms of Trade (NTT): - Formula: - (Value of Exports / Value of Imports) × 100 - India 2018–19: - Exports = $330B, Imports = $510B ⇒ NTT ≈ 64.7 - Interpretation: - NTT < 100 implies unfavorable ToT (imports costlier than exports). - Gross (Barter) Terms of Trade (GTT): - Formula: - (Quantity of Imports / Quantity of Exports) × 100 - India: - Typically < 100 - Example: - India exports 10M tonnes of rice, imports 5M tonnes of oil ⇒ GTT < 100 - Income Terms of Trade (ITT): - Formula: - NTT × Export Quantum Index - Significance: - Shows real purchasing power from exports. - Relevant for countries like India with high volume exports (e.g., IT). - UPSC Note: - ITT less asked in Prelims, more useful for Essay or GS3. - Benefits of International Trade: -

- Export Composition in terms of value (ES24): - Consumer goods: - 40% - Intermediate goods: - 30% - Capital goods: - 20% - Raw materials: - 10% - Types of Economies: - Closed Economy: - Minimal trade, high self-sufficiency, restricted capital flows (e.g., North Korea, trade <5% of GDP). - Open Economy: - High trade and capital flows, liberalized markets (e.g., India post-1991, trade-to-GDP ratio ~40%; Singapore, 130%). - Mixed Economy: - Balances trade openness with domestic protection (e.g., India’s partial PSU dominance and private sector growth post-1991). - Developed vs. Developing: - Developed economies (e.g., USA, Germany) have advanced infrastructure, high-value exports (e.g., machinery, tech). Developing economies (e.g., India, Vietnam) focus on agriculture, services, labor-intensive goods. -

- Circular Flow of Income & Import/Export: - Exports: - Inject foreign income into the economy, increasing household income, business revenues, and government tax collections (e.g., $208B service exports in 2018-19 boosted IT sector wages). - Imports: - Represent leakages, as domestic income is spent abroad (e.g., $510B goods imports in 2018-19 reduced domestic liquidity). - Impact: - Trade balances affect GDP, employment, and inflation. Surplus (exports > imports) stimulates growth; deficit (imports > exports) may weaken currency (e.g., INR depreciation in 2018). - Entry into International Business - Modes/Types: - Import/Export: - Direct trade of goods (e.g., India exporting basmati rice to UAE, importing crude oil from Saudi Arabia). - Contract Manufacturing: - Producing for foreign brands (e.g., Foxconn assembling iPhones in Chennai for Apple). - Outsourcing: - Delegating production/services (e.g., Godrej producing Dettol soaps for Reckitt Benckiser). - Franchising (Services): - Licensing brand and business model (e.g., McDonald’s via Westlife Foodworld in India). - Licensing (Goods): - Allowing production under brand (e.g., Pepsi via Varun Beverages for bottling). - Joint Venture: - Shared ownership (e.g., Maruti Suzuki, 56% Suzuki, 44% Indian stakeholders; Hero Honda ended 2010). - Wholly Owned Subsidiaries: - Full foreign ownership (e.g., Amazon India, 100% owned by Amazon USA). -

- FAQs - Difference between contract manufacturing, licensing, joint venture? - Contract Manufacturing: - Produces for another brand, no IP ownership (e.g., Foxconn for Apple). - Licensing: - Grants IP rights for production (e.g., Pepsi formula to bottlers). - Joint Venture: - Shared ownership/control (e.g., Maruti Suzuki). - Benefits of partnerships? - Access to capital, technology transfer, risk-sharing, market knowledge, innovation (e.g., Maruti Suzuki’s R&D from Japan). - Documents Related to Import/Export: - Quotation/Proforma Invoice: - Exporter’s offer (price, quantity, delivery date; e.g., tea exporter quoting $5/kg). - Indent/Receipt of Order: - Importer’s acceptance (e.g., UAE firm confirming tea order). - Importer-Exporter Code (IEC): - DGFT-issued license for trade (mandatory since 1993). - Certificate of Inspection: - Issued by Export Inspection Council (EIC) for quality (e.g., marine products). - Certificate of Origin: - Proves product’s origin (e.g., Darjeeling tea for EU markets). - End-User Certificate (EUC): - Ensures sensitive goods (e.g., defense equipment) aren’t resold to restricted nations. - Shipping Documents: - Bill of lading (sea), airway bill (air), packing list. - Demurrages: - Penalties for port delays (e.g., $10,000/day at Mundra Port). -

- Documents Related to Loans: - Bill of Exchange: - Definition: - Exporter’s written order to importer for payment at a future date (e.g., 90 days post-shipment). - Use: - Facilitates trade credit, often bank-guaranteed (e.g., SBI discounting exporter’s bill). - Example: - Indian textile exporter draws $100,000 bill on US importer, payable in 60 days. - Export Credit Guarantee/NIRVIC Scheme: - ECGC covers 90% of bank losses if exporter defaults (e.g., textile firm failing to repay export loan). - Letter of Credit/Undertaking: - Importer’s bank guarantees payment (e.g., HSBC issuing LoC for Nirav Modi’s diamond imports). - FAQ: - Export credit guarantee vs. letter of credit? - ECGC: - Protects exporter’s bank (e.g., SBI covering textile exporter’s default). - LoC: - Protects exporter by ensuring importer’s payment (e.g., HSBC for US buyer). -

- Pravasi Bharatiya Diwas (PBD): - Overview: - It is a government-organized event to celebrate and honor the contributions of the Indian diaspora (NRIs/PIOs) to India. - Held around January 9th, to mark the return of Mahatma Gandhi from South Africa in 1915 — seen as a symbolic date for the Indian diaspora's connection with India. - First celebrated in 2003 under PM Vajpayee (NDA-I). - Since 2015, it is held biennially (every 2 years) instead of annually. - Every edition has a theme and is hosted in a different city. - Timeline: -

Focus on trends (deficit vs. surplus). - BoP - Current Account - Imports - Oil: - Context: - India imports 85% of crude oil ($140B, 2018-19). - Goal (2015): - Reduce oil imports by 10% by 2022 via domestic production, renewables. - Outcome: - Target missed; imports rose to 88% by 2022 due to limited domestic output. - Strategy: - Enhance exploration (HELP policy), promote ethanol blending (20% target by 2025), green energy (500 GW renewable capacity by 2030). - Domestic Oil Exploration Policies: - Nodal: - Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH), Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. - Pre-1991: - Only PSUs (ONGC, Oil India) explored oil/gas. - Post-1991: - Private players (Reliance, Cairn) allowed under NELP, HELP policies. -
PeriodPolicyPlayers
Pre-1991PSU MonopolyONGC, Oil India
Post-1991NELP, HELPReliance, Cairn, ONGC
- NELP’s Primary Limitations: - New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP, 1997-2016): - Auction-based contracts for oil/gas blocks. - Issues: - Separate licenses for each hydrocarbon (oil, gas, shale). - Production-sharing contracts led to cost inflation (e.g., Reliance overstated KG Basin costs). - Reduced government revenue due to profit-sharing model. - High regulatory burden (multiple inspections, approvals). -
IssueDescriptionImpact
Separate LicensesOne license per hydrocarbonIncreased complexity
Cost InflationProducers overstated costsLower government revenue
Regulatory BurdenMultiple inspectionsDelayed projects
- HELP Policy: - Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy (2016) replaced NELP. - Features: - Single Uniform License: - Applicable to all types of hydrocarbons including oil, natural gas, shale gas, and coal bed methane (CBM). - Simplifies the regulatory framework and reduces delays. - Revenue-Sharing Model: - The government receives a fixed percentage of gross revenue from the contractor. - Replaces the earlier cost-recovery model under NELP. - Enhances transparency, reduces disputes, and ensures predictable revenue for the government. - Market and Pricing Freedom: - No control on pricing or marketing of crude oil and natural gas. - Promotes competition and enhances ease of doing business. - Open Acreage Licensing Policy (OLAP): - Companies are allowed to choose exploration blocks based on their own assessment. - No need to wait for formal bidding rounds. - Over 50 blocks awarded under this provision by 2023. - Relaxed Offshore Norms: - Reduced number of environmental and regulatory clearances for offshore exploration activities. - Encourages offshore investment and faster project implementation. - Impact: - Increased private sector participation in upstream exploration. - For example, Vedanta’s operations in Rajasthan. - Boost to domestic energy production and reduction in import dependency. - India’s Strategic Oil Reserves: - Objective: - Ensure energy security during crises (war, supply cuts). - Locations: - Visakhapatnam (1.33M tonnes), Chandikhol (1M tonnes), Padur (2.5M tonnes), Mangalore (1.5M tonnes). - Storage: - Underground rock caverns (cost-effective, secure). - Operator: - Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Ltd (ISPRL), under Ministry of Petroleum. - Capacity: - 5.33M tonnes (15 days of India’s oil needs, 2024). - Leasing Out: - Feb 2024, ISPRL leased 1M tonnes of vacant storage to private firms (e.g., ADNOC) due to funding constraints, generating revenue. -
LocationCapacity (M Tonnes)Features

Chandikhol1Odisha, operational 2020
Padur2.5Karnataka, largest
Mangalore1.5Karnataka, operational 2016
- Crude Oil Prices & OPEC: - OPEC: - Established 1961, HQ Vienna, 14 members (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Iran, Iraq; Qatar exited 2019). - Price Drivers: - Supply: - OPEC cuts (e.g., 2022 raised prices to $100/barrel), Houthi attacks (Red Sea disruptions). - Demand: - Global growth (post-COVID travel), slowdowns (2020 lockdown). - India’s Suppliers (2021): - Iraq (23%), USA (15%), Saudi Arabia (14%). - Russia-Ukraine War (2022): - War spiked prices ($120/barrel, Feb 2022); OPEC (UAE, Iraq) increased output, prices fell 17% ($100/barrel, Mar 2022); India imported discounted Russian oil (20% of imports by 2023, $30/barrel savings). - Price Cap (2022): - G7 capped Russian oil at $60/barrel; India rejected, bought at $70/barrel, saved $5B (2022-23). - G7 & EU said: - “Hey Russia, you can’t sell oil above $60 if you're using our ships, banks, insurance, etc.” - India replied: - “Cool, we won’t use your ships, banks, or insurance. We’ll make our own deals with Russia.” -
FactorPrice UpPrice DownExample
SupplyOPEC cuts, Houthi attacksOPEC increases, US shale2022: $100/barrel
DemandGlobal growth, travel surgeLockdowns, slowdown2020: -$40/barrel (WTI)
- Crude Oil - GK: - Cartel: - Definition: - An association of producers or suppliers formed to regulate supply and manipulate prices for mutual benefit. - Example/Context: - Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), especially during the 1973 oil crisis. - Sweet Crude: - Definition: - Crude oil with low sulfur content (typically less than 0.5%), making it easier and less costly to refine. - Example/Context: - Brent Crude is a prominent example of sweet crude. - Sour Crude: - Definition: - Crude oil with high sulfur content (generally above 1%), requiring complex refining processes. - Example/Context: - Commonly sourced from the Middle East. - Brent Index: - Definition: - A widely used international benchmark for pricing crude oil traded globally. - Example/Context: - Derived from North Sea oil fields; traded around $80 per barrel in 2023. - Barrel (bbl): - Definition: - The standard unit of measurement for crude oil volume in international trade. - Example/Context: - 1 barrel = 159 liters = 42 US gallons. - Fall of Crude Oil Prices in Negative: - Apr 2020: - WTI prices fell to -$40/barrel due to COVID lockdowns, storage shortages. - WTI stands for West Texas Intermediate — it's a benchmark crude oil used to set oil prices globally, especially in the U.S - India’s Impact: - Limited benefit (imports tied to Brent, not WTI; Middle East focus). - ES21: - India saved $10B on oil imports in 2020 due to low prices. - BoP - Current Account - Imports - Gold: - Context: - India 2nd largest gold consumer ($33B imports, 2018-19) after China. - Drivers (2010-14): - High inflation (8-12%), negative real interest rates, cultural demand (weddings, festivals). - Impacts: - Widens Current Account Deficit ($10B+ annually), weakens INR, encourages black​ money (unreported gold purchases). - ES24: - Gold imports rose 30% in 2023-24 due to global uncertainty, festival demand. - RBI’s 80:20 Scheme (2013-14): - Rule: - 20% of imported gold must be exported (e.g., as jewelry). - Objective: - Curb CAD, reduce INR depreciation. - Outcome: - Reduced gold imports by 10% in 2014; scheme ended as demand stabilized. - Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme (2015): - Issued by: - RBI, sold via banks, post offices. - Features: - Interest-bearing (2.5% p.a.), 8-year tenure, redeemable in cash, linked to market prices. - Objective: - Reduce physical gold imports, promote financial savings. - Impact: - ₹1.2 lakh crore issued by 2024, reduced gold imports by 5%. - Gold Monetization Scheme (2015): - Mechanism: - Deposit idle gold (min. 30g) in banks for 1-15 years; used for coins, jewelry, electronics. - Interest Rates: - Short-term (1-3 years, bank-decided), Medium-term (5-7 years, 2.25%), Long-term (12-15 years, 2.5%). -
TypeDurationInterest (%)Authority
Short-Term1-3 yearsBank-decidedBank
Medium-Term5-7 years2.25Govt

- What is GMS interest rate based on? - Interest is paid in gold terms, not rupees. - That means: - If you deposit 100 grams of gold at 2.5% annual interest, - After 1 year, your account shows 102.5 grams of gold (not ₹ equivalent). - Impact: - Low uptake (20 tonnes deposited by 2023 vs. 1000 tonnes target). - Discontinued (2025): - Mar 2025, medium/long-term deposits stopped due to high gold prices (₹90,000/10g), low participation; short-term deposits optional for banks. - Taxes on above schemes: -

- Gold-Related GK: - Mines: - Nevada (USA, 5% global output), Muruntau (Uzbekistan, 80 tonnes/year), Grasberg (Indonesia, 50 tonnes/year). - Producers: - China (400 tonnes), Australia (330 tonnes), Russia (300 tonnes), Canada, USA. - China has vast natural gold reserves and has heavily invested in mining technology. Extracts the most gold but keeps most of it. - Exporters: - Switzerland (40% of global trade), UK, USA, South Africa, Australia. - Why Switzerland is the Largest Exporter of Gold? - Gold Refining Hub: - Switzerland is not a major gold producer, but it houses four of the world's largest gold refineries. - Import and Re-export Model: - Switzerland imports large quantities of raw or semi-refined gold from countries like the USA, Africa, and even China. - Neutral Financial Reputation: - Switzerland’s historical neutrality, stable banking system, and strong logistics infrastructure make it a preferred transit and storage hub. - Central Bank Reserves: - USA (8133 tonnes), Germany (3359 tonnes), Italy (2451 tonnes), France (2436 tonnes), Russia (2298 tonnes). - Importers - India is consistently the largest importer of gold in the world. - Lab Grown Diamonds (LGD): - Natural Diamonds: - Formed in Earth’s mantle (1-3B years), costly ($2000/carat), ethical issues (deforestation, child labor in Africa). - LGD: - Produced via CVD/HPHT in labs (2-4 weeks), cheaper ($800/carat), ethical, identical properties. -

- Budget-2023: - Reduced customs duty (5% to 0%), R&D grants to IITs, seed funding for LGD startups. - Impact: - India’s LGD exports doubled to $1B (2023-24). - BoP - Current Account - Exports - GI Tag: - Geographical Indication (GI): - Identifies products with specific origin (e.g., Darjeeling tea, Banarasi saree). - Benefits: - Premium pricing (e.g., Darjeeling tea at $100/kg vs. $10/kg for regular tea), higher export revenue, cultural protection. - Governance: - WTO’s TRIPS Agreement, India’s GI Act (1999, 10-year validity, renewable). - Nodal: - World Intellectual Property Organization (global), GI Registry (Chennai, India). - Stats: - 400+ GI tags by 2024 (e.g., Alphonso mango, Basmati rice). - GI Logo: - Commerce Ministry’s logo: - “Invaluable Treasures of Incredible India,” used on GI products (e.g., Kancheepuram silk). -

- Government initiatives and various policies - Trade Policy – Stakeholder Consultation (2025): - Reform: - Mandatory stakeholder consultation (exporters, states, MSMEs) before modifying the Foreign Trade Policy (FTP). - Benefits: - Enhanced transparency via public feedback portals. - Greater accountability in policy design. - 20% faster policy implementation due to inclusive planning. - E-Governance Initiatives: - CBIC SWIFT: - Single-window interface for facilitating trade approvals. - Components include E-Sanchit (paperless documentation) and Turant Customs (facilitated clearance). - India Trade Webportal / Niryat Mitra App: - Developed by DGFT and FIEO. - Provides export schemes, market intelligence, and procedural guidance. - 10,000+ exporters onboarded (as of 2024). -

- Merchanting Trade @ GIFT City: - Definition: - Triangular trade where goods are purchased from one country and sold to another without entering Indian territory. - Example: - Singapore-origin electronics sold to UAE via India-based firm. - FTP-2023: - Recognizes and promotes merchanting activities in GIFT City IFSC. - Offers tax-free, dollar-denominated operations. - Impact: - $5 billion merchanting trade facilitated by 2024. - Export Improvement – Miscellaneous Schemes: - Export Promotion Mission (Budget 2025): - Facilitates faster working capital loans for MSMEs. - Introduces factoring for liquidity and addresses non-tariff barriers (e.g., EU’s phytosanitary standards). - ₹500 crore fund allocated. - BharatTradeNet (BTN) Portal: - Unified digital platform integrating trade documentation, logistics, and finance. - Linked with ULIP (Unified Logistics Interface Platform). - 10,000 active users (2024). - Trade Connect e-Platform: - Developed by DGFT to link Indian exporters with global buyers. - Example: - 5000 Indian exporters connected to African markets. -

- Interest Equalisation Scheme for MSME Exporters (2015): - Subsidy: - 3–5% interest subvention on export credit. - Beneficiaries include sectors like textiles, leather, and handicrafts. - Extension: - Valid till 2026. - ₹1000 crore allocated in Budget 2024. - Tax Credit for Exporters: - MEIS (Merchandise Exports from India Scheme): - 2–7% duty credit on merchandise exports. - Example: - Apparel sector eligible for 5% credit. - Status: - WTO-noncompliant. - SEIS (Service Exports from India Scheme): - 3–5% duty credit on services exports (e.g., IT sector). - Phase-Out: - Both MEIS and SEIS phased out by 2021. - RoDTEP (Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products): - Replaced MEIS to comply with WTO norms. - Refunds various embedded taxes: customs duty, VAT, mandi tax, stamp duty, electricity duty. - Covers 8000+ export products. - Disbursement: $500M to textiles sector in 2023. - Refund rates: 2–4%. -

- Port Logistics – Authorised Economic Operator (AEO): - Status: - CBIC certification for compliant exporters and logistics providers. - Example: Tata Steel holds AEO status. - Benefits: - Expedited customs clearance (24 hours vs. regular 3 days). - Fewer inspections (5% vs. 20% general cargo). - Global Alignment: - Harmonized with WCO’s SAFE Framework (Brussels). - Stats: - Over 5000 AEOs registered in India by 2024. - Krishi Udan Scheme v2.0 (2020): - Objective: - Promote air freight of perishable agricultural produce. - Example: Nagaland king chillies, Assam jackfruit. - Focus: - Special support to North-East, tribal, and hilly regions. - Offers 50% freight subsidy on select agri-exports. - Impact: - Agricultural exports grew 10% in FY 2023–24. - Assemble in India – Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme: - Sectors: - Electronics ($6B), Pharmaceuticals ($2B), Textiles ($1.5B). - Impact: - India achieved $100B electronics exports by 2024. - Example: Apple iPhones assembled in Chennai. - Objective: - Promote domestic manufacturing. - Reduce import dependence. - Export Problems - Canals in Negative News: - Red Sea Attacks (Dec 2023): - Houthi rebels disrupted 40% of global trade. - Sectoral impact: - $500M loss in India’s rice exports due to shipping delays. - Overall impact: - Estimated $10B loss to India due to increased freight, insurance, and delayed exports across sectors. - Panama Canal Drying (2023): - El Niño-induced drought cut shipping capacity by 50%. - Why? - Panama Canal depends on freshwater from artificial lakes (mainly Gatun Lake) to operate its lock system. - Each ship passing through uses over 50 million gallons of freshwater. - El Niño (2023) led to less rainfall and high evaporation, causing water levels to drop drastically. - Sectoral impact: - $200M loss to India’s textile exports. - Overall impact: - $1B export loss across multiple products due to delays and rerouting. - Strait of Hormuz: - Vital for 21% of global petroleum trade. - Iranian naval threats raised geopolitical tensions. - Impact: - $5B increase in India’s import bill due to higher crude oil prices and insurance premiums. - Global Uncertainty Harming Global Trade (ES25): - Factors: - Geopolitical conflicts (Ukraine, Palestine), US election tariffs (Trump’s 10% tariff proposal), China’s slowdown. - Impacts: - Higher capital costs (borrowing rates up 2%), increased defaults ($50B NPAs globally), reduced GDP (1% global decline), unemployment (2M jobs lost). - India: - Exports fell 5% in 2024 due to global demand slump. - Global Policy Uncertainty Consequences: - Investor Risk: - Higher risk premiums (e.g., 3% higher bond yields). - Borrowing Costs: - Interest rates up (e.g., ECB rates at 4% in 2024). - NPAs: - $10B potential defaults in India (2024). - Demand: - Global trade growth slowed to 1% (WTO, 2024). - RBI’s India-GUI Index: - Measures uncertainty via Google trends on fiscal, monetary, trade policies; 2024: 120 (100 = neutral, reflecting high uncertainty). - BoP - Capital Account - Investment - Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI): - Definition: - Foreign entity registered with SEBI, holding up to 10% equity/shares in an Indian company (different limits for corporate bonds, government securities). - History: - Previously Foreign Institutional Investors (FII) and Qualified Foreign Investors (QFI); merged into FPI in 2013 per K.M. Chandrasekhar committee. - Objective: - Profit from buying/selling shares in capital/share markets; not involved in company operations/management. - Participatory Notes (P-Notes): - Issued by FPIs to non-SEBI-registered foreign investors (see Pillar#1C: SEBI). - Hot Money: - FPI funds that quickly exit India for better returns elsewhere, weakening the Indian Rupee and Sensex. - FPI to FDI Conversion (2024 Rules): -

- Reason: - Corona-led slowdown reduced Indian company valuations; prevents Chinese takeovers at low prices to protect strategic/economic interests. - Criticism: - China claims violation of WTO norms; Australia/Germany imposed similar restrictions (see Pillar#3B: WTO). - What kind of WTO violations? - Most-Favoured Nation (MFN) Principle: - WTO’s GATS Article I and TRIMs Agreement Article 3 mandate equal treatment for all WTO members. - India's selective targeting of border-sharing countries (mainly China) is viewed as discriminatory. - Market Access Commitments: - If India has committed to opening specific sectors (e.g. telecom, IT) under GATS, denying automatic FDI entry to China could breach these commitments. - Transparency Violation: - WTO norms require timely notification of trade/FDI restrictions. - Critics argue India's abrupt rule change lacked due WTO notification. - India’s Defence: - National Security Exception: - GATS Article XIV bis allows exceptions for actions taken to protect essential national security interests. - India can cite: - Galwan Valley border clash, - Broader geopolitical tensions with China, - Risk of strategic assets being compromised. - Global Precedent: - Countries like Australia, Germany, and the USA imposed similar FDI restrictions during COVID-19. - India can argue it acted in line with global norms during a global crisis. - International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) / GIFT City - Overview: - IFSC: - Hub of financial institutions (banks, stock markets, insurance, fund managers, FinTech). - Features: - Relaxed local taxation/investment norms, 100% capital account convertibility, 0% income tax (e.g., Dubai IFSC: 50 years), DTAA with most countries, independent judiciary, quick visas. - Benefits: - Attracts international financial companies, creates jobs (e.g., for accountants, hoteliers, taxi operators). - Global Examples: - London, New York, Hong Kong, Singapore. - India’s IFSC: - Gujarat International Finance Tec (GIFT) City, near Ahmedabad (est. 2015). - Challenges: - Limited international company presence due to less attractive tax benefits compared to Singapore/Hong Kong. - Development: - 50:50 joint venture by IL&FS and Gujarat Urban Development Company Limited (GUDCL); post-IL&FS crisis, Gujarat government acquired IL&FS’s 50% share. - Budget-2019: - Companies in GIFT City IFSC: - 100% corporation tax exemption for 10 years. - 2024: - Liquor prohibition lifted in GIFT City (despite Gujarat’s state-wide ban). - Gujarat government amended rules to allow controlled liquor consumption and sale within this special zone. - IFSC Authority Act, 2019: - IFSCs (e.g., GIFT City) established under SEZ Act. - Exemptions: - Relaxed Indian tax laws, RBI (CRR, SLR, PSL), SEBI, IRDAI norms for IFSC bank branches. - IFSC Authority: - Composition: - Chairperson + 1 member each from RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA + Finance Ministry members. - Tenure: - 3 years, re-appointment possible. - Role: - Regulates financial services/products/institutions in IFSCs. - HQ: - Gandhinagar, Gujarat (2020-April). - Controversy: - Maharashtra demands HQ in Mumbai. - Budget-2023 (IFSCA): - Enhanced powers to IFSCA to reduce dual regulation with SEZ/other authorities. - Single-window IT portal for banks/NBFCs to register with IFSCA, SEZ, GSTN, RBI, SEBI, IRDAI. - Foreign University in GIFT City: - 2023: - Deakin University (Australia) established first International Branch Campus (IBC). - Regulation: - By IFSC Authority, not University Grants Commission (UGC). - Data Embassy (Budget-2023): - Definition: - Secure data storage in another country to protect against disasters/cyber-attacks. - Plan: - Encourage data embassies in GIFT City. - Variable Capital Companies (VCC) in GIFT City: - Definition: - Companies managing collective investment schemes (e.g., shares, bonds, real estate, startups, FPI in other nations). - Advantages: - More operational flexibility than mutual funds, hedge funds, REITs, LLPs, private limited companies (see Pillar#1C). - Global Prevalence: - Singapore, UK, Luxembourg. - 2021: - K.P. - Sterilization - Definition: - Sterilization is the process by which the RBI neutralizes the impact of foreign exchange interventions on the domestic money supply to prevent inflation or deflation. - Mechanism: - When RBI sells dollars to stabilize the rupee, it injects rupees into the market, increasing money supply and risking inflation. To counter this, RBI conducts Open Market Operations (OMO), selling government securities to absorb excess rupees. - Step-by-step: - Suppose rupee is depreciating sharply (e.g., ₹85 per USD). - To stabilize the rupee, RBI sells US dollars from its forex reserves in the open market (to banks, importers, etc.). - How Rupee Weakening is Stabilized by Selling Dollars? - When rupee weakens (e.g., ₹85/$ from ₹82/$), it means: - High demand for dollars, or - Low supply of dollars, or - Low demand for rupees. - Causes: - oil import bills, FPI outflow, global dollar strengthening, etc. - These market participants pay rupees to RBI in exchange for USD. - Hence, RBI gives dollars and receives rupees from buyers. - But when RBI gives dollars to the banks, those dollars become bank assets, and the equivalent rupee amount is credited back into the banking system as liquidity. - In effect, the overall rupee liquidity in the system rises. - Why Liquidity Rises: - The commercial bank now has more dollar assets it can use to settle forex deals or lend to importers. - RBI’s forex reserve (USD) is reduced, and rupees are effectively injected into the system to finance these deals. - Importers who need USD get them → pay rupees to banks → banks now have more rupees circulating. - Why this is considered "injection" of rupees: - Though RBI receives rupees, they are not retired or removed. - The transaction increases the supply of rupees in circulation because: - The buyer of USD (say, a bank) now has dollars and has passed rupees into circulation (say, paid on behalf of an importer). - This stimulates money supply and may cause inflationary pressure if not sterilized. - Example: - In 2018-19, RBI sold $3 billion to balance BoP, requiring sterilization to manage rupee liquidity. - Significance: - Prevents inflationary pressure from excess rupee circulation, ensuring monetary stability while maintaining exchange rate targets. - Mundell-Fleming Trilemma - Definition: - The Mundell-Fleming Trilemma, proposed by economists Robert Mundell and Marcus Fleming in the 1960s, states that a country cannot simultaneously achieve a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility, and an independent monetary policy. Only two of these objectives can be pursued effectively at the same time. - Application to India (2020): - During the COVID-19 pandemic, RBI prioritized exchange rate stability due to supply-demand mismatches causing potential inflation. It allowed limited capital mobility and adjusted monetary policy (e.g., lowering interest rates) to support economic recovery, illustrating the trilemma’s trade-offs. - Implications: - India’s managed float exchange rate regime balances these constraints, allowing RBI to intervene in forex markets while maintaining partial control over monetary policy. - India’s Balance of Payments Crisis (1991) - Context: - In 1991, India faced a severe BoP crisis due to a high current account deficit, inadequate capital account surplus, and depleted foreign exchange reserves, exacerbated by external shocks like the Gulf War and internal policy inefficiencies. - Causes of Disequilibrium: - Macroeconomic Imbalances: - High fiscal deficit (12.7% of GDP in 1990-91) and current account deficit (3.1% of GDP) due to excessive government spending and import reliance. - External Shocks: - Gulf War (1990-91) increased oil import costs by 60%, straining reserves as India relied on Iraq and Kuwait for oil. - Policy Constraints: - Pre-1991 Nehruvian socialist policies nationalized key sectors (e.g., banking, insurance), restricted private sector growth via Licence-Quota-Inspector Raj, and limited FDI/FPI due to fears of foreign influence, reducing export competitiveness and capital inflows. - Structural Issues: - Poor infrastructure and technological backwardness hindered export growth, leading to persistent trade deficits. - Consumerism: - Demand for imported luxury goods (e.g., Swiss watches, sports cars) increased the trade deficit. - Impact: - Foreign exchange reserves fell to $1.2 billion by January 1991, covering only three weeks of imports, risking default on external debt. - Rupee devaluation in two steps (July 1991) increased import costs, exacerbating inflation (13% in 1991-92). - India pledged 67 tonnes of gold to IMF for a $2.2 billion emergency loan, with 47 tonnes airlifted to the Bank of England and 20 tonnes to Union Bank of Switzerland. - Resolution: - The crisis prompted the New Economic Policy (LPG reforms: Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization) under Finance Minister Manmohan Singh, reducing import tariffs, devaluing the rupee, and opening the economy to FDI/FPI, fostering long-term stability. - Disequilibrium in BoP: - Definition: - When Credit (Receipts, Income, Inflows) = Debit (Payments, Outflows), BoP is in equilibrium (BoP = 0). - If not equal, BoP is in disequilibrium. - Causes of Disequilibrium: - Development Disequilibrium: - Developing or poor countries need to import more (e.g., food grains, medicines). - Imports > Exports → Adverse BoP. - Secular or Long-term Disequilibrium: - Seen in newly independent/young nations. - Such countries often have weak industrial base and heavy import dependence. - Example: - India post-independence till 1990s. - Persistent imbalance due to structural development lag. - Consumerism and Demonstration Effect: - Citizens imitate consumption patterns of developed countries. - Leads to high imports of luxury goods like Swiss watches, sports cars. - Results in adverse BoP due to non-essential import surge. - Structural Disequilibrium: - Arises due to: - Poor infrastructure (transport, electricity, ports). - Technological backwardness. - Limits export competitiveness → export stagnation → BoP stress. - Cyclical Disequilibrium: - Happens when trading partner countries are in different phases of business cycles. - E.g., one country in boom (high imports), other in recession (low exports). - Mismatch in trade, FDI, remittances → temporary BoP imbalance. - RBI’s Foreign Exchange Reserves - Definition: - Foreign exchange reserves are assets held by the RBI in foreign currencies, gold, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), and Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) with the IMF, used to stabilize the rupee, meet external obligations, and buffer economic shocks. - In what form does RBI hold these currencies? - Not as physical notes. - RBI keeps foreign reserves mainly in the form of: - Foreign government bonds (especially US Treasury securities) - Deposits with foreign central banks or commercial banks - IMF's SDR assets - Components: - Foreign Currency Assets (FCA): - Includes major currencies (e.g., US dollar, euro) and foreign government securities (e.g., US Treasury bonds). Accounts for ~87% of reserves ($616 billion in September 2024). - Gold Reserves: - Held as a hedge against inflation and economic uncertainty (695.31 metric tonnes in March 2021, with 10.4% of reserves in December 2024). - Special Drawing Rights (SDRs): - IMF-allocated reserve assets ($18.547 billion in September 2024). - Reserve Tranche Position (RTP): - India’s quota contribution to IMF, accessible as emergency credit ($4.3 billion in September 2024). - Current Status (2024-2025): - India’s forex reserves reached $704.89 billion in September 2024, the fourth largest globally after China ($3 trillion), Japan (~$1.2 trillion), and Switzerland. - Covers ~90% of external debt ($700+ billion) and over 11 months of imports, indicating robust adequacy. - Gold Repatriation (2024): - RBI moved 100 metric tonnes of gold from the Bank of England to India in 2024, reducing reliance on foreign storage due to geopolitical risks (e.g., Western sanctions on Russia in 2022). Total gold: 822 metric tonnes, with 408 tonnes now stored domestically. - Reserve Dynamics: -
Factor Reserves Increase Reserves Decrease
BoP Transactions RBI buys dollars in surplus scenarios (e.g., high FDI/FPI inflows). RBI sells dollars to cover deficits (e.g., high current account deficit).
RBI Interventions RBI buys dollars to prevent rupee appreciation, aiding exporters. RBI sells dollars to stabilize rupee during depreciation.
Valuation Effect Market value of assets (e.g., gold, euro) rises. Market value of assets falls (e.g., gold price drop in 2023).
- Significance: - Stabilizes exchange rates by enabling RBI interventions to manage rupee volatility. - Absorbs external shocks (e.g., oil price spikes, global crises like Sri Lanka’s 2022 default). - Enhances creditworthiness, attracting FDI and supporting external debt payments. - Adequacy Indicators (IMF): - Reserves to Imports Ratio: - Should cover at least 6 months of imports (India: ~11 months in 2024). - Reserves to External Debt Ratio: - Should cover short-term debt for 1 year (India: ~90% of total external debt). - Reserves to Monetary Aggregates (e.g., M3): - Ensures liquidity relative to money supply; specific thresholds vary. - Negative Implications: - Opportunity Costs: - Funds locked in reserves are unavailable for domestic priorities (e.g., health, education, infrastructure). - Imported Inflation: - Deliberate currency weakening to boost exports can increase import costs (e.g., crude oil), fueling inflation. - Neglect of Non-Tradable Sectors: - Focus on export-driven tradable sectors (e.g., IT, manufacturing) may underfund non-tradable sectors like healthcare and education, impacting social development. - Remittances and BoP Stability - Definition: - Remittances are funds sent by migrant workers to their home country, classified as unilateral transfers under the Current Account’s “invisibles.” - Role in BoP: - Remittances provide stable foreign currency inflows, narrowing trade and current account deficits, especially for import-dependent countries like India. - Unlike FDI/FPI, remittances are less volatile, offering consistent support during economic downturns (Economic Survey 2024 observation). - Relationship with Oil Prices and Exchange Rates: - Oil Prices: - Higher global oil prices increase jobs and remittances from Indian workers in oil-rich Middle Eastern countries. Conversely, falling oil prices reduce jobs and remittances. - Exchange Rates: - A weaker rupee increases the rupee value of remittances (e.g., $1,000 sent from abroad rises from ₹75,000 to ₹84,000), boosting inflows. - Significance: - India is the world’s largest recipient of remittances (~$100 billion annually), supporting BoP stability and household consumption, particularly in states like Kerala and Punjab. - Additional Insights: - Remittances are more stable than FDI/FPI, which are pro-cyclical (increase during booms, decrease during crises), making them a critical buffer for India’s BoP. - Pillar 3B2: Currency Exchange Rate - Definition & overview: - Definition: - The currency exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, determined by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market. It influences international trade, investment, and economic stability, with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) managing volatility to stabilize the Indian rupee. - Context: - Exchange rates are critical for India’s Balance of Payments (BoP), affecting export competitiveness, import costs, and foreign investment. India operates a managed float regime, balancing market forces with RBI interventions to ensure economic stability. - Key Concepts: - Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) - Definition: - Geometric weighted average of the Indian Rupee (INR)’s bilateral exchange rates against a basket of up to 36 major trading partner currencies. - Weights are assigned based on trade volume with India. - Characteristics: - Captures INR’s relative strength or weakness beyond just USD (includes Euro, Pound, Yen, Yuan, etc.). - Not adjusted for inflation → "nominal" measure. - Interpretation: - NEER ↑ → Rupee has appreciated (strengthened) against basket. - NEER ↓ → Rupee has depreciated (weakened). - Analogy: - Acts as a "report card" of INR's performance against major global currencies. - Trend (ES25, 2024): - NEER has remained stable in the 90–92 range (Index Base Year = 2015–16). - Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) - Definition: - NEER adjusted for inflation differentials between India and its trading partners, typically using Consumer Price Index (CPI). - Purpose: - Reflects INR’s true purchasing power and export competitiveness. - Interpretation: - REER > 100 → Rupee is overvalued → Indian exports become less competitive, imports become cheaper. - REER < 100 → Rupee is undervalued → Exports become cheaper, more competitive. - Example (per NCERT): - Measures the quantity of Indian goods needed to purchase a basket of foreign goods. - Trend (ES25, 2024): - REER appreciated from 103 to 107 → stronger INR in real terms. - 2018 Context: - INR weakened against USD ($1 = ₹63 → ₹74), but remained relatively stable against other currencies as per NEER/REER. - Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) - Definition: - Economic theory that suggests exchange rates should adjust so that identical goods cost the same in different countries. - Example: - If coffee costs ₹20 in India and $2 in the US → PPP exchange rate = ₹10/$ → ₹20 ÷ $2. - OECD Estimate: - Based on PPP: $1 = ₹17 (hypothetical, assumes perfect markets). - Utility: - Helps compare: - Cost of living. - Real GDP of countries. - Currency valuation over long term. - GDP Rankings (PPP basis): - 1. USA - 2. China - 3. India - 4. Japan - 5. Germany - Limitations: - Doesn’t hold in short term due to: - Tariffs, taxes, transport costs, regulatory barriers, etc. - Big Mac Index: - Informal PPP tool published by *The Economist*. - Compares price of McDonald’s Big Mac burger in different countries. - Example: - If Big Mac = $5 in US, ₹250 in India → PPP exchange rate = $1 = ₹50 → ₹250 ÷ $5. - Purpose: - Indicates whether a currency is undervalued or overvalued relative to USD. - Twin Deficit Problem - Definition: - A situation where both: - Fiscal Deficit (excess govt. expenditure over revenue), and - Current Account Deficit (CAD) (excess imports over exports) are high. - Implications: - Reflects macroeconomic vulnerability. - May lead to: - Rupee depreciation. - Inflation. - Weakening of investor confidence. - Rating downgrades. - Often cited during economic crises or periods of high oil import bills and low tax/GDP ratios. - Special Drawing Rights (SDRs): - SDR is not a currency. It’s an international reserve asset created by the IMF. - It helps countries boost their forex reserves. - Its value is based on a basket of 5 major currencies: - US Dollar (USD) - Euro (EUR) - Chinese Yuan (CNY) - Japanese Yen (JPY) - British Pound (GBP) - Countries can exchange SDRs for actual foreign currency with other IMF members. - As of 2024, India holds $18.547 billion worth of SDRs. - Quantitative Easing (QE): - Definition: - Quantitative Easing is a non-conventional monetary policy tool used by central banks (such as the US Federal Reserve) wherein the central bank creates new money (base money) to purchase government securities or other financial assets from the market, with the objective of injecting liquidity into the economy, lowering long-term interest rates, and stimulating economic activity—especially during times of recession or financial crises. - Context (2007–08 Subprime Mortgage Crisis): - The US housing market collapsed due to widespread defaults on subprime mortgage loans. - Banks and NBFCs held large volumes of toxic assets (e.g., mortgage-backed securities or MBS), causing a credit crunch. - The US Federal Reserve launched QE by printing new dollars and purchasing these toxic assets from banks to restore liquidity and confidence in the financial system. - Impact: - Injected large volumes of USD into the global financial system. - Lowered interest rates, encouraged lending, revived investment activity. - Also contributed to currency depreciation pressures in emerging markets due to capital inflows. - QE During COVID-19 (2020): - Action: - In response to the economic shock of the COVID-19 pandemic, the US Federal Reserve restarted QE by buying US government bonds and MBS in large quantities to increase money supply and ensure credit availability. - Reference: - See Pillar#1A2 (Monetary Policy tools) and Pillar#1C (Global financial environment and USD liquidity). - Impact: - While it boosted the US economy, it also caused a global credit squeeze due to strong USD demand. - Borrowers in other countries with USD-denominated loans faced higher repayment costs, impacting corporates and sovereigns dependent on foreign debt. - Federal Tapering: - Definition: - Tapering refers to the gradual rollback of the quantitative easing (QE) program by a central bank, i.e., the reduction in the pace of asset purchases, thereby slowing the infusion of new money into the economy and preparing to normalize monetary policy. - Context (2013): - The US Federal Reserve, after years of QE post-2008 crisis, announced a slowdown in its bond-buying program. - Outcome (Taper Tantrum): - Fears of USD liquidity drying up led investors to pull out capital from emerging markets (like India) and repatriate funds to the US. - Resulted in INR depreciation, stock market volatility, and bond yield spike in India and other EMEs (Emerging Market Economies). - Currency Depreciation (ES25 Data): - Definition: - Decline in a currency’s value relative to another currency in a floating exchange rate system. -

- Global Factors Affecting Exchange Rates (ES25): - USD movement, FDI/FPI capital flows, interest rates, demand for gold/crude oil, Current Account Deficit (CAD), geopolitical issues (e.g., Ukraine, Palestine). - Afghan Currency case (2023): - Key Highlights: - The Afghan Afghani (AFN) appreciated significantly in 2023 — gaining ~26% against the US dollar despite sanctions and frozen reserves. - It was among Asia’s best-performing currencies in Q3 2023, rising by ~9% in that period and ~14% year‑on‑year. - Reasons for Appreciation: - Strict currency controls imposed by the Taliban regime prevented dollarisation. - International cash aid was converted into AFN on the domestic market. - Tight control over the informal hawala system and import smuggling. - Scarcity of banknotes (new printing initiatives, withdrawal of old notes) reduced supply. - Modest export growth despite trade isolation. - Other Facts: - Managed by Da Afghanistan Bank (DAB), AFN was redenominated in 2002 and is subdivided into 100 puls (no pul coins in use). - Exchange rate ranged from ~AFN 91/USD at its weakest (early 2023) to ~AFN 69–70/USD by year-end. - RBI’s Role: - Manages exchange rate volatility through forex interventions, interest rate adjustments, and open market operations to stabilize the rupee and control imported inflation. - Significance: - Exchange rates impact trade competitiveness, import costs, and inflation. A weaker rupee boosts exports but raises import costs (e.g., crude oil), affecting India’s BoP. - Stable exchange rates enhance India’s global trade competitiveness, reduce imported inflation (e.g., from oil prices), and support financial inflows like remittances and foreign investments, aligning with goals of economic self-reliance (Atmanirbhar Bharat). - Exchange Rate Regimes: Theory - Definition: - An exchange rate regime is the set of rules governing how a country’s currency is exchanged with foreign currencies, influencing economic policy and trade. - Types of Regimes: - Fixed/Pegged Exchange Rate: - Currency value is tied to another currency (e.g., US dollar) or asset (e.g., gold), requiring central bank interventions to maintain the peg. - Floating Exchange Rate: - Currency value is determined by market forces with minimal central bank intervention (e.g., US dollar). - Managed Float: - Hybrid system where the currency fluctuates within a range, with central bank interventions to stabilize excessive volatility (India’s current regime since 1993). - Appreciation vs. Depreciation: - Appreciation: - Currency increases in value relative to others (e.g., $1 = ₹60 to ₹40), benefiting importers but hurting exporters. - Depreciation: - Currency decreases in value (e.g., $1 = ₹60 to ₹80), boosting exports but increasing import costs. -
Scenario Indian Exporter (e.g., Tea) Indian Importer (e.g., Dell Laptops)
Weaker Rupee ($1 = ₹60 → ₹80) Benefits: Higher rupee earnings from exports Loss: Higher costs for imports
Stronger Rupee ($1 = ₹60 → ₹40) Loss: Lower rupee earnings from exports Benefits: Lower costs for imports
- Foreign Exchange Market: - The market where currencies are traded, operated by Authorized Dealers (ADs) like banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), registered under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999. - ADs set different buying and selling rates (e.g., ICICI: $1 buy at ₹67.95, sell at ₹72.76) to earn profits, with transactions subject to GST based on the amount exchanged. - Runaway Inflation and Depreciation - Runaway Inflation: - Uncontrollable, rapid increase in prices of goods and services, often triggered by excessive money supply or supply chain disruptions (e.g., Zimbabwe’s hyperinflation in 2008). - Runaway Depreciation: - Rapid decline in a currency’s value relative to others (e.g., Pakistani rupee: $1 = PKR 175 in 2022 to PKR 300 in 2023), exacerbating inflation by increasing import costs. - Interlinkage: - Depreciation fuels inflation by raising import prices (e.g., oil, electronics), while inflation erodes currency value, creating a vicious cycle. - Fixed/Pegged System Challenges: Sri Lanka (2022) - Context: - Sri Lanka’s 2022 economic crisis saw its rupee collapse due to a fixed exchange rate system, high debt, and depleted forex reserves, leading to default on external debt. - Challenges: - Insufficient Reserves: - Sri Lanka’s central bank lacked adequate forex reserves to defend the pegged rate, unable to supply dollars to meet import demands. - External Shocks: - Rising oil prices and tourism collapse post-COVID increased the current account deficit, straining the peg. - Policy Failures: - Excessive borrowing and populist policies (e.g., tax cuts) led to fiscal deficits, undermining the fixed rate’s sustainability. - Outcome: - Rupee devaluation and shift to a floating regime, coupled with IMF bailout conditions, highlighted the risks of fixed systems in volatile economies. - Managed Float System Challenges - Currency Speculation: - Speculators bet on currency movements, increasing volatility. RBI counters this by buying/selling dollars to stabilize the rupee. - Interest Rate Arbitrage: - Higher interest rates in one country (e.g., US Federal Reserve’s tapering) attract capital, strengthening that currency and weakening others like the rupee. - Currency Manipulation: - Central banks may buy dollars to weaken their currency, boosting exports. The US Treasury monitors such actions, listing countries like India and China on its “watch list” for alleged lack of transparency. - Example (2024-2025): - FPI outflows from India’s stock market (October 2024) weakened the rupee to $1 = ₹86.70 by January 2025. RBI’s non-intervention reflected a shift to market-driven rates to conserve forex reserves. - Currency War and Global Dynamics - Currency War (2018): - US accused China, Russia, and Japan of deliberately weakening their currencies to gain trade advantages, making their exports cheaper. China’s Yuan was allegedly kept weak to counter US tariffs. - Mar-a-Lago Accord (2025): - Proposed by US President Trump to weaken the dollar, similar to the 1985 Plaza Accord, to boost US exports. It involves foreign central banks selling dollars from their reserves to reduce dollar strength (deal pending as of April 2025). - Reverse Currency War: - Refers to competitive currency appreciation to attract investment, though less relevant for UPSC unless highlighted in future Economic Surveys. - RBI lets Rupee depreciate (2025) - 2024-Oct: - FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) withdrew from Indian share markets. (Reason for this capital flight explained in Pillar 1C.) - Impact: - Rupee weakened sharply due to outflow of dollars. - RBI intervened by selling ~$50 billion from its forex reserves. - Objective: - To control exchange rate volatility. - 2025-Jan: - Rupee depreciated further: - from ₹85/USD to ₹86.70/USD. - RBI did not intervene this time. - Reason: - New RBI Governor’s policy stance: - Avoid wasting forex reserves in artificially defending the rupee. - Let market forces determine the rupee-dollar exchange rate. - Belief: - Trying to keep the exchange rate within a tight band is inefficient and drains resources. - Soft vs. Hard Currency - Definitions: - Hard Currency: - Stable, widely accepted currencies with low volatility (e.g., US dollar, euro, pound sterling), held as reserves by central banks. - Soft Currency: - High volatility currencies from developing nations (e.g., African, Asian currencies), less trusted globally. - Factors Affecting Soft Currency: - Customer Income: - Lower purchasing power reduces currency demand. - Forex Supply/Demand: - Scarcity of dollars increases depreciation pressure. - Interest Rate Arbitrage: - Capital flows to high-interest countries, weakening soft currencies. - Speculation: - Speculative trading exacerbates volatility. - Soft vs. Hard Dollars: - A technical concept related to US mutual fund commissions, not critical for UPSC exams. - Bad Money Drives Out Good Money (Gresham’s Law) - Gresham’s Law: - When two currencies circulate, the “bad” (less valued) currency drives out the “good” (more valued) currency, as people hoard the good currency and spend the bad. - Thiers’ Law: - Contrarily suggests good money drives out bad money, as people prefer higher-quality currency. Applicability depends on context and MCQ framing. - Modern Examples: - Zimbabwe (2008): - Hyperinflation (e.g., bread costing 10 million Zimbabwe dollars) led to preference for US dollars (good money) over local currency (bad money). - Zimbabwe Gold Coin (2022): - Introduced as Mosi-oa-Tunya ($1,800 per coin) to counter hyperinflation, but lacked foreign acceptance. - Sri Lanka (2022): - Foreigners rejected the fixed-rate Sri Lankan rupee ($1 = LKR 200) due to its perceived low value. - Historical Exchange Rate Regimes - Gold Standard (1870-1914): - Currencies were backed by gold (e.g., $1 = 14g gold, £1 = 73g gold), enabling fixed exchange rates based on gold ratios. Bimetallism (gold/silver backing) was used when gold supplies dwindled. - Collapsed during World War I due to excessive money printing beyond gold reserves. - Bretton Woods System (1946-1971): - US dollar was pegged to gold ($35 = 1 ounce), and other currencies were pegged to the dollar (e.g., ₹1 = $0.30). Managed by the IMF, it enforced devaluation for excessive money printing. - Collapsed in 1971 when the US ended gold convertibility to fund Cold War expenses, shifting to floating/managed float systems. - Currency Exchange in India: - Pre-1991: - Fixed Fiduciary System (1860s): - British India issued rupees backed by government securities (up to ₹10 crore) and gold/silver beyond that. - Proportional Reserve (1935): - RBI required 40% gold backing for currency. - Bretton Woods (1946): - Rupee pegged to the dollar, which was pegged to gold. - Minimum Reserve System (1956): - RBI mandated to hold ₹400 crore in forex/gold, with excess currency backed by government securities. - Post-1991: - Shift to managed float (1993) with minimal reserve requirements (₹115 crore gold), allowing RBI to print currency backed by assets like government securities and forex. - Liberalization of Currency Exchange - Context: - Triggered by the 1991 BoP crisis, India undertook reforms to liberalize exchange rates and boost exports. - Key Reforms: - 1991: - Rupee devalued by 18-19% to enhance export competitiveness. - 1992: - Dual exchange rate system introduced (market rate + RBI-fixed rate for importers). - 1993: - Unified managed float system adopted, discontinuing dual rates. - Outcome: - Rupee depreciation improved exports, attracted FDI, and supported economic recovery post-1991. - IMF Special Drawing Rights (SDR) - Definition: - SDR is an artificial currency created by the IMF to supplement member countries’ reserves, used to settle BoP crises or convert into other currencies. - Composition (2022): -

- Valuation: - 1 SDR = $1.40 (₹98 at $1 = ₹70). Known as “paper gold” due to its accounting nature, not backed by physical gold. - Usage: - Traded among IMF members to settle BoP deficits or converted into dollars for import payments. Additional SDR loans are available with interest. - Quota Reforms (2016-2021): - India’s IMF quota increased to 2.76% (8th largest), granting ~$17-18 billion in SDRs from the 2021 $650 billion allocation. - Governance: - Voting power is tied to quotas, exercised by India’s Finance Minister (ex-officio IMF Governor) or RBI Governor (Alternate Governor). - Challenges for India: - Indian rupee is not in the SDR basket due to limited export volume and partial capital account convertibility. - Currency Convertibility - Overview: - India uses a managed floating exchange rate system: - Currency exchange rates are determined by market forces (supply/demand), but RBI intervenes during high volatility by buying/selling USD/INR to stabilize rates. - Unrestricted conversion of INR to foreign currency would cause excessive volatility, unmanageable by RBI. - Legal Framework: - Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 (FERA): - Initial restrictions on currency convertibility. - Replaced by Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA): - Governs current convertibility rules. - RBI Restrictions on Capital Account Convertibility: - External Commercial Borrowing (ECB): - Ceiling: - $1.5 billion/year per Indian company (or equivalent in other currencies). - Example: - Even if Bank of America offers $3 billion to Reliance, only $1.5 billion can be brought to India. - Violation (e.g., via Hawala): - Enforcement Directorate (ED) takes action under FEMA. - Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI): - Limits: - Up to 5% in government securities (G-secs), 20% in corporate bonds. - Impact: - Prevents unlimited FPI inflows (e.g., Morgan Stanley cannot bring unrestricted funds). - Foreign Direct Investment (FDI): - Governed by government FDI policy; RBI controls currency conversion. - Example: - FDI prohibited in casinos. - Outcome: - Indian rupee is not fully convertible for capital account transactions, limiting unrestricted foreign investments. - Current Account Convertibility: - General Rule: - Since 1994, INR considered fully convertible for current account transactions (imports, exports, remittances, income transfers, gifts, donations). - Exception (2013-14): - RBI’s 80:20 Gold Import Rule: - Mandated 20% of imported gold be exported before jewelers/bullion dealers could convert INR to USD for next gold consignment. - Full Convertibility of Rupee: - Definition: - Unrestricted conversion of INR to foreign currency for both current and capital account transactions. - Benefits: - Attracts more FDI, leading to new factories, jobs, GDP growth. - Risks (Anti-Arguments): - East Asian Crisis (1997): - Countries (South Korea, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Philippines) allowed full capital account convertibility to attract FDI. - Result: - Bankruptcy of local companies (e.g., automobile, steel) led to panic; foreign investors sold shares/bonds, converted local currency to USD, and exited (hot money). - Outcome: - Extreme currency depreciation (e.g., $1 = 2000 to 18,000 Indonesian Rupiah), high inflation (petrol/diesel), social unrest, riots, political instability. - Central banks lacked forex reserves to manage crisis; GDP growth turned negative (e.g., Indonesia: -13.7%). - India/China avoided crisis, grew at 6-8% due to restricted convertibility. - S.S. Tarapore Committee (1997): - Recommended full Capital Account Convertibility (CAC) only when economic fundamentals are strong: - RBI forex reserves sufficient for 6 months of imports. - Fiscal deficit ≤ 3.5% of GDP. - Inflation between 3-5%. - Banks’ NPAs ≤ 5% of total assets. - Conclusion: - India not yet ready for full CAC. - RBI Reforms (2004-2019): - Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS, 2004): - Indian residents (including minors) can remit up to $250,000/year abroad for current or capital account transactions (e.g., college fees, buying shares, bonds, properties, bank accounts). - Controversy: - Panama Papers alleged Bollywood celebrities used LRS to shift money to tax-haven shell companies for tax avoidance (see black​ money Handout). - ECB Norms Relaxation: -

- Prohibited Sectors: - ECB not allowed for farmhouses, tobacco, betting, gambling, lotteries. - FEMA Rules for Overseas Investment (2022-Aug): - Indian residents cannot invest in foreign companies involved in gambling or real estate. - Wilful defaulters require No Objection Certificate (NOC) from RBI/ED for overseas financial commitments (e.g., new loans from USA). - Prepaid Forex Cards: - Description: - Prepaid cards loaded with foreign currency after paying INR to banks/NBFCs. - Example: - HDFC Hajj Umrah Card (₹2.65 lakh for 12,000 Saudi Riyal balance). - Benefits: - Eliminates need to carry physical foreign currency; used for shopping abroad. - Zero Forex Cards: - FinTech companies (e.g., Niyo Global) partner with banks to offer forex cards with 0% transaction fees (vs. standard 3-5%). - Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS): TCS on Foreign Transactions - Overview: - Under RBI’s LRS, Indian residents can remit up to $250,000 (₹2.07 crore at $1=₹83) annually overseas without RBI approval. - Remittances exceeding $250,000 require RBI approval. - Tax Collection at Source (TCS) on LRS (Effective 1/Oct/2023): - Applicability: -

- Notes: - Separate rules exist for medical trips and education loans, but basic understanding sufficient for prelims (not CA exam). - TCS Objectives: - Discourage excessive foreign shopping to reduce Current Account Deficit (CAD), supporting BoP/exchange rate stability. - Enable data surveillance on tax evaders. - Clarification: - TCS is not an additional tax; it’s adjusted against income tax liability, similar to TDS (see Pillar#2A1). - Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA), 2010: - Purpose: - Regulates foreign money inflows to prevent misuse (e.g., NGOs/universities becoming puppets of foreign entities like ISI, China, CIA). - Rules: - NGOs/universities must register with Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and submit annual reports. - Non-compliance prohibits receiving foreign donations. - FCRA on Remittances: -
