- PLI 2.0 for IT Hardware (2023) - Boss: - MeitY. - Products: - Laptops, tablets, all-in-one PCs, servers, semiconductors, integrated chips. - Benefits: - 5% incentive on incremental sales of IT hardware made in India. - Tenure: - 6 years from registration. - PLI 1.0 IT manufacturers automatically upgraded to PLI 2.0. - PLI Scheme Benefits and other information: - Reduces imports, increases exports, boosts jobs and GDP. - Economic Survey 2023: - India’s global export share (2.2% in 2021) to improve. - Mobile Sector: - ₹10 lakh crore GDP contribution, 60% export share, 2 lakh direct jobs, 6 lakh indirect jobs. - Automobiles: - 7.5 lakh jobs. - Drones: - 10,000 jobs. - Encourages MNCs (Foxconn, Wistron, Pegatron) to shift from China to India (e.g., Tata’s acquisition of Wistron’s Bengaluru factory for iPhone production). - PLI Lapsed (March 2025) - Reasons for Lapse: - Improved pharma and mobile manufacturing but failed to raise manufacturing’s GDP share from 17% to 25%. - Many firms did not start production or meet targets. - Indian steel, textiles, solar panels uncompetitive against Chinese firms globally. - Industrialists cite bureaucratic delays in subsidy release. - Electric Vehicles: FAME & PMP Schemes - Covered in Pillar #5 (Infrastructure - Transport). - Balance Sheet Deleveraging (Economic Survey 2023) - Definition: - Reducing corporate debt through loan repayment, restructuring, asset sales, or profit increases. - Progress: - Reforms (IBC Code, Bad Bank, ECLGS, PLI) facilitated deleveraging. - Indicators: - Interest Coverage Ratio: - Improved from 3 (2020) to 5 (2022). - Debt to Equity Ratio: - Reduced from 0.8 (2020) to 0.4 (2022). - Startup India (2016) - Boss: - Commerce Ministry, DPIIT. - Definition (2019): - Companies not older than 10 years, with turnover < ₹100 crore, working on innovative goods/services. - Features: - 3-year exemption from income and corporation tax. - Self-certification for EPFO and ESIC compliance. - Relaxed public procurement norms (e.g., no experience/turnover requirements). - Simplified exit norms under I&B Code (90-day liquidation). - Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS): - Provides capital to startup schemes. - Support for industry-academia partnerships, incubation, patent filing (low/zero fees). - Foreign Venture Capital Investors (FVCI): - Relaxed TDS and currency convertibility norms. - Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS, 2021): - Financial aid to 3600 startups over 4 years. - Prarambh Summit (2021): - Commerce Ministry + BIMSTEC countries for startup collaboration. - Unicorn Company - Definition: - Privately held startup valued at $1 billion or more (not listed on stock exchanges). - Origin: - Coined by Aileen Lee (2013). - Examples: - Swiggy, Byju’s, Unacademy. - Data (Jan 2022): - India (80+), China (300+), USA (400+). - Network Effect & Related Concepts - Network Effect: - A product/service becomes more valuable as more people use it (e.g., social media platforms attract more advertisers with larger user bases). - Metcalfe’s Law: - Similar to network effect, applied to telecom networks (value grows with user connections). - Free Riders: - Users benefiting from services without payment (e.g., using Starbucks’ Wi-Fi without buying coffee; tax evaders using public infrastructure). - National Policy on Electronics (NPE, 2019) - Boss: - MeitY. - Objective: - Make India a global hub for Electronics System Design and Manufacturing (ESDM). - Features: - Tax benefits, subsidies for R&D, and skill development in 5G, IoT, AI, machine learning, VR, drones, robotics, medical electronics, automotive electronics, and defense electronics. - Sovereign Patent Fund (SPF): - Government buys patents/IPR to enable MSMEs to use them without heavy royalties. - Targets (2025): - Produce 100 crore mobile handsets, export 60 crore units. - Create 1 crore jobs. - Achieve $1 trillion digital economy (Economic Survey 2023). - Electronics Development Fund (EDF, 2015) - Boss: - MeitY, managed via Canara Bank’s CANBANK Venture Capital Funds Ltd. - Features: - Fund of Funds model, investing in SEBI-registered venture capital funds for electronics startups. - Design Linked Incentive (DLI) for Semiconductors - Boss: - MeitY, implemented by C-DAC. - Features: - 4-6% subsidy for Indian companies designing semiconductors, ICs, chipsets to reduce reliance on Taiwan. - National Digital Communications Policy (2018) - Boss: - Ministry of Communications, Dept of Telecom. - Status: - Outdated for 2025-26 prelims, compressed in notes. - National Policy on Software Products (2019) - Boss: - MeitY. - Targets (2025): - 10,000 startups, 35 lakh jobs, 10% of India’s GDP. - Electronics & Startups: Notable Schemes/Portals (2022) -

- Quantum Technology (2020) - Definition: - Quantum computers use qubits, leveraging quantum mechanics for faster processing (e.g., Google’s Sycamore: 200 seconds vs. 10,000 years for conventional supercomputers). - Applications: - Computing, communications, cybersecurity. - Budget 2020: - National Mission on Quantum Technologies (5 years). - Related: - 5G, public data (Pillar #5: Communication Infrastructure). - Startup Criticism / Challenges: - High Failure Rate: - Most startups fail within the first 3–5 years due to poor product-market fit, lack of scalability, or flawed business models. - Funding Challenges: - Early-stage startups often struggle to raise capital. - Overvaluation or undervaluation may lead to investor dissatisfaction. - Equity dilution and dependency on multiple rounds can be problematic. - Regulatory and Compliance Issues: - Many startups lack clarity on regulations (e.g., data privacy, environmental norms), especially in sectors like fintech, healthcare, and ed-tech. - Compliance costs can be high for small ventures. - Talent Retention & Team Building: - Founders struggle to attract and retain skilled talent due to limited salary and benefits. - Cultural clashes and misaligned expectations can disrupt team cohesion. - Market Competition: - Intense competition from incumbents, other startups, or global players. - Copycat products and price wars can reduce margins. - Technology Risk & Obsolescence: - Rapid tech evolution may render a startup’s core offering obsolete. - Investments in R&D require balancing risk and pace. - Business Sustainability: - Many startups focus on growth over profitability. - Reliance on investor funding without focusing on unit economics can lead to unsustainable burn rates. - Governance & Ethical Concerns: - Issues like insider trading, misuse of user data, and lack of corporate governance surface as startups scale. - Founder-led decision-making without checks and balances poses risk. - Access to Market and Distribution: - Scaling beyond metro cities remains a challenge due to infrastructure or logistical constraints. - User acquisition costs can be prohibitively high. - Financial Literacy & Financial Management: - Many first-time entrepreneurs lack financial skills; poor accounting and cash-flow management are common. - Exit & Valuation Concerns: - IPO or acquisition timelines are uncertain; valuation corrections may disappoint investors. - Secondary sales or shareholder conflicts can cause governance complications. - Societal & Ethical Pushback: - Startups like food delivery, ride-sharing, and social media may face criticism over labor practices, environmental impact, and data misuse. - Startup Shutdown - Exit of Sick Industries - Definition: - Sick industries have accumulated losses exceeding net worth (assets minus liabilities). - Causes: - Internal: - Mismanagement, low worker morale, strikes. - External: - Rising energy/raw material costs, falling demand. - Historical Context: - 1985: - Sick Industrial Companies Act (PM Rajiv Gandhi) created Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) (under Finance Ministry) to identify, revive, or shut down sick industries. - Problems with BIFR (termed "Issues"): - Delayed decision-making processes. - Prolonged government support led to inefficient resource use. - Described in Economic Surveys as the “Chakravyuh challenge” (trapped in procedural delays with no clear exit). - Post-2016 (PM Modi): - Repealed Sick Industrial Companies Act; cases transferred to National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). - Process: - Wilful/incapable defaulters: - Liquidation under SARFAESI Act. - Others: - Insolvency Professional (IP) creates resolution plan within specified days; if unacceptable, liquidation follows. - Voluntary shutdown: - Startups can liquidate within 90 days under I&B Code, enhancing ease of doing business. - Pillar 4B1-ii: Manufacturing & Services - Intellectual Property Rights - Definition: - Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) are legal rights protecting creations of the mind, such as inventions, literary/artistic works, designs, symbols, and names, governed by WTO’s TRIPS Agreement (1995), covering Copyright, Trademarks, Geographical Indications, Industrial Designs, Patents, Integrated Circuits, and Trade Secrets. - Global Authority: - World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), a UN specialized agency (HQ: Geneva, Switzerland), oversees global IPR standards and initiatives. - WIPO - Key Functions - Global Innovation Index (GII): - Ranks countries based on innovation performance across seven pillars: knowledge/technology outputs, market sophistication, human capital/research, institutions, business sophistication, infrastructure, and creative outputs. - Marrakesh Treaty (2013): - Mandates nations to enhance accessibility of copyrighted books for visually challenged individuals. - India was the first to ratify, launching Sugamya Pustakalaya e-library for visually impaired, in collaboration with Daisy Forum of India (NGO) and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment’s Divyangjan Department. - - Copyright Related Bodies - Copyright Office - Boss: - Commerce Ministry (DPIIT), earlier Education Ministry. - Nature: - Statutory, quasi-judicial, full-time. - Function: - Registration of copyrights through the Registrar of Copyright. - Copyright Board - Nature: - Statutory, quasi-judicial, part-time. - Functions: - Resolves disputes related to copyright registration and fixes royalty rates for music, books, etc. - Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) - Established: - 2003, to hear appeals under Trademark Act, GI Act, Patent Act, and Copyright Act. - Abolished: - 2021, due to delays in delivering justice; appeals now filed in High Courts. - Copyright Act - Automatic Existence - Copyright exists automatically upon creation of a work, requiring no formal registration. - Registration with Copyright Office is advisable to establish ownership in legal disputes (e.g., piracy cases). - Covered Works - Original literary, software, musical, and artistic works. - Cinematographic films. - Sound recordings. -

- What Cannot Be Patented - Frivolous inventions (e.g., schoolbag, laptop bag). - Inventions harmful to public order, morality, humans, animals, plants, or environment (e.g., stone-pelting machine). - Atomic energy-related inventions. - Mere discovery of scientific principles, abstract theories, or natural substances (living/non-living). - Plant/seed varieties and their biological production processes. - Animal breeding or medical treatments for humans/animals. - New forms of known substances without enhanced efficacy. - Mere rearrangement/duplication of known devices. - Aggregation of component properties (e.g., lemon + sugar + water = juice). - Mathematical formulas, business methods, game methods (e.g., Dhoni’s helicopter shot). - Computer programs or information presentation. - Integrated circuits (protected under Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act). - Literary, dramatic, musical, artistic works, or cinema/TV shows (protected under Copyright Act). - Traditional knowledge (e.g., Ayurvedic information). - Patent: Discovery vs. Invention -
AspectDiscoveryInvention
DefinitionHighlighting an existing phenomenonCreating something novel/unique
ExampleNewton discovering gravityBell inventing the telephone
PatentableNoYes
- IPR: Biopiracy & Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) - Biopiracy: - Exploitation of traditional knowledge or genetic material without consent of local communities (e.g., neem oil for skin diseases, turmeric for wound healing). - TKDL (2001): - Boss: - CSIR (Science Ministry) and AYUSH Ministry. - Objective: - Prevent biopiracy by documenting traditional knowledge. - Features: - Digital database of over 3 lakh Indian traditional medicines/techniques (Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Sowa Rigpa, Yoga) in five languages (English, German, French, Japanese, Spanish) for patent examiners. - Impact: - Helped revoke/ban over 200 biopiracy-related patents. - Compulsory Licensing - Definition: - Government can use, manufacture, import, or sell a patented invention without the patent holder’s consent in public interest, permitted under WTO’s TRIPS Agreement. - Example (2012): - Anticancer drug Nexavar (Bayer Pharma, Germany) was priced at ₹2.5 lakh per 120 tablets. - Indian government issued compulsory license to NATCO to produce it at ₹8,880 per 120 tablets, with 6% royalty to Bayer. - Concerns: - US and EU oppose compulsory licensing, citing losses to their MNCs due to low prices and royalties. - Patent Pools - Definition: - Voluntary agreements among patent holders to pool patents, managed by a third party, licensing production to others at low cost and distributing royalties. - Context: - Proposed by Costa Rica and other developing nations for COVID-19 drugs/vaccines. - Opposition: - Pharma MNCs (US, UK) resist due to reduced monopoly and profits. - TRIPS Waiver Demand by India & South Africa - Proposal (2020): - India and South Africa sought a TRIPS waiver for COVID-19 drugs, vaccines, diagnostics, PPE, and medical technologies to enable production in developing nations. - Outcome: - Approved at 2022 WTO Geneva Summit, allowing third-world countries to use patented technologies without penalties at WIPO/WTO. - Evergreening of Patents - Definition: - Extending patent life beyond 20 years by slightly modifying the original invention to file a new patent, an unethical practice prohibited under Indian Patent Act (Section 3(d)). - Examples: - 2013: - Novartis’ blood cancer drug Glivec patent expired; Supreme Court rejected their new patent application, allowing Indian companies to produce generic versions at lower costs. - 2023: - Similar case with Johnson & Johnson’s TB drug Bedaquiline. - Utility Patents - Definition: - Recognize minor/superficial improvements to existing products (e.g., adding a speaker to a microwave to announce food readiness). - Status: - Commerce Ministry opposes amending Patent Act to allow utility patents, citing risks of exacerbating evergreening. - National IPR Policy (2016) - Boss: - Commerce Ministry. - Motto: - Creative India; Innovative India. - Features: - Shifted Copyright Office and IPAB from Education Ministry to Commerce Ministry (DPIIT). - Conducts IPR awareness for industry, police, customs, and judiciary to combat counterfeiting/piracy. - Offers new IPR courses in higher education, reduces patent fees for startups and grassroots innovators. - Digital India FutureLABS (2024) - Boss: - MeitY, implemented by C-DAC. - Objective: - Foster collaboration between government labs, startups, and large companies in mobile, IT, electronics, and automobiles. - Interim Budget 2024 - Allocates ₹1 lakh crore fund for R&D, offering 50-year interest-free loans to the private sector to scale up research and innovation. - ADITI Scheme (2024) - Boss: - Ministry of Defence, Department of Defence Production, under iDEX framework. - Features: - Up to ₹25 crore grants for startups’ R&D in defence technology. - Related Schemes: - Defence India Startup Challenge (DISC), iDEX Prime, iDEX Internship. - Budget 2025 - Startup/IPR/Manufacturing - Fund of Funds: - ₹10,000 crore for startups. - Atal Tinkering Labs: - 50,000 labs in government schools. - Focus Product Scheme: - Footwear & Leather, Toy Sector, Food Processing. - R&D Observations (Economic Survey 2025) - India ranks 6th globally in patent filings. - Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD): - ₹1,27,381 crore (2020), 0.64% of GDP. - Private sector R&D contribution: - 36% in India vs. >70% in China, Japan, South Korea, USA. - Issue: - Indian companies rely on “jugaad” mentality, underinvesting in R&D despite subsidies and tax benefits. - Notable Schemes -

- Pillar 4B1-iii: Sectors of Economy - Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) - Definition: - Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) measures how conducive a country’s regulatory environment is to starting and operating a business, assessed through various parameters like registration, taxation, and contract enforcement. - Ease of Doing Business Report - World Bank’s Doing Business Index (Discontinued 2020): - Measured business ease based on 10 parameters (e.g., registering property, getting electricity, paying taxes) using a simple average. - Discontinued in August 2020 due to allegations of data manipulation, particularly regarding China’s rank. - World Bank’s B-READY (Business-Ready) Index (2026) - Replacement for the Doing Business Index. - India’s B-READY report to be published in 2026. - Commerce Ministry (DPIIT) coordinates with World Bank for data collection. - Indian States Business Reforms Action Plan (BRAP) Ranking - Boss: - Commerce Ministry (DPIIT) with World Bank. - Parameters: - Access to information, single window system, labour, environment, etc. - 2024 Rankings: - Top: - Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh. - Worst: - Arunachal Pradesh, Telangana, Punjab, Puducherry. - Economic Freedom of the World - Boss: - Fraser Institute, Canada. - Measures individuals’ ability to make economic decisions (e.g., starting a business, accessing loans, government regulations). - Note: - Low-profile report, not critical for memorization. - Budget-2023 Announcements - Vivad se Vishwas I – Relief for MSMEs - Context: - MSMEs failing to complete government/CPSE contracts during COVID (Feb 19, 2020 - Mar 31, 2022) had bid security/earnest money/performance security forfeited. - Budget-2023: - 95% of forfeited amount to be refunded to MSMEs. - Vivad se Vishwas II – Settling Contractual Disputes - Context: - Contractual disputes (e.g., NHAI/ONGC penalties on contractors) pending in courts. - Budget-2023: - Offers voluntary out-of-court settlement via arbitrator/mediator, targeting 500 cases worth ₹1 trillion. - PAN Card as Common Business Identifier - Objective: - Use PAN as a unified identifier for businesses across platforms (e.g., GSTIN, LIN, CIN, Udyam number). - Benefits: - Simplifies login/registration on government portals. - Enhances tax authorities’ ability to detect fraud/tax​ evasion. - Aids bankers in assessing financial capacity for loans. - Unified Filing Process - Context: - Companies submit multiple compliance documents to various ministries (Labour, Corporate Affairs, Commerce, MSME). - Budget-2023: - Proposes a common portal for unified filing to reduce time/effort. - EoDB for MSME: GSTN gets AA Status - Account Aggregator (AA): - NBFC that collects/provides financial data with client consent. - RBI granted AA status to GST Network (GSTN). - Benefit: - MSMEs can share GST tax data to secure loans more easily from banks/NBFCs. - One-Stop Solution for Identity and Address Updating - Context: - Personal data stored across multiple government platforms (e.g., driving license, property tax, scholarship portals). - Budget-2023: - Proposes a single portal using Aadhaar and DigiLocker for updates. - DigiLocker: - MeitY’s app/portal (2015) for storing documents (e.g., marksheets, licenses). - Training of Civil Servants in Mission Karmayogi - Mission Karmayogi (2020): - Ministry of Personnel’s training/skill development program for civil servants. - iGOT Karmayogi: - Online training portal for Union/State/UT civil servants. - Budget-2023: - Training to make civil servants more citizen- and business-friendly. - EoDB 2.0 in Budget-2022 - EoDB 1.0: - Removed ~1,500 laws and 25,000 compliances. - EoDB 2.0 Focus: - Trust-based governance. - Digitization of manual processes. - Integration of Central and State systems via IT bridges. - Citizen-centric services. - Removal of overlapping compliances. - Crowdsourcing suggestions for reforms. - Pro-Business vs Pro-Crony (Economic Survey 2020, Vol 1, Ch 3) - Crony Capitalism: - Business success driven by political-business nexus rather than hard work or innovation. - Economic Harm: - Leads to rent-seeking, high prices, and reduced wealth creation as profits are used for debauchery or further cronyism rather than R&D. - Cronyism: - David Ricardo & Rent Seeking - Example: - Mobile company pays bribes for spectrum/license, raising consumer prices to recover costs, profits, and bribes. - Other Examples: - High coal-based electricity prices, toll fees, private hospital/school fees. - Ricardo’s Term: - Rent-seeking behavior, extracting abnormal profits at public expense without contributing to wealth creation. - Enforcing Contracts Portal (2021-June) - Boss: - Department of Justice (Ministry of Law). - Features: - Provides case statistics for commercial/civil courts in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata. - Offers access to commercial laws for reference. - International Arbitration Centre @GIFT City (Budget-2022) - Arbitration: - Out-of-court dispute resolution using an impartial third party. - Context: - Foreign companies vs. Indian entities currently use arbitration centers in Singapore, Netherlands, etc. - Budget-2022: - Establishes an International Arbitration Centre in GIFT City for timely dispute resolution under international jurisprudence. - Transparency International - Corruption Perceptions Index - Boss: - Transparency International (1993, HQ: Berlin, Germany), a global anti-corruption NGO. - 2021 Rankings: - #1 (Denmark, Finland), #180 (South Sudan), India #85. - India’s Rank Trend: - 2018 (86), 2019 (80), 2020 (86), 2021 (85), 2024 (93/180). - Recommendations: - Address conflicts of interest and preferential treatment. - Regulate electoral financing and election integrity. - Control lobbying activities. - Labour Reforms - Context: - Multiple Central labour laws (e.g., Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Wages Act 1936, Payment of Bonus Act 1965, Equal Remuneration Act 1976) require extensive compliance and inspections, hindering EoDB. - - Pre-Code Reforms: - Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017: - Applies to factories, mines, plantations, shops. - Maternity leave: - 26 weeks (1st/2nd child), 12 weeks (3rd child onwards or adoption/surrogacy). - Creche required for 50+ workers; minimum 4 daily visits allowed for mothers. - Option for work-from-home post-maternity leave. - Written notification of rights to female workers. - Payment of Wages (Amendment) Act, 2017: - Allows salary payment via cheque/NEFT, reducing cash transactions. - Child Labour (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016: - Bans employment of children under 14, except in TV/cinema/sports (not circus) or non-hazardous family enterprises after school hours. - Adolescents (14-18) allowed in non-hazardous work. - Criticism: - Removal of certain occupations (e.g., chemical mixing, battery recycling) from hazardous list may lead to adolescent exploitation. - Apprentices (Amendment) Act, 2014: - Relaxes 1961 Act’s strict rules (e.g., stipend, holidays, overtime set by employer, not government). - Violations result in fines, not jail. - Maternity Leave for Construction Workers (2024) - Boss: - Ministries of Road Transport and Highways, Housing and Urban Affairs. - Provisions: -

- Additional facilities: - Latrines, urinals, washing areas, creches, accommodation. - Digital wage payments mandated. - Fixed Term Employment (2018) - Removed from 2025-26 syllabus as outdated. - Minimum Wages - Definition (ILO): - Minimum remuneration an employer is legally required to pay, expressed per day/hour. - Origin: - Concept dates to Arthashastra (2nd Century BCE); British-era Payment of Wages Act 1936 ensured timely payments but lacked minimum wage provisions. - Arthashastra (2nd century BCE, authored by Kautilya / Chanakya) does mention the concept of minimum wages, though not in modern legal terms. - Constitutional Mandate (DPSP): - Article 43: - Secure living wage and decent standard of life. - Article 39: - Adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work for men and women. - Minimum Wage Reform: Anoop Satpathy Committee (2019) - Set up by: Ministry of Labour and Employment - Objective: - To recommend a scientific methodology for fixing the National Minimum Wage (NMW) across India, replacing outdated norms. - Key Recommendations: - Proposed a national minimum wage of ₹375/day (₹9,750/month) for a standard household (3 consumption units). - Suggested additional housing allowance of ₹55/day for urban workers. - Recommended 5 different regional minimum wages based on food, clothing, housing, fuel, and education needs. - Emphasized regular adjustment based on inflation (CPI-IW). - Significance: - Aimed to ensure minimum living standards, reduce wage disparity, and bring uniformity across states. - Minimum Wages - Code on Wages 2019 - Objective: - Merges Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Wages Act 1936, Payment of Bonus Act 1965, Equal Remuneration Act 1976. - Floor Wage: - Definition: - A minimum benchmark wage set by the Central Government below which no state can fix its minimum wage, though they may set it higher. - Legal Basis: - Introduced under the Code on Wages, 2019. - Purpose: - To bring uniformity in wage structures across states. - Prevents extreme wage disparity and protects low-income workers in weaker states. - Determination: - Based on living standards, cost of living, geographical conditions, and other socio-economic factors. - Difference from Minimum Wage: - Floor Wage is a *national threshold* fixed by the Centre. - Minimum Wage is fixed by both Centre and State for different skill levels, industries, or locations—but must not fall *below* the floor wage. - As of 2023: - Government had not yet formally notified a floor wage. - Domains: -
DomainSectors CoveredFeatures
Union GovernmentAir transport, railways, ports, mines, oil fields, telecom, banking, insurance, Central Government jobs, CPSEs, autonomous bodiesCentral Advisory Body sets floor wages based on minimum living standards

- Update Frequency: - Revised every 5 years or less. - Salient Features - Overtime Pay: - Minimum 2x normal wages for extra hours. - Payment Frequency: - Daily, weekly, fortnightly, or monthly via cash, cheque, or e-transfer. - Deductions: - Allowed for penalties, absence, rent, loans. - Right to Bonus: - 8.33% of wages or ₹100 (higher) for workers earning <3x specified amount, capped at 20% of annual wages. - Gender Discrimination: - Prohibited; equal pay for equal work. - Penalty: - Up to 3 months jail, ₹1 lakh fine. - Status: - Passed by Parliament, but implementation delayed due to COVID (rules and minimum wages pending notification). - Factories Act Reforms - Factories Act 1881: - Focused on child labour prevention. - Factories Act 1948: - Regulates worker safety, health, welfare. - Definition: - Premises with manufacturing using power and 10+ workers (or 20+ without power) in the last 12 months. - Requirements: - Washrooms, drinking water, spittoons, creches, etc. - Restrictions: - No women in night shifts or near dangerous machinery; mandatory inspections with risk of arrests for violations. - Factories (Amendment) Bill, 2014 - Proposals: - Redefines factory (20+ workers) to exempt smaller units. - Allows women in night shifts and near machinery with safety measures. - Replaces arrests with fines for minor violations. - Status: - Pending in Parliament; states like Rajasthan amended state laws (labour in Concurrent List). - Industrial Disputes Act 1947, 2010 - Provisions: - Factories with 100+ workers require state government approval for retrenchment. - Advance notice needed for changes in work hours, holidays; workers can complain to Labour Ministry. - Issues: - Hinders EoDB by restricting adoption of labour-saving technologies or emergency work hour increases. - Reforms: - 2010 Amendment: - Technical relaxations by Union. - State Reforms: - Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh relaxed norms to attract investment (labour in Concurrent List). - Economic Survey 2019: - Rajasthan progressed in employment and investment; inflexible states (West Bengal, Bihar, Kerala) lag in jobs, capital, and wages due to low productivity. - Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Bill, 2022 - Amends 42 Acts to reduce compliance and decriminalize offenses. - Examples: -

Investment Friendliness Index for States. - Shram Suvidha Portal (2014) - Boss: - Labour Ministry. - Features: - Labour inspectors upload reports within 48 hours, reducing bribery and record tampering. - Online registration/payment for ESIC/EPFO. - Compliance document uploads for labour/factory acts. - Samadhan Portal: - Handles industrial disputes between workers, trade unions, and industrialists. - Corona: Suspension of Labour Laws - Context: - States like UP, Gujarat, MP suspended labour laws for 3 years (or 1,000 days for new factories). - Provisions: - Small factories exempt from inspections. - Increased work hours without clear overtime wage guidelines. - Implications (Trade Union Concerns): - Reduced investment in worker safety/amenities (washrooms, creches). - Forced extra hours without adequate overtime/bonus. - Arbitrary hiring/firing without recourse due to suspended laws. - Undermines EPFO, ESIC, bonus, job/social security rights. - Corona Suspension Labour Laws: Union Says No - Constitutional Context: - Labour in Concurrent List (7th Schedule). - Article 254(1): - Parliament’s laws prevail over state laws. - Article 254(2): - State law amendments require President’s assent (guided by PM). - Union Response: - Rejected state suspensions (e.g., UP’s 3-year, MP’s 1,000-day suspensions). - Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979: - Union may enforce to protect migrant workers if needed. - Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979 - Contractor Obligations: - Regular wage payments. - Equal pay for equal work (gender-neutral). - Suitable work conditions. - Residential accommodation. - Free medical facilities. - Protective clothing. - Reporting fatal accidents to government. - Banking as Public Utility Service - Industrial Disputes Act: - Statutory right to strike, except for government employees and public utility services (e.g., electricity, telecom). - Implications of Strikes in Public Utility: - Deemed illegal; workers can be dismissed or required to pay compensation. - 2020-April: - Banking declared a public utility service to prevent strike-related delays in MSME loans and economic revival. - Building Homes & Running Shops - Model Shops & Establishments Bill, 2016 - Boss: - Union Government (circulated to States/UTs). - Subject: - State List; each state has its own Shops and Establishments Act for wages, hours, holidays. - Features: - Allows 24/7, 365-day shop/mall operations. - Permits women in night shifts with safety measures. - Adoption: - Gujarat adopted in 2019 with modifications. - Benefits: - EoDB, overtime pay, increased employment (day/night shifts). - Real Estate Regulation & Development Act (RERA), 2016 - Boss: - Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation. - Subject: - Land (State List), but contracts (Concurrent List). - Features: - Establishes State-level Real Estate Regulatory Authorities (RERAs) and Appellate Tribunals. - Mandatory project registration on RERA website (includes facilities like fire systems, sewage plants). - No advertisements or payments before registration. - Real estate agents must register with RERAs. - Project details published online for buyer verification/complaints. - Separate bank account for buyer payments. - Builder liable for interest on buyer’s loans if project delayed; RERA can order refunds or project completion. - Free repairs for defects within 5 years. - Penalties: - Up to 3 years jail + fines. - Benefits: - Online registration reduces bribery. - Enhances consumer protection. - Separate accounts curb tax​ evasion and malpractices (e.g., selling same property twice). - Challenges: - Increased compliance costs may raise home prices. - Pre-RERA projects face legal loopholes for justice. - Some states (non-BJP) lack RERA chairpersons/websites. - Real Estate GRETI Index - Boss: - JLL and LaSalle (foreign companies). - India’s Rank: - 31st out of 89 countries (2024). - Pillar 4B2-i: Sectors of Economy - Manufacturing, Textile, MSME - Sectors of Economy - Manufacturing, Textile & MSME - Overview: - Focuses on key sectors contributing to India's economy, with emphasis on textiles and Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). - Textiles Ministry - Organizations: - CPSEs: - Cotton Corporation of India, Jute Corporation of India, National Textile Corporation Ltd. - Attached Offices: - Development Commissioners for Handloom and Handicrafts. - Statutory Bodies: - National Jute Board, Central Silk Board, National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT). - Others: - Autonomous bodies, export promotion councils, research associations, advisory boards for apparel, textile, wool, silk, carpet. - Industry Significance (ES25): - Indian textile industry: - 2nd largest manufacturer and exporter globally. - Employment: - 4.5 crore direct jobs, 6 crore in allied sectors. - Contribution: - 11% of India’s manufacturing GDP. - Rankings: - #2 in cotton, silk, man-made fiber production; #6 in textile/apparel exports. - Notable Schemes/Initiatives - Jute Packaging Material (JPM) Act, 1987: - Mandates 100% foodgrains and 20% sugar be packed in jute bags to support jute industry against plastic competition. - Technical Textiles: - Includes fishing nets, bulletproof jackets, surgical gowns, parachutes. - Applications: - Automobile, aerospace, architecture, occupational therapy, sports, apparel. - Budget-2020: - National Technical Textiles Mission (2020-21 to 2023-24) to reduce $16 billion import dependency. - Project India Size: - Develops India-specific size charts for shoes, shirts, pants, replacing UK/US standards. - India Handloom Brand Logo (2015): - Certifies handmade products (e.g., saris, bedsheets) for quality, zero defects, eco-friendliness, and traditional design. - Application: - Online via Textile Ministry’s Development Commissioner for Handloom. - Pehchan Cards (2016): - Aadhaar-linked cards for handicraft artisans to access scheme benefits. - e-Cocoon App: - Mobile app for quality certification in silkworm seed sector. - E-Dhaga App & BunkarMitra Helpline: - Advises weavers on business operations. - PM Mega Investment Textiles Parks (PM-MITRA, Budget-2021): - Seven parks with 30% Union subsidy, 1,000-acre land from states. - Locations: - Virudhunagar (TN), Warangal (TS), Kalaburagi (KA), Amravati (MH), Navsari (GJ), Dhar (MP), Lucknow (UP). - 5F Formula: - Farm → Fiber → Factory → Fashion → Foreign Export. - Central Sector Schemes (100% Union-funded): - National Handloom Development Programme: - Weavers Mudra Scheme (interest subvention, credit guarantee for loans). - Amended Technology Upgradation Funds Scheme (ATUFS): - Funds for machinery upgrades (also Power Tex for powerlooms). - Ambedkar Hasthshilp Vikas Yojana & Handloom Weaver Comprehensive Welfare Scheme (HWCWS): - Training, skill development, marketing support. - Pradhan Mantri Paridhan Rojgar Protsahan Yojana (2016): - Textile Ministry pays employer’s EPFO contribution for 3 years to boost formal jobs. - Samarth Scheme (2017): - Capacity building via training by MSDE-hired institutes, funded by Textile Ministry. - Rebate of State and Central Taxes and Levies (RoSCTL, 2019): - Input Tax Credit for textile/garment exporters until March 31, 2024 (similar to RODTEP, Pillar 3A). - Kasturi Cotton Bharat (2022) - Boss: - Textile Ministry, Cotton Corporation of India, trade bodies, industry. - Features: - Certifies high-quality Indian cotton with brand logo. - Uses blockchain and QR codes for supply chain monitoring. - Textile Problems (ES25) - Complex, non-localized value chain (e.g., cotton from Gujarat/MP/Andhra to Tamil Nadu for yarn, then Maharashtra/Gujarat for fabric). - Export competition from China, Vietnam. - Trade barriers: - US tariffs, EU’s climate/deforestation rules (Ref: Pillar 3C). - Man-Made Fibers (MMF): - India produces <10% of global output, facing competition from Vietnam, China, Taiwan. - Leather Industry - Tamil Nadu (ES25) - Tamil Nadu excels in leather and non-leather footwear, employing 2 lakh people. - Hosts: - Central Leather Research Institute, Council for Leather Exports, Footwear Design and Development Institute. - Manufacturing & Services - MSME Ministry - Organizations: - Government Company: - National Small Industries Corporation Limited (NSIC), an NBFC under RBI, founded 1955, HQ: Delhi, aids MSME loan access. - Attached Office: - Development Commissioner (MSME). - Statutory Bodies: - Khadi & Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Coir Board. - MSME - Truckload of Schemes/Initiatives - PM’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP, 2008) - Boss: - MSME Ministry via Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), central Sector Scheme, 100% Union-funded. - Beneficiary: - Std. 8 pass individuals/SHGs starting new non-farm micro-enterprises. - Funding: - Entrepreneur (5-10%), KVIC (15-35%), rest via bank loans (credit-linked subsidy). - Criteria: - Varies by rural/urban area, General/SC/ST/Women/PH/Minorities/Ex-Servicemen/North East. - Public Procurement Order (2012) - Mandates Central Ministries/Departments/Govt Companies to procure: - 25% of goods/services from Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs). - 3% of 25% from women-owned MSEs. - 4% of 25% from SC/ST-owned MSEs. - Preferences: - Local suppliers, minimum 50% local content (Make in India). - Monitoring: - MSME-Sambandh web portal. - Legal Basis: - MSME Development Act, 2006. - Public Procurement - GeM Portal - Government e-Marketplace: - Online portal for Union/State/PRIs/PSUs to buy goods/services (e.g., stationery). - Boss: - Commerce Ministry’s not-for-profit GeM Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV). - Benefits: - Transparency, efficiency, cost savings vs. traditional tendering. - SWAYATT Initiative: - Promotes startups, women, youth entrepreneurs via GeM. - ES22: - Highlights GeM’s significance (Ch. 02, Fiscal Development, p. 73). - One District One Product (ODOP, 2021) - Boss: - Commerce Ministry with Union/State support. - Objective: - Transform each district into an export hub by promoting products with export potential (e.g., Jaipur’s Blue Pottery). - Support: - Marketing, branding, logistics, infrastructure, incubation, training, R&D. - Subordinate Debt for stressed MSMEs. - Equity: - Infusion via Fund of Funds. - Procurement Protection: - Foreign companies excluded from tenders up to ₹200 crore. - Swavalamban Challenge Fund: - Supports non-profits, educational institutes, social startups for entrepreneurship, financial inclusion, green tech (Boss: SIDBI, UK-based org). - Replaces Entrepreneurs’ Memorandum; provides unique Udyog Aadhaar ID. - Benefits: - Access to MSME schemes; retail/wholesale traders eligible for Priority Sector Lending (Ref: Pillar 1A2). - CHAMPIONS Web Portal (2020-May): - Service Sector - Overview: - The service sector is a critical component of India's economy, contributing significantly to GDP and employment. - Service Sector – 3/4/5 Level Classification - Tertiary Sector: - Basic and traditional services involving tangible or direct customer interaction. - Includes: - Trade and Commerce - Transport (Road, Rail, Air, Waterways) - Communication (Postal, Telecom, Internet services) - Banking and Financial Services - Insurance - Real Estate and Housing - Tourism and Hospitality - Education and Healthcare (basic level) - Quaternary Sector: - Knowledge-oriented and information-based services. - Involves handling, generation, and dissemination of information. - Includes: - IT and Software Services - Data Analysis and Management - Financial Analytics and Advisory - Research and Development (R&D) - Educational Services (advanced and specialized) - Media and Publishing - Legal and Intellectual Property Services - Quinary Sector: - High-level decision-making and advanced professional services. - Involves creation, reorganization, and interpretation of complex data and ideas. - Driven by human capital and intellect – "Gold Collar" professions. - Includes: - Top Executives and Policy Makers (Government, Corporates, NGOs) - Senior Consultants and Advisors - Scientists, Academicians, and Think Tanks - Innovators and Futurists (e.g., AI ethicists, tech philosophers) - Cultural, Spiritual, and Social Leaders - Outsourcing vs. Home-Shoring - Outsourcing: - Contracting work to an external agency to improve efficiency and reduce costs (e.g., Apple phones made by Tata, US bank call centers in Bengaluru). - Home-Shoring: - Employees work from home instead of company offices to save on office maintenance costs (e.g., Infosys employees coding from home). - BPO vs. KPO - Business Process Outsourcing (BPO): - Basic tasks like customer support, data entry. - Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO): - Advanced tasks like VFX for Hollywood, legal/pharma writing, online SAT coaching by Indian professionals. - Service Sector Data (ES25) - Global GDP: - 62% from services. - Indian GDP: - FY14 (50.6%), FY25 (55%). - Global Service Exports (2023): - #1 USA (13%), #7 India (4.3%). - Employment: - 30% of Indian workers. - States like Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Mizoram: - >33% Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) from trade, repair, hotels, restaurants (tourism-driven). - Servicification of Industrial Sector (ES25) - Services enhance manufacturing value addition (e.g., clinical trials for pharmaceuticals, fashion design for garments, online support for cars/laptops). - Subscription-based models (e.g., Maruti Suzuki’s car ownership) integrate services into products. - Service Sector - Public Administration (ES25) - Public administration (government services) contributes to GDP. - Rich/industrialized states: - Low % GDP from public administration due to high industrialization. - Poor/North-Eastern states: - Higher % GDP from public administration due to low industrialization. - ES25 (Ch. 8, p. 237): - Detailed analysis, low prelims utility. - Knowledge Economy of India - Threats/Challenges - Definition: - Economy based on intangible assets like workers’ knowledge, IPR (e.g., space, pharma, IT, e-learning). - Challenges: - Competition from China in space, pharma, IT. - Philippines, Indonesia offering English-proficient graduates in IT, engineering to MNCs. - Space sector growth driven by ISRO support, but electronics/hardware lacks similar backing. - Pharma: - Private sector-driven but insufficient R&D investment (ES25). - Brain drain of talent since the 1970s. - Service Sector Recommendations (ES25) - Defend - Preserve and Strengthen Core Services - IT & Business Services: - Maintain India’s global leadership and quality standards. - Support scale‑ups, cybersecurity readiness, and capacity building. - Ease of Doing Business: - Improve contract enforcement and litigation delays. - Simplify MSME compliance and enable single-window service export clearances. - Policy & Institutional Coordination: - Align Center-State-industry initiatives. - Create a Services Export Promotion Council. - Accelerate - Scale up High‑Growth Sectors - Transport, Trade & Repair, Financial Services, Education: - Deepen and broaden service delivery across states. - Foster global partnerships and certifications. - Infrastructure & Connectivity: - Boost logistics, power, and digital infrastructure. - Leverage PM Gati‑Shakti, smart city frameworks. - Skill Development: - Tailor training for export-led services (edtech, fintech, healthcare). - Expand vocational and soft-skills training programs. - Transform - Innovate in Emerging Sectors - Travel, Tourism, Healthcare, Personal & Cultural Services: - Use digital platforms, AI-driven booking, and telemedicine. - Create holistic travel circuits (heritage, wellness, adventure). - Digital Services & SaaS: - Encourage global IT‑BPM and SaaS exports. - Strengthen data protection frameworks and trust. - Financial & Professional Services: - Position India as an arbitration and financial center. - Expand fintech, insuretech, and GIFT City as hubs. - Untapped - Unlock High-Potential/Newer Sectors - Insurance, Pensions, Audio‑Visual, Media, Telecom & Postal Services: - Improve regulatory clarity. - Encourage formalization and private investment. - MSME‑led Services: - Promote enterprises in niche service domains. - Expand in Tier‑2 and Tier‑3 cities through credit, training, and cluster development. - Cross‑cutting Enablers: - Promote flexible models like gig economy and WFH to boost youth and women participation. - Expand remote-service delivery infrastructure. - Maintain continuous monitoring via service-sector dash-boards and digital metrics. - Sunrise Sector (Budget-2022) - Definition: - New sectors with rapid growth potential. - Sectors: - AI, geospatial systems, drones, semiconductors, space, genomics, pharmaceuticals, green energy, clean mobility. - Objective: - Government support to foster growth. - E-Commerce - E-Commerce vs. E-Business - E-Commerce: - Buying/selling via digital platforms (subset of E-Business). - E-Business: - Broader, includes e-commerce, production, supply chain, management, product development, HR, finance. - E-Commerce Transaction Types - B2B: - Business-to-business (e.g., Infosys developing SBI’s e-banking website). - B2G: - Business-to-government (e.g., Infosys developing GST portal). - B2C: - Business-to-consumer (e.g., Amazon selling to individuals). - C2B: - Consumer-to-business (e.g., warranty claims on Dell’s website). - C2C: - Consumer-to-consumer (e.g., selling used goods on OLX, reporting traffic on Google Maps). - E-Commerce Challenges - Anti-competitive practices: - Exclusive partnerships (e.g., Flipkart/Amazon restricting Xiaomi/Oppo sales to their platforms). - Marketplace model issues: - E-commerce giants (e.g., Amazon’s Cloudtail) offer deep discounts, harming other online/offline merchants. - Investigation: - Competition Commission of India (CCI, Corporate Affairs Ministry) probing Amazon/Flipkart (2021); legal battles ongoing. - Predatory Pricing - Definition: - Selling products at unrealistically low prices to eliminate competitors. - Issue (2024-Aug): - Commerce Minister accused e-commerce platforms of predatory pricing, harming 10 million retail stores (electronics, apparel). - E-Commerce Rules (2019-Feb) - Boss: - Consumer Affairs Ministry (under Consumer Protection Act, 2019). - Rules: - Ban on exclusive agreements (e.g., Flipkart cannot restrict Xiaomi sales to its platform). - Stricter norms on cashbacks, discounts, and shell companies selling at deep discounts. - Mandatory disclosure: - Expiry date, country of origin, return/refund policies, seller address, customer care, ratings. - Consumer-friendly rules; logical reasoning for MCQs (e.g., banning fake reviews is correct). - Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 - Fall-back liability: - E-commerce platforms (e.g., Amazon) liable if suppliers fail to deliver, causing consumer loss. - Country of origin identification for goods. - Fair opportunity for domestic sellers via product suggestions. - Ban on dictating commission rates (to avoid misuse of dominant position). - No sharing of customer data without consent. - Criticism Against E-Commerce Rules - Foreign companies: - Rules push “Make in India” via Consumer Protection Act, argue competitive domestic products don’t need such measures. - Overlap: - Consumer Protection Authority encroaching on Competition Commission of India (CCI’s) domain. - Data rules: - Should be under Personal Data Protection Bill, not Consumer Protection Act. - Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) - Boss: - Commerce Ministry’s DPIIT (non-profit, 2021). - Objective: - Digital platform to connect buyers/sellers, using open-source protocol to prevent exploitation by e-commerce giants. - Comparison: - Platform fees: - Swiggy/Zomato (25-40%) vs. ONDC (2-10%). - Example: - McDonald’s burger ₹250 (Swiggy) vs. ₹200 (ONDC). - Benefits: - Ends duopoly (Amazon-Flipkart, Ola-Uber, Swiggy-Zomato), product-agnostic (allows food, taxi bookings). - Analogy: - UPI/BHIM reduced seller fees (Paytm) and product prices; ONDC does similar for e-commerce. - ONDC Observations (ES25) - Transactions: - >14 million across 1,100+ cities (Nov 2024). - Sellers: - 7 lakh+ active. - Saarthi App: - AI-driven (with Bhashini) for buyer-side app creation. - Affordable onions in NCR region. - E-Commerce Rules vs. ONDC - E-Commerce Rules (Consumer Affairs): - Focus on buyer protection, some seller safeguards. - ONDC (Commerce): - Protects both buyers and sellers. - Issue: - Some stakeholders or experts have suggested to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) that: - The E-Commerce Rules and ONDC initiatives should be merged, coordinated, or harmonized. - This would avoid policy fragmentation, streamline digital commerce, and increase effectiveness. - Q-Commerce (Quick Commerce) - Delivery: - 15 minutes to 1 hour (vs. 1-3 days for e-commerce). - Examples: - Dunzo, Swiggy Instamart, Blinkit, Zepto (vs. Amazon, Flipkart). - E-Commerce Anti-Fake Review Framework (BIS) - Boss: - Bureau of Indian Standards (Consumer Affairs Ministry). - Guideline: - Indian Standard (IS) 19000:2022 to combat fake reviews. - Measures: - Verify/ban fake reviewers (via email/OTP), penalize merchants paying for fake reviews. - Voluntary framework, not legally binding. - E-Commerce Google App Store Anti-Trust (CCI Order) - Issue: - Google mandated pre-installation of Play Store with Android, charging 15-30% commission, creating a monopoly. - CCI (2022): - Fined Google $161 million (₹1,337.76 crore). - Appeals: - Google lost at NCLAT and Supreme Court. - Mergers & Acquisitions (M&A) - CCI Threshold - Issues: - Data misuse, cartelization, monopoly from Mergers and Acquisitions (M&As) (e.g., Sun Pharma-Ranbaxy, Tata-Vistara/Air India). - Competition Act 2002 (Amended 2023): - CCI approval needed if: - Deal value >₹2,000 crore. - Target company has substantial business operations in India. - Retail Trade - Itinerant Retailers & Cheap Jacks - Itinerant Traders: - No fixed place, move with wares (e.g., peddlers, hawkers). - Cheap Jacks: - Itinerant with temporary shops (e.g., watch/shoe repair, street-side salons). - Manufacturing - Bodies for Quality Standards - Consumer Affairs Ministry - Statutory - BIS (1986) - Bureau of Indian Standards: - Apex regulator for standardization, quality certification. - Certifies ISI mark for goods (e.g., helmets, gas stoves) meeting standards. - Nodal for ISO standards, WTO’s Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) agreement (Ref: Pillar 3B). - BIS & Gold-Silver Hallmarking - Certifies purity of gold (14, 18, 22 carat) and silver. - Mandatory since June 2021 (previously voluntary since 2000). - Exemptions: - Jewelers with turnover <₹40 lakh. - Benefits: - Assures gold quality, enables tax authorities to monitor trade for tax​ evasion. - BIS Certificate for Mitticool Refrigerator (2022) - Developed by Mansukh Bhai Prajapati (Gujarat), uses evaporative cooling (clay-based, no electricity). - BIS Standard (IS 17693:2022): - Specifies clay type, dimensions, temperature. - Supports 6/17 UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (e.g., no poverty, zero hunger, clean energy). - Power Ministry - Statutory - BEE (2001-02) - Bureau of Energy Efficiency (Energy Conservation Act, 2001). - Star Labeling: - Mandatory for ACs, refrigerators, tubelights, TVs, geysers, inverters, LED lamps; voluntary for computers, LPG stoves, fans. - Chiller Star Labeling: - For commercial HVAC systems. - RAISE Program: - Improves AC quality/efficiency (EESL, USAID joint initiative). - Health Ministry - Statutory - FSSAI (2006) - Food Safety and Standards Authority of India: - Sets scientific standards for food manufacture, storage, distribution, sale, import. - Repealed Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954, other food-related laws. - Labeling: - Green circle (vegetarian), brown circle (non-vegetarian/egg). - Bans: - Recycled plastic/newspaper for food packing, calcium carbide/acetylene for fruit ripening (ethylene permitted). - Limits: - Trans Fatty Acids <2% (2022), no mustard oil blending (2021, due to dropsy/allergy risks). - MSG Issue: - Maggi Noodles Controversy: - Trigger: - In 2015, samples of Maggi noodles tested by FSSAI (Food Safety and Standards Authority of India) were found to allegedly contain: - Lead: - beyond permissible limits. - MSG (Monosodium Glutamate): - without proper labeling (though naturally occurring in some ingredients). - Immediate Action: - FSSAI ordered nationwide ban and recall of Maggi noodles. - Nestlé India withdrew the product from the market. - Industry Impact: - Major loss of public trust. - Financial loss and stock impact for Nestlé. - Ripple effect on packaged food industry in India. - Legal Outcome: - Bombay High Court (2015): - Lifted the ban. - Allowed Maggi to be sold again after passing fresh lab tests. - Reintroduction: - Maggi was relaunched in the market after clearing the tests from accredited labs. - Lessons and Reforms: - Boost in consumer awareness on food safety. - FSSAI introduced stricter norms on labeling and contaminants. - Food Safety Mitra (2019): - Trained youth assist food businesses with FSSAI compliance. - Food Safety Index: - Compares states. - AGMARK: - Advisory bodies for awareness. - Consumer Protection Act - Features - Product Liability: - Companies liable for injury, damage, or death from defective goods/services. - Unfair Contracts: - Excessive deposits, unilateral terminations penalized. - E-Filing: - Complaints via electronic means, video conferencing hearings. - Penalties: - Up to ₹50 lakh fine, 5 years jail; ₹50,000 fine for frivolous complaints. - Celebrity Ads: - Misleading ads lead to bans, financial penalties. - Consumer Protection - Dark Patterns - Definition: - Manipulative e-commerce practices (e.g., drip pricing, disguised ads, bait-and-switch, false urgency). - CCPA issued guidelines to curb these. - Consumer Protection - Drip Pricing - Definition: - Partial price advertised, additional charges (e.g., shipping, platform fees) revealed at checkout. - Example: - Shoes ₹4,700 + ₹300 hidden fees = ₹5,000. - Consumer Affairs Ministry warned against this (May 2024). - Consumer Protection - Spam Protection in USA - CAN-SPAM Act (2003): - Regulates commercial emails for products/services. - Mains Questions - Focus: - 4th Industrial Revolution, Make in India, manufacturing improvement, LPG reforms’ impact. - Covered in separate Mains-QEP course, not Raftaar (PCB) Prelims. - Pillar 4C1: Economic Planning, NITI Aayog, and Statistical Systems - Definition: - Economic planning is the process through which a government identifies socio-economic challenges such as poverty, inequality, low agricultural productivity, and inadequate industrial or infrastructural development, setting strategic goals and policies to address them, ensuring sustainable growth and equitable resource distribution. - Context: - India’s economic planning has evolved from centralized, Soviet-inspired models to a more decentralized, cooperative framework under NITI Aayog, emphasizing innovation, inclusivity, and data-driven governance to align with global economic trends and national development goals. - Significance for India: - Economic planning drives India’s vision of becoming a developed nation by 2047, fostering cooperative federalism, sustainable development, and robust statistical systems to enhance policy effectiveness and global credibility. - Economic Systems - Definition: - An economic system is a structured mechanism through which a society organizes the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services, shaped by ownership structures, resource allocation, and decision-making processes. - Types of Economic Systems: -
Economic System Capitalism Mixed Economies Socialism
Ownership of Industries Private sector dominates. Few industries reserved for public sector; rest by private sector. Public sector/government/collective ownership; no private property.
Production Decisions Market forces (supply and demand) decide what to produce (e.g., more bikes or books). Essential goods/services by public sector; others by private sector. Government decides what and how much to produce.
Production Methods Cheaper mode (labor or capital) chosen by private entities. Public sector: government decides; private sector: entrepreneurs decide. Preference for labor-intensive methods.
Distribution Only consumers who can afford goods/services can purchase them. Essential goods: government may fix prices (e.g., NPPA for stents); others: market-driven. Government distributes via subsidies/rationing shops.
- Global Context: - Most nations, including India and the USA, operate mixed economic systems. China, officially socialist, functions as a mixed economy in practice. Pure socialist systems (e.g., North Korea, Cuba) face economic hardships. Communism, a branch of socialism, often involves totalitarian governance with single-party control. - Anarcho-Capitalism and Libertarianism - Libertarianism: - Emphasizes individual liberty with minimal government intervention, prioritizing personal and economic freedom. - Anarchism: - Advocates a society without government or rulers, relying on voluntary cooperation. - Anarcho-Capitalism: - Concept by Murray Rothbard (1950s, USA), advocating complete privatization of all functions, including police and judiciary, replaced by private arbitrators. -
Aspect Capitalism Anarcho-Capitalism
Government Role Controls law, order, contracts, judiciary. All functions, including police and judiciary, privatized.
Trade and Taxes Taxes on imports; protects local industries. No taxes on imports; free trade prioritizes cheap goods.
- Relevance: - Gained attention due to Argentina’s President Javier Milei advocating anarcho-capitalism, highlighting debates on government roles in economic systems. - Closed vs. Open Economy -
Closed Economy Open Economy
No imports, exports, or economic relations with other countries (e.g., North Korea). Engages in imports, exports, FDI, and FPI with global markets (e.g., India).
- Significance: - Closed economies aim for self-sufficiency (autarky) but face resource constraints. Open economies leverage global trade for growth, as seen in India’s liberalization post-1991. - Great Reset Initiative by World Economic Forum (WEF) - Concept: - Proposed by WEF founder Klaus Schwab, it calls for a “reset” of capitalism to create a new social contract emphasizing equality in health, finance, energy, and education. - Context: - Revived post-COVID-19 due to its impact on vulnerable populations, highlighting the need for inclusive economic models. - Relevance: - Aligns with global discussions on sustainable and equitable growth, influencing India’s policy focus on inclusive development. - Miscellaneous Economic Terms - Washington Consensus (1980s): - A set of economic policy recommendations by IMF, World Bank, and U.S. Treasury for developing nations, focusing on liberalization, privatization, and reduced government control, similar to India’s LPG reforms. - Reaganomics (1980s): - Policies under U.S. President Reagan, emphasizing reduced government spending, tax cuts for businesses, and deregulation to stimulate economic growth. - Thatcheromics (1980s): - Policies under UK PM Margaret Thatcher, focusing on privatization of public enterprises and reducing government control to enhance market efficiency. - Autarky: - An economic system of self-sufficiency with minimal global trade, akin to a closed economy (e.g., North Korea). - Adam Smith’s Invisible Hand: - Refers to the self-regulating nature of markets, where individual self-interest drives efficient resource allocation through supply and demand. - Economic Planning - Definition: - Economic planning involves a government preparing a roadmap to address socio-economic issues like poverty, inequality, and underdevelopment by setting goals, allocating resources, and implementing policies. - Types of Economic Planning: -
Type Description
Totalitarian vs. Democratic Totalitarian: Centralized control (e.g., USSR, North Korea). Democratic: Participatory, as in India post-independence.
Centralized vs. Decentralized Centralized: Top-down planning (e.g., USSR). Decentralized: Local participation, as in India after 73rd and 74th Amendments.
Inducement vs. Direction Inducement: Incentives like subsidies guide actions. Direction: Central authority sets mandatory targets.
Indicative vs. Imperative Indicative: Flexible guidelines with public/private consultation (e.g., India, France). Imperative: Rigid state control (e.g., USSR).
Financial vs. Physical Financial: Resource allocation in monetary terms. Physical: Allocation in terms of labor, materials, machinery.
Timeframe-Based Operational (up to 1 year), Tactical (3-7 years), Strategic/Perspective (10+ years).
- Economic Planning Before Independence - Key Plans: - Hind Swaraj (1909, Gandhi): - Advocated minimal wants, self-reliance, and small-scale production (khadi, cottage industries), opposing industrialization. - Planned Economy for India (1934, M. Visvesvaraya): - Proposed a 10-year plan focusing on industrial development, authored by the engineer and Bharat Ratna recipient. - Congress Plan (1938, Nehru): - Proposed a National Planning Commission, stalled due to World War II. - Bombay Plan (1944): - A 15-year investment plan by industrialists like JRD Tata and GD Birla, emphasizing industrial growth. - Gandhian Plan (1944, Sriman Narayan Agrawal): - Focused on agricultural and rural economy with a decentralized approach. - People’s Plan (1945, MN Roy): - Socialist-leaning, advocating state-controlled resource distribution and agricultural mechanization. - Sarvodaya Plan (1950, Jayprakash Narayan): - Based on Vinoba Bhave’s philosophy, prioritizing agriculture and cottage industries. - Economic Planning After Independence - Establishment: - Inspired by the Soviet model, PM Nehru established the Planning Commission in March 1950 to draft Five-Year Plans (FYPs). - National Development Council (NDC, 1952) approved FYPs, comprising PM, CMs, and others. - Planning Commission dissolved in 2014 by PM Modi, replaced by NITI Aayog in January 2015. - Five-Year Plans (FYPs): -
Plan Period Theme/Model/Target Outcome
1st 1951-56 Harrod-Domar Model; focus on agriculture, irrigation, power. Successful: Exceeded GDP growth target.
2nd 1956-61 P.C. Mahalanobis Model; socialist pattern, rapid industrialization, heavy industries. Successful: Achieved GDP growth target.
3rd 1961-66 Sukhmoy Chakraborty & John Sandy Model (Gadgil Yojana); economic independence. Failed: Due to droughts, wars with Pakistan and China.
Plan Holiday 1966-69 Annual plans due to 3rd FYP failure. -
4th 1969-74 Ashok Rudra & Alon Manney Model; growth with stability, self-reliance; “Garibi Hatao” slogan. Failed: Due to Bangladeshi refugee crisis, drought.
5th 1974-79 C. Subramaniam, later D.P. Dhar; agriculture prioritized; poverty removal, self-reliance. Terminated in 1978 under Morarji Desai.
Rolling Plan 1978-80 Morarji Desai’s annual progress evaluation. -
6th 1980-85 Poverty removal via IRDP, NREP, TRYSEM schemes. Moderate success.
7th 1985-90 Pranab Mukherjee Model; focus on employment, private sector priority. Moderate success.
Annual Plans 1990-92 Due to political instability. -
8th 1992-97 John W. Miller Model; LPG reforms under PV Narasimha Rao; focus on employment, education, health. Successful: Exceeded GDP growth target.
9th 1997-02 Growth with social justice, equity; 7 Basic Minimum Services; indicative planning. Failed: Due to Asian Financial Crisis.
10th 2002-07 Target 8% GDP growth, double per capita income, reduce poverty to 15%. Failed: Targets not achieved.
11th 2007-12 C. Rangarajan; faster, inclusive growth; 9% GDP growth, 70 million jobs. Failed: Due to US subprime crisis.
12th 2012-17 Faster, inclusive, sustainable growth; 9% GDP, 4% agriculture, 10% manufacturing; 50 million jobs. Failed: Due to global slowdown.
- Planning Commission Limitations - Centralized Approach: - Top-down planning ignored state-specific needs, reducing flexibility. - Bureaucratic Inefficiency: - Slow decision-making and rigid targets hindered adaptability. - Limited Private Sector Role: - Nehruvian socialist bias restricted private sector participation. - Inadequate Monitoring: - Weak focus on implementation and outcome evaluation. - Financial Dependence: - States relied heavily on central funds, undermining cooperative federalism. - Planning Commission vs. NITI Aayog: Structure -
Aspect Planning Commission NITI Aayog
Establishment 1950-2014 2015 onwards
Chairman Prime Minister Prime Minister
Vice Chairman Cabinet Minister rank (e.g., Montek Singh Ahluwalia). Arvind Panagariya (2015-17), Rajiv Kumar (2017-22), Suman K Bery (2022-present).
CEO Member-Secretary (IAS). Secretary-level bureaucrat (e.g., Parameswaran Iyer).
Ex-Officio Members Finance Minister, Planning Minister. Up to 4 Union Ministers (Home, Defense, Finance, Agriculture).
Full-Time Members 4-7, Minister of State rank. Economists, scientists (e.g., Arvind Virmani, Ramesh Chand, V.K. Saraswat, Vinod Kumar Paul).
Special Invitees None. Union Ministers (e.g., Transport, Health); list dynamic.
Part-Time Members None. Tech experts (none as of July 2024).
Governing Council National Development Council (PM, CMs, UT Lieutenant Governors). PM, CMs, UT Lieutenant Governors; promotes cooperative federalism.
Regional Councils None. Ad hoc councils for regional issues (e.g., irrigation, Naxalism).
- Planning Commission vs. NITI Aayog: Functions -
Planning Commission NITI Aayog
Drafted Five-Year Plans; allocated funds for centrally sponsored schemes and state plans using Gadgil-Mukherjee formula. Drafts Three-Year Action Agenda, Seven-Year Strategy, Fifteen-Year Vision (2017-32); Strategy for New India @ 75 (2017-23). No fund allocation; Finance Commission/Ministry handles this.
Focused on plan implementation. Serves as a think tank; designs policies, monitors schemes via dashboards (e.g., SDG India Index, School Education Quality Index).
- NITI Aayog Notable Initiatives - Darpan Portal (2017): - NGOs register for unique IDs to access government grants for schemes. - Aspirational Districts Programme (2018): - Transforms 115 backward districts across 49 KPIs (health, education, infrastructure); monitored via “Champions of Change” portal. - Strategic Disinvestment: - Recommended disinvestment of loss-making CPSEs (e.g., Air India, Pawan Hans). - POSHAN Abhiyaan: - Aims for malnutrition-free India by 2022, focusing on women and children; led by NITI Vice-Chairman. - Policy and Legislative Support: - Frames policies on energy, minerals; model acts for agricultural land leasing, livestock selling. - Agricultural Reforms: - Revamped MSP via price deficiency payments (PM-AASHA) and fertilizer subsidies through DBT. - Sustainable Development Goals (SDG): - Developed SDG India Index to track 17 SDG goals; promotes methanol/biofuel economy. - GIRG Dashboard: - Monitors India’s performance on global indices (e.g., UNDP’s Multidimensional Poverty Index). - Output Outcome Monitoring Framework: - Enhances monitoring of government scheme implementation. - Seminars and Innovation: - Organizes workshops, conferences; runs Atal Innovation Mission (AIM) with grants for incubators and Mentor India program. - State Support Mission (2022): - Funds state-level think tanks (State Institutions of Transformation) to design policies and ensure effective scheme implementation by 2047. - Prime Minister’s Economic Advisory Council (PM-EAC) - Establishment: - Non-constitutional, non-statutory body formed in the 2000s to advise the PM on economic issues; reconstituted in 2017 post-demonetization and GST. - Composition: - Chaired by Bibek Debroy (died 2024); includes 7 full/part-time members; supported by NITI Aayog. - Recommendations: - GST Council-like body for public expenditure. - Reduce GST slabs and direct taxes to boost economic growth. - PRAGATI - Overview: - Pro-Active Governance and Timely Implementation (2015), a PMO web platform for monitoring scheme implementation and addressing public grievances (e.g., tax refunds, EPFO claims). - Mechanism: - PM conducts monthly video conferences with Union ministries and state chief secretaries. - Other Related Organizations - eSamikSha (2014): - Cabinet Secretariat portal to monitor decisions/follow-ups post-PM meetings, ensuring timely action by officials. - Project Monitoring Group (PMG, 2013): - Fast-tracks approvals for public, private, and PPP projects via the e-Nivesh Monitor portal. - Investment Commission (2004-09): - Chaired by Ratan Tata; recommended investment-friendly policies; revival considered in 2016 but faded. - CPGRAMS (2007): - Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System under DARPG; allows citizens to file complaints against central ministries for corruption, delays, etc., via portal and “My Grievance” app. - Apex/Independent Offices - Offices not under any ministry: - President’s Secretariat, Cabinet Secretariat (includes RAW), Prime Minister’s Office (includes NSA), NITI Aayog, Department of Atomic Energy, Department of Space, National Security Council Secretariat. - Statistical Systems - Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI): - Headed by Secretary & Chief Statistician of India (Indian Statistical Service officer). - Components: - National Statistical Office (NSO): - Formed in 2019 by merging Central Statistics Office (CSO) and National Sample Survey Office (NSSO). - CSO: - Computes GDP, GSDP, IIP, ASI, CPI, and Economic Census (6th in 2013). - NSSO: - Collects data on socio-economic indicators, rural-urban prices, and Annual Survey of Industries (ASI). - Plans for a National-Level Data Warehouse for centralized statistical data and big data analytics. - Programme Implementation Wing: - MPLADS (1993): - MPs suggest development works worth ₹5 crore annually per constituency. - Twenty Point Programme (2006): - Monitors schemes for poverty alleviation, employment, health, etc. - Infrastructure and project monitoring. - National Statistical Commission (NSC) - Establishment: - Set up in 2005 via Cabinet resolution, based on C. Rangarajan Committee recommendations; non-constitutional, non-statutory. - Structure: - Part-time chairman, 4 part-time members, NITI CEO as ex-officio member; Chief Statistician serves as Secretary. - Functions: - Sets standards for data collection and publication; coordinates among agencies; replaced NSSO’s Governing Council. - Controversy (2019): - Two members resigned, citing government sidelining; alleged suppression of 2017-18 Employment Survey showing job losses post-demonetization/GST. - Implications: - Data manipulation risks undermining confidence in India’s statistical systems, affecting IMF voting rights and credit ratings by agencies like S&P, Moody’s, and Fitch. - Standing Committee on Statistics (SCoS) - Establishment: - Formed as SCES in 2019; renamed SCoS in 2023; dissolved in September 2024. - Role: - Advised on survey methodologies and results; chaired by Pronab Sen. - Dissolution: - Official reason: - Replaced by Steering Committee for National Sample Surveys. - Unofficial reason: - Pronab Sen’s criticism of delayed population census. - Mahalanobis National Award - Overview: - Awarded by MoSPI for outstanding contributions to statistics; named after P.C. Mahalanobis, father of Indian statistics and architect of 2nd FYP. - Recipient: - C. Rangarajan (2020), former RBI governor. - Pillar 4C2: Indicators → Unemployment - Disclaimer on Data Consistency - Data on employment/unemployment may vary across sources (e.g., PLFS, Economic Survey) due to revisions by the government and selective reporting. Focus on trends rather than specific figures for exams, as cross-referencing all data is impractical. - International Labour Organization (ILO) - Established: - 1919, under Treaty of Versailles, post-World War I. - Status: - UN specialized agency, headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. - Key Report: - World Employment and Social Outlook. - ILO Core Conventions - India ratified 6 out of 8 core conventions: -
