- Wage Theories - Subsistence Wage Theory (Adam Smith) - Definition: - Proposes that wages naturally settle at a level just sufficient to enable workers to survive and maintain their families — i.e., at the subsistence level. - Economic Logic: - Rooted in Classical Economics and Smith’s concept of “natural price,” where wages are a component. - Mechanism of Adjustment: - If actual wages > subsistence wage: - Living standards improve. - Population increases (more births, lower mortality). - Labor supply expands → Increased competition → Downward pressure on wages → Wages fall back to subsistence. - If actual wages < subsistence wage: - Living standards decline. - Higher mortality, lower birth rates, or emigration. - Labor supply contracts → Reduced competition → Upward pressure on wages → Wages rise to subsistence. - Implication: - Long-term wage levels are stable and self-correcting around subsistence. - Offers little hope for sustained wage improvement without productivity growth or institutional changes. - Natural Wage Theory (David Ricardo) - Also known as: - Iron Law of Wages (popularized later by Ferdinand Lassalle based on Ricardo's insights). - Definition: - Real wages tend to stabilize around the “natural wage,” defined as the minimum level required to sustain a worker and maintain labor supply over time. - Key Features: - Closely related to Smith’s subsistence theory, but with greater emphasis on population dynamics and capital accumulation. - Ricardo introduced the idea of diminishing returns in agriculture, which influences wage stagnation. - Mechanism: - If wages temporarily rise: - Worker well-being improves. - Population grows → Increased labor supply → Wages decline. - If wages fall below the natural level: - Workers cannot sustain themselves. - Population falls → Labor supply tightens → Wages rise. - Implication: - In the absence of technological progress or institutional reforms, real wages cannot rise significantly above subsistence. - Capital accumulation increases labor demand but is offset by rising population → keeping wages low. - Criticism: - Too deterministic. - Neglects role of state policy, labor unions, and productivity improvements. - Miscellaneous Wage Theories -
Theory Description
Residual-Claimant Theory Wages are what remains after paying rent, interest, and profits to other factors of production (land, loans, investors).
Bargaining Theory Wages determined through negotiations between workers, employers, and trade unions.
Marginal Productivity Theory Wages depend on the value a worker adds to the company, based on their productivity.
- Occupational Structure of Indian Workers -
Sector 2017–18 Share (%) 2023–24 Share (%)
Agriculture 44.1 46.1
Manufacturing 12.1 11.4
Services 31.1 29.7
Total 87.3 87.2
- Note: - Total is less than 100% as sectors like mining, construction, and utilities are excluded. - Additional details: - Rise in Agriculture (from 44.1% to 46.1%) - Reverse migration during COVID-19: - Many workers returned to rural areas and took up farm work. - Low-entry barrier: - Agriculture acts as a fallback employment during crises. - Informal rural employment increased post-pandemic, boosting agri share. - Lack of alternate rural jobs like construction or manufacturing. - Fall in Services (from 31.1% to 29.7%) - Pandemic impact: - Hospitality, tourism, retail, and education sectors faced disruption. - Digital transformation may have reduced low-skill service jobs. - Some part of the workforce moved back to informal/agri sectors. - Manufacturing's fall (12.1% → 11.4%) is due to: - Automation, low investment in labor-intensive sectors. - Low job creation in formal sector. - Unemployment: Involuntary Types - Voluntary Unemployment: - Individuals choose not to work, seeking higher wages or preferring not to work. - Involuntary Unemployment: - Individuals willing to work at prevailing wages but unable to find jobs due to external factors. - Causes of involuntary: - Slow economic growth vs. rapid population growth. - Defective education system and lack of employable skills. - Insufficient banking, transport, and communication infrastructure. - Social discrimination (e.g., against SC/ST, women, physically handicapped). - Major Types of involuntary - Types: -
Type Features
Cyclical Occurs during economic downturns (recession/depression); mass layoffs (e.g., Maruti laid off 3000 workers in 2019 due to low car sales).
Frictional Transitional unemployment when individuals search for new jobs.
Disguised Workers appear employed but contribute zero marginal productivity (e.g., excess workers in farming).
Seasonal Jobs tied to specific seasons (e.g., agriculture, tourism, sugar mills).
Underemployment Workers employed below their qualifications/salary potential (e.g., M.Com as delivery boy).
Technological Job losses due to automation (e.g., handloom workers vs. textile machines). WEF (2018) predicts 75 million jobs lost by 2025, but 133 million new jobs in tech-related fields.
Structural Mismatch between workers’ skills and job requirements (e.g., C++ programmer in a Python-demand market).
Natural Rate of Unemployment (NRU) Sum of frictional and structural unemployment; baseline unemployment in a healthy economy.
Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU) Refer to Pillar 4E (Inflation and Phillips Curve).
- Employment-Related Terms in News - Baumol’s Cost Disease Theory (1965) - By William J. Baumol and William G. Bowen. - Wages rise in certain sectors (e.g., doctors, professors in USA; farm laborers in Punjab/Haryana) despite no increase in productivity, due to labor shortages (e.g., MGNREGA reducing farm labor supply). - Moonlighting - Undertaking additional jobs alongside primary employment. - Issue: - Companies like Wipro and Infosys have terminated employees for moonlighting due to risks of leaking trade secrets, software codes, or client lists. - Unemployment: NSO Survey Types -
Aspect Quinquennial Employment and Unemployment Surveys Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS)
Frequency Every 5 years (1972–2011/12; discontinued). Annual, since 2017; includes workers aged 15+.
Households Surveyed Non-agriculture workers in rural/urban areas. All sectors (agriculture, non-agriculture) in rural/urban areas.
- PLFS Details: - Annual Reports: - Report #1 (2019-May): - July 2017–June 2018. - Report #6 (2023-Oct): - July 2022–June 2023. - Quarterly Bulletins: - Released for specific periods (e.g., Q2 2020: August 2021). - Note: - Quarterly data has low cost-benefit for exam preparation. - Indicators: Unemployment Rate (UR) - Definition: - Percentage of involuntarily unemployed individuals in the labor force. - Formula: - UR = (Number of involuntarily unemployed / Labor force) × 100. - Example: - 2018 UR = (3 crore unemployed / 51.8 crore labor force) × 100 = 5.8%. - Measurement Approaches: -
Approach Criteria
Current Weekly Status (CWS) Unemployed if no work for even 1 hour in a week.
Current Daily Status (CDS) Unemployed if no work for even 1 hour in a day within a week.
Usual Status (US) Employed if worked at least 30 days in 365 days; otherwise, unemployed. Subdivided into Principal Activity Status (PS) and Subsidiary Economic Activity Status (SS). Official reports prioritize US.
- PLFS 2017–18: - UR = 6.0% (Usual Status), highest in 45 years.' - Economic Survey Insights: - High UR: - Arunachal Pradesh, Kerala, Manipur, Bihar. - Low UR: - Gujarat, Karnataka, West Bengal, Sikkim. - UR highest among urban youth (20%), lowest among illiterates (1.1%). - Worker Population Ratio (WPR) - Definition: - Percentage of employed persons in the total population. - Formula: - WPR = (Number of employed persons / Total population) × 100. - Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) - Definition: - Percentage of the working-age population (usually 15 years and above) that is either employed or actively seeking employment (i.e., part of the labor force). - Formula: - LFPR = [(Number of employed + Number of involuntarily unemployed) / Total population] × 100. - 2017: - All-India LFPR = 37% (male + female, rural + urban). - Female LFPR: -
Year All-India Female LFPR (%) Rural Female LFPR (%)
2017–18 23.3 24.6
2023–24 41.7 47.6
- Insights: - Sikkim has the highest female LFPR (56.9%). - Urban female LFPR is lower than rural due to women pursuing higher education or staying home as housewives. - Over 75% of rural female workers are in agriculture. - Female LFPR is significantly lower than male LFPR. - Economic Survey 2025 (ES25) Reasons for Female LFPR Increase: - Rising rural women participation. - Better capture of unpaid female work in PLFS. - Government schemes promoting women’s employment (see Pillar 6D). - Why Female LFPR Declined (2004–2018) - From 45% (2004) to 23% (2017): - Increased pursuit of higher education, delaying job market entry. - Rising rural male incomes, leading women to take domestic roles. - Mechanization in agriculture/animal husbandry reducing female labor demand. - Declining textile/leather exports due to US/EU protectionism. - Slowdown in real estate, reducing construction jobs for women. - Cultural and patriarchal norms limiting women’s mobility. - Lack of computer/English skills for emerging startup jobs. - NSO Time Use Survey (2019): - Women spend 7.5 hours on unpaid domestic/caregiving tasks vs. 5.7 hours on paid work. - Solutions to Improve LFPR - Invest in childcare/daycare, paid parental leave, family-friendly workplaces, elderly care facilities. - Ensure equal pay, career progression, and social security (EPFO/ESIC) for women. - Government schemes for women’s skill development and entrepreneurship (see Pillar 6: HRD). - Augmented Female LFPR - Definition: - Regular Female LFPR + unpaid women workers (e.g., domestic duties, collecting vegetables/firewood for household use). - Issue: - PLFS excludes unpaid domestic work, underrepresenting female labor force participation. - ES25 Unemployment Data -

- Requirement: - India needs to generate 78.5 lakh non-farm jobs annually until 2030. - Salaries of Indian Workers (ES25) - Profit vs. Salary Trends - Average salary: - ₹15,885 (FY19) to ₹20,702 (FY24), a 30% increase. - Company profits: - Increased 300% (4x) in the same period. - Issue: - FY24 profits rose 22%, but new hiring only 1.5%, with mass layoffs prevalent. - Japanese Model for High Salaries - Japan’s social contract: - Consumers overpay for goods/services; companies invest in R&D, infrastructure, and decent wages; government supports with tax-funded infrastructure. - India’s Issue: - Consumers overpay, but companies underinvest in R&D/wages, limiting job and salary growth. - Worker Types by National Statistical Office (NSO) -

- Unorganized Sector - Definition: - Firms not registered under laws like Shop Establishment Act, Factory Act, or Companies Act; workers lack social security (EPFO/ESIC). - Features: - Casual/seasonal work, irregular payments, no trade union protection. - Legislation: - Unorganized Sector Workers’ Social Security Act, 2008, provides life/disability cover, health/maternity benefits, and old-age protection. - Formalization: - Increasing proportion of formal workers indicates job formalization. - Informal Workers - Definition: - Workers not in formal records/contracts, even in organized sectors (e.g., drivers, security guards in companies like Reliance). - Sectors with High Informal Workers: - Construction (>80%), mining (>30%), transport/hotels/restaurants (>10%). - Issues: - Lack minimum wages, EPFO/ESIC benefits; vulnerable to economic shocks (e.g., 60 lakh migrant workers fled cities during COVID-19 via Shramik Special trains, May–August 2020). - Unorganized Workers: E-Shram Portal (2021) - Overview: - National database by Ministry of Labour & Employment for ~38 crore unorganized workers (e.g., construction workers, street vendors, domestic workers). - Features: - Free registration; issues e-Shram card with Universal Account Number (UAN). - Benefits: - ₹1 lakh for partial disability, ₹2 lakh for accidental death; access to social security schemes. - ES23 Data: - 28 crore registered; highest from UP (29%), Bihar (10%), West Bengal (9%); sectors: agriculture (52%), domestic workers (9.8%), construction (9.1%). - Gig Workers & Two-Sided Market - Definition: - Temporary workers outside traditional employer-employee setups (e.g., delivery boys, app-based taxi drivers, freelancers). - Data: - 7.5 million gig workers (2020–21), projected to reach 20 million in 8 years. - Two-Sided Market: - Buyers and sellers interact via platforms (e.g., Amazon, Ola, Uber). - Decisions of one group (e.g., customer ratings) affect the other (e.g., delivery boy’s payment). - Characteristics: - Workers classified as independent contractors, not employees, depriving them of EPFO/ESIC benefits. - Short-term, temporary contracts; payment based on piece rate, ratings, or profit share. - Code on Social Security 2020 aims to address social security gaps. - Formal Temporary Flexi Workers - Definition: - Temporary workers hired through staffing companies (e.g., TeamLease supplying cleaners to Infosys). - Features: - Staffing companies handle wages, social security; 1% of Indian workforce (vs. 2.2% in Europe); mostly aged 21–30, earning ₹20,000–22,000 in low-skill jobs (e.g., data operations, sales). - AI & Job Loss: Engel’s Pause Analogy - Concept: - "Engel’s Pause" refers to a historical phase during Britain’s Industrial Revolution (late 18th–early 19th century) when: - Productivity and output increased rapidly due to mechanization. - But wages remained stagnant, and workers didn’t initially benefit. - Named after economist Friedrich Engels, who observed this worker-capital divide. - This analogy is now used to highlight: - A similar risk in the AI revolution—where tech boosts profits and efficiency, but displaces workers, especially low/mid-skill jobs. - Fear: - Economic gains may accrue to a small elite (coders, tech firms) while masses suffer job insecurity. - ILO Findings: - International Labour Organization (ILO) estimates: - Over 75 million jobs globally could be displaced by AI and automation by 2025. - Vulnerable sectors include: - Routine office tasks (clerical, accounting) - Manufacturing - Customer support - Transportation (self-driving tech) - However, AI also creates new jobs, but they often require reskilling and high digital literacy. - Economic Survey 2024–25 (ES25) Recommendations: - In response to AI-led disruption, ES25 proposes a balanced approach: - 1. Reskilling & Upskilling: - Launch large-scale training programs in: - Data analysis, robotics, coding, digital marketing. - Emphasis on women, rural youth, and informal workers. - Public-private partnerships for curriculum alignment with industry needs. - 2. Establish Stewarding Institutions: - Independent regulatory-cum-research bodies to: - Monitor ethical AI development. - Prevent biases, protect privacy and data rights. - Ensure equity in AI deployment across regions/sectors. - 3. Rational Taxation on AI Companies: - Avoid excessive taxation on AI profits, as: - It may lead to R&D slowdown or capital flight. - Especially dangerous in early-stage AI ecosystems like India’s. - Suggests adopting a graduated tax or AI investment credits instead. - 4. Encourage AI for Public Good: - Promote AI in: - Healthcare diagnostics (rural clinics) - Agriculture (crop pattern prediction) - Education (personalized tutoring tools) - This balances job creation with social utility. - Job Elasticities vs. AI-Induced Job Loss -
Sector AI Job Loss Risk Reason
Teachers High AI-based tutors may replace ineffective teachers, though regulations (e.g., UGC/NEP) can mandate minimum teacher hiring.
Telecom Workers High Oligopolistic market (e.g., Jio, Airtel) allows companies to collude, lay off workers, and maintain high prices.
Financial Sector Low Requires salesmen, auditors, and analysts to oversee AI-driven processes.
Medical Sector Low Nurses and doctors remain essential.
Retail/Wholesale Low Salesmen, laborers, and transporters still needed.

- Sectors: - Expert services (51 lakh, e.g., manpower agencies), trading-commercial establishments, engineering. - India Employment Report 2024 - Released by: - ILO and Institute of Human Development (IHD). - Relevance: - Less critical for prelims; focuses on broader employment trends. - Pillar 4D: Indicators → GDP - Gross Domestic Product (GDP) - Definition: - GDP measures the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s borders over a specific period. It reflects economic activity and is used to assess growth, living standards, and policy impacts. - Domestic Territory: - Includes political frontiers, territorial waters, ships, aircraft, fishing vessels operated by residents, and embassies/consulates abroad (per NIOS). - GDP Potential: - Maximum output a country can produce using available labor and capital at a constant innovation rate. - GDP Gap: - Difference between potential GDP and real GDP. - GDP Calculation Methods: - Basic Concepts: - Three Methods: - Expenditure Approach: - Measures spending on final goods/services. - Production (GVA) - Approach: Measures value added in production. - Income Approach: - Measures income generated from production. - Current vs. Constant Prices: - Current Market Price: - GDP using current year prices. - Constant Market Price: - GDP adjusted for inflation (e.g., base year 2011) to reflect real growth. - Expenditure Approach: - Definition: - The expenditure approach calculates GDP as the sum of all spending on final goods and services in an economy: \( \text{GDP} = C + I + G + (X - M) \), where \( C \) is consumption, \( I \) is investment, \( G \) is government spending, and \( X - M \) is net exports. - Components: - Consumption (C): - Spending by households on new goods/services (e.g., cars, mobiles, notional rent for self-occupied houses). Excludes second-hand goods and new house construction (counted in investment). - Investment (I): - Spending on tangible assets (e.g., houses, factories, machinery), intangible assets (e.g., patents, software), and unsold inventory. Excludes financial investments like shares/bonds. - Government Spending (G): - Government purchases of goods/services (e.g., salaries, computers, vehicles). Excludes transfer payments (e.g., subsidies, scholarships) as they’re counted in consumption. - Net Exports (X - M): - Exports (foreign spending on Indian goods/services) minus imports (Indian spending on foreign goods/services). - Real-Life Application (NSO Data 2022-23, Approx): - Private Final Consumption Expenditure (PFCE): - ₹164 lakh crore (~60% of GDP). - Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) + Change in Stocks (CIS): - ₹79 lakh crore (~30%). - Government Final Consumption Expenditure (GFCE): - ₹28 lakh crore (~10%). - Net Exports: - -₹12 lakh crore (negative due to higher imports). - Discrepancies: - ₹6 lakh crore (errors in data collection/estimation). - Total GDP: - >₹270 lakh crore (current prices), ~₹159 lakh crore (constant prices, 2011 base). - Growth Rate: - Example: - 2021-22 GDP (constant prices) = ₹149 lakh crore; 2022-23 = ₹159 lakh crore. Growth rate = \( \frac{159 - 149}{149} \times 100 \approx 6.71\% \). - Production (GVA) Approach: - Definition: - The production approach calculates GDP as the Gross Value Added (GVA), the value of final goods/services minus intermediate goods used in production. - Formula: - GVA = Total value of final goods - Value of intermediate goods. - GDP = GVA (basic price) + Indirect Taxes - Subsidies. - Sectoral Contributions: - Typically: - Agriculture (~15%), Industry (~30%), Services (~55%). - Key Concept: - GVA focuses on the supply-side (producers’ perspective), avoiding double-counting by subtracting intermediate goods (e.g., steel used in engines). - Real-Life Example (LPG Cylinder): - GVA = ₹600, Taxes = ₹100, Subsidies = ₹200. - GDP = \( 600 + 100 - 200 = 500 \). - Example: -
StageTotal ProductionIntermediate GoodsValue Added
Mining (Steel)₹1 lakh₹0₹1 lakh
Engine Company₹5 lakh₹1 lakh (Steel)₹4 lakh
Tractor Company₹10 lakh₹5 lakh (Engine)₹5 lakh
Total₹16 lakh₹6 lakhGVA = ₹10 lakh
- Income Approach: - Definition: - The income approach calculates GDP as the sum of all incomes generated in production: \( \text{GDP} = W + I + P + R \), where \( W \) is wages, \( I \) is interest, \( P \) is profits, \( R \) is rent. - Components (NSO): - Compensation: - Employee salaries + employer contributions (e.g., EPFO/ESIC). - Operating Surplus and Mixed Income: - Profits and income from family-run enterprises. - Consumption of Fixed Assets: - Depreciation. - Result: - GDP at factor cost (excludes taxes/subsidies). - Additional Concepts: - Discrepancies: - Errors in data collection/estimation (e.g., ₹6 lakh crore in 2022-23) arise due to differences in data sources or methods, ensuring all three approaches yield the same GDP theoretically. - Current vs. Constant Prices: - Current prices reflect actual market values; constant prices (base year 2011) adjust for inflation to show real growth. - Growth Rate & Deflator - Growth Rate Formula: - \( \text{Growth Rate} = \frac{\text{GDP}_{\text{new}} - \text{GDP}_{\text{old}}}{\text{GDP}_{\text{old}}} \times 100 \). - Inflation Impact: - Use base year (2011) to convert current prices to constant prices. - GDP Deflator: - Also called Implicit Price Deflator. - GDP Deflator Formula: - (Nominal GDP @ Current Prices / Real GDP @ Constant Prices) × 100 - Example (ES22, 2019): -

- GDP Misc Topics - 2015 Calculation Reform - Compliance with UN System of National Accounts (SNA-2008). - Changes: - Base year changed from 2004 to 2011. - Updated data collection/classification for: - Crop and livestock data, handicraft industries. - Meat value calculation. - Services by local bodies (municipal bus, school, water, sanitation). - Informal sector (e.g., domestic maids). - Sand extraction, construction, mining. - Company data: - From Annual Survey of Industries (ASI)/Index of Industrial Production (IIP) to Ministry of Corporate Affairs’ balance sheets. - Financial services: - Improved data capture with RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA. - Private coaching, hotel-tourism: - Use service-tax data for cross-checking. - Backseries Controversy - Outdated topic, removed for prelims. - Changing Base Years to 2017 & 18 - MoSPI (2018-Feb) proposed: - GDP & IIP: - From 2011 to 2017-18. - CPI: - From 2012 to 2018-19. - Reason: - Accommodate economic changes (GST, Demonetization, RERA). - Economic Cycle - Phases: - Expansion/Prosperity/Boom: - Rising GDP. - Recession: - Negative growth for two consecutive quarters (e.g., USA 2007-09, subprime crisis). - Depression: - Severe, prolonged recession (e.g., USA 1929-39, stock market crash). - Recovery: - From recession/depression to prosperity. - Technical Recession: - Negative GDP growth for two consecutive quarters. - Recessionary Phase: - GDP growth lower than previous quarter. - Expansionary Phase: - GDP growth higher than previous quarter. - Post-Corona: V-Shaped Recovery for India - V-Shaped: - Sharp decline followed by quick recovery (e.g., USA 1918-20 Spanish Flu: –3.5% to 7.5%). - U-Shaped: - Slow recovery. - W-Shaped: - Recovery, decline, then recovery again. - K-Shaped: - Some sectors recover (e.g., e-learning, e-commerce), others lag (e.g., tourism, restaurants). - ES21 Projection: V-shaped recovery due to: - Mass vaccination boosting contact-sensitive sectors (trade, hotels, transport, tourism). - Unlocking pent-up demand. - Low base effect. - Low Base Effect in GDP Growth - Smaller denominator (previous year’s GDP) inflates % growth. - Example: - 2021 GDP growth ~9% due to low base from Corona 2020 (vs. usual 6-7%). - Misc. Terms: - Animal Spirit - John Maynard Keynes: - Investors/consumers driven by psychological urges, not rational analysis. - 2019 RBI Report: - Weak domestic demand, animal spirit not reviving, causing slowdown. - Pent-Up Demand - Postponed shopping during recession; surges during recovery or festivals. - 2020 Diwali: - Surge in online/offline shopping due to discounts, but critics argue it’s temporary. - Lipstick Effect / Little Luxuries - During slowdown, people buy small luxuries (e.g., lipstick) for psychological thrill, not expensive items. - Hysteresis - Economic effects persist after cause is removed (e.g., reduced spending post-Corona due to lockdown/job-loss fears). - Doom Loop - One negative condition creates another, amplifying the first (e.g., Pakistan’s lack of funds → no schemes → poor manufacturing → low taxes → lack of funds). - Financial Contagion - Financial disruptions spread across countries/sectors (e.g., Silicon Valley Bank collapse → Indian startups → IT sector → banks/share market). - Goldilocks Scenario - Ideal economic growth: - Not too high (causing inflation) nor too low (causing slowdown). - Headwinds & Tailwinds - Headwinds: - Challenges (e.g., inflation, global slowdown, oil prices). - Tailwinds: - Opportunities (e.g., young population, favorable monsoon). - GDP Growth Rate & 5 Trillion Economy - World Bank-ICP’s GDP Series (PPP) - Outdated topic, removed. - Budget-2019: $5 Trillion Economy - GDP (Current Prices): - 2014-15: - $1.85 trillion - 2018-19: - $2.70 trillion - 2019-20: - $2.90 trillion - Target: - $5 trillion by 31/3/2025, $7 trillion (CEA Nageswaran). - ES19: - Blueprint for $5 trillion economy. - Counterview (C. Rangarajan): - Unachievable by 2025, requires 9-10% annual growth (current: 5-6%). - Note: - $5 trillion target still valid for Mains answers, as government hasn’t officially abandoned it. - GDP Growth Rate Before Corona - Growth Rate Decline (Pre-Corona) - Causes: - Protectionism (China, USA), US-Iran tensions → reduced global trade. - Sharp decline in automobile purchases (worsened by Bharat-6 norms’ higher costs). - Slow investment due to Twin Balance Sheet Syndrome (TBS), IL&FS-NBFC crisis. - Demonetization, GST: - Short-term harm, long-term benefit (per ES20). - Negative GDP Growth (Post-Independence) - Occurred 4 times: -

- GDP → $5 Trillion → How to Achieve: ES Strategy - Savings: - Income excess of consumption (private: households/businesses; public: government). - Includes household financial savings (deposits, insurance), corporate retained earnings, and govt surplus (if any). - Investment: - Domestic savings + foreign capital in physical assets (machines, buildings, roads, unsold inventory). - Key for capacity creation → boosts employment, productivity, and exports. - Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF): - Investment – disposal of assets; ignores depreciation, land purchases. - Proxy for productive investment → tracked in GDP expenditure method. - High GFCF/GDP ratio = healthy capital formation. - Capital Output Ratio: - Capital needed per unit of output. - Lower ratio → more efficient use of capital. - Example: - USA: - $3 lakh plant → 2 lakh bottles → Ratio = 1.5 (better). - India: - $3 lakh plant → 1 lakh bottles → Ratio = 3 (worse). - High ratio in India: - Reason for subdued growth. - Causes: - outdated tech, infrastructure gaps, low human capital productivity. - Incremental Capital Output Ratio (ICOR): - Additional capital needed for additional output. - Indicator of marginal capital productivity. - India: - 3.8 (2016) → 4.9 (2018) → 6.9 (2019). - Higher ICOR = less efficient production. - Target: - Reduce ICOR to 3–4 through reforms and efficiency. - Investment More Important Than Savings: - ES18: - To achieve 9% growth, prioritize investment → GFCF increase → automatic growth and savings increase. - Strategies: - Resolve TBS (Twin Balance Sheet), promote Make in India, Startup India, reform tax/labor/environment/FDI laws. - Investment-led growth → demand for goods, jobs → higher income → savings improve later. - Savings mobilization (PMJDY, pension, gold bonds, demonetization) important but not urgent. - Purpose: - widen financial inclusion, improve formal channel savings. - Capital Intensity Ratio (CIR): - Definition: - CIR tells how much capital (like machines, equipment, buildings) is used compared to labour in producing output. - It shows whether a production process is capital-intensive or labour-intensive. - Macroeconomics Formula: - CIR = Total Capital Employed ÷ Total Labour Employed - High CIR → More machines used, fewer workers. - Low CIR → More workers used, fewer machines. - Accounting Formula: - CIR = Total Assets ÷ Total Sales - Indicates how much capital is needed to generate ₹1 of sales revenue. - High CIR Sectors (Capital-Intensive): - Oil Refineries - Steel Plants - Automobile Manufacturing - Infrastructure Projects - Characteristics: - High fixed costs (plant, machinery) - Lower employment generation - Low CIR Sectors (Labour-Intensive): - Textiles and Garments - MSMEs (Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises) - Services (restaurants, tourism, etc.) - Construction - Characteristics: - More employment per unit of investment - Suitable for labour-surplus economies like India - Significance: - For job creation, focus on sectors with low CIR. - For productivity and growth, capital-intensive sectors are also essential. - Paradox of Savings / Paradox of Thrift - John Maynard Keynes (1936): - Individual saving → reduced demand → GDP/job loss → less savings nationally. - Counterargument: - Savings → bank loans → R&D/innovation → future demand (long-term benefit). - - Misc. Terms: Chinese Atma-Nirbhar / Dual Circulation - China’s post-Corona strategy: - Boost local production with foreign tech/investment (details not important). - GDP Growth → ES Observations - Frontloaded Economic Stimulus (USA/EU) - Economic Stimulus: - Definition: - Government policy tools used during downturns to revive demand and production. - Includes fiscal (tax cuts, subsidies, transfers) and monetary (rate cuts, liquidity) interventions. - Objective: - Jumpstart the economy during crises (e.g., COVID-19 pandemic, 2008 crisis). - Instruments: - Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT) - Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Schemes (ECLGS) - Interest subvention, tax holidays, loan moratoriums - Fed’s QE (Quantitative Easing), ECB stimulus packages - Frontloading: - Definition: - Delivering the bulk of the stimulus in the early phase of the crisis period. - Example: - Fund Disbursement: 3-3-1-1 (₹8000 cr in Year 1, 8000 cr in Year 2, 2000 cr in Year 3 & 4) vs. 2-2-2-2 (even spread across four years). - Rationale: - Faster recovery and confidence restoration - Avoid prolonged recession/deflation cycles - Drawbacks: - Can lead to overheating if demand outpaces supply capacity - Potential for wasteful spending if planning/execution is weak - Overheating: - Definition: - A phase where rapid demand growth leads to inflation, asset bubbles, and capacity strain. - Symptoms: - High CPI/WPI inflation - Wage-price spiral - Central banks forced to tighten interest rates - ES23 Observation: - Post-COVID, USA and EU’s frontloaded stimulus led to high inflation once pandemic supply chains were restored but demand stayed elevated. - Fed and ECB had to increase interest rates sharply in 2022–23. - Lessons for India: - Need for calibrated stimulus, balancing speed with sustainability. - Prefer targeted spending (Capex, Infrastructure, MSMEs) over blanket handouts. - 4 Structural Challenges to GDP Growth (CEA V. Anantha Nageswaran, 2024) - Challenge #1: Onshoring, Friendshoring & Home-shoring - Friendshoring: - Definition: - Reconfiguring global supply chains to rely more on friendly or geopolitically aligned countries. - Example: - USA importing semiconductors from Taiwan and South Korea rather than China. - Implication for India: - India's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme may lose traction if major manufacturers prefer friendlier nations over India. - Onshoring: - Definition: - Bringing production and supply chains back to the domestic economy from abroad. - Example: - Tesla shifting its focus from China to set up plants in the USA. - Implication for India: - Reduces potential for foreign direct investment and job creation in India if global firms prioritize home markets. - Home-shoring: - Definition: - Remote work strategies that allow firms to reduce operational costs by letting employees work from home. - Example: - Infosys and TCS adopting hybrid/remote work models post-COVID. - Implication: - Urban economic patterns may shift, demand for real estate and services in business hubs may decline. - Overall Impact: - Weakens India's export potential. - Indicates a retreat from hyper-globalization. - Contributes to geo-economic fragmentation. - Challenge #2: Energy Security vs. Green Transition - Key Tension: - Ensuring reliable energy access while transitioning to sustainable sources. - Example: - India continues to use coal to meet base power demands even while investing in solar and wind. - Trade-off: - Subsidies for renewables reduce fiscal space for other sectors. - Climate activism (domestic/international) adds pressure to cut down on fossil fuels rapidly. - Implication: - Energy transition must be balanced, or it may threaten both growth and climate goals. - Challenge #3: Disruptive Potential of Artificial Intelligence - IMF Warning: - Up to 40% of global jobs are at risk of automation due to AI (higher in advanced economies). - Nature of Threat: - Routine and cognitive tasks are more exposed to AI displacement. - Raises inequality: - those with digital/AI skills benefit disproportionately. - Implication: - India must invest in AI regulation, upskilling, and adapting labor laws to changing job landscapes. - Challenge #4: Shortage of Talented & Skilled Workforce - Skill Mismatch: - Rapid technological change outpaces the current educational and vocational training systems. - Sectoral Gaps: - Shortages in key areas like semiconductor design, advanced manufacturing, data science, clean energy. - Implication: - Constraints on productivity, innovation, and global competitiveness. - Solution Path: - Expand and reform skilling programs (e.g., PMKVY). - Link education with industry needs through stronger apprenticeships and internships. - GDP → GNP to NNP to Per Capita Income - Primary Income: - Includes factor incomes earned through production: wages (labor), interest (capital), profits (entrepreneurship), and rent (land). - Secondary Income: - Includes unilateral transfers with no production involved: gifts, donations, foreign remittances, aid; excluded from GNP as they’re not earned through factor services. - Gross National Product (GNP): - Formula: - GDP + Net Primary Income from Abroad. - Net Primary Income = Income earned by Indian residents abroad – Income earned by foreigners in India. - GNP highlights the income accruing to Indian nationals, regardless of geographic production. - Net National Product (NNP): - Formula: - GNP – Depreciation. - Depreciation: - Loss in asset value over time due to wear and tear; deducted to reflect net production. - NNP at Factor Cost (National Income): - Formula: - NNP at Market Price – Indirect Taxes + Subsidies. - Factor Cost: - Reflects actual income earned by factors of production, excluding market distortions like taxes or subsidies. - Per Capita Income: - Formula: - National Income ÷ Total Population. - Indicates average income per person; key metric for comparing living standards across regions or time. - Data: -

- Budget-2023: - Govt claimed Per capita income doubled to ₹1.97 lakh since 2014; actual figures vary by MoSPI methodology. - SBI Research: - Projected per capita income (nominal) by 2046–47: ₹14.9 lakh. - Net Domestic Product (NDP): - Formula: - GDP – Depreciation. - Focuses only on domestic output; excludes foreign income. - Depreciation rates defined by Ministry of Commerce via asset classification. - Misc. Concepts: - Gross National Income (GNI): - Similar to GNP but includes both factor incomes and net transfers like taxes/subsidies with the rest of the world. - National Disposable Income: - Formula: - NNP + Net current transfers (e.g., remittances, gifts, donations); reflects total resources available for consumption/savings. - Personal Income: - Theoretical concept involving national income, corporate tax, undistributed profits, government transfers etc.; not UPSC-priority. - Personal Disposable Income: - Formula: - Personal Income – Personal Taxes – Non-tax Payments (e.g., traffic fines); indicates what households can actually spend/save. - National Income Accounting: - Covered in NCERT Class 12 (Introductory Macroeconomics); foundational for understanding macro indicators and budgeting. - Depreciation of Fixed Assets - Fixed Assets: - Long-term tangible assets used in production over multiple years, not consumed in a single cycle (e.g., machinery, buildings, vehicles, computers). - Depreciation: - Systematic decline in fixed asset value over time due to usage, wear, and market changes; recorded annually in accounts to reflect asset aging. - Factors Causing Depreciation: - Wear and tear from regular use (e.g., factory machines). - Obsolescence due to tech upgrades or new models (e.g., smartphones, software). - Natural deterioration from climate or environment (e.g., rusting, moisture, heat). - Accidental damage (e.g., earthquakes, floods, fires). - Features: - Gradual, irreversible loss in value; not random or one-time. - Treated as business expense for tax deduction: - reduces taxable profits (Profit ₹50,000 – Depreciation ₹10,000 = Taxable Income ₹40,000). - Non-cash expense: - doesn’t involve immediate outflow but reflects economic cost. - Provides realistic asset valuation and true profit/loss estimation. - Depletion and Amortization: - Depletion: - Similar to depreciation; applied to exhaustible natural resources (e.g., oil wells, coal mines). - Amortization: - Applied to intangible assets (e.g., trademarks, patents, licenses); spreads cost over useful life. - Types of Nations: - High Income, Low Income - World Bank Classification (2020, per capita GNI basis): - High-Income: - ≥$12,696 (e.g., USA, Germany, Israel). - Upper-Middle-Income: - $4,096–$12,695 (e.g., China, Malaysia). - Lower-Middle-Income: - $1,046–$4,095 (e.g., India, with $1,928 in 2020). - Low-Income: - ≤$1,045 (e.g., Chad, Somalia). - IBRD: - Imposes additional surcharges on loans to high-income countries since 2018. - 2022 WTO Dispute: - India filed complaint against China for retaining developing country benefits despite upper-middle-income status. - Advanced Economies (AE) - IMF Criteria: - High per capita income with consistent growth. - Export diversification (not reliant on single commodities). - Deep integration into global financial markets. - Includes most OECD members pre-1990s (e.g., USA, UK, Japan). - EMDEs - Emerging Market and Developing Economies (non-AEs). - Subgroups: - Low-Income Countries (LIC): - Low productivity, poor HDI (e.g., Afghanistan, Nepal). - Emerging Market Economies (EM): - Rapidly industrializing, high investment inflows (e.g., India, Brazil, Indonesia). - Bangladesh Transition from LDC to Developing Country: - UN ECOSOC-CDP LDC Graduation Criteria: - Per Capita GNI: - ≥$1,230 (3-year average). - Economic & Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI): - Sensitivity to shocks (natural disasters, export instability). - Human Assets Index (HAI): - Health, education, and nutrition metrics. - November 2021: - Bangladesh, Nepal, and Laos to graduate by 2026. - Negative Outcomes: - Loss of WTO duty-free-quota-free access. - Stricter compliance with WTO rules (e.g., IPR, agri subsidies). - No longer eligible for interest-free/mildly concessional loans from multilateral agencies. - Reduced aid/grants from donors and climate funds. - Positive Outcomes: - Reflects economic progress and political stability. - Increases investor confidence, boosts FDI, jobs, and growth. - Bangladesh Per Capita GDP Higher Than India: - Now outdated; gap narrowed post-pandemic recovery. - Bhutan Graduates from LDC (2023): - Bhutan exited LDC list in December 2023 after meeting all graduation thresholds; mirrors Bangladesh’s transition pathway. - India as a Developed Country: - PM Modi (2022): - Announced vision for India to become a developed nation by 2047 (centenary of independence). - Indicators of Developed Status: - High GDP and per capita income. - Strong HDI (health, education, life expectancy). - Social equity, urban infrastructure, industrial base. - Strategic Path: - Build upon economic pillars like manufacturing (PLI, Make in India), services (Digital India), infrastructure (PM Gati Shakti), and governance reforms (Ease of Doing Business, FDI liberalization). - GDP & Per Capita Income → Criticism / Limitations - GDP Issues: - Unorganised Sector Exclusion: - Informal/unregistered economic activities often go unaccounted. - Example: - Street vendors, small-scale artisans, daily-wage laborers. - tax​ evasion: - Firms underreport turnover to evade taxes → leads to underestimation in GDP calculation. - National Statistical Office (NSO) relies heavily on reported data. - Parallel Economy: - Shadow economy involving black​ money, cash-based transactions not routed via banking channels → excluded from formal GDP. - Example: - Real estate sector with cash components in deals. - Ignores Qualitative/Necessary Environmental Externalities: - Pollution vs. Output Paradox: - Coal-based power generation boosts GDP, but causes environmental degradation → cost not deducted. - Environmental degradation reduces sustainability of growth. - Green Accounting / Green GDP: - Introduced by Peter Wood (1980s). - Adjusts GDP by subtracting ecological costs. - GEP (Gross Environment Product): - Uttarakhand (2021) became first Indian state to adopt GEP. - Includes value of forests, air, water, soil – integrated into state GSDP. - Non-Market Activities Ignored: - Activities with real economic value but not bought/sold in the market are excluded. - Example: - Unpaid domestic work by homemakers, volunteer work, child-rearing, etc. - Opportunity Cost Ignored: - GDP measures "what is", not "what could be". - Example: - A child laborer producing ₹50,000 worth of fireworks adds to GDP. - But loses the chance to earn ₹5,00,000 over life as a skilled engineer → hidden cost not reflected. - Ignores Inequality: - GDP aggregates income, but doesn’t show how it’s distributed. - India’s rising GDP may coexist with high Gini coefficient. - Example: - Top 10% may own 77% of wealth (Oxfam). - Alternatives to capture human well-being: - Gross Happiness Index (Bhutan). - Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI). - Human Development Index (HDI) – explained under Pillar 6. - GDP ≠ Economic Development: - Economic Growth: - Quantitative rise in GDP. - May coexist with poverty, malnutrition, illiteracy. - Economic Development: - Qualitative improvements: - education, healthcare, equality, sustainability. - Includes structural transformation (shift from agri to industry/services). - Important Distinction: - A country may grow rich (GDP ↑) without becoming truly developed (HDI remains stagnant). - Conceptual Add-ons: - Per Capita Income (PCI) Limitations: - Hides intra-country disparities. - Skewed by few ultra-rich → raises average artificially. - Doesn’t indicate standard of living or purchasing power. - Doesn’t Account for: - Leisure time. - Social capital (trust, community networks). - Happiness and mental health. - Related Indexes/Approaches: - Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) → considers health, education, standard of living. - OECD’s Better Life Index → includes housing, income, jobs, community, etc. - Pillar 4E: Economic Indicators - Inflation and Production - Definition: - Economic indicators are statistical measures that assess the health, performance, and trends of an economy, providing critical insights into inflation, production, and consumption patterns for policymaking and economic analysis. - Context: - In India, indicators like the Consumer Price Index (CPI), Wholesale Price Index (WPI), and Index of Industrial Production (IIP) are essential for UPSC examinations, reflecting the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) inflation targeting, industrial performance, and economic policy effectiveness, particularly in the post-COVID recovery context. - Significance for India: - These indicators guide RBI’s monetary policy, government fiscal strategies, and reforms aimed at sustainable growth, financial inclusion, and stability in a globalizing economy, supporting India’s vision of becoming a developed nation by 2047. - Inflation: Concepts and Dynamics - Definition: - Inflation is the sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time, reducing purchasing power. Deflation is the persistent decline in prices, often signaling economic stagnation or recession. - Inflationary and Deflationary Gaps: - Inflationary Gap: - Occurs when aggregate demand (AD = Consumption + Investment + Government Spending + Net Exports) exceeds aggregate supply at full employment, leading to price increases. - Causes: - Increased money supply (e.g., RBI printing money). - Higher propensity to consume (e.g., increased disposable income from schemes like MNREGA or PM-KISAN). - Increased investment or government expenditure. - Rising net exports due to global demand. - High economic growth driving excessive demand. - Deflationary Gap: - Occurs when aggregate demand falls below aggregate supply, causing price declines. - Causes: - Reduced money supply (e.g., tight monetary policy). - Increased propensity to save or delayed purchases expecting further price drops. - Decreased investment or government spending (e.g., fiscal consolidation). - Reduced net exports due to global economic slowdown. - Economic depression or recession lowering demand. - Inflationary and Deflationary Spirals: - Inflationary Spiral: - Rising prices lead workers to demand higher wages, increasing production costs, which firms pass on as higher prices, further fueling inflation. - Deflationary Spiral: - Falling prices reduce firm profits, leading to lower production, wage cuts, or layoffs, reducing demand and further lowering prices. - Combating Inflation and Deflation - Combating Inflation: - RBI’s Monetary Policy: - Tight or hawkish policy: - Increasing interest rates (e.g., repo rate) to make loans costlier, reducing money supply and demand. - Issuing inflation-indexed bonds or sovereign gold bonds to absorb excess liquidity. - Government Measures: - Increase direct taxes to reduce disposable income. - Curtail fiscal deficits to limit public spending. - Reduce subsidies that increase money supply without boosting production. - Implement Essential Commodities Act, stock limits, or minimum export prices to control prices. - Use schemes like FCI’s Open Market Sale or Operation Greens for price stabilization. - Combating Deflation: - RBI’s Monetary Policy: - Easy or dovish policy: - Lowering interest rates to make loans cheaper, encouraging spending and investment. - Government Measures: - Provide tax deductions, exemptions, or subsidies to consumers to boost consumption (e.g., GST cuts on consumer goods). - Increase public expenditure on infrastructure (e.g., highways, dams) to stimulate demand in industries like steel and cement. - Neutral and Natural Rate of Interest - Definition: - The neutral rate of interest (or natural rate) is the theoretical interest rate at which monetary policy neither stimulates nor restricts economic growth, balancing aggregate demand and supply at full employment. - Significance: - Guides RBI in setting policy rates to achieve stable inflation (2-6% as per RBI Act) without causing overheating or slowdown. - Under the RBI Act (amended in 2016), the RBI is legally mandated to maintain CPI inflation at 4% ± 2%, i.e., within the 2% to 6% band. - This is part of India's Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) Framework, and the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is held accountable for meeting this target. - NAIRU and Phillips Curve: - Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU): - Definition: - It is the lowest level of unemployment that an economy can sustain without triggering accelerating inflation. - Below this level: - Excess demand for goods/services and labor causes wages and prices to rise. - Employers bid up wages to attract scarce labor → cost-push inflation. - NAIRU ≠ Natural Rate of Unemployment: - NAIRU is empirical and may vary due to structural factors (e.g., technology, labor laws, productivity). - Policy Relevance: - If actual unemployment < NAIRU → signal for RBI to tighten monetary policy. - If actual unemployment > NAIRU → risk of output loss, unemployment → policy may ease. - Example: - If NAIRU is estimated at 5% and current unemployment is 3.5%, inflationary pressure is likely. - Phillips Curve: - Short-term Phillips Curve (STPC): - Shows inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment. - Mechanism: - Lower unemployment → higher demand → firms raise prices → inflation. - Higher employment → workers demand higher wages → cost-push inflation. - Shape: - Downward sloping, valid only in the short run when inflation expectations are static. - Example: - If unemployment falls from 6% to 4%, inflation may rise from 3% to 6%. - Long-term Phillips Curve (LTPC): - Conceptualized by Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps. - Assumes people adjust expectations; no long-term trade-off between inflation and unemployment. - Shape: - Vertical at NAIRU → inflation can rise or fall, but unemployment returns to NAIRU. - Implication: - Any attempt to keep unemployment below NAIRU permanently leads to accelerating inflation. - Example: - Unemployment fixed at 3% → inflation may be 4% in Year 1, 6% in Year 2, 9% in Year 3, etc. - Criticism & Modern View: - 1970s stagflation (high inflation + high unemployment) challenged the classical Phillips Curve. - Modern version incorporates expectations-augmented Phillips Curve and anchored inflation expectations. - Recent observations (e.g., post-2008 crisis, post-COVID recovery) show flattening of Phillips Curve: - Even with low unemployment, inflation remained subdued until supply shocks like in 2021–22. - Inflation Types: - Based on Causation - Demand-Pull Inflation: - Occurs when excessive demand (“too much money chasing too few goods”) outstrips supply, often due to schemes like MNREGA, Pay Commission, or Universal Basic Income increasing disposable income. - Monetary Inflation: - Results from excessive money supply, often due to RBI monetizing fiscal deficits (e.g., printing money to finance government debt). - Cost-Push Inflation: - Arises from increased input costs, such as: - High crude oil prices increasing transport costs. - Wage hikes from trade or labor union actions. - Natural disasters reducing agricultural output (e.g., lower potato production raising chip prices). - Profit-Push Inflation: - Caused by cartels or monopolists deliberately reducing supply or hiking prices for profit (e.g., OPEC oil production cuts). - Built-In Inflation: - Linked to wage-price spirals, where rising prices prompt wage demands, increasing costs and further raising prices. - Repressed Inflation: - Occurs when government imposes price controls or rationing (e.g., during wars), but prices surge once controls are lifted due to pent-up demand. - Stagflation: - Combines high inflation, high unemployment, and low growth, leading to a stagnant economy. - Skewflation: - Episodic price rises in specific commodities (e.g., pulses, onions) while general inflation remains stable. - Structural Inflation: - Embedded in the economic system, requiring policy overhaul to address (e.g., MSP hikes for wheat but not pulses, causing pulse shortages). - Shrinkflation: - Companies reduce product size while maintaining prices (e.g., Vim Soap from 155 gm to 135 gm for ₹10). - Taxflation: - Price increases due to higher indirect taxes (e.g., excise or VAT on petrol/diesel). - black​ money-Induced Inflation: - tax​ evasion increases disposable income, boosting lavish spending and driving prices (e.g., real estate). - Black Marketing and Hoarding: - Traders artificially reduce supply, causing price spikes. - Credit Inflation: - Cheap loans from banks increase demand, pushing prices up. - Based on Speed/Quantum - Creeping Inflation: - Moderate, ~4% per annum, considered safe for job creation and growth. - Walking/Trotting Inflation: - Above 4%, transitioning to double-digit rates. - Running Inflation: - Double-digit inflation, significantly impacting purchasing power. - Galloping/Hyperinflation: - Extremely high rates (20%–10,000%+), rendering money nearly worthless (e.g., post-Versailles Germany, modern Venezuela, Zimbabwe, Iran). - Runaway Inflation and Depreciation: - Runaway Inflation: - Uncontrollable, rapid price increases (e.g., hyperinflation scenarios). - Runaway Depreciation: - Rapid decline in local currency value (e.g., Pakistani rupee: $1 = 175 PKR in 2022 to 300 PKR in 2023). - Inflation: Base Effect - Definition: - The base effect refers to the impact of the price level in the previous year (the base year) on the year-on-year inflation rate. - A low base tends to inflate the current inflation figure, while a high base tends to deflate it — even if absolute price change is similar. - This can distort the interpretation of inflation trends and misguide policy responses if not understood properly. - Example: - Suppose prices of onions: - ₹100 in 2010 → ₹110 in 2011 → ₹120 in 2012. - Absolute rise = ₹10 each year (same). - Calculated YoY inflation: - 2011: - (110 - 100)/100 = 10% - 2012: - (120 - 110)/110 = 9.09% - Even though the price rise is constant, inflation appears lower in 2012 because the base is higher. - Real-World Context: - COVID-19 and Oil Prices: - In 2020, crude oil prices crashed globally → low base. - In 2021, moderate recovery in oil prices → artificially high inflation due to base effect. - CPI spike in 2022-23: - High food inflation in 2022 made 2023's CPI look relatively cooler, not necessarily due to improvement in fundamentals. - Implications: - Monetary Policy: - RBI (or any central bank) must consider base effects while interpreting inflation trends and deciding interest rate changes. - Reacting to base-driven inflation can lead to pro-cyclical errors (e.g., hiking rates in response to base effect rather than real demand-pull inflation). - Communication: - Government and RBI often cite the base effect while explaining temporary inflation surges or disinflation in press releases. - Related Concepts: - Headline vs. Core Inflation: - Base effect often impacts headline inflation more (due to food/fuel volatility), while core inflation (ex-food & fuel) is more stable. - Statistical Illusion: - It is a form of statistical illusion in inflation measurement that policymakers and analysts need to adjust for. - WPI vs CPI Base Years: - Changes in base year (e.g., WPI revised from 2004–05 to 2011–12) also affect trend comparison due to recalibration. - Notes: - When inflation is very high in the base year, the next year might show disinflation or even deflation without prices falling in absolute terms. - Base effect is temporary, and its distortion usually fades after 12 months unless external shocks persist. - Effects of Inflation and Deflation - On Individuals and Groups: -
Group During Inflation During Deflation
Businessmen/Borrowers Gain due to faster-rising product prices compared to input costs, increasing profits. Face losses as product prices fall faster than production costs, leading to layoffs.
Fixed-Income Groups/Lenders Suffer as real purchasing power declines due to reduced real interest rates. Benefit from increased purchasing power, but risk job losses per Phillips Curve.
Currency Exchange Rate Rupee weakens as purchasing power falls, reducing foreign demand for Indian goods. Rupee strengthens, boosting export competitiveness.
- Inflating Away Debt: - Definition: - A strategy where governments or central banks allow or induce moderate inflation to reduce the real burden of existing debt. - Mechanism: - Inflation reduces the real value (purchasing power) of money, so the fixed nominal repayments on government bonds or loans cost less in real terms. - Tools: - Quantitative easing (QE): - central bank buys government securities to increase money supply. - Accommodative monetary policy: - lower interest rates stimulate demand and inflation. - Motivation: - Helps manage high debt-to-GDP ratios without explicit defaults or austerity. - Limitations: - Only effective if inflation remains moderate and controlled. - Can lead to loss of investor confidence if perceived as deliberate debasement. - Inflation Impact on Exports: - Currency Depreciation: - High domestic inflation erodes the value of the currency (e.g., rupee), making imports costlier and increasing trade deficits. - Export Competitiveness: - If inflation is higher than trading partners, domestic goods become relatively expensive, reducing price competitiveness. - Example: - Onion exports: - If onions were ₹50/kg (with ₹75/USD rate, $0.66), and rise to ₹100/kg while currency depreciates to ₹80/USD, the new price is $1.25/kg—nearly double—hurting foreign demand. - Exceptions: - If the currency depreciates more than inflation, exports can still benefit. - Inelastic or quality-dependent goods may not be impacted heavily. - Global Perception: - Persistent inflation signals economic mismanagement, reducing trust in trade partners and investments. - Inflation and Production Indices - Laspeyres, Paasche, and Fisher Indices: - Laspeyres Index: - Uses a fixed basket of goods with base-year weights to calculate CPI, WPI, and IIP, measuring price/production changes against a base year. - Paasche Index: - Uses current-year quantities to calculate what today’s goods would cost at base-year prices. - Fisher Index: - Geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche indices for a balanced measure. - Consumer Price Index (CPI): - Measures retail price changes for a basket of goods and services, base year 2012, by NSO, MoSPI. - Components (All India, weights): - Food & Beverages: - 45.86% - Services (Transport, Communication, Health, Education, Recreation): - 20.62% - Housing: - 10.07% - Fuel & Light: - 6.84% - Clothing & Footwear: - 6.53% - Miscellaneous (Personal Care, Household Goods): - 7.69% - CPI Variations: - Rural: - No housing weight, higher food weight (54.18%). - Urban: - Includes housing, lower food weight. - CPI-Industrial Workers (CPI-IW): - Base year 2016, by Labour Bureau, monitors prices for industrial workers. - CPI-Rural/Agricultural Labourers: - Base year 1986 (proposed change to 2019), by Labour Bureau. - Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI): - Tracks food prices (cereals, meat, fish, eggs, milk, oils, fruits, vegetables, pulses, sugar, spices), excluding non-alcoholic beverages and prepared meals. - Wholesale Price Index (WPI): - Measures wholesale price changes, base year 2011, by Economic Advisor, DPIIT. - Components (weights): - Manufactured Products: - ~64% - Primary Articles (Unprocessed Food, Crude Petroleum, Minerals): - ~23% - Fuel & Power: - ~13% - Wholesale Price Index (WPI) vs Consumer Price Index (CPI) Divergence: - CPI includes indirect taxes and services, WPI excludes them. - CPI gives higher weight to food (~46%) than WPI (~19% for primary articles). - Example: - April-July 2020, WPI was negative, while CPI inflation exceeded 6% due to food price volatility. - Index of Industrial Production (IIP) - Definition: - A monthly index by NSO, base year 2011, using Laspeyres formula, measuring production across 407 item groups in mining, manufacturing, and electricity. - Classification by Use (Weights): - Primary Goods: - 34% (ores, minerals, crude oil, electricity). - Capital Goods: - 8% (machinery, boilers, vehicles). - Infrastructure/Construction Goods: - 12% (cement, cables, paints). - Intermediate Goods: - 17% (yarn, steel tubes, fasteners). - Consumer Durables: - 13% (TVs, cars, jewelry). - Consumer Non-Durables: - 15% (food, beverages, cigarettes). - Sector-Based Weights: - Manufacturing: - 77.63% - Mining: - 14.37% - Electricity: - 7.99% - Trends: - 2018-2019: - IIP declined due to NPA issues, ILFS-NBFC crisis, protectionism, and reduced demand in automobiles and real estate. - 2020: - IIP hit a low in April due to COVID lockdown, later recovered. - 2021: - IIP surged 22% in March due to base effect. - 2024: - Economic Survey notes healthy IIP growth. - Index of Eight Core Industries - Definition: - A monthly index by EA-DPIIT, base year 2011, focusing on eight core industries with 40.27% weight in IIP. - Components (Descending Weight): - Refinery Products, Electricity, Steel, Coal, Crude Oil, Natural Gas, Cement, Fertilizers. - Other Economic Indices - Producer Price Index (PPI): - Measures price changes from sellers’ perspective, covering goods and services, unlike WPI (goods only). - Experimental Service Price Index: - By EA-DPIIT, covers railway, port, air, postal, telecom, banking, and insurance services. - Banking Business Service Price Index: - By RBI, tracks fees for NEFT, RTGS, card transactions, and DEMAT accounts, base year 2011. - Inflation Expectation Survey: - RBI’s quarterly survey of ~5,000 households across 18 cities on expected inflation. - Business Inflation Expectations Survey: - By IIM Ahmedabad, assesses business expectations on price trends. - Housing Inflation: - National Housing Bank’s RESIDEX (HPI, base year 2017) tracks residential house prices. - RBI’s Home Price Index monitors housing market trends. - Causes: - Post-COVID cheap loans and investment demand increased housing prices. - Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (2022-23) - Overview: - Conducted by NSO, MoSPI, released in February 2024, covering Monthly Per Capita Consumption Expenditure (MPCE) from August 2022 to July 2023. - MPCE Without Imputation: -

- High-Frequency Indicators (HFIs) - Definition: - HFIs are frequently updated economic data providing real-time insights into economic activity, unlike slower indicators like annual GDP. - Examples (Economic Survey 2021-22): - Inflation: - Retail CPI. - Financial: - UPI/ATM transactions, currency in circulation, SENSEX, NIFTY, G-Sec yields. - Taxation: - Monthly GST, E-way bills. - Rural/Agro: - APMC mandi arrivals, tractor sales, MNREGA work demand. - Production: - IIP, power consumption, vehicle sales. - Transport: - Railway, port, airway traffic, road toll collection. - Global Trade: - FDI, FPI, crude oil prices, Baltic Dry Index, forex reserves. - Pros and Cons: - Pros: - Enable rapid policy responses and targeted interventions. - Cons: - High noise-to-signal ratio (e.g., market fluctuations due to rumors may not reflect economic fundamentals). - Thalinomics (Economic Survey 2020) - Definition: - Thalinomics estimates the cost of a typical Indian thali (food platter) to assess food affordability across regions. - Trends: - 2015-2018: - Thali prices decreased for both vegetarian and non-vegetarian options across India. - 2019: - Prices increased, but affordability improved for poor households, saving families of five ~₹10,000 annually. - 2020 (June-December): -

- Significance: - Reflects success of Modi-era schemes (e.g., PM-KISAN, FCI operations) in enhancing food production and affordability. - Inflation in Other Countries - Economic Survey 2024: - India’s inflation remained moderate compared to many global economies, reflecting effective monetary and fiscal policies. - Pillar 5A1: Infrastructure - Mining and Basic Industries - Definition: - Infrastructure refers to the set of basic facilities that enable an economy to function and grow, including energy, irrigation, roads, railways, and telecommunications. - Characteristics of Infrastructure: - Natural Monopoly: - Infrastructure sectors often display natural monopoly features due to high fixed costs and low marginal costs, economies of scale making a single provider most efficient. - What are fixed and marginal costs? - Fixed Cost: - Definition: - Cost that does not change with the level of output. - Examples: - Rent for a factory - Salaries of permanent staff - Cost of installing railway tracks, airport runways, power grids - Marginal Cost: - Definition: - The cost of producing one additional unit of output. - Examples: - Fuel cost for running one extra train - Cost of producing one more unit of electricity - Examples: - Railways (track laying, signaling). - Aviation (pre-LPG era dominated by Indian Airlines). - Telecom (before liberalization, monopolized by BSNL/MTNL). - High Sunk Costs: - Capital-intensive investments with low or zero resale value. - Once invested, funds cannot be recovered if project is abandoned. - Examples: - Airport runways, ports, tunnels, power transmission lines. - Implication: - Leads to entry barriers; requires long-term commitment and planning. - Non-Tradable Output: - Infrastructure services are location-bound and cannot be exported/imported. - Examples: - Roads, bridges, irrigation canals, metro systems. - Implication: - Regional development depends on local infrastructure provisioning. - Intangible Nature: - Some infrastructure assets are non-physical but critical. - Examples: - Radio spectrum for telecom. - Electricity as a flow (cannot be stored easily). - Implication: - Requires strong regulatory oversight and pricing mechanisms. - Non-Rival Consumption: - One person's use does not diminish availability to others (up to a limit). - Examples: - Street lighting, highways, public broadcasting. - Implication: - Justifies public funding or subsidies for universal access. - Price Exclusion Difficulty: - Hard to exclude non-payers from usage. - Examples: - Rural or village roads, public parks, street lighting. - Implication: - Market-based provisioning inefficient → government intervention necessary. - Positive Externalities: - Infrastructure stimulates broader economic and social benefits. - Examples: - A new railway station leads to: - Rise in local commerce. - Better job opportunities. - Enhanced connectivity to nearby towns. - Implication: - Public investment in infrastructure leads to multiplier effects on the economy. - Sectors with Infrastructure Status (Finance Ministry - Dept. of Economic Affairs): - Transport & Logistics: - Roads, bridges, ports, shipyards, inland waterways, airports, railways, tunnels, transport infrastructure. - Energy: - Electricity, oil, gas. - Water & Sanitation: - Water supply, treatment, sewage, solid waste management, irrigation. - Communication: - Telecommunications. - Social & Commercial Infrastructure: - Hospitals, educational institutions, sports infrastructure, tourism (hotels, ropeways), industrial/food/textile parks, SEZs, cold storage, soil-testing labs, affordable housing. - Benefits of Infrastructure Status: - Tax benefits, subsidized public land leases, faster environmental/FDI approvals. - RBI relaxes External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) norms, debt restructuring (e.g., 5/25 rule), and Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms. - SEBI relaxes REITs/InvITs norms for easier capital mobilization. - IRDAI/PFRDA mandates minimum investment in infrastructure by insurance/pension companies. - Easier funding from World Bank and multilateral banks. - Budget 2022: - Infrastructure status granted to data centers, energy storage systems, grid-scale battery systems, and EV charging infrastructure. - Mining / Basic Industries - Basic Industries: - Supply raw materials for other goods (e.g., iron, steel, copper, aluminum, chemicals). - Capital Goods Industries: - Produce goods used in manufacturing (e.g., textile machinery, conveyor belts, mining equipment). - Heavy Industries: - Manufacture large/heavy products (e.g., shipbuilding, bulldozers, industrial machinery, transformers). - Reference: - Ministries and departments differ as per forms of government organizations (see unacademy.com/lesson/mrunals-yearbook-ministries-and-departments). - [Yearbook] Ministry of Heavy Industries - Departments: - Department of Heavy Industry. - Department of Public Enterprises: - Manages Ratna status allocation and Public Enterprises Survey (shifted to Finance Ministry in 2021, see Pillar 2A). - Attached/Subordinate/Statutory: - Not MCQ-worthy. - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP): - Implements FAME-India for electric vehicle adoption. - Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (BHEL). - Cement Corporation of India Ltd. (1965, approved for strategic disinvestment 2019). - Hindustan Newsprint Ltd., Scooters India Ltd., Bharat Pumps and Compressors Ltd., Andrew Yule (tea plantations), Braithwaite, Burn & Jessop Construction, Hindustan Salts (salt, bromine, magnesium chloride), Rajasthan Electronics Ltd. (joint venture for solar panels). - Notable Schemes: - Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Electric Vehicles (FAME-India). - National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage. - Productivity Linked Incentive (PLI) for automobile and auto components. - [Yearbook] Ministry of Steel - Departments: - None. - Attached/Subordinate/Statutory: - Not MCQ-worthy. - CPSEs: - Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL). - Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. (RINL). - National Mineral Development Corporation (NMDC, iron ore). - Salem Steel Plant (Tamil Nadu), Bhadravati Steel Plant (Karnataka), Ferro Scrap Nigam Ltd. (approved for disinvestment 2019). - E-Governance: - Steel Import Monitoring System (SIMS) portal. - Targets (National Steel Policy 2017): - Increase per capita steel consumption from 74 kg to 160 kg by 2031. - Reduce coking coal imports from 85% to 65% by 2030-31. - 100% indigenous high-grade automobile steel production. - Rankings (Yearbook 2024): - Crude Steel Production: - #1 China (54%), #2 India (6%), #3 Japan. - China is the largest producer of crude steel in the world, contributing about 54% of global production. - Steel Consumption: - #1 China (49%), #2 USA, #3 India (6%). - China also consumes the most steel in the world, about 49% of global steel consumption. - Why China producing and consuming almost 50% of the world steel alone? - Infrastructure Development: - Massive public works: - roads, bridges, high-speed rail, airports - Mega projects: - dams (e.g., Three Gorges), ports, power plants - All require large volumes of structural steel - Urbanization and Real Estate: - Rapid urbanization (60%+ population in cities) - Construction of residential apartments, office complexes, malls - High steel demand in building frames, reinforcements - Manufacturing Hub: - World’s largest producer of: - Automobiles - Appliances - Machinery - Electronics - All depend heavily on steel components and structures - Export-Oriented Steel Products: - Exports of finished goods (cars, tools, electronics) - Exports of semi-finished/finished steel - Competitive pricing due to domestic steel surplus - State Industrial Policy: - Government-backed steel overcapacity - Strategic support to drive: - Economic growth - Employment generation - Global industrial influence - Belt and Road Initiative (BRI): - Infrastructure projects in Asia, Africa, Europe - Chinese steel used in BRI countries - Boosts steel demand and exports simultaneously - Purvodaya Initiative (2020) - Focus: - Eastern states (Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, Northern Andhra Pradesh) with 80% of India’s iron reserves. - Objective: - Establish new steel plants and transport infrastructure, coordinated by Steel Ministry with central/state governments and private companies. - [Yearbook] Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers - Departments: - Chemicals and Petrochemicals. - Fertilizers. - Pharmaceuticals. - Attached/Subordinate/Statutory: - Fertilizers Industry Coordination Committee (FICC). -
