National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research (NIPER). - Central Institute of Plastics Engineering & Technology (CIPET, Ranchi). - CPSEs: - Hindustan Insecticide Ltd. (HIL): - Manufactures DDT for mosquito control in National Vector Borne Disease Control Program. - Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals, Bengal Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals, Hindustan Antibiotics, Karnataka Antibiotics & Pharma, Hindustan Fluorocarbon Ltd., Madras Fertilizer, Brahmaputra Valley Fertiliser, Aravali Gypsum (approved for disinvestment 2019). - Notable Schemes: - Plastic parks for the plastic industry. - Petroleum, Chemical, and Petrochemical Investment Regions (PCPIRs): - Andhra Pradesh (Vishakhapatnam), Gujarat (Dahej), Odisha (Paradeep), Tamil Nadu (Cuddalore, Nagapattinam). - Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana for affordable medicines. - [Yearbook] Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas - Departments: - None. - Attached/Subordinate: - Directorate General of Hydrocarbons: - Regulates upstream activities (oil/gas exploration and production, 2018 statutory status proposal rejected). - Statutory: - Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (2006): - Regulates downstream activities (pipelines, fuel marketing). - CPSEs: - Bharat Petroleum Corp Ltd., Hindustan Petroleum Corp Ltd. (approved for disinvestment 2019). - Engineers India Ltd.: - Consultancy for petroleum refineries. - Gas Authority of India, Indian Oil Corporation, Oil India, ONGC, ONGC Videsh Ltd. (foreign projects: Sakhalin-Russia, Al-Furat-Syria, Greater Nile-Sudan, San Cristobal-Venezuela). - Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserve Ltd. (ISPRL): - Stores crude oil in Vishakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur (see Pillar 3A). - Dutch Disease & Resource Curse (Economic Survey 2016-17) - Dutch Disease: - Discovery of natural gas in the Netherlands led to foreign currency inflows, strengthening local currency, reducing non-energy exports (e.g., agriculture, textiles), causing food shortages, hyperinflation, and riots. - Resource Curse/Paradox of Plenty: - Despite large oil reserves, countries like Venezuela face economic crises due to Dutch Disease effects. In India, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand’s mineral wealth fuels mining mafia, Naxalism, corruption, and poverty. - Crude Oil Prices, Petrol/Diesel Taxes, Oil Bonds, NELP-HELP Policies - Reference: - See Pillar 2A2 (Indirect Taxes) and Pillar 3A (Import-Export). - [Yearbook] Ministry of Mines - Departments/Statutory/Attached/Subordinate: - National Mineral Exploration Trust: - Funds mineral exploration. - Geological Survey of India (1851): - Focuses on coal, landslide, and glacial disaster research. - Indian Bureau of Mines (1948): - Regulates mining activities. - CPSEs: - National Aluminium Company Ltd. (NALCO, Bhubaneswar). - Hindustan Copper Ltd. (HCL, Kolkata). - Mineral Exploration Corporation Ltd. (MECL, Nagpur). - Autonomous Bodies: - National Institute of Rock Mechanics (Kolar Gold Fields, Karnataka). - National Institute of Miners’ Health (Karnataka, merged with ICMR-NIOH, Ahmedabad, 2020). - Statutory: - District Mineral Foundations (DMF) in mining districts for local welfare. - Mineral Products in India - Categories: - Hydrocarbon Energy Minerals: - Coal, lignite, petroleum, natural gas (4 types). - Atomic Minerals: - Ilmenite, rutile, zircon, uranium, monazite (5 types). - Metallic Minerals: - 10 types. - Non-Metallic Minerals: - 21 types. - Minor Minerals: - 55 types (Total: 95 types). - Regulation: - Major Minerals (Union List): - Atomic minerals, bauxite, iron, coal, petroleum, natural gas. - Minor Minerals (State List): - Sand, mica, marble, granite, agate, chalk, gypsum, shale. - National Mineral Policy (NMP) 2019 - Replaces NMP 2008, under Ministry of Mines. - Targets (Non-Fuel/Non-Coal Minerals): - Allow transfer of mining leases for mergers/acquisitions. - Grant ‘industry’ status to mining for tax/scheme benefits. - Harmonize taxes/royalty rates with global benchmarks. - Enhance FDI (100% allowed in exploration) via ease of doing business. - Promote R&D, skilling, and environmental conservation. - Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 2015 - Replaces MMDR Act 1957 for ease of doing business. - Key Provisions: - Mining leases granted via auction, not discretionary allotment. - Lease duration: - 50 years, followed by re-auction (no renewal). - National Mineral Exploration Trust: - Funded by mining companies for exploration. - District Mineral Foundations (DMF): - Not-for-profit trusts in mining districts, funded by companies for local welfare, with state-prescribed guidelines. - Higher penalties/jail terms for illegal mining. - MMDR Amendment Bill/Act, 2021 - Excludes coal and atomic minerals. -
Aspect Before After
Captive Mining Policy Mines reserved for captive use (e.g., Tata’s iron ore only for its steel plant) No captive use restrictions; companies can sell minerals to others
Minor Mineral Auctions States conducted auctions, often delayed Union sets auction timelines; if states fail, Union conducts auctions
Mining Lease Expiry Lease expires if no mining for 2 years Up to 3-year extension allowed (e.g., delays due to COVID, labor, disasters)
- Royalty Rates for Critical Minerals Reduced (2023) - Context: - India is rich in certain critical minerals essential for future technologies (EVs, renewables, electronics). - Earlier high royalty rates (12%) discouraged private sector mining and foreign investment. - Royalty rates refer to the percentage of revenue or profit that mining companies must pay to the government for extracting natural resources such as minerals, oil, or gas from public or government-owned land. - When a private company extracts a mineral (like lithium or iron) from Indian soil, they don’t own it — it belongs to the nation. So they must pay the government a fee — this is called royalty. - To boost domestic exploration and reduce import dependence, the government slashed royalty rates in October 2023. - Revised Royalty Rates: -
Mineral Before (Royalty Rate) After (Royalty Rate) Key Uses
Lithium 12% 3%
  • Batteries (mobiles, laptops, EVs)
  • Pacemakers
Niobium 12% 3%
  • Superconducting materials
  • Jet engines, rockets, pipelines
  • MRI scanners
Rare Earth Elements (REEs) 12% 1%
  • 17 critical elements incl. scandium, yttrium, cerium
  • Catalysts, magnets, alloys, electronics
  • EVs, wind turbines, LEDs
- Sales Pricing: - Based on international benchmarks like London Metal Exchange (LME). - Benefits: - Boosts profitability for miners, encouraging exploration and production. - Enhances foreign and domestic investment in the mining sector. - Reduces battery costs → cheaper EVs → supports green energy goals. - Helps meet Net-Zero Emissions target by 2070. - Reduces reliance on imports → lowers Current Account Deficit → stabilizes INR (see Pillar 3B). - Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) (MMDR) Amendment, 2023 -
Aspect Before After
Private Sector in Atomic Mineral Mining
  • Mining of six atomic minerals restricted to government entities.
  • Included: beryl/beryllium, lithium, niobium, titanium, tantalum, zirconium.
  • These six minerals delisted from 'atomic minerals' category.
  • Private sector now allowed to explore and mine them.
New Mining Licenses
  • Only four types: Reconnaissance, Prospecting, Mining, Composite.
  • Composite = Prospecting + Mining.
  • New license category introduced: Exploration license for Reconnaissance + Prospecting.
Specified Minerals & Licensing Power
  • No unified clarity on Union vs. State roles.
  • Specified Minerals: Gold, silver, copper, cobalt, nickel, lead, potash, rock phosphate, beryl/beryllium, lithium, niobium, titanium, tantalum, zirconium.
  • Exploration License: By State government with Union’s auction terms.
  • Mining & Composite License: By Union government.
Reconnaissance: Sub-Surface Activity
  • Only surface-level methods permitted (aerial/geophysical/geochemical surveys, geological mapping).
  • Sub-surface activities like trenching, drilling, excavation were prohibited.
  • Now allows sub-surface methods like trenching, drilling, excavation under Reconnaissance license.
- Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Amendment, 2023 - Amends: - Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act, 2002 - Objective: - Streamline offshore mineral exploration and production; curb corruption; ensure security and sustainability. -
Aspect Before (2002 Act) After (2023 Amendment)
License Duration 30 years + 20-year renewal (often misused) Single 50-year license to promote long-term investment
Mode of Allocation Administrative discretion (opaque, risk of cronyism) Transparent competitive bidding/auction mechanism
Atomic Mineral Mining No restriction; open to private players Only government companies allowed (national security concern)
Mineral Development Fund No statutory trust or fund Creation of Offshore Areas Mineral Trust:
  • Funded by royalties paid by mining companies
  • Used for research, conservation, disaster mitigation
Penalties for Illegal Mining Lower penalties; ineffective deterrence Enhanced fines and imprisonment to ensure compliance
- National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) - Launch Year: - 2025 - Total Funding: - ₹34,300 crore (₹16,300 crore by Central Govt + ₹18,000 crore by PSUs) - Objectives: - Accelerate exploration of critical minerals (e.g., lithium, cobalt, REEs) - Promote recycling and circular economy - Fast-track approvals for mining projects - Acquire strategic mineral assets abroad (e.g., lithium reserves in Argentina's Catamarca province) - Critical Minerals from Tailings - Definition: - Tailings: - Residual material left after extracting primary minerals. - Example: - Cobalt extraction from copper ore tailings. - Budget 2025 Initiative: - Promotes recovery of critical minerals from tailings to reduce import dependency and ensure resource efficiency. - Coal Mining - Global Coal Reserves: - Top 5 Countries: - USA: - ~250 billion tonnes, Wyoming (Powder River Basin), high-quality bituminous/sub-bituminous. - Russia: - ~160 billion tonnes, Siberian Kuznetsk Basin, anthracite and bituminous. - China: - ~140 billion tonnes, Shanxi/Inner Mongolia, mostly bituminous for industrial use. - Australia: - ~140 billion tonnes, Queensland/New South Wales, high-quality coking coal for steel exports. - India: - ~100 billion tonnes, Jharkhand/Odisha/Chhattisgarh, predominantly bituminous. - India: - Production: - 2nd largest globally (~780 MT, 2023-24), yet imports ~250 MT (~₹1.7 lakh crore) annually. - Why Import Coal: - High demand: - Power (70% of India’s electricity), steel, cement industries outstrip domestic supply. - Quality issues: - Indian coal has high ash content (30-40%), low calorific value; imported coal (e.g., Australian/Indonesian) has lower ash, higher energy. - Coking coal scarcity: - India’s coking coal (for steel) is limited; imports ~50 MT from Australia/South Africa. - Logistical constraints: - Transport bottlenecks, mining inefficiencies increase reliance on imports. - Import Sources: - Australia (coking coal), Indonesia (steam coal), South Africa, USA. - Uses: - Electricity: - ~70% of India’s power generation (thermal plants). - Steel: - Coking coal for blast furnaces. - Cement, Paper, Brick Kilns: - Steam coal for energy. - Emerging: - Coal gasification (methanol, ammonia), coal-to-chemicals (ethylene, propylene). - Coal Types: - Peat: - 40% carbon, high moisture, smoky, low energy, not mined commercially in India. - Lignite/Brown Coal: - 40-60% carbon, high moisture, low calorific value (~2500-4000 kcal/kg). - Found in: - Neyveli (Tamil Nadu), Gujarat (Kutch), Rajasthan (Bikaner). - Use: - Power generation (e.g., Neyveli Lignite Corporation plants). - Bituminous/Black Coal: - 60-80% carbon, releases bitumen on heating, high calorific value (~5000-7000 kcal/kg). - Types: - Coking Coal: - For steel production (blast furnaces). - Steam Coal: - For thermal power plants. - Gas Coal: - For coal gasification. - Found in: - Jharkhand (Jharia, Dhanbad), Odisha (Talcher), Chhattisgarh (Korba), West Bengal (Raniganj), Madhya Pradesh (Singrauli). - Anthracite/Hard Coal: - 80-90% carbon, low moisture, high calorific value (~7000-8000 kcal/kg), burns with short blue flame. - Found in: - Limited deposits in Jammu & Kashmir (Kalakot). - Use: - High-energy applications, domestic heating, niche industries. - [Yearbook] Coal Ministry: - Attached/Subordinate: - Coal Controller’s Organization: - Functions: - Collects production/sales data, monitors coal quality, resolves disputes on coal-bearing area notifications. - CPSEs: - Coal India Ltd. (CIL): - Kolkata, Maharatna, world’s largest coal producer (~620 MT, 2023-24). - Neyveli Lignite Corporation (NLC India Ltd.): - Tamil Nadu, lignite mining and power generation. - Singareni Collieries Company Ltd. (SCCL): - Telangana (51% state, 49% Union), bituminous and lignite mining. - Statutory: - Coal Mines Provident Fund Organization: - Manages provident funds via C-CARES portal. - Nationalization & Private Sector Entry: - Captive Mining - Mining of minerals (like coal, iron ore, limestone) by a company solely for use in its own industrial operations (e.g., power plants, steel plants, cement factories), not allowed to sell the mineral in the open market - Timeline: -
Year Event / Legislation Details
1973 Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act
  • Nationalized private coal mines
  • Transferred ownership to Coal India and other CPSEs
  • Objective: Ensure coal supply for thermal power and core industries
1993 Amendment to Coal Act
  • Allowed captive mining for private players in steel, cement, aluminium sectors
  • Led to irregular allocations and coal block scams (e.g., UPA-era)
2014 Supreme Court Judgement
  • Cancelled 204 coal block allocations
  • Reason: Lack of transparency and fairness in allocation process
2015 Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act
  • Allowed commercial coal mining by private and public sector entities
  • Ended Coal India’s monopoly
  • Retained captive mining rights for previously allocated firms
- Mineral Laws (Amendment) Act, 2020: - Amends: - MMDR Act 1957, Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act 2015. - Changes: - Eligibility: - Any India-registered company can bid (earlier restricted to iron, steel, power, coal firms). - Experience: - No prior mining experience required (earlier mandatory). - Licensing: - Composite prospecting-cum-mining lease (earlier separate licenses). - Payment: - Revenue-sharing model (minimum 4% revenue share, higher bids win) vs fixed per-tonne payment. - Usage: - Captive miners can sell up to 50% of production (earlier restricted to own use). - Impact: - Encourages FDI, competition, reduces import dependence. - Shakti Policy (2017): - Purpose: - Transparent coal allocation to power plants/industries. - National Coal Index: - Tracks domestic/imported coal price changes, base year 2017-18. - Apps: - Coal Mitra App (Power Ministry): - Facilitates coal buying/selling. - UTTAM App (Coal Ministry): - Monitors coal quality from mines. - Atma-Nirbhar Bharat: - PM Garib Kalyan: - District Mineral Foundation (DMF): - Funds used for COVID-19 testing, healthcare infrastructure in mining areas. - Mineral Index: - Proposed for tracking prices of various minerals (details pending). - Joint Auction: - Bauxite and coal blocks auctioned together to reduce aluminum smelting costs. - Coal Gasification and Liquefaction: - Definition: - Technologies that convert coal into gaseous or liquid fuels like syngas, methanol, ammonia, diesel, etc. - Purpose: - Reduces dependence on imported natural gas and crude oil. - Supports "Atmanirbhar Bharat" in energy security. - Applications: - Syngas: - Used in power generation and as feedstock in petrochemicals. - Methanol: - Used as a fuel blend, in marine sector and transport. - Ammonia: - Used for fertilizers and industrial processes. - Liquid fuels: - For transport, reducing crude oil dependency. - Advantages: - Utilizes low-grade, high ash Indian coal efficiently. - Reduces carbon footprint compared to direct coal combustion. - Promotes cleaner coal technologies. - Enables monetization of unmineable coal reserves. - Energy Consumption in Coal Gasification/Liquefaction: - Conversion Process: - Involves breaking down coal into syngas (CO + H2) using heat, pressure, and controlled oxygen/steam. - Further conversion into methanol, ammonia, etc., also requires energy. - Energy Balance: - Net Energy Gain: - Depends on process efficiency and quality of coal. - Generally, gasification is ~60-70% efficient; liquefaction even lower. - Auxiliary Energy Consumption: - Power is required to operate reactors, compressors, purification units. - Water-intensive process; energy used in water handling and treatment. - Environmental & Economic Trade-off: - Pros: - Reduces reliance on imported natural gas, methanol, ammonia. - Promotes domestic energy security. - Cons: - High capital cost and operational energy burden. - Potential increase in CO₂ emissions unless CCS (Carbon Capture & Storage) is used. - India’s Target: - 100 MT coal gasification/liquefaction capacity by 2030. - Goal: - Substitute natural gas, methanol, ammonia imports. - Coal Bed Methane (CBM): - Definition: - Methane gas extracted directly from coal seams before, during, or after mining. - Coal Seams are layers or beds of coal found underground between layers of rock. - Importance: - Alternative clean energy resource. - Reduces methane emissions (a potent greenhouse gas). - Promotes gas-based economy in line with India’s energy transition targets. - Applications: - Power generation. - Domestic and industrial fuel. - Feedstock for fertilizer and chemical industries. - Policy Support: - Blocks allocated through auction by Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas. - Pricing and marketing freedom provided for CBM projects. - Examples: - ONGC, Reliance, Essar operate CBM blocks in Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal. - Commercial Mining: - Revenue-sharing model, 41 blocks auctioned (2020-23), aims to boost domestic production. - Economic Survey Suggestions/Observations: - Carbon Imperialism: - First-world nations push restrictive energy norms on developing countries to sell nuclear fuel/technology, deflect global warming blame. - India’s GHG contribution: - <10% globally, per capita emissions <2 tons (vs global avg. ~4.7 tons). - Coal Necessity: - Renewables (wind/solar) non-dispatchable, nuclear fuel import challenges, land constraints for solar, coal plant closures risk unemployment. - Budget 2020: - Close old, high-emission thermal plants, repurpose land for renewable projects. - Budget 2022: - Co-fire 5-7% biomass pellets in thermal plants to reduce emissions, support farmer income, curb stubble burning. - Promote coal gasification and coal-to-chemicals (formaldehyde, ethylene, propylene, acetic acid). - Interim Budget 2024: - Target: - 100 MT coal gasification/liquefaction capacity by 2030 to cut imports of natural gas, methanol, ammonia. - ES22 (World Bank): - Clean energy needs copper, aluminum, iron, manganese, nickel, lithium, graphite; India lacks sufficient reserves, increasing import reliance. - Energy Transition in First-World Nations: -
Year Event / Transition
1700s Wood to coal transition due to industrialization, causing deforestation.
1946 Oil and gas overtook coal as primary energy sources in developed nations.
1970s Yom Kippur War oil embargo: France shifted to nuclear power (~70% of electricity today).
2022 EU’s REPowerEU plan: Reduce Russian gas reliance post-Ukraine war, boost renewables.
2023 USA: Approved largest oil drilling project in Alaska (Willow Project).
2026 AI data centers to consume ~6% of US electricity, increasing coal/gas reliance.
- Economic Survey 2025: Energy/Climate Change: - India: - 7th most vulnerable to climate change (heatwaves, floods, droughts). - 2024 UNFCCC Summit (Baku, Azerbaijan): - ‘Finance COP’ for New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) on climate finance. - Issue: - First-world contributions inadequate (~$100 billion/year pledged vs $1 trillion needed). - Vertical Gardens: - Benefits: - Carbon sequestration, biodiversity, air quality improvement, urban heat island mitigation. - Europe: - Gas plants used when wind turbine output is low, highlighting renewable unreliability. - Solar Panels: - Issue: - Recycling difficult/expensive, creates waste at end of 25-30 year lifecycle. - Vegetarianism: - Reduces carbon footprint by up to 2.1 tons annually per person. - Mining Miscellaneous Schemes, Apps, Portals, Issues: - Illegal Mining: - Impacts: - Environmental degradation, royalty loss (~₹10,000 crore annually). - Mining Surveillance System (MSS): - Satellite-based monitoring by Indian Bureau of Mines. - Khan Prahari App: - Reports illegal coal mining activities. - cVIGIL App: - Election Commission’s app for model code violation reporting (not mining-specific). - TAMRA App/Portal (2017): - Transparent Auction & Monitoring of Resource Allocation for mining bids. - PRAKASH Portal (2019): - Power and Railways for Coal Supply Honesty: - Links coal companies, railways, thermal plants for efficient supply chain. - Satyabhama Portal (2020): - Mining Ministry’s portal for funding mining-related research. - CIMS/AIMS: - Copper/Aluminium Import Monitoring Systems to track imports, promote domestic production. - Pollution: - Red Mud: - Bauxite-to-aluminum waste, used in cement/ceramics to reduce landfill. - Fly Ash: - Thermal plant pollutant, used in cement, bricks, tiles, roads; monitored via ASH TRACK App. - Lakshya Portal (2021): - Boss: - Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. - Purpose: - Lists items imported by oil/gas companies to encourage domestic manufacturing (Atma-Nirbhar Bharat). - Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (2015): - Uses DMF funds for drinking water, health, sanitation, education, skill development, women/child care in mining-affected areas. - Star Rating of Mines (2016): - Indian Bureau of Mines rates mines (0-5 stars) based on social, economic, environmental impact. - Pillar 5A2: Infrastructure - Energy, Electricity, and Cooking - Overview: - Electricity is critical for modern life, powering irrigation pumps, mobile phones, agricultural growth, and digital connectivity. - Historical Context: - Electricity supply began in Darjeeling (1897) and Shivasamudram hydropower station (1902, Karnataka). Pre-independence, power supply was primarily private and urban-centric. - Significance: - Increased energy access drives economic growth and human development. India aims to quadruple per capita energy consumption to improve Human Development Index (HDI). - Data (Yearbook 2023): - India’s per capita energy consumption is ~1/3rd of the global average. - India, with ~18% of the world’s population, consumes ~6% of global energy. - India is the 3rd largest energy consumer globally (after USA, China), 3rd largest crude oil importer, and 4th largest LNG importer. - Energy Index Global Reports: - World Energy Investment Report (IEA): - 2021: - Top energy consumers: - 1) China, 2) USA, 3) EU, 4) India.' - By 2040: - India projected to surpass EU as 3rd largest. - Global Energy Transition Index (World Economic Forum, Geneva): - Measures CO2/pollution in energy production and commitment to reduction. - 2023 Ranking: - 1) Sweden, 2) Denmark, 3) Norway, 67) India (improving rank). - World Energy Transitions Outlook (IRENA, Abu Dhabi): - Highlights global renewable energy trends. - India Energy Outlook Report (IEA, Paris): - 2021: - India as 4th largest energy consumer. - By 2030: - India to become 3rd largest, with fuel import bill tripling in 20 years. - State Energy Efficiency Index: - By BEE and Alliance for an Energy Efficient Economy (AEEE). - Basic information - Electricity Generation by Ownership: - Union-Owned: - 25% - State-Owned: - 26% - Private Sector: - 49% - Total: - 100% - [Yearbook] Ministry of Power: - Departments: - None (no MCQ-worthy departments). - Statutory Bodies: - Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission (JERC): - For UTs like J&K, Ladakh, Goa, Manipur, Mizoram. - Central Electricity Authority (CEA): - Sets standards for electrical plants and lines. - Central & State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (CERC/SERC): - Fix electricity tariffs. - Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL): - Handles appeals against CERC/SERC decisions. - Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE): - Promotes energy efficiency. - Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC): - Manages power and water in Damodar Valley. - Bhakra Beas Management Board: - Manages Bhakra-Nangal and Beas projects. - Autonomous Bodies: - Central Power Research Institute: - Conducts power research. - National Power Training Institute: - Trains power sector professionals. - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC): - Thermal power generation. - National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC): - Hydropower generation. - SJVN Ltd.: - Satluj hydropower (GoI: 62%, Himachal: 27%, others: 11%). - Power Finance Corporation (PFC): - Finances power projects. - Power Grid Corporation of India (POWERGRID): - Manages national grid. - Power System Operation Corporation (POSOCO): - Operates power systems. - Energy Efficiency Services Ltd. (EESL): - Joint venture (NTPC, PFC, REC, POWERGRID) for UJALA LED bulbs. - THDC India Ltd.: - Tehri hydropower (GoI: 75%, UP: 25%, approved for disinvestment 2019). - Rural Electrification Corporation (REC): - Supports rural electrification (DDUGJY). - North Eastern Electric Power Corporation (NEEPCO): - Power generation in Northeast. - Power Ministry’s Apps/Portals: - Examples: - Garv, Deep, Tarang, National Power Portal (NPP). - Purpose: - Monitor electricity data (generation, distribution, consumption). - Electricity Distribution Reforms - National Electricity Distribution Company: - Context: - PM Modi’s 24x7 power goal by 2022 was hindered by NPA/debt issues in state and private Electricity Distribution Companies (DISCOMs). - Formation (2019): - 50:50 joint venture between NTPC and POWERGRID. - Objective: - Expand electricity distribution on a pan-India basis to address Electricity Distribution Company (DISCOM) inefficiencies. - Indian Energy Exchange (IEX): - Private sector company facilitating electricity trading. - Note: - Limited exam relevance due to poor cost-benefit ratio for current affairs (CA) preparation. - NPA Resolution - UDAY (2015): - Objective: - Address Electricity Distribution Companies (DISCOMs’) non-performing assets (NPAs) and debt. - Mechanism: - States take over the loans (debts) of their DISCOMs from banks/financial institutions. - DISCOM Debt Takeover by States: - This is not a waiver, but a transfer of liability from the DISCOM to the state government. - It's not a celebration — it's more like a bailout with strings attached. - Objective: - DISCOMs get financial breathing space to focus on improving operational efficiency (reducing losses, improving billing, metering, etc.). - States then repay the loans over time, often under better repayment terms (lower interest, longer tenure) negotiated with lenders. - State government steps in not out of kindness, but because DISCOMs failure is hurting everyone — power supply, banks, economy, and even the state's own fiscal health. - Incentives: - Union provides additional funding for Deendayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY), Integrated Power Development Scheme (IPDS), and Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) schemes. - Outcome (2019-20): - First phase completed, but failed to fully resolve Electricity Distribution Company (DISCOM) issues. - UDAY 2.0: - Proposed by Power Minister with enhanced features, but no progress yet. - Electricity Reforms under Atma-Nirbhar Bharat Abhiyan: - Focus: - Improve DISCOM (Distribution Company) efficiency and financial health. - Promote consumer-centric reforms and 24x7 power supply. - Measures: - Privatization of DISCOMs in Union Territories. - ₹3.05 lakh crore reform-based, result-linked power distribution scheme. - Smart metering, feeder separation, and reduction in AT&C (Aggregate Technical & Commercial) losses. - Electricity (Amendment) Bill 2022: - Context: - Electricity is on the Concurrent List; Union law prevails in conflicts. - Responsibilities: - Union: - Electricity generation, transmission. - States: - Electricity distribution. - Objective: - Amend Electricity Act 2003 to improve efficiency, but controversial and faded from focus. - Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020: - Boss: - Ministry of Power (under Electricity Act 2003). - Requirements: - DISCOMs must provide 24/7 electricity, grievance redressal, and compensation mechanisms. - Exception: - Agricultural consumers may have reduced supply hours to prevent groundwater over-exploitation. - Benefit: - Addresses DISCOM monopolies, ensuring consumer rights where alternatives are unavailable. - Time-of-Day (ToD) Tariff (2023): - Boss: - Ministry of Power (under Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Amendment Rules, 2023). - Mechanism: - Varies electricity prices by time: - Normal sunny hours: - 20% below normal price. - Peak hours (e.g., evening): - 1.10-1.20x normal price (varies by consumer type). - Analogy: - Similar to surge pricing in taxis during high-demand periods. - Faster Connection Rules (Feb 2024): - Boss: - Ministry of Power (under Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules). - Features: - Separate electricity connections for EV charging. - Reduced time for new connections. - Simplified rules for rooftop solar installations. - “Prosumers”: - Consumers producing electricity via rooftop solar. - Mandatory additional meter installation for billing disputes. - Rural Electrification Schemes - Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY, 2015): - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by REC (Central Sector Scheme, 100% Union-funded). - Target: - 24x7 metered electricity for rural households by 2022. - Features: - Separate feeder lines for rural households and agricultural use. - Strengthen sub-transmission and distribution networks to reduce losses. - Install electricity meters. - Benefit: - Reduces kerosene use, pollution, and import/subsidy bills. - Predecessor: - Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (Manmohan Singh). - PM Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (Saubhagya, 2017): - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by REC (Central Sector Scheme). - Target: - Electrify all un-electrified rural and urban households. - Implementation: - Identify beneficiaries using SECC-2011 data. - Free metered electricity connections. - Solar cells, DC battery packs, and LED lights for remote households. - Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS, June 2021): - Boss: - Ministry of Power (funding: >₹3 lakh crore). - Umbrella Scheme: - Subsumes DDUGJY, Saubhagya, IPDS, and PMDP (J&K, Ladakh). - Features: - Separate agricultural feeder lines. - Solarization of feeder lines under KUSUM (farmers sell excess solar power). - AI-monitored smart meters for non-agricultural users. - Modernize state-level distribution infrastructure. - Extra funding for special category states (e.g., J&K, Ladakh, Andaman, Lakshadweep). - DISCOMs need ≥60% performance score for funding. - Outcome (ES22): - 96% of Indian households electrified. - Power Transmission and Grid Integration - One Nation-One Grid: - What is a grid? - The electricity grid is a network of transmission lines, substations, transformers, and more that delivers electricity from power plants to homes, industries, and businesses. - It's called a "grid" because of how the electrical infrastructure is physically and logically laid out — it resembles a grid-like pattern of interconnected lines and nodes, much like a mesh or a checkerboard. - The word “grid” comes from Latin "cratis" → meaning lattice or framework. It entered English to describe anything laid out in intersecting lines — like graph paper, city roads, or wiring systems. - Initial Setup: - Five regional grids (Northern, Eastern, Western, North Eastern, Southern) interconnected, but surplus electricity was limited to regional trading. - Objective: - Integrate all regional grids into a single national grid for seamless transfer of surplus electricity to deficit regions. - Mechanism: - Trading via power exchanges like Power Exchange of India (PXIL) and Indian Energy Exchange (IEX). - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by POWERGRID. - Green Energy Corridor Project: - Objective: - Enable renewable energy flow into the national grid, allowing states like Rajasthan (solar) and Tamil Nadu (wind) to sell surplus electricity. - Phase-II (2022): - Union provides 33% subsidy on project costs. - Green Credit Programme (Budget 2023): - Notified under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. - Objective: - Promote environmentally beneficial activities (e.g., water saving, waste management) through voluntary participation. - Trading Mechanisms - RPO, PAT, CCTS, GCP: -

- GREEN Grids / OSOWOG (One Sun, One World, One Grid): - Background: - Concept proposed in 2018 by India under the International Solar Alliance (ISA), headquartered in Gurugram. - Officially launched in 2021 at COP26 (Glasgow) by Indian PM Narendra Modi and UK PM Boris Johnson. - Positioned as part of India’s global climate leadership and energy transition diplomacy. - Objective: - To create a global interconnected solar power grid that allows countries to: - Access solar energy across time zones (e.g., importing solar power from countries where the sun is shining). - Maximize renewable energy usage and minimize storage needs. - Reduce dependence on fossil fuels by ensuring 24x7 green power availability. - Key Features: - Based on the idea of "sun never sets" on solar energy — by linking different countries’ grids, one can always tap solar power somewhere. - Involves regional grids (Africa, Asia, Europe) that will eventually be unified. - Enables energy sharing between surplus and deficit regions. - Strategic Relevance: - Enhances energy security and resilience. - Reduces global carbon footprint. - Strengthens India’s leadership in global climate governance and renewable technology. - Partners and Collaborations: - International Solar Alliance (ISA). - UK Government. - World Bank and other multilateral energy bodies. - Implementation Challenges: - Cross-border transmission agreements. - Harmonization of grid standards and infrastructure. - Financing and geopolitical alignments. - Complementary Initiatives: - ISA’s Global Solar Atlas. - India's domestic Green Energy Corridor. - GGI-OSOWOG (Green Grids Initiative-OSOWOG) umbrella. - Integrated Power Development Scheme (IPDS, 2014): - Boss: - Ministry of Power (Central Sector Scheme, 100% Union-funded). - Target: - Strengthen urban power infrastructure. - Implementation: - Financial assistance to Electricity Distribution Companies (DISCOMs) for improving distribution networks. - Installation of ICT-enabled smart meters for billing. - Solar panel installation in areas not feasible for grid connection. - Prepaid Smart Meters: - Features: - Internet-enabled: - Equipped with SIM cards or IoT tech to enable real-time data transfer. - Allow remote monitoring, billing, and disconnection/reconnection. - Prepaid Recharge Model: - Consumers buy electricity in advance like mobile recharges. - Promotes consumption awareness and budgeting. - Anti-theft Measures: - Tamper alerts and encryption prevent unauthorized usage. - Remote cutoff discourages illegal connections. - Consumer Benefits: - No estimated billing or meter reader dependency. - Transparency through mobile apps, SMS, web portals. - Utility Benefits: - Improved billing efficiency and collection. - Reduced transmission and distribution losses. - Load forecasting through real-time demand data. - Budget 2020: - Announcement: - Nationwide plan to replace all conventional electricity meters with prepaid smart meters. - Timeline: - Targeted completion within 3 years. - Implementation: - In coordination with Energy Efficiency Services Limited (EESL) and Electricity Distribution Companies (discoms). - Related Schemes: - Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS): - Launched 2021 to improve discom viability via smart metering and loss reduction. - National Smart Grid Mission (NSGM): - Supports integration of smart meters and grid automation. - Energy Efficiency: - Definition: - Using less energy for the same output (e.g., LED vs. incandescent bulbs). - Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) Mechanism: - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) under National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE, part of NAPCC 2008). - Target: - 8 energy-intensive industries (Thermal Power, Aluminium, Cement, Fertilizer, Iron-Steel, Pulp-Paper, Textiles, Chlor-Alkali). - Mechanism: - Industries must reduce energy consumption as per assigned quotas or face penalties. - Incentives: - Overachievers earn Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts) via BEE’s PATNET portal, tradable to underachieving firms (similar to Priority Sector Lending Certificates). - Regulator: - Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) sets ESCert prices. - National LED Programme: - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by Energy Efficiency Services Ltd. (EESL). - Components: - Unnat Jeevan by Affordable LEDs and Appliances for All (UJALA): - Subsidized LED bulbs for households (previously Domestic Efficient Lighting Program, DELP). - Street Lighting National Program: - The Street Lighting National Program (SLNP) aims to replace conventional streetlights (like halogen or sodium-vapor lamps) with LED lights, which consume much less electricity and last longer. - Energy Efficiency Services Limited (EESL) replaces halogen streetlights with LEDs at no cost. - What “no cost” means here? - Local bodies (like municipalities) do not need to pay any upfront cost for the installation or procurement of LED streetlights. - Instead, EESL bears the initial cost of buying and installing LEDs. - EESL recovers this cost over time from the energy savings that the municipality achieves. - Gram Ujala Programme: - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by EESL’s Convergence Energy Services Ltd. (CESL). - Mechanism: - Villagers exchange working incandescent bulbs and pay ₹10 for LED bulbs (3-year warranty, max 5 bulbs per villager). - Benefits: - 12W LED bulb equals 100W incandescent bulb, reducing CO2 emissions. - Longer lifespan, lower energy bills, and reduced waste. - Miscellaneous Energy Efficiency Schemes: - ESCO Company (Budget 2022): - Promote energy efficiency in large commercial buildings. - Atal Jyoti Yojana (AJAY): - Free solar LED streetlights in special category states, Assam, Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, aspirational districts, Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep (75% MNRE, 25% MPLADS funding). - SAATHI: - Ministry of Power and Textiles funds EESL to provide energy-efficient equipment to small/medium powerlooms. - Star Label: - BEE’s labeling for energy-efficient appliances (see Pillar 4B). - Smart Electricity Meters: - EESL assists DISCOMs with IT-enabled meters for remote monitoring, reducing theft. - FCI Ethanol (2019): - Ethanol production from surplus rice/maize with Food Corporation of India (see Pillar 4A). - UNNATEE: - BEE’s 2017-2031 strategy for national energy efficiency. - SIDHIEE: - Power Ministry’s portal for energy efficiency best practices in MSMEs. - Eco-Niwas Samhita: - BEE’s energy conservation standards for residential buildings. - Building Energy Efficiency Programme (BEEP): - EESL’s initiative for commercial buildings. - Renewable Energy Infrastructure: - Context: - Under UNFCCC Paris Accord (2015), India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) include: - By 2030: - Reduce emission intensity of GDP by 33-35% from 2005 levels. - 40% of installed power capacity from non-fossil fuel sources. - Target (2022): - 175 GW renewable capacity (100 GW solar, 60 GW wind, 10 GW biomass, 5 GW small hydro). - PM Modi’s Panchamrit @ COP-26 Glasgow (2021): - Announced at UNFCCC COP-26 Summit, UK, with Lifestyle for Environment (LiFE) proposal. - Updated NDCs (2022): - By 2030: - 500 GW renewable energy capacity (not in NDC). - 50% of energy from non-fossil fuels (included in NDC). - Reduce emission intensity by 45% from 2005 levels (included in NDC). - Net-zero emissions (not in NDC). - Reduce 1 billion tonnes of projected carbon emissions (not in NDC). - Carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes via afforestation (included in NDC). - Budget 2022: - 280 GW solar capacity by 2030, with Production Linked Incentive (PLI) for solar cell manufacturing (see Pillar 4B). - [Yearbook] Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE): - Departments/Statutory Bodies: - None MCQ-worthy. - Autonomous Bodies: - National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE, Gurugram): - Developed Solar Atlas of India. - National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE, Chennai): - Developed Wind Atlas of India. - Sardar Swaran Singh National Institute of Renewable Energy (SSS NIRE, Kapurthala, Punjab). - National Institute of Bio Energy (NIBE, Kapurthala, Punjab). - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA, Delhi). - Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI, Delhi): - Set up India’s largest Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Rajnandgaon, Chhattisgarh. - Portals: - India Renewable Idea Exchange (IRIX) Portal. - Akshay Urja Portal and Magazine. - KUSUM (2019): - Full Name: - Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan. - Boss: - MNRE. - Components: - Install solar pump tube wells for irrigation (reduces diesel use). - Farmers/panchayats/cooperatives install up to 2 MW renewable plants on barren/cultivable land. - Sell excess electricity to DISCOMs (prices set by SERC). - Funding: - Union (30%), State (30%), Bank Loan (30%), Farmer (10%). - Benefit: - Reduces diesel/thermal electricity use, cuts 27 million tonnes CO2 annually, increases farmer income. - Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (2009-10): - Part of National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) 2008 (Manmohan Singh). - Targets: - Original (Manmohan): - 20,000 MW by 2022. - Modi: - 100 GW by 2022. - Budget 2022: - 280 GW by 2030. - Boss: - MNRE. - Initiatives: - SRISTI: - Subsidies for rooftop solar equipment. - Tax-free solar bonds. - Rooftop solar in government complexes. - State building bye-laws mandating rooftop solar in large private buildings. - Solar parks on wastelands. - Net-metering for residential/commercial solar power sales to DISCOMs. - Surya Mitra: - 90-day skill development for solar equipment installation/repair. - ARUN Mobile App: - Assists rooftop solar installation. - Solar City Initiative (2012-17): - 60 cities to replace 10% conventional energy with solar. - Amending Electricity Act for RPO and Renewable Generation Obligation (RGO). - Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO): - Applicable: - DISCOMs, large electricity consumers, captive power plants. - Requirement: - Purchase a minimum percentage of electricity from renewable sources (set by MNRE). - Quotas: - 2014 (11.5%), 2018 (17%), 2019 (17.5%), 2022 (21%), with internal solar/non-solar and Hydropower Purchase Obligation (HPO) quotas. - Pricing: - Set by CERC (interstate) or SERC (intrastate). - Related: - Renewable Generation Obligation (RGO) mandates coal-based thermal plants to generate/procure a percentage of renewable energy. - World’s Largest Hybrid Renewable Energy Park (Khavda): - Location: - Kutch, Gujarat (near Indo-Pakistan border). - Capacity: - 30,000 MW (solar + wind) over 72,600 hectares. - Operators: - Adani Green, Gujarat State Electricity Company, etc. - Renewable/Energy Efficiency Rankings/Portals: - SARAL Index: - By MNRE, Shakti Sustainable Energy Foundation, ASSOCHAM, Ernst & Young; ranks states for rooftop solar attractiveness. - SAATHEE Portal: - Power Ministry’s portal to monitor state-level energy efficiency. - PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (Interim Budget 2024): - Boss: - MNRE. - Loan: - Interest Rate: - Repo + 0.5% (currently 7%). - Collateral: - Not required. - Subsidy: - Up to 2 kW: - 60% (₹30,000 for 1 kW, ₹60,000 for 2 kW). - 2-3 kW: - 40% (₹78,000 for 3 kW). - Above 3 kW: - No subsidy. - Eligibility: - Indian citizen. - Owns a house with a suitable roof for solar panels. - Valid electricity connection. - No prior solar panel subsidy availed. - Benefits: - Saves electricity bills. - Earns income by selling surplus power to DISCOMs. - Example: - 3 kW panel with 300 units/month usage saves ~₹15,000/year. - Fossil Fuel Reduction Strategies - E20 Ethanol Blending: - Context: - Dr. Rakesh Sarwal Committee (2021) roadmap for ethanol blending (2020-2025). - Sources of Ethanol: - Primary Feedstocks: - Sugarcane molasses: - C-heavy molasses, ~80% of India’s ethanol production. - Damaged food grains: - Rice, wheat unfit for human consumption (FCI surplus). - Maize: - Promoted for sustainability, less water-intensive than sugarcane. - Emerging Feedstocks: - Agricultural residues: - Straw, bagasse for 2G ethanol (cellulosic). - Non-food crops: - Sweet sorghum, energy cane for higher yield, lower environmental impact. - Production Process: - Fermentation of sugars (molasses, grains) or cellulosic biomass (2G ethanol). - Distillation to achieve 99.5% pure ethanol for blending. - Ethanol Types: - 1G Ethanol: - From sugarcane, grains; widely used but competes with food security. - 2G Ethanol: - From agricultural residues; eco-friendly, reduces stubble burning, no food crop diversion. - Targets: - E10 (10% ethanol in petrol): - Achieved by 2022. - E20 (20% ethanol in petrol): - By 2025, reduces CO emissions by 30-50%, hydrocarbons by 20%. - Ultimate Goal: - E100 (100% ethanol vehicles). - Support Mechanisms: - R&D funding: - For E20-compliant vehicle engines (e.g., flex-fuel engines). - Tax/subsidy: - Incentives for E20-compliant vehicles (GST reduction, road tax waivers). - Feedstock Strategy: - Divert surplus sugarcane/rice for ethanol. - Promote maize/non-food crops to ensure food security and sustainability. - Loan interest subsidies: - For ethanol distilleries (up to 6% interest subvention). - Benefits: - Economic: - Saves ₹30,000 crore in fuel imports annually, enhances energy security. - Environmental: - Reduces CO2 emissions, hydrocarbons, and stubble burning. - Social: - Boosts farmer income (~₹20,000 crore annually), creates jobs (~7 lakh in ethanol sector). - Environmental Risks: - Water-intensive sugarcane cultivation: - Depletes groundwater in states like Maharashtra, Karnataka. - Soil degradation: - Monoculture sugarcane farming reduces soil fertility. - Food security: - Diversion of grains risks price volatility (mitigated by 2G ethanol focus). - Effluent discharge: - Molasses-based distilleries produce wastewater, requires zero-liquid discharge compliance. - Policy Context: - Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme (2003): - Initial 5% blending mandate. - National Biofuel Policy (2018): - Promotes 2G ethanol, targets E20 by 2025. - Biogas Blending in Natural Gas: - Boss: - Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. - Process: - Biogas Production: - Anaerobic decomposition of agriculture residue (straw, husk), cattle dung, municipal solid waste, sewage. - Purification: - Removal of CO2, H2S, moisture to produce Compressed Biogas (CBG, >95% methane). - Blending: - CBG mixed with CNG (vehicles) or PNG (cooking) via city gas distribution pipelines. - Sources: - Cattle dung: - ~300 million cattle in India, major biogas source. - Agricultural waste: - Paddy straw, sugarcane bagasse (~500 MT annually). - Municipal waste: - Urban areas generate ~60 MT organic waste yearly. - Blending Targets: - 2024-25: - Voluntary. - 2025-26: - 1%. - 2026-27: - 3%. - 2027-28: - 4%. - Applications: - Transport: - CBG as CNG substitute in buses, auto-rickshaws. - Domestic: - Blended with PNG for cooking in urban households. - Industrial: - Used in small-scale industries for heating. - Benefits: - Economic: - Reduces LNG imports (~₹10,000 crore savings annually), saves forex. - Environmental: - Lowers CO2 emissions, utilizes waste, promotes circular economy. - Social: - Creates rural jobs (~2 lakh in CBG plants), reduces stubble burning. - Logistical: - Decreases LPG cylinder transport, reducing air pollution and logistics costs. - Environmental Risks: - Methane leakage: - Improper handling during production/storage risks GHG emissions. - Land use: - Large-scale biogas plants may compete with agricultural land. - Water pollution: - Improper slurry disposal from biogas plants can contaminate water bodies. - Policy Context: - SATAT (2018): - Promotes CBG as automotive fuel, targets 5,000 CBG plants by 2030. - GOBARdhan (2018): - Supports biogas plant setup, waste-to-wealth model. - Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF): - Definition: - Liquid fuel for aviation from food waste, used cooking oil, green/municipal waste, non-food crops (jatropha, algae), blended with conventional jet fuel. - Production Process: - Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA): - Converts oils/fats into jet fuel. - Fischer-Tropsch (FT): - Biomass gasification to produce synthetic fuel. - Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ): - Ethanol/methanol converted to jet fuel. - Sources: - Used cooking oil: - Collected from restaurants, households. - Municipal waste: - Organic fraction from urban waste. - Non-food crops: - Jatropha, camelina, pongamia grown on marginal lands. - Benefits: - Environmental: - Reduces CO2 emissions by up to 80%, lowers particulate matter. - Economic: - Reduces jet fuel import dependence (~₹15,000 crore annually). - Social: - Promotes non-food crop cultivation, creates jobs in rural areas. - Targets: - 2027: - 1% SAF blending (international flights). - 2028: - 2% SAF blending (international flights). - Environmental Risks: - Land use conflict: - Large-scale non-food crop cultivation may encroach on arable land. - Biodiversity loss: - Monoculture plantations (e.g., jatropha) may reduce biodiversity. - High energy input: - SAF production (e.g., FT process) requires significant energy. - Policy Context: - National Biofuel Policy (2018): - Encourages SAF development. - CORSIA (ICAO): - Global carbon offset scheme mandates SAF use for international flights. - Green, Grey, Blue Hydrogen: - Green Hydrogen: - Production: - Electrolysis of water using renewable energy (solar, wind). - Emissions: - Zero carbon emissions. - Cost: - High (~₹350/kg, expected to drop to ₹150/kg by 2030 with scale). - Applications: - Heavy industries (steel, cement), transport (fuel cells), power generation. - Blue Hydrogen: - Production: - Steam Methane Reforming (SMR) with carbon capture and storage (CCS). - Emissions: - Low (~90% CO2 captured). - Cost: - Moderate (~₹200/kg). - Applications: - Industrial heating, ammonia production. - Grey Hydrogen: - Production: - SMR without CCS. - Emissions: - High (~10 kg CO2 per kg H2). - Cost: - Low (~₹100/kg). - Applications: - Current dominant source for industrial hydrogen (e.g., fertilizers). - SMR Process: - CH4 + H2O → CO + 3H2 (synthesis gas/syngas). - CO + H2O → CO2 + H2 (water-gas shift reaction). - Environmental Risks: - Green: - High water use in electrolysis (~9 liters/kg H2), renewable energy land requirements. - Blue: - CCS infrastructure leakage risks, energy-intensive capture process. - Grey: - High GHG emissions, unsustainable long-term. - Policy Context: - National Hydrogen Mission (2021): - Prioritizes green hydrogen for energy transition. - Global Context: - EU’s Hydrogen Strategy, US Inflation Reduction Act support green hydrogen. - National Hydrogen Mission (Budget 2021, PM Modi’s August 2021 Speech): - Boss: - Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). - Focus: - Green hydrogen production, use, and export to position India as a global hub. - Targets by 2030: - Production: - 5 MMT green hydrogen. - Energy: - 125 GW from green hydrogen. - Investment: - ₹8 lakh crore. - Jobs: - 6 lakh jobs. - GHG Reduction: - 50 MMT annually. - Crude Oil Import Reduction: - ₹1 lakh crore. - SIGHT Subsidy Program: - Full Name: - Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition. - Subsidies: - Electrolyzer manufacturing: - ₹4,440 crore allocated (2023-28). - Green hydrogen production: - ₹5,000 crore for cost reduction. - Objective: - Reduce green hydrogen cost to compete with grey hydrogen. - SHIP Partnership: - Full Name: - Strategic Hydrogen Innovation Partnership. - Objective: - Public-private R&D for green hydrogen technologies (e.g., fuel cells, storage). - Environmental Risks: - Water scarcity: - Electrolysis requires significant water, challenging in water-stressed regions. - Land use: - Large solar/wind farms for green hydrogen may impact ecosystems. - Infrastructure: - High initial emissions for building hydrogen plants. - Policy Context: - Green Hydrogen Policy (2022): - Tax exemptions, land allocation, grid connectivity for producers. - International Collaboration: - India-Germany H2 Partnership, ISA’s Green Hydrogen Program. - MAHIR Research for Energy (2023): - Full Name: - Mission on Advanced and High-Impact Research. - Boss: - Ministry of Power and MNRE. - R&D Focus: - Battery Alternatives: - Sodium-ion, solid-state batteries for EVs. - Nanotechnology: - High-efficiency EV battery materials. - Electric Cookers: - Modified for Indian cooking (e.g., high-heat tandoors). - Solid-State Refrigeration: - Energy-efficient cooling without refrigerants. - Green Hydrogen: - High-efficiency fuel cells for mobility. - Carbon Capture: - Next-gen CCS for blue hydrogen, thermal plants. - Geothermal Energy: - Exploration in Himalayan, Deccan regions. - Environmental Risks: - Nanotechnology: - Potential toxicity of nanomaterials in battery production. - Geothermal: - Seismic risks in unstable regions (e.g., Himalayas). - CCS: - Long-term CO2 storage leakage risks. - Policy Context: - Aligns with Atma-Nirbhar Bharat: - Promotes indigenous clean energy tech. - Complements FAME-II, PLI schemes for EV and battery manufacturing. - Miscellaneous Fossil Fuel Reduction Schemes: - Methanol Economy Fund (2017, NITI Aayog): - Objective: - Reduce petrol/diesel use with methanol (CH3OH) from bio-waste, coal gasification. - Sources: - Biomass: - Agricultural residues, municipal waste. - Coal: - High-ash Indian coal for methanol via gasification. - Benefits: - Environmental: - No particulate matter, sulfur, or nitrogen emissions. - Economic: - Reduces fuel imports (~₹12,000 crore annually). - Social: - Utilizes waste, creates jobs in methanol plants. - Applications: - Transport: - Methanol-blended fuels (M15, M100). - Power: - Methanol-based generators. - Cooking: - Methanol stoves as LPG alternative. - Environmental Risks: - Coal-based methanol: - High CO2 emissions unless paired with CCS. - Toxicity: - Methanol is hazardous if mishandled. - Policy Context: - NITI Aayog’s Methanol Economy Roadmap: - Targets 10% fuel blending by 2030. - PM JI-VAN Yojana (2019): - Full Name: - Pradhan Mantri Jaiv Indhan-Vatavaran Anukool Fasal Awashesh Nivaran. - Boss: - Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (100% Union-funded). - Objective: - Financial assistance for 2G bioethanol projects using lignocellulosic biomass. - Sources: - Agricultural residues: - Rice straw, wheat straw, bagasse. - Municipal solid waste: - Organic fraction for ethanol. - Benefits: - Environmental: - Reduces stubble burning, CO2 emissions. - Economic: - ₹6,000 crore investment in 2G ethanol plants. - Social: - Farmer income from crop residue (~₹2,000 crore annually). - Environmental Risks: - Biomass transport: - High logistics emissions if not localized. - Water use: - Biomass pretreatment requires water, risks in dry regions. - Policy Context: - National Biofuel Policy (2018): - Targets 12 2G ethanol plants by 2025. - Complements EBP Programme for ethanol blending. - LPG and Cooking Fuel Schemes - Pratyaksh Hanstantrit Labh (PAHAL, 2015): - Boss: - Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (Central Sector Scheme, 100% Union-funded). - Mechanism: - Direct Benefit Transfer for LPG (DBTL); consumers buy LPG at market price, subsidy transferred to bank account linked to customer ID. - Subsidy: - Up to 12 cylinders (14.2 kg) per year; 5 kg cylinders receive lower subsidy. - Ineligible: - Restaurants, commercial enterprises, individuals with taxable income >₹10 lakh. - Price Trends: - 2014: - Market ₹1241, Subsidy ₹800 (to companies), Effective ₹441. - 2018: - Market ₹941, Subsidy ₹434, Effective ₹507. - 2020-21: - Market ₹885, Subsidy ₹0 (paused), Effective ₹885. - 2023: - Market ₹703, Subsidy ₹300, Effective ₹603. - LPG PAHAL Subsidy Paused (2020-21): - Since May 2020: - Subsidy paused, saving >₹25,000 crore but causing hardship for middle-class families. - 2022-23: - Subsidy resumed for PM Ujjwala Yojana beneficiaries. - 2024: - Subsidy continuation announced. - Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana 1.0 (PMUY, 2016): - Boss: - Petroleum Ministry (Central Sector Scheme). - Features: - Deposit-free LPG connections, rubber tube, pressure regulator for BPL women (SECC-2011 data, later expanded to forest dwellers, island residents). - Cost: - Beneficiaries pay for stove and cylinders. - Benefits: - Reduces firewood/kerosene use, indoor pollution, improves health/environment. - Milestone: - Himachal Pradesh achieved 100% LPG coverage (2019). - COVID-19 Relief (2020): - 3 free cylinders for PMUY beneficiaries until June 30, 2020. - Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana 2.0 (2021): - Boss: - Petroleum Ministry. - Features: - Deposit-free LPG connection, free first cylinder, free hotplate/stove. - Target: - Poor households not covered in PMUY 1.0, poor migrant workers (no ration card/address proof required, self-declaration suffices). - Eligibility: - Adult women from poor households, SECC-listed, SC/ST, PMAY (Gramin), AAY, tea garden workers, forest dwellers, island residents. - Kerosene Subsidy Stopped (2020): - Mechanism: - Similar to PAHAL, kerosene sold at market price with subsidy transferred to poor families’ accounts. - Context: - Saubhagya and PMUY reduced kerosene demand. - Since March 2020: - Subsidy stopped; kerosene sold at PDS stores without subsidy. - GOBARdhan (2018): - Boss: - Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (under Swachh Bharat Mission - Gramin). - Funding: - Core scheme (Union + State contributions). - Objective: - Convert cattle dung and biowaste into biogas and organic manure. - Support: - Up to ₹20 lakh for gram panchayats to set up projects. - Unified GOBARdhan Portal: - By Ministries of Agriculture, Animal Husbandry, Petroleum, Jal Shakti. - Budget 2023: - 500 new “waste to wealth” plants, 5% mandatory CBG blending in natural gas. - Natural Gas and Related Initiatives - Natural Gas Price: Kirit Parikh Panel (2022-23): - Gas Production Ownership: - Government (83%), Private (17%). - 2014: - New formula for domestic natural gas pricing. - 2023 Recommendations: - Before: - Separate pricing for public (ONGC, Oil India) and private companies. - After: - Prices linked to international markets, with ceiling ($6.5/MMBtu) and floor ($4/MMBtu). - Benefit: - ~10% price reduction for PNG/CNG consumers. - Miscellaneous Gas Schemes: - PM Urja Ganga (2016): - Objective: - Natural Gas Grid Pipeline across UP, Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal (Jagdishpur-Haldia/Bokaro-Dhamra Pipeline, JHBDPL). - Benefit: - Supplies PNG to homes, hotels, fertilizer/electricity companies, fostering a gas-based economy. - City Compost Scheme (2016): - Boss: - Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. - Objective: - Subsidize compost production from municipal waste for farmers. - SATAT (2018): - Boss: - Petroleum Ministry. - Objective: - Promote Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG, >95% methane) as automotive fuel. - SAMARTH: - Boss: - Ministry of Power. - Objective: - Thermal plants to use 5-10% biomass/crop residue with coal. - Flex Engine: - Vehicles capable of using petrol/diesel, ethanol, or methanol. - Unified Gas Price System (2020): - Boss: - Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB). - Objective: - Reduce natural gas costs for distant users. - Nuclear Energy Development - Applications: - Research Reactors: - Produce medical isotopes for cancer treatment. - Irradiation Facilities: - Preserve food. - Economic Survey 2025 - Nuclear Power Challenges: - Safety: - Chernobyl (1986, Ukraine), Fukushima (2011, Japan). - Limited access to uranium and reactor technologies. - By 2040: - Shortage of sulfuric acid (petrochemical byproduct) for uranium extraction. - Budget 2024 - Energy Focus: - Nuclear Energy: - Key for Viksit Bharat. - Initiatives: - Bharat Small Reactors, R&D for Small Modular Reactors, and newer nuclear technologies. - Advanced Ultra Super Critical (AUSC) Thermal Coal Power: - NTPC-BHEL joint venture for 800 MW plant, reducing GHG emissions by 11% compared to super-critical plants. - Budget 2025 - Energy/Mining/Nuclear: - Clean Tech Manufacturing: - Support for solar PV cells, EV batteries, electrolyzers, wind turbines. - Target: - 100 GW nuclear energy by 2047. - Legislative Amendments: - Proposed amendments to the Atomic Energy Act and Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act to facilitate nuclear energy expansion. - Nuclear Energy Mission: - Focus: - Research and development of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs). - Target: - At least 5 indigenously developed SMRs operational by 2033. - Budget 2024/2025 Context: - Emphasis on nuclear energy for Viksit Bharat. - Initiatives: - Bharat Small Reactors, R&D for SMRs, and advanced nuclear technologies. - Target: - 100 GW nuclear energy capacity by 2047. - Pillar 5A3: Infrastructure - Water & Sanitation - Overview: - Historical Context: - Ancient Indus Valley Civilization prioritized sanitation with integrated systems in town planning. However, by 2012, over 50% of Indians practiced open defecation due to neglect by policymakers. - Significance: - Access to clean water and sanitation is critical for public health, dignity (especially for women), and environmental sustainability. - Related Reference: - Pillar 4A (Agriculture) for irrigation and drinking water schemes. - Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM, 2014) - Introduction: - Launched on October 2, 2014, by PM Narendra Modi, restructured from Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (2012, PM Manmohan Singh). - Boss: - Originally Ministry of Drinking Water & Sanitation, now under Ministry of Jal Shakti. - Funding: - Core scheme (not 100% Union-funded; 60:40 or 90:10 Union-State ratio) with Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) contributions. - Recognition: - PM Modi received the Global Gatekeeper Award (2019) from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation for SBM. - Objective: - Achieve a clean and open defecation-free (ODF) India by promoting sanitation, waste management, and behavioral change. - Phases: - Phase 1 (2014-2019): - Focused on toilet construction, ODF status, and awareness. - Phase 2 (2020-2025): - Reinforces ODF status, emphasizes waste management and sustainability. - Target of Swachhta Diwas (October 2, 2019) - Gandhi’s 150th Birth Anniversary: - Open Defecation Free (ODF) India. - Eradication of manual scavenging. - Improved Municipal Solid Waste Management (MSWM). - Outcome: - Approximately 90 million toilets constructed by 2019, per government data. - How to Achieve Targets: - Construction: - Financial assistance for building individual household toilets, community toilets, bathing houses, and public toilets at bus stations, schools, and temporary construction sites. - Solid Waste Management: - Funding for trucks, garbage disposal units, and infrastructure. - Awareness Campaigns: - Information, Education, and Communication (IEC) initiatives via Swachhta Doots, social media, posters, and advertisements. - Darwaza Band Campaign: - Promotes toilet use to prevent open defecation. - Research and Development: - Innovations in sanitation technologies. - Mobile Applications: - Platforms for reporting unclean areas and public grievances. - Citizen Engagement: - Encourages large-scale participation through community clean-ups and sustainable practices. - Who Implements the Scheme: - Rural Areas: - Department of Drinking Water & Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti. - Urban Areas: - Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA). - Gramin Phase 2 (2020-2025): - Objective: - Ensure sustained toilet use and expand waste management. - Features: - Plastic waste management. - Animal and biodegradable solid waste management. - Greywater management (used domestic water, excluding toilet wastewater). - Fecal sludge management. - Progress (2023): - 50% of villages achieved ODF Plus status, with Telangana at 100% ODF Plus. - Village Types: - Aspiring: - Sustains ODF status + arrangements for either solid or liquid waste management. - Rising: - Sustains ODF status + arrangements for both solid and liquid waste management. - Model (ODF Plus): - Rising category + visual cleanliness (minimal litter, stagnant wastewater, no plastic waste dumps) + displays ODF Plus IEC messages. - Urban 2.0 (Budget 2021): - Timeline: - 2021-2026. - Funding: - Over ₹1 lakh crore. - Features: - Management of fecal sludge and wastewater. - Garbage segregation. - Reduction in single-use plastics. - Decreased air pollution from construction and demolition activities. - Bioremediation of dumpsites. - Emphasis on circular economy principles. - Protocols: - ODF (Open Defecation Free) Protocol: - Definition: - No visible faeces in environment + every household has access to safe toilet. - ODF+: - Sustained toilet usage + safe disposal of faecal sludge. - ODF++: - ODF+ + complete faecal sludge and sewage management in all households and institutions. - GFC (Garbage Free City) Protocol: - Launched by: - Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. - Rating: - 1-star to 7-star based on solid waste management performance. - Parameters: - Door-to-door waste collection. - Source segregation. - Scientific processing of waste (composting, recycling). - No visible garbage in public spaces. - Bulk waste generators must process waste on-site. - Water+ Protocol: - Applicable to cities with ODF++ certification. - Ensures: - All wastewater is safely collected, transported, treated, and reused or disposed. - Promotes treated wastewater reuse in agriculture, industry, and construction. - Sanitation Rating Protocol: - For: - Cities and towns. - Focuses on cleanliness of public toilets, water availability, and maintenance. - SafaiMitra Suraksha Protocol: - Objective: - Ensure safety of sanitation workers. - Prohibits manual entry into sewers and septic tanks. - Mandates mechanized cleaning and proper Personal Protective Equipment (PPE). - Swachh Survekshan: - Annual cleanliness survey of cities and towns since 2016. - Evaluates cities based on service-level progress, citizen feedback, and field assessment. - Achievements: - Over 100 million toilets constructed in rural India. - 6+ lakh villages declared ODF. - Massive behavioural change and community participation. - Increased awareness of waste segregation and sanitation rights. - Swachh Bharat Abhiyan (Urban) – Monitoring, Ranking, and Support Schemes - Swachh Sarvekshan 2023 (MoHUA, January 2024): - Overview: - World’s largest urban sanitation survey, conducted since 2016 by MoHUA, covering 4,416 urban local bodies, 61 cantonments, and 88 Ganga towns. - Cleanest Cities: - Rank 1 (Tie): - Indore (7th consecutive year) and Surat. - Rank 3: - Navi Mumbai. - Top States: - Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh. - Subcategories: - Awards for cities with populations <1 lakh, states with <100 local bodies, etc. (low MCQ relevance due to poor cost-benefit for memorization). - Prerak Dauur Samman (2021): - Introduced by MoHUA under SBM to recognize waste segregation, construction waste management, landfill management, and sanitation efforts. - Subcategories: - Divya (Platinum), Anupam (Gold), Ujjwal (Silver), Udit (Bronze), Aarohi (Aspiring). - Note: - Latest rankings have poor cost-benefit for memorization in MCQ context. - Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan 2024 (Clean Air Ranking): - Boss: - Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. - Event: - Awards presented on International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies (September 7). - Rankings (2023, million-plus population cities): - Rank 1: - Surat. - Rank 2: - Jabalpur. - Rank 3: - Agra. - Super Swachh League (2024): - Criteria: - Cities in the top 3 for at least 2 of the last 3 years (2021-2023). - Categories and Cities: - Very Small Cities (<20,000): - Panchgani, Patan. - Small Cities (20,000-50,000): - Vita, Sasvad. - Medium Cities (50,000-3 lakh): - Ambikapur, Tirupati, New Delhi Municipal Council. - Big Cities (3-10 lakh): - Noida, Chandigarh. - Million Plus (>10 lakh): - Navi Mumbai, Indore, Surat. - Swachhta Udyami Yojana (2014): - Boss: - Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, implemented by National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation. - Features: - Concessional loans to Safai Karamcharis/manual scavengers for: - Building community toilets with user fee revenue. - Purchasing sanitation-related vehicles for municipal garbage collection contracts. - Related Scheme: - Self Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of Manual Scavengers (SRMS) provides skill training and financial assistance. - Economic Survey 2025 - Water-Related Portals: - Bhu-Neer Portal: - Developer: - Central Ground Water Authority. - Objective: - Manage groundwater resources, monitor usage, and ensure sustainability. - FloodWatch India App (v2.0): - Developer: - Central Water Commission. - Objective: - Provide real-time flood forecasts and warnings. - Pillar 5B1: Infrastructure - Transport (Inland Waterways, Shipping & Ports) - Overview: - Transport infrastructure, including inland waterways and ports, is critical for economic growth, trade, and connectivity. - Economic Survey 2025: - India’s navigable waterway length is approximately 14,850 km, with 26 operational waterways spanning over 4,800 km. - Significance: - Inland Waterways Transport (IWT) and ports facilitate low-carbon, cost-effective cargo movement, reducing road/rail congestion. - Inland Waterways - Benefits of Inland Waterways Transport (IWT): - Lower CO2 emissions and fuel consumption per tonne of cargo compared to rail/road. - Minimal land acquisition required compared to rail/road infrastructure. - Eases traffic congestion on road/rail networks. - Inland Waterway Authority of India (IWAI): - Boss: - Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. - Status: - Statutory body established under the Inland Waterways Authority of India Act, 1985. - Functions: - Develops and regulates inland waterways for navigation and transport. - National Waterways: - Legal Basis: - 7th Schedule (Union List); Parliament can legislate on inland waterways. - National Waterways Act, 2016: - Declared 111 national waterways, including 5 pre-existing ones. - Key National Waterways (Operational): - NW-1: - Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly River System (Haldia-Allahabad, 1,620 km, UP/Bihar/Jharkhand/WB). - NW-2: - Brahmaputra River (Dhubri-Sadiya, 891 km, Assam). - NW-3: - West Coast, Champakara, and Udyogmandal Canals (205 km, Kerala). - NW-4: - Krishna, Godavari, and Canals (2,890 km when completed, TN/Andhra/Telangana). - NW-5: - Mahanadi Delta Rivers and Canals (588 km, Odisha/WB). - NW-40: - Ghagra/Saryu River (354 km, UP; planned for Ramayan Cruise Tour, Ayodhya). - Others: - NW-68 (Mandovi, Goa), NW-111 (Zuari, Goa), NW-97 (Sundarbans). - Note: - Over 20 waterways are currently operational, per Economic Survey 2025. - Jal Marg Vikas Project (2014): - Objective: - Develop infrastructure for commercial navigation on NW-1 (Varanasi-Haldia stretch of Ganga). - Challenges: - Low depth upstream of Farakka, limiting large vessel navigation. - Features: - Construction of navigational locks and infrastructure. - Roll on-Roll off (Ro-Ro) ferries. - Digital tools: - River Information System (RIS) and Vessel Traffic Management System (VTMS). - Multi-modal terminal at Varanasi (inaugurated November 2018 by PM Modi, received cargo ship MV Rabindranath Tagore from Kolkata). - Funding: - Central Sector Scheme (100% Union-funded) with World Bank (IBRD) loans and Public-Private Partnership (PPP). - Completion: - Targeted for March 2023, aimed at transforming Ganga into “Arth Ganga” (River of Wealth). - Additional: - Varanasi designated as India’s first freight village for cargo operations. - Arth-Ganga (August 2022): - Objective: - Promote sustainable economic development along the Ganga beyond cleaning. - Six Pillars: 1. Zero Budget Natural Farming: - Chemical-free farming within 10 km of Ganga, promoting cow dung fertilizers via GOBARdhan scheme. 2. Sludge and Wastewater Management: - Recycling for irrigation and industrial use. 3. Cultural Heritage: - Boat tourism, adventure sports, and yoga activities. 4. Livelihood Opportunities: - Local markets for products, medicinal plants, and Ayurveda 5. Local Administration Improvement 6. Public Participation Enhancement - MV Ganga Vilas - Longest River Luxury Cruise: - Overview: - World’s longest river cruise, covering 3,200 km in 51 days across 27 rivers. - Route: - Varanasi (UP) to Dibrugarh (Assam) via Bangladesh. - Coverage: - 50 tourist spots, including world heritage sites, national parks, river ghats, and cities (Patna, Sahibganj, Kolkata, Dhaka, Guwahati). - Operator: - Antara Luxury River Cruises (Kolkata-based private company). - Ticket Price: - ₹25,000/day onwards. - Inland Vessels Act, 2021: - Note: - Outdated/low-profile topic, removed from study material due to limited exam relevance. - Harit Nauka Initiative: - Objective: - Promote green fuels/technology in inland waterway vessels. - Milestone (February 2024): - PM Modi launched India’s first hydrogen cell-powered inland waterway vessel, manufactured by Cochin Shipyard. - Green Hydrogen Hub: - V.O. Chidambaranar Port (Tuticorin) designated as India’s first Green Hydrogen Hub Port. - Jalvahak Scheme (2025): - Boss: - Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. - Feature: - 35% subsidy on cargo transportation costs via NW-1 (Ganga), NW-2 (Brahmaputra), and NW-16 (Barak). - Shipping & Ports - Context: - India’s coastline: - ~7,517 km. - Trade: - ~95% of trade by volume and 68% by value transported via sea. - Alang-Sosiya (Gujarat): - World’s largest ship recycling yard, operational since 1983. - [Yearbook] Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways: - Old Name: - Ministry of Shipping (renamed in 2020). - Statutory Bodies: - Inland Waterway Authority of India (IWAI). - Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP): - Sets fees for major ports. - Indian Maritime University (IMU, Chennai): - Established via IMU Act, 2008, for maritime education, training, and research. - Directorate General of Shipping (Mumbai): - National Authority for Ship Recycling under Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 (office in Gandhinagar, Gujarat). - Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships. - Minor Ports Survey Organisation. - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Shipping Corporation of India (Mumbai, approved for disinvestment in 2019). - Dredging Corporation of India Ltd. - Kamarajar Port Ltd. (Ennore, Tamil Nadu). - Cochin Shipyard Ltd. (Cochin). - Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. - Hooghly Dock & Port Engineers Ltd. - Sethusamudram Corporation Ltd. - Global Cooperation: - International Maritime Organization (IMO, London): - UN agency for shipping regulation. - Hong Kong International Convention (2009, ratified by India in 2019): - Safe and environmentally sound ship recycling. - UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, 1982, Jamaica): - Regulates maritime activities; notable for 2012 Enrica Lexie case (Italian marines killed Indian fishermen off Kerala). - 2012 Enrica Lexie case: - Two Italian marines aboard the Italian tanker "Enrica Lexie" shot dead two Indian fishermen off the Kerala coast. - Led to diplomatic and legal conflict; referred to international arbitration. - Reason: - They mistook the fishing boat for a pirate vessel. - At that time, merchant vessels in the Indian Ocean and Arabian Sea were on high alert due to frequent Somali pirate attacks. - Polar Code (IMO): - Safety guidelines for ships in polar waters (e.g., ice removal equipment, thermal clothing). - Miscellaneous: - Ropax Service (Roll-on/Roll-off cum Passenger Ferry): - Launched: - March 2020. - Route: - Mumbai to Mandwa (Maharashtra). - Purpose: - Reduces road travel time (110 km) to sea travel (18 km). - Cuts travel time from ~3 hours to just 1 hour. - Promotes eco-friendly and economical transport. - Features: - Can carry both passengers and vehicles (cars, buses, motorcycles). - Reduces traffic congestion and fuel consumption. - Types of Ports - Major and Minor Ports: - Legal Basis: - Indian Ports Act, 1908. - Major Ports: - 12 operational, regulated by Union Government (Union List, 7th Schedule). - Minor Ports: - Over 200, regulated by State Governments (Concurrent List). - Note: - Government reports list 12 operational major ports, though new ports (e.g., Galathea Bay) are notified. - List of Major Ports in India (A: Artificial, N: Natural Harbor): - West Coast (6): - Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Nhava Sheva, Maharashtra, N, 1989): - Largest container port of India (per NCERT). - Functions as a satellite port to Mumbai Port to reduce congestion. - Mumbai Port (Maharashtra, N): - Largest oil terminal in India. - Deendayal Port (Kandla, Gujarat, N): - Tidal port, first Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in India/Asia, developed post-Partition. - Mormugao Port (Goa, N): - Tidal port at Zuari estuary, exports iron ore to Japan. - New Mangalore Port (Karnataka, A): - Deep-water, all-weather port (1974-75). - Cochin Port (Kerala, N): - Willingdon Island, developed during British Raj, known as Queen of the Arabian Sea. - East Coast (6): - Kolkata Port (West Bengal, N): - Oldest major port, riverine port on Hooghly River with Kolkata and Haldia docks; requires constant dredging due to silt. - Vishakhapatnam Port (Andhra Pradesh, N): - Land-locked harbor, Eastern Naval Command base. - Paradeep Port (Odisha, A): - Manmade lagoon in Mahanadi Delta, Union-owned since 1965. - V.O. Chidambaranar Port (Tuticorin, Tamil Nadu, N): - Gulf of Mannar. - Chennai Port (Tamil Nadu, A): - All-weather port (1875), less suitable for large ships due to shallow waters. - Kamarajar Port (Ennore, Tamil Nadu, A): - Corporate port under Companies Act, primarily for thermal coal for Tamil Nadu Electricity Board. - Additional Developments: -
