- Budget 2020: - Plan to corporatize at least one major port and list its shares on stock exchanges. - Note: - For state PSC exams, assume 12 operational major ports unless options specify otherwise. - Vizhinjam International Seaport (Kerala, Under Construction): - Overview: - India’s first deep-water transshipment port with a natural depth of over 20 meters. - Transshipment refers to the process of transferring cargo (usually containers) from one ship to another at an intermediate port before it reaches its final destination. - Located near the international shipping route (~10 nautical miles from East-West trade corridor). - Being developed by Adani Ports and SEZ Ltd. on a PPP model with Kerala government. - Features: - Capable of berthing ultra-large container ships (ULCS) like Triple-E class. - Fully mechanized cargo handling. - Smart, green, and sustainable infrastructure (e.g., renewable energy use, minimal dredging). - First phase capacity: - ~1 million TEUs (Twenty-foot Equivalent Units). - The unit TEU stands for Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit, and it is the standard measurement used in the shipping and port industry to measure cargo capacity, especially container capacity. - Connectivity planned via rail, NH-66 highway, and potential inland waterways. - Significance: - Reduces India’s dependency on foreign ports like: - Colombo (Sri Lanka) - Singapore - Port Klang (Malaysia) - Helps retain transshipment revenue within India. - Strategic location for naval, trade, and geopolitical interests in the Indian Ocean Region. - Enhances export-import (EXIM) competitiveness by reducing time and cost. - Timeline: - Foundation stone laid in 2015. - Delayed due to protests, cyclone damage, and land acquisition issues. - Expected operationalization: - By 2025 (Phase I). - Mundra Port, Gujarat: - Overview: - Located on the northern shores of the Gulf of Kutch, Mundra Port is India’s first greenfield port developed under the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model. - A greenfield port refers to a completely new port built from scratch on undeveloped land where no previous port infrastructure exists. - Operated by Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Ltd. (APSEZL), part of the Adani Group. - Developed as a multi-cargo, all-weather, deep-draft port with world-class infrastructure. - Model: - Build, Own, Operate, and Transfer (BOOT) model. - Adani Group retains operational control for 30 years, after which the port will be transferred to the Gujarat government. - Demonstrates a successful example of private sector participation in major port development. - Infrastructure: - Features over 30 berths handling containers, bulk, liquid, automobiles, and LNG cargo. - Equipped with mechanized cargo handling systems, rail and road connectivity, and dedicated freight corridors. - Houses India’s largest commercial port-based SEZ (Special Economic Zone). - Capacity & Connectivity: - Annual handling capacity of over 250 million tonnes of cargo. - Direct connectivity to Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC), Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC), and Western Railway network. - Status: - Currently the largest privately owned and operated port in India. - Also among the top 30 container ports in the world (by throughput). - Plays a pivotal role in India’s trade logistics, especially for the western hinterland states (Rajasthan, Gujarat, MP, Delhi, etc.). - Significance: - Enhances India’s maritime trade competitiveness. - Reduces logistics costs by offering end-to-end integrated logistics solutions. - Contributes significantly to Gujarat’s port-led industrial development. - Classification by Function and Geography of Ports: - Dry Ports: - Inland terminals connected to seaports by rail/road (e.g., Patna, Bihar; Hazira, Gujarat; 20+ under development since 2018). - Industrial Ports: - Handle bulk cargo (grain, sugar, ore, oil, chemicals). - Commercial Ports: - Handle general cargo and passengers. - Comprehensive Ports: - Combine industrial and commercial facilities. - Packet Stations: - Ferry ports for short-distance passenger/mail transport (e.g., Dover, England; Calais, France). - Inland Ports: - Located away from sea via rivers/canals (e.g., Kolkata, Memphis, Rhine, Manchester). - Out Ports: - Deep-water ports built away from main ports for large ships (e.g., Piraeus for Athens, Greece). - Ports of Call: - Anchor points for refueling, watering, and food supplies (e.g., Aden, Honolulu, Singapore). - Entrepot Ports: - Collection centers for goods from various countries for export (e.g., Singapore, Rotterdam, Copenhagen). - Naval Ports: - For warship repair/construction (e.g., Kochi, Karwar). - Major Port Authorities Bill, 2020: - Note: - Technical topic, removed from study material due to low exam relevance. - Ports - Challenges in India: - Neglected Infrastructure: - Aging fleets, manpower shortages, and lack of world-class ports; large ships unload at Sri Lanka for transshipment to India. - Congestion and Delays: - High turnaround times, excessive paperwork, slow customs clearance/inspection. - Connectivity Issues: - Inadequate road/rail links to hinterland. - Major Port Inefficiencies: - Labor union issues and politicization of Boards of Directors; minor ports (privately owned) are more efficient. - Land and Environmental Issues: - Challenges in land acquisition and environmental clearances for new ports. - Underdeveloped Shipbuilding: - Domestic shipping companies rely on costly foreign ships due to weak domestic industry. - Sagar Aankalan - Guidelines for Indian Port Performance Index: - Boss: - Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. - Objective: - Monitor and improve port performance metrics. - India Stops Trans-shipment Facility to Bangladesh (2025): - Context: - India discontinued the facility that allowed Bangladesh to export goods to third countries via Indian seaports and airports (notably through Kolkata and Delhi). - Official Reason: - Bangladeshi cargo led to significant logistical delays, port congestion, and adversely impacted Indian exporters' schedules and competitiveness. - Unofficial/Strategic Reason: - Diplomatic signal to Bangladesh after its Chief Adviser, Md Yunus, sought Chinese investments in Bangladeshi port infrastructure. - He reportedly cited India’s Northeast as a landlocked region needing access through Bangladesh, suggesting Chinese ports could serve this role. - China could help build ports in Bangladesh that India’s Northeast could use for trade. - Why it's controversial? - It suggests that India’s Northeast might rely on Chinese-built ports, which India sees as a strategic and security concern. - Seen as undermining India’s Act East Policy and regional connectivity ambitions. - Implications: - May impact Bangladesh’s reliance on Indian logistics. - Potential boost to China’s influence in Bay of Bengal if Bangladesh pivots further east. - Could affect bilateral ties and SAARC/BIMSTEC cooperation. - Policies and schemes - National Logistics Policy (NLP) 2022: - Boss: - Ministry of Commerce and Industry. - Objective: - Reduce logistics costs (currently 13-14% of GDP) to single-digit levels, aligning with global standards (8-9% of GDP). - Features: - Integration of Digital System (IDS). - Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP). - Ease of Logistics (ELOG). - System Improvement Group (SIG). - Mechanism: - Seamless goods movement via Gati Shakti project (see Pillar 5C: PPP). - Cooperation: - Involves Ministries of Road Transport, Railways, Customs, Aviation, and Commerce. - Multimodal Parks by Ministry of Road Transport and Highways: - Objective: - Develop logistics parks for cargo aggregation, distribution, storage, and warehousing. - Budget 2023: - 100 critical transport infrastructure projects for last-mile connectivity to ports, coal, steel, fertilizer, and food grain sectors. - Example: - First multimodal park near Chennai, developed with Reliance. - Logistics Ranking: - World Bank’s Logistics Performance Index (LPI): - Released: - Every 2 years. - 2023: - India ranked 38 out of 139 countries. - NLP Target: - Top 25 by 2030 (not achieved by 2023). - LEADS Index (Logistics Ease Across Different States): - Boss: - Ministry of Commerce. - 2021: - Gujarat #1, Haryana #2, Punjab #3. - 2022 Onwards: - No ranks; states/UTs categorized into three groups (Achievers, Fast Movers, Aspirers). - Note: - Low priority for memorization due to limited exam relevance. - Sagarmala Project: - History: - Proposed by PM Vajpayee (2003), ignored by Manmohan Singh, revived by PM Modi (2015). - Boss: - Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. - Funding: - Central Sector Scheme (0% state funding), implemented via Sagarmala Development Company Ltd. (2016) through Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) with state/private participation. - Objectives: - Develop/improve ports and encourage coastal shipping. - Establish Coastal Economic Zones (CEZs) for manufacturing and employment. - Enhance hinterland connectivity via rail, road, and inland water transport. - Skill development for coastal communities. - Related Initiatives: - SAGAR-SETU: - Mobile app to improve Ease of Doing Business. - Harit Sagar: - Vision for zero carbon emissions from ports. - Sagar Manthan: - Incorrectly noted as a fish production mission (not relevant to Shipping Ministry). - Costa Serena: - First international cruise liner in India. - Blue Economy Policy 2021: - Boss: - Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES). - Objective: - Sustainable use of ocean resources for job creation and GDP growth, aligning with UN SDG #14 (Life Below Water). - Context: - India’s coastline: - ~7,500 km, 12 major ports, 9 coastal states, 1,300+ islands, 2 million sq.km Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). - Resources: - Living (algae, fish, prawns) and non-living (oil, gas, polymetallic nodules). - Features: - Fisheries and marine food processing. - Deep-sea mining and offshore energy. - Research and skill development. - Interim Budget 2024: - Blue Economy 2.0 focuses on coastal aquaculture and mariculture (see Pillar 4A). - Related: - Sethusamudram Project (1997) to create a shipping canal between Palk Bay and Gulf of Mannar; pending in Supreme Court due to marine biodiversity and Ram Sethu concerns. - Maritime Vision 2030: - Objective: - Enhance ships, ports, exports, and create 7-10 lakh jobs. - Note: - Overlaps with Blue Economy Policy; low-priority technical details. - Multi-Modal Transportation of Goods Bill, 2019: - Definition: - Multimodal transport uses multiple modes (rail, road, sea) for goods movement. - Original Act (1993): - Governs registration and liability for cargo delays/damage. - 2019 Proposal: - Replace 1993 Act with updated provisions (technical, low exam relevance). - Pillar 5B2: Infrastructure - Transport (Roads) - Overview: - Importance: - A robust road network is essential for economic growth, connecting remote areas, opening backward regions, and facilitating access to markets, trade, and investment. - Data: - India has the world’s second-largest road network (64 lakh km) after the USA (66 lakh km). National Highways (NH) constitute 2% of the total network (146,195 km) but carry 40% of road freight traffic (Economic Survey 2025). - Economic Contribution: - Road transport generates the highest Gross Value Added (GVA) within transport services. - [Yearbook] Ministry of Road Transport & Highways: - Statutory Bodies: - National Highways Authority of India (NHAI): - Manages national highways. - Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE): - National Highways and Infrastructure Development Corporation (NHIDCL). - Autonomous Bodies: - Indian Academy of Highway Engineers (IAHE): - Training for highway engineers. - Indian Road Congress (IRC): - Organizes conferences on road construction, maintenance, and development. - Number Plates: - 2019: - ‘LA’ number plates for vehicles registered in Ladakh UT. - 2021: - ‘BH’ series for Defense personnel, government employees, and private companies with offices in 4+ states/UTs. - Green Number Plates: - Notified for electric vehicles. - E-Governance Initiatives: - Vahan Portal: - Vehicle registration, taxation, permits, and fitness services. - Sarathi Portal: - Driving licenses, learner licenses, and driving school services. - mParivahan App: - Combines features of Vahan and Sarathi portals. - Integrated Road Accident Database (iRAD): - Developed with IIT Madras and National Informatics Centre (NIC) for accident data analysis. - Bhoomi-Rashi Portal: - Facilitates land acquisition for highways. - Data Lake and Project Management Software: - NHAI’s digital platform for paperless decision-making and dispute resolution in highway construction. - Road Types: - National Highways: - Responsibility: - Union Government (NHAI). - Connects: - State capitals, major cities, ports. - State Highways: - Responsibility: - State Government (Public Works Department - PWD). - Connects: - State capital to district headquarters. - District Roads: - Responsibility: - Zila Parishad. - Connects: - District headquarters to tehsils and blocks. - Village Roads: - Responsibility: - Gram Panchayat. - Connects: - Villages to neighboring towns. - Expressways: - Responsibility: - Public-Private Partnership (PPP) or Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV), often under NHAI. - Features: - Six- to eight-lane high-class highways (e.g., Ahmedabad-Vadodara Expressway by NHAI and IRB Infrastructure Developers). - Associated Organizations: - NHAI, State PWD, Border Roads Organisation (BRO, under Ministry of Defence). - Road Length Hierarchy (largest to smallest): - Other roads > State highways > National highways > Expressways. - Authorities - National Highways Authority of India (NHAI, 1988): - Status: - Statutory body under Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Funding Sources: - Road and Infrastructure Cess on petrol/diesel (Central Road and Infrastructure Fund, non-lapsable, 2000). - External assistance (World Bank, ADB, Japan Bank for International Cooperation). - Market borrowings and PPP. - 2019: - NHAI established Infrastructure Investment Trust (InvITs) for fundraising (see Pillar 1C). - GATI Portal (2020): - Monitors highway construction progress, allows contractors to file complaints (e.g., against delays or corruption). - NHAI Functions: - Develop, maintain, and manage national highways. - Collect fees (tolls) on national highways. - Regulate vehicle size/weight on highways. - Provide consultancy and construction services in India and abroad. - Conduct research on highway development. - Projects and programmes - National Highways Development Programme (NHDP, 1998): - Launched by: - PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee. - Components: - Golden Quadrilateral (GQ): - Connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata. - North-South Corridor: - Connects Srinagar to Kanyakumari. - East-West Corridor: - Connects Silchar to Porbandar. - Related Term: - Diamond Quadrilateral (High-Speed Railways connecting major metros). - Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY, 2000): - Boss: - Ministry of Rural Development. - Funding: - Centrally Sponsored Core Scheme (60:40 for general states, 90:10 for special category states). - Objective: - Construct all-weather single-lane roads for unconnected rural habitations. - Targets (by 2019): - Habitations with ≥500 population (plains, per 2001 Census). - Habitations with ≥250 population (special category states, tribal districts, desert areas). - Habitations with 100-249 population in Naxal/Left-Wing Extremism (LWE) areas by 2020. - Phases: - PMGSY-II (2013): - Repair existing rural roads and construct new ones. - PMGSY-III (2019-2025): - Upgrade 1,25,000 km of roads, including bridges, connecting agricultural markets, schools, and hospitals. - Technology: - Uses green technologies (waste plastic, cold mix) to reduce carbon footprint. - Monitoring: - eMARG portal (scheme progress), Meri-Sadak App (citizen feedback). - Benefits (World Bank Study, 2019): - Increased school enrollment, institutional deliveries, and vaccination rates in rural areas. - Bharatmala Pariyojana (2017): - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (NHAI). - Funding: - Cess, PPP, SPV. - Objective: - Upgrade and expand highways from NHDP, focusing on coastal areas, economic corridors, and border regions (for troop movement and trade with Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar). - Phase 1: - Upgrade 24,800 km of national highways by 2022. - Green National Highways Corridor Project (2016): - Objective: - Develop eco-friendly national highways. - This includes: - Using recycled materials (like fly ash, plastic waste) in road construction - Planting green belts (trees/vegetation) along the highways to absorb pollution - Managing rainwater harvesting and soil erosion control - Promoting electric vehicle infrastructure (e.g., charging stations) - Using solar lighting and energy-efficient technologies - Ensuring wildlife crossings to protect biodiversity - Coverage: - Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh. - E-Toll Collection via FASTag (2017): - Reference: - Pillar 1A-1 (Digital Payments). - Features: - RFID-based toll collection to reduce delays at toll plazas. - Satellite-Based Toll Collection: - Transition from FASTag: - Before: - Vehicles slow down at toll plazas for RFID scanning (~50 seconds). - After: - GPS-based system using Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) tracks distance traveled, deducts tolls directly from bank accounts. - Benefits: - Zero wait time at toll plazas. - Pay only for distance traveled (e.g., 80 km instead of full 180 km). - Eliminates need for FASTag recharges. - Status (March 2025): - Postponed due to security and privacy concerns. - NoWAIT@Railway Crossing - Setu Bharatam: - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Funding: - Central Sector Scheme (100% Union-funded). - Objective: - Eliminate railway level crossings on national highways by constructing Railway Over Bridges (ROB) or Railway Under Bridges (RUB). - Deadline: - 2019. - Benefits: - Reduced traffic congestion, fewer accidents, and lower staffing needs for railway crossings. - Char Dham Mahamarg Vikas Pariyojana: - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Objective: - Build/renovate roads connecting four pilgrimage sites in Uttarakhand: Gangotri, Yamunotri, Kedarnath, Badrinath. - Fossil Fuel Reduction - Electric Vehicles (EVs): - Definition: - EVs are propelled by rechargeable batteries, classified as: - Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs): - Fully electric. - Hybrid Electric Vehicles (HEVs): - Run on both battery and petrol/diesel. - Context: - Transport sector is India’s second-largest CO2 emitter after industry. EVs reduce emissions and oil imports. - Data: - EV market share in India <1% (vs. 2% in China, 40% in Norway). - EVs in India - Steps to Promote: - 100% FDI via automatic route in the automobile sector. - National Electric Mobility Mission Plan (NEMMP, 2013): - Promotes electric and hybrid vehicles. - FAME Scheme (2015, Ministry of Heavy Industries): - FAME stands for Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid &) Electric Vehicles in India. - Phase I: - Initial promotion of EV adoption. - Phase II (2019-2024): - Targets 2,700 charging stations (3x3 km grid in cities, every 25 km on highways), electrifies public transport, reduces GST on EVs to 5%. - Budget 2019: - Income tax deduction on EV loans. - Green Number Plates: - For EVs. - E-AMRIT Portal: - Launched at COP26 (2021, Glasgow) by NITI Aayog and UK Government to promote EV awareness. - Phased Manufacturing Program (PMP): - Objective: - Provide tax benefits for manufacturing EVs, components, and other electronics (e.g., smart watches, touchscreens). - Boss: - Ministries of Heavy Industries (EVs) and Electronics (other devices). - Note: - Low-profile scheme, less exam-relevant compared to RODTEP/PLI/FAME. - 100% EV Adoption - NITI vs. Highway Ministry: - 2017: - NITI Aayog proposed 40% private transport to be electric by 2030. - 2019 (June): - NITI proposed only EVs to be sold post-2030. - 2019 (August): Union Minister Nitin Gadkari clarified: - No ban on petrol/diesel vehicles. - No deadline for automakers to switch to EVs. - NITI Aayog lacks authority to set EV deadlines. - Economic Survey 2019 - EVs: Charging Challenges: - Comparison: - Norway leads EV adoption (40% market share) due to tax incentives, toll waivers, and free parking. - Challenges in India: - Limited EV battery range requires widespread charging stations. - Charging time varies (30 minutes to 8 hours), necessitating universal standards. - Need for GPS-based apps/maps to locate charging stations. - High temperatures reduce battery life, requiring R&D for heat-resistant batteries. - Lithium supply: - China dominates global supply; India needs to secure resources. - Implication: - Without charging infrastructure, consumers prefer internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles. - Khanij Bidesh India Ltd (KABIL, 2019): - Established by: - NALCO, Hindustan Copper, Mineral Exploration Ltd. - Objective: - Acquire strategic minerals (e.g., lithium, cobalt) globally. - Milestone: - 2020, acquired a lithium mine in Argentina. - EV New Policy (March 2024): - Boss: - Ministry of Commerce (handles import-export policies, Pillar 3). - Objective: - Promote EV manufacturing in India with tax relief on imports. - EV Policy Conditions: - Minimum Investment: - ₹4,150 crore (USD 500 million), no upper limit. - Factory Setup: - Within 3 years. - Domestic Value Addition (DVA): - 25% by year 3, 50% by year 5. - EV Policy - Tax Relief on Imported EV Cars: - Before: - 60-100% customs duty based on price/engine model. - After: - 15% customs duty for 5 years if manufacturer (e.g., Tesla) commits to investment and factory setup with bank guarantee. - EV Policy - Quota System on Import Duty Relief: - Annual Limit: - 8,000 imported cars per company. - Total Limit (5 years): - 40,000 cars per company. - Price Threshold: - Imported cars must cost >$35,000 (~₹30 lakh). - Additional Condition: - $800 million investment for full 40,000-car quota. - Note: - Technical details have poor cost-benefit for exam preparation. - PM E-DRIVE Scheme (2024): - Full Name: - PM Electric Drive Revolution in Innovative Vehicle Enhancement. - Boss: - Ministry of Heavy Industries. - Replaces: - FAME Scheme and Electric Mobility Promotion Scheme (EMPS). - Features: - Subsidies for e-two-wheelers (up to ₹10,000), e-three-wheelers, e-ambulances, e-trucks, and emerging EVs. - E-Vouchers: - Linked to Aadhaar and mobile number for subsidies. - Funding for public charging stations. - Criticism: - No subsidies for e-cars (four-wheelers). - Electric Vehicle Miscellaneous Updates (2023-24): - Induction/Wireless Charging on Golden Quadrilateral: - Concept: - Inductive (wireless) charging via electrified roads. - Scope: - Planned for 6,000 km of Golden Quadrilateral (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata). - Note: - Details pending; Germany uses overhead power lines for e-highways. - PM-eBus Sewa Scheme (2023): - Objective: - Operate 10,000 electric buses via PPP model. - Boss: - Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. - Gigacasting: - Normal Car: - Underbody made of multiple parts. - Gigacasting: - Single die-cast underbody (e.g., Tesla’s method). - EV Conclusion: - Importance: - EVs are key for sustainable mobility, reducing GHG emissions, and boosting employment/export earnings. - Priority: - Address charging infrastructure, R&D, and mineral supply chains. - Fossil Fuel Emission – Bharat Stage (BS) Norms: - Governing Authority: - Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) - Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) - Objective: - Regulate and reduce vehicular air pollutants (e.g., PM, NOx, CO, SOx) from internal combustion engines. - Progression of Standards: - Based on Euro emission norms, adapted to Indian conditions. - BS-I to BS-IV (2000–2017): - Gradual tightening of emission limits for 2-wheelers, 3-wheelers, passenger cars, and commercial vehicles. - BS-IV: - Mandatory nationwide from April 2017. - Sale and registration of BS-III vehicles banned by Supreme Court from April 2017. - Manufacturing and sale banned from April 2020. - BS-V: - Skipped to leapfrog directly to BS-VI to address worsening air quality and meet global climate commitments. - BS-VI: - Enforced from April 2020 nationwide. - Key changes: - Sulphur content reduced from 50 ppm (BS-IV) to 10 ppm. - Significant reduction in NOx (Nitrogen Oxide) and PM (Particulate Matter) emissions. - Mandatory Onboard Diagnostics (OBD) and Real Driving Emissions (RDE) testing in phases. - Compatible only with BS-VI-grade fuel. - Impacts: - Environment: - Cleaner air, lower health burden from air pollution in urban areas. - Automobile Sector: - Increased vehicle costs due to engine and technology upgrades (DPF, SCR, etc.). - Contributed to 2019 slowdown in auto sales. - Lower resale value for BS-IV vehicles post-2020. - Related Emission Control Regulation: - Corporate Average Fuel Efficiency (CAFE) Norms: - Introduced by Ministry of Heavy Industries in 2017. - Sets fleet-wide average CO₂ emission targets (measured in g/km) for auto manufacturers. - Encourages production of fuel-efficient and hybrid/electric vehicles. - BS vs CAFE: - BS Norms: - Aim to reduce harmful vehicular emissions such as particulate matter (PM), nitrogen oxides (NOx), hydrocarbons (HC), and carbon monoxide (CO). - CAFE Norms: - Aim to improve fuel efficiency and reduce carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions per kilometer across a manufacturer’s vehicle fleet. - Decarbonizing Transport in India (June 2020): - Project: - 5-year initiative by NITI Aayog and OECD’s International Transport Forum. - Goal: - Reduce transport sector’s 13% contribution to India’s CO2 emissions. - Vehicle Scrappage Policy (Budget 2021): - Official Name: - Voluntary Vehicle-Fleet Modernisation Programme. - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (amends Motor Vehicles Act). - Targets: - Commercial vehicles (e.g., taxis, trucks) >15 years. - Personal vehicles (e.g., bikes, cars) >20 years. - Exemptions: - Vintage/museum vehicles >50 years (not for daily use). - Process: - Vehicles failing fitness tests after specified age are seized/destroyed. - Voluntary scrapping at authorized centers yields a certificate for 4-6% discount on new vehicle purchase (transferable). - Exemptions: - Registration fees and state road tax relaxations. - Scrapping centers linked to National Police database to track stolen/criminal vehicles. - Budget 2023: - Loans to states for replacing old vehicles and ambulances. - Benefits: - Cleaner emissions, fuel efficiency, improved safety (e.g., airbags), 35,000 jobs, ₹10,000 crore GDP boost. - India to Produce Reference Fuels: - Definition: - Reference Fuels are high-purity, standardized petrol and diesel used by automobile manufacturers for: - Vehicle/engine calibration. - Emission testing. - Compliance certification under BS-VI norms and CAFE standards. - They are not meant for retail sale but for regulatory and R&D purposes. - Need: - Calibration and emission tests require uniform chemical composition fuels to ensure accurate and reproducible results. - Ensures consistency with global emission norms (like Euro standards). - Earlier Practice: - India used to import reference fuels from Europe and other nations, increasing costs and dependency. - Milestone: - In 2023, Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) started domestic production of BS-VI grade reference fuels at: - Paradip Refinery (Odisha). - Panipat Refinery (Haryana). - Significance: - Reduces foreign dependency and import bill. - Supports Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat in the auto and energy sectors. - Facilitates: - Faster emission testing. - More accurate R&D by vehicle manufacturers. - Export potential for reference fuels. - Budget 2022 on Road Transport/EVs: - Expand National Highways by 25,000 km in 2022-23. - Battery Swapping Policy: - Addresses space shortages for charging stations. - Promote public transport in urban areas. - Special Mobility Zones: - Zero fossil-fuel policy with EV focus. - Bharat New Car Assessment Program (NCAP, 2022): - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Launched: - April 1, 2023. - Objective: - Award star ratings to M1 category vehicles (≤8 seats + driver) based on crash test performance. - Benefit: - Helps consumers choose safer vehicles. - Road Transport and Highway Reforms - Motor Vehicle Amendment Act, 2019: - Context: - ~1.5 lakh annual road accident deaths prompted amendments to Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. - Key Provisions: - Steep penalties (e.g., drunk driving fine increased from ₹2,000 to ₹10,000). - Penalties for road contractors/engineers for faulty infrastructure causing accidents. - Aadhaar mandatory for driving licenses and vehicle registration. - Good Samaritan Protection: - No harassment in civil/criminal cases; identity disclosure to police/doctors not mandatory. - Penalties for vehicle companies for sub-standard components; government can order recalls. - Simplified registration for vehicles modified for persons with disabilities (Divyang). - Motor Vehicle Accident Fund: - Mandatory insurance for road users. - Technical reforms in third-party insurance and claims. - Legal Basis: - Concurrent List (Entry 35); Union law prevails, but states can revise penalties (some reduced fines). - Truck Drivers Eye Checkup - Project Abhay: - Objective: - Conduct eye checkups for truck drivers. - Partners: - IIT Delhi, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Motor Vehicle Amendment Act, 2019 - Gig Drivers: - Guidelines for cab aggregators (e.g., Ola, Uber): - Provide health and term life insurance for drivers. - Norms on surge pricing linked to Wholesale Price Index (WPI, see Pillar 4C). - Data storage on Indian servers. - Driver training and gender sensitization. - Humsafar Policy for Highway Amenities (2024): - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Objective: - Develop integrated, user-friendly Way Side Amenities (WSAs) along national highways to: - Improve commuter experience. - Ensure safety, hygiene, and comfort. - Promote economic activity and tourism. - Way Side Amenities (WSA): - Definition: - Facilities developed along highways to provide comfort, safety, and essential services to travelers, including truck drivers and tourists. - Implemented under: - Humsafar Policy for Highway Amenities (2024), Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH). - Components: - Fuel station (petrol/diesel, EV charging) - Hygienic toilets (male, female, disabled-friendly, baby-care) - Drinking water facility - Restaurants / Dhabas / Food courts - Retail outlets / Convenience stores / ATMs - Parking for cars, buses, trucks - Dormitories / resting facilities for drivers - First aid room / Emergency medical clinic - Emergency helipad - Tourist information kiosks / Guide maps - Surveillance cameras / Police post / Security - Examples: - Delhi–Mumbai Expressway: - Integrated WSA plaza with helipad, food court, fuel, first aid - NH48: - Food court with brands like McDonald’s, EV charger, clean toilets - Project Abhay: - Eye checkup clinics for truckers as part of WSA - Significance: - Reduces driver fatigue and road accidents - Promotes tourism, hygiene, and rural employment - Enables EV adoption via charging infrastructure - Enhances quality of highway travel experience - Integrated Road Accident Database (iRAD): - Developer: - IIT Madras and National Informatics Centre (NIC). - Objective: - Centralized digital platform to collect, analyze, and report road accident data for evidence-based safety interventions. - Features: - Real-time data: - Captures accident details (location, vehicle type, cause) via mobile app/web portal. - Stakeholders: - Police, transport, highways, and health departments for coordinated response. - Analytics: - Identifies accident-prone areas, informs infrastructure upgrades. - Strategic Importance: - Supports Vision Zero: - Aims to reduce road fatalities (India: ~1.5 lakh deaths annually, WHO 2023). - Enhances road safety policy under Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019. - Challenges: - Data accuracy: - Relies on manual input by police, risks inconsistencies. - Digital divide: - Limited tech access in rural areas hampers implementation. - Policy Context: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), aligns with Bharat New Car Assessment Programme (BNCAP). - Indian Bridge Management System (IBMS): - Objective: - Monitor structural health of 50,000+ bridges on National Highways for maintenance and safety. - Features: - Inventory: - Digital database of bridge details (age, material, load capacity). - Sensors: - IoT-based monitoring for stress, corrosion, and vibrations. - Traffic management: - Diverts heavy vehicles from structurally weak bridges. - Strategic Importance: - Enhances safety: - Prevents bridge collapses (e.g., Morbi bridge tragedy, 2022). - The 2022 Morbi bridge (suspension bridge) collapse in Gujarat killed over 135 people due to overcrowding (capacity was 100, but 400 were present) and faulty renovation by a private firm. The bridge was built in 1877 and had just reopened after renovation by the Oreva Group. - Investigations revealed poor renovation, no firness certificate, and rusted cables. The Gujarat High Court took suo moto cognizance of the tragedy. - The incident raised questions on public infrastructure safety and private accountability. - Economic: - Extends bridge lifespan, reduces repair costs (~₹10,000 crore annually). - Challenges: - Funding: - High cost of sensor installation across all bridges. - Maintenance backlog: - Older bridges require urgent retrofitting. - Environmental Concerns: - Construction waste from repairs impacts local ecosystems. - Policy Context: - MoRTH initiative, aligns with National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP). - Bridges, Tunnels, and Miscellaneous - Maitri Setu: - Location: - Connects Sabroom (Tripura) to Ramgarh (Bangladesh) over Feni River. - Objective: - Facilitate Northeast exports via Chattogram port (Bangladesh, 80 km away). - Features: - Length: - 1.9 km, double-lane road bridge. - Infrastructure: - Customs station, integrated check post at Sabroom. - Strategic Importance: - Economic: - Boosts Tripura’s trade (tea, rubber) via Bangladesh ports. - Geopolitical: - Strengthens India-Bangladesh ties, supports Act East Policy. - Connectivity: - Reduces dependence on Siliguri Corridor for Northeast. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Feni River ecosystem risks from construction, vehicular pollution. - Security: - Proximity to Bangladesh border requires robust monitoring. - Policy Context: - India-Bangladesh Protocol on Inland Water Transit and Trade (PIWTT). - Bogibeel Bridge: - Location: - India’s longest rail-cum-road bridge (4.94 km) over Brahmaputra, connecting Dhemaji to Dibrugarh (Assam). - Objective: - Enhance connectivity between North and South Assam, support Northeast development. - Features: - Dual purpose: - Upper deck for vehicles, lower for trains. - Seismic resilience: - Designed for Zone V earthquake-prone area. - Inaugurated: - 2018, cost ₹5,920 crore. - Strategic Importance: - Economic: - Facilitates trade (tea, oil) and passenger movement. - Defense: - Enhances military mobility near China border (Arunachal). - Challenges: - Environmental: - Brahmaputra’s seasonal flooding risks structural stress. - Maintenance: - High costs due to riverbed erosion, siltation. - Policy Context: - Aligns with SARDP-NE, Bharatmala Pariyojana. - Dhola-Sadiya Bridge: - Location: - India’s longest road bridge (9.15 km) over Lohit River, connecting Dhola (Assam) to Sadiya (Arunachal Pradesh). - Objective: - Improve connectivity to Arunachal’s border areas, reduce travel time. - Features: - Inaugurated: - 2017, cost ₹2,056 crore. - Design: - Beam bridge, withstands heavy military vehicles. - Strategic Importance: - Defense: - Critical for troop movement near China border (LAC). - Economic: - Boosts tourism, trade in Arunachal’s remote regions. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Impacts Lohit River’s aquatic ecosystems, flood patterns. - Maintenance: - High costs in monsoon-prone region. - Policy Context: - Supports Act East Policy, Northeast Vision 2020. - Dhubri-Phulbari Bridge: - Location: - 19.3 km road bridge over Brahmaputra, connecting Dhubri (Assam) to Phulbari (Meghalaya). - Objective: - Set to become India’s longest bridge upon completion (2026-27). - Features: - Cost: - ₹5,000 crore, cable-stayed design. - Connectivity: - Links Assam, Meghalaya, and Bangladesh border areas. - Strategic Importance: - Economic: - Enhances trade, reduces travel time by ~200 km. - Regional: - Strengthens Northeast connectivity, supports BIMSTEC trade. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Risks to Brahmaputra’s biodiversity (e.g., Gangetic dolphin). - Funding: - Delays due to high costs, land acquisition issues. - Policy Context: - Bharatmala Pariyojana, SARDP-NE. - Difo Bridge: - Location: - Over Difo River, Arunachal Pradesh. - Objective: - Improve access to remote border areas near LAC. - Features: - Strategic military bridge, supports heavy vehicle movement. - Length: - ~200 meters, inaugurated 2019. - Strategic Importance: - Defense: - Enhances military logistics in Arunachal’s Dibang Valley. - Connectivity: - Links rural communities to markets. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Construction impacts Difo River’s fragile ecosystem. - Security: - Proximity to China border requires constant vigilance. - Policy Context: - Aligns with India’s border infrastructure push under MoRTH. - River Ropeway: - Location: - India’s longest (2 km) over Brahmaputra, connecting Kachari Ghat to North Guwahati, Assam. - Objective: - Provide eco-friendly passenger transport, reduce road congestion. - Features: - Cable car system, capacity ~250 passengers/hour. - Cost: - ₹56 crore, inaugurated 2020. - Strategic Importance: - Tourism: - Enhances Guwahati’s appeal, connects to Umananda Temple. - Economic: - Reduces travel time across Brahmaputra. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Minimal, but bird migration paths may be affected. - Maintenance: - High costs for cable system upkeep. - Policy Context: - Aligns with Smart City Mission (Guwahati), tourism promotion. - Special Accelerated Road Development Programme for Northeast (SARDP-NE): - Objective: - Develop 10,000+ km of roads in Northeast to enhance connectivity. - Features: - Phases: - I-A (completed), I-B, II (ongoing, target 2030). - Focus: - National Highways, state roads, border roads. - Strategic Importance: - Economic: - Boosts trade, tourism in Northeast (e.g., tea, bamboo). - Defense: - Enhances military access to LAC, Myanmar border. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Deforestation, soil erosion in hilly terrains. - Funding: - High costs (~₹1.5 lakh crore), delays in land acquisition. - Policy Context: - Aligns with Act East Policy, Bharatmala Pariyojana. - Sela Tunnel: - Location: - Arunachal Pradesh, through Sela Pass (13,000+ feet), connects Tezpur to Tawang. - Objective: - Ensure all-weather connectivity to Tawang, reduce distance by 10 km. - Features: - Twin tunnels: - 1.5 km (main), 0.5 km (escape), cost ₹700 crore. - Inaugurated: - 2024, built by Border Roads Organisation (BRO). - Strategic Importance: - Defense: - Critical for troop movement near China border (LAC). - Economic: - Boosts tourism, trade in Tawang region. - Challenges: - Environmental: - High-altitude construction risks avalanches, glacial ecosystems. - Technical: - Extreme weather complicates maintenance. - Policy Context: - Aligns with India’s border infrastructure strategy, Vibrant Villages Programme. - Mavala Machine: - Location: - Mumbai Coastal Road Project, South Mumbai to Worli (undersea tunnel). - Objective: - India’s first undersea road tunnel, reduces travel time by 20 minutes. - Features: - Tunnel Boring Machine (TBM): - Largest in India (12.2 meters diameter). - Length: - 2.07 km twin tunnels, cost ₹12,000 crore. - Completion: - 2024 (part of Mumbai Coastal Road). - Strategic Importance: - Urban mobility: - Eases Mumbai’s traffic congestion (~1.5 crore vehicles). - Economic: - Boosts coastal trade, tourism. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Marine ecosystem disruption (Arabian Sea), reclamation impacts. - Cost overruns: - Delays due to complex underwater engineering. - Policy Context: - Aligns with Smart Cities Mission, Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development. - Sudarshan Setu / Signature Bridge (2024): - Location: - Connects Okha mainland to Beyt Dwarka, Gujarat, over Arabian Sea. - Objective: - India’s longest cable-stayed bridge, enhances pilgrimage and tourism. - Features: - Length: - 2.32 km (PIB) or 4.7 km (Indian Express, including approach roads). - Design: - Cable-stayed, solar panels on footpath, Bhagavad Gita verses on railings. - Cost: - ₹980 crore, inaugurated 2024. - Strategic Importance: - Religious: - Connects Dwarkadhish Temple, attracts 20 lakh pilgrims annually. - Economic: - Boosts Gujarat’s coastal economy, tourism. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Impacts marine life, coastal erosion risks. - Maintenance: - High costs due to saline corrosion. - Policy Context: - Aligns with Sagarmala Programme, Gujarat’s tourism promotion. - Longest Road Tunnels in India: - Atal Road Tunnel: - Location: - Rohtang Pass, Himachal Pradesh (9.02 km). - Objective: - Longest high-altitude tunnel (10,000 feet), reduces Leh-Manali distance by 46 km, travel time by 4 hours. - Features: - Cost: - ₹3,200 crore, inaugurated 2020. - Design: - Single-tube, double-lane, emergency escape tunnel. - Strategic Importance: - Defense: - All-weather access to Ladakh near LAC. - Economic: - Boosts tourism, trade in Lahaul-Spiti. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Glacial melt, landslide risks in Himalayan ecology. - Technical: - Ventilation, snow clearance in extreme weather. - Policy Context: - Built by BRO, aligns with border infrastructure strategy. - Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee (Chenani-Nashri) Tunnel: - Location: - Jammu & Kashmir (9.34 km, NH-44). - Objective: - Longest road tunnel in India, reduces Jammu-Srinagar distance by 30 km, travel time by 2 hours. - Features: - Cost: - ₹3,720 crore, inaugurated 2017. - Design: - Twin-tube, escape cross-passages, advanced ventilation. - Strategic Importance: - Economic: - Enhances Kashmir’s connectivity, boosts tourism, trade. - Defense: - Supports military logistics in J&K. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Impacts Pir Panjal ecosystem, water seepage risks. - Security: - Militancy in J&K requires constant surveillance. - Policy Context: - Aligns with Bharatmala Pariyojana, J&K development plans. - Transborder Connectivity - International Container Transshipment Port: - Location: - Galathea Bay, Great Nicobar Island, Andaman & Nicobar Islands. - Objective: - Develop a transshipment hub to handle large cargo vessels, reducing reliance on Singapore/Colombo ports. - Strategic Importance: - Enhances India’s maritime influence in Indo-Pacific, counters China’s String of Pearls strategy. - Supports Act East Policy, strengthens trade links with ASEAN. - Features: - Deep-water port: - Handles mega-container ships (18,000+ TEUs). - Connectivity: - Links to Southeast Asia, Bay of Bengal, and Indian Ocean trade routes. - Infrastructure: - Includes port, airport, township, and power plant. - Environmental Concerns: - Located in ecologically sensitive Nicobar Islands, risks to tribal communities (Shompen, Nicobarese). - Deforestation and coral reef damage due to construction. - Policy Context: - Sagarmala Programme: - Aligns with port-led development. - Budget 2022: - ₹6,000 crore allocated for project phase-I. - Kartarpur Sahib Corridor (2019): - Location: - Ravi River bank, Narowal district, Pakistan, 4.5 km from India-Pakistan border (Dera Baba Nanak, Punjab). - Significance: - Religious: - Guru Nanak’s final resting place, spent 18 years until death in 1539. - Diplomatic: - Symbol of India-Pakistan goodwill, opened on Guru Nanak’s 550th birth anniversary. - Features: - Visa-free access: - For Indian citizens and OCI cardholders (up to 5,000 pilgrims/day). - Infrastructure: - 4.1 km corridor with integrated check post, 800-acre complex in Pakistan. - Cost: - India-funded (₹500 crore), Pakistan charges $20 service fee per pilgrim. - Challenges: - Security concerns: - Proximity to border, potential for misuse. - Fee disputes: - India seeks waiver of $20 fee to ease pilgrim access. - Policy Context: - Aligns with India’s soft diplomacy, promotes cultural connectivity. - Kaladan Multi-Modal Project: - Objective: - Connect Haldia/Kolkata Port (West Bengal) to Sittwe Port (Myanmar) via sea, then Kaladan River and road to Paletwa (Myanmar) and Zorinpui (Mizoram). - Purpose: - Alternate route for Northeast India, bypassing Bangladesh’s Chittagong port. - Enhances trade, connectivity for landlocked Northeast states. - Components: - Sea Route: - Kolkata to Sittwe (539 km). - River Route: - Sittwe to Paletwa via Kaladan River (158 km). - Road Route: - Paletwa to Zorinpui, Mizoram (100 km). - Strategic Importance: - Strengthens India-Myanmar ties, supports Act East Policy. - Counters China’s influence in Myanmar (e.g., Kyaukpyu port). - Challenges: - Delays: - Insurgency in Rakhine (Arakan Army), Myanmar coup (2021). - Environmental: - River dredging risks aquatic ecosystems. - Funding: - India-funded ($484 million), cost overruns due to delays. - Policy Context: - India-Myanmar Friendship Project, aligns with BIMSTEC connectivity goals. - Sonamura-Daudkandi (September 2020): - Route: - Riverine connectivity: - Sonamura (Tripura, Gomati River) to Daudkandi (Bangladesh, Meghna River). - Objective: - Enhance trade and passenger movement between Tripura and Bangladesh. - Features: - Protocol on Inland Water Transit and Trade (PIWTT): - India-Bangladesh agreement. - Infrastructure: - Inland water terminals, customs facilities at Sonamura. - Cargo: - Food grains, cement, consumer goods. - Strategic Importance: - Boosts Northeast economy, reduces dependence on Siliguri Corridor. - Strengthens India-Bangladesh ties, supports BIMSTEC framework. - Challenges: - Seasonal: - Low river depth in dry seasons limits navigation. - Environmental: - River pollution from cargo spills, dredging impacts. - Policy Context: - India-Bangladesh Joint Rivers Commission oversees riverine trade routes. - India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway (IMT): - Route: - Moreh (Manipur, India) to Mae Sot (Thailand) via Mandalay, Myanmar (~1,360 km). - Objective: - Enhance trade, tourism, and connectivity with ASEAN nations. - Features: - Road upgrades: - 69 bridges, 3-lane sections in Myanmar. - Extensions: - Proposed links to Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam. - Strategic Importance: - Supports Act East Policy, integrates Northeast with ASEAN markets. - Counters China’s BCIM corridor (dropped in 2019). - Challenges: - Delays: - Myanmar political instability, funding issues. - Security: - Insurgency in Manipur, Myanmar’s border areas. - Environmental: - Deforestation, wildlife habitat disruption. - Policy Context: - India-ASEAN Summit (2023): - Pledged completion by 2027. - Funding: - India ($250 million), ADB support. - BBIN Motor Vehicles Agreement (2015): - Members: - Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal. - Objective: - Seamless cross-border movement of passenger and cargo vehicles. - Features: - Single permit system: - Reduces border delays, lowers logistics costs. - Routes: - Covers key trade corridors (e.g., Kolkata-Dhaka-Agartala). - Status: - Implemented by Bangladesh, India, Nepal; Bhutan yet to ratify due to environmental concerns. - Strategic Importance: - Boosts sub-regional trade (~$50 billion potential). - Enhances connectivity for landlocked Nepal, Bhutan. - Challenges: - Infrastructure gaps: - Poor road conditions in border areas. - Environmental: - Increased vehicular emissions, pressure on Himalayan ecosystems (Bhutan’s concern). - Political: - Bhutan’s reluctance delays full implementation. - Policy Context: - Aligns with SAARC, BIMSTEC trade facilitation goals. - International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC, 2000): - Members: - India, Iran, Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Belarus, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Oman, Ukraine, Syria (Observer: Bulgaria). - Objective: - Multimodal (ship, rail, road) cargo transport from Mumbai to Moscow via Chabahar (7,200 km). - Features: - Route: - Mumbai-Chabahar (sea), Chabahar-Bandar Abbas-Zahedan (rail/road), Russia via Caspian Sea. - Reduces transit time: - 20-25 days vs 40-60 days (Suez Canal route). - Strategic Importance: - Access to Central Asia, Afghanistan, bypassing Pakistan. - Counters China’s OBOR, strengthens India-Russia-Iran ties. - Challenges: - Geopolitical: - US sanctions on Iran delay funding, operations. - Environmental: - Rail/road construction impacts desert ecosystems in Iran. - Infrastructure: - Incomplete rail links (e.g., Chabahar-Zahedan). - Policy Context: - India’s $500 million investment in Chabahar, aligns with Eurasian Economic Union trade goals. - Ashgabat Agreement (2011): - Members: - Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Iran, Oman, Pakistan (2016), India (2018). - Objective: - Multimodal goods transport from Central Asia to Persian Gulf, synergizes with INSTC. - Features: - Route: - Connects Caspian Sea ports to Persian Gulf via rail/road. - Customs harmonization: - Simplifies cross-border trade. - Strategic Importance: - Enhances India’s access to Central Asian markets (energy, minerals). - Complements Chabahar port operations. - Challenges: - Geopolitical: - Tensions between Iran, Pakistan affect coordination. - Environmental: - Desertification risks from infrastructure in arid regions. - Policy Context: - Aligns with India’s Connect Central Asia Policy (2012). - Gwadar Port: - Location: - Balochistan, Pakistan, developed by China under CPEC. - Strategic Importance: - Part of China’s String of Pearls, secures energy routes from Persian Gulf. - Competes with India’s Chabahar port (~100 km away). - Features: - Deep-water port, handles oil, gas, and cargo. - Infrastructure: - China-funded ($1.6 billion), includes highways, pipelines. - Challenges: - Security: - Baloch insurgency disrupts operations. - Environmental: - Coastal erosion, marine pollution from port activities. - India’s Concerns: - Strategic encirclement by China via CPEC, Gwadar’s proximity to Chabahar. - Chabahar Port (Shahid Beheshti, Iran): - India’s Role: - 2016 Agreement: - India to develop port, build Chabahar-Zahedan railway (628 km). - Investment: - $500 million for port, $1.6 billion for railway. - Strategic Importance: - Access to Afghanistan, Central Asia without Pakistan. - Counters China’s Gwadar port, strengthens India-Iran ties. - Developments: - 2020: - Iran dropped India from railway project citing funding delays, pursued China for 25-year pact. - 2024: - India signed 10-year contract to operate port terminals. - Challenges: - Geopolitical: - US sanctions on Iran limit foreign investment. - Environmental: - Dredging impacts Persian Gulf marine ecosystems. - Security: - Balochistan (Pakistan) instability spills over to Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan. - Policy Context: - Aligns with INSTC, India’s Indo-Pacific strategy. - Build Back Better World (B3W, 2020): - Proposed by: - US President Joe Biden at G7 Summit (2021). - Objective: - Post-COVID infrastructure development in developing nations, countering China’s OBOR. - Features: - Focus: - Climate-resilient infrastructure, digital connectivity, health systems. - Funding: - G7 nations, private sector (~$40 trillion by 2035). - India’s Role: - Supports as alternative to OBOR, aligns with Quad (India, US, Japan, Australia). - Challenges: - Environmental: - Large-scale projects risk ecological damage. - Financial: - Funding delays due to G7 economic constraints. - Policy Context: - Complements India’s Indo-Pacific vision, SAGAR initiative. - Blue Dot Network (2019): - Proposed by: - USA, Japan, Australia (India not joined). - Objective: - Certify infrastructure projects for quality, transparency, sustainability. - Features: - Voluntary certification: - Based on OECD, G20 standards. - Attracts private investment for certified projects. - Strategic Importance: - Counters China’s debt-trap diplomacy (e.g., OBOR). - Promotes high-standard infrastructure in Indo-Pacific. - Challenges: - Environmental: - Certification may overlook local ecological impacts. - Limited participation: - India’s absence reduces regional influence. - Policy Context: - Aligns with Quad’s infrastructure focus, India monitors but prioritizes own initiatives. - One Belt One Road (OBOR, 2013): - Proposed by: - China, under Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). - Corridors: - New Eurasia Land Bridge Economic Corridor: - China to Europe via Russia. - China-Mongolia-Russia Economic Corridor: - Enhances trade in Northeast Asia. - China-Central Asia-West Asia Economic Corridor: - Links to Persian Gulf. - China-Indochina Peninsula Economic Corridor: - Connects ASEAN nations. - Bangladesh-China-India-Myanmar (BCIM) Economic Corridor: - Dropped in 2019 due to India’s objections. - China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC): - Gwadar to Kashgar, passes through Gilgit-Baltistan (Indian territory). - Strategic Importance: - China’s global trade dominance: - ~140 countries, $6 trillion investment. - Secures energy routes, expands geopolitical influence. - India’s Concerns: - Sovereignty: - CPEC violates India’s territorial integrity in PoK. - Debt traps: - Sri Lanka, Pakistan face repayment issues (e.g., Hambantota port). - Environmental: - Massive infrastructure damages ecosystems (e.g., CPEC highways). - Status: - Debt restructuring: - China offers relief to partner nations (2023). - India’s stance: - Non-participant, promotes INSTC, Chabahar as alternatives. - Policy Context: - India counters with Quad, SAGAR, and Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF). - Pillar 5B3: Transport and Infrastructure - Definition: - Transport infrastructure encompasses the physical and organizational systems facilitating the movement of people, goods, and services, including railways, aviation, and tourism-related facilities, critical for economic growth, connectivity, and regional development in India. - Context: - India’s transport sector, managed by ministries like Railways, Civil Aviation, and Tourism, is undergoing modernization to enhance efficiency, safety, and sustainability, aligning with initiatives like Atmanirbhar Bharat and Gati Shakti for integrated infrastructure development. - Significance for India: - Robust transport infrastructure supports India’s economic ambitions by improving trade logistics, fostering tourism, and enhancing regional connectivity, particularly in underserved areas like the Northeast, while addressing environmental and safety challenges. - Basic information - Project Types Based on Land/Asset Use: - Greenfield Projects: - Definition: - Projects built from scratch on previously unused land. - Features: - No existing infrastructure present. - Requires full setup: land acquisition, environment clearance, etc. - Examples: - Jewar Noida International Airport - New Smart Cities under DMIC - Bullet Train Mumbai-Ahmedabad (largely greenfield) - Brownfield Projects: - Definition: - Projects involving modification, renovation, or expansion of existing infrastructure. - Features: - Existing land/assets reused. - Less time-consuming and less risky. - Examples: - Redevelopment of old railway stations (e.g., Rani Kamalapati station) - Expansion of existing metro lines - Asset monetization of operational highways via TOT model - Bluefield Projects (Not a starndard term): - Definition: - Hybrid of Greenfield + Brownfield; upgrades old assets and adds new ones simultaneously. - Features: - Partial reuse of infrastructure with partial new development. - Examples: - Upgradation + expansion of existing ports - Railway electrification + laying of 3rd track - Yellowfield Projects (Not a standard term): - Definition: - Operational brownfield assets are leased/franchised to private players. - Features: - Used mostly under PPP models like HAM, TOT. - Examples: - NHAI leasing operational highways under TOT - Airport leasing by AAI (Adani Group managing Lucknow, Ahmedabad airports etc.) - Railways - Definition: - Indian Railways, the fourth-largest rail network globally, spans over 68,000 route-km, serving as a lifeline for passenger and freight transport, with significant modernization efforts to enhance efficiency, safety, and sustainability. - Historical Context: - Established in 1853 with the first Mumbai-Thane line (34 km) under Governor General Dalhousie, Indian Railways has evolved significantly, merging its budget with the general budget in 2017 under PM Modi, streamlining financial planning. - Organizational Structure: - Ministry of Railways oversees: - Railway Board (statutory body under the Indian Railway Board Act, 1905). - Subordinate offices: - Railway Recruitment Boards, Railway Staff College (Vadodara), Indian Railway Engineering Institute (Pune), Research Design and Standards Organisation (RDSO, Lucknow). - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - IRCON (construction), IRFC (finance), IRCTC (catering/tourism), Konkan Railway Corporation, Rail Vikas Nigam Ltd., RailTel (communication), Dedicated Freight Corridor Corp., CONCOR (approved for privatization in 2019). - Zonal Headquarters: - Indian Railways operates 18 zones, with headquarters including: - Central (Mumbai), Eastern (Kolkata), Northern (New Delhi), Southern (Chennai), South Coast (Visakhapatnam, 2025). - 18th Zone: - South Coast Railway (2025), carved from East Coast and South Central zones, headquartered in Visakhapatnam, per the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014. - Key Concepts: - Cross Subsidization: - Passenger fares kept low to ensure affordability, offset by higher freight charges, impacting operational revenue. - Operating Ratio: - Ratio of operating expenses to revenues; 2017: 98.4% (1.6% surplus), 2018: 96.2%, targeted at 95% in Budget 2019. - Modified Economic Internal Rate of Return (MEIRR): - Pre-2019: - Projects required minimum 12% profit. - Post-2019: - Projects approved with 2-3% profit for remote connectivity, pollution reduction, or traffic decongestion, with NITI Aayog consultation for projects over ₹500 crore. - Challenges: - Cross-subsidization strains finances, compromising sanitation, service quality, and safety. - Over two-thirds of cargo transported by trucks, which are slower, costlier, and more polluting than rail. - Excessive stoppages for political reasons reduce train speeds. - Modernization Efforts: - Personnel Reforms (Unification of Services): - Pre-2019: - Eight services (e.g., Indian Railway Service of Engineers, Traffic, Accounts) recruited via UPSC exams, causing coordination issues. - Post-2019: - Merged into Indian Railways Management Service (IRMS) for improved efficiency; Indian Railway Medical Service renamed to Indian Railway Health Service (IRHS). - Controversy: - Officers fear seniority loss; non-engineers managing technical roles criticized as irrational. - Organizational Reforms: - Railway Board restructured (2019) with a CEO and four functional members, plus independent experts in industry, finance, and economics. - Private Train Operators: -
Before After (Post-2019)
- Indian Railways solely operated trains, collected fares. - Affluent passengers preferred airlines for speed and comfort. - Private operators run trains on select routes, using their own trains and staff, with market-linked fares. - Government provides tracks, signaling, and timetable; operators share revenue. - Premium trains (e.g., Vande Bharat, Tejas) introduced, but limited government funds necessitate private investment.
- Benefits: - Improved services (no hawkers, hygienic facilities), faster journeys (minimum 60 kmph, fewer stops). - 2006: - Private container trains allowed. - 2019: - Lucknow-Delhi Tejas Express (IRCTC-operated) launched as a semi-private trial. - 2020: - Proposal for 150 private trains on 100 routes under Design, Build, Finance, Operate (DBFO) model, with 35-year concessions.
- Pre-2019 Modernization: - Project Unigauge (1990s): - Converted tracks to broad gauge (1,676 mm) for uniformity. - Project Saksham (2018): - Employee training program. - Mission Avataran (2016): - Focused on speed, safety, and profitability. - Yatri Mitra Sewa (2016): - Wheelchair and porter services for differently-abled passengers. - Rail Drishti Portal: - For customer complaints and train information. - Fare Reforms: - Rail Development Authority (2017, non-statutory) suggests fares, efficiency standards, and technological upgrades, but Railway Board retains final authority. - Tatkal Tickets: - For emergency bookings. - Flexi-Fare/Dynamic Pricing (2016): - Increased fares by percentage as seats filled on premium trains (Rajdhani, Shatabdi, Duronto); phased out by 2018 due to high costs. - Green Initiatives: - Solar/wind energy at stations, green curtains, bio-toilets (DRDO-developed, using anaerobic bacteria), 5% biodiesel blending. - Green Corridors: - Trains with bio-toilets to prevent excreta discharge. - Electric Traction (100% by 2022): - Replaced diesel/coal engines, despite high costs (₹1 lakh crore) and topography challenges in J&K and Northeast. - Greenwashing Criticism: - Electric traction uses coal-based electricity, reducing environmental benefits. - National Rail Plan (NRP) 2030: - Increase freight share to 45%, average speed to 50 kmph, 100% electrification, 160 kmph on key routes (Delhi-Howrah, Delhi-Mumbai), new freight and high-speed corridors, and station upgrades. - Safety Initiatives: - Rashtriya Rail Sanraksha Kosh (2017): - Funds safety projects like Train Collision Avoidance System. - 182 Helpline, RPGRAMS, Rail Madad App, Rail Drishti dashboard for grievances and operations. - NINA-UAV drones for track/station surveillance. - Railways Protection Force (RPF) Initiatives (2019): - Commando for Railway Security (CORAS): - A specialized RPF unit formed to tackle terrorism, naxal threats, and sabotage in the Indian Railways network with quick response capabilities and high-intensity training. - Operation Thirst: - Curb unauthorized water bottle vendors at railway stations and on trains. - Ensure passengers get safe and clean drinking water from authorized sources only. - Meri Saheli: - Enhances women’s security. - Involves identifying women travelers, especially those traveling alone, and providing them with constant support and assistance from boarding to destination. - Rail Types: -

- Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC, 2006): - 2,800 km for cargo: - Eastern (Ludhiana-Dankuni), Western (Dadri-JNPT Mumbai). - Increases cargo speed to 60 kmph from 20 kmph. - Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS, NAMO BHARAT): - Connects Delhi with Panipat, Meerut, and Alwar, managed by NCRTC under MoHUA. - Metro Rail: - Mass Rapid Transit System (MRTS) for urban commuters, operational in Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai. - Challenges: - High capital costs, land acquisition issues, long cost-recovery periods. - Metro Rail Policy (2017): - MoHUA oversees; projects approved after cost-benefit analysis. - Funding: - 50:50 Union-State joint ventures or PPP with Viability Gap Funding. - Metrolite/Metro Neo (2021): - Cheaper metro systems for smaller cities (e.g., Nashik, Jammu). -
