- PPP-Related Terms/Schemes (2022-24) - Viability Gap Funding (VGF) - Boss: - DEA, Ministry of Finance. - Purpose: - Provides financial assistance for economically desirable but financially unviable PPP projects (e.g., wastewater treatment, water supply, solid waste management, health, education). - India Infrastructure Project Development Fund Scheme (IIPDF, 2022) - Boss: - DEA, Ministry of Finance. - Purpose: - Funds consultants/advisors to prepare high-quality PPP project blueprints; supports project structuring and feasibility studies. - Government Land Information System (GLIS) Portal - Announcement: - Budget 2019. - Purpose: - Tracks unused CPSE land assets for monetization (e.g., sale or lease). - India Infrastructure Report 2023 - Publishers: - IDFC Foundation, Infrastructure Development Corporation (Karnataka) Ltd. (iDeCK), National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA). - Purpose: - Analyzes infrastructure development trends, challenges, and opportunities in India. - Miscellaneous General Knowledge - Sustainable Investments in Infrastructure and Innovation (S3i) Initiative - Boss: - United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS, Copenhagen, Denmark). - Launched: - 2019-21 (exact year varies by source). - Focus Areas: - Affordable housing, renewable energy, health infrastructure. - Status: - Discontinued in February 2023 due to mismanagement. - Stability and Growth Pact of EU - Established: - 2014. - Purpose: - Guidelines for EU member states to: - Control fiscal deficits. - Implement structural reforms. - Invest in job creation and GDP growth. - Asian Development Bank (ADB) Commitment - Commitment: - $25 billion over five years to support PM Gati Shakti, social development, and climate action initiatives in India. - Pillar 6A1: Demography, Health, and Hunger - Introduction: - Demography studies population dynamics, including size, growth, and structure, which are critical for economic development, social upliftment, and policy planning. Health and hunger are closely linked to demographic indicators, influencing productivity, life expectancy, and quality of life. - Managed by the Ministry of Home Affairs (Census), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (health policies), and other agencies like NITI Aayog for health and demographic indices. - Population Census - Overview: - First conducted in 1872 under Lord Mayo; systematic decadal census began in 1881 under Lord Ripon. - Constitutional Basis: - Union List, Entry 69; governed by Census Act, 1948. - Administered by: - Registrar General and Census Commissioner under the Ministry of Home Affairs; district-level operations overseen by District Magistrates (IAS). - Post-Independence: - Conducted every 10 years; 2011 was the 7th Census of independent India. - Data Collection (Until 2011): -
Period SC/ST Data OBC Data
Until 1931 Collected & Published Collected & Published
1941 Collected & Published Not Collected
1951-2011 Collected & Published Collected but Not Published
- Why was OBC data not published (1951–2011)? - Post-Independence Policy Shift: - After 1947, the Indian state moved away from caste enumeration (except SC/ST) to avoid reinforcing caste divisions. - Emphasis was on promoting equality and treating caste as a private/social identity, not a public administrative category (beyond SC/ST). - OBC Identification Remained Politically Sensitive: - OBCs were not constitutionally recognized as a separate group until the Mandal Commission (1979–80). - Post-Mandal (1990), OBC reservations were implemented but no national-level caste census was taken for OBCs due to: - Political backlash and polarisation risks - Fear of inflaming identity-based politics - Disputes over methodology and accuracy - SECC 2011 - Data Collected but Not Released - Socio-Economic and Caste Census (SECC) 2011 was the first post-independence attempt to gather caste data for all. - However: - The data was found to be error-prone, inconsistent, and politically controversial - The Rangarajan Committee flagged its poor data quality - So, while economic data from SECC was used, the caste component was never officially released to the public. - Census 2021 (Postponed) - Funding: - ₹8,700 crore allocated by Union Cabinet in December 2019. - Data Points: - Housing conditions, amenities/assets, demography, religion, SC/ST, language, literacy, economic activity, migration, fertility. - Innovation: - First-time use of a mobile app for data collection. - Phases: - House Listing and Housing Census: - April to September 2020. - Population Enumeration: - February 9 to February 28, 2021. - National Population Register (NPR): - The National Population Register (NPR) is a register of the usual residents of the country. - Usual resident: - A person who has resided in a local area for the past 6 months or intends to reside there for the next 6 months or more. - Updated concurrently (except in Assam) under Citizenship Act, 1955. - Why is NPR updated concurrently with Census? - Operational Efficiency: - Since both the Census and NPR require house-to-house visits and demographic data collection, it is cost-effective and time-saving to update NPR along with the Census House Listing phase. - Data Synergy: - NPR and Census collect overlapping information like name, age, gender, address, etc. - Updating both simultaneously avoids duplication and ensures data consistency. - Legal & Administrative Requirements: - The Census is governed by the Census Act, 1948 while NPR is governed by Citizenship Rules, 2003. - Updating NPR helps the government prepare for any future National Register of Citizens (NRC), though the NRC is a separate and controversial exercise. - Why Assam is excluded? - Assam already completed an NRC exercise under Supreme Court supervision. - NRC (National Register of Citizens) in Assam was published in August 2019. - Its purpose: - Identify illegal immigrants from Bangladesh. - Over 19 lakh people were excluded from Assam NRC. - To avoid duplication/conflict between NRC and NPR: - The Union Home Ministry decided to exclude Assam from NPR rollout. - NPR is not a Supreme Court-mandated exercise, but NRC in Assam was. - Status: - Postponed due to COVID-19; rescheduled for 2024-25. - Demand for OBC Caste Census - Background: - Mandal Commission (1979) estimated OBC population at 52%. Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC) 2011 collected caste data but not released publicly. - Need: - Lack of OBC population, education, and income data hinders effective policy-making for OBC welfare. - Demand: - Political groups advocate including OBC enumeration in the next census. - Government Response (2021): - No caste-wise enumeration except for SC/ST in Census (Lok Sabha statement). - State Initiatives (2023-25): - Bihar, Karnataka, and others began state-level caste censuses. - Caste Census Inclusion (April 2025) - Announcement: - Modi government decided to include caste enumeration in the 2025 Census. - Rationale: - Census is a Union subject (Article 246, Seventh Schedule, Item 69). - State-level caste surveys lack transparency and are politically motivated, risking social fabric. - Centralized caste enumeration in the main census ensures credibility and avoids political bias. - Demographic Transition (Census Perspective) -
Phase Period Birth Rate Death Rate Remarks
Stagnant Population 1901-1921 High High Population declined (-0.31%) in 1921 due to WW1, droughts, epidemics, Spanish Flu. 1921 known as the "Great Demographic Divide."
Steady Growth 1921-1951 High Medium Mortality-induced growth due to declining death rates.
Rapid High Growth 1951-1981 High Low Fertility-induced growth due to agricultural revolution (reduced famines), medical advancements (contained epidemics), and increased life expectancy.
High Growth with Slowing 1981-2011 Medium to Low Lower Birth rate declined due to family planning, nuclear families, and high living costs.
- Demographic Transition (Theoretical Perspective) - Significance: - Population change reflects economic development, social upliftment, and cultural/historical context. - Stages: -
Stage Birth Rate Death Rate Period in India Remarks
High Stationary High High Up to 1920 Stable population.
Early Expanding High Medium 1921-1951 Population growth due to declining mortality.
Late Expanding Medium Low 1971 onwards India currently in this phase.
Low Stationary Lower Lower ~2026 onwards Most developed countries; India expected to enter soon.
Declining Lowest (below Death Rate) Lowest Not yet Population shrinks (e.g., Japan).
- Malthusian Theory of Population Growth - Proposed by: - Thomas Robert Malthus (1798). - Theory: - Population grows geometrically (exponential), while food production grows arithmetically (linear). - Natural equilibrium achieved through "Positive Checks" (e.g., famines, epidemics, earthquakes) or "Preventative Checks" (e.g., family planning, celibacy, late marriages). - Family Planning - Definition: - Spacing or preventing births to control population growth and improve women’s health. - Methods: - Awareness campaigns. - Free contraceptives. - Tax disincentives for large families (e.g., China’s former one-child policy tax). - Cases: - Sikkim's Incentives for Government Employees (2023) - Context: - Sikkim, India’s least populous state (~7 lakh), has the lowest Total Fertility Rate (TFR) of 1.1. - Policy: - From January 1, 2023, state government employees receive a bonus salary for having a second or third child to boost population growth. - Assam Two-Child Policy - Background: - Announced by Assam Government in 2017 to control population growth. - Came into effect from 1 January 2021. - Influenced by similar laws in other Indian states like Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh. - Provisions: - Employment Restrictions: - Individuals with more than two children: - Ineligible for government jobs. - May be denied promotions in government services. - Panchayat Elections: - Under Assam Panchayat (Amendment) Act, 2018: - Individuals with more than two children barred from contesting panchayat elections. - Government Schemes: - People with more than two children may be disqualified from: - Benefiting from state-funded welfare schemes. - Receiving subsidies and housing assistance. - Exemptions: - Twins in second pregnancy not counted as violating the norm. - Policy not applied retroactively. - Certain tribal communities may be exempt (subject to notification). - Objectives: - Population control for better resource allocation. - Promote access to healthcare, education, employment. - Encourage small family norms. - Criticism: - Rights and Welfare Concerns: - May violate reproductive rights (Article 21). - Disproportionately affects women and marginalized groups. - Effectiveness: - Experts (e.g., UNFPA) argue coercive population policies are ineffective. - Emphasis should be on: - Women's education and empowerment. - Access to family planning services. - Demographic Indicators - Overview: - Demographic indicators provide statistical data about a population. - Help analyze population structure, health, growth trends, and social development. - Crucial for planning policies in health, education, employment, and welfare. -
Indicator Definition 2011 Data/Recent Data
Population Density Number of people per square kilometer. 382 (2011).
Natural Growth Births minus Deaths. -
Actual Growth Births minus Deaths plus In-Migration minus Out-Migration. -
Decadal Population Growth Rate (Latest Census - Previous Census) / Previous Census. 17.7% (2001-2011).
Birth Rate Live births per 1,000 population. ~20 (2018, SRS).
Death Rate Deaths per 1,000 population. ~6 (2018, SRS).
Crude Birth Rate (CBR) (Live births × 1,000) / Mid-year population. -
Crude Death Rate (CDR) (Deaths × 1,000) / Mid-year population. -
Population Growth Rate Birth Rate minus Death Rate. Positive: Population increasing; Near zero: Stabilized or replacement level.
Fertility Rate Live births per 1,000 women (15-49 years). -
Total Fertility Rate (TFR) Hypothetical number of children a woman would have over her reproductive years. 2.2 (2015) to 2.0 (2019, ES22); Target: 2.1 (Replacement level).
Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) Infant deaths (<1 year) per 1,000 live births. 34 (2016); 32 (2018, SRS).
Child Mortality Rate (CMR) Child deaths (<5 years) per 1,000 live births. ~50 (2016); SDG-2030 Target: 11.
Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) Women dying in childbirth per 1 lakh live births. ~130 (2016); SDG-2030 Target: 70.
Life Expectancy Average years a person is expected to live. Females: 70; Males: 67 (ES22); Urban: 72.6; Rural: 68.0; Highest: Kerala, Delhi (75); Lowest: Chhattisgarh (65).
Sex Ratio Females per 1,000 males. 943 (2011); Child Sex Ratio: 919 (2011, down from 927 in 2001).
Doctor-Patient Ratio Doctors per 1,000 people. 1:834 (ES23, includes Allopathic and AYUSH); WHO recommends 1:1,000.
Age Pyramid Distribution of population across age groups. Reflects proportion of working-age vs. dependent population.
Dependency Ratio (Population <15 and >64) / Population (15-64). Lower ratio indicates demographic dividend.
- Additional Notes (ES22): - TFR Decline: - Achieved through contraceptives, family planning, and girls’ education. - Sex Ratio at Birth: - Improved in most states (2019-21 vs. 2015-16), except Himachal Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Meghalaya, Goa, and Nagaland. - Global Sex Ratio: - ~102 males per 100 females; Asia has a lower sex ratio (more males). - Healthcare Expenditure (ES25) - Source: - National Health Accounts (2021-22, Ministry of Health). -

- Census 2011- Migration and Occupation - Migration: - Definition: - A person settled in a place different from their previous residence (permanent, temporary, or seasonal). - Types: - Rural-to-Rural, Rural-to-Urban, Urban-to-Urban, Urban-to-Rural (e.g., reverse migration during COVID-19 lockdowns). - Immigrants: - People moving into a new place. - Emigrants: - People moving out of a place. - Statistics: - 37% of Indians are internal migrants; 70% are female, primarily due to marriage (70% for females, 28% for males due to work/employment). - Factors: -

- Reports: - NITI Aayog Healthy States, Progressive India (Health Index) - Published: - Since 2017; latest for 2019-20 (released December 2021). - Measures: - 24 indicators across three pillars: - Health Outcomes, - Governance and Information, - Key Inputs/Processes. - Rankings: - Top-3 States: - Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Telangana. - Bottom-3 States: - Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh (lowest). - Note: - West Bengal did not participate. - Reason for West Bengal’s Non-Participation: - West Bengal Government declined to share health data with NITI Aayog. - Cited reasons: - Alleged duplication with existing state-level data collection. - Concern over central interference in state matters. - Political tensions between the state and central government. - Sub-Categories: - Larger states, smaller states, Union Territories. - National Family Health Survey (NFHS) - Conducted by: - International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), Mumbai, under Ministry of Health. - Rounds: - 1992-93, 1998-99, 2005-06, 2015-16, 2019-21 (NFHS-5). - NFHS-5: - Phase 1: - Data for 22 States/UTs (December 2020). - Phase 2: - Data for remaining States/UTs (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Haryana, Chhattisgarh) (November 2021). - Key Findings: - Total Fertility Rate (TFR): - Declined from 2.7 (2005) to 2.2 (2015) to 2.0 (2019); still >2.1 in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh. - Improvements: - Increased contraceptive use, vaccinations, institutional births, breastfeeding, women’s bank accounts, and mobile phone access. - Challenges: - Child malnutrition persists; anaemia among children and women remains a concern. - Other Health Surveys -

- National Population Policy 2000 - Objectives: - Achieve TFR of 2.1 (replacement level) by 2010 (now targeted for 2025). - Actual Progress: - TFR in 2019 (NFHS-5 Phase 1) -> 2.2 - TFR in 2021 (NFHS-5 Phase 2) -> 2.0 - Indicates target achieved with delay. - Stabilize population by 2045 (stable growth rate and age pyramid). - Promote family planning, contraceptives, safe abortions, HIV control, universal immunization, and mandatory birth/death registration. - Recommendations: - Freeze Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha seats based on 1971 Census until 2026 to discourage population growth for political gains. - Bodies Established: - National Commission on Population: - Chaired by the Prime Minister, includes CMs, Union Ministers, NGOs, and experts (appears defunct). - Population Stabilization Fund (2005): - Autonomous body chaired by Health Minister; promotes awareness, community participation, and fundraising. - Schemes: - Prerna Scheme: - Encourages delayed marriage, childbirth, and spacing; ASHA workers provide counseling and contraceptives. - Santushti Scheme: - Public-Private Partnership for sterilization services. - Global Reports and Rankings - World Population Prospects 2022 - Published by: - UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (July 2022). - Key Findings: - India surpassed China as the world’s most populous nation in 2023 (142.86 crore). - Basis of Estimation: - Not based on Census (India’s last census was in 2011, 2021 postponed). - Projections derived from: - Civil Registration System (CRS) data. - Sample Registration System (SRS). - National Family Health Surveys (NFHS). - International databases (e.g., UN, World Bank, IIPS). - Statistical modelling and demographic estimation techniques. - Methodology: - Uses fertility rates, mortality rates, life expectancy, and migration data. - Demographic models project annual population changes for each country. - Adjusts for under-reporting and data gaps using statistical corrections. - UN’s declaration based on best available data and modeling. - Global population estimates: - 8.5 billion (2030), 9.7 billion (2050), 10.4 billion (2100). - State of World Population Report - Published by: - United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), New York. - Theme (2023): - “8 Billion Lives, Infinite Possibilities: The Case for Rights and Choices.” - Key Finding: - India became the most populous nation by mid-2023 (142.86 crore). - Population ageing and inverted pyramid - Definition: - Increasing proportion of elderly (65+) in the population due to declining birth rates and rising life expectancy. - Example: - Japan, with a shrinking working-age population and high elderly dependency. - Implications: - Increased healthcare costs, pension burdens, and reduced workforce. - Pro-Natalist Policy (2024) - Definition: - Government policies encouraging higher birth/fertility rates. - Examples (2024): - Andhra Pradesh CM Chandrababu Naidu and Tamil Nadu CM M.K. Stalin urged citizens to have more children. - Rationale: - States with larger populations secure more parliamentary seats. - Higher population increases tax devolution under Finance Commission formulas. - Additional topics: - Demographic Dividend - Definition: - A period when the dependency ratio declines, and the working-age population (15-64) is proportionately larger, boosting economic productivity. - In economics and finance, a "dividend" refers to a return or reward received from an investment. - Analogy: - When a country has a high proportion of working-age people, it's like having a high-yield investment opportunity. - If the government and society invest well in education, health, skills, and jobs: - The large workforce becomes productive. - Generates higher economic output and tax revenues. - Leads to accelerated economic growth, just like receiving a "reward" (dividend) from the demographic investment. - Temporality: - Temporary in nature; the demographic dividend is not permanent. - The working-age population will eventually age and become dependent again. - Repercussions of Wasted Demographic Dividend: - Rising Unemployment: - If adequate jobs are not created, a large youth population remains idle. - Leads to economic stagnation and under-utilization of human capital. - Social Unrest: - Frustrated unemployed youth may turn to crime, extremism, or violence. - Increases law-and-order issues and weakens social fabric. - Demographic Burden: - When the large working-age cohort ages without retirement security: - Burdens healthcare, pensions, and social security systems. - Shrinking workforce must support a growing elderly population. - Missed Economic Growth: - Countries that fail to invest in education, skills, and infrastructure: - Miss the chance to boost productivity and GDP growth. - Fall into the "middle-income trap" or remain underdeveloped. - Comparative Loss: - Other nations (e.g., South Korea, China) that harnessed their demographic window: - Gained rapid economic advancement. - Countries like India risk falling behind if the window closes without capitalizing. - Silver Dividend - Definition: - Refers to the economic and social gains that can be derived from the ageing population — especially active and healthy senior citizens — who continue to contribute meaningfully to society. - Seen as a potential counterbalance to the challenges of population ageing (e.g., pension burden, healthcare costs). - Rationale: - With improvements in healthcare and longevity, many elderly remain physically fit, mentally alert, and professionally capable beyond retirement age. - Aging population is often seen as a liability, but with the right ecosystem, they can become an asset. - Contributions: - Economic: - Elderly professionals offering consulting, mentoring, part-time, or freelance services. - Entrepreneurship by retirees (second careers). - Reduced burden on pension systems if older citizens continue earning. - Social: - Participation in voluntary activities, local governance, and social welfare programs. - Transfer of values, experience, and institutional memory to younger generations. - Familial: - Grandparental caregiving reduces pressure on nuclear families. - Elderly often play key roles in child-rearing, especially in dual-income households. - Examples: - Japan: - Senior citizens work in retail, teaching, and small-scale enterprises. - Community-led initiatives for elderly engagement in rural areas. - India: - Government promoting voluntary retirement re-engagement programs. - NGOs involving seniors in educational and health awareness campaigns. - Some states offer incentives for employing elderly in low-risk sectors. - Policy Implications: - Need for: - Flexible retirement and pension policies. - Lifelong learning and reskilling programs for elderly. - Age-friendly infrastructure and digital literacy. - Promotion of health and wellness among seniors to ensure "active aging". - Significance: - Complements demographic dividend by ensuring intergenerational contribution. - Supports inclusive growth and social cohesion in an ageing society. - Helps mitigate negative effects of rising old-age dependency ratio. - Pillar 6A2: Human Resource Development - Health - Definition: - Human resource development in health focuses on improving healthcare access, infrastructure, and outcomes to ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all, aligning with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3, which targets reducing maternal and child mortality, combating communicable and non-communicable diseases, and enhancing healthcare systems by 2030. - Health Sector Overview - SDG Goal 3 Targets and India’s Progress: - Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR): - 130 per 1 lakh live births (baseline); target to reduce to 70 by 2030. Achieved in Kerala, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu while Uttar Pradesh, Assam report over 200 deaths. - Under-5 Child Mortality Rate: - Refers to the number of children who die before reaching their 5th birthday. - 50 per 1000 live births; target to reduce to 11. Only Kerala has achieved (7). - Annual Reported TB Cases: - 138 per 1 lakh population; target to eliminate by 2030. - Government Doctors, Nurses, Midwives: - 221 per 1,00,000 population; target to increase to 550. Only Kerala has achieved (700). - Additional Goals: - Reduce road accidents, alcohol and tobacco abuse, mental illness, and eliminate HIV/AIDS, malaria, hepatitis, and other communicable diseases (no quantifiable targets set by India). - Ministry of Science and Technology - Departments: - Department of Science and Technology (DST): - Oversees Survey of India (national mapping organization), National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation (NATMO), Science and Engineering Research Board, Technology Development Board, National Innovation Foundation, and Indian Science Congress Association (Kolkata). - Department of Scientific and Industrial Research: - Supports scientific research initiatives. - Department of Biotechnology: - Includes National Institute of Immunology and Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC). - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Bharat Immunological and Biological Corporation: - Focuses on vaccine production. - Indian Vaccine Corporation Ltd (IVCOL): - Supports vaccine development. - Central Electronics Ltd: - Approved for strategic disinvestment (privatization) in 2019. - Note: - Department of Pharmaceuticals falls under Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers (Pillar 5). - Ministry of Health and Family Welfare - Departments: - Department of Health and Family Welfare: - Manages healthcare delivery and policy. - Department of Health Research: - Oversees research initiatives. - Attached Offices: - Directorate General of Health Services: - To launch National Tele Mental Health Programme (Budget 2022). - Budget Allocation: - 2020: - Rs. 70,000 crore by Union (0.3% of GDP); combined Union + State spending at 1.6% of GDP. - Economic Survey 2022: - Union + State spending increased to 2.1% of GDP. - National Health Policy 2017: - Targets 2.5% of GDP by 2025. - WHO Recommendation: - Minimum 5% of GDP for public healthcare. - CPSEs: - Hospital Services Consultancy Ltd (HSCC): - Approved for privatization in 2019. - HLL Lifecare: - Approved for privatization in 2019. - World Health Organization (WHO) - Established: - Founded on 7 April 1948 as a specialized agency of the United Nations. - Headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. - Primary role: - Direct and coordinate international health within the UN system. - Objectives: - Attainment by all peoples of the highest possible level of health. - Universal Health Coverage (UHC), emergency response, health research, setting international norms/standards. - Governance Structure: - World Health Assembly: - Supreme decision-making body, comprises delegates from all 194 member states. - Meets annually to set policies, approve budgets, and appoint the Director-General. - Executive Board: - Consists of 34 technically qualified members elected for 3-year terms. - Implements decisions and policies of the Health Assembly. - Director-General: - Elected by the World Health Assembly for a 5-year term. - Heads the Secretariat and oversees WHO’s global operations. - Funding: - Two types of contributions: - Assessed Contributions: - Compulsory, based on a country’s wealth and population. - ~16% of WHO’s budget. - Voluntary Contributions: - ~84% of budget. - Includes funds from member states, philanthropic foundations (e.g., Gates Foundation), private sector, and international organizations. - Key Roles and Functions: - International health surveillance and response (e.g., pandemics). - Issuing International Health Regulations (IHR). - Promoting access to essential medicines and vaccines. - Global initiatives on disease eradication (e.g., polio, TB, malaria). - Controversies: - Taiwan’s Observer Status: - Taiwan seeks observer status at WHA (enjoyed between 2009–2016 as “Chinese Taipei”). - Observer status is a diplomatic position that allows an entity (country, organization, or region) to participate in the activities of an international organization without having full membership or voting rights. - Blocked by China, citing One-China Policy. - Accusations of Chinese Influence: - During COVID-19, WHO was accused of favoring China’s narrative and delaying pandemic alerts. - USA’s Exit from WHO (Announced July 2020, formally set for Jan 2021): - President Donald​Trump’s Justifications: - WHO’s alleged mismanagement of the COVID-19 pandemic. - Delayed response and “pro-China bias.” - Excessive US financial burden (US was the largest contributor). - Criticism of WHO’s stance on issues like: - Support for sex-change procedures and LGBT+ rights. - Advocacy for abortion rights. - Climate change policy involvement. - Note: - President Joe Biden reversed the decision and rejoined WHO in January 2021. - On January 20, 2025, immediately after being inaugurated for his second term, Trump signed an executive order (EO 14155) directing the U.S. to withdraw from the WHO once again - The formal withdrawal process requires a one-year notice and the settlement of dues, meaning the U.S. is set to officially leave the WHO by January 22, 2026 - WHO Global Initiative on Digital Health (GIDH) - Launch: - August 19, 2023, during the G20 Health Ministers’ Meeting in Gandhinagar, India. - Jointly announced by the G20 Presidency (India) and WHO. - Objective: - Strengthen digital health infrastructure globally. - Promote inclusive, secure, and interoperable digital health systems. - Facilitate knowledge sharing, capacity-building, and technical assistance. - Relevance: - Supports SDG Goal 3 (Good Health and Well-being). - Aims to close digital divides between developed and developing nations in healthcare. - AYUSH Ministry - Overview: - Promotes Ayurveda, Yoga (attributed to Maharshi Patanjali), Naturopathy, Unani (notable figure: Hakim Ajmal Khan), Siddha (Tamil Siddhar Saints), Homoeopathy (German physician), and Sowa-Rigpa (Tibetan, added in 2017). - Naturopathy (or Naturopathic Medicine) is a system of alternative medicine based on the belief that the body has an innate ability to heal itself using natural therapies and lifestyle changes. - Autonomous Bodies: - Morarji Desai National Institute of Yoga, Delhi. - National Institutes: - Ayurveda (Jaipur), Naturopathy (Pune, Nisarga Gram), Unani Medicine (Bengaluru), Siddha (Chennai), Homoeopathy (Kolkata), Sowa-Rigpa (Leh). - Jaipur (Code: 4). - National Institute of Homoeopathy - Kolkata (Code: 3). - National Institute of Unani Medicine - Bengaluru (Code: 2). - National Institute of Siddha - Chennai (Code: 1). - Correct Code: - (c) 4, 3, 2, 1. - AYUSH Regulation - Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Sowa-Rigpa: - Regulated by Indian Medicine Central Council Act, 1970, under NCISM, New Delhi. - Homoeopathy: - Regulated by Homoeopathy Central Council Act, 1973, under NCH, New Delhi. - Yoga and Naturopathy: - No governing body yet. - AYUSH elements in detail - Yoga - Key Texts: - Charak Samhita and Sushruta Samhita (circa 2500 BC). - Definition by Panini: - Yoga means “Yujir” (union) or “Yuja” (samadhi, highest state of mind and knowledge). - Union of what? - That depends on the philosophical or spiritual tradition: - Union of Individual Self with Universal Consciousness - Union of Body, Mind, and Spirit - Union of Prakriti (nature) and Purusha (consciousness) - Union of Opposites - Union through Discipline and Practice - International Yoga Day Themes: -

- Unani System - Origin: - Greece, integrating knowledge from Egypt, Arabia, Iran, China, Syria, and India. - Medicines: - Primarily herbal, with animal, marine, and mineral products. - Key Texts: - Al-Qanoon by Sheikh Abu-Ali Sina (Avicenna, 980-1037 AD); Al-Havi by Razi (850-923 AD). - Introduction to India: - Eighth century. - Siddha System - Origin: - Ancient Tamils/Dravidians, flourishing during Indus Valley Civilization (10000-4000 BC). - Key Terms: - Siddha: - Achievements. - Siddhars: - Practitioners who achieved medicinal perfection. - Vaathuvas: - 96 tools or principles of Siddha. - Focus: - Science of life, drugs, kayakalpam, anatomy, physiology, pathology, diagnostics, surgery, alchemy, astrology, atomic theory. - Homoeopathy - Founder: - Dr. Christian Friedrich Samuel Hahnemann (German physician). - Introduction to India: - 1810 by European missionaries. - Official Recognition: - 1948 by Constituent Assembly resolution. - Principle: - Similia Similibus Curentur (like cures like). - It means that a substance that causes symptoms in a healthy person can be used in very small amounts to treat similar symptoms in a sick person. - The logic is that the body can be stimulated to heal itself by introducing a diluted version of the substance that causes the symptoms. - Example: - If a substance causes fever and chills in a healthy person, that same substance (in a highly diluted form) might be used to treat fever and chills in someone who is ill. - Sowa-Rigpa - History: - Over 2,500 years, practiced in Himalayan regions (Leh, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Darjeeling). - Efficacy: - Effective for chronic diseases like asthma, bronchitis, arthritis. - Philosophy: - Emphasizes five cosmological physical elements. - Health-Related Notable Policies - National Health Policy 2017 - Goals: - Increase public health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP by 2025. - Transform primary healthcare into Health and Wellness Centres. - Establish NDHA/NeHA for telemedicine and remote diagnostics. - Promote generic drugs, affordable medical devices, Make in India, and AYUSH systems. - HIV/AIDS: - 90:90:90 target by 2020; End AIDS by 2030. - HIV Prevention Act, 2017; NACO as nodal body; World AIDS Day (December 1). - Reduce non-communicable diseases in a time-bound manner. - Five Pillars of Health Policy (as per Economic Survey 2025) - 1. Preventive Healthcare - 2. Timely Diagnosis - 3. Affordable Medicines & Treatment - 4. Quality Healthcare in Small Towns & Villages - 5. Expansion of Technology in Healthcare :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1} - National Policy for Rare Diseases 2021 - Examples: - Spinal Muscular Atrophy, Lysosomal Storage Disorders, Cystic Fibrosis. - Classification: - Divides rare diseases into three groups. - Financial Support: - Up to ₹50 lakh through Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi. - Initiatives: - Encourages crowdfunding and donations; ICMR to maintain rare disease database (e.g., Hemophilia, Thalassemia, Sickle Cell). - Policies related to medicine: - Cheap medicine: - NPPA Price Control - National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA): - Established in 1997 under Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. - Powers: - Derived from Essential Commodities Act, 1955, and Drugs Prices Control Orders (DPCO) 1995, 2013; sets price ceilings on over 800 essential medicines. - Tools: - Pharma Sahi Daam: - App/portal for checking drug prices. - Pharma Jan Samadhan: - Web portal for filing complaints on drug pricing/availability. - Coronary Stents: - 2017 price ceilings to prevent profiteering by companies and hospitals. - Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP) - Administered by: - Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers via Bureau of Pharma PSUs of India (BPPI), registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860. - Objective: - NGOs/individuals open Jan Aushadhi Stores (JAS) to sell generic medicines at affordable prices, supplied by BPPI, located at district hospitals and public places. - Budget 2020: - Expand JAS to all districts by 2024. - Jan Aushadhi Diwas: - Celebrated annually on March 7. - Terminology: - Generic Drugs: - Non-proprietary drugs produced after patent expiry or compulsory licensing. - Fixed Dose Combinations (FDCs): - Mixtures of two or more drugs; many banned (e.g., Corex, Saridon, D’Cold, Vicks Action 500) due to safety concerns. - Free Medicine: - Free Drugs Service Initiative (FDSI, 2015) - Under National Health Mission (NHM), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. - Objective: - Provides funds to states/UTs for free medicines in government hospitals and Primary Healthcare Centres (PHCs). - National Health Mission (NHM, 2005) - Administered by: - Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Core Scheme (60:40 or 90:10 funding). - Objectives: - Reduce MMR to 100 per 1 lakh live births. - Reduce Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) to 25 per 1000 live births. - Reduce Total Fertility Rate (TFR) to 2.1. - Reduce anaemia in women aged 15–49. - Decrease household healthcare expenditure. - Focus on tuberculosis, leprosy, malaria; eliminate Kala-azar (target 2015, not fully achieved per WHO). - Sub-Missions: - National Rural Health Mission (2005): - Enhances rural healthcare. - National Urban Health Mission (2013): - Reduces healthcare expenditure for urban poor. - Mother and Child Healthcare - SDG Targets: - Reduce MMR to 70 per 1 lakh live births (from 130); reduce under-5 mortality to 11 per 1000 live births (from 50). - Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS, 1975) - Administered by: - Ministry of Women and Child Development; Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10). - Beneficiaries: - Children (0-6 years), pregnant and lactating mothers. - Components: - Anganwadi Services Scheme: - Nutrition and health services. - Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana: - Rs. 5,000 for childbirth. - SABLA: - Empowerment of adolescent girls (11-18 years). - POSHAN Abhiyaan: - Nutrition improvement. - National Creche Scheme: - Creches for working mothers. - Child Protection Scheme: - Supports children in difficult circumstances. - Benefits: - Reduces IMR, MMR, anaemia; provides immunization, health check-ups, pre-school education. - Mothers’ Health - Administered by: - NHM, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. - Key Initiatives: - Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA): - Provide Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (RMNCH+A) services. - Interim-Budget 2024: - ASHA workers, Anganwadi workers, and helpers eligible for PM-JAY (Rs. 5 lakh health insurance). - Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) - Objective: - Reduce maternal and neonatal mortality by promoting institutional deliveries among Below Poverty Line (BPL) women. - Conditional Cash Transfers: - Low Performing States (LPS: Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Assam, Rajasthan, Odisha, Jammu and Kashmir): - Urban: - Rs. 1,000. - Rural: - Rs. 1,400. - High Performing States (HPS: Others): - Urban: - Rs. 600. - Rural: - Rs. 700. - ASHA Bonus: - Rs. 400–600 per beneficiary mother. - Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) - Services: - Free normal/caesarean deliveries, food, medicines, and transport (dial 102) in public hospitals; covers sick infants up to 1 year. - Other Notable Schemes - Surakshit Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN, 2019): - Ensures dignified treatment; complaints via helpline/SMS/portal with zero tolerance for violations; reduces IMR, MMR. - Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyaan (2016): - Free check-ups, iron folic acid, calcium tablets on the 9th of each month for antenatal care; private doctors volunteer. - Laqshya (2017): - Ensures sterilized delivery rooms with necessary equipment. - Mother’s Absolute Affection (MAA, 2016): - Promotes breastfeeding for first six months to enhance child health. - Mission Parivar Vikas (2016): - Targets high TFR states (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Assam) for family planning; offers free contraceptives (Chhaya: non-hormonal, weekly; Antara: injectable, quarterly); aims to reduce TFR from 2.2 (2016) to 2.1 (2025). - Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY, 2017) - Administered by: - Ministry of Women and Child Development; Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10). - History: - Renamed from Indira Gandhi Matritva Sahyog (2014). - Benefits: - Rs. 6,000 total (Rs. 1,000 + Rs. 2,000 + Rs. 2,000 via PMMVY; Rs. 1,000 via JSY for BPL women) for first child; Rs. 5,000 for second child if a girl, to support rest and breastfeeding, reducing MMR and IMR. - Eligibility: - Excludes women in government/PSU jobs or under 19 years. - Alignment: - Fulfills National Food Security Act (NFSA) 2013 requirement for Rs. 6,000 to pregnant/lactating mothers. - Paalan 1000 - Journey of the First 1000 Days - Administered by: - Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. - Objective: - Provides parental guidance via app for child’s physical, mental, emotional, cognitive, and social health in the first two years. - Kilkari Audio Training Messages - Objective: - Delivers 72 free weekly audio messages on pregnancy, childbirth, and childcare to mothers’ mobile phones. - ANMOL Tablet App - Objective: - Tablet-based app for health workers (Auxiliary Nurse Midwives) to streamline beneficiary registration and daily tasks. - Vaccination - Administered by: - Ministry of Health and Family Welfare with 100% union funding, supported by WHO and UNICEF. - Universal Immunization Programme (UIP, 1985): - Vaccines: - BCG (TB, tubercular meningitis), Oral Polio Vaccine (India polio-free since 2014), Rotavirus (diarrhoea), Japanese Encephalitis (selected areas), Measles-Rubella (MR), Pentavalent (Diphtheria, Tetanus, Pertussis, Influenza Type B, Hepatitis B). - Coverage: - Only 65% of children covered by 2014. - Mission Indradhanush (2014) - Objective: - Achieve 100% immunization for children under 2 against seven diseases (diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, polio, tuberculosis, measles, hepatitis B). - Additional Vaccines: - Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV), Rotavirus, Measles-Rubella, Japanese Encephalitis (adults in Assam, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal), Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV), Tetanus and Adult Diphtheria (Td). - Pregnant Women: - Vaccinated for selected diseases. - Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI, 2017): - Targets 90% coverage for children under 2 and pregnant women by December 2018. - e-VIN: - Electronic Vaccine Network, supported by UNDP, monitors vaccine stocks. - Interim-Budget 2024: - Cervical cancer vaccination for girls aged 9-14 (linked to Human Papilloma Virus). - Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI) 3.0 (2021) & 4.0 (2022-23) - Focus: - Children and pregnant women who missed non-COVID vaccine doses during the pandemic; targets migrants and hard-to-reach areas. - Approach: - Staggered vaccination to reduce crowding. - Fully Immunized Child - Criteria - Vaccines by First Birthday: - BCG, Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV), Pentavalent (Diphtheria, Tetanus, Pertussis, Hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type B), Measles-Rubella. - Coverage: - 93% of children fully immunized (2023-24). - Side note: - How Vaccines Work: - Purpose: - Train the immune system to recognize and fight pathogens (viruses or bacteria) without causing disease. - Process: - 1. Introduction of Vaccine: - Contains: - Weakened or inactivated virus/bacteria (e.g., measles, polio) - A fragment of the pathogen (e.g., protein subunit like in HPV) - Genetic material (e.g., mRNA in COVID vaccines like Pfizer/Moderna) - 2. Immune System Response: - Detects the vaccine components as foreign. - Produces: - Antibodies via B cells to neutralize the threat. - T cells to destroy infected cells and coordinate the immune response. - 3. Creation of Memory Cells: - Body retains a "memory" of the pathogen. - Memory B and T cells remain in the body for long-term immunity. - 4. Future Exposure: - If exposed to the actual pathogen later: - Immune system recognizes it immediately. - Rapid immune response destroys the pathogen before illness develops or limits severity. - Analogy: - Vaccine = “Wanted poster” for the immune system. - Prepares the body for a real attack without experiencing the full disease. - Adolescent Boys and Girls - Women and Child Development Ministry: - SAKSHAM: - Targets boys aged 11-18 for health, hygiene, nutrition, and vocational training. - SABLA (Rajiv Gandhi Scheme): - Empowers adolescent girls (11-18) with health, hygiene, nutrition, adolescent reproductive and sexual health (ARSH), Iron-Folic Acid supplementation, and vocational skills. - Kishori Health Cards: - Track weight, height, BMI for girls aged 11-18. - Health Ministry: - Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram: - Targets boys aged 10-19 for similar objectives. - Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK): - Screens children aged 0-6 for birth defects, deficiencies, diseases, and developmental delays; provides annual check-ups for ages 6-18 in government schools. - Saksham Anganwadis (Budget 2022) - Objective: - Upgrade 2 lakh Anganwadi centres under ICDS with improved infrastructure, audio-visual aids, and clean energy for family planning, nutrition, and pre-school activities. - Ayushman Bharat National Health Protection Mission (AB-NHPM) - Definition: - A flagship healthcare initiative launched in 2018 to provide comprehensive health services and financial protection to India’s population, particularly the poor, through upgraded health facilities and insurance coverage. - Components: - Health and Wellness Centres (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs): - Upgrades Primary Health Centres (PHCs) into Health and Wellness Centres to deliver free drugs, diagnostic checkups, mother-child care, family planning, and treatment for non-communicable diseases (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, oral/breast/cervical cancers), communicable diseases (e.g., malaria, measles), mental health, ENT, ophthalmology, oral health, geriatric care, and palliative care (e.g., for HIV/AIDS, cancer). - Promotes yoga, wellness activities, and healthy lifestyles through initiatives like anti-tobacco campaigns, marathons, laughter clubs, and open gyms. - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY): - Provides Rs. 5 lakh per poor family per year for health insurance, covering secondary and tertiary care, including 3 days of pre-hospitalization and 15 days of post-hospitalization expenses. - As of January 2023, enrolled 22 crore people, significantly reducing out-of-pocket healthcare costs for the poor. - Ayushman Bhav Campaign (2023): - An awareness and enrollment drive for Ayushman health insurance cards, generating Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) digital IDs, and raising awareness about government health schemes, tuberculosis, and sickle cell disease. - Components: - Ayushman Apke Dwar 3.0: - Door-to-door beneficiary registration. - Ayushman Melas: - Health camps at Community Health Centres (CHCs). - Ayushman Sabhas: - Awareness events in villages and panchayats. - Duration: - September 17 to October 2, 2023 (Seva Pakhwada, aligned with Gandhi Jayanti). - Health Cess (2020): - A 5% cess on customs duty for imported medical devices to fund hospital construction under Ayushman Bharat in Public-Private Partnership (PPP) mode, particularly in Aspirational Districts (backward districts identified by NITI Aayog). - Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Nidhi (PMSSN, 2021): - A non-lapsable fund under the Public Account, funded by a 4% Health and Education Cess on direct taxes (e.g., income tax, corporation tax). - Objectives: - Supports Ayushman Bharat schemes, including PM-JAY. - Funds Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY) for establishing AIIMS-like institutions and upgrading government medical colleges. - Supports National Health Mission (NHM) and health emergency responses (e.g., COVID-19). - PMSSY Objectives: - Correct regional imbalances in tertiary healthcare services. - Augment facilities for quality medical education. - National Health Mission (NHM) - Definition: - A comprehensive initiative to improve public health systems, focusing on both communicable and non-communicable diseases, maternal and child health, and rural healthcare access. - Components: - Communicable Diseases: - National Vector-Borne Disease Control Programme: - Targets malaria, dengue, filaria, kala-azar, Japanese encephalitis, and chikungunya through mosquito prevention strategies like Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS), Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLIN), larvivorous fish, and bio-larvicides. - Leprosy Eradication Programme: - Aims to eliminate leprosy through early detection and treatment. - HIV/STD Programme: - Focuses on prevention, testing, and treatment. - Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP): - Monitors diseases like swine flu, Ebola, Nipah, Zika, and COVID-19. - TB Elimination - Target: - 2025 - National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) uses Directly Observed Treatment Short course (DOTS) strategy. - Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyan (2022): - Encourages community support through Nikshay Mitras (donors) via the NIKSHAY web portal, providing Rs. 500/month to TB patients for nutrition and vocational training. - SAANS Initiative (2019): - Social Awareness and Actions to Neutralize Pneumonia Successfully, reducing childhood pneumonia deaths. - Non-Communicable Diseases: - National Mental Health Programme (NMHP): - Addresses mental health issues. - National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases, and Stroke (NPCDCS): - Focuses on screening and management. - Blindness and Tobacco Control Programmes: - Includes COTPA Act, 2003, mandating 85% health warnings on cigarette and tobacco packaging. - Fluorosis Prevention: - Targets excessive fluoride in drinking water (desirable limit: 1.0–1.5 mg/litre), linked to Anemia Mukt Bharat. - eDantSeva Portal: - Promotes oral health awareness. - Global Fund to Fight AIDS, TB, and Malaria (2002): - Headquartered in Geneva, supported by the UN and Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. - Promotes 3-in-1 TLD pill (tenofovir, lamivudine, dolutegravir) for HIV treatment, recommended by WHO for its efficacy and low cost (<$45/year). - Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM, 2021) - Definition: - Launched on October 2021 (announced August 2020), ABDM aims to create a digital health ecosystem for seamless healthcare access and data management. - Features: - Managed by the National Health Authority (NHA), also responsible for PM-JAY. - Provides a 14-digit Unique Health ID (UHID) for citizens, linked to mobile numbers or Aadhaar (optional), storing records of diseases, diagnoses, reports, and medications. - Consent-based, voluntary, with opt-out and data deletion options; allows nominee access (e.g., for guardians). - Integrates with digital health services like digi-doctor, telemedicine, and e-pharmacy. - Budget 2022: - Plans digital registries for doctors, hospitals, and patient records. - Health Data Management Policy: - Covers patients, doctors, governments, insurance, pharma, and research bodies. - Ensures patient rights to remove data, correct errors, restrict disclosures, and request data copies. - Data sharing complies with applicable laws and international standards. - Includes awareness programs on data privacy. - E-Sanjeevani Telemedicine - Definition: - A telemedicine platform developed by the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC, Mohali) under the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY). - Features: - Offers patient registration, audio-video consultations with doctors, and e-prescriptions. - Types: - Doctor-to-Doctor (eSanjeevani). - Patient-to-Doctor (eSanjeevani OPD). - PM Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM, 2021) - Definition: - Renamed from PM AtmaNirbhar Swasth Bharat Yojana, launched in 2021 to strengthen public health infrastructure (tenure: 2021–2026). - Features: - Centrally sponsored scheme with state contributions. - Aims to detect and cure new/emerging diseases, manage pandemics, and enhance primary, secondary, and tertiary healthcare systems. - Focuses on IT-enabled surveillance, public health labs, and National Centre for Disease Control. - 15th Finance Commission Grants (2021–2026): - Rs. 70,000 crore for local bodies. - Rs. 15,000 crore for critical care hospitals (e.g., ICU, ventilators, dialysis). - Rs. 13,000 crore for training allied healthcare workers (e.g., lab technicians, ASHA workers). - Rs. 2,000 crore for doctor training in district hospitals. - Recommendations: - Union and state governments to spend 2.5% of GDP on healthcare by 2025. - Propose All India Medical and Health Service under All-India Services Act, 1951, for UPSC recruitment to address doctor shortages. - Address concentration of medical colleges and super-specialty hospitals in western/southern India. - COVID-19 Response - Vaccination Timeline: - Jan 2021: - Health and frontline workers (e.g., policemen). - Apr 2021: - Citizens aged 45+. - May 2021: - Citizens aged 18+. - Jan 2022: - Teenagers aged 15–18. - Health Apps and Portals: - COVAX Network: - Led by WHO, GAVI, and CEPI to procure vaccines for member countries. - Controversy: - Alleged insufficient vaccine supply for poor nations; deals only with union governments, not states (e.g., Punjab denied). - CoWIN App/Portal: - Managed by NHA for vaccination slot registration and certificate downloads. - Supports non-Aadhaar IDs (e.g., voter ID, driving license). - Open-sourced in 2021 for global use. - COVAID Portal: - NITI Aayog portal for importing/donating COVID relief materials (e.g., oxygen cylinders, ventilators, Remdesivir). - Aarogya Setu (2020): - Uses Bluetooth and GPS to track COVID infections and contacts. - Developed by National Informatics Centre (NIC) with NITI Aayog and private IT experts. - Privacy concerns: - Data hacking/misuse risks. - AarogyaPath: - CSIR portal for real-time availability of masks, PPE, and critical healthcare supplies. - Suraksha Store Initiative: - Department of Consumer Affairs monitors health-safety guidelines at retail stores with tech startups Safejob and Seekify. - Corona Strategies: - R0 (Basic Reproduction Number): - R0 < 1: - Disease fades. - R0 = 1: - Disease persists without epidemic. - R0 > 1: - Epidemic possible. - R0 > 10/100: - Super-spreader event. - Mitigation vs. Suppression: -
Mitigation Suppression
- Slows pandemic spread (e.g., R0 from 100 to 2) using masks, social distancing, contact tracing, and partial lockdowns. - Reduces economic damage while cutting deaths by ~50%. - Stops/reverses spread (R0 < 1) via nationwide complete lockdowns. - Causes significant economic damage.
- Barbell Strategy: - Initial nationwide lockdown to save lives and flatten the epidemic curve, followed by gradual unlocking to save livelihoods, combined with social distancing, contact tracing, and vaccination. - Origin of term: - Term originally used in investment and risk management - In finance, it refers to: - Investing heavily in two extreme ends (very safe + very risky assets) - Avoiding the "middle risk" options - The barbell shape: - heavy weights on both ends, nothing in the center - The "two ends" of the barbell in covid context: - One end: - Harsh initial lockdown (to flatten the curve, save lives) - Other end: - Gradual unlocking and economic revival (to protect livelihoods) - Middle avoided: - Partial, indecisive, or weak measures that could fail at both - Miscellaneous Health Schemes - Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY): - Central sector scheme to establish AIIMS-like institutions and upgrade government medical colleges to address regional healthcare imbalances. - Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi (RAN): - Provides financial aid for Below Poverty Line (BPL) patients with life-threatening diseases to access free treatment at super-specialty hospitals. - National Pharmacovigilance Programme: - Monitors adverse drug reactions and spurious/fake drugs. - Deworming: - Administers Albendazole tablets to children for intestinal worm infections, observed on National Deworming Day (Feb 10, Aug 10). - Atal Jai Anusandhan Biotech Missions (2019): - Sub-missions: - GARBH-ini: - Research on preterm birth causes. - IndCEPI: - Affordable vaccines for endemic diseases. - UNaTI: - Bio-fortified and protein-rich crops. - Antimicrobial Resistance: - Addresses drug-resistant infections. - Swachh Bharat: - Innovative technologies for sanitation. - National Ayush Mission (2014): - Promotes AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy) through new colleges, hospitals, and medicinal plant cultivation. - PM Vrikshayush Yojana: - Supports cultivation and post-harvest management of medicinal plants. - e-AUSHADHI Portal: - Facilitates online licensing and information on AYUSH drugs, including cancelled/spurious drugs. - Yoga Initiatives: - BHUVAN-YOGA App (ISRO): - Tracks International Yoga Day participation. - Yoga Locator: - Identifies venues for International Yoga Day. - Important Days: - June 21: - International Yoga Day (since 2015, UNGA). - Jan 4: - Siddha Day (since 2018, Ayush Ministry). - Dec 1: - World AIDS Day. - Disease Elimination: - India eliminated polio, guinea worm disease, yaws, maternal, and neonatal tetanus (Economic Survey 2022). - MERA and TruNAT: - MERA: - ICMR’s Malaria Elimination Research Alliance. - TruNAT: - ICMR’s low-cost TB detection project. - AMRIT Outlets: - Affordable Medicines and Reliable Implants for Treatment, offering cancer/cardiovascular drugs and cardiac implants at 60–90% discounts. - SUGAM Portal: - CDSCO portal for drug approvals, clinical trial reports, and complaints. - U-Win Platform: - Records vaccinations for pregnant women and children up to 16 years under Mission Indradhanush. - Interim Budget 2024: - Cervical cancer vaccination for girls aged 9–14 (linked to Human Papillomavirus). - ASHA and Anganwadi workers/helpers eligible for PM-JAY Rs. 5 lakh insurance. - Budget 2025: - Day Care Cancer Centres in all district hospitals within three years. - Other Initiatives: - Drones for Medicine Delivery: - ‘Medicines from the Sky’ (WEF, Telangana, Arunachal) and i-DRONE (ICMR, Northeast). - AI in Healthcare: - Rajasthan’s AI for silicosis detection; Uttarakhand’s eSwasthya Dham for Char Dham Yatra pilgrims. - Toxic Work Culture (Economic Survey 2025): - Impacts mental health, low prelims relevance. - Ultra-Processed/Junk Food: - Linked to obesity, cardiovascular diseases, and mental health issues. - Suggestions: - Higher GST, stricter advertising, and labeling rules. - Hunger and Malnutrition - Definitions: - Hunger: - Distress from insufficient calorie/food intake. - Malnutrition: - Deficiency from insufficient calories and/or nutrients. - Food Security: - Availability of nutritious food at stable, affordable prices year-round. - Causes of Malnutrition: - Income Inequality: - Poor cannot afford nutrient-rich foods (e.g., milk, vegetables); ~21% of India’s population is Below Poverty Line (2011). - Gender Inequality: - Women eating last/least; >1/3rd of Indian women have low BMI. - Social Inequality: - Marginalized groups (SC/ST) lack economic opportunities for nutritious food. - Water-Sanitation Issues: - Open defecation causes intestinal worms and enteropathy. - Psychological Issues: - Disorders like anorexia nervosa, exacerbated by social media body image pressures. - Dietary Habits: - Vegetarian diets may lack protein, per Western research. - Food Security Pillars and India’s Efforts: -
Pillar India’s Efforts
Availability Union: MSP, fertilizer subsidies, PM-KISAN. States: Cheap canal water, electricity for farmers.
Affordability National Food Security Act (NFSA) provides subsidized grains to the poor.
Nutrition Poshan Abhiyaan, Mid-Day Meal, Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) ensure nutritious food for children and women.
Stability Food Corporation of India (FCI) maintains buffer stocks for distribution during inflation or disasters.
- Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution - Departments: - Department of Consumer Affairs: - Manages INGRAM portal for consumer complaints. - Department of Food and Public Distribution: - Oversees food security schemes. - Attached/Subordinate Offices: - Directorate of Sugar and Vegetable Oils: - Includes National Sugar Institute. - Indian Grain Storage Management & Research Institute. - Statutory Bodies: - Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (2007). - National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. - Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS): - Manages ISI and gold hallmarking. - Enforces Essential Commodities Act, 1955. - Commercial Undertakings: - Food Corporation of India (FCI, 1964): - Procures, stores, and distributes food grains. - Central Warehousing Corporation (1962). - Central Railside Warehouse Company Limited. - Hindustan Vegetable Oils Corporation Limited. - National Food Security Act (NFSA, 2013) - Definition: - A legal framework to provide subsidized food grains to ~67% of India’s population (75% rural, 50% urban), converting food entitlements into legal rights. - Features: - Boss: - Department of Food and Public Distribution. - Union procures grains at Minimum Support Price (MSP) and sells to states at Central Issue Price (CIP, not exceeding MSP). - Food Subsidy: - Food Corporation of India's (FCI’s) economic cost minus CIP. - States distribute grains via Fair Price Shops (FPS)/Public Distribution System (PDS). - Budget 2019: - Allocated >Rs. 1.5 lakh crore. - Beneficiary Categories: - Priority Households (PH): - 5 kg grains per person at Rs. 3/kg (rice, market price: ₹30–₹45), Rs. 2/kg (wheat, market price: ₹25–₹35), Rs. 1/kg (coarse grains, market price: ₹20–₹30). - The prices are as of August 2025 - Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY): - 35 kg grains per family at same rates, regardless of family size. - 2023: - Grains made free (Jan–Dec) under PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY). - Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT): - States like Chandigarh, Puducherry, Dadra & Nagar Haveli provide cash for market purchases. - Food Security Allowance: - Paid if states fail to provide grains on time. - Women Empowerment: - Eldest woman (18+) is household head for ration cards. - Additional Benefits: - Pregnant/lactating mothers: - 600-calorie take-home ration, free Anganwadi meals, Rs. 6,000 maternity benefits (PM Matru Vandana Yojana). - Children (6–14): - Free hot meals or take-home rations in government schools (Mid-Day Meal Scheme). - One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC, 2019): - Enables inter-state and intra-state portability of PDS benefits. - Implemented nationwide by July 31, 2021 (per Supreme Court order). - Portals: - IMPDS: - Manages national-level portability. - Annavitran: - Displays sales data via e-Point of Sale (e-PoS) devices. - Food Distribution Reforms - GPS and RFID: - Tracks trucks transporting subsidized grains to prevent black-market diversion. - ePoS Devices: - Installed at FPS for systematic distribution tracking. - Aadhaar: - Removes duplicate/ghost beneficiaries. - Toll-Free Helpline: - Addresses grievances. - Jan Poshan Kendra: - Renames FPS to focus on nutrition-rich foods (50% inventory) and household items (50%). - FPS Sahay Loan App: - Provides collateral-free loans to FPS dealers. - Rice Fortification: - Adds micronutrients (iron, folic acid, vitamin B12) to rice under NFSA/PMGKAY/ICDS. - Central sector scheme, fully funded by Union, valid till Dec 2028. - How Rice Fortification Is Done? - Fortification Process: - 1. Fortified Rice Kernels (FRKs) are prepared in factories by blending micronutrient premix with broken rice powder and forming them into rice-like grains. - 2. These FRKs are then blended with normal rice at a ratio of 1:100 (i.e., 1 kg FRK with 100 kg regular rice). - 3. The fortified rice looks, cooks, and tastes like regular rice but contains added nutrients. - PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY): - Launched during COVID-19 (Apr 2020–Dec 2024, extended to 2029). - Provided 5 kg free grains (wheat/rice) + 1 kg pulses per month (2020 phases). - Merged with NFSA in Jan 2023, making 5 kg grains free. - Estimated cost: - Rs. 11.8 lakh crore over 5 years. - Bharat Atta (2023): - Subsidized wheat flour (Rs. 27.50/kg vs. Rs. 36/kg market rate) sold via mobile vans, NAFED outlets due to price hikes from Russia-Ukraine crisis, exports, and festival demand. - Other Initiatives: - Free LPG cylinders for PM-Ujjwala beneficiaries (3 months, 2020). - Non-NFSA migrants: - 5 kg grains + 1 kg chana per family for 2 months (2020). - Poshan Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission, 2018) - Definition: - A flagship program to achieve nutritional security by addressing malnutrition among children, women, and adolescents, launched with the motto “Sahi Poshan, Desh Roshan.” - Features: - Boss: - Ministry of Women and Child Development. - Core scheme with 60:40/90:10 funding (Union:States), half-funded by World Bank/MDBs. - Interventions: - Iron-folic acid tablets, nutritious food via Anganwadi/schools, convergence with women/child schemes, online monitoring, IEC awareness, e-learning, yoga. - Bharatiya Poshan Krishi Kosh: - Database of crops across 128 agro-climatic zones for nutritional outcomes. - Poshan Anthem: - By Prasoon Joshi and Shankar Mahadevan. - Rashtriya Poshan Mah: - Celebrated annually in September. - Objectives and Targets: - Reduce stunting (0–6 years) from >35% to 25% by 2022. - Reduce stunting, undernutrition, low-birthweight by 2% annually (till 2020). - Reduce anemia in children (0–6), adolescent girls, women by 3% annually (till 2020). - Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) Strategy (2018): - 6x6x6 Approach: - The Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) Strategy is called the 6x6x6 strategy because it is based on six target beneficiary groups, six interventions, and six institutional mechanisms. - 6 Target Population Groups: - Children (6–59 months) - Children (5–9 years) - Adolescents (10–19 years) - Pregnant women - Lactating women - Women of reproductive age (15–49 years) - 6 Interventions: - Iron-folic acid supplementation - Deworming - Delayed cord clamping (3 minutes post-delivery) - Digital methods for hemoglobin testing - Fortified foods in government programs - Addressing non-nutritional causes (malaria, hemoglobinopathies, fluorosis) - 6 Institutional Mechanisms: - Inter-ministerial coordination - National AMB Unit - Centre of Excellence for Anemia - Convergence across ministries - Strengthening supply chain and logistics - Monitoring via AMB Dashboard/Portal - National Council on India’s Nutrition Challenges: - Chairman: - Vice Chairman, NITI Aayog. - Members: - NITI Aayog CEO, ministers (Women and Child, Drinking Water, Tribal Affairs, Rural Development), CMs of backward states, Health Ministry secretaries. - Mission Poshan 2.0 (2021): - Merges Poshan Abhiyaan and Supplementary Nutrition Scheme (ICDS sub-scheme). - Provides hot-cooked meals/take-home rations (rice, wheat, pulses, eggs, etc.) for children (6 months–6 years), pregnant/lactating mothers, and out-of-school adolescent girls (11–14). - Focuses on first 1,000 days (pregnancy to child’s second birthday). - Portals: - Poshan Tracker: - Monitors pregnant women, lactating mothers, children, adolescents. - Poshan Gyan: - Digital repository for nutrition knowledge, led by NITI Aayog with Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. - Global Hunger Index (GHI) - Definition: - An annual report by Concern Worldwide (Ireland) and Welthungerhilfe (Germany), measuring hunger through four weighted indicators: - Undernourishment: - Share of population with insufficient calorie intake (energy-deficient diets). - Child Wasting: - Low weight-for-height in children under 5 years; indicates acute undernutrition. - "To waste" in English means to gradually lose strength, health, or weight. - Child Stunting: - Low height-for-age in children under 5 years; indicates chronic undernutrition. - Child Mortality: - Mortality rate of children under 5; reflects fatal synergy of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environment. - Scoring Method: - Each indicator is given a standardized score out of 100; weighted and combined to calculate a composite GHI score. - GHI Score Categories: -
GHI Score Range Hunger Level
0–9.9 Low
10–19.9 Moderate
20–34.9 Serious
35–49.9 Alarming
50+ Extremely alarming
- India’s Rank: - 94th (2020), 101st (2021), 107th (2022), 111th (2023), 105th (2024) - Reasons for India's declining rank: - High levels of child wasting and stunting. - Persistent undernourishment in a significant portion of the population. - Child mortality (under 5 years) still a concern in some regions. - Data quality issues: - India rejected GHI rankings in recent years, citing outdated or flawed data sources (e.g., FAO’s PoU estimates). - Disruptions from COVID-19 (2020–2022): - Impact on food security, healthcare, and nutrition services. - Socio-economic disparities: - Unequal access to nutrition, sanitation, and healthcare in rural and marginalized areas. - Implementation challenges in public distribution and child welfare schemes. - 2024 Theme: - Gender justice for climate resilience and zero hunger - Analysis of theme: - Why gender justice matters here: - Women are central to food production (especially in agriculture in developing countries). - But they often have: - Less land ownership - Less access to finance, education, and technology - Less decision-making power - Empowering women = better nutrition, crop diversity, climate resilience. - In essence: - Without gender equality, efforts to fight hunger and adapt to climate change will fail. - India's GHI Score: - Score of 28.8 in 2023 → categorized as "serious" - NITI Aayog Critique: - Claims international methodologies are flawed and outdated. - Argues GHI uses small sample surveys and does not reflect India's national data from NFHS, CNNS, etc. - Suggests that improvements in child nutrition are visible in Indian government surveys. - Criticism of India's Rank in Global Hunger Index (GHI): - Too much weight on child undernutrition: - GHI gives 33% importance to stunting + wasting (both are undernutrition in children). - This gives lower rank to countries like India, which have high child population and undernutrition. - Problem with child mortality as a factor: - Child mortality is affected by many things, not just food. - Example: - dirty water, poor healthcare, bad sanitation. - So using it to measure "hunger" is not fully accurate. - Other Related Reports: - World’s Children Report (UNICEF): - 2019: - Every second Indian child is malnourished (includes stunting, wasting, underweight). - Global Nutrition Report: - Highlights India’s burden of anemia (especially in women and adolescent girls). - Reports high prevalence of stunting among Indian children under 5. - State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (FAO, WHO, IFAD, UNICEF, WFP): - Uses Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES) to measure moderate and severe food insecurity. - Food Waste Index (UNEP): - 50 kg food wasted per person annually in Indian homes (2021 report). - Contradiction - Food Waste vs Malnutrition in India - Food Waste Index (UNEP 2021): - Indian households waste around 50 kg of food per person every year. - But India also has high malnutrition (Global Hunger Index): - High levels of child stunting, wasting, and undernourishment. - Why both exist together? - Unequal distribution: - Plenty of food is produced or available, but not everyone gets it. - Rich urban households waste food, while poor rural families may not have enough to eat. - Poor supply chain and infrastructure: - Food gets spoiled during transport, storage, or at markets. - Cold storage and logistics are weak in many areas. - Lack of awareness: - People often cook more than needed, especially in functions or hotels. - Cultural habit of serving excess food leads to wastage. - Policy and system failures: - Public Distribution System (PDS) has leakages and corruption. - Malnutrition persists despite food availability due to poor outreach and targeting. - Conclusion: - India doesn’t have a food shortage — it has a distribution and utilization problem. - Hunger Hotspots Report (FAO/WFP): - Identifies critical hunger zones: - Ethiopia, Madagascar, Yemen, South Sudan, Nigeria. - Warns of worsening food insecurity due to conflict, climate shocks, economic crises. - One Health Approach - Definition: - A collaborative, multisectoral, and transdisciplinary approach recognizing the interdependence of human, animal, and environmental health. - Especially crucial for prevention, detection, and control of zoonotic diseases (diseases transmitted from animals to humans). - Significance: - Over 60% of known infectious diseases and ~75% of emerging infectious diseases (EIDs) are zoonotic in origin. - Factors like deforestation, intensive farming, wet markets, antibiotic misuse, and climate change increase human-animal-environment interface risks. - Aims to prevent future pandemics by integrating surveillance, early warning, and response mechanisms across sectors. - Examples of Zoonotic Outbreaks: - Nipah Virus (India/Bangladesh): - Origin: - Fruit bats → pigs → humans. - Triggered by habitat destruction (deforestation), bat migration, and pig farming proximity. - Ebola (West Africa): - Transmission via consumption of bushmeat (e.g., monkeys, antelopes). - High mortality and rapid human-to-human transmission. - COVID-19 (Global): - Suspected origin: - Wildlife meat markets in Wuhan, China. - Led to global pandemic with over 6 million deaths. - Avian Influenza & Swine Flu: - Frequent cross-species transmission due to industrial farming practices. - Institutional Support: - Global: - FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization) - WHO (World Health Organization) - OIE (World Organisation for Animal Health) - UNEP (United Nations Environment Programme) - Quadripartite support for One Health Joint Plan of Action (2022–2026). - National (India): - "National One Health Mission" proposed under Department of Animal Husbandry. - ICMR, ICAR, MoEFCC, and health ministry coordinating surveillance efforts. - National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) hosts zoonotic disease cell. - Regular inter-ministerial One Health workshops/seminars held. - Applications: - AMR (Antimicrobial Resistance) Surveillance: - Integrated AMR tracking in human health, livestock, aquaculture, and environment. - Pandemic Preparedness: - Early detection and containment of potential zoonoses. - Sustainable Agriculture: - Reduce indiscriminate use of antibiotics in animal husbandry. - Pillar 6B1: Human Resource Development - Education - Definition: - Education is the systematic process of acquiring knowledge, skills, values, and attitudes through structured instruction, typically in schools or universities, fostering individual and societal development. - Context: - Education is a cornerstone of human resource development, driving economic growth, social equity, and national progress. In India, education reforms aim to achieve universal access, improve quality, and align with global standards like SDG Goal 4, targeting inclusive and equitable education by 2030. - Significance for India: - India’s education system is pivotal for leveraging its demographic dividend, reducing poverty, and fostering innovation. Initiatives like NEP 2020 and digital platforms aim to enhance access, quality, and employability, aligning with Atmanirbhar Bharat and global competitiveness. - Education Statistics and Metrics - Definition: - Education metrics like literacy rate, Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER), and dropout rates measure access, participation, and retention, guiding policy interventions for equitable education. - Literacy Rate: - As per Census 2011, India’s literacy rate is 73%, with urban areas surpassing rural and males outpacing females. Literacy is defined as the ability of a person aged 7 or above to read and write with understanding in any language. - Adult Literacy Rate: - Measured for individuals aged 15 and above, focusing on functional literacy for economic and social participation. - Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER): - GER = (Number of students enrolled in a specific age group or standard) / (Total population in that age group). A GER of 97% indicates 3% of children are out of school, while GER >100% suggests underage admissions. - Economic Survey 2025 Data: - Primary GER (Classes I–V; Age group 6–10 years): - 77.4% — indicates significant enrolment gap despite RTE Act guarantees. - Secondary GER (Classes IX–X; Age group 14–15 years): - 56.2% — reflects dropout rates post-primary due to socio-economic, cultural, and infrastructure factors. - Higher Secondary GER (Classes XI–XII; Age group 16–17 years): - 14.1% — extremely low, pointing to affordability issues, early marriage in some regions, and vocational migration. - NEP 2020 Target: - Achieve 100% GER in school education (Pre-primary to Secondary) by 2030. - Includes Early Childhood Care & Education (ECCE) integration to improve transition into primary education. - Gender Parity Index (GPI): - GPI = Ratio of female to male students enrolled in a specific age or standard group. Budget 2020 notes higher GER for girls than boys at all levels (elementary, secondary, higher secondary), driven by schemes like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao. - School Dropout Data (Economic Survey 2025): - Dropout rate is the proportion of students discontinuing education between school years (e.g., enrolled in Class 9 but not continuing to Class 10). - Rates: - Primary (1.9%), Upper Primary (5.2%), Secondary (14.1%). - Dropout rates being low doesn’t automatically mean that Gross Enrollment Ratio (GER) is high. - GER also depends on how many kids ever get enrolled in the first place and whether they’re enrolled at the right age. - Factors Contributing to Dropouts: - Lack of interest due to traditional gender, societal, or occupational norms. - Girls engaged in domestic work or early marriage. - Financial constraints leading to child labor. - Inaccessible schools, unsuitable timings, or lack of transport. - Teacher absenteeism, poor teaching quality, or language barriers for tribal students. - Post-Class 8 dropout surge due to cessation of free mid-day meals and increased academic/family pressure. - Retention Rate (Economic Survey 2025): - Percentage of first-grade students expected to reach the last grade of their level: - Primary (I-V): - 85.4% - Elementary (I-VIII): - 78% - Secondary (I-X): - 63.8% - Higher Secondary (I-XII): - 45.6% - SDG Goal 4.1 - Universal Primary and Secondary Education: - India’s Baseline (2025) vs. SDG Target 2030: - Enrollment ratio (Class 1-10): - 75% → 100% - Dropout rate (Secondary): - 17% → 10% - Schools with Pupil-Teacher Ratio ≤30%: - 70% → 100% - Learning outcomes (Maths, Language, Science): - 57-67% score → Improved outcomes. - School, Student, and Teacher Data (Economic Survey 2025): - 2023-24: - 24.8 crore students, 14.72 lakh schools, 98 lakh teachers. -
