- Educational Bodies and Institutions - Overview: - India’s education system is governed by multiple bodies under the Ministry of Education (formerly HRD), ensuring curriculum development, examinations, funding, and quality standards. - Key Bodies: - Department of School Education and Literacy: - Oversees primary and secondary education, focusing on access and quality. - Department of Higher Education: - Manages universities, colleges, and technical education institutions. - Statutory Bodies: - All India Council of Technical Education (AICTE, 1987): - Regulates technical education, runs schemes like Pragati, Saksham, Prerana, Samridhi, and Ishan Uday for scholarships and research funding for girls, SC/ST, PH, and Northeast students. - University Grants Commission (UGC, 1956): - Coordinates and funds higher education; to be replaced by Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) per NEP 2020. - Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) – Proposed Replacement: - Vision (NEP 2020): - Create a single unified body to oversee regulation, accreditation, funding, and academic standards—replacing UGC, AICTE, and NCTE. - Proposed Structure (Four Vertical Model): - 1. National Higher Education Regulatory Council (NHERC) – Regulation - 2. National Accreditation Council (NAC) – Accreditation - 3. Higher Education Grants Council (HEGC) – Funding - 4. General Education Council (GEC) – Academic Standards - Status Update: - As of mid-2025, the Education Ministry has drafted the HECI bill and is preparing for its introduction in Parliament. - No firm timeline yet for its passage or full implementation. - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Higher Education Financing Agency (HEFA, 2016): - Non-profit company (91% Education Ministry, 9% Canara Bank), registered as a non-deposit-taking NBFC with RBI. Provides loans to IITs, IIMs, NITs, AIIMS, Kendriya Vidyalayas, and Navodaya Vidyalayas for infrastructure and equipment upgrades. - RISE-2022: - Budget 2018 allocated additional funds for HEFA to support infrastructure revitalization by 2022. - Educational Consultants of India Limited (EdCIL): - Provides consultancy services for educational projects. - Autonomous Bodies: - National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT, 1961): - Develops curricula, textbooks, and teacher training programs. Units include: - National Institute of Education (NIE), New Delhi - Central Institute of Education Technology (CIET), New Delhi - Pandit Sunder Lal Sharma Central Institute of Vocational Education, Bhopal - Regional Institutes of Education (RIEs): - Ajmer, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Mysuru, Umiam (Meghalaya) - Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE, 1929): - Conducts Class 10 and 12 board exams, Central Teachers Eligibility Test (CTET), admission tests for Navodaya Vidyalayas, National Achievement Survey, and SAFAL tests (Classes 3, 5, 8). - Sets quality standards for Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navodaya Vidyalayas. - National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS, 1989): - Provides open schooling for pre-degree learners unable to attend physical schools. Levels: A (Class 3), B (Class 5), C (Class 8), Secondary (Class 10), Senior Secondary (Class 12). - Offers vocational courses (e.g., computer training, office secretary training) and life enrichment programs. Operates Radio Vahini FM 91.2 MHz for educational podcasts. - Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS): - Runs Kendriya Vidyalayas (since 1962) for government employees’ children (Class 1-12, in India and abroad). Launched Project Balvatika for ages 3-5. MP quota for admissions removed in 2022. Uses Shaala Darpan e-governance platform. - Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS): - Manages Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas, free residential schools for talented rural children (Class 6-12), requiring entrance exams. Established under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, with states providing 30 acres of land. - National Testing Agency (NTA): - Conducts common entrance exams for higher education admissions. - National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE): - Regulates teacher education programs. - Indian Council of Historical Research (ICHR): - Promotes historical research. - National Book Trust (NBT) and National Bal Bhavan: - NBT promotes publishing; Bal Bhavan runs Bal Kendras for children’s activities. - National Institution of Industrial Engineering, Mumbai: - Focuses on industrial engineering education. - Advisory Body: - Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE, 1920): - Advises Union and State governments on education policy. Chaired by the Education Minister, includes Union/State ministers, MPs, and heads of educational bodies. - International Organization: - UNESCO (1946, Paris): - UN agency promoting education, science, and culture globally. - Miscellaneous: - Central Tibetan Schools Administration (CTSA, 1961): - Funds schools, hostels, and scholarships for Tibetan refugee children in Shimla, Dalhousie, Darjeeling, Kalimpong, Mussoorie, and Herbetpur. - Bharatiya Shiksha Board (2019): - Standardizes Vedic education (e.g., Acharyakulam, Vidya Bharati, Gurukuls) with new syllabi, exams, and certifications, addressing non-recognition by CBSE/State boards. - Notable Union-Funded Schools: - Kendriya Vidyalayas (KVS): - Established 1962, for government employees’ children (Class 1-12). Managed by KVS under the Societies Registration Act, using Shaala Darpan for e-governance. - Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV): - Residential girls’ schools (Class 5-12) for SC, ST, OBC, minorities, and BPL families. Reservations: 75% for SC/ST/OBC/minorities, 25% for BPL girls. - Eklavya Model Residential Schools: - Residential schools in high ST-population areas, managed by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs. - Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas: - Free residential schools (Class 6-12) for talented rural children, requiring entrance exams. Managed by NVS under the Societies Registration Act. - Seema Darshan: - Initiative by Education, Defence, and Home Ministries to take KVS/NVS students to border areas to foster patriotism through interactions with armed forces. - New Education Policy (NEP) 2020 - Introduction: - NEP 2020, based on the Dr. K. Kasturirangan Committee (2017-19), replaces the 1986 National Policy on Education, aiming for transformative reforms from pre-primary to higher education. - Historical Context: -

- Key Features: - Targets 100% GER from pre-school to secondary by 2030. - Promotes flexibility in academic streams, integrating vocational and academic education. - Enhances critical thinking, emotional intelligence, and 21st-century skills. - Primary Education Reforms: - National Mission on Foundational Literacy and Numeracy: - Ensures all Class 3 students achieve basic reading and math skills by 2025. - Flexible Streams: - Eliminates rigid separation between science, commerce, arts, curricular/extracurricular, and vocational/academic streams to promote holistic learning. - Counseling and Social Work: - Schools to employ counselors and social workers to address psychological issues, sexual harassment, bullying, and depression. - Open/Distance Learning: - Expanded through NIOS for Classes 3, 5, and 8, targeting 2 crore out-of-school children. - Curriculum Changes: - National Curricular Framework for School Education (NCFSE): - Developed by NCERT for Classes 1-12, focusing on core concepts and reducing rote learning. - Structure (5+3+3+4): - Foundational (5 years: 3 years pre-primary, 2 years Classes 1-2) - Preparatory (3 years: Classes 3-5) - Middle (3 years: Classes 6-8) - Secondary (4 years: Classes 9-12) - Emphasis on critical thinking, emotional intelligence, scientific temper, and 21st-century skills. - Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE): - National Curricular and Pedagogical Framework for ECCE (NCPFECCE): - Developed by NCERT for up to Class 8, implemented by Ministries of Education, Women and Child Development, Health, and Tribal Affairs. - Programs: - Aadharshila (Birth to 3 years): - Focuses on holistic development, maternal mental health, and Garbh Sanskar (pregnancy practices). - Navchetana (3-6 years): - Emphasizes play-based learning for foundational skills. - Poshan bhi Padhai bhi (PBPB): - Trains Anganwadi workers on malnutrition, Aadharshila, and Navchetana to enhance early education and nutrition. - Peer Teaching and Student Champions: - Older/bright students mentor younger/weaker peers, as per SARTHAQ guidelines (Students’ and Teachers’ Holistic Advancement through Quality Education). - Social and Emotional Learning - Tim Tim Tare (TTT): - Launched in Tamil Nadu (2009), now expanding nationwide. - Based on WHO’s Life Skills Framework, TTT promotes soft skills like communication, empathy, critical thinking, etiquette, time management, and social well-being. - Language and Medium: - Mother tongue/regional language as medium of instruction up to Class 5, with efforts to extend to Class 8 and beyond. - Sanskrit offered at all levels; foreign languages at secondary level. - Three-language formula: - Students learn three languages, at least two native Indian (e.g., mother tongue + Hindi/Sanskrit + English/French). - No language imposed, addressing concerns about Hindi imposition in non-Hindi states. - New Organizations: - National Institute for Pali, Persian, and Prakrit - Indian Institute of Translation and Interpretation (IITI) - PM Schools for Rising India (PM SHRI, 2022): - Upgrades 14,000+ existing schools (2022-27) with advanced infrastructure (labs, smart classrooms, libraries, sports facilities). - Acts as role models for nearby schools; post-2027, states/UTs handle maintenance. - Vocational Education: - Introduced from Class 6 with internships, targeting 50% learner exposure by 2025. - Secondary schools collaborate with ITIs, polytechnics, and local industries; skill labs established. - Higher Education Reforms: - GER Target: - Increase from 26% (2018) to 50% (2035) by adding 3.5 crore seats. - Multi-disciplinary courses (e.g., philosophy and architecture) and college autonomy. - Vocational education integration for employability. - Academic Bank of Credits (ABC, 2021): - Digitally stores credits from multiple courses/institutions, enabling flexible degree completion. - National Credit Framework (NCrF, 2022): - Integrates educational and vocational training for seamless credit transfer. - Multiple Entry and Exit Points: - Allows flexible degree completion with certifications: - 1 year: - Certificate - 2 years: - Advanced Diploma - 3 years: - Bachelor’s Degree - 4 years: - Bachelor’s with Research - Example: - IITs offer BSc after 3 years, BTech after 4 years. - Flexible Degree Completion (UGC, 2024): - Accelerated Degree Programs (ADP): - Bright students complete degrees faster (e.g., 4-year degree in 3 years) by earning more credits per semester. Limited to top 10% of students. - Extended Degree Programs (EDP): - Weaker students complete degrees slower (e.g., 4-year degree in 5 years) with fewer subjects per semester. - Both treated as equivalent to standard degrees by UPSC/State PSCs. - Higher Education Commission of India (HECI): -
Before HECI After HECI
Multiple regulators (UGC, AICTE, NMC, Bar Council). Single umbrella body for higher education (excl. medical, legal).
Bribery in inspections/fund approvals. Faceless inspections using technology.
Different rules for public/private colleges. Uniform rules for all institutions.
HECI Verticals: - National Higher Education Regulatory Council (NHERC): Regulation - General Education Council (GEC): Standard setting - Higher Education Grants Council (HEGC): Funding - National Accreditation Council (NAC): Accreditation
- UGC Budget Cut (Interim-Budget 2024): - Allocation reduced from ₹5,000+ crore (2023) to ₹2,500 crore (2024) to transition to HECI. - Other Higher Education Organizations: - Multidisciplinary Education and Research Universities (MERUs): - Equivalent to IITs/IIMs, focusing on research and teaching-intensive courses. - National Research Foundation (NRF): - Apex body for research, established under NRF Act 2023. - University Definition Expansion: - Includes more institutions offering research and teaching-intensive courses. - Ministry Renaming: - HRD Ministry renamed to Ministry of Education per NEP 2020. - SARTHAQ: - Plan to implement NEP 2020, focusing on holistic advancement. - SATH-E (Outdated, 2017-20): - NITI Aayog’s roadmap for school education in Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha. - Adult and Divyang Education: - Targets 100% adult literacy through life-enrichment programs. - National Book Promotion Policy to encourage reading and publishing. - Uniform Indian Sign Language (ISL) for hearing-impaired students. - Open, Distance, and E-Learning: - Expanded through NIOS for Classes 3, 5, 8. - Promotes MOOCs for online learning in regional languages. - Divyang-friendly educational software. - National Educational Technology Forum (NETF): - Facilitates technology use in learning, exams, and administration. - Student Assessment: - Holistic Progress Card (HPC): - Tracks progress via inputs from students, peers, parents, and teachers. - Assesses strengths (e.g., collaboration, creativity) and weaknesses (e.g., lack of attention). - Formative vs. Summative Assessment: -
Before After
Summative: End-of-semester exams testing factual knowledge. Formative: Ongoing assessments (oral questions, homework) for analytical thinking.
High-stake board exams focusing on memory. Low-stake board exams testing core concepts and application, with school assignments counted.
- Assessment Bodies: - PARAKH (Performance Assessment, Review, and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic Development): - NCERT’s standard-setting body for assessments. - National Testing Agency (NTA): - Conducts common entrance exams for higher education. - School Assessment: - State School Standards Authority (SSSA): - Requires schools to disclose seats, facilities, fees, and board exam results for public oversight and accountability. - Teacher Recruitment and Training: - Minimum qualification by 2030: - 4-year integrated B.Ed. - Frameworks by NCTE and NCERT: - National Curriculum Framework for Teacher Education (NCFTE) - National Professional Standards for Teachers (NPST) - Transparent recruitment, merit-based promotions, and operational freedom. - National Mission for Mentoring: - Engages senior/retired faculty to mentor college teachers. - NEP 2020 Funding: - Current public investment (Union + States): - ~4.4% of GDP. - NEP Target: - Increase to 6% of GDP. - Expanded National Scholarship Portal for SC/ST/OBC, SEDGs (women, transgender). - Gender Inclusion Fund for girls’ education. - Special Education Zones for disadvantaged regions. - Encourages private college scholarships. - NEP 2020 Criticism: - Insufficient clarity on funding and fee regulation, risking privatization. - Inadequate focus on girls and weaker sections. - Unaddressed teacher demands for job security, salaries, and work conditions. - Limited attention to students’ emotional needs and competition-related stress. - Alleged Sanskrit promotion for political agendas. - Non-adoption of best practices from previous committees or foreign systems. - NEP 2020 Conclusion: - Aligns with SDG Goal 4 for inclusive, equitable education and lifelong learning. - Reforms aim to universalize education, leverage demographic dividends, and achieve sustainable development. - PRAGYATA Guidelines on Digital Education (2020): - Launched by the Ministry of Education during the COVID-19 lockdown, addressing 240 million children unable to attend school. - Types of Digital Education: - Synchronous: - Real-time (live) teaching. - Asynchronous: - Non-real-time (e.g., recorded programs, articles). - Eight Steps: - Plan, Review, Arrange, Guide, Yak (talk), Assign, Track, Appreciate. - Screen Time Recommendations: -
Class Level Screen Time (Synchronous)
Pre-Primary ≤30 minutes
Classes 1-8 ≤2 lectures (30-45 minutes each)
Classes 9-12 ≤4 lectures (30-45 minutes each)
- Teacher Guidelines: - Teach ≤2-3 hours online daily to ensure physical (back pain, eye strain) and mental well-being, cyber safety, and digital privacy. - Mid-Day Meal Scheme (MDM, 2001-2020): - Boss: - Ministry of Education. - Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10 funding by Union:States). - Provides free hot-cooked meals for 200 days/year to students in government/government-aided schools, madrassas, and maqtabs (up to Class 8). - Nutritional Standards: - Lower Primary (Classes 1-5): - ≥450 calories, 12g protein. - Upper Primary (Classes 6-8): - ≥700 calories, 20g protein. - Benefits: - Enhances nutritional security and class attendance for poor children. - Tithi Bhojan: - Community contributions (money/food/sweets) for celebrations (e.g., birthdays). Adopted as Sampriti Bhojan (Assam), Dham (Himachal Pradesh), Sneh Bhojan (Maharashtra), etc. - Challenges: - Siphoning of rations, unhygienic food preparation, resistance to Dalit cooks, poison/pesticide mixing, and lack of take-home rations during COVID-19 closures. - Food Security Allowance: - Provided if MDM is unavailable due to food/cook shortages. - PM Poshan Scheme (2021-2026): - Renamed from MDM, covering Classes 1-8 in government/government-aided schools. - Validity: - 2021-22 to 2025-26. - Excludes pre-school children (covered under ICDS/Mission Poshan). - Features: - School nutrition gardens for students to grow fruits/vegetables. - Cooking competitions to promote healthy eating. - Supplies from Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs) and Self-Help Groups (SHGs). - Compulsory social audits by local communities and college students to ensure food quality. - Food Allotment: -

- Funding: - Per meal cost: - Balvatika/Primary (₹11.54), Upper Primary (₹16.74). - Union covers 100% food-grain and transport costs, linked to CPI-Rural Laborers. - Criticism: - NEP 2020’s breakfast recommendation not implemented. - Social audits not conducted in many states. - Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA, 2001): - Boss: - Ministry of Education. - Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10 funding). - Legal Framework: - 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002): - Article 21A: - Fundamental right to free and compulsory education (ages 6-14). - Article 51A(k): - Parental duty to ensure education. - Right to Education Act (2009): - Operationalizes Article 21A, including 25% EWS reservation in private schools. - Prarambhik Shiksha Kosh (2004): - Non-lapsable fund from education cess on direct taxes. - Features: - Funds school construction, free uniforms/textbooks, teacher recruitment, computer labs, and libraries to achieve universal education. - Subschemes: - Shagun Portal: - Monitors school quality under SSA. - Padhe Bharat Badhe Bharat (2014): - Enhances Class 1-2 education with ≥4 hours/day teaching in math/reading/writing, mentoring for weak students, minimum PTR (30:1), 200 school days, and 75% student/95% teacher attendance. - NIPUN Bharat (2021): - Improves foundational literacy and numeracy for Class 3 by 2026-27. - Rashtriya Avishkar Abhiyan (2015): - Promotes science, math, and technology (ages 6-18) via science melas and mentoring. - Vidyanjali: - Engages volunteers (NRIs, retired teachers, professionals) for teaching, mentoring, and providing resources (e.g., fans, water purifiers, digital devices). - Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan (RMSA, 2009): - Boss: - Ministry of Education. - Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10 funding). - Madhyamik and Uchchtar Shiksha Kosh (2007): - Non-lapsable fund from education cess. - Objective: - Achieve 100% retention up to Class 10 by 2020 (no dropouts). - Features: - Funds school infrastructure (libraries, labs, toilets, hostels), teacher recruitment, and salaries. - CBSE Syllabus Reduction (2020-21): - Reduced by 30% due to COVID-19, excluding topics like federalism, nationalism, and secularism (one-time measure, later re-added). - Samagra Shiksha Scheme (2018): - Boss: - Ministry of Education. - Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10 funding). - Merges SSA, RMSA, and Teacher Education into a single scheme (pre-school to Class 12). - Focus: - E-learning, skill development, funding, and stipends. - Subcomponents: - NISHTHA (2019): - Trains teachers/headmasters on gender rights, PH rights, and POCSO Act. - NISHTHA 2.0 (2021): - Online training for secondary teachers via DIKSHA. - NISHTHA 3.0: - Trains primary teachers for reading/math skills. - NISHTHA 4.0 (ECCE): - Trains master trainers for early childhood education. - Atal Tinkering Labs (ATL): - Research/innovation labs (Class 6-12) with ₹10 lakh funding for high-performing schools. - Salary and Grants: - Supports teacher salaries, Hindi teachers in non-Hindi states, library/sports grants. - Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV): - Residential girls’ schools with hostel facilities and self-defense training. - Free Textbooks: - Provided up to Class 8. - Rashtriya Avishkar Abhiyan: - Promotes science/math (ages 6-18). - e-Pathshala: - NCERT books in digital format. - Prashikshak: - Online teacher training portal (now merged into DIKSHA). - Pariksha Pe Charcha: - PM’s interaction with students, parents, and teachers to address exam stress. - GANIT Week: - Promotes math in CBSE schools, commemorating Srinivasa Ramanujan’s birth anniversary (22nd December, National Mathematics Day). - Madrassa Education: - Union Funding: - Up to ₹50 lakh for teaching formal subjects (Science, Math, Social Studies, Hindi, English). - NIOS affiliation enables board exams for Class 10-12 certifications, aiding college admissions and jobs. - Assam Madrassa Conversion (2021-23): - 1,281 madrassas converted to Middle English (ME) schools by 2023, following repeal of state funding laws for religious education. - Scholarships for Classes 9-12 - National Means-cum-Merit Scholarship Scheme (NMMSS): - Launched: - 2008, extended till 2025-26. - Boss: - Department of School Education and Literacy, Ministry of Education. - Beneficiaries: - Bright students in Classes 9-12 from families with annual income ≤ ₹3.5 lakh. - Selection: - State/UT governments conduct exams to identify eligible students. - Scholarship: - ₹1,000/month (₹12,000/year) for Classes 9-12. - Funding: - 100% by Union Government, disbursed via Public Financial Management System (PFMS) to Aadhaar-linked bank accounts through National Scholarship Portal (NSP). - National Scheme of Incentive to Girls for Secondary Education (NSIGSE): - Launched: - 2008. - Boss: - Department of School Education and Literacy, Ministry of Education. - Beneficiaries: - SC/ST girls in Classes 9-12. - All girls in Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas (irrespective of caste). - Scholarship: - ₹3,000 fixed deposit, withdrawable only if: - Student completes Classes 9-12. - Remains unmarried until age 18. - Funding: - 100% by Union Government, disbursed via PFMS to Aadhaar-linked accounts through NSP. - Criticism: - Allegations of fund discontinuation since 2018, though scheme remains active. - Rankings for School Education - Annual Status of Education Report (ASER): - Published by: - NGO Pratham. - Latest: - ASER 2022 (released January 2023). - Key Findings: - Government school enrollment increased from 65% (2018) to 73% (2022) due to unaffordable private school fees. - Only 20% of Class 3 students can read Class 2-level texts, highlighting learning gaps. - Other Notable Reports: - Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA): - Conducted by: - OECD, every 3 years, assessing 15-year-olds in reading, math, and science. - India’s Participation: - Poor performance in 2009 led to boycott in 2012, 2015, 2018; rejoined via 2019 agreement for 2021 tests. - National Achievement Survey (NAS): - Conducted by: - CBSE/NCERT under Ministry of Education. - Assesses students in Classes 3, 5, 8, and 10 to evaluate learning outcomes. - Purpose: - Counter ASER/PISA methodologies with government-led assessments. - School Education Quality Index (SEQI): - Published by: - NITI Aayog. - Evaluates school education quality across states/UTs. - Performance Grading Index (PGI): - Published by: - Ministry of Education for 2019-20. - Data Sources: - UDISE+, NAS, Mid-Day Meal Scheme. - Ranking: - 10 levels (Level 1 = highest). No state reached Level 1; Punjab scored highest, Meghalaya lowest. - World Bank’s Ending Learning Poverty Report: - Defines learning poverty as inability to read/understand simple text by age 10. - India: - 54.8% of 10-year-olds face learning poverty (Sweden: 2%). - Right to Education (RTE) Act and Amendments - RTE Act, 2009: - Provides free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 under Article 21A. - Key Provision: - No child can be failed till Class 8 (No Detention Policy). - Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation (CCE): - Teachers assess students via assignments, essays, mentoring, and remedial classes. - Challenges: - CCE implemented superficially due to teacher workload (low salaries, contractual jobs, auxiliary duties like election work, Swachh Bharat patrolling). - Lax student performance led to poor ASER scores. - RTE Amendment, 2019: - Regular exams at Classes 5 and 8. - Failure leads to re-test within 2 months; if failed again, states may detain student for one year, ending the No Detention Policy. - RTE Amendments - 25% Quota: - Provision: - Private schools reserve 25% Class 1 seats for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) and disadvantaged groups, with fee concessions subsidized by state governments. - State Rules to Avoid Quota: - Kerala (2011), Karnataka (2018), Maharashtra (2024): - No quota if government school exists within 1 km of private school. - Bombay High Court (May 2024): - Stayed Maharashtra’s rule, pending further hearing. - Other RTE Amendments: -
Year Provision
2012 Exempts madrassas, Vedic pathshalas, and religious training institutions from RTE Act.
2017 Technical amendments for teacher qualifications.
2019 Ends No Detention Policy; allows exams at Classes 5 and 8 with potential detention.
- CBSE Class 12 Result (2020-21): - COVID-19 led to cancellation of Class 12 board exams. - Marks calculated using 30:30:40 formula (30% Class 10, 30% Class 11, 40% Class 12 internal assessments). - National Testing Agency (NTA) - Established: - 2017, under Ministry of Education, registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860. - Funding: - Initial ₹25 crore; self-sustained via exam fees. - Structure: - Board of Governors: - Chaired by a noted educationist, includes members from institutes for which NTA conducts exams. - CEO/Director General: - Manages daily operations. - Exams Conducted: - Joint Entrance Examination (JEE) for engineering. - National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) for medical (replaced AIPMT, conducted twice yearly since 2019). - UGC National Eligibility Test (NET) for assistant professorship and research fellowships (twice yearly). - Graduate Pharmacy Aptitude Test (GPAT) for pharmacy. - Common Management Admission Test (CMAT) for management. - Hotel Management Joint Entrance Examination. - Entrance exams for 45 Central universities. - NEET Controversies: - Age limit criteria (maximum age limit removed in 2022). - Stringent security checks, wrong questions/translations, perceived bias against non-English medium students. - Opposition from Tamil Nadu government. - Higher Education Colleges and Universities - Growth Since Independence (Press Information Bureau (PIB) report): - 1947: - ~20 universities, ~500 colleges. - 2022: - Over 1,000 universities (50x increase), over 40,000 colleges (80x increase). - Rashtriya Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan (RUSA) / PM-USHA: - Boss: - Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education. - Type: - Centrally Sponsored Scheme (Union + State funding). - Launched: - 2013 as RUSA; renamed PM Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan (PM-USHA) in 2024. - Features: - Funds new colleges, faculty recruitment, research grants, scholarships, market-linked courses, industry connections, internships, and e-learning, aligned with NEP 2020. - Coverage: - Government and government-aided institutions in States/UTs. - Higher Education Institutes (Economic Survey 2025): -

- Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) in Higher Education: - 2014-15: - 23.7%. - 2021-22: - 28.4%. - NEP 2020 Target: - 50% by 2035 (adding 3.5 crore seats). - Higher Education Rankings: - Atal Ranking of Institutions on Innovation Achievements (ARIIA): - Ranks centrally funded technical institutions, state universities, private universities, and colleges in categories like innovation and technical/non-technical performance. - National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF): - Conducted annually since 2016 by Ministry of Education. - Categories: - Overall, universities, engineering, management, pharmacy, medical, architecture, law, dental, research. - Top Rank (2024): - IIT Madras (overall). - NIRF 2025: - Release stayed by Madras High Court (March 2025) due to PIL alleging baseless rankings based on unverified, emailed data. - National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC): - Funded by UGC, rates colleges/universities from A++ to D. - Paramarsh Scheme: - Ministry of Education mentors institutions for NAAC accreditation. - Quacquarelli Symonds (QS) World University Rankings: - Top-200 Indian institutes: - IIT Bombay, IIT Delhi, IISc Bengaluru. - Institutions of Eminence (IoE): - Budget 2016: - Plan to develop 20 world-class institutions (10 public, 10 private) with ₹1,000 crore over 5 years. - Selection: - N. Gopalaswami Committee (2018) shortlisted 6 IoEs (3 public, 3 private), including Jio Institute (Reliance Foundation, Pune) as a greenfield project, sparking controversy. - Deemed-to-be Universities: - Granted by Ministry of Education based on UGC recommendations, allowing autonomy in courses, syllabus, admissions, and fees. - Issue: - Over 40 institutes blacklisted post-UPA era for deficient faculty/infrastructure. - 2017: - Supreme Court barred Deemed Universities from using “university” in names (e.g., Manipal University renamed Manipal Academy of Higher Education). - Central Sanskrit Universities: - Central Sanskrit Universities Act, 2020 converted three institutions into Central Universities: - Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan, New Delhi. - Shri Lal Bahadur Shastri Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeth, New Delhi. - Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeth, Tirupati. - Libraries for Children and Teenagers (Budget 2023): -
Digital Library Physical Libraries
National-level, device-agnostic (works on Android, Apple, Microsoft, etc.). At Panchayat and Municipal ward levels, funded by 50-year interest-free Union loans to states.
- Loans and Scholarships for Higher Education - PM-Vidyalaxmi Scheme: - Boss: - Ministry of Education. - Eligibility: - Students admitted to top-860 NIRF-ranked higher education institutes. - Features: - Collateral-free, guarantor-free loans; 75% credit guarantee by government; 3% interest subvention for families with income ≤ ₹8 lakh/year. - Validity: - 2024-31. - PM Uchchatar Shiksha Protsahan - Central Sector Interest Subsidy (CSIS): - Boss: - Ministry of Education. - Features: - Full interest waiver on education loans for students with family income ≤ ₹4.5 lakh/year. - Other Schemes: - Swami Vivekananda Scholarship (UGC): - Covers college fees for girls, prioritizing only-girl-child families. - SAKSHAM Scholarship (AICTE): - Supports differently-abled students pursuing technical education. - Pragati Scholarship (AICTE): - Supports girl students in technical courses. - Post-COVID Education Portals and Initiatives - Abhyas App: - By: - NTA. - Purpose: - Mobile app for IIT-JEE mock tests. - VidyaDaan 2.0 (April 2020): - By: - Ministry of Education. - Purpose: - Educators contribute e-learning content via DIKSHA portal. - YUKTI 2.0: - By: - Ministry of Education. - Purpose: - Portal for sharing research, innovation, and startup ideas, especially COVID-related. - Bharat Padhe Online (April 2020): - By: - Ministry of Education. - Global Education Coalition (UNESCO, May 2020): - Purpose: - Coordinates educational activities post-COVID. - Akhil Bharatiya Shiksha Samagam (2022): - By: - Ministry of Education, UGC, Banaras Hindu University. - - Conclusion - SDG Goal #4: - Aim: - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all. - Note: - Without achieving SDG-4, India cannot meet: - SDG-1: - No Poverty - SDG-5: - Gender Equality - Significance of Education: - Enables individuals to lead productive lives in a globalising world. - Enhances: - Health and nutritional status of society - Economic growth and workforce productivity - Population control through awareness - Empowerment of women and marginalized communities - Way Forward: - Aforementioned schemes, initiatives, and challenges need to be: - Acknowledged as foundational to achieving broader development goals - Addressed with urgency and priority in policy and governance - Pillar 6B2: Human Resource Development - Skilling, Vocational Training, Recruitment - Definition and Significance: - Skill: - The ability to perform a task proficiently, enhancing employability and productivity. - Vocational Training: - Methods to improve skills for specific trades (e.g., auto repair, plumbing, carpentry, welding). - Demographic Dividend: - Economic growth potential when the working-age population (15-59 years) exceeds the dependent population (<15 or >65 years). India’s population: >65% below 35 years (Economic Survey 2025). - Dependency Ratio (Economic Survey 2025): -
Year Dependency Ratio
2011 64.6%
2021 55.7%
2026 (Projected) 54.3%
- Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2017-18: - Only 14% of the workforce (15-59 years) received formal training; most rely on self-learning, family, or on-the-job training. - Context: - By 2020, India’s average population age was 29 years (vs. USA: 40, EU: 46, Japan: 47). Over the next 20 years, India’s labor force is projected to grow by 32%, while developed nations’ decline by 4%. Skilling is critical to harness this demographic dividend. - Challenge: - Over 40% of India’s workforce is in agriculture (vs. <25% in advanced economies like USA: 4%, UK: 5%, France: 14%, Australia: 16%). Skilling is essential to shift workers to manufacturing and service sectors. - Yearbook: Recruitment and Training-Related Ministries - Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions: - Departments: - Department of Personnel and Training (DoP&T). - Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare (DPPW): - Manages Jeevan Pramaan digital life certificate with MEITY (Ref: Pillar 1D). - Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG): - Celebrates Civil Services Day on April 21 since 2006. - Operates CPGRAMS portal for citizen complaints. - Publishes Good Governance Index (2019: Tamil Nadu > Maharashtra > Karnataka). - Attached/Subordinate Offices: - Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA): - Trains IAS probationers. - Staff Selection Commission (SSC). - Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM). - Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB). - Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI): - Derives powers from Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946. - Constitutional Body: - Union Public Service Commission (UPSC). - Statutory Bodies: - Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT, 1985). - Central Vigilance Commission (CVC): - Established in the 1960s (Santhanam Committee), statutory status in 2003. - Central Information Commission (CIC): - Under Right to Information Act, 2005. - Lokpal: - Established under Lokpal Act, 2013; first Lokpal Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose (2019). - Autonomous Bodies: - National Recruitment Agency (NRA): - Conducts Common Eligibility Test (CET) to screen candidates for SSC, Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs), and Institute of Banking Personnel Selection (IBPS). - CET scores enable candidates to appear for domain-specific tests for final recruitment. - National Centre for Good Governance (NCGG): - Set up under LBSNAA, chaired by Cabinet Secretary. - Subsumes National Institute of Administrative Research (NIAR). - Mission Karmayogi (September 2020): - Full Name: - National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building (NPCSCB). - Purpose: - Train government employees for New India’s governance needs. - Components: - Public Human Resources Council: - Headed by the Prime Minister. - Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV): - Not-for-profit company for e-training. - iGOT Karmayogi Platform: - Integrated Government Online Training for civil servants. - Ministry of Labour and Employment: - Attached/Subordinate Offices: - Director General Employment. - Chief Labour Commissioner. - Labour Bureau: - Publishes Consumer Price Index for industrial and agricultural rural workers. - Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS). - Statutory Bodies: - Employees State Insurance Corporation (ESIC). - Employees Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO). - Central Government Industrial Tribunal-cum-Labour Courts (Industrial Disputes Act, 1947). - Autonomous Body: - V.V. Giri National Labour Institute, Uttar Pradesh. - Ministry of Skill Development & Entrepreneurship: - Attached Office: - Directorate General of Training (DGT): - Ensures common syllabus and training modules for Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) in States/UTs. - Statutory Bodies: - None. - Related Company: - National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC, 2008). - Autonomous Bodies: - 30+ Sector Skill Councils (e.g., Beauty & Wellness, Construction, Furniture & Fittings). - National Institute for Entrepreneurship & Small Business Development (NIESBUD), Noida. - Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship (IIE), Guwahati, Assam. - Non-Statutory Regulatory Bodies (via Gazette): - National Council for Vocational Training (NCVT, 1956). - National Skill Development Agency (NSDA, 2013). - Merged in 2020 into National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET). - Notable Schemes: - Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY). - Jan Shikshan Sansthan (JSS): - Adult education and vocational training. - National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC, 2008, HQ: Delhi): - Structure: - Not-for-profit public limited company (Section 8, Companies Act, 2013). - Shareholding: - 49% Ministry of Skill Development, 51% private sector (ASSOCHAM, CII, FICCI). - Objectives: - Fund skill programs via debt, equity, and grants. - Create market-based, profitable skill training models to ensure seriousness among trainees. - Implement skills voucher program (e.g., ₹1,000 voucher for learners to pay for approved training centers). - Train trainers in collaboration with states. - Skill Development Bodies: - National Skill Development Fund (NSDF, 2009): - Operated by: - Ministry of Skill Development via NSDC. - Purpose: - Receives funds from schemes and private donors, disburses to ministries for skill programs. - National Skill Development Agency (NSDA, 2013): - Autonomous body under Ministry of Skill Development. - Responsibilities: - Develops National Labour Market Information System (LMIS) database. - Implements National Quality Assurance Framework (NQAF) to align training with job requirements. - National Skills Qualifications Framework (NSQF): - Purpose: - Organizes qualifications by levels of knowledge, skills, and aptitude, including Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL). - Example: -

- National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET, 2018): - Type: - Non-statutory regulatory body under Ministry of Skill Development, established via Gazette. - Structure: - Chairman and members. - Responsibilities: - Advises on short- and long-term vocational programs/syllabi. - Oversees Sector Skill Councils (SSCs) and skill certification/assessment bodies. - Indirectly regulates ground-level vocational training institutes via SSCs (recognition, regulation, inspection, certification). - Manages grievance redressal, research, awareness, and information dissemination. - National Skill Development Mission (NSDM, 2015): - Boss: - Ministry of Skill Development. - Focus Areas: - Institutional Training. - Infrastructure. - Convergence. - Trainers. - Overseas Employment. - Sustainable Livelihoods. - Leveraging Public Infrastructure. - Skill India Campaign (2015): - Boss: - Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. - Components: - National Skill Development Mission (NSDM, 2015): - SANKALP (Skills Acquisition and Knowledge Awareness for Livelihood Promotion, 2018): - Type: - Centrally Sponsored Core Scheme (states contribute funds). - Purpose: - Establishes new training institutes, upgrades infrastructure, trains trainers/assessors, encourages women, SC/ST/PH participation. - STRIVE (Skill Strengthening for Industrial Value Enhancement, 2017): - Type: - Central Sector Scheme (100% Union-funded). - Purpose: - Strengthens NSDC, NSDA, and related bodies. - Funding: - Supported by World Bank for both SANKALP and STRIVE. - Skill Loan Scheme: - Loan Amount: - ₹5,000 to ₹1.5 lakh for skill courses. - Features: - Up to 7-year tenure, no processing fees/collateral, credit guarantee by National Credit Guarantee Trust Company Ltd (NCGTC). - Interest Subsidy: - Optional by government/banks. - National Policy for Skill Development & Entrepreneurship (2015). - Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY). - National Policy for Skill Development & Entrepreneurship (2015): - Challenges: - Social stigma views vocational training (e.g., mason, carpenter) as inferior to graduation degrees. - Strategies: - Raise awareness to break stigma and inferiority complex. - Integrate vocational skilling from Class 9. - Ensure market-driven training to increase seriousness (avoid free training’s casual approach). - Conduct sector-wise skill gap analysis, update syllabi, and train workforce with Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL). - Use IT-based monitoring, evaluation, and placement systems. - Establish new ITIs in PPP mode. - Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY): - Boss: - Ministry of Skill Development, funds NSDC and State Skill Development Missions. - Type: - Centrally Sponsored Core Scheme (states contribute funds). - Target: - Skill 40 crore people by 2022. - Components: - Short-Term Training (STT): - 150-300 hours at public (ITI, Polytechnics) and empanelled private Kaushal Vikas Kendras. - Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL): - Certifies skills of informally trained workers (e.g., tailors, masons) for bridge courses. - Special Projects: - Training for sectors/persons not covered by STT. - Additional Activities: - Training melas, rozgar melas, placement tracking. - PMKVY Phase 3.0 (2020): - Phases: - Phase 1.0 (2015-16), Phase 2.0 (2016-2020), Phase 3.0 (2020-21). - Target: - Train 8 lakh people in 2020-21. - Feature: - Greater powers to district administrations to address local skill demands. - PM Kaushal Vikas 4.0 (Budget 2023): - Focus: - New-age Industry 4.0 skills (coding, AI, robotics, mechatronics, IoT, 3D printing, drones, soft skills). - Methods: - On-job training, industry partnerships, syllabus alignment. - Duration: - Next three years (2023-2026). - PM-VIKAS / Vishwakarma Kaushal Samman (Budget 2023): - Refer: - Pillar 1D (not detailed here as per source instruction). - Skill India Digital Platform (Budget 2023): - Purpose: - Offers online formal skill training courses. - Feature: - Demand-based, open enrollment 365 days a year (unlike fixed-seat traditional courses). - ₹6,000. - Monthly stipend: - ₹5,000 for 12 months (₹4,500 by government, ₹500 by company). - CSR Compliance: - Company spending counts toward CSR quota (Ref: Pillar 1C). - Insurance: - Covered under PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana and PM Suraksha Bima Yojana (Ref: Pillar 1D). - Boss: - Skill Ministry. - Purpose: - Group A service, recruited via UPSC’s Indian Engineering Service Examination (first batch 2019, trained in Mysuru). - SAMVAY (Skills Assessment Matrix for Vocational Advancement of Youth): - Purpose: - Credit framework for vertical/lateral mobility in vocational education, similar to Academic Bank of Credits. - Pillar 6C: Human Resource Development - Poverty - Definition: - Poverty is the lack of sufficient money to meet the minimum standard of living, including food, clothing, shelter, health, and education. - Poverty in India - Factors Responsible for Poverty in India: - Poor fiscal capacity due to tax​ evasion, leading to inadequate public healthcare, education, housing, water, and sanitation infrastructure. - Poor educational outcomes resulting in illiteracy and lack of vocational skills, causing unemployment, underemployment, and disguised unemployment (Ref: Pillar 4C). - Unhygienic slums leading to diseases, loss of wages, savings, and school days. - Lack of family planning increases birth rates, leading to child labor and reduced education opportunities. - Large families result in insufficient food, malnutrition, and limited mental/physical capacity for better economic opportunities. - Unprofitable agriculture due to monsoon vagaries and structural bottlenecks in APMC markets. - Low asset base (e.g., lack of land, milch animals, farm machinery, or bank deposits) reduces self-employment/business opportunities, perpetuating a vicious trap of low savings, low investment, and low income. - Lack of financial planning, with money wasted on tobacco, liquor, social rituals, and pilgrimages. - Lack of financial inclusion, leading to debt traps by informal moneylenders. - Majority of labor in the unorganized/informal sector, where minimum wages are not enforced. - Poor insurance density and lack of social security, pushing families into poverty if the breadwinner dies or becomes permanently disabled. - Social barriers faced by SC/ST/minorities in economic advancement in rural areas. - Low female labor force participation rate, weak enforcement of Maternity Benefits Act and Equal Wages Act, and gender inequality in education/nutrition, confining women to unpaid domestic work. - Misgovernance, terrorism, and secessionism in Special Category States, leading to underdeveloped infrastructure, industries, and tourism. - Corruption and leakages in poverty removal programs, with inadequate accountability by Finance Commission and planning machinery. - Delayed economic reforms compared to China, with India’s industrialists constrained by license, quota, and inspector raj, and archaic factory/labor laws hindering manufacturing job creation. - Vicious Circle of Poverty: - Supply Side: - Low income leads to low savings, low investment/capital, inability to start/expand businesses, and persistent poverty. - Demand Side: - Low income results in low demand for goods (e.g., mobiles, TVs, fridges), reducing company/factory investments, leading to fewer jobs and more poverty. - Implication: - Poor individuals lack money for quality food/education, reducing productivity and perpetuating low income. This cycle also explains low development in Least Developed Countries (LDCs). - Economics Nobel 2019 for Global Poverty Alleviation: - Awarded to Abhijit Banerjee (Mumbai-born, MIT, USA), Esther Duflo (France), and Michael Kremer (USA) for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty. - Prize: - 9 million Swedish krona, shared equally. - Approach: - Divide poverty into smaller, manageable questions (e.g., improving educational outcomes via extra classes for weak students, enhancing child health through vaccination incentives like food grains for parents). - Economics Nobel 2024 for Importance of Institutions for Economic Growth: - Awarded to Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, and James A. Robinson (USA) for highlighting the role of institutions and rule of law in economic growth. - Findings: - Inclusive Institutional Framework (e.g., democracy, law and order, property rights protection) in countries like USA and Canada, where European colonial masters settled permanently. - Extractive Institutional Framework (e.g., lack of rule of law, autocracy, concentrated power) in African and Asian countries, where Europeans did not settle due to malaria, heat, or large local populations, leading to exploitation and stunted growth. - Counterarguments: - Model does not fully explain China’s growth. - USA exploited African slaves and Native Americans. - Britain’s industrial revolution relied on labor exploitation, challenging the notion of an inclusive framework for all citizens. - Poverty Measurement/Estimation: - World Bank (Videshi Methods): - International Poverty Line (IPL): - $2.15/day (PPP exchange rate, 2017). - Absolute Poverty: - A person spending less than $2.15/day is classified as poor, measured via Poverty Head Count Ratio (HCR). - 2011: - 21.2% of India’s population below IPL, the highest globally; by 2018, Nigeria surpassed India. - World Bank Goal: - Eliminate extreme poverty by 2030 (Reports: Poverty and Shared Prosperity 2016, 2018, 2020). - 2020 Report: - Noted COVID-19 could push 150 million into poverty by 2021; criticized India for lacking recent poverty data but praised Mumbai’s Dharavi slum community support during COVID. - Relative Poverty: - Households earning less than 60% of median income (e.g., UK standard). - World Bank Poverty Line Changed (September 2022): -

- Composite/Multidimensional Measurement of Poverty: - Uses a composite index aggregating multiple indicators into a single score, capturing broader wellbeing dimensions (health, education, living standards). - Examples: - UNDP’s Human Development Index (HDI, Ref: Pillar 6E), UNDP’s MPI, NITI’s MPI. - UNDP-MPI (2022 Report): - Measures poverty beyond income, focusing on deprivations in health, education, and living standards. - Prepared by UNDP and Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI). - 10 Indicators (3 Dimensions): - Health: - Nutrition, child mortality. - Education: - Years of schooling, school attendance. - Living Standards: - Cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets (e.g., radio, TV, bicycle). -

- Progress: - 41.5 crore people moved out of MPI poverty (2005-2021). - Global Ranking: - India (22.8 crore poor) ranks #1, followed by Nigeria. - Global MPI: - 19.1% (120 crore) people live in multidimensional poverty. - FAQ: - Is MPI a Poverty Line? - MPI is not an absolute or relative poverty line but a composite measurement, providing a more refined picture of poverty by capturing multiple deprivations. - Videshi Methods - Inequality: - Gini Coefficient (Corrado Gini, 1912): - Measures income/wealth inequality (0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality). - Used by World Bank, Credit Suisse, etc. - Global Wealth Report (Credit Suisse): - India’s richest 10% own over 70% of wealth; over 70% of Indians have personal wealth below $10,000. - Inclusive Wealth Report (UN Environment): - Biennial report measuring economic sustainability and wellbeing (last report: 2018). - Global Social Mobility Report (World Economic Forum, 2019 onwards): - Measures access to health, education, technology, work opportunities, and social protection. - 2020 Ranking: - #1 Denmark, #76 India, #82 Ivory Coast. - World Inequality Report 2022 (World Inequality Lab, Paris): - Richest 10% globally own 60-80% of wealth; poorest 50% own less than 5%. - Women earn one-third of global labor income. - India: - Bottom 50% earn <₹55,000/year; top 10% earn >₹11 lakh/year. - Suggestion: - Higher taxes on the rich. - Oxfam Inequality Index (Commitment to Reducing Inequality, CRI): - Measures government efforts via social sector spending, progressive taxation, and labor rights. - 2018 Ranking: - #1 Denmark, #147 India, #157 Nigeria. - 2020 Report (WEF-Davos): - India’s 1% hold four times more wealth than 70% of the poor; a female domestic worker would need 22,277 years to earn a top tech CEO’s annual income. - Period Poverty: - Social taboos and hygiene issues around menstruation hinder women’s education and employment potential. - Issues: - Lack of sanitary products/separate toilets leads to school absenteeism; Chhaupadi practice in rural Nepal forces menstruating women into separate huts, risking infection/death. - Initiatives: - Scotland (2020) passed a law for free sanitary products; India applies 0% GST on sanitary napkins; Rajasthan’s Udaan scheme provides free sanitary napkins. - Deshi Methods (Below Poverty Line - BPL): - Alagh Committee (1979): - Defined BPL as adult daily calorie intake of 2100 (urban), 2400 (rural). - Lakdawalla Committee (1993): - Included calorie intake, clothing, and shelter. - Suresh Tendulkar Committee (2005-09): - Defined poverty line at monthly per capita expenditure (MPCE): - ₹816 (rural, ~₹27/day), ₹1000 (urban, ~₹33/day). - Used all-India urban poverty line basket as a reference for both rural and urban estimates. - State-specific poverty lines adjusted using CPI inflation. - 2011-12: - 21.9% (all India), 25.7% (rural), 13.7% (urban) below poverty line. - Used by NITI Aayog and Modi government in official documents. - States with >21.9% poverty: - Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Assam, Odisha, Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Jharkhand, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Chhattisgarh (highest). - C. Rangarajan Committee (2012-14): - Poverty line for a family of five: - ₹4860/month (rural), ₹7035/month (urban). - Components: - Food: - Based on average calorie, fat, and protein requirements. - Normative Non-Food: - Clothing, housing, mobility, education. - Behavioral Non-Food: - Other expenses based on actual spending patterns. - SBI Research Paper (2024): -

- Application: - Excluded households ineligible for schemes; included households prioritized; deprivation-based households ranked by deprivation level for schemes like PM Awas Yojana, PM Ujjwala, PM Jan Arogya Yojana (₹5 lakh health insurance for 10 crore families). - Process: - Rural survey results verified at Gram Sabha; urban methodology differs slightly; caste census data not released. - Deshi Methods - NITI-MPI (2022-23): - First Indian MPI by NITI Aayog (November 2021), inspired by Alkire-Foster methodology. - Alkire-Foster Methodology: - Developed by Sabina Alkire and James Foster (OPHI). - Flexible technique for measuring poverty/wellbeing, similar to UNDP-MPI. - NITI-MPI Indicators: - 3 Dimensions (equal weight): Health, Education, Standard of Living. - 12 Indicators: -
Indicator Deprivation Criteria
Nutrition Any woman (15-49 years) or man (15-54 years) with BMI <18.5 kg/m²; or child under 5 with stunting/underweight (below -2 SD of reference population median).
Child-Adolescent Mortality Any child under 18 died in the household in the past 5 years.
Maternal Health Any woman (last 5 years) with <4 antenatal care visits or no skilled medical assistance during recent childbirth.
Years of Schooling No household member (10+ years) completed 6 years of schooling.
School Attendance Any school-aged child not attending school up to class completion age.
Cooking Fuel Household uses dung, agricultural crops, shrubs, wood, charcoal, or coal.
Sanitation Unimproved/no sanitation facility or improved but shared with other households.
Drinking Water No access to improved drinking water or safe water is ≥30-minute walk (round trip).
Housing Inadequate housing (natural floor or rudimentary roof/wall materials, e.g., mud, clay).
Electricity No electricity.
Assets Does not own >1 of: radio, TV, telephone, computer, animal cart, bicycle, motorbike, refrigerator; and does not own a car/truck.
Bank Accounts No household member has a bank/post office account.
- Data Source: - National Family Health Survey (NFHS). - NITI-MPI 2024 Report: - Poverty Reduction: - 24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty (2013-14 to 2022-23), ~2.75 crore annually. - 2022-23: - 11.28% of Indians poor. - Projection: - India to reach single-digit poverty levels in 2024, ahead of SDG target to halve poverty by 2030. - Best Performing States (2024 Report): - Highest Poverty (2021): - Bihar (52%), Jharkhand (42%), Uttar Pradesh (38%), Madhya Pradesh (36%), Meghalaya (32%). - Lowest Poverty (2021): - Kerala (0.71%), Goa (3.76%), Sikkim (3.82%), Tamil Nadu (4.89%), Punjab (5.59%). - Most Progress (2013-14 to 2022-23): - Uttar Pradesh: - 5.94 crore escaped poverty. - Bihar: - 3.77 crore. - Madhya Pradesh: - 2.30 crore. - Rajasthan: - 1.87 crore. - Bare Necessities Index (BNI, Economic Survey 2021): - Concept: - Poverty as failure to achieve minimum basic needs (Amartya Sen), including food, housing, water, sanitation, electricity, clean cooking fuel. - BNI Structure: 5 dimensions, 26 indicators (notable ones listed): -
Dimension Indicators Implications Related Scheme
Water Source (e.g., tanker, river); distance from source; collection method (tap, pot). Distant water sources reduce daughters’ education due to water hauling. Jal Jeevan Mission (piped water).
Sanitation Toilet type (exclusive/community). Open defecation causes infections, diseases, higher IMR/MMR, reduced girls’ school attendance, malnutrition. Swachh Bharat Mission.
Housing House condition, wall/roof materials. Dilapidated housing increases vulnerability to crime, disasters, diseases. Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana.
Micro-Environment Drainage system; flies/mosquitoes issues and government response. Poor drainage increases diarrhea, jaundice, malaria risks. -
Other Facilities Electricity; cooking fuel (LPG, firewood, dung); kitchen/bathroom type. Wood/dung fuel causes indoor air pollution, affecting mother/child health; firewood collection reduces girls’ education and causes deforestation; electricity enables education and democratic awareness. Saubhagya (electricity), PM Ujjwala (LPG).
- Scoring: - Arithmetic mean, score range 0-1; higher score indicates better access to bare necessities. - Visualization: - Green, yellow, red colors on state maps to show access levels. - BNI Findings: - Highest Progress: - Kerala, Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat, Uttarakhand, Delhi, Goa, Mizoram, Sikkim. - Lowest Progress: - Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura. - Urban areas score better than rural areas. - Schemes Praised: - Swachh Bharat Mission, National Rural Drinking Water Programme, PM Awas Yojana, Saubhagya, Ujjwala Yojana. - Progress: - BNI improved for all states from 2012 to 2018, with better infant mortality and health outcomes (NFHS data). - BNI Analysis - Conclusion/Significance: - Tracks SDG progress (Goal 6: water/sanitation; Goal 7: electricity/clean fuel). - Improves scheme implementation via real-time monitoring, geo-tagging, social audits, and DBT. - Enhances transparency, accountability, and good governance. - Poverty Removal in Rural Areas (Economic Survey 2023): - Rural Population: - 80% (1960), 70% (2007), 65% (2021). - Agriculture Dependency: - 47% of population (ES23). - Schemes Praised: - Insurance, pension, loans, financial inclusion (Ref: Pillar 1D, e.g., Jeevan Jyoti, Mudra, Vay Vandana, Shram Yogi Maan-Dhan). - Poverty Removal (SDG Goal 1 - End Poverty): - Target: - Halve BPL population by 2030 (2011 baseline: 21.9% to 10.95%). - Indicators and Targets: -

- Schemes: - NSOAP (pension/insurance for poor, Ref: Pillar 1D), PMJDY (Jan Dhan accounts). - Poverty Removal - MGNREGA (2005): - Act: - Enacted in 2005, launched in 2006 (200 districts), expanded nationwide in 2008 as Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme. - Boss: - Ministry of Rural Development (Centrally Sponsored Core Scheme, partial Union funding). - Structure: - Central Employment Guarantee Council (chaired by Rural Development Minister) advises on implementation. - Features: - Guarantees 100 days of unskilled manual labor to rural households volunteering for it. - Unemployment allowance if work not provided within 15 days. - Creates durable assets (e.g., ponds, wells, cattle sheds, granaries, vermicompost plants, anganwadi centers, school buildings). - No contractors/machinery allowed; ≥60% of district work linked to agriculture/allied activities. - Funding: - 60% wages, 40% materials; Union covers 100% wage cost, 75% material cost. - Data: - Over 5 crore households employed; >50% workers were women (2018-2022). - Social Audit: - Conducted by Gram Sabha every 6 months. - MGNREGA Wages: - Linked to Consumer Price Index (Agricultural Labour); proposed shift to CPI-Rural. - 2020 (COVID): - Wages increased from ₹182 to ₹202/day (₹2000 extra for 100 days). - State Variations (due to inflation differences): -

- 2025-26: - Wages hiked by 2-7%. - MGNREGA - DBT (Mixed Model): - Wages paid via Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) using: - Aadhaar-Based Payment System (ABPS, 95% workers, Aadhaar mandatory). - National Automated Clearing House (NACH, 5% workers, Aadhaar not required). - 2023: - Plan to phase out NACH, but operational issues led to continuation of mixed model. - 2024: - Controversy over shifting fully to ABPS. - MGNREGA Budget 2023: - Allocation reduced (₹86,000 crore in 2025) due to expected economic recovery post-COVID, assuming villagers would return to urban jobs. - Bare Foot Technicians (BFT, 2015): - Rural Development Ministry trains 10,000 young workers in basic civil engineering. - Benefits: - Skill upgradation for construction sector jobs; improved MGNREGA work planning, layout, measurement, and supervision. - MGNREGA Reforms/Apps/Portals: -

- MGNREGA Problems/Suggested Reforms: - Delayed wage payments despite legal guarantee of 15-day payment under the Act. - Fund shortages due to delayed central government release, leading to halted work. - Underemployment: - Average days of employment provided is far below the guaranteed 100 days. - Poor asset quality due to lack of proper planning and technical supervision. - Leakages and corruption through fake job cards, ghost beneficiaries, and inflated muster rolls. - Weak social audit implementation, reducing transparency and accountability. - Political interference in work allocation and beneficiary selection. - Insufficient use of technology like GIS-based monitoring and Aadhaar-based payments in some states. - Lack of skilled-based work diversification; mostly focuses on unskilled manual labor. - Suggested Reforms: - Ensure timely release of funds from Centre to states. - Strengthen social audits and community monitoring mechanisms. - Increase convergence with other development schemes to create durable assets. - Introduce more skilled work and training programs for rural workers. - Implement end-to-end digital payment systems to reduce leakages. - Provide adequate staff and technical support at Gram Panchayat level. - Link MGNREGA works with climate resilience projects like water harvesting and afforestation. - PM Garib Kalyan Rojgar Abhiyaan (GKRA, 2020): - Launched in Bihar’s Telihar village to support returnee migrants. - Boss: - Rural Development Ministry, coordinating with ministries like Roads, Mines, Jal Shakti. - Coverage: - 6 states (Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Odisha). - Duration: - 125 days. - Activities: - Building panchayat bhavans, community toilets, rural mandis, roads, cattle sheds, anganwadi bhavans. - Rajasthan Indira Gandhi Shehri Rozgar Guarantee Yojana (2022): - Urban equivalent of MGNREGA, guaranteeing 100 days of work. - Activities: - Tree plantation, pond cleaning, garbage collection, stray animal management, environmental/water conservation, cleanliness, sanitation, property defacement prevention, heritage conservation. - Rajasthan Minimum Guaranteed Income Bill (2023): - Features: - 125 days of employment guarantee for all rural/urban families; minimum ₹1000/month pension for aged/disabled/single women, with 15% annual increase. - Controversy: - Financial strain on state, compounded by reverting to Old Pension Scheme (Ref: Pillar 1D). - National Livelihood Missions (Skill + Loan): - Evolution: - Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) and TRYSEM (1970s) → Swarnjayanti Gram/Sahari Rozgar Yojana (1997-99) → National Rural Livelihood Mission (NRLM, 2011) and National Urban Livelihood Mission (NULM, 2013) → prefixed with Deen Dayal Antyodaya Yojana. - Structure: -
Scheme Deen Dayal Antyodaya Yojana: NULM Deen Dayal Antyodaya Yojana: NRLM

- NRLM Institutions/Funds: - Institutions: - SHGs, livelihood collectives, producer cooperatives/companies, production hubs. - Training: - Via SHGs, federations, government, bankers, NGOs, CRPs. - Funds: - Community Investment Support Fund (CIF): Formed via SHGs to support poor families. - Vulnerability Reduction Fund (VRF): Part of CIF for interest-free loans to poor families. - National Special Fund Support: With state governments to reduce poverty and empower rural poor. - Infrastructure/Marketing: - Market research, intelligence, technology extension, backward/forward linkages, livelihoods collectives. - Support Structures: - National, state, district, sub-district levels with dedicated professionals. - Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (DDU-GKY): - Objective: - Free skill training for rural youth via public/private training organizations. - Timeline: - 1999: - Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) launched from IRDP. - 2010: - SGSY split into NRLM (SHGs) and Aajeevika Skills. - 2014 (25th September, Antyodaya Diwas): - Aajeevika Skills renamed DDU-GKY. - Three-Tier Structure: - National Unit: - Policy, central investments, technical support (Ministry of Rural Development). - State Skills Missions: - State investments, implementation, monitoring. - Project Implementing Agencies (PIAs): - Public/private partners for skill training and placements. - Funding Quota: - 50% for SC/ST, 33% for women, 15% for minorities, 3% for physically handicapped (PH). - Beneficiaries: - Rural youth (15-35 years, higher for SC/ST/women/PH) from: - MGNREGA worker families (≥15 days work). - Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana (RSBY, now PM-JAY) households. - Antyodaya Anna Yojana cardholders. - BPL PDS cardholders. - NRLM-SHG households. - SECC-2011 auto-inclusion households. - Placement/Jobs: - Minimum 70% trainees must secure jobs with ≥₹6000/month or state minimum wage (whichever is higher). - Special Focus: - ROSHNI: - For Left-Wing Extremist areas (9 states), mandatory residential course, 40% women coverage. - Himayat: - For all youth in Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, 100% central funding. - Poverty Removal - DISHA Committees (2016): - Boss: - Ministry of Rural Development. - Full Name: - District Development Coordination and Monitoring Committee. - Members: - Elected representatives (Parliament, state legislature, PRI, ULB). - Objective: - Implements schemes with greater vigilance/accountability via Gram Panchayats, NGOs, SHGs, ASHA workers. - Target: - ≥50,000 Gram Panchayats poverty-free by 2020. - RUDSETI (RSETI): - Full Name: - Rural Development and Self-Employment Training Institute. - Objective: - Trains unemployed rural youth (18-45 years) via a three-way partnership (Ministry of Rural Development, state governments, banks). - Requirement: - Banks must establish ≥1 RSETI per district. - Courses: - Papad/pickle/masala making, embroidery, fabric painting, costume jewelry, women’s tailoring, house aya, beauty parlor management. - Certification: - By Assessment and Certification Board. - SMILE 75: - Boss: - Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. - Objective: - Makes 75 cities begging-free through rehabilitation, medical facilities, education, skill development, and economic opportunities. - ~40% food subsidies benefit non-poor families. - Exclusion Error: - ~40-60% needy families miss scheme benefits. - Leakage: - 20-36% PDS/MGNREGA funds lost to corruption. - Tendulkar Poverty Line (2011): - Rural (≥₹816/month, ₹9800/year), Urban (≥₹1000/month, ₹12000/year) considered non-poor. - Economic Survey 2017: - Proposed UBI to transfer money directly to poor individuals’ bank accounts to enhance purchasing power. - Constitutional Protection - Constitution does not define "minority" but provides: - Article 25-28: - Right to freedom of religion. - Article 25(2): - Sikhs have the right to wear and carry kirpans. - Article 29(1): - Right to conserve distinct language, script, or culture. - Article 30(1): - Minorities’ right to establish and administer educational institutions. - Article 350B: - Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities. - Minorities - Legal Protection - 1955: - Durgah Khwaja Saheb Act empowers Union to administer Durgah of Khwaja Moin-ud-din Chishti at Ajmer. - 1992: - National Commission for Minorities Act, Section 2(c) recognizes six national minorities: Muslims, Christians, Buddhists, Sikhs, Zoroastrians (Parsis), Jains (added in 2014). - 1995: - Waqf Act establishes Waqf Councils at Union and State levels for managing donated Muslim properties. - 2002: - Haj Committee Act. - 2004: - Minority Educational Institutions Act. - Minorities - Census 2011 - Population Share: - Hindu (79.8%), Muslim (14.2%), Christian (2.3%), Sikh (1.7%), Buddhist (0.7%), Jain (0.4%), Parsis (0.06%), Animist & others (0.72%). - Decadal Growth Rate (2001-2011): - Hindus (16.8%), Muslims (24.6%), Christians (15.5%), Sikhs (8.4%), Buddhists (6.1%), Jains (5.4%). - Jain Population Share: - Maharashtra (1.3%), Rajasthan (1.2%), Delhi (1.1%), Gujarat (1.0%). - Non-Hindu Majority Areas: - Muslims (J&K, Lakshadweep), Sikhs (Punjab). - Hindu Minority States/UTs: - Lakshadweep, Mizoram, Nagaland, Meghalaya, J&K, Arunachal, Manipur, Punjab (per PIL in Supreme Court). - Minorities - Religious Freedom Reports - United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) 2020 Report: - Labeled India as a Country of Special Concern (CSC) due to communal violence. - India’s Ministry of External Affairs rejected the report, deeming it biased. - State Commission for Minorities - Statutory bodies in 18 states/UTs: - Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Delhi, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Uttarakhand, West Bengal, Punjab. - Example: - Rajasthan State Minorities Commission Act, 2001. - Linguistic Minorities - Constitutional Rights -
Article Provision
29, 30 Right to conserve distinct language, script, or culture; establish and administer educational institutions.
347 Official recognition of any language as specified by the President.
350 Right to submit complaints in any language used in Union/states.
350A Instruction in mother tongue at primary education stage for linguistic minority children.
350B Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities (est. 1957, HQ: Delhi, zonal offices: Belagavi, Chennai, Kolkata).
- Ministry of Minority Affairs - CPSE: - National Minorities Development & Finance Corporation (NMDFC), non-profit under Companies Act, 73% Union-owned, state/UT share proportional to minority population. Virasat: NMDFC loan scheme for craftsmen. - Autonomous: - Maulana Azad Education Foundation (MAEF), named after India’s first Education Minister. - Statutory: - National Commission for Minorities, Waqf Council, Haj Committee. - Constitutional: - Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities (Art 350B). - Minority Schemes - PM Janvikas Karykram (PMJVK, 2018) - Evolution: - 2005-06 Sachar Committee → 2005 PM’s 15-Point Programme → 2008 Multi-sectoral Development Programme (MsDP) → 2018 PMJVK. - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs, Centrally Sponsored Scheme (60:40, 90:10 funding). - Coverage: - Village clusters with ≥25% minority population (earlier MsDP covered ≥50% minority areas, ~90 districts). - Focus: - Health (PHCs, Anganwadi centers), Education (schools, classrooms, labs), Skills (ITIs, Polytechnics), Community Halls, Marketsheds, Rural Housing, Water, Toilets. - Allocation: - 80% for health, education, skills; 33-40% for women-centric projects. - PMJVK Sub-component - CyberGram - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs. - Objective: - Provide computer training to Madressa students. - Minority Scheme - Education/Exams -
Scheme Details
Nai Roshni Leadership development for minority women, training to interact with government and banks for assertiveness and confidence.
Nai Manzil For Madressa pass-outs and school dropouts (17-35 years), provides employable skills (e.g., computer, accounting) and NIOS certification for organized sector jobs; ≥30% seats for minority girls.
Naya Savera Central Sector Scheme, 100% Union-funded, free coaching for minority students for competitive exams (UPSC, SSC, State PCS).
Nai Udaan Financial support for minority students clearing prelims of UPSC, SSC, State PCS (gazetted posts), family income ≤₹6 lakh, max 2000 students annually, first-come-first-serve.
Padho Pardesh Education loan subsidy for minority students pursuing higher education overseas.
Maulana Azad National Fellowship Five-year financial assistance for M.Phil/Ph.D. for Buddhists, Christians, Jains, Muslims, Parsis, Sikhs; discontinued in 2022-23 due to overlap with other schemes.
Pre-matric Scholarship Earlier for Class 1-10, from 2022 only for Class 9-10.
- Minority Skilling - USTTAD - Full Name: - Upgrading Skills & Training in Traditional Arts/Crafts for Development. - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs, Central Sector Scheme (100% Union-funded). - Beneficiaries: - Minority craftsmen (≥30 years, 10 years experience), trained with stipends to become master trainers (Ustads) to teach younger generations. - Examples: - Phulkari embroidery (Sikh), Kashmiri shawls/carpets, Aligarh handmade locks (Muslims), Thanka painting (Buddhist), Parsi Gara hand-embroidered sarees. - Related: - Hunar Haat (trade mela for craftsmen), Virasat (NMDFC credit scheme). - Minority Skilling - Seekho Aur Kamao (Learn & Earn) - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs, Central Sector Scheme (100% Union-funded). - Beneficiaries: - Minority persons (min Class 5 pass, 14-45 years). - Training: - Modern trades (saloon, restaurant, computer data entry) or traditional crafts (carpets, handicrafts) with stipends; followed by placement/self-employment support. - Minority Skill/Culture - PM VIKAS (2022) - Full Name: - Pradhan Mantri Virasat Ka Samvardhan (earlier Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Ko Kaam Karykram). - Umbrella scheme covering Seekho Aur Kamao, USTTAD, Hamari Dharohar, Nai Roshni, Nai Manzil. - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs. - Beneficiaries: - ≥33% women. - Minority Skilling - MANAS Academy - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs via NMDFC and Maulana Azad National Academy for Skills (MANAS). - Functions: - Uses government scheme funds and donations to set up PPP training institutes, provide concessional loans for skill courses/businesses, and offer technical/marketing support. - Monitoring: - Online portal with Skill Ministry to oversee private training institutes. - Shahari Waqf Sampatti Vikas Yojana - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs via Central Waqf Council. - Objective: - Interest-free loans up to ₹2 crore for constructing economically viable buildings (e.g., commercial complexes, marriage halls, hospitals, cold storage) on Waqf land. - Preserving Community/Culture/Pilgrimage -
Scheme Details
Jiyo Parsi (2013) Central Sector Scheme, encourages Parsi couples to have children to reverse population decline; supports infertility treatment, IVF, advocacy, counseling.
Hamari Dharohar Ministry of Minority Affairs with Culture Ministry, preserves minority culture, heritage, manuscripts.
- Pilgrim - Hajj Subsidy - 1932: - British India started subsidized sea transport for Hajj pilgrims. - Modern Era: - Civil Aviation Ministry provided subsidies to Air India for cheap transport/meals. - 2012: - Supreme Court ordered phasing out Hajj subsidy, redirecting funds to Muslim education/social development. - 2018: - Subsidy canceled based on Afzal Amanullah Committee (2017) report. - Pilgrim - Hajj Mehram - Earlier: - Muslim women required a Mehram (husband, son, or male first blood relation) for Hajj. - Post-2017: - PM Modi allowed women ≥45 years to travel without Mehram in groups of ≥4, per Afzal Amanullah Committee. - App: - E-MASIHA health app for Hajj pilgrims. - Scheduled Tribes (ST) - ST - Constitutional Protection - Article 23: - Abolishes human trafficking and bonded labor. - Article 164: - Tribal Welfare Minister in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha (Bihar excluded via 94th Amendment, 2006). - Articles 330, 332: - SC/ST reservation in Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha. - Articles 243D, 243T: - Reservation in PRI and ULB. - Article 338A: - National Commission for ST (bifurcated from NCSC via 89th Amendment, 2003). - 2021: - Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order (Amendment) Bill updates tribe names in Arunachal Pradesh. - 5th & 6th Schedules: - Special provisions for tribal areas (Ref: Laxmikanth). - ST - Legal Protection - 1955: - Protection of Civil Rights Act. - 1976: - Bonded Labour System Abolition Act. - 1989: - Prevention of Atrocities Act for SC/ST. - 1996: - Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas Act (PESA). - 2006: - Scheduled Tribes & Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act. - ST - Census 2011 - Population: - 8.6% of India’s population. - Sex Ratio: - 990 (better than national 943). - Literacy: - 59% (below national 73%). - ST Share (%): - Lakshadweep > Mizoram > Nagaland > Meghalaya > Dadra & Nagar Haveli. - Absolute Numbers: - Madhya Pradesh > Maharashtra > Odisha > Jharkhand > Gujarat > Rajasthan. - No ST notified in Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, Delhi, Puducherry. - Ministry of Tribal Affairs - Cooperative/Autonomous: - TRIFED (1987): - Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation, under Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act, markets Minor Forest Produce (MFP) under TRIBES INDIA; 2020 launched TRIFOOD for mahua drink, amla/jamun juice. - National Education Society for Tribal Students (NESTS), autonomous under Society Registration Act. - CPSE: - National Scheduled Tribes Finance & Development Corporation, non-profit under Companies Act. - Constitutional: - National Commission for ST (Art 338A). - E-Governance: - Swasthya Portal: - Health/nutrition info for tribals. - GOAL: - Leadership development for ST students. - ALEKH: - Newsletter for tribal communities. - Shramshakthi Portal: - For migrant workers. - ADIGRAMS Portal: - Monitors funds/schemes. - Adiprashikshan Portal: - Training/capacity building. - Days: - 15th Nov (Janjatiya Gaurav Divas, Birsa Munda’s birthday, from 2021); 9th Aug (World Tribal Day). - ST - Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) - 1960s: - Dhebar Commission identified tribes with pre-agricultural technology, isolation, low literacy, declining/stagnant population (earlier called Primitive Tribal Groups, now PVTGs). - Current: - 75 PVTGs across 18 states and Andaman-Nicobar. - Examples: -
State/UT PVTGs
Andhra & Telangana Bodo Gadaba, Bondo Poroja, Chenchu, Dongria Khond, Gutob Gadaba, Khond Poroja, Kolam, Kondareddis, Konda Savaras, Kutia Khond, Parengi Poroja, Thoti
Gujarat Kathodi, Kohvalia, Padhar, Siddi, Kolgha
Karnataka Jenu Kuruba, Koraga
MP & Chhattisgarh Abujh Macias, Baigas, Bharias, Hill Korbas, Kamars, Saharias, Birhor
Maharashtra Katkaria (Kathodia), Kolam, Maria Gond
Rajasthan Seharias
Tamil Nadu Kattu Nayakans, Kotas, Kurumbas, Irulas, Paniyans, Todas
Andaman & Nicobar Negrito (Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa, Sentinalese), Mongoloid (Nicobarese, Shompens)
