- Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Unnat Gram Abhiyan (2024-Sep) - Centrally Sponsored Scheme for tribal-majority villages and aspirational districts. - Saturation approach to cover every ST family. - Focus: - Socio-economic improvement via schemes like PM Awas, PMJAY, Jal Jeevan Mission, PM Ujjwala. - Tourism Ministry funds tribal homestays. - Faster land title clearances under Forest Rights Act. - AIIMS to research sickle cell anemia (genetic blood disorder affecting red blood cells). - ST - Tribal Sub Plan (1974) - Strategy for rapid socio-economic development of STs. - Union ministries allocate funds to states proportional to ST population for infrastructure (e.g., schools, roads, hospitals). - Continues despite abolition of Planning Commission and plan/non-plan budget merger. - ST - Vanbandhu Kalyan Yojana (2014) - Boss: - Ministry of Tribal Affairs. - Focus: - Better implementation of existing schemes, additional funds for schools, hospitals, roads, irrigation, housing in tribal areas. - Emphasis: - Sickle cell anemia, tribal cultural heritage, sports promotion. - ST - Van Dhan Yojana - Boss: - Ministry of Tribal Affairs via TRIFED. - Establishes Van Dhan Vikas Kendras in forested tribal districts. - Forms SHGs for non-timber forest produce (e.g., tamarind, mahua, chironji). - Provides training, finance, and marketing linkages for value addition and sales. - ST - MSP for Minor Forest Produce - Boss: - Ministry of Tribal Affairs via TRIFED’s Pricing Cell. - MSP for items like chironji, tamarind, wild honey, mahua seeds, karanj seeds, baheda, shikakai pods, guggul, arjuna bark. - Seasons: -
Season Notable MFPs
Jan-Mar Lac, mahua flower, tamarind
Apr-Jun Tendu leaves, sal seeds, chironji
Jul-Sep Chironji, mango, mahua fruits, silk cocoons, bamboo
Oct-Nov Lac, kullu gum, incense stick resins
- Benefit: - Prevents exploitation by forest contractors/merchants. - ST - Central Tribal University - Per Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, Union to establish tribal universities in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. - 2019: - Central Tribal University planned in Araku, Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh. - ST Villages - Pradhan Mantri Adi Adarsh Gram Yojana - Renamed from Special Central Assistance to Tribal Sub-Scheme. - Boss: - Ministry of Tribal Affairs. - Coverage: - Villages with ≥50% ST population (36,000+ villages). - Validity: - 2021–2026. - Funding: - ~₹20 lakh/village + additional scheme funds. - Focus: - Road/telecom connectivity, schools, Anganwadi centers, health sub-centers, drinking water, drainage, solid waste management. - ST - Adivasi Mahila Sashaktikaran Yojana (AMSY) - Boss: - National Scheduled Tribes Finance and Development Corporation (NSTFDC). - Objective: - Economic development of ST women via cheap business loans up to ₹50,000. - Part of Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission, implemented via Van Dhan Kendras and TRIFED for fair returns on collection/processing. - Bhagwan Birsa Munda Memorial Udyan cum Freedom Fighters Museum - Established in Ranchi (2021), highlights tribal freedom fighters like Budhu Bhagat, Sidhu-Kanhu, Nilambar-Pitambar, Diwa-Kisun, Telanga Khadiya, Gaya Munda, Jatra Bhagat, Poto H, Bhagirath Manjhi, Ganga Narayan Singh. - Plan: - Tribal Ministry to set up museums in 10 states. - ST - Partnership with Private/Global Players -

- Scheduled Castes (SC) - SC - Constitutional Protection - Article 17: - Abolishes untouchability. - Article 23: - Abolishes human trafficking and bonded labor. - Article 25(2)(b): - Ensures entry to Hindu temples. - Articles 330, 332: - SC/ST reservation in Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha. - Articles 243D, 243T: - Reservation in PRI and ULB. - Article 338: - National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC). - SC - Legal Protection - 1955: - Protection of Civil Rights Act. - 1976: - Bonded Labour System Abolition Act. - 1989: - Prevention of Atrocities Act for SC/ST. - 2006: - Central Educational Institutions Reservation in Admission Act. - 2013: - Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers & Rehabilitation Act. - SC - Census 2011 - Population: - 16.6% of India’s population (1,200+ SCs). - SC Share (%): - Punjab > West Bengal > Himachal > Uttar Pradesh > Haryana. - Absolute Numbers: - Uttar Pradesh > West Bengal > Bihar > Tamil Nadu > Andhra Pradesh > Maharashtra. - No SC notified in Nagaland, Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep. - SC Sub-categorisation - Madiga in Telangana (2023) - Madiga community: - ≥50% of Telangana’s SC population. - Issue: - Madigas allege Mala community corners most SC reservation benefits, demand sub-quota. - SC Sub-categorisation - Article 341 (2024) - Article 341: - Parliament solely authorizes inclusion/exclusion from SC list; states have recommendatory role. - Past Attempts: - Punjab, Bihar, Tamil Nadu tried SC sub-categorization laws. - 2005: - Attorney General supported sub-categorization with data justification. - NCSC Opposition: - Prioritize existing scheme benefits for all SCs. - 2023: - PM Modi met Madiga activists in Hyderabad, promised action. - 2024: - Karnataka (Congress) requested Union to amend Article 341(3) for sub-quota. - Aug 2024: - Supreme Court ruled states can sub-classify SCs for preferential treatment in employment/education. - Aug 2024: - Union Government stated no plans for SC/ST sub-categorization, citing no creamy layer provision in Constitution. - Oct 2024: - Haryana BJP CM supported SC sub-categorization. - Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment - Departments: - Social Justice & Empowerment, Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (renamed from derogatory term). - Constitutional: - NCSC (Art 338), National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC, Art 338B, 102nd Amendment, 2018; earlier statutory body, 1993). - Statutory: - Rehabilitation Council of India (1992), National Council for Transgender Persons (2019). - Non-statutory: - National Commission for Safai Karamcharis (NCSK, Act expired 2004), National Commission for Denotified, Nomadic & Semi-Nomadic Tribes (2003, reconstituted 2005, 2015 under Bhiku Ramji Idate). - Autonomous: - Development & Welfare Board for DNTs (2019), Dr. Ambedkar Foundation, Babu Jagjivan Ram National Foundation, National Institute of Social Defence (Delhi). - CPSE: - National Scheduled Castes Finance & Development Corporation (NSFDC), corporations for Backward Classes, Safai Karamcharis, Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation (ALIMCO). - Days: - 26th Nov (Constitution Day, from 2015), 14th Apr (Ambedkar’s birthday). - Committees: - Justice G. Rohini (OBC sub-categorization), Justice K.G. Balakrishnan (SC reservation for converts to non-Hindu/Buddhist/Sikh religions). - Ministry of Law & Justice - Departments: - Legal Affairs, Legislative, Justice. - Executive: - Law Commission of India (non-statutory, non-constitutional, 22nd Commission 2020). - Statutory: - National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), State Legal Services Authority (SALSA) for free legal aid, Bar Council of India, Delimitation Commission. - Constitutional: - Election Commission. - Apps: - Nyay Bandhu (connects poor with pro bono advocates), Tele-Law (legal aid for rural/poor). - Index: - Rule of Law Index by World Justice Project (#1 Denmark, #79 India), focuses on government openness, rights, justice, anti-corruption. - SC Welfare Schemes - Part of Centrally Sponsored Schemes, Umbrella Program for SC Development (not 100% Union-funded). -
Scheme Details
Post-matric Scholarship (2020) For 4 crore SC students over 5 years, 90:10/60:40 funding, direct transfer to accounts.
VISVAS Yojana 5% loan interest subvention for SC/OBC business loans, applicable to SHGs/individuals.
SCDC (1979) State Scheduled Castes Development Corporations, 49:51 Union:State share, provide concessional loans.
Inter-caste Marriages Dr. Ambedkar scheme, ₹7 lakh in two installments for SC/non-SC couples.
PM Adarsh Gram Yojana Develops villages with >50% SC population via better scheme implementation.
ASIIM (2020) Ambedkar Social Innovation & Incubation Mission, supports 1000 SC youth startups over 4 years via venture capital.
Standup India Bank loans (₹10 lakh–₹1 crore) for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs, 7-year tenure, under FinMin’s Dept of Financial Services.
SHRESHTA Admission to top residential schools for meritorious SC students via NTA entrance exam.
NAMASTE Mechanized sanitation, skill development, behavioral change to support sanitation workers.
- SC Welfare - Pradhan Mantri Anusuchit Jaati Abhyuday Yojana (PM-AJAY) - Merges three schemes: - PM Adarsh Gram Yojana, Special Central Assistance to SC Sub Plan, Babu Jagjivan Ram Chatrawas Yojana. - Components: 1. Develop SC-dominated villages into Adarsh Grams. 2. Grants for skill development, business loans, infrastructure (e.g., SC women cooperatives). 3. Hostels for SC students in schools/colleges. - Skill Development - PM Daksha - Full Name: - Pradhan Mantri Dakshta Aur Kushalta Sampann Hitgrahi. - Free skill training for SCs, OBCs, EBCs, DNTs, sanitation workers, waste pickers (18-45 years). - Implemented via NSFDC, NBCFDC, NSKFDC under Social Justice Ministry. - DNT - SEED (Scheme for Economic Empowerment of DNTs) - Context: - 1871 Criminal Tribes Act (repealed 1952), DNTs categorized as SC/ST/OBC or none. - 2008: - Renke Commission for DNT development. - 2019: - Development & Welfare Board for DNTs (autonomous). - 2022: - SEED Scheme by Social Justice Ministry with four components: 1. Free coaching for competitive exams (Civil Services, NEET, IIT, MBA). 2. Health insurance via PMJAY. 3. Employment/livelihood support. 4. Housing via PMAY. - DNT - Nanaji Deshmukh Scheme - Provides hostel facilities for DNT students. - Weaker Section - OBC & EWS - OBC Sub-categorization - Ref: - Pillar 6A (Census, demand for OBC caste census). - EWS Reservation - 2019: - 103rd Constitutional Amendment provides 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) among unreserved categories (non-SC/ST/OBC). - Gujarat: - First state to implement EWS quota. - Boss: - Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment. - PM-YASASVI - Full Name: - PM Young Achievers Scholarship Award Scheme for Vibrant India. - Provides scholarships for Class 9-12 students from OBC, EBC, and DNT communities. - Pillar 6D2: Human Resource Development and Education for Weaker Sections - Women, Children, Persons with Disabilities, Elderly, and LGBT - Introduction - Overview: - India’s human resource development (HRD) and education policies prioritize weaker sections—women, children, persons with disabilities (PH), elderly, and LGBT—aligning with constitutional mandates and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 5 (Gender Equality). - Women: - Constitute 48.5% of India’s population (Census 2011) but face socio-economic disparities despite 78 years of independence, with persistent challenges in education, health, and workforce participation (LFPR 37%, PLFS 2022-23). - Children: - Represent 26% of the population (NFHS-5, 2019-21), requiring protection from exploitation and access to education under Article 21A. - Persons with Disabilities (PH): - 2.68 crore (2.21% of population, Census 2011), necessitating inclusive policies. - Elderly: - 10.1% of population (Census 2011), projected to rise to 13.1% by 2031 (UNFPA), requiring welfare focus. - LGBT: - Emerging focus post-2018 decriminalization, addressing social inclusion. - Global Context: - UNDP Gender Inequality Index (GII) ranks India 102/191 (2023), and World Economic Forum (WEF) Global Gender Gap Report ranks 129/146 (2024), highlighting persistent gaps. - Women: Empowerment and Development - Constitutional Framework -
Article Provision
14 Equality before law, foundational for gender justice.
15 No discrimination; enables affirmative action for women and children.
15(3) Special provisions for women and children, e.g., reservations.
16 Equal opportunity in government jobs, promoting workforce inclusion.
23 Prohibits forced labour and human trafficking, protecting vulnerable women.
39(d) Equal pay for equal work, yet India’s gender wage gap remains 34% (ILO, 2023).
39A Equal justice and free legal aid, supporting marginalized women.
42 Just and humane work conditions; maternity relief, e.g., Maternity Benefit Act.
44 State to endeavor for Uniform Civil Code, debated for gender equity.
46 Promote educational and economic interests, protect from injustice.
47 Raise nutrition levels and standard of living, linked to ICDS.
51A(e) Duty to renounce practices derogatory to women’s dignity, e.g., dowry.
243D 1/3rd reservation for women in PRIs/ULBs (50% in Gujarat, Bihar, MP).
106th Amendment, 2023 33% reservation in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies for 15 years.
- Legal Safeguards -
Year Legislation/Act Details
1860 Indian Penal Code (IPC) Sections 376, 498A, 509; Section 497 decriminalized in 2018.
1952 Cinematograph Act Censor Board curbs violence glorification; OTT regulation pending post-2019 Supreme Court directive.
1956 Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act Amended 1986 to strengthen anti-trafficking measures.
1961 Dowry Prohibition Act Amended 1986; reduced dowry deaths from 8,391 (2010) to 6,923 (2022, NCRB).
1961 Maternity Benefit Act Ensures maternity leave, amended 2017 for 26 weeks.
1971 Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act Regulates safe abortions, amended 2021 for gestational limits.
1976 Equal Remuneration Act Promotes wage equality, yet gaps persist (34%, ILO 2023).
1986 Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act Addresses maintenance post-divorce.
1987 Sati (Prevention) Act Penalizes Sati practice, rare enforcement cases.
1990 National Commission for Women Act Established NCW for women’s rights advocacy.
1992 Infant Milk Substitutes Act Regulates infant food marketing.
1994 PCPNDT Act Prohibits sex selection, reduced sex ratio at birth to 929 (NFHS-5).
2000 Juvenile Justice Act Amended 2015 for child protection.
2005 Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act Addresses domestic abuse, 33% cases reported (NCRB 2022).
2005 Commission for Protection of Child Rights Act Established NCPCR.
2006 Prohibition of Child Marriage Act Replaced 1929 Act, enforces age 18.
2012 POCSO Act Protects children from sexual offences.
2013 POSH Act Based on 1997 Vishakha Guidelines, ensures workplace safety.
2019 Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act Bans Triple Talaq, effective 1st August.
- International Cooperation: Beijing+25 - 1995: - UN Beijing Declaration set gender equality goals. - 2010: - UN Women established (HQ: New York). - 2020: - Beijing+25 review assessed progress, India’s score improved from 0.54 to 0.60 (UN Women). - Demographic Insights (Census 2011) - Sex Ratio: - National 943; Highest - Kerala (1,084), Puducherry (1,038); Lowest - Haryana (879), Punjab (895). - Policy Link: - Beti Bachao Beti Padhao targets skewed ratios. - Institutional Framework - Ministry of Women and Child Development (WCD) - Statutory Bodies: - National Commission for Women (NCW), National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR), Central Adoption Resource Agency (CARA). - Autonomous Bodies (Pre-2023 Shutdown): - NIPCCD (HQ: Delhi), Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (RMK), Central Social Welfare Board, Food and Nutrition Board. - International Partner: - UNICEF (1946, HQ: New York). - Policies: - 2001 National Policy for Empowerment of Women; 2016 Draft Policy. - Observances: - 8th March - International Women’s Day (Nari Shakti Puraskar named after historical figures). - Gender Disparities and Son-Meta Preference - Son-Meta Preference: - Couples prioritize sons, leading to 21 million “unwanted girls” (Economic Survey 2017-18). - Consequences: - Neglect (anaemia in 57% women, NFHS-5), high Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR: 103/100,000), child marriages (26% of girls, UNICEF 2023). - Mitigation: - PCPNDT Act enforcement reduced sex ratio at birth from 918 (2011) to 929 (NFHS-5). - Policy Initiatives: Marriage Age Reform -
Year Initiative Details
1929 Sharda Act Minimum marriage age 15, raised to 18 in 1978.
2020 Jaya Jaitley Task Force Proposed raising to 21, linked to nutrition and career outcomes.
2021 Prohibition of Child Marriage (Amendment) Bill Awaiting passage to enforce age 21.
- Global Recognition - Nobel 2023 - Claudia Goldin - Research: - U-shaped female LFPR with economic growth, driven by education and service sector expansion. - India Context: - LFPR rose from 23.3% (2017-18) to 37% (PLFS 2022-23) due to skill programs. - Gender Indices - UNDP Gender Inequality Index (GII, 2023) -

- Institutional Support - National Council for Transgender Persons (2019): - Statutory body with 5 transgender members. - SMILE Scheme - Support for transgender welfare and beggars’ rehabilitation. - Conclusion - HRD for weaker sections requires integrated policy action, addressing constitutional commitments, global benchmarks, and societal attitudes for equitable development. - Pillar 6E1: Human Development - Introduction: - Human development, a paradigm shift from traditional economic growth metrics, evaluates the richness of human life through well-being, education, and living standards, as conceptualized by economists Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen. It reflects India’s evolving policy focus on inclusive growth, aligning with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047. - Three foundations: - Live a healthy and creative life (e.g., access to healthcare and cultural expression). - Be knowledgeable (e.g., universal education and skill development). - Achieve a decent standard of living (e.g., adequate income and housing). - Four pillars: - Equity (reducing disparities across gender, caste, and regions). - Sustainability (balancing development with environmental conservation). - Productivity (enhancing human capital for economic output). - Empowerment (fostering agency and participation in governance). - Four approaches (NCERT): -
Approach Description
Income Approach Oldest method; assumes higher income correlates with better human development, criticized for ignoring non-monetary well-being (e.g., India’s GDP growth vs. poverty persistence).
Welfare Approach Views people as passive beneficiaries, necessitating state intervention via schemes like Ayushman Bharat and Samagra Shiksha, prevalent in post-colonial welfare states.
Basic Needs Approach Proposed by the International Labour Organisation (ILO) in the 1970s post-oil crisis, emphasizes six needs: health, education, food, water supply, sanitation, housing, influencing India’s rural development programs.
Capability Approach Developed by Amartya Sen, focuses on expanding human capabilities (e.g., health, education, resource access) rather than mere outcomes, underpinning India’s focus on skill development and women’s empowerment.
- Social Capital: - NCERT classification of social resources: -
Type Description Examples
Economic Capital Material assets and income, critical for accessing opportunities in a market economy. Money for college admission, property ownership.
Cultural/Educational Capital Educational qualifications and social status, shaping employability and social mobility. Degrees, certifications, cultural heritage knowledge.
Social Capital Networks of contacts and social associations, vital for job opportunities and community support in India’s diverse society. Connections aiding access to advice, jobs, or political influence.
- Relevance: Strengthens community resilience (e.g., SHGs under NRLM) and governance (e.g., Panchayati Raj Institutions). - Social Overhead Capital: - Encompasses infrastructure like transportation, education, healthcare, water, and electricity utilities, foundational for long-term economic growth and human development. - Economic Survey 2023: - Highlighted India’s ₹10 lakh crore investment in social overhead capital (e.g., PM Gram Sadak Yojana, Jal Jeevan Mission), addressing rural-urban disparities. - Policy Implication: - Critical for achieving SDG targets like Goal 6 (clean water) and Goal 9 (infrastructure). - UNDP Human Development Report: - Published annually by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in New York, under the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), since 1990, based on the pioneering work of Mahbub ul Haq (Pakistan) and Amartya Sen (India). - Mahbub ul Haq’s legacy: - Shifted global focus from GDP to human-centric development, influencing India’s Five-Year Plans. - Themes: -
Year Theme
2020-Dec Next frontier: Human development and the Anthropocene (addressing climate change impacts).
2021 No report published (due to global disruptions from COVID-19).
2022-Sep Uncertain times, unsettled lives: Shaping our future in a transforming world (covers 2021-22, post-pandemic recovery).
2023-24 Breaking the gridlock: Reimagining cooperation in a polarized world (ranks for 2022, emphasizes global collaboration).
2025-May A matter of choice: People and possibilities in the age of AI (ranks for 2023, explores AI’s role in human development).
- Provides five indices: - Human Development Index (HDI, 1990): - Measures health, education, and income. - Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI, 2010): - Captures deprivations in health, education, and living standards (e.g., India’s MPI declined from 55.1% in 2005-06 to 16.4% in 2019-21 per NITI Aayog). - Gender Inequality Index (GII, 2010): - Assesses gender disparities in reproductive health, empowerment, and labor market participation. - Gender Development Index (GDI, 2014): - Compares female and male HDI. - Planetary Pressures-adjusted HDI (PHDI, 2020): - Adjusts HDI for environmental impact (e.g., CO2 emissions). - UNDP Human Development Index (HDI): - Geometric average of three dimensions: -

- Analysis: - Steady improvement reflects policy interventions, but 2020-21 dip highlights vulnerability to global shocks. - UNDP Inequality Adjusted HDI: - Adjusts HDI for inequality in health, education, income. - India: - HDI (0.644), Inequality-adjusted HDI (0.444; 31% loss due to inequality), indicating significant disparities (e.g., rural vs. urban). - Relevance: - Highlights need for targeted schemes like PMAY-G. - UNDP Gender Development Index (GDI): - Ratio of Female HDI to Male HDI. - Nations grouped (1–5), not ranked; India in Group 5 (with Niger, Chad) due to low female labor force participation (23.3% vs. 82% male, PLFS 2022-23). - GDI >1 possible if female indicators surpass males (e.g., Estonia, Latvia due to male health issues). - UNDP Planetary Pressures-adjusted HDI (PHDI): - Started 2020, adjusts HDI for carbon dioxide emissions (India: - 1.7 tons per capita) and material footprint. - Scores (2024): - Iceland (HDI: 0.972, PHDI: 0.735), India (HDI: 0.685, PHDI: 0.656). - Policy Link: - Aligns with India’s net-zero target by 2070. - UNSDSN World Happiness Report: - Annual since 2012 by the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network, based on Gallup World Poll data. - Scores (0–10) derived from income, freedom, life expectancy, social support, generosity, corruption perception. - Rankings: -

- Comparative Analysis: - China (56/143), Pakistan (108/143), Nepal (93/143), Bhutan (87/143), Sri Lanka (128/143), Bangladesh (115/143) rank higher, reflecting India’s challenges with mental health, income inequality, and social trust. - Policy Implication: - Necessitates focus on mental health (e.g., National Mental Health Programme) and social cohesion. - World Bank Human Capital Index: - Launched 2018, measures health and education impact on future productivity. - Components: - Child survival rate (under-5 mortality: India 28/1,000 live births, NFHS-5). - Expected years of schooling (India 13 years, UDISE+ 2022). - Health (under-5 stunting: 31.7%, adult survival rate: 87%). - India rejected the report (2018), citing methodological flaws (e.g., underestimation of health infrastructure) and data gaps, sparking a debate on global indices’ applicability to developing nations. - Human Development Miscellaneous Indicators: -
Indicator Details
Gross National Happiness Index (GNHI) Coined 1972 by Bhutan’s fourth king Jigme Singye Wangchuck; measures sustainable development, environmental conservation, culture, governance via nine domains (e.g., psychological well-being, education), influencing India’s Gross National Happiness initiatives in the Northeast.
Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI) Developed mid-1970s by Morris D Morris to complement GDP; scores (1–100) based on life expectancy (India: 70), infant mortality (India: 28/1,000), literacy rate (India: 77.7%), used in early development planning.
Human Poverty Index Developed 1997 by UNDP to measure deprivation; replaced by MPI in 2010 due to its broader scope, reflecting India’s shift to multidimensional poverty assessment.

- Structure of the India Economy & Demographics PYQs - [1995] - Q1: According to the 1991 Census, the highest percentage of population in India is to be found in the age group of: - Options: (a) 60 years and above (b) 35 to 55 years (c) 25 to 34 years (d) 5 to 14 years - Answer: (d) 5 to 14 years - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The 1991 Census, conducted by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, captured India’s demographic profile during the onset of economic liberalization (1991). With a population of ~846 million, India had a youthful demographic due to high fertility rates (Total Fertility Rate ~4.5 in the 1970s–1980s) and improving life expectancy (~60 years). The 5–14 age group, representing school-age children, formed the largest segment, reflecting a broad-based population pyramid. - This youth bulge drove policies like Operation Blackboard (1986) for education and the Universal Immunization Programme (1985) for health, aiming to leverage the demographic dividend. - Why Not Others?: - (a) 60 years and above: Incorrect—Elderly population was ~6–7%, smaller due to lower life expectancy compared to developed nations. - (b) 35 to 55 years: Incorrect—Middle-aged workforce was significant but smaller than the youth cohort due to the pyramid’s tapering structure. - (c) 25 to 34 years: Incorrect—Young adults were a growing segment, but the 5–14 group was larger due to high birth rates in prior decades. - Additional Evidence: - 1991 Census Data: ~36–38% of the population was under 15 years, with the 5–14 age group being the largest single segment. - Population Pyramid: Broad base, narrow top, with 5–14 years as the widest band, driven by high fertility. - NFHS-1 (1992–93): High dependency ratio (0.95), with children (0–14 years) dominating, especially 5–14 years. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Demographic Transition: India in Stage 2 (high birth rates, declining death rates), explaining the youth bulge (links to Q10 [1996] on population and income). - Rajiv Gandhi: His policies (1984–1989) targeted youth education (e.g., Operation Blackboard), addressing the 5–14 group’s needs. - Family Planning Programme (1952–): Slow impact in the 1980s kept child population high. - Amartya Sen: His human development work (e.g., Q13 [1997] on HDI) emphasized education for young populations. - Key Takeaway: - The 1991 Census highlighted a youthful India, with the 5–14 age group dominant, driving policies for education and health to harness the demographic dividend. - Q2: Which of the following pairs are correctly matched? - List-I: 1. Increase in - Monetary expansion 2. Low import growth rate in India - Recession in Indian industry 3. Euro-issues - Shares held by Indian companies in European countries 4. Portfolio investment - Foreign institutional investors - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 4 (b) 3 & 4 (c) 1, 2 & 3 (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (a) 1, 2 & 4 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In 1991, India’s economic liberalization, led by Manmohan Singh and P.V. Narasimha Rao, addressed a balance of payments crisis, opening markets to foreign investment. Pair 1 (Increase in - Monetary expansion) reflects RBI’s use of money supply growth to stimulate the economy. Pair 2 (Low import growth - Recession) captures pre-reform industrial stagnation due to forex shortages. Pair 4 (Portfolio investment - FIIs) aligns with post-1991 FII entry into Indian markets. Pair 3 (Euro-issues) is incorrect, as Euro-issues are financial instruments (e.g., GDRs) issued abroad, not shares held in European firms. - Why Not Others?: - (b) 3 & 4: Incorrect—Pair 3 is wrong; Euro-issues are not shares in European companies. - (c) 1, 2 & 3: Incorrect—Pair 3 is wrong, invalidating this option. - (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4: Incorrect—Pair 3’s error excludes this. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Reforms (1991): FIIs were allowed via SEBI, with $1.6 billion inflows by 1993–94 (Pair 4). Forex reserves fell to $1.1 billion in 1990, causing low imports and industrial recession (Pair 2). RBI used monetary expansion via CRR cuts (Pair 1). Euro-issues like Reliance’s GDRs (1992) raised capital abroad, not shares held in Europe (Pair 3). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Manmohan Singh: Architect of 1991 reforms, enabling FIIs and Euro-issues. - Narasimham Committee: Recommended FII liberalization (Q4 [1995]). - SEBI (1992): Regulated FIIs, ensuring market transparency. - Key Takeaway: - The 1991 reforms introduced monetary expansion, FII portfolio investments, and addressed pre-reform industrial challenges, with Euro-issues misunderstood as local shareholding. - Q3: Which one of the following is true regarding the Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY)? - Options: (a) It was launched during the Prime Ministership of Indira Gandhi (b) It aims at creating one million jobs annually (c) The target group of JRY are the urban poor living below the poverty line (d) Under the scheme 30% of the employment generated is reserved for women - Answer: (d) Under the scheme 30% of the employment generated is reserved for women - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY), launched in April 1989 under Rajiv Gandhi’s government, was a flagship rural employment scheme consolidating earlier programs like the National Rural Employment Programme (NREP) and Rural Landless Employment Guarantee Programme (RLEGP). It aimed to provide wage employment to rural poor below the poverty line, with a mandate to reserve 30% of jobs for women to promote gender equity in rural labor markets. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Launched in 1989 under Rajiv Gandhi, not Indira Gandhi (PM until 1984). - (b) Incorrect: JRY aimed to provide employment, not specifically one million jobs annually; targets varied by region and funding. - (c) Incorrect: JRY targeted rural poor, not urban poor, focusing on village-level infrastructure development. - Additional Evidence: - JRY Guidelines: Emphasized 30% women’s participation, implemented through Panchayati Raj institutions, with funds allocated to village-level projects (e.g., roads, wells). - Economic Survey (1989–90): Noted JRY’s focus on rural employment, with ~700 million person-days of work generated annually, prioritizing marginalized groups like women. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Rajiv Gandhi: Launched JRY, aligning with rural development goals (links to Q150 [2023-I] on Janani Suraksha Yojana). - Poverty Alleviation: JRY was part of India’s anti-poverty strategy, alongside IRDP (Q10 [1995]). - MGNREGA (2005): JRY’s successor, also reserving 33% jobs for women, reflecting continuity (Q54 [2019-I]). - Key Takeaway: - JRY’s 30% reservation for women reflects India’s commitment to gender-inclusive rural employment in the late 1980s, a precursor to modern schemes like MGNREGA. - Q4: The Narasimham Committee for financial sector reforms has suggested reduction in: - Options: (a) SLR and CRR (b) SLR, CRR and Priority Sector Financing (c) SLR and Financing to capital goods sector (d) CRR, Priority Sector Financing and Financing to capital goods sector - Answer: (b) SLR, CRR and Priority Sector Financing - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Narasimham Committee (1991) recommended reducing Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) and Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) to enhance bank liquidity and rationalizing priority sector lending to improve efficiency, aligning with India’s 1991 liberalization goals. - Why Original Answer (a) Incorrect: - The original answer (a) omitted priority sector financing, a key reform area where the committee suggested refining targets, not just reducing SLR/CRR. - Why Not Others?: - (c) Incorrect: No specific recommendation targeted capital goods sector financing. - (d) Incorrect: Capital goods financing was not a focus. - Additional Evidence: - Narasimham Committee Report (1991): Proposed SLR reduction from 38.5% to 25%, CRR from 15% to 10%, and priority sector lending rationalization. - RBI Annual Report (1992–93): Implemented phased reductions, with priority sector targets adjusted. - Related Concepts/Figures: - M. Narasimham: Led banking reforms. - Financial Liberalization: Supported credit flow (Q2 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - The committee’s reforms, including priority sector adjustments, shaped India’s banking efficiency post-1991. - Q5: Corporation tax: - Options: (a) is levied and appropriated by the States (b) is levied by the Union and collected and appropriated by the States (c) is levied by the Union and shared by the Union and the States (d) is levied by the Union and belongs to it exclusively - Answer: (d) is levied by the Union and belongs to it exclusively - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Corporation tax, levied on company profits, is a Union tax under Article 246, Seventh Schedule. Post-2000, the 80th Constitutional Amendment made it non-shareable with states, unlike pre-2000 when it was shared via the Finance Commission. - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - In 1995, corporation tax was shareable (10th Finance Commission), but by 2025, post-2000 reforms, it’s exclusively Union revenue, making (d) correct. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: States cannot levy corporation tax. - (b) Incorrect: States neither collect nor appropriate it. - Additional Evidence: - Constitution (80th Amendment, 2000): Made corporation tax non-shareable. - Economic Survey (2024–25): Corporation tax ~15% of Union revenue, retained fully. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Federalism: Evolved post-2000 (Q149 [2023-I]). - Finance Commission: Excludes corporation tax now. - Key Takeaway: - Corporation tax’s exclusive Union status post-2000 reflects India’s centralized fiscal policy. - Q6: One of the reasons for India's occupational structure remaining more or less the same over the years has been that: - Options: (a) investment pattern has been directed towards capital intensive industries (b) productivity in agriculture has been high enough to induce people to stay with agriculture (c) ceiling on land holdings have enabled more people to own land and hence their preference to stay with agriculture (d) people are largely unaware of the significance of transition from agriculture to industry for economic development - Answer: (a) investment pattern has been directed towards capital intensive industries - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In the post-independence era (1947–1990s), India’s occupational structure remained predominantly agrarian (~70% in agriculture in 1991), with slow industrial growth. The Second Five-Year Plan (1956–61) emphasized capital-intensive industries (e.g., steel, heavy machinery) under the Mahalanobis model, prioritizing industrial growth over labor-intensive sectors, limiting job creation and structural shift. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Agricultural productivity was low, with stagnant yields (e.g., 1.3 tons/ha for rice in 1990s). - (c) Incorrect: Land ceiling laws (1960s–70s) redistributed land but didn’t significantly increase ownership or retain workers in agriculture. - (d) Incorrect: Awareness existed, but structural constraints limited transitions. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (1994–95): Agriculture employed ~65% of the workforce, with industry at ~15%. - Planning Commission: Capital-intensive focus in Five-Year Plans restricted labor absorption. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Mahalanobis Model: Prioritized heavy industries (Q7 [1995]). - Green Revolution: Boosted agriculture but not enough to retain workers (Q150 [2023-I]). - Amartya Sen: Highlighted structural issues in occupational shifts. - Key Takeaway: - Capital-intensive investment patterns post-independence hindered occupational diversification, keeping India’s workforce agrarian. - Q7: The main reason for low growth rate in India, inspite of high rate of savings and capital formation is: - Options: (a) high birth rate (b) low level of foreign aid (c) low capital output ratio (d) high capital output ratio - Answer: (d) high capital output ratio - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In the 1990s, India had high savings (~23% of GDP) and capital formation but low GDP growth (~5–6%) due to a high Incremental Capital Output Ratio (ICOR), indicating inefficiency in capital utilization. A high ICOR (e.g., 4–5) meant more capital was needed per unit of output, reflecting inefficiencies in public sector enterprises and infrastructure. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: High birth rates increased population but weren’t the primary growth constraint. - (b) Incorrect: Foreign aid was low but not the main issue post-1991 liberalization. - (c) Incorrect: A low ICOR would imply efficient growth, contrary to India’s case. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (1994–95): ICOR was ~4.5, indicating capital inefficiency. - World Bank Reports: Highlighted India’s public sector inefficiencies in the 1990s. - Related Concepts/Figures: - ICOR: Measures capital efficiency (Q6 [1995]). - P.C. Mahalanobis: His model led to high ICOR via capital-intensive focus. - 1991 Reforms: Aimed to reduce ICOR through privatization. - Key Takeaway: - High ICOR in the 1990s reflected inefficient capital use, limiting India’s growth despite high savings and investment. - [1996] - Q8: Which one of the following is correct regarding stabilization and structural adjustment as two components of the new economic policy adopted in India? - Options: (a) Stabilization is a gradual, multi-step process while structural adjustment is a quick adaptation process (b) Structural adjustment is a gradual multi-step process, while stabilization is a quick adaptation process (c) Stabilization and structural adjustment are very similar and complimentary policies (d) Stabilization mainly deals with a set of policies which are to be implemented by the Central government while structural adjustment is to be set in motion by the State governments - Answer: (a) Stabilization is a gradual, multi-step process while structural adjustment is a quick adaptation process - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The 1991 New Economic Policy (NEP) included stabilization (e.g., fiscal deficit control, monetary tightening) as a phased process and structural adjustment (e.g., trade liberalization) as rapid reforms to align with global markets. - Why Original Answer (b) Incorrect: - The original answer reversed the timelines; stabilization was gradual (e.g., deficit reduction over years), while structural adjustment (e.g., delicensing) was implemented quickly in 1991–92. - Why Not Others?: - (c) Incorrect: They are distinct, with different timelines. - (d) Incorrect: Both are Central government policies. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (1991–92): Structural reforms like devaluation were immediate, stabilization phased. - IMF Loan (1991): Supported rapid structural changes. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Manmohan Singh: NEP architect (Q2 [1995]). - Balance of Payments: Stabilization focus (Q2 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - NEP’s rapid structural adjustments contrasted with gradual stabilization, shaping India’s economy. - Q9: One of the important goals of the economic liberalisation policy is to achieve full convertibility of the Indian rupee. This is being advocated because: - Options: (a) convertibility of the rupee will stabilize its exchange value against major currencies of the world (b) it will attract more foreign capital inflow in India (c) it will help to promote exports (d) it will help India secure loans from the world financial markets at attractive terms - Answer: (a) convertibility of the rupee will stabilize its exchange value against major currencies - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Full rupee convertibility, pursued post-1991, aimed to stabilize exchange rates by aligning the rupee with market forces, reducing volatility via current and capital account convertibility (achieved partially in 1994). - Why Original Answer (b) Incorrect: - While convertibility attracted FDI, the primary goal was exchange rate stability, as volatility deterred trade and investment in the 1990s. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: FDI was a secondary benefit. - (c) Incorrect: Exports were aided but not the primary goal. - (d) Incorrect: Loan terms depend on creditworthiness. - Additional Evidence: - Tarapore Committee (1997): Emphasized convertibility for stability. - RBI Report (1995–96): Convertibility reduced rupee volatility. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Tarapore Committee: Guided convertibility (Q20 [1998]). - FDI/FII: Secondary outcomes (Q2 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - Convertibility aimed to stabilize the rupee, a key liberalization goal. - Q10: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R): - Assertion (A): Though India's national income has gone up several fold since 1947, there has been no marked improvement in the per capita income level. - Reason (R): Sizeable proportion of the population of India is still living below the poverty line. - Options: (a) Both A & R are true & R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A & R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (b) Both A & R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Post-1947, India’s national income (GDP) grew significantly due to industrialization and Green Revolution, but per capita income remained low (~$300 in 1991) due to high population growth (~2% annually). Poverty remained high (~36% below the poverty line in 1993–94), but it doesn’t directly explain stagnant per capita income, which is more tied to population growth diluting GDP gains. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Poverty (R) doesn’t directly cause low per capita income; population growth does. - (c) Incorrect: R is true; poverty was prevalent. - (d) Incorrect: A is true; per capita income growth was slow. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (1995–96): GDP grew ~5% annually, but per capita income growth was ~2–3% due to population. - NFHS-1 (1992–93): High fertility rates (~4.5) drove population growth, diluting income gains. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Demographic Dividend: Population growth’s impact (Q1 [1995]). - Amartya Sen: Analyzed poverty and income (Q13 [1997]). - Planning Commission: Tracked poverty trends (Q3 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - India’s post-1947 growth was offset by population growth, not poverty alone, limiting per capita income gains. - Q11: A redistribution of income in a country can be best brought about through: - Options: (a) progressive taxation combined with progressive expenditure (b) progressive taxation combined with regressive expenditure (c) regressive taxation combined with regressive expenditure (d) regressive taxation combined with progressive expenditure - Answer: (b) progressive taxation combined with regressive expenditure - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Progressive taxation (higher rates for higher incomes) paired with regressive expenditure (broad-based spending benefiting all, e.g., infrastructure) effectively redistributes income by taxing the wealthy and funding universal services. - Why Original Answer (a) Incorrect: - Progressive expenditure (targeting only the poor) is less effective in 1990s India, where broad infrastructure spending had wider redistribution impacts. - Why Not Others?: - (c) Incorrect: Regressive systems favor the wealthy. - (d) Incorrect: Regressive taxation undermines redistribution. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (1995–96): Infrastructure spending (regressive) complemented progressive taxes. - Income Tax Act (1961): Progressive slabs (10–40%). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Policy: Redistribution tool (Q5 [1995]). - JRY: Broad expenditure example (Q3 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - Progressive taxation with regressive expenditure balanced redistribution in 1990s India. - Q12: As per the 1991 Census, the average size of households in terms of number of persons per household in respect of the given states follows the sequence (highest first, lowest last): - Options: (a) Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Tamil Nadu (b) Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Gujarat, Kerala (c) Gujarat, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal (d) Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Kerala - Answer: (b) Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Gujarat, Kerala - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The 1991 Census reported average household sizes influenced by fertility rates, cultural practices, and urbanization. Uttar Pradesh had the highest (~6.5 persons) due to high fertility (~5.0 TFR). West Bengal (~5.5) and Gujarat (~5.3) followed, with Kerala lowest (~4.5) due to advanced demographic transition (TFR ~2.0). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Haryana’s household size (~5.8) was lower than Uttar Pradesh. - (c) Incorrect: Gujarat higher than Uttar Pradesh is incorrect. - (d) Incorrect: Tamil Nadu (~4.8) was higher than Kerala. - Additional Evidence: - 1991 Census: Uttar Pradesh (6.5), West Bengal (5.5), Gujarat (5.3), Kerala (4.5). - NFHS-1 (1992–93): Kerala’s low TFR and high literacy reduced household size. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Demographic Transition: Kerala’s advanced stage (Q1 [1995]). - Family Planning: Influenced household sizes (Q10 [1996]). - T.N. Madan: Sociologist studying Indian family structures. - Key Takeaway: - The 1991 Census showed regional household size variations, with Uttar Pradesh highest and Kerala lowest, reflecting fertility and development differences. - [1997] - Q13: Human Development Index comprises literacy rates, life expectancy at birth and: - Options: (a) Gross National Product per head in the US dollars (b) Gross Domestic Product per head at real purchasing power (c) Gross National Product in US dollars (d) National Income per head in US dollars - Answer: (d) National Income per head in US dollars - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Human Development Index (HDI), introduced by UNDP in 1990, used national income per head in USD in 1997 to measure economic well-being, alongside literacy and life expectancy. - Why Original Answer (b) Incorrect: - GDP per capita at PPP became standard later; in 1997, HDI used national income in USD for simpler global comparisons. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: GNP per head was not used. - (b) Incorrect: PPP was adopted post-1997. - (c) Incorrect: Total GNP is not per capita. - Additional Evidence: - UNDP HDR (1997): Used national income in USD. - India’s HDI: ~0.45, with national income ~$450. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Amartya Sen: HDI co-developer. - UNDP: Publishes HDI (Q23 [1998]). - Key Takeaway: - HDI’s 1997 use of national income in USD reflected economic well-being. - Q14: In India, inflation is measured by the: - Options: (a) Wholesale Price Index number (b) Consumers Price Index for urban non-manual workers (c) Consumers Price Index for agricultural workers (d) National Income Deflation - Answer: (a) Wholesale Price Index number - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In the 1990s, India measured inflation primarily via the Wholesale Price Index (WPI), which tracks price changes of goods at the wholesale level. WPI was preferred for its broad coverage of commodities, unlike CPI, which was sector-specific. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: CPI (urban non-manual) was used for specific groups, not general inflation. - (c) Incorrect: CPI (agricultural workers) was limited to rural labor. - (d) Incorrect: National Income Deflation is not an inflation measure. - Additional Evidence: - RBI Reports (1990s): WPI-based inflation was ~8–10% in the mid-1990s. - Economic Survey (1996–97): WPI as the primary inflation metric. - Related Concepts/Figures: - RBI: Manages inflation (Q147 [2023-I]). - WPI vs. CPI: Shift to CPI in 2011 (Q14 [1997]). - P.V. Narasimha Rao: Oversaw inflation control post-1991. - Key Takeaway: - WPI was India’s primary inflation measure in the 1990s, reflecting its commodity-focused economy. - Q15: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R): - Assertion (A): The emergence of economic globalism does not imply the decline of socialist ideology. - Reason (R): The ideology of socialism believes in Universalism and globalism. - Options: (a) Both A & R are true & R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A & R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (b) Both A & R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In 1990s India, globalism (via liberalization) coexisted with socialist policies (e.g., JRY). Socialism’s universalist ideals align with globalism, but this doesn’t explain socialism’s persistence, which was due to political and welfare priorities. - Why Original Answer Correct: - The original answer aligns with the correct reasoning; socialism persisted due to India’s mixed economy, not just universalism. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Universalism doesn’t explain socialism’s persistence. - (c) Incorrect: R is true; socialism supports universalism. - (d) Incorrect: A is true; socialism continued. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (1996–97): Mixed economy retained socialist policies. - Planning Commission: Welfare focus post-1991. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Mixed Economy: India’s model (Q8 [1996]). - 1991 Reforms: Balanced globalism, socialism. - Key Takeaway: - Socialism persisted in 1990s India despite globalism, not solely due to universalism. - Q16: National Income is: - Options: (a) Net National Product at market price (b) Net National Product at factor cost (c) Net Domestic Product at market price (d) Net Domestic Product at factor cost - Answer: (b) Net National Product at factor cost - Analysis: - Historical Context: - National Income in India is measured as Net National Product (NNP) at factor cost, reflecting income earned by residents, adjusted for depreciation and subsidies/taxes. In the 1990s, this was the standard metric for economic planning. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: NNP at market price includes indirect taxes, not reflecting true factor income. - (c) Incorrect: NDP excludes foreign income, unlike NNP. - (d) Incorrect: NDP at factor cost is domestic-focused, not national. - Additional Evidence: - CSO (1990s): Used NNP at factor cost for National Income. - Economic Survey (1996–97): Reported NNP at factor cost as ~₹10 lakh crore. - Related Concepts/Figures: - CSO: Tracks national income (Q10 [1996]). - National Income Accounting: Basis for GDP metrics. - Montek Singh Ahluwalia: Shaped 1990s economic data policies. - Key Takeaway: - NNP at factor cost as National Income captures India’s economic output accurately, central to 1990s planning. - Q17: The Minimum Alternative Tax (MAT) was introduced in the Budget of the Government of India for the year: - Options: (a) 1991-92 (b) 1992-93 (c) 1995-96 (d) 1996-97 - Answer: (d) 1996-97 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT), introduced in the 1996–97 Union Budget by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, ensured companies with high book profits but low taxable income (due to exemptions) paid a minimum tax, addressing tax avoidance post-liberalization. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: 1991–92 focused on liberalization, not MAT. - (b) Incorrect: 1992–93 had no MAT introduction. - (c) Incorrect: 1995–96 preceded MAT’s introduction. - Additional Evidence: - Finance Act (1996): Introduced MAT under Section 115JA at ~7.5% of book profits. - Economic Survey (1996–97): Highlighted MAT to boost tax revenue. - Related Concepts/Figures: - P. Chidambaram: Introduced MAT (Q18 [1997]). - Tax Reforms: Linked to Narasimham Committee (Q4 [1995]). - Corporate Tax: Shared with states (Q5 [1995]). - Broader Connection: - Links to tax policy (Q5 [1995]), reforms (Q18 [1997]), and fiscal measures (Q149 [2023-I]). Reflects post-liberalization tax restructuring. - Key Takeaway: - MAT’s 1996 introduction addressed tax avoidance, strengthening India’s fiscal framework post-liberalization. - Q18: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer: - List-I (Committee): A. Disinvestment of shares in Public Sector Enterprises B. Industrial Sickness C. Tax Reforms D. Reforms in Insurance Sector - List-II (Chaired by): 1. Rajah Chelliah 2. Omkar Goswami 3. R.N. Malhotra 4. C. Rangarajan - Options: (a) A-1, B-4, C-2, D-3 (b) A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3 (c) A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3 (d) A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2 - Answer: (b) A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Post-1991, committees addressed economic challenges. C. Rangarajan (Disinvestment), Omkar Goswami (Industrial Sickness, 1993), Rajah Chelliah (Tax Reforms, 1992), and R.N. Malhotra (Insurance Reforms, 1994) led key reforms to align with liberalization goals. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Mismatches A, B, C. - (c) Incorrect: Swaps B and C incorrectly. - (d) Incorrect: Mismatches all pairs. - Additional Evidence: - Rangarajan Committee (1991): Recommended PSE disinvestment. - Goswami Committee (1993): Addressed sick industries. - Chelliah Committee (1992): Proposed tax rationalization. - Malhotra Committee (1994): Suggested insurance liberalization. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Narasimham Committee: Banking reforms (Q4 [1995]). - 1991 Reforms: Context for these committees (Q8 [1996]). - P. Chidambaram: Implemented tax reforms (Q17 [1997]). - Key Takeaway: - Specialized committees in the 1990s drove India’s liberalization, addressing disinvestment, industrial sickness, taxes, and insurance. - Q19: What is the correct sequence of the descending order of the following States in respect of female literacy rates as per the 2001 census? - List: 1. Mizoram 2. Kerala 3. Goa 4. Nagaland - Options: (a) 2, 1, 3, 4 (b) 2, 3, 4, 1 (c) 2, 4, 1, 3 (d) 1, 2, 4, 3 - Answer: (a) 2, 1, 3, 4 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The 2001 Census reported female literacy rates: Kerala (~87.7%), Mizoram (~86.7%), Goa (~75.4%), Nagaland (~61.5%). Kerala’s lead reflects its social development model, while Mizoram’s high literacy stems from missionary education. Goa’s urbanized society and Nagaland’s tribal context explain their rankings. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Goa higher than Mizoram is wrong. - (c) Incorrect: Nagaland higher than Mizoram is incorrect. - (d) Incorrect: Mizoram higher than Kerala is wrong. - Additional Evidence: - 2001 Census: Confirmed Kerala’s lead, followed by Mizoram, Goa, Nagaland. - NFHS-2 (1998–99): Supported high literacy in Kerala and Mizoram. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Kerala Model: High literacy and HDI (Q13 [1997]). - Missionary Education: Boosted Mizoram’s literacy. - Amartya Sen: Linked literacy to development. - Key Takeaway: - The 2001 Census underscored Kerala’s lead in female literacy, reflecting its social development success, followed by Mizoram, Goa, and Nagaland. - [1998] - Q20: The Capital Account Convertibility of the Indian Rupee implies: - Options: (a) that the Indian Rupee can be exchanged by the authorised dealers for travel (b) that the Indian Rupee can be exchanged for any major currency for the purpose of trade in goods and services (c) that the Indian Rupee can be exchanged for any major currency for the purpose of trading financial assets (d) None of the above - Answer: (c) that the Indian Rupee can be exchanged for any major currency for the purpose of trading financial assets - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Capital Account Convertibility (CAC) allows unrestricted exchange of the rupee for financial assets (e.g., stocks, bonds) abroad. In 1998, India had partial current account convertibility (1994) but was cautious about full CAC due to volatility risks, as recommended by the Tarapore Committee (1997). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Travel-related exchange is current account, not capital account. - (b) Incorrect: Trade in goods/services is current account convertibility. - (d) Incorrect: CAC is correctly defined in (c). - Additional Evidence: - Tarapore Committee (1997): Outlined CAC roadmap (Q9 [1996]). - RBI Reports (1998): Noted cautious approach to CAC post-Asian Financial Crisis. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Tarapore Committee: Guided CAC (Q9 [1996]). - 1991 Reforms: Set stage for convertibility (Q8 [1996]). - SEBI: Regulated FIIs under CAC (Q2 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - CAC focuses on financial asset trading, a cautious liberalization goal in 1998 to boost capital flows. - Q21: A consumer is said to be in equilibrium, if: - Options: (a) he is able to fulfil his need with a given level of income (b) he is able to live in full comforts with a given level of income (c) he can fulfil his needs without consumption of certain items (d) he is able to locate new sources of income - Answer: (a) he is able to fulfil his need with a given level of income - Analysis: - Historical Context: - In microeconomics, consumer equilibrium occurs when a consumer maximizes utility within their budget constraint, allocating income to fulfill needs optimally. In 1990s India, rising consumer markets post-liberalization made this concept relevant. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: “Full comforts” is subjective, not economic equilibrium. - (c) Incorrect: Non-consumption of items doesn’t define equilibrium. - (d) Incorrect: New income sources are irrelevant to equilibrium. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Theory: Utility maximization at budget constraint (Varian, Microeconomics). - Economic Survey (1997–98): Rising consumption post-liberalization reflected consumer behavior. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Utility Theory: Basis for consumer equilibrium. - Amartya Sen: Linked consumer behavior to welfare (Q13 [1997]). - Market Reforms: Boosted consumer markets (Q8 [1996]). - Key Takeaway: - Consumer equilibrium involves optimal need fulfillment within income, a key microeconomic concept in 1990s India. - Q22: The supply-side economics lays greater emphasis on the point of view of: - Options: (a) producer (b) global economy (c) consumer (d) middle-man - Answer: (a) producer - Analysis: - Historical Context: - Supply-side economics, prominent in the 1980s–90s globally, emphasizes boosting production through tax cuts, deregulation, and incentives for producers. In India, 1991 reforms (e.g., industrial delicensing) aligned with supply-side principles to enhance producer efficiency. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Global economy is secondary; focus is on domestic producers. - (c) Incorrect: Consumer focus is demand-side economics. - (d) Incorrect: Middlemen are not the primary focus. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (1997–98): Deregulation boosted industrial production. - Narasimham Committee: Supported producer-friendly banking reforms (Q4 [1995]). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Supply-Side Policies: Tax cuts, deregulation (Q8 [1996]). - Manmohan Singh: Implemented producer-friendly reforms. - Reaganomics: Global supply-side influence. - Key Takeaway: - Supply-side economics prioritizes producers, aligning with India’s 1991 reform strategy to boost industrial output. - Q23: Human Poverty Index was introduced in the Human Development Report of the year: - Options: (a) 1994 (b) 1995 (c) 1996 (d) 1997 - Answer: (d) 1997 - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Human Poverty Index (HPI), introduced by UNDP in 1997, measures deprivation in health, education, and living standards, complementing HDI (Q13 [1997]). India’s HPI in 1997 highlighted persistent poverty despite economic growth. - Why Not Others?: - (a), (b), (c) Incorrect: HPI was launched in 1997 HDR. - Additional Evidence: - UNDP HDR (1997): Introduced HPI, focusing on multidimensional poverty. - India’s HPI: ~40% in 1997, reflecting health and education gaps. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Amartya Sen: Influenced HPI’s multidimensional approach (Q13 [1997]). - UNDP: Developed HPI/HDI metrics. - Poverty Alleviation: Linked to JRY (Q3 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - HPI’s 1997 introduction emphasized deprivation, guiding India’s poverty alleviation efforts. - Q24: The current Price Index (base 1960) is nearly 330. This means that the price of: - Options: (a) all items cost 3.3 times more than what they did in 1960 (b) the price of certain selected items have gone upto 3.3 times (c) weighted mean of price of certain items has increased 3.3 times (d) gold price has gone up 3.3 times - Answer: (c) weighted mean of price of certain items has increased 3.3 times - Analysis: - Historical Context: - A Price Index (e.g., WPI in 1998) measures the weighted average price change of a basket of goods relative to a base year (1960). A value of 330 indicates prices rose 3.3 times, reflecting inflation in a weighted basket, not all items or specific ones like gold. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Not all items; only a selected basket. - (b) Incorrect: Not selected items individually but their weighted mean. - (d) Incorrect: Gold prices are not the focus of the general price index. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (1997–98): WPI inflation averaged 8–10% annually since 1960. - RBI: WPI as primary index (Q14 [1997]). - Related Concepts/Figures: - WPI: Inflation metric (Q14 [1997]). - RBI: Tracks price indices (Q147 [2023-I]). - Inflation: Impacts growth (Q7 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - A Price Index of 330 reflects a 3.3-fold rise in the weighted mean price of a goods basket, capturing inflation trends since 1960. - [1999] - Q25: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R): - Assertion (A): Devaluation of a currency may promote export. - Reason (R): Price of the country's products in the international market may fall due to devaluation. - Options: (a) Both A & R are true & R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A & R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A & R are true & R is the correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Devaluation, a deliberate reduction in a currency’s value by a government (e.g., India’s 1991 devaluation of the rupee), makes exports cheaper in foreign markets, boosting competitiveness. In 1991, India devalued the rupee by ~19% to address a balance of payments crisis, increasing export demand. The reason (R) correctly explains this, as lower export prices in foreign currencies drive higher demand. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: R directly explains A by linking price reduction to export promotion. - (c) Incorrect: R is true; devaluation reduces export prices. - (d) Incorrect: A is true; devaluation promotes exports. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (1991–92): Post-devaluation, exports grew ~40% in 1991–92. - RBI Report (1991): Rupee devaluation from ₹17.5 to ₹21.2 per USD enhanced export competitiveness. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Balance of Payments: Devaluation addressed 1991 crisis (Q2 [1995]). - Manmohan Singh: Oversaw 1991 devaluation as Finance Minister. - Export-Led Growth: Key post-1991 strategy (Q9 [1996]). - Key Takeaway: - Devaluation boosts exports by lowering prices in international markets, a critical 1991 reform strategy for India. - Q26: Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R): - Assertion (A): Fiscal deficit is greater than budgetary deficit. - Reason (R): Fiscal deficit is the borrowing from the Reserve Bank of India plus other liabilities of the Government to meet its expenditure. - Options: (a) Both A & R are true & R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A & R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A & R are true & R is the correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Fiscal deficit (expenditure minus receipts excluding borrowings) exceeds budgetary deficit (expenditure minus receipts including some borrowings) due to RBI borrowings and other liabilities in 1999 (~5.4% GDP). - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - The original answer assumed R was false, but fiscal deficit includes RBI borrowings and liabilities, making R a correct explanation. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: R explains A accurately. - (c) Incorrect: R is true. - (d) Incorrect: A is true. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (1998–99): Fiscal deficit included RBI borrowings. - Public Finance Statistics: Broader liabilities in fiscal deficit. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Deficit: Key metric (Q38 [2001]). - RBI: Deficit financing role (Q147 [2023-I]). - Key Takeaway: - Fiscal deficit’s broader scope, including RBI borrowings, explains its size in 1999. - Q27: Persons below the poverty line in India are classified as such based whether: - Options: (a) they are entitled to a minimum prescribed food basket (b) they get work for a prescribed minimum number of days in a year (c) they belong to agricultural labourer household and the scheduled caste/tribe social group (d) their daily wages fall below the prescribed minimum wages - Answer: (a) they are entitled to a minimum prescribed food basket - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In the 1990s, India’s poverty line was defined by the Planning Commission using a calorie-based approach, ensuring a minimum food basket (e.g., 2400 kcal/day rural, 2100 kcal/day urban). This was based on the Lakdawala Committee (1993), focusing on consumption expenditure for basic nutrition. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Employment days (e.g., JRY, Q3 [1995]) are outcomes, not poverty criteria. - (c) Incorrect: Social groups are correlated with poverty but not the definition. - (d) Incorrect: Wages are a factor, but poverty is consumption-based, not wage-based. - Supporting Evidence: - Lakdawala Committee (1993): Defined poverty line via calorie norms. - Economic Survey (1998–99): ~36% below poverty line based on consumption. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Poverty Line: Calorie-based metric (Q10 [1996]). - Planning Commission: Set poverty norms (Q29 [1999]). - JRY: Targeted poverty alleviation (Q3 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - India’s 1990s poverty line was based on a minimum food basket, reflecting a consumption-based approach to deprivation. - Q28: Which one of the following statements regarding the levying, collecting and distribution of Income Tax is correct? - Options: (a) The Union levies, collects and distributes the proceeds of income tax between itself and the states (b) The Union levies, collects and keeps all the proceeds of income tax to itself (c) The Union levies and collects the tax but all the proceeds are distributed among the states (d) Only the surcharge levied on income tax is shared between the Union and the states - Answer: (a) The Union levies, collects and distributes the proceeds of income tax between itself and the states - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Under the Indian Constitution (Article 270), income tax is levied and collected by the Union but shared with states per Finance Commission recommendations. In 1999, the 10th Finance Commission (1995–2000) allocated ~29% of income tax to states, ensuring fiscal federalism. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Income tax is shared, not retained entirely by the Union. - (c) Incorrect: Not all proceeds go to states; the Union retains a share. - (d) Incorrect: Surcharge is not typically shared, unlike the main tax. - Supporting Evidence: - 10th Finance Commission (1995): Recommended 29% tax devolution. - Constitution (Article 270): Mandates income tax sharing. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Federalism: Union-state tax sharing (Q5 [1995]). - Finance Commission: Sets devolution norms (Q149 [2023-I]). - P.V. Narasimha Rao: Oversaw 1990s fiscal policies. - Key Takeaway: - Income tax sharing reflects India’s cooperative federalism, balancing Union and state fiscal needs. - Q29: Among which one of the following sets of social/religious groups is the extent of poverty the highest, as per Government statistics for the nineties? - Options: (a) Muslims in Kerala, Gujarat and A.P. (b) Tribals in Bihar, Orissa, M.P. and Maharashtra (c) Scheduled Caste in Punjab, Western UP, Northern Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu (d) Christians in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Assam - Answer: (b) Tribals in Bihar, Orissa, M.P. and Maharashtra - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In the 1990s, tribals (Scheduled Tribes) in states like Bihar, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, and Maharashtra faced the highest poverty rates (~50–60%) due to landlessness, lack of infrastructure, and marginalization. The Planning Commission’s 1993–94 data highlighted their economic deprivation compared to other groups. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Muslims in these states had lower poverty rates (~30–40%). - (c) Incorrect: Scheduled Castes faced poverty (~40%) but less severe than tribals. - (d) Incorrect: Christians had relatively lower poverty rates. - Supporting Evidence: - NSSO (1993–94): Tribal poverty rate ~55% in these states. - Economic Survey (1998–99): Highlighted tribal socio-economic challenges. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Poverty Line: Calorie-based metric (Q27 [1999]). - Planning Commission: Tracked poverty data (Q10 [1996]). - Tribal Development: Focus of schemes like JRY (Q3 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - Tribals in Bihar, Orissa, M.P., and Maharashtra faced the highest poverty in the 1990s, reflecting their socio-economic marginalization. - Q30: The first Indian State to have its Human Development Report prepared and released by Amartya Kumar Sen in Delhi is: - Options: (a) West Bengal (b) Kerala (c) Madhya Pradesh (d) Andhra Pradesh - Answer: (c) Madhya Pradesh - Madhya Pradesh HDR (1995): Launched by Sen, first state-level report. - UNDP: Inspired state-level HDRs (Q13 [1997]). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Amartya Sen: HDI pioneer (Q13 [1997]). - HDI: Development metric (Q33 [2000]). - Madhya Pradesh: Early adopter of HDR. - Key Takeaway: - Madhya Pradesh’s 1995 HDR, led by Amartya Sen, pioneered state-level development analysis in India. - [2000] - Q31: In an open economy, the national income (Y) of the economy is: (C, I, G, X, M stand for Consumption, Investment, Govt. Expenditure, total exports and total imports respectively.) - Options: (a) Y = C + I + G + X (b) Y = I + G - X + M (c) Y = C + I + G + (X - M) (d) Y = C - G + I + (X - M) - Answer: (c) Y = C + I + G + (X - M) - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In an open economy, national income (Y) is calculated using the expenditure approach: Y = C + I + G + (X - M), where X - M is net exports. This accounts for domestic consumption, investment, government spending, and trade balance, reflecting India’s open economy post-1991 liberalization. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes imports, overestimating income. - (b) Incorrect: Incorrectly subtracts exports and adds imports. - (d) Incorrect: Subtracts government expenditure, which is incorrect. - Supporting Evidence: - National Income Accounting: CSO uses Y = C + I + G + (X - M). - Economic Survey (1999–2000): Applied this formula for GDP estimates. - Related Concepts/Figures: - National Income: NNP at factor cost (Q16 [1997]). - Open Economy: Post-1991 trade liberalization (Q9 [1996]). - CSO: Tracks GDP (Q40 [2001]). - Key Takeaway: - The open economy national income formula includes net exports, reflecting India’s global trade integration. - Q32: Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: - List-I: A. Boom B. Recession C. Depression D. Recovery - List-II: 1. Business activity at high level with increasing income, output and employment at macro level 2. Gradual fall of income, output and employment with business activity in a low gear 3. Unprecedented level of under employment, and unemployment, drastic fall in income output and employment 4. Steady rise in the general level of prices, income, output and employment - Options: (a) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4 (b) A-1, B-2, C-4, D-3 (c) A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3 (d) A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4 - Answer: (a) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Business cycles include Boom (high activity), Recession (gradual decline), Depression (severe downturn), and Recovery (steady rise). In 2000, India’s economy was recovering post-1997 Asian Financial Crisis, with growth ~6%. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: C-4 and D-3 mismatch; depression is severe, not a price rise. - (c) Incorrect: A-2 and B-1 reverse boom and recession. - (d) Incorrect: A-2 and C-3 mismatch cycle definitions. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (1999–2000): India’s recovery phase with GDP growth ~6%. - Business Cycle Theory: Standard economic definitions (Mankiw). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Business Cycles: Economic fluctuations (Q2 [1995]). - RBI: Monitors cycles (Q147 [2023-I]). - Asian Financial Crisis: Context for 1990s cycles. - Key Takeaway: - Correct matching of business cycle phases reflects India’s economic dynamics in 2000, post-crisis recovery. - Q33: Indian Human Development Report does not give for each sample village: - Options: (a) Infrastructure and Amenities Index (b) Education Related Index (c) Health Related Index (d) Unemployment Related Index - Answer: (d) Unemployment Related Index - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The Indian Human Development Report (HDR), pioneered by Madhya Pradesh in 1995 (Q30 [1999]), includes village-level indices for infrastructure, education, and health but not unemployment, which is typically aggregated at state/national levels due to data limitations. - Excise duty - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 & 4 (c) 1 & 3 (d) 2 & 3 - Answer: (b) 2 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Customs and excise duties are indirect taxes, collected by the Union and not shareable with states in 2001, unlike direct taxes (corporation, wealth) which were shareable. - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - Corporation and wealth taxes were shareable, not customs and excise, which aligns with (b). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes excise duty. - (c) Incorrect: Includes shareable taxes. - (d) Incorrect: Wealth tax is direct. - Additional Evidence: - Constitution (Article 270): Direct taxes shareable. - 11th Finance Commission (2000–05): Customs, excise retained by Union. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Tax Sharing: Fiscal federalism (Q5 [1995]). - Finance Commission: Tax devolution (Q28 [1999]). - Key Takeaway: - Indirect taxes like customs and excise were Union-exclusive in 2001. - Q40: The term National Income represents: - Options: (a) gross national product at market prices minus depreciation (b) gross national product at market prices minus depreciation plus net factor income from abroad (c) gross national product at market prices minus depreciation and indirect taxes plus subsidies (d) gross national product at market prices minus net factor income from abroad - Answer: (c) gross national product at market prices minus depreciation and indirect taxes plus subsidies - Analysis: - Economic Context: - National Income is Net National Product (NNP) at factor cost, calculated as GNP at market prices minus depreciation (netting capital wear) and indirect taxes plus subsidies (adjusting to factor cost).
