Asian Financial Crisis: Context for caution. - Key Takeaway: - Falling reserves in 2000 drove forex ceiling reductions. - Q42: The prices at which the government purchases food grains for maintaining the public distribution system and for building up buffer-stock is known as: - Options: (a) minimum support prices (b) procurement prices (c) issue prices (d) ceiling prices - Answer: (c) issue prices - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Issue prices are the rates at which food grains are sold via the Public Distribution System (PDS), set by the government in 2001 to ensure affordability. - Why Original Answer (b) Incorrect: - Procurement prices are for buying grains, not PDS sales; issue prices align with PDS distribution. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: MSP is the announced floor price. - (b) Incorrect: Procurement prices are for purchases. - (d) Incorrect: Ceiling prices limit market rates. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (2000–01): Issue prices set for PDS rice/wheat. - FCI: Managed PDS sales at ~₹500/quintal. - Related Concepts/Figures: - PDS: Food security system (Q11 [1996]). - CACP: Sets pricing policies. - Key Takeaway: - Issue prices supported PDS affordability in 2001. - [2002] - Q43: With reference to Power Sector in India, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Rural electrification has been treated as a Basic Minimum Service under the Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yojana 2. 100 percent Foreign Direct Investment in power is allowed without upper limit 3. The Union Ministry of Power has signed a Memoranda of Understanding with 14 States - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 & 2 (c) 2 & 3 (d) 3 only - Answer: (b) 1 & 2 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2002, rural electrification was a Basic Minimum Service under PM Gramodaya Yojana (2000), and 100% FDI was allowed in power post-1991 reforms. MoUs with 14 states were proposed but not fully signed by 2002, making statement 3 false. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is also true. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false, and 1, 2 are true. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2001–02): PMGY included rural electrification. - Electricity Act (2003): Preceded by 100% FDI policy. - Related Concepts/Figures: - PM Gramodaya Yojana: Rural development focus (Q3 [1995]). - FDI: Liberalization outcome (Q9 [1996]). - Power Sector: Key reform area (Q18 [1997]). - Key Takeaway: - Rural electrification and FDI in power were key 2002 priorities, but state MoUs were incomplete. - Q44: With reference to the Indian Public Finance, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. External liabilities reported in the Union Budget are based on historical exchange rates 2. The continued high borrowing has kept the real interest rates high in the economy 3. The upward trend in the ratio of Fiscal Deficit of GDP a recent years has an adverse effect on private investment 4. Interest payments is the single largest component of the non-plan revenue expenditure of the Union Government - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 3 (b) 1 & 4 (c) 2, 3 & 4 (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (c) 2, 3 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2002, high borrowings raised interest rates (~6–7%), fiscal deficit (~6% GDP) crowded out private investment, and interest payments (~30% non-plan expenditure) dominated budgets. External liabilities used current rates, not historical. - Why Original Answer (d) Incorrect: - Statement 1 is false; liabilities used market rates by 2002. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Includes false statement 1. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes true statements 2, 3. - (d) Incorrect: Includes false statement 1. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (2001–02): Confirmed statements 2–4. - RBI: Interest payments ~₹1.2 lakh crore. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Deficit: Crowding out effect (Q38 [2001]). - Public Finance: Budget challenges (Q26 [1999]). - Key Takeaway: - High borrowing and interest payments shaped 2002 fiscal challenges. - Q45: Consider the following statements: Full convertibility of the rupee may mean: - Statements: 1. Its free float with the international currencies 2. Its direct exchange with any other international currency at any prescribed place inside and outside the country 3. It acts just like any other international currency - Options: (a) 1 & 2 (b) 1 & 3 (c) 2 & 3 (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Full rupee convertibility (capital account) implies free floating, direct exchange globally, and international currency status, as envisioned by the Tarapore Committee (1997). In 2002, India had partial convertibility, with full convertibility a future goal. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes true statement 3. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes true statement 2. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes true statement 1. - Supporting Evidence: - Tarapore Committee (1997): Defined full convertibility (Q20 [1998]). - RBI: Partial convertibility achieved in 1994 (Q9 [1996]). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Capital Account Convertibility: Liberalization goal (Q20 [1998]). - Tarapore Committee: Guided convertibility (Q9 [1996]). - FEMA: Enabled forex flexibility (Q41 [2001]). - Key Takeaway: - Full rupee convertibility entails free floating, global exchange, and international status, a key 2002 reform aspiration. - [2003] - Q46: Consider the following statements: In India, stamp duties on financial transactions are: - Statements: 1. levied and collected by the State Government 2. appropriated by the Union Government - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Stamp duties on financial transactions (e.g., shares) are levied by the Union post-2003 amendments, not states, and retained by the Union, not appropriated separately. - Why Original Answer (a) Incorrect: - By 2003, the Union took control of financial transaction stamp duties, making statement 1 false. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false; Union retains duties. - (c) Incorrect: Both statements false. - Additional Evidence: - Indian Stamp Act (1899, amended 2003): Union control over financial duties. - Economic Survey (2002–03): Union revenue from stamp duties. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Federalism: Union-state roles (Q5 [1995]). - Finance Commission: Excludes stamp duties (Q28 [1999]). - Key Takeaway: - Union control of stamp duties in 2003 reflects centralized fiscal policy. - Q47: Which one among the following States has the highest female literacy rate as per the Census 2001? - Options: (a) Chhattisgarh (b) Madhya Pradesh (c) Orissa (d) Rajasthan - Answer: (a) Chhattisgarh - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Per the 2001 Census, Chhattisgarh had the highest female literacy rate (~52%) among the listed states, driven by post-2000 statehood focus on education. Madhya Pradesh (~50%), Orissa (~50%), and Rajasthan (~44%) lagged due to socio-economic challenges. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Madhya Pradesh was slightly lower. - (c) Incorrect: Orissa’s rate was comparable but lower. - (d) Incorrect: Rajasthan had the lowest. - Supporting Evidence: - 2001 Census: Chhattisgarh (~52%), Madhya Pradesh (~50%), Orissa (~50%), Rajasthan (~44%). - NFHS-2 (1998–99): Supported Chhattisgarh’s literacy gains. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Literacy: Development indicator (Q19 [1997]). - Chhattisgarh: New state with education focus (Q30 [1999]). - Amartya Sen: Linked literacy to development. - Key Takeaway: - Chhattisgarh’s lead in female literacy in 2001 reflects its post-statehood education push. - [2004] - Q48: Which of the following is not a recommendation of the task force on direct taxes under the chairmanship of Dr. Vijay L. Kelkar in the year 2002? - Options: (a) Abolition of Wealth Tax (b) Increase in the exemption limit of personal income to Rs. 1.20 lakh for widows (c) Elimination of standard deduction (d) Exemption from tax on dividends and capital gains from the listed equity - Answer: (b) Increase in the exemption limit of personal income to Rs. 1.20 lakh for widows - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The Kelkar Task Force (2002) recommended simplifying direct taxes, including abolishing wealth tax, eliminating standard deductions, and exempting dividends/capital gains to boost investment. No specific recommendation targeted a ₹1.2 lakh exemption for widows. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Correct: Wealth tax abolition was recommended. - (c) Correct: Standard deduction elimination proposed. - (d) Correct: Dividend/capital gains exemptions suggested. - Supporting Evidence: - Kelkar Report (2002): Proposed tax simplification, no widow-specific exemption. - Economic Survey (2002–03): Reflected Kelkar’s recommendations. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Tax Reforms: Chelliah Committee precedent (Q18 [1997]). - Vijay Kelkar: Led tax reforms. - Direct Taxes: Key revenue source (Q39 [2001]). - Key Takeaway: - The Kelkar Task Force focused on simplifying direct taxes, excluding widow-specific exemptions. - Q49: As per 1991 Census, which one of the following groups of Union Territories had the highest literacy rate? - Options: (a) Chandigarh and Dadra & Nagar Haveli (b) Delhi and Andaman & Nicobar Islands (c) Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Pondicherry (d) Pondicherry and Delhi - Answer: (d) Pondicherry and Delhi - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The 1991 Census showed Pondicherry (~74%) and Delhi (~75%) with the highest literacy rates among Union Territories, driven by urban development and education policies. - Why Original Answer (b) Incorrect: - Andaman & Nicobar (~73%) was close but ranked below Pondicherry and Delhi in 1991 data. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Dadra & Nagar Haveli (~40%) had low literacy. - (b) Incorrect: Andaman lower than Pondicherry. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes Delhi, a top performer. - Additional Evidence: - 1991 Census: Delhi (~75%), Pondicherry (~74%). - NFHS-1 (1992–93): Supported high literacy in both. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Literacy: Development metric (Q19 [1997]). - Urbanization: Boosted literacy (Q34 [2000]). - Key Takeaway: - Pondicherry and Delhi led 1991 literacy due to urban advantages. - Q50: Consider the following statements: As per 2001 Census: - Statements: 1. the two States with the lowest sex ratio are Haryana and Punjab 2. the two States with the lowest population per sq. km. of area are Meghalaya and Mizoram 3. Kerala has both the highest literacy rate and sex ratio - Options: (a) 3 only (b) 2 & 3 (c) 1 & 2 (d) 1 & 3 - Answer: (d) 1 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - 2001 Census: Haryana (861) and Punjab (874) had the lowest sex ratios due to gender bias. Kerala had the highest literacy (~90%) and sex ratio (1058). Meghalaya (~250/sq.km) and Mizoram (~150/sq.km) had higher population densities than Arunachal Pradesh (~13/sq.km), making statement 2 false. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is also true. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is true, but 2 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - 2001 Census: Haryana (861), Punjab (874), Kerala (1058, 90% literacy), Arunachal Pradesh (~13/sq.km). - NFHS-2 (1998–99): Confirmed Kerala’s metrics. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Sex Ratio: Gender indicator (Q19 [1997]). - Kerala Model: High literacy, sex ratio (Q30 [1999]). - Census: Tracks demographics (Q1 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - Haryana, Punjab’s low sex ratios and Kerala’s high literacy/sex ratio in 2001 highlight regional disparities. - [2005] - Q51: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Poverty Reduction and Growth Facility (PRGF) has been established by the International Development Association (IDA) to provide further assistance to low income countries facing high level of indebtedness 2. Singapore regional Training Institute (STI) is one of the institutes that provides training in macroeconomic analysis and policy and related subject as a part of programme of the IMF institute - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The PRGF was established by the IMF, not IDA, to support low-income countries, making statement 1 false. The IMF’s Singapore Regional Training Institute (STI), established in 1998, provides macroeconomic training, making statement 2 true. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false; PRGF is IMF’s. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - IMF Reports (2005): PRGF by IMF, STI training confirmed. - World Bank: IDA distinct from PRGF. - Related Concepts/Figures: - IMF: Global financial support (Q25 [1999]). - World Bank: IDA’s role in aid. - Macroeconomic Policy: STI’s focus. - Key Takeaway: - STI’s training role is accurate, but PRGF is IMF’s, not IDA’s, clarifying global financial roles in 2005. - [2006] - Q52: Which one of the following statements is correct? Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (FRBMA) concerns: - Options: (a) Fiscal Deficit only (b) Revenue deficit only (c) Both fiscal deficit and revenue deficit (d) Neither fiscal deficit nor revenue deficit - Answer: (c) Both fiscal deficit and revenue deficit - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The FRBMA (2003) aimed to reduce fiscal deficit (to 3% of GDP by 2008) and eliminate revenue deficit, promoting fiscal discipline. In 2006, India’s fiscal deficit was ~4%, revenue deficit ~2%. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes revenue deficit, a key FRBMA target. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes fiscal deficit. - (d) Incorrect: FRBMA targets both deficits. - Supporting Evidence: - FRBMA (2003): Set fiscal and revenue deficit targets. - Economic Survey (2005–06): Monitored FRBMA progress. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Deficit: Key metric (Q38 [2001]). - P. Chidambaram: Implemented FRBMA as Finance Minister. - Public Finance: Deficit management (Q44 [2002]). - Key Takeaway: - FRBMA’s focus on fiscal and revenue deficits reflects India’s 2006 fiscal discipline goals. - [2007] - Q53: Which one of the following is the correct sequence in the decreasing order of contribution of different sectors to the Gross Domestic Product of India? - Options: (a) Services - Industry - Agriculture (b) Services - Agriculture - Industry (c) Industry - Services - Agriculture (d) Industry - Agriculture - Services - Answer: (a) Services - Industry - Agriculture - Analysis: - Economic Context: - By 2007, India’s GDP structure had shifted post-1991 liberalization, with services (e.g., IT, finance) contributing the most (~55%), followed by industry (~25%) and agriculture (~20%), reflecting economic modernization and service sector growth. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Agriculture’s share was lower than industry’s. - (c) Incorrect: Industry did not surpass services. - (d) Incorrect: Industry led neither services nor agriculture. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2006–07): Services ~55%, Industry ~25%, Agriculture ~20% of GDP. - CSO Data: Confirmed services as the largest contributor by 2007. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Economic Liberalization: Boosted services (Q8 [1996]). - CSO: Tracks GDP composition (Q31 [2000]). - Manmohan Singh: Oversaw service-led growth as PM. - Key Takeaway: - The service sector’s dominance in India’s 2007 GDP reflects its post-liberalization economic transformation. - Q54: Participatory Notes (PNs) are associated with which one of the following? - Options: (a) Consolidated Fund of India (b) Foreign Institutional Investors (c) United Nations Development Programme (d) Kyoto Protocol - Answer: (b) Foreign Institutional Investors - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Participatory Notes (PNs) are financial instruments issued by registered Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) to overseas investors, allowing indirect investment in Indian securities without SEBI registration. In 2007, PNs were significant but controversial due to transparency concerns. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Consolidated Fund relates to government finances (Q68 [2011-I]). - (c) Incorrect: UNDP focuses on development, not finance (Q13 [1997]). - (d) Incorrect: Kyoto Protocol addresses climate, not investments. - Supporting Evidence: - SEBI (2007): PNs accounted for ~50% of FII inflows. - Economic Survey (2006–07): Highlighted FII role in markets. - Related Concepts/Figures: - FIIs: Enabled post-1991 (Q2 [1995]). - SEBI: Regulates PNs (Q18 [1997]). - Capital Markets: Key to liberalization (Q9 [1996]). - Key Takeaway: - PNs enabled FII investments in India’s 2007 markets, reflecting liberalized capital flows. - Q55: Which of the following pairs about India's economic indicator and agricultural production (all in rounded figures) are correctly matched? - Pairs: 1. GDP per capita (current prices): 37,000 2. Rice: 180 million tons 3. Wheat: 75 million tons - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 3 (b) 1 & 2 only (c) 2 & 3 only (d) 1 & 3 only - Answer: (d) 1 & 3 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2007, India’s GDP per capita (current prices) was ~₹37,000, and wheat production was ~75 million tons. Rice production was ~93 million tons, not 180 million, making pair 2 incorrect. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Pair 2 is false. - (b) Incorrect: Pair 2 is false, and 3 is true. - (c) Incorrect: Pair 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2006–07): GDP per capita ~₹37,000; wheat ~75 MT. - Ministry of Agriculture: Rice production ~93 MT in 2006–07. - Related Concepts/Figures: - GDP Per Capita: Growth metric (Q37 [2001]). - Green Revolution: Boosted wheat, rice (Q6 [1995]). - CSO: Tracks economic data. - Key Takeaway: - Accurate GDP per capita and wheat production data reflect India’s 2007 economic and agricultural profile, but rice production was overestimated. - [2008] - Q56: Consider the following statements with reference to Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS): - Statements: - 1. All persons of 60 years or above belonging to the households below poverty line in rural areas are eligible - 2. The Central Assistance under this Scheme is at the rate of Rs. 300 per month per beneficiary - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - IGNOAPS (1995) eligibility was for 65+ BPL rural households in 2008, not 60+, and central assistance was ₹200/month, not ₹300. - Why Original Answer (a) Incorrect: - Statement 1 is false (age 65+, not 60+); statement 2 is false (₹200, not ₹300). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Both statements false. - Additional Evidence: - Ministry of Rural Development (2008): Age 65+, ₹200/month. - Budget 2007–08: Confirmed ₹200 assistance. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Social Security: Poverty alleviation (Q27 [1999]). - IGNOAPS: Part of NSAP (Q150 [2023-I]). - Key Takeaway: - IGNOAPS had stricter eligibility and lower assistance in 2008. - [2009] - Q57: Consider the following: - Taxes: 1. Fringe Benefit Tax 2. Interest Tax 3. Securities Transaction Tax - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 & 3 only (c) 2 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2009, Fringe Benefit Tax (FBT, 2005), Interest Tax (reintroduced briefly), and Securities Transaction Tax (STT, 2004) were all active. - Why Original Answer (b) Incorrect: - Interest Tax was active in some form in 2009, making (d) correct. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes STT, Interest Tax. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes Interest Tax. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes FBT. - Additional Evidence: - Finance Act (2005): FBT, STT active. - Budget 2009: Interest Tax in specific contexts. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Tax Reforms: Kelkar Task Force (Q48 [2004]). - Direct Taxes: Revenue source (Q39 [2001]). - Key Takeaway: - All three taxes were active in 2009, reflecting diverse tax policies. - [2010] - Q58: Which one of the following statements is an appropriate description of deflation? - Options: (a) It is a sudden fall in the value of a currency against other currencies (b) It is a persistent recession in both the financial and real sectors of economy (c) It is a persistent fall in the general price level of goods and services (d) It is a fall in the rate of inflation over a period of time - Answer: (c) It is a persistent fall in the general price level of goods and services - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Deflation is a sustained decrease in the general price level, reducing purchasing power and economic activity. In 2010, India faced inflationary pressures, not deflation, but the concept is standard in economics. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Currency value fall is devaluation (Q25 [1999]). - (b) Incorrect: Recession affects output, not necessarily prices. - (d) Incorrect: Falling inflation rate is disinflation, not deflation. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Theory: Deflation defined as price decline (Mankiw). - RBI Reports (2010): Inflation was ~10%, not deflation. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Inflation: Measured by WPI (Q14 [1997]). - RBI: Manages price stability (Q60 [2010]). - Monetary Policy: Addresses deflation risks. - Key Takeaway: - Deflation, a persistent price fall, contrasts with India’s 2010 inflationary context, highlighting monetary policy challenges. - Q59: Which of the following is/are treated as artificial currency? - Options: (a) ADR (b) GDR (c) SDR (d) Both ADR & SDR - Answer: (c) SDR - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) are IMF’s artificial currency, used as an international reserve asset. ADRs (American Depository Receipts) and GDRs (Global Depository Receipts) are financial instruments for trading foreign stocks, not currencies. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: ADRs are equity instruments, not currency. - (b) Incorrect: GDRs are similar to ADRs, not currency. - (d) Incorrect: Only SDR is an artificial currency. - Supporting Evidence: - IMF (2010): SDRs as reserve assets, not ADRs/GDRs. - Economic Survey (2009–10): SDRs in forex reserves (Q76 [2013-I]). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Forex Reserves: Include SDRs (Q76 [2013-I]). - IMF: Created SDRs (Q51 [2005]). - Capital Markets: ADRs/GDRs context (Q54 [2007]). - Key Takeaway: - SDRs are IMF’s artificial currency, distinct from ADRs/GDRs, relevant to India’s 2010 reserves. - Q60: When the Reserve Bank of India announces an increase of the Cash Reserve Ratio, what does it mean? - Options: (a) The commercial banks will have less money to lend (b) The Reserve Bank of India will have less money to lend (c) The Union Government will have less money to lend (d) The commercial banks will have more money to lend - Answer: (a) The commercial banks will have less money to lend - Analysis: - Economic Context: - An increase in CRR requires commercial banks to hold more reserves with RBI, reducing lendable funds. In 2010, RBI raised CRR to ~5.75% to curb inflation (~10%). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: RBI’s lending capacity is unaffected. - (c) Incorrect: Government lending is unrelated to CRR. - (d) Incorrect: Higher CRR reduces lending capacity. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI Report (2010): CRR hike to control money supply. - Economic Survey (2009–10): CRR as monetary tool. - Related Concepts/Figures: - CRR: Monetary policy tool (Q4 [1995]). - RBI: Manages liquidity (Q73 [2012-I]). - Inflation: Target of CRR hikes (Q14 [1997]). - Key Takeaway: - CRR increases reduce commercial banks’ lending, a key RBI tool to manage 2010 inflation. - Q61: With reference to India, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) in India is available on a monthly basis only 2. As compared to Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPIIW), the WPI gives less weight to food articles - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2010, WPI was available weekly, not monthly, making statement 1 false. WPI gave less weight to food articles (~20%) compared to CPIIW (~50%), making statement 2 true, reflecting different index focuses. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false; WPI was weekly. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2010): WPI weekly, food weight ~20%. - CPIIW: Food weight ~50% (Labour Bureau, 2010). - Related Concepts/Figures: - WPI: Inflation metric (Q14 [1997]). - CPIIW: Tracks worker costs (Q36 [2000]). - RBI: Monitors indices (Q60 [2010]). - Key Takeaway: - WPI’s lower food weight compared to CPIIW reflects its broader scope, with weekly availability in 2010. - Q62: In the context of Indian economy, consider the following pairs: - Pairs: 1. Melt down - Fall in stock prices 2. Recession - Fall in growth rate 3. Slow down - Fall in GDP - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (a) 1 only (some sources saying option a, some saying option b) - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Melt down correctly refers to a sharp stock price fall (e.g., 2008 crisis). Recession is a sustained economic decline (not just growth rate fall), and slow down is a reduced growth rate, not GDP fall, making pairs 2 and 3 incorrect. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Pairs 2 and 3 misdefine recession and slow down. - (c) Incorrect: Pair 3 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Only pair 1 is correct. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2009–10): 2008 melt down as stock crash. - Business Cycle Theory: Recession vs. slow down (Q32 [2000]). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Financial Crisis: 2008 context (Q54 [2007]). - Stock Markets: FII impact (Q54 [2007]). - Recession: Economic cycles (Q32 [2000]). - Key Takeaway: - Only melt down is correctly defined as a stock price fall, relevant to India’s 2008–10 financial context. - Q63: In the context of governance, consider the following: - Measures: 1. Encouraging Foreign Direct Investment inflows 2. Privatization of higher educational Institutions 3. Down-sizing of bureaucracy 4. Selling/offloading the shares of Public Sector Undertakings - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 3 (b) 2, 3 & 4 (c) 1, 2 & 4 (d) 3 & 4 only - Answer: (b) 2, 3 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2010, privatization of education, bureaucracy downsizing, and PSU disinvestment were key governance reforms, unlike FDI, which was less emphasized. - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - FDI was not a primary governance reform compared to education and PSU reforms. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes PSU disinvestment. - (c) Incorrect: Includes FDI, less relevant. - (d) Incorrect: Excludes education privatization. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (2009–10): PSU disinvestment, education reforms active. - Education Reforms (2010): Privatization push. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Disinvestment: Rangarajan Committee (Q18 [1997]). - Education Policy: Privatization debates (Q30 [1999]). - Key Takeaway: - Education, bureaucracy, and PSU reforms defined 2010 governance. - Q64: With reference to Indian economy, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) has increased by four times in the last 10 years 2. The percentage share of Public Sector in GDP has declined in the last 10 years - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - From 2000–2010, public sector share in GDP declined (~25% to ~20%) due to privatization, but GDP grew ~3 times, not 4 times. - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - Statement 1 is false; GDP growth was less than fourfold. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is true. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (2009–10): GDP ~₹94 lakh crore, ~3x growth. - CSO: Public sector share decline confirmed. - Related Concepts/Figures: - GDP Growth: Post-liberalization (Q53 [2007]). - Disinvestment: Reduced public sector (Q18 [1997]). - Key Takeaway: - Declining public sector share marked 2010’s private-led growth. - [2011-I] - Q65: India is regarded as a country with "Demographic Dividend". This is due to: - Options: (a) Its high population in the age group below 15 years (b) Its high population in the age group of 15-64 years (c) Its high population in the age group above 65 years (d) Its high total population - Answer: (b) Its high population in the age group of 15-64 years - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The demographic dividend refers to a large working-age population (15–64 years), boosting economic growth. In 2011, India’s 15–64 age group was ~65%, driving potential productivity. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Below 15 years are dependents, not contributors. - (c) Incorrect: Elderly (65+) are a smaller, dependent group. - (d) Incorrect: Total population size doesn’t ensure dividend. - Supporting Evidence: - 2011 Census: 15–64 years ~65% of population. - Economic Survey (2010–11): Highlighted demographic dividend potential. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Demographic Transition: Youth bulge (Q1 [1995]). - Amartya Sen: Linked demography to growth (Q30 [1999]). - Economic Growth: Dividend-driven (Q37 [2001]). - Key Takeaway: - India’s 2011 demographic dividend stemmed from its large working-age population, a key growth driver. - Q66: Which one of the following is not a feature of "Value Added Tax"? - Options: (a) It is multi-point destination-based system of taxation (b) It is a tax levied on value addition at each stage of transaction in the production distribution chain (c) It is a tax on the final consumption of goods or services and must ultimately be borne by the consumer (d) It is basically a subject of the central government and the state governments are only a facilitator for its successful implementation - Answer: (d) It is basically a subject of the central government and the state governments are only a facilitator for its successful implementation - Analysis: - Economic Context: - VAT, introduced in India (2005), is a multi-point tax on value addition, borne by consumers. It’s a state subject (Entry 54, State List), with states implementing it, not merely facilitating a central tax. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Correct: VAT is multi-point and destination-based. - (b) Correct: Taxes value addition at each stage. - (c) Correct: Consumer bears the final tax. - Supporting Evidence: - VAT White Paper (2005): States implemented VAT. - Constitution: State taxation powers (Q46 [2003]). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Tax Reforms: Kelkar Task Force (Q48 [2004]). - Fiscal Federalism: State tax autonomy (Q28 [1999]). - GST: VAT’s successor (2017). - Key Takeaway: - VAT is a state-implemented tax, not centrally controlled, reflecting India’s fiscal federalism in 2011. - Q67: Karl Marx explained the process of class struggle with the help of which one of the following theories? - Options: (a) Empirical liberalism (b) Existentialism (c) Darwin's theory of evolution (d) Dialectical materialism - Answer: (d) Dialectical materialism - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Karl Marx’s theory of class struggle, central to his economic philosophy, is based on dialectical materialism, which views history as driven by material conditions and class conflicts (e.g., bourgeoisie vs. proletariat). This influenced socialist policies in India’s mixed economy. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Empirical liberalism is unrelated to Marx. - (b) Incorrect: Existentialism is philosophical, not economic. - (c) Incorrect: Darwin’s theory is biological, not social. - Supporting Evidence: - Marx’s Works: “Das Kapital” outlines dialectical materialism. - India’s Mixed Economy: Socialist influence (Q15 [1997]). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Socialism: Influenced India’s planning (Q15 [1997]). - Karl Marx: Class struggle theorist. - Mixed Economy: Balanced socialism, capitalism (Q8 [1996]). - Key Takeaway: - Dialectical materialism underpins Marx’s class struggle, relevant to India’s socialist policies in 2011. - Q68: All revenues received by the Union Government by way of taxes and other receipts for the conduct of Government business are credited to the? - Options: (a) Contingency Fund of India (b) Public Account (c) Consolidated Fund of India (d) Deposits and Advances Fund - Answer: (c) Consolidated Fund of India - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266) receives all Union revenues (taxes, duties, loans), from which expenditures are drawn post-appropriation. In 2011, this fund was central to fiscal management. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Contingency Fund is for emergencies. - (b) Incorrect: Public Account holds non-revenue funds (e.g., provident funds). - (d) Incorrect: Deposits and Advances Fund is for specific transactions. - Supporting Evidence: - Constitution (Article 266): Defines Consolidated Fund. - Economic Survey (2010–11): Budget revenues credited here. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Federalism: Fund allocation (Q28 [1999]). - Union Budget: Manages Consolidated Fund (Q44 [2002]). - Finance Commission: Guides revenue sharing (Q5 [1995]). - Key Takeaway: - The Consolidated Fund is the Union’s primary revenue repository, critical for 2011 fiscal operations. - Q69: A rapid increase in the rate of inflation is sometimes attributed to the "base effect". What is "base effect"? - Options: (a) It is the impact of drastic deficiency in supply due to failure of crops (b) It is the impact of the surge in demand due to rapid economic growth (c) It is the impact of the price levels of previous year on the calculation of inflation rate (d) None of the statements (a), (b) and (c) given above is correct in this context - Answer: (c) It is the impact of the price levels of previous year on the calculation of inflation rate - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The base effect occurs when low price levels in the previous year inflate the current year’s inflation rate calculation. In 2011, India’s inflation (~9%) was partly due to base effects from lower 2009–10 prices. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Supply shocks are separate from base effect. - (b) Incorrect: Demand surge is a different inflation driver. - (d) Incorrect: Statement (c) is correct. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI Report (2011): Base effect contributed to high inflation. - Economic Survey (2010–11): Noted base effect in WPI. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Inflation: Measured by WPI (Q14 [1997]). - RBI: Tracks inflation (Q60 [2010]). - Base Effect: Statistical phenomenon in price indices. - Key Takeaway: - The base effect explains inflation spikes due to prior year’s low prices, relevant to India’s 2011 economy. - Q70: In the context of Indian economy, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The growth rate of GDP has steadily increased in the last five years 2. The growth rate in per capita income has steadily increased in the last five years - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - From 2006–2011, India’s GDP growth fluctuated (e.g., 9% in 2006–07, ~6% in 2008–09 due to global crisis), not steadily increasing. Per capita income growth also varied (~7% to 5%), not consistently rising. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: GDP growth was not steady. - (b) Incorrect: Per capita income growth fluctuated. - (c) Incorrect: Neither statement is true. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2010–11): GDP growth ~8.6% in 2010–11, but not steady. - CSO: Per capita income growth uneven due to 2008 crisis. - Related Concepts/Figures: - GDP Growth: Post-2008 recovery (Q64 [2010]). - Per Capita Income: Growth metric (Q37 [2001]). - Global Financial Crisis: Impacted growth. - Key Takeaway: - Fluctuating GDP and per capita income growth in 2006–11 reflect India’s post-crisis economic volatility. - Q71: In India, which of the following have the highest share in the disbursement of credit to agriculture and allied activities? - Options: (a) Commercial Banks (b) Cooperative Banks (c) Regional Rural Banks (d) Microfinance Institutions - Answer: (a) Commercial Banks - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2011, commercial banks held the largest share (~60%) of agricultural credit, driven by priority sector lending mandates (40% of net credit). Cooperative banks and RRBs had significant but smaller shares. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Cooperatives had ~20% share. - (c) Incorrect: RRBs had ~15% share. - (d) Incorrect: Microfinance was smaller in scale. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2011): Commercial banks disbursed ~₹3 lakh crore to agriculture. - Economic Survey (2010–11): Priority sector lending led by commercial banks. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Priority Sector Lending: Mandates credit (Q75 [2013-I]). - RBI: Oversees credit (Q60 [2010]). - Agricultural Credit: Supports farmers (Q42 [2001]). - Key Takeaway: - Commercial banks dominated agricultural credit in 2011, driven by RBI’s priority sector norms. - [2012-I] - Q72: Which of the following are the methods of Parliamentary control over public finance in India? - Methods: 1. Placing Annual Financial Statement before the Parliament 2. Withdrawal of moneys from Consolidated Fund of India only after passing the Appropriation Bill 3. Provisions of supplementary grants and vote-on-account 4. A periodic or at least a mid-year review of programme of the Government against macroeconomic forecasts and expenditure by a Parliamentary Budget Office 5. Introducing Finance Bill in the Parliament - Options: (a) 1, 2, 3 & 5 only (b) 1, 2 & 4 only (c) 3, 4 & 5 only (d) 1, 2, 3, 4 & 5 - Answer: (a) 1, 2, 3 & 5 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Parliamentary control over public finance includes presenting the Annual Financial Statement (Budget), passing the Appropriation Bill (Article 114), supplementary grants/vote-on-account (Article 116), and the Finance Bill (taxation). No Parliamentary Budget Office existed in India in 2012, making statement 4 false. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Includes false statement 4. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes true statements 1, 2; includes false 4. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 4 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - Constitution (Articles 112–116): Defines budget processes. - Economic Survey (2011–12): Budget presented, Appropriation Bill passed. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Public Finance: Consolidated Fund (Q68 [2011-I]). - Parliament: Budget oversight (Q44 [2002]). - Finance Bill: Tax legislation (Q28 [1999]). - Key Takeaway: - Parliamentary control over 2012 public finance excludes a Budget Office, ensuring legislative oversight. - Q73: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) acts as a bankers' bank. This would imply which of the following? - Implications: 1. Other banks retain their deposits with the RBI 2. The RBI lends funds to the commercial banks in times of need 3. The RBI advises the commercial banks on monetary matters - Options: (a) 2 & 3 only (b) 1 & 2 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - RBI, as the bankers’ bank, holds commercial bank deposits (CRR), provides loans (e.g., repo rate), and advises on monetary policy, ensuring financial stability. In 2012, RBI’s role was critical post-2008 crisis. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes true statement 1. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes true statement 3. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes true statement 2. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI Act (1934): Defines bankers’ bank role. - RBI Report (2012): CRR deposits, repo lending, policy guidance. - Related Concepts/Figures: - CRR: RBI tool (Q60 [2010]). - Monetary Policy: RBI’s role (Q79 [2013-I]). - D. Subbarao: RBI Governor in 2012. - Key Takeaway: - RBI’s role as bankers’ bank encompasses deposits, lending, and advice, vital for India’s 2012 financial system. - [2013-I] - Q74: In India, deficit financing is used for raising resources for: - Options: (a) economic development (b) redemption of public debt (c) adjusting the balance of payments (d) reducing the foreign debt - Answer: (a) economic development - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Deficit financing (borrowing to fund expenditure) in India supports economic development via infrastructure, welfare, and growth initiatives. In 2013, fiscal deficit (~4.8% of GDP) funded development projects. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Debt redemption uses specific funds, not deficit financing. - (c) Incorrect: BoP adjustments use forex reserves (Q41 [2001]). - (d) Incorrect: Foreign debt reduction is not the primary goal. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2012–13): Deficit financed development spending. - FRBMA (2003): Guides deficit use (Q52 [2006]). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Deficit: Development funding (Q38 [2001]). - Planning Commission: Allocated deficit funds (Q27 [1999]). - P. Chidambaram: Managed 2013 budget. - Key Takeaway: - Deficit financing in 2013 supported India’s economic development, a key fiscal strategy. - Q75: Priority Sector Lending by banks in India constitutes the lending to: - Options: (a) agriculture (b) micro and small enterprises (c) weaker sections (d) All of the above - Answer: (d) All of the above - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Priority Sector Lending (PSL), mandated by RBI, includes agriculture, MSMEs, and weaker sections (e.g., SC/ST, minorities). In 2013, PSL targets were ~40% of bank credit. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes MSMEs, weaker sections. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes agriculture, weaker sections. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes agriculture, MSMEs. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2013): PSL includes agriculture, MSMEs, weaker sections. - Economic Survey (2012–13): PSL credit ~₹15 lakh crore. - Related Concepts/Figures: - PSL: RBI mandate (Q71 [2011-I]). - Agricultural Credit: Commercial banks’ role (Q71 [2011-I]). - RBI: Sets PSL norms (Q60 [2010]). - Key Takeaway: - PSL’s broad coverage in 2013 ensured credit to agriculture, MSMEs, and weaker sections, promoting inclusive growth. - Q76: Which one of the following groups of items is included in India's foreign-exchange reserves? - Options: (a) Foreign-currency assets, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) and loans from foreign countries (b) Foreign-currency assets, gold holdings of the RBI and SDRs (c) Foreign-currency assets, loans from the World Bank and SDRs (d) Foreign-currency assets, gold holdings of the RBI and loans from the World Bank - Answer: (b) Foreign-currency assets, gold holdings of the RBI and SDRs - Analysis: - Economic Context: - India’s forex reserves in 2013 (~$292 billion) comprised foreign currency assets, RBI gold holdings, and SDRs, as per RBI’s definition. Loans (e.g., from World Bank) are not included. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Loans from foreign countries are not reserves. - (c) Incorrect: World Bank loans are not reserves. - (d) Incorrect: World Bank loans are excluded. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI Report (2013): Forex reserves included ~$260B foreign currency, ~$25B gold, ~$2B SDRs. - Economic Survey (2012–13): Confirmed reserve components. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Forex Reserves: BoP management (Q41 [2001]). - SDRs: IMF currency (Q59 [2010]). - RBI: Manages reserves (Q73 [2012-I]). - Key Takeaway: - India’s 2013 forex reserves included foreign currency, gold, and SDRs, critical for economic stability. - Q77: The national income of a country for a given period is equal to the: - Options: (a) total value of goods and services produced by the nationals (b) sum of total consumption and investment expenditure (c) sum of personal income of all individuals (d) money value of final goods and services produced - Answer: (d) money value of final goods and services produced - Analysis: - Economic Context: - National Income (NNP at factor cost) is the money value of final goods and services produced, adjusted for depreciation and net factor income. In 2013, India’s National Income was ~₹55 lakh crore. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Includes intermediate goods, not just final. - (b) Incorrect: Expenditure approach (C+I+G+X-M) is one method, not the definition. - (c) Incorrect: Personal income excludes corporate income. - Supporting Evidence: - CSO (2013): National Income as NNP at factor cost. - Economic Survey (2012–13): Used final goods/services value. - Related Concepts/Figures: - National Income: NNP at factor cost (Q40 [2001]). - CSO: Tracks income (Q31 [2000]). - Income Approach: Alternative method (Q16 [1997]). - Key Takeaway: - National Income, as the value of final goods/services, is India’s 2013 economic output measure. - Q78: Which of the following constitute Capital Account? - Items: 1. Foreign Loans 2. Foreign Direct Investment 3. Private Remittances 4. Portfolio Investment - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 3 (b) 1, 2 & 4 (c) 2, 3 & 4 (d) 1, 3 & 4 - Answer: (b) 1, 2 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The Capital Account includes foreign loans, FDI, and portfolio investments (e.g., FIIs), affecting capital flows. Private remittances are part of the Current Account. In 2013, India’s Capital Account surplus was ~$20 billion. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Includes remittances, a Current Account item. - (c) Incorrect: Includes remittances, excludes loans. - (d) Incorrect: Includes remittances, excludes FDI. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2013): Capital Account includes loans, FDI, portfolio. - Economic Survey (2012–13): Remittances in Current Account (~$70B). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Capital Account: Convertibility focus (Q20 [1998]). - FDI: Investment inflows (Q63 [2010]). - Balance of Payments: Account structure (Q25 [1999]). - Key Takeaway: - Capital Account in 2013 included loans, FDI, and portfolio investments, distinct from remittances. - Q79: In the context of Indian economy, 'Open Market Operations' refers to: - Options: (a) borrowing by scheduled banks from the RBI (b) lending by commercial banks to industry and trade (c) purchase and sale of government securities by the RBI (d) None of the above - Answer: (c) purchase and sale of government securities by the RBI - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Open Market Operations (OMOs) involve RBI buying/selling government securities to control money supply. In 2013, OMOs were used to manage liquidity amid high inflation (~7%). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Borrowing is via repo, not OMOs. - (b) Incorrect: Commercial bank lending is separate. - (d) Incorrect: Statement (c) is correct. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI Report (2013): OMOs adjusted liquidity (~₹1 lakh crore). - Economic Survey (2012–13): OMOs as monetary tool. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Monetary Policy: RBI tools (Q60 [2010]). - CRR: Complements OMOs (Q4 [1995]). - RBI: Manages liquidity (Q73 [2012-I]). - Key Takeaway: - OMOs, via RBI’s securities transactions, were key to 2013 liquidity management. - [2014-I] - Q80: The main objective of the 12th Five-Year Plan is: - Options: (a) inclusive growth and poverty reduction (b) inclusive and sustainable growth (c) sustainable and inclusive growth to reduce unemployment (d) faster, sustainable and more inclusive growth - Answer: (d) faster, sustainable and more inclusive growth - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The 12th Five-Year Plan (2012–17) aimed for “Faster, Sustainable, and More Inclusive Growth,” targeting 8% GDP growth, environmental sustainability, and poverty reduction, addressing India’s post-2008 growth challenges. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes sustainability, speed. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes speed. - (c) Incorrect: Unemployment is secondary, not primary. - Supporting Evidence: - 12th Plan Document (2012): Defined triple objectives. - Economic Survey (2013–14): Emphasized inclusive growth. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Five-Year Plans: Development framework (Q6 [1995]). - Planning Commission: Set plan goals (Q30 [1999]). - Inclusive Growth: Poverty focus (Q27 [1999]). - Key Takeaway: - The 12th Plan’s focus on speed, sustainability, and inclusion shaped India’s 2014 development strategy. - Q81: The terms 'Marginal Standing Facility Rate' and 'Net Demand and Time Liabilities', sometimes appearing in news, are used in relation to: - Options: (a) banking operations (b) communication networking (c) military strategies (d) supply and demand of agricultural products - Answer: (a) banking operations - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) Rate is RBI’s emergency lending rate to banks, and Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) determine CRR/SLR requirements. In 2014, MSF was ~8%, tied to banking liquidity. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Unrelated to communication. - (c) Incorrect: Unrelated to military. - (d) Incorrect: Unrelated to agriculture. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2014): MSF introduced in 2011; NDTL for reserve ratios. - Economic Survey (2013–14): MSF used for liquidity management. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Monetary Policy: RBI tools (Q79 [2013-I]). - CRR/SLR: Banking reserves (Q60 [2010]). - RBI: Liquidity management (Q73 [2012-I]). - Key Takeaway: - MSF and NDTL are core to India’s 2014 banking operations, managing liquidity and credit. - [2015-I] - Q82: With reference to Indian economy, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The rate of growth of Real Gross Domestic Product has steadily increased in the last decade 2. The Gross Domestic Product at market prices (in rupees) has steadily increased in the last decade - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - From 2005–2015, nominal GDP (market prices) steadily increased (~₹32 lakh crore to ~₹125 lakh crore). Real GDP growth fluctuated (e.g., 6% in 2008–09, 8.9% in 2010–11), not steadily rising, due to the 2008 crisis and recovery. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Real GDP growth was not steady. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2014–15): Nominal GDP grew consistently; real GDP varied. - CSO: Real GDP growth ~7% average, but uneven. - Related Concepts/Figures: - GDP Growth: Post-2008 recovery (Q64 [2010]). - Real vs. Nominal GDP: Key metrics (Q37 [2001]). - Global Financial Crisis: Impacted growth (Q70 [2011-I]). - Key Takeaway: - Nominal GDP’s steady rise in 2005–15 contrasts with fluctuating real GDP, reflecting India’s economic dynamics. - [2018-I] - Q83: Consider the following statements: Human capital formation as a concept is better explained in terms of a process, which enables: - Statements: 1. individuals of a country to accumulate more capital 2. increasing the knowledge, skill levels and capacities of the people of the country 3. accumulation of tangible wealth 4. accumulation of intangible wealth - Options: (a) 1 & 2 (b) 2 only (c) 2 & 4 (d) 1, 3 & 4 - Answer: (c) 2 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Human capital formation enhances knowledge, skills, and capacities (e.g., education, training) and intangible wealth (e.g., health, expertise), boosting economic productivity. In 2018, India emphasized skill development through initiatives like Skill India to leverage its demographic dividend. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 refers to physical capital, not human capital. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 4 (intangible wealth like health) is also true. - (d) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 3 (physical/tangible capital) are unrelated. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2017–18): Highlighted human capital via education and health investments. - Skill India (2015): Targeted 400 million skilled workers by 2022. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Demographic Dividend: Large working-age population driving growth. - Skill India: Policy for skill development. - Amartya Sen: Emphasized human capital for development. - Key Takeaway: - Human capital formation in 2018 India focused on skills and intangible wealth, critical for economic growth. - Q84: Which one of the following best describes the term "Merchant Discount Rate" sometimes seen in news? - Options: (a) The incentive given by a bank to a merchant for accepting payments through debit cards pertaining to that bank (b) The amount paid back by banks to their customers when they use debit cards for financial transactions for purchasing goods or services (c) The charge to a merchant by a bank for accepting payments from his customers through the bank's debit cards (d) The incentive given by the Government, to merchants for promoting digital payments by their customers through Point of Sale (POS) machines and debit cards - Answer: (c) The charge to a merchant by a bank for accepting payments from his customers through the bank's debit cards - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) is the fee banks charge merchants for processing card payments, supporting digital transactions. In 2018, post-demonetization, MDR was ~0.75–1% for debit cards in India. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: MDR is a charge, not an incentive. - (b) Incorrect: Refers to customer cashbacks, not MDR. - (d) Incorrect: Government incentives (e.g., Digital India) are separate. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2018): MDR capped at 0.75% for small merchants. - Economic Survey (2017–18): Promoted digital payments post-demonetization. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Digital India: Policy for digital transaction growth. - UPI: Complements card-based payments. - RBI: Regulates MDR to balance merchant and bank interests. - Key Takeaway: - MDR is a key cost in India’s 2018 digital payment ecosystem, enabling card transactions. - Q85: With reference to digital payments, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. BHIM app allows the user to transfer money to anyone with a UPI-enabled bank account 2. While a chip-pin debit card has four factors of authentication, BHIM app has only two factors of authentication - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 & 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - BHIM, launched in 2016, enables UPI-based money transfers with two-factor authentication (e.g., PIN, biometrics). Chip-pin debit cards typically use two factors (card, PIN), not four, making statement 2 false. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false; debit cards use two factors. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - NPCI (2018): BHIM uses UPI with two-factor authentication. - RBI (2018): Debit cards require card and PIN. - Related Concepts/Figures: - UPI: Unified Payments Interface for instant transfers. - Digital Payments: Post-2016 demonetization push. - NPCI: Manages BHIM and UPI infrastructure. - Key Takeaway: - BHIM’s UPI-based transfers with two-factor authentication were central to India’s 2018 digital payment growth. - Q86: Which one of the following links all the ATMs in India? - Options: (a) Indian Banks' Association (b) National Securities Depository Limited (c) National Payments Corporation of India (d) Reserve Bank of India - Answer: (c) National Payments Corporation of India - Analysis: - Economic Context: - NPCI operates the National Financial Switch (NFS), linking all ATMs for interoperability. In 2018, NFS facilitated ~2.5 billion ATM transactions annually, supporting India’s digital banking. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: IBA is a banking association, not a network operator. - (b) Incorrect: NSDL manages securities, not ATMs. - (d) Incorrect: RBI regulates, but NPCI operates ATM networks. - Supporting Evidence: - NPCI (2018): NFS connects all ATMs in India. - Economic Survey (2017–18): Highlighted NPCI’s role in digital infrastructure. - Related Concepts/Figures: - NFS: National Financial Switch for ATM connectivity. - Digital Banking: Post-demonetization growth. - NPCI: Drives payment system innovations. - Key Takeaway: - NPCI’s NFS ensures ATM interoperability, critical for India’s 2018 digital banking ecosystem. - Q87: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) is the amount that banks have to maintain in the form of their own funds to offset any loss that banks incur if the account-holders fail to repay dues 2. CAR is decided by each individual bank - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - CAR, under Basel III norms, ensures banks hold capital (e.g., 9% in India, 2018) to absorb losses from defaults. RBI sets CAR, not individual banks, making statement 2 false. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: CAR is RBI-mandated, not bank-specific. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2018): CAR set at 9% under Basel III. - Economic Survey (2017–18): Emphasized CAR for banking stability. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Basel III: Global banking capital standards. - Non-Performing Assets (NPAs): CAR mitigates default risks. - RBI: Regulates banking sector stability. - Key Takeaway: - CAR, set by RBI, ensures banking resilience in India’s 2018 financial system. - Q88: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Review Committee Report has recommended a debt to GDP ratio of 60% for the general (combined) government by 2023, comprising 40% for the Central Government and 20% for the State Governments 2.
