As per the Constitution of India, it is mandatory for a State to take the Central Government's consent for raising any loan if the former owes any outstanding liabilities to the latter - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (c) 1 & 3 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The FRBM Review Committee (2017, N.K. Singh) recommended a 60% debt-to-GDP ratio by 2023 (40% Centre, 20% states). Statement 2 is false; in 2018, Centre’s domestic liabilities were ~46% of GDP, states ~25%. Statement 3 is true per Article 293(3). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 3 is also true. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false; debt figures are reversed. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - FRBM Review Committee (2017): 60% debt-to-GDP target. - Economic Survey (2017–18): Centre’s debt ~46%, states ~25%. - Constitution (Article 293): State borrowing consent. - Related Concepts/Figures: - FRBM Act: Guides fiscal discipline. - Fiscal Federalism: Centre-state financial relations. - N.K. Singh: Chaired FRBM Review Committee. - Key Takeaway: - FRBM’s debt targets and constitutional borrowing rules shaped India’s 2018 fiscal framework. - Q89: Consider the following items: - Items: 1. Cereal grains hulled 2. Chicken eggs cooked 3. Fish processed and canned 4. Newspaper containing advertising material - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 1, 2 & 4 only (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (c) 1, 2 & 4 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2018, GST exempted hulled grains, cooked eggs, and newspapers (0% tax), but canned fish was taxed at 5%, excluding it from exempt items. - Why Original Answer (d) Incorrect: - Canned fish (statement 3) was not exempt, unlike others. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes eggs, newspapers. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes grains, includes taxed fish. - (d) Incorrect: Includes taxed fish. - Additional Evidence: - GST Council (2018): 0% tax on grains, eggs, newspapers; 5% on canned fish. - Economic Survey (2017–18): GST exemptions for essentials. - Related Concepts/Figures: - GST: Unified tax regime (2017). - Essential Goods: Low-tax focus. - Key Takeaway: - GST exemptions in 2018 targeted essentials like grains, eggs, newspapers. - Q90: With reference to India's decision to levy an equalization tax of 6% on online advertisement services offered by non-resident entities, which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: - 1. It is introduced as a part of the Income Tax Act - 2. Non-resident entities that offer advertisement services in India can claim a tax credit in their home country under the "Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements" - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The 6% equalization levy (2016) was introduced via Finance Act, not Income Tax Act, and DTAAs did not universally allow tax credits for this levy in 2018. - Why Original Answer (b) Incorrect: - Statement 2 is false; DTAA credits were limited for the levy. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false; not under Income Tax Act. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Both statements false. - Additional Evidence: - Finance Act (2016): Introduced levy. - OECD BEPS: Limited DTAA applicability. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Equalization Levy: Digital economy tax. - DTAA: Tax credit limitations. - Key Takeaway: - The 2018 levy was a standalone tax, not DTAA-compatible. - Q91: Despite being a high saving economy, capital formation may not result in significant increase in output due to: - Options: (a) weak administrative machinery (b) illiteracy (c) high population density (d) high capital-output ratio - Answer: (d) high capital-output ratio - Analysis: - Economic Context: - A high capital-output ratio (ICOR) means more capital is needed per unit of output, reducing efficiency. In 2018, India’s ICOR was ~4, reflecting inefficiencies in capital use despite high savings (~30% of GDP). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Administrative issues are secondary to ICOR. - (b) Incorrect: Illiteracy affects human capital, not directly capital formation. - (c) Incorrect: Population density doesn’t directly impact capital efficiency. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2017–18): ICOR ~4, indicating capital inefficiency. - Planning Commission: Linked high ICOR to low output growth. - Related Concepts/Figures: - ICOR: Measures capital efficiency. - Savings Rate: India’s high savings (~30% GDP). - Economic Survey: Tracks capital formation trends. - Key Takeaway: - High ICOR limits output growth despite India’s 2018 high savings rate. - [2019-I] - Q92: Which of the following is not included in the assets of a commercial bank in India? - Options: (a) Advances (b) Deposits (c) Investments (d) Money at call and short notice - Answer: (b) Deposits - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Commercial bank assets include advances (loans), investments (e.g., securities), and money at call/short notice (interbank lending). Deposits are liabilities, as they are owed to customers. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Advances are assets (loans given). - (c) Incorrect: Investments are assets (e.g., bonds). - (d) Incorrect: Money at call/short notice is an asset. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2019): Bank balance sheet structure. - Economic Survey (2018–19): Deposits as liabilities (~₹125 lakh crore). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Bank Balance Sheet: Assets vs. liabilities. - Priority Sector Lending: Part of advances. - RBI: Regulates bank accounting. - Key Takeaway: - Deposits, as liabilities, are not assets in India’s 2019 banking system. - Q93: In the context of India, which of the following factors is/are contributor/contributors to reducing the risk of a currency crisis? - Factors: 1. The foreign currency earnings of India's IT sector 2. Increasing the government expenditure 3. Remittances from Indians abroad - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 & 3 only (c) 2 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (b) 1 & 3 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - IT sector earnings (~$80 billion in 2019) and remittances (~$80 billion) boost forex reserves, reducing currency crisis risk. Increased government expenditure, if deficit-financed, may weaken the rupee, not stabilize it. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Remittances (statement 3) also contribute. - (c) Incorrect: Expenditure may increase crisis risk. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2019): Forex reserves ~$430 billion, driven by IT and remittances. - Economic Survey (2018–19): Highlighted IT and remittance inflows. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Forex Reserves: Buffer against currency crises. - Balance of Payments: Tracks inflows. - Raghuram Rajan: Strengthened reserves as RBI Governor. - Key Takeaway: - IT earnings and remittances bolster India’s 2019 currency stability. - Q94: The Chairman of public sector banks are selected by the: - Options: (a) Banks Board Bureau (b) Reserve Bank of India (c) Union Ministry of Finance (d) Management of concerned bank - Answer: (a) Banks Board Bureau - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The Banks Board Bureau (BBB), established in 2016, recommends appointments of chairmen and directors for public sector banks (PSBs) to enhance governance. In 2019, BBB streamlined PSB leadership. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: RBI regulates, not appoints. - (c) Incorrect: Ministry approves, but BBB recommends. - (d) Incorrect: Banks don’t self-appoint chairmen. - Supporting Evidence: - BBB (2019): Mandated for PSB appointments. - Economic Survey (2018–19): Noted BBB’s governance role. - Related Concepts/Figures: - PSB Reforms: Post-NPA crisis governance. - Basel Norms: Drive banking oversight. - P.J. Nayak Committee: Recommended BBB creation. - Key Takeaway: - BBB’s role in PSB chairman selection reflects India’s 2019 banking governance reforms. - Q95: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) is the first regulatory body set up by the Government of India 2. One of the tasks of PNGRB is to ensure competitive markets for gas 3. Appeals against the decisions of PNGRB go before the Appellate Tribunals of Electricity - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (b) 2 & 3 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - PNGRB (2006) regulates gas markets, ensuring competition (statement 2). Appeals go to the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (statement 3). Statement 1 is false; TRAI (1997) was earlier. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 2 is also true. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - PNGRB Act (2006): Defines PNGRB’s role and appeals. - Economic Survey (2018–19): Noted PNGRB’s market regulation. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Energy Regulation: PNGRB’s role in gas markets. - TRAI: Earlier regulatory body. - Competition Policy: Ensures market fairness. - Key Takeaway: - PNGRB’s regulatory and appellate framework supports India’s 2019 gas market competition. - Q96: Consider the following statements: The Reserve Bank of India's recent directives relating to 'Storage of Payment System Data', popularly known as data diktat command the payment system providers that: - Statements: 1. They shall ensure that entire data relating to payment systems operated by them are stored in a system only in India 2. They shall ensure that the systems are owned and operated by public sector enterprises 3. They shall submit the consolidated system audit report to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India by the end of the calendar year - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 & 2 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - RBI’s 2018 data localization directive mandated payment system data storage in India (statement 1). Systems can be privately owned, and audits go to RBI, not CAG, making statements 2 and 3 false. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false; private ownership allowed. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false; audits to RBI. - (d) Incorrect: Only statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2018): Data localization for payment systems. - Economic Survey (2018–19): Highlighted data security policies. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Data Localization: Enhances data security. - Digital Payments: UPI and card growth. - RBI: Regulates payment systems. - Key Takeaway: - RBI’s 2019 data localization ensures payment data security in India. - [2020-I] - Q97: What is the importance of the term "Interest Coverage Ratio" of a firm in India? - Statements: 1. It helps in understanding the present risk of a firm that a bank is going to give a loan to 2. It helps in evaluating the emerging risk of a firm that a bank is going to give a loan to 3. The higher a borrowing firm's level of Interest Coverage Ratio, the worse is its ability to service its debt - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 2 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (a) 1 & 2 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR, EBIT/interest) measures a firm’s ability to pay interest, assessing present (statement 1) and emerging risks (statement 2). Higher ICR indicates better debt servicing, making statement 3 false. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statement 1 is also true. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false; higher ICR is better. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2020): ICR used in credit risk assessment. - Economic Survey (2019–20): Highlighted corporate debt risks. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Credit Risk: ICR assesses loan repayment ability. - Non-Performing Assets: Linked to low ICR. - Basel III: Guides bank risk management. - Key Takeaway: - ICR is critical for assessing firm-level debt risks in India’s 2020 banking sector. - Q98: With reference to the Indian economy, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. 'Commercial Paper' is a short-term unsecured promissory note 2. 'Certificate of Deposit' is a long-term instrument issued by the Reserve Bank of India to a corporation 3. 'Call Money' is a short-term finance used for interbank transactions 4. 'Zero-Coupon Bonds' are the interest bearing short-term bonds issued by the Scheduled Commercial Banks to corporations - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 4 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (c) 1 & 3 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Commercial Paper (CP) is a short-term unsecured note (~90–180 days, statement 1). Call Money is short-term interbank lending (statement 3). Certificates of Deposit are short-term, issued by banks, not RBI (statement 2 false). Zero-Coupon Bonds are non-interest bearing, long-term, not short-term (statement 4 false). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 4 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statements 2 and 4 are false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2020): CP and Call Money definitions. - Economic Survey (2019–20): Money market instruments. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Money Market: CP and Call Money as instruments. - Liquidity Management: RBI’s role. - Financial Markets: Short-term financing tools. - Key Takeaway: - CP and Call Money are key short-term instruments in India’s 2020 financial markets. - Q99: In the context of the Indian economy, non-financial debt includes which of the following? - Items: 1. Housing loans owed by households 2. Amounts outstanding on credit cards 3. Treasury bills - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 & 2 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Non-financial debt includes household debts (housing loans, credit cards) and treasury bills, as they represent borrowing outside financial securities in 2020. - Why Original Answer (b) Incorrect: - Treasury bills, as government borrowing, are included in non-financial debt definitions in some contexts. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes credit cards, treasury bills. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes treasury bills. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes household debts. - Additional Evidence: - RBI (2020): Household debt ~11% GDP; treasury bills included in broader debt. - Economic Survey (2019–20): Debt composition data. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Household Debt: Loans, credit cards. - Treasury Bills: Government borrowing. - Key Takeaway: - Non-financial debt in 2020 included diverse borrowing types. - [2021-I] - Q100: The money multiplier in an economy increases with which one of the following? - Options: (a) Increase in the Cash Reserve Ratio in the banks (b) Increase in the Statutory Liquidity Ratio in the banks (c) Increase in the banking habit of the people (d) Increase in the population of the country - Answer: (c) Increase in the banking habit of the people - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The money multiplier (M3/M0) increases when more people deposit money in banks, expanding credit creation. In 2021, India’s banking penetration grew post-Jan Dhan Yojana. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Higher CRR reduces multiplier by locking funds. - (b) Incorrect: Higher SLR limits lending, reducing multiplier. - (d) Incorrect: Population growth doesn’t directly affect multiplier. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2021): Money multiplier ~5.5, driven by deposits. - Economic Survey (2020–21): Jan Dhan boosted banking. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Money Multiplier: Links deposits to credit creation. - Jan Dhan Yojana: Expanded banking access. - RBI: Manages CRR and SLR. - Key Takeaway: - Increased banking habits boost India’s 2021 money multiplier, enhancing credit creation. - Q101: With reference to Indian economy, demand-pull inflation can be caused/increased by which of the following? - Factors: 1. Expansionary policies 2. Fiscal stimulus 3. Inflation-indexing wages 4. Higher purchasing power 5. Rising interest rates - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 4 only (b) 3, 4 & 5 only (c) 1, 2, 3 & 5 only (d) 1, 2, 3, 4 & 5 - Answer: (a) 1, 2 & 4 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Demand-pull inflation occurs when demand exceeds supply, driven by expansionary monetary policies (e.g., low rates), fiscal stimulus (e.g., deficit spending), and higher purchasing power. Inflation-indexed wages and rising interest rates (cost-push factors) don’t directly cause demand-pull inflation. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statements 3 and 5 are cost-push factors. - (c) Incorrect: Includes 3 and 5, excludes 4. - (d) Incorrect: Includes 3 and 5. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2020–21): Demand-pull inflation post-COVID stimulus. - RBI (2021): Noted fiscal stimulus effects. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Demand-Pull Inflation: Excess demand dynamics. - Fiscal Policy: Government spending drives demand. - RBI: Manages monetary policy. - Key Takeaway: - Demand-pull inflation in 2021 India was driven by expansionary policies, stimulus, and purchasing power. - Q102: Which among the following steps is most likely to be taken at the time of an economic recession? - Options: (a) Cut in tax rates accompanied by increase in interest rate (b) Increase in expenditure on public projects (c) Increase in tax rates accompanied by reduction of interest rate (d) Reduction of expenditure on public projects - Answer: (b) Increase in expenditure on public projects - Analysis: - Economic Context: - During a recession, governments increase public spending (fiscal stimulus) to boost demand, as seen in India’s 2021 COVID recovery (~₹2.6 lakh crore stimulus). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Higher interest rates curb demand. - (c) Incorrect: Higher taxes reduce demand. - (d) Incorrect: Cutting expenditure worsens recession. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2020–21): Stimulus for post-COVID recovery. - Keynesian Economics: Advocates public spending in recessions. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Stimulus: Boosts demand in recessions. - Counter-Cyclical Policy: Government spending strategy. - Nirmala Sitharaman: Finance Minister during 2021 stimulus. - Key Takeaway: - Public expenditure increases are key to India’s 2021 recession recovery strategy. - Q103: Indian Government Bond yields are influenced by which of the following? - Factors: 1. Actions of the United States Federal Reserve 2. Actions of the Reserve Bank of India 3. Inflation and short-term interest rates - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 2 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Bond yields are influenced by US Fed actions (global capital flows), RBI actions (e.g., repo rate, OMOs), and domestic inflation/short-term rates. In 2021, 10-year G-sec yields were ~6%. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes inflation/rates (statement 3). - (b) Incorrect: Excludes Fed and inflation. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes Fed and RBI. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2021): G-sec yields ~6%, influenced by repo rate. - Economic Survey (2020–21): Global and domestic factors in yields. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Bond Yields: Reflect borrowing costs. - Open Market Operations: RBI’s yield management tool. - Global Financial Markets: US Fed’s impact. - Key Takeaway: - India’s 2021 bond yields reflect global and domestic monetary dynamics. - [2022-I] - Q104: With reference to the Indian economy, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. If the inflation is too high, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is likely to buy government securities 2. If the rupee is rapidly depreciating, RBI is likely to sell dollars in the market 3. If interest rates in the USA or European Union were to fall, that is likely to induce RBI to buy dollars - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (b) 2 and 3 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - High inflation prompts RBI to sell securities (OMOs) to reduce money supply, making statement 1 false. Selling dollars curbs rupee depreciation (statement 2). Lower US/EU rates attract capital to India, prompting RBI to buy dollars to manage rupee appreciation (statement 3). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2022): Sold dollars to stabilize rupee. - Economic Survey (2021–22): Noted RBI’s forex interventions. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Open Market Operations: RBI’s inflation control tool. - Forex Interventions: Manage rupee value. - Shaktikanta Das: RBI Governor in 2022. - Key Takeaway: - RBI’s 2022 actions focused on curbing depreciation and managing capital flows. - Q105: With reference to the Indian economy, what are the advantages of "Inflation-Indexed Bonds (IIBs)"? - Statements: 1. Government can reduce the coupon rates on its borrowing by way of IIBs 2. IIBs provide protection to the investors from uncertainty regarding inflation 3. The interest received as well as capital gains on IIBs are not taxable - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - IIBs (relaunched 2013) adjust returns for inflation, lowering coupon rates (statement 1) and protecting investors (statement 2). Interest and capital gains are taxable, making statement 3 false. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false; IIBs are taxable. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2022): IIBs linked to CPI, taxable. - Economic Survey (2021–22): IIBs as inflation hedge. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Inflation Protection: IIBs’ core feature. - CPI: Basis for IIB adjustments. - RBI: Issues IIBs. - Key Takeaway: - IIBs reduce borrowing costs and protect investors in India’s 2022 economy. - Q106: With reference to the Indian economy, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. A share of the household financial savings goes towards government borrowings 2. Dated securities issued at market-related rates in auctions form a large component of internal debt - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (c) Both 1 and 2 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Household savings (~20% of GDP in 2022) fund government borrowings via bonds. Dated securities (e.g., G-secs) are a major part of internal debt (~₹80 lakh crore), auctioned at market rates. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is also true. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 1 is also true. - (d) Incorrect: Both statements are true. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2021–22): Household savings in G-secs. - RBI (2022): Dated securities ~50% of internal debt. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Government Securities: Key borrowing tool. - Household Savings: Finance public debt. - Debt Management Office: Manages internal debt. - Key Takeaway: - Household savings and dated securities are central to India’s 2022 public borrowing. - Q107: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Tight monetary policy of US Federal Reserve could lead to capital flight 2. Capital flight may increase the interest cost of firms with existing External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) 3. Devaluation of domestic currency decreases the currency risk associated with ECBs - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - US Fed’s tight policy (e.g., rate hikes) causes capital flight from India (statement 1), raising ECB interest costs due to rupee depreciation (statement 2). Devaluation increases currency risk for ECBs, making statement 3 false. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2022): Capital outflows during Fed rate hikes. - Economic Survey (2021–22): ECB risks with depreciation. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Capital Flight: Response to global rates. - ECBs: External borrowing risks. - RBI: Manages currency risks. - Key Takeaway: - US Fed’s policies impact India’s 2022 capital flows and ECB costs. - Q108: In India, which one of the following is responsible for maintaining price stability by controlling inflation? - Options: (a) Department of Consumer Affairs (b) Expenditure Management Commission (c) Financial Stability and Development Council (d) Reserve Bank of India - Answer: (d) Reserve Bank of India - Analysis: - Economic Context: - RBI controls inflation via monetary policy (e.g., repo rate ~6.5% in 2022), targeting 4% ± 2% under the 2016 framework. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Consumer Affairs handles pricing, not inflation. - (b) Incorrect: EMC focuses on expenditure, not inflation. - (c) Incorrect: FSDC oversees financial stability, not price control. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2022): Inflation targeting at ~6%. - Economic Survey (2021–22): RBI’s inflation role. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Monetary Policy: Repo rate and CRR tools. - Inflation Targeting: 2016 RBI framework. - Shaktikanta Das: RBI Governor in 2022. - Key Takeaway: - RBI’s monetary policy is key to India’s 2022 inflation control. - Q109: With reference to Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. They enable the digital representation of physical assets 2. They are unique cryptographic tokens that exist on a blockchain 3. They can be traded or exchanged at equivalency and therefore can be used as a medium of commercial transactions - Options: (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3 - Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - NFTs represent physical or digital assets (e.g., art) on blockchains, being unique tokens (statements 1 and 2). They are non-fungible, not interchangeable at equivalency, making statement 3 false. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false; NFTs are non-fungible. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2022): NFTs as unique blockchain assets. - Economic Survey (2021–22): Emerging digital asset market. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Blockchain: Underpins NFT uniqueness. - Digital Assets: NFTs as new investment class. - Crypto Regulation: RBI’s cautious stance. - Key Takeaway: - NFTs’ unique, blockchain-based nature defines their role in India’s 2022 digital economy. - [2024-I] - Q110: The total fertility rate in an economy is defined as: - Options: (a) the number of children born per 1000 people in the population in a year (b) the number of children born to a couple in their lifetime in a given population (c) the birth rate minus death rate (d) the average number of live births a woman would have by the end of her child-bearing age - Answer: (d) the average number of live births a woman would have by the end of her child-bearing age - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman has during her reproductive years (15–49). In 2024, India’s TFR was ~2, below replacement level (2.1). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Refers to crude birth rate, not TFR. - (b) Incorrect: TFR is per woman, not per couple. - (c) Incorrect: Describes natural population growth. - Supporting Evidence: - NFHS-5 (2019–21): India’s TFR ~2. - Economic Survey (2023–24): TFR decline impacts demographics. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Demographic Transition: Falling TFR in India. - Population Policy: Family planning initiatives. - Census of India: Tracks TFR trends. - Key Takeaway: - TFR defines India’s 2024 demographic trends, critical for economic planning. - Q111: With reference to the sectors of the Indian economy, consider the following pairs: - Pairs: 1. Storage of agricultural produce - Secondary 2. Dairy farm - Primary 3. Mineral exploration - Tertiary 4. Weaving cloth - Secondary - Options: (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) Only three (d) All four - Answer: (b) Only two - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Dairy farming is primary (resource extraction). Weaving cloth is secondary (manufacturing). Storage is tertiary (services), and mineral exploration is primary, not tertiary. Only pairs 2 and 4 are correct. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Two pairs (2 and 4) are correct. - (c) Incorrect: Pair 3 is incorrect. - (d) Incorrect: Pairs 1 and 3 are incorrect. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2023–24): Sectoral GDP contributions. - CSO: Defines primary, secondary, tertiary sectors. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Economic Sectors: Primary, secondary, tertiary classification. - Structural Transformation: Shift to services. - CSO: Tracks sectoral data. - Key Takeaway: - Correct sector classification is key to understanding India’s 2024 economic structure. - Q112: With reference to physical capital in Indian economy, consider the following pairs: - Pairs: 1. Farmer's plough - Working capital 2. Computer - Fixed capital 3. Yarn used by the weaver - Working capital 4. Petrol - Working capital - Options: (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) Only three (d) All four - Answer: (b) Only two - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Fixed capital (e.g., computers) is long-term; working capital (e.g., yarn, petrol) is short-term. Plough is fixed capital, not working. Pairs 2 and 3 are correct. - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - Pair 4 (petrol) is not working capital in strict definitions; it’s a consumable. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Two pairs correct. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes petrol as working capital. - (d) Incorrect: Plough, petrol incorrect. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (2023–24): Capital formation ~30% GDP. - CSO: Fixed vs. working capital definitions. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Capital Formation: Economic growth driver. - Fixed vs. Working Capital: Investment types. - Key Takeaway: - Correct capital classification is key for 2024 investment analysis. - Poverty, Planning, Finance and Economic/Social Development - [1995] - Q1: Which one of the following Five Year Plans recognised human development as the core of all development efforts? - Options: (a) The Third Five Year Plan (b) The Fifth Five Year Plan (c) The Sixth Five Year Plan (d) The Eighth Five Year Plan - Answer: (d) The Eighth Five Year Plan - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The Eighth Five Year Plan (1992–97) explicitly prioritized human development (education, health, and poverty reduction) as central to economic growth, aligning with the post-1991 liberalization era’s focus on inclusive development. Earlier plans focused more on industrial and agricultural growth. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Third Plan (1961–66) emphasized agriculture and industry. - (b) Incorrect: Fifth Plan (1974–79) focused on poverty alleviation but not explicitly human development. - (c) Incorrect: Sixth Plan (1980–85) prioritized infrastructure and energy. - Supporting Evidence: - Planning Commission (1992): Eighth Plan emphasized human development. - Economic Survey (1994–95): Highlighted education and health investments. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Human Development Index (HDI): Introduced by UNDP in 1990, HDI (measuring life expectancy, education, and income) influenced India’s shift toward human-centric planning in the 1990s, as reflected in the Eighth Plan’s focus on literacy and healthcare. - Liberalization Reforms: The 1991 reforms under Manmohan Singh shifted planning toward inclusive growth, integrating human development with economic progress. - Amartya Sen: His work on human development and capability approach shaped India’s policy focus on education and health as development pillars. - Key Takeaway: - The Eighth Plan marked India’s 1995 shift toward human development as a core economic strategy, reflecting global and domestic policy evolution. - Q2: Which of the following are among the non-plan expenditures of the Government of India? - Items: 1. Defence expenditure 2. Subsidies 3. All expenditures linked with the previous plan periods 4. Interest payment - Options: (a) 1 & 2 (b) 1 & 3 (c) 2 & 4 (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Non-plan expenditure includes recurring costs not tied to new development projects, such as defence (~₹22,000 crore in 1995), subsidies (e.g., food, fertilizer), interest payments (~₹50,000 crore), and expenditures from past plans (e.g., maintenance of projects). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes interest payments and past plan expenditures. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes subsidies and interest payments. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes defence and past plan expenditures. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (1994–95): Non-plan expenditure ~70% of total budget. - Union Budget (1995–96): Defence, subsidies, interest as major non-plan items. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Non-Plan vs. Plan Expenditure: Non-plan expenditure covers operational and maintenance costs, while plan expenditure funds new developmental projects, a distinction critical in India’s 1990s fiscal planning. - Fiscal Deficit: High non-plan expenditures, especially interest payments, drove India’s fiscal deficit (~5.7% of GDP in 1995), necessitating fiscal reforms. - P. Chidambaram: As Finance Minister (1996–98), he emphasized controlling non-plan expenditure to stabilize public finances. - Key Takeaway: - Non-plan expenditures in 1995, including defence, subsidies, and interest, dominated India’s budget, highlighting fiscal management challenges. - Q3: What is the annual rate aimed in the Eighth Five Year Plan? - Options: (a) 5.6% (b) 6% (c) 6.5% (d) 7% - Answer: (a) 5.6% - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Eighth Five Year Plan (1992–97) initially targeted 5.6% annual GDP growth, reflecting cautious optimism post-1991 liberalization, later revised to ~6.5% as reforms took effect. - Q4: The largest source of financing the public sector outlay of the Eighth Five Year Plan comes from: - Options: (a) balance from current revenue (b) contribution of public enterprises (c) government borrowings (d) deficit financing - Answer: (d) deficit financing - Analysis: - Historical Context: - The Eighth Plan’s outlay (~₹4.34 lakh crore) relied heavily on deficit financing (~45%), as borrowings and revenue were insufficient post-1991 fiscal reforms. - The Seventh Five Year Plan covered the period: - Options: (a) 1987-1992 (b) 1986-1991 (c) 1985-1990 (d) 1988-1994 - Answer: (c) 1985-1990 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The Sixth Plan ran from 1980–85, the Seventh from 1985–90, and the Eighth from 1992–97, with 1990–92 as a period of annual plans due to political instability. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: 1987–92 includes annual plan years. - (b) Incorrect: 1986–91 overlaps with annual plans. - (d) Incorrect: 1988–94 is misaligned with plan cycles. - Supporting Evidence: - Planning Commission (1985): Seventh Plan 1985–90. - Economic Survey (1996–97): Plan period timelines. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Five Year Plans: India’s centralized planning framework, initiated in 1951, guided economic development through set periods, with the Seventh Plan focusing on modernization. - Annual Plans: The 1990–92 gap due to political changes delayed the Eighth Plan, reflecting planning flexibility. - Planning Commission: Under Rajiv Gandhi’s oversight in 1985, it shaped the Seventh Plan’s goals. - Key Takeaway: - The Seventh Plan (1985–90) bridged India’s economic planning in the 1997 context. - [1998] - Q11: Economic Survey in India is published officially, every year by the: - Options: (a) Reserve Bank of India (b) Planning Commission of India (c) Ministry of Finance, Govt. of India (d) Ministry of Industries, Govt. of India - Answer: (c) Ministry of Finance, Govt. of India - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The Economic Survey, an annual pre-budget document, is published by the Ministry of Finance, analyzing economic performance and trends. Q22: The growth rate of per capita income at current prices is higher than that of per capita income at constant prices, because the latter takes into account the rate of: - Options: (a) growth of population (b) increase in price level (c) growth of money supply (d) increase in the wage rate - Special securities issued to RBI - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 & 2 (c) 2 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2000, government financing included market borrowings (e.g., G-secs), treasury bills (short-term), and special securities to RBI (e.g., ad-hoc T-bills), all funding fiscal deficits (~5.5% of GDP). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes T-bills and RBI securities. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes RBI securities. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes market borrowings and RBI securities. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2000): Market borrowings ~₹1 lakh crore, T-bills ~₹30,000 crore. - Economic Survey (1999–2000): Deficit financing sources. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Deficit Financing: Market borrowings, T-bills, and RBI securities funded India’s fiscal gap in the 1990s, reflecting borrowing reliance. - Government Securities: G-secs and T-bills were key debt instruments, shaping public finance. - RBI: Managed government borrowing, including special securities, in 2000. - Key Takeaway: - Diverse borrowing instruments funded India’s 2000 fiscal deficit. - [2001] - Q24: Global capital flows to developing countries increased significantly during the nineties. Elections in 1977 led to the Janata Party’s victory, ending Congress rule and impacting economic policy continuity. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Third Plan (1961–66) predates Emergency. - (b) Incorrect: Fourth Plan (1969–74) ended before Emergency. - (d) Incorrect: Sixth Plan (1980–85) was post-Emergency. - Supporting Evidence: - Planning Commission (1974): Fifth Plan timeline. - Economic Survey (2008–09): Historical context of Emergency. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Emergency (1975–77): Imposed by Indira Gandhi, it disrupted economic planning and led to political shifts, affecting the Fifth Plan’s poverty alleviation focus. - Janata Party Government: Its 1977 election introduced policies like rural development, altering the Fifth Plan’s trajectory. - Indira Gandhi: Her leadership during the Emergency shaped India’s 1970s economic and political landscape. - Key Takeaway: - The Fifth Plan’s alignment with the 1975–77 Emergency and Janata Party’s 1977 election marked a turbulent period in India’s 2009 historical economic context. - Q29: Consider the following statements regarding Indian Planning: - Statements: 1. Why? - Options: (a) India has preference for certain countries as regards receiving FDI (b) India has double taxation avoidance agreement with Mauritius (c) Most citizens of Mauritius have ethnic identity with India and so they feel secure to invest in India (d) Impending dangers of global climatic change prompt Mauritius to make huge investments in India - Answer: (b) India has double taxation avoidance agreement with Mauritius - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) with Mauritius (1982) allowed tax benefits, routing ~40% of India’s FDI in 2010 due to favorable tax treatment, unlike UK/France. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: No explicit country preference; DTAA drives flows. - (c) Incorrect: Ethnic ties are not a primary factor. - (d) Incorrect: Climate change irrelevant to FDI routing. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2010): Mauritius FDI ~₹40,000 crore. - Economic Survey (2009–10): DTAA’s role in FDI. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA): The 1982 India-Mauritius DTAA minimized tax liabilities, making Mauritius a preferred FDI route. - FDI Routing: Tax havens like Mauritius facilitated FDI inflows, raising concerns about round-tripping in the 2000s. - Manmohan Singh: As Prime Minister in 2010, oversaw FDI policy debates, including DTAA revisions. - Key Takeaway: - Mauritius’ DTAA drove significant FDI to India in 2010, leveraging tax benefits. - Q34: India-based Neutrino Observatory is included by the Planning Commission as a mega science project under the 11th Five-Year Plan. Q69: A rise in general level of prices may be caused by: - Causes: 1. an increase in the money supply 2. a decrease in the aggregate level of output 3. an increase in the effective demand - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 & 2 only (c) 2 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Inflation (~9% in 2013) results from increased money supply (1), reduced output (2, supply shock), and higher demand (3, demand-pull), as seen in India’s 2013 food and fuel price spikes. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes true statements 2 and 3. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes true statement 3. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes true statement 1. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2012–13): Inflation drivers. - RBI (2013): Monetary tightening for inflation control. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Inflation Types: Demand-pull (3), cost-push (2), and monetary (1) inflation shaped India’s 2013 price challenges. - Monetary Policy: RBI’s rate hikes (~7.5% repo rate) addressed inflation in 2013. - Raghuram Rajan: As RBI Governor, tackled inflation in 2013. - Key Takeaway: - Multiple factors drove India’s 2013 inflation, requiring robust policy responses. - Q70: Which one of the following is likely to be the most inflationary in its effect? - Options: (a) Repayment of public debt (b) Borrowing from the public to finance a budget deficit (c) Borrowing from banks to finance a budget deficit (d) Creating new money to finance a budget deficit - Answer: (d) Creating new money to finance a budget deficit - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Creating new money (deficit financing, 4) directly increases money supply, fueling inflation (~9% in 2013). Debt repayment (1) and public borrowing (2) are less inflationary, while bank borrowing (3) is indirect. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Debt repayment reduces money supply. - (b) Incorrect: Public borrowing redistributes existing money. - (c) Incorrect: Bank borrowing is less direct than money creation. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2013): Deficit financing’s inflationary impact. - Economic Survey (2012–13): Fiscal deficit ~5%. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Deficit Financing: Printing money to fund deficits increases inflation, a concern in India’s 2013 fiscal policy. - Monetary Policy: RBI’s efforts to curb money supply growth countered deficits. - Raghuram Rajan: As RBI Governor, addressed deficit-driven inflation in 2013. - Key Takeaway: - Creating new money in 2013 was the most inflationary deficit financing method. - Q71: Supply of money remaining the same when there is an increase in demand for money, there will be: - Options: (a) a fall in the level of prices (b) an increase in the rate of interest (c) a decrease in the rate of interest (d) an increase in the level of income and employment - Answer: (b) an increase in the rate of interest - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Fixed money supply with rising demand (e.g., for investment) increases interest rates, as seen in India’s 2013 tight monetary policy (repo rate ~7.5%). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Prices may not fall; interest rates rise. - (c) Incorrect: Interest rates increase, not decrease. - (d) Incorrect: Income/employment not directly affected. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2013): Interest rate hikes for demand control. - Economic Survey (2012–13): Money demand dynamics. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Money Demand: Increased demand with fixed supply raises borrowing costs, influencing 2013 monetary policy. - Liquidity Preference Theory: Keynes’ theory explains interest rate rises, relevant to 2013. - Raghuram Rajan: As RBI Governor, raised rates in 2013 to manage demand. - Key Takeaway: - Rising money demand in 2013 increased interest rates, reflecting tight monetary policy. - Q72: Economic growth in country X will necessarily have to occur if: - Options: (a) there is technical progress in the world economy (b) there is population growth in X (c) there is capital formation in X (d) the volume of trade grows in the world economy - Answer: (c) there is capital formation in X - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Capital formation (investment in infrastructure, industry) directly drives growth in country X (~6% GDP growth in 2013). Global factors (1, 4) or population growth (2) are not guaranteed drivers. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Global progress doesn’t ensure X’s growth. - (b) Incorrect: Population growth may strain resources. - (d) Incorrect: Global trade growth is external, not internal. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2012–13): Capital formation ~35% of GDP. - World Bank (2013): Investment-growth link. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Capital Formation: Investment in fixed assets drives production and growth, key to India’s 2013 economy. - Solow Growth Model: Emphasizes capital accumulation for growth, relevant to 2013. - P. Chidambaram: As Finance Minister, promoted investment in 2013. - Key Takeaway: - Capital formation in 2013 was essential for economic growth in India. - [2014-I] - Q73: If the interest rate is decreased in an economy, it will: - Options: (a) decrease the consumption expenditure in the economy (b) increase the tax collection of the Government (c) increase the investment expenditure in the economy (d) increase the total savings in the economy - Answer: (c) increase the investment expenditure in the economy - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Lower interest rates (e.g., RBI repo rate cut to ~7% in 2014) reduce borrowing costs, boosting investment expenditure (~₹10 lakh crore in 2014). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Consumption may increase with lower rates. - (b) Incorrect: Tax collection not directly affected. - (d) Incorrect: Savings may decrease as borrowing rises. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2014): Interest rate cuts for growth. - Economic Survey (2013–14): Investment trends. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Monetary Policy: Lower rates stimulate investment, a key 2014 RBI strategy. - Investment Expenditure: Drives GDP growth, critical for India’s 2014 recovery. - Raghuram Rajan: As RBI Governor, initiated rate cuts in 2014. - Key Takeaway: - Lower interest rates in 2014 boosted India’s investment expenditure. - Q74: With reference to Union Budget, which of the following is/are covered under Non-Plan Expenditure? - Items: 1. Defence expenditure 2. Interest payments 3. Salaries and pensions 4. Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes true statements 2, 3, 4. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes true statements 1 and 4. - (d) Incorrect: All statements are true. - Supporting Evidence: - Union Budget (2014–15): Non-Plan Expenditure breakdown. - Economic Survey (2013–14): Budget expenditure categories. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Non-Plan Expenditure: Covers recurring costs, constraining India’s 2014 fiscal flexibility. - Fiscal Deficit: Non-Plan spending (~60% of budget) challenged deficit targets (~4%). - Arun Jaitley: As Finance Minister, managed 2014 budget allocations. - Key Takeaway: - Non-Plan Expenditure in 2014 covered critical recurring costs, impacting fiscal policy. - Q75: The sales tax you pay while purchasing a toothpaste is a: - Options: (a) tax imposed by the Central Government (b) tax imposed by the Central Government but collected by the State Government (c) tax imposed by the State Government but collected by the Central Government (d) tax imposed and collected by the State Government - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Sales tax is State, not Central. - (b) Incorrect: States collect sales tax. - (c) Incorrect: Centre doesn’t collect sales tax. - Supporting Evidence: - Constitution (Entry 54, List II): State taxation powers. - Chidambaram: As Finance Minister (pre-2014), laid groundwork for GST transition. - Key Takeaway: - Sales tax in 2014 was a State-driven revenue source, pre-GST. - Q76: What does venture capital mean? - Options: (a) A short-term capital provided to industries (b) A long-term start-up capital provided to new entrepreneurs (c) Funds provided to industries at times of incurring losses (d) Funds provided for replacement and renovation of industries - Answer: (b) A long-term start-up capital provided to new entrepreneurs - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Venture capital provides long-term funding to startups, supporting innovation (~₹20,000 crore invested in 2014). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Venture capital is long-term, not short-term. - (c) Incorrect: Not for loss-making industries. - (d) Incorrect: Not for replacement/renovation. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2013–14): Venture capital growth. - SEBI (2014): VC regulations. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Venture Capital: High-risk, high-reward funding for startups, boosting India’s 2014 entrepreneurial ecosystem. - Startup Ecosystem: VC growth supported India’s emerging tech sector. - SEBI: Regulated VC funds, ensuring investor protection in 2014. - Key Takeaway: - Venture capital in 2014 fueled India’s startup growth, supporting innovation. - Q77: Which of the following are associated with 'Planning' in India? - Entities: 1. The Finance Commission 2. The National Development Council 3. The Union Ministry of Rural Development 4. The Union Ministry of Urban Development 5. Finance Commission (1) handles tax devolution, not planning; Ministries (3, 4) implement, not plan. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Finance Commission (1) not involved in planning. - (b) Incorrect: Ministries (3, 4) implement, not plan. - (d) Incorrect: Only 2 and 5 are correct. - Supporting Evidence: - Planning Commission (2014): NDC and Parliament roles. - Economic Survey (2013–14): Planning process. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Planning Commission: Guided India’s planning until 2014, replaced by NITI Aayog. - National Development Council: Ensured Centre-State plan coordination in 2014. - Montek Singh Ahluwalia: As Planning Commission Deputy Chairman, shaped 2014 plans. - Key Takeaway: - NDC and Parliament were central to India’s 2014 planning process. - [2015-I] - Q78: A decrease in tax to GDP ratio of a country indicates which of the following? - Indicators: 1. Slowing economic growth rate 2. Less equitable distribution of national income - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - A falling tax-to-GDP ratio (~16% in 2015) often signals slowing growth (1), as revenue collection lags GDP, but not necessarily inequality (2). - Why Original Answer (d) Incorrect: - Slowing growth (1) is linked to lower tax revenue, unlike inequality. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Inequality not directly tied. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes inequality link. - (d) Incorrect: Growth slowdown is relevant. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (2014–15): Tax-to-GDP trends. - World Bank (2015): Growth-revenue correlation. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Tax-to-GDP: Fiscal capacity indicator. - Arun Jaitley: Led 2015 tax reforms. - Key Takeaway: - Falling tax-to-GDP in 2015 signaled growth challenges. - Q79: With reference to 'Indian Ocean Rim Association for Regional Cooperation (IOR-ARC)', consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. AIBP (1996–97, 1) funds irrigation projects, not specifically poor farmers’ loans. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false; AIBP isn’t for poor farmers’ loans. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - Ministry of Water Resources (2015): AIBP, CADP details. - Economic Survey (2014–15): Irrigation programs. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Irrigation Development: AIBP and CADP boosted agricultural productivity, critical for India’s 2015 rural economy. - Water-Use Efficiency: CADP addressed water scarcity, supporting sustainable agriculture. - Ministry of Water Resources: Oversaw irrigation programs in 2015. - Key Takeaway: - CADP’s focus on water efficiency in 2015 supported India’s agricultural growth. - Q81: With reference to inflation in India, which of the following statements is correct? - Options: (a) Controlling the inflation in India is the responsibility of the Government of India only (b) The Reserve Bank of India has no role in controlling the inflation (c) Decreased money circulation helps in controlling the inflation (d) Increased money circulation helps in controlling the inflation - Answer: (c) Decreased money circulation helps in controlling the inflation - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Reducing money circulation (e.g., via higher interest rates, ~8% repo rate in 2015) controls inflation (~5%). RBI and government share roles; increased circulation fuels inflation. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: RBI also controls inflation. - (b) Incorrect: RBI has a key role via monetary policy. - (d) Incorrect: Increased circulation raises inflation. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2015): Monetary tightening for inflation. - Economic Survey (2014–15): Inflation trends ~5%. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Monetary Policy: RBI’s rate adjustments control money supply, curbing inflation in 2015. - Inflation Targeting: Adopted in 2015, aimed at ~4–6% inflation. - Raghuram Rajan: As RBI Governor, implemented inflation targeting in 2015. - Key Takeaway: - Reduced money circulation in 2015 was key to India’s inflation control. - Q82: There has been a persistent deficit budget year after year. It avoided sector-specific grants (2), focusing on untied funds. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: No sector-specific grants. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - 14th Finance Commission Report (2015): 42% devolution. - Economic Survey (2014–15): Fiscal federalism. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fiscal Federalism: 14th FC’s higher State share strengthened decentralized governance in 2015. - Tax Devolution: Increased State autonomy, aligning with 2015 cooperative federalism. - Y.V. Q113: If a commodity is provided free to the public by the Government, then: - Options: (a) the opportunity cost is zero (b) the opportunity cost is ignored (c) the opportunity cost is transferred from the consumers of the product to the tax-paying public (d) the opportunity cost is transferred from the consumers of the product to the Government - Answer: (c) the opportunity cost is transferred from the consumers of the product to the tax-paying public - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Free commodities (e.g., food subsidies, ~₹1.4 lakh crore in 2018) shift opportunity cost to taxpayers via funding, not consumers or government directly. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Opportunity cost exists (resource allocation). - (b) Incorrect: Cost isn’t ignored, it’s redistributed. - (d) Incorrect: Government transfers cost to taxpayers. - Supporting Evidence: - Subsidies: Tax-funded welfare programs like PDS shifted costs to taxpayers. - Arun Jaitley: As Finance Minister, managed 2018 subsidy budgets. - Key Takeaway: - Free commodities in 2018 transferred opportunity costs to taxpayers. - Women with two children get reduced entitlements - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 2 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (c) 3 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Maternity Benefit Act (2017) provides 26 weeks’ leave (1 false, not 3+3 months), no specific creche visit mandate (2 false), and reduced leave (12 weeks) for women with two children (3 true). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 2 are false. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Only statement 3 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - Maternity Benefit Act (2017): Provisions. - Economic Survey (2018–19): Women’s welfare policies. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Maternity Benefit Act: Enhanced women’s workplace rights in 2017. - Gender Equality: Supported female workforce participation (~24% in 2019). - Maneka Gandhi: As WCD Minister, drove 2017 amendments. - Key Takeaway: - 2017 Maternity Benefit Act reduced entitlements for women with two children. - Q119: Considering the following statements: - Statements: 1. Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) exchange rates are calculated by the prices of the same basket of goods and services in different countries 2. In terms of PPP dollars, India is the sixth largest economy in the world - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - PPP exchange rates use a common goods basket (1 true). India was third largest in PPP terms (~$8 trillion, 2019, 2 false). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - IMF (2019): PPP rankings (India 3rd). - Economic Survey (2018–19): PPP methodology. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Purchasing Power Parity: Measures real economic size, critical for 2019 global rankings. - GDP (PPP): India’s $8 trillion PPP GDP reflected its 2019 economic strength. - IMF: Provided 2019 PPP data, ranking India third. - Key Takeaway: - PPP in 2019 accurately measured India’s economic size, not sixth-ranked. - Q120: Which one of the following is not the most likely measure the Government/RBI takes to stop the slide of Indian rupee? - Options: (a) Curbing imports of non-essential goods and promoting exports (b) Encouraging Indian borrowers to issue rupee denominated Masala bonds (c) Easing conditions relating to external commercial borrowing (d) Following an expansionary monetary policy - Answer: (d) Following an expansionary monetary policy - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Rupee depreciation (₹70/$ in 2019) is countered by curbing imports (a), Masala bonds (b), and ECB easing (c). Expansionary policy (d) increases money supply, worsening depreciation. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Reduces forex demand. - (b) Incorrect: Attracts forex via bonds. - (c) Incorrect: Boosts forex inflows. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2019): Rupee stabilization measures. - Economic Survey (2018–19): Forex management. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Rupee Depreciation: 2019 pressures from oil imports and CAD (~1.8%). - Masala Bonds: Rupee-denominated, attract foreign investment. - Shaktikanta Das: As RBI Governor, managed 2019 rupee stability. - Key Takeaway: - Expansionary policy in 2019 was least likely to stabilize the rupee. - Q121: The money multiplier in an economy increases with which one of the following? - Options: (a) Increase in the cash reserve ratio (b) Increase in the banking habit of the population (c) Increase in the statutory liquidity (d) Increase in the population of the country - Answer: (b) Increase in the banking habit of the population - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Banking habit (b) increases deposits, boosting money multiplier (~5 in 2019). CRR (a) and SLR (c) reduce lending capacity; population (d) is indirect. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: CRR reduces multiplier. - (c) Incorrect: SLR reduces multiplier. - (d) Incorrect: Population doesn’t directly affect multiplier. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2019): Money multiplier dynamics. - Economic Survey (2018–19): Banking trends. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Money Multiplier: Measures money creation from deposits, key to 2019 monetary policy. - Banking Penetration: PMJDY boosted deposits, enhancing multiplier. - Shaktikanta Das: As RBI Governor, oversaw 2019 banking reforms. - Key Takeaway: - Increased banking habits in 2019 raised India’s money multiplier. - [2020-I] - Q122: If another global financial crisis happens in the near future, which of the following actions/policies are most likely to give some immunity to India? - Actions: 1. Not depending on short-term foreign borrowings 2. Opening up to more foreign banks 3. Maintaining full capital account convertibility - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 & 2 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Low short-term borrowings (1) reduce crisis vulnerability (India’s external debt ~20% GDP in 2020). Foreign banks (2) and full convertibility (3) increase exposure. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Foreign banks increase risk. - (c) Incorrect: Full convertibility risks capital flight. - (d) Incorrect: Only statement 1 is correct. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2020): External debt management. - Economic Survey (2019–20): Crisis resilience. - Related Concepts/Figures: - External Debt: Low short-term debt (~4% of total) enhanced 2020 stability. - Capital Account Convertibility: Partial convertibility protected against 2020 volatility. - Shaktikanta Das: As RBI Governor, ensured 2020 financial stability. - Key Takeaway: - Minimizing short-term borrowings in 2020 bolstered India’s crisis immunity. - Q123: If you withdraw 1,00,000 in cash from your Demand Deposit Account at your bank, the immediate effect on aggregate money supply in the economy will be: - Options: (a) to reduce it by ₹1,00,000 (b) to increase it by ₹1,00,000 (c) to increase it by more than 1,00,000 (d) to leave it unchanged - Answer: (d) to leave it unchanged - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Cash withdrawal shifts money from deposits to currency (M0), leaving total money supply (M3, ~₹170 lakh crore in 2020) unchanged. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Money supply doesn’t decrease. - (b) Incorrect: No new money is created. - (c) Incorrect: No multiplier effect occurs. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2020): Money supply components. - Economic Survey (2019–20): Monetary aggregates. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Money Supply (M3): Includes currency and deposits, unchanged by withdrawal in 2020. - Monetary Base (M0): Shifts within M3 don’t affect total supply. - RBI: Tracks money supply dynamics in 2020. - Key Takeaway: - Cash withdrawals in 2020 didn’t alter India’s money supply. - Q124: Along with the Budget, the Finance Minister also places other documents before the Parliament which include 'The Macro Economic Framework Statement'. The aforesaid document is presented because this is mandated by: - Options: (a) Long standing parliamentary convention (b) Article 112 and Article 110(1) of the Constitution of India (c) Article 113 of the Constitution of India (d) Provisions of the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 - Answer: (d) Provisions of the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - FRBM Act (2003) mandates the Macro Economic Framework Statement to ensure fiscal transparency (~₹30 lakh crore budget in 2020). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Not a convention, legally mandated. - (b) Incorrect: Articles 112, 110(1) cover budget, not specific documents. - (c) Incorrect: Article 113 covers demands, not statements. - Supporting Evidence: - FRBM Act (2003): Budget document mandates. - Economic Survey (2019–20): Fiscal transparency. - Related Concepts/Figures: - FRBM Act: Enforces fiscal discipline, critical for 2020 budget transparency. - Macro Economic Framework: Outlines economic projections, guiding policy. - Nirmala Sitharaman: As Finance Minister, presented 2020 budget documents. - Key Takeaway: - FRBM Act mandated the 2020 Macro Economic Framework Statement. - Q125: Under the Kisan Credit Card scheme, short-term credit support is given to farmers for which of the following purposes? - Purposes: 1. Working capital for maintenance of farm assets 2. Purchase of combine harvesters, tractors and mini trucks 3. Consumption requirements of farm households 4. Post-harvest expenses 5. Construction of family house and setting up of village cold storage facility - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 5 only (b) 1, 3 & 4 only (c) 2, 3, 4 & 5 only (d) 1, 2, 3, 4 & 5 - Answer: (b) 1, 3 & 4 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - KCC (1998) provides short-term credit for working capital (1), consumption (3), and post-harvest expenses (4, ~₹7 lakh crore disbursed by 2020). Harvesters/tractors (2) and housing/storage (5) are long-term. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 5 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statements 2 and 5 are false. - (d) Incorrect: Statements 2 and 5 are false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2020): KCC guidelines. - Economic Survey (2019–20): Agricultural credit. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Kisan Credit Card: Enhances farmer liquidity, supporting 2020 agricultural growth. - Agricultural Credit: KCC disbursements boosted rural economy. - Narendra Singh Tomar: As Agriculture Minister, oversaw KCC in 2020. - Key Takeaway: - KCC in 2020 supported short-term farmer needs effectively. - Q126: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The weightage of food in Consumer Price Index (CPI) is higher than that in Wholesale Price Index (WPI) 2. The WPI does not capture changes in the prices of services, which CPI does 3. Reserve Bank of India has now adopted WPI as its key measure of inflation and to decide on changing the key policy rates - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 2 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (a) 1 & 2 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - CPI has higher food weight (~46% vs. WPI’s ~24% in 2020, 1 true). WPI excludes services, unlike CPI (2 true). RBI adopted CPI for inflation targeting (3 false). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Excludes true statement 1. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2020): CPI-based inflation targeting. - Economic Survey (2019–20): CPI vs. WPI. - Related Concepts/Figures: - CPI vs. WPI: CPI’s broader coverage drives 2020 monetary policy. - Inflation Targeting: CPI focus (~4–6%) stabilized 2020 prices. - Shaktikanta Das: As RBI Governor, enforced CPI targeting in 2020. - Key Takeaway: - CPI’s food and service coverage made it RBI’s 2020 inflation metric. - Q127: With reference to the Indian economy after the 1991 economic liberalization, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Worker productivity per worker (at 2004-05 prices) increased in urban areas while it decreased in rural areas 2. The percentage share of rural areas in the workforce steadily increased 3. In rural areas, the growth in the non-farm economy increased 4. The growth rate in rural employment decreased - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 3 & 4 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 4 - Answer: (b) 3 & 4 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Post-1991, rural non-farm growth increased (3, ~40% of rural jobs by 2020). Rural employment growth slowed (4, ~1% annually). Urban/rural productivity trends (1) and rural workforce share (2) didn’t align as stated. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 2 are false. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes true statement 4. - (d) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 2 are false. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2019–20): Rural economy trends. - NSSO (2020): Employment data. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Non-Farm Economy: Rural diversification reduced agricultural dependence in 2020. - Rural Employment: Slowed due to mechanization and urban migration. - NITI Aayog: Analyzed 2020 rural economic shifts. - Key Takeaway: - Post-1991, 2020 saw rural non-farm growth and slower employment growth. - Q128: In India, under cyber insurance for individuals, which of the following benefits are generally covered, in addition to payment for the loss of funds and other benefits? - Benefits: 1. Cost of restoration of the computer system in case of malware disrupting access to one's computer 2. Cost of a new computer if some miscreant wilfully damages it, if proved 3. Cost of hiring a specialized consultant to minimize the loss in case of cyber extortion 4. Cost of defence in the Court of Law if any third party files a suit - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 4 only (b) 1, 3 & 4 only (c) 2 & 3 only (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (b) 1, 3 & 4 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Cyber insurance (2020) covers malware restoration (1), extortion consultants (3), and legal defense (4). Physical damage (2) is typically excluded. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes true statements 1 and 4. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - IRDAI (2020): Cyber insurance guidelines. - Economic Survey (2019–20): Digital economy risks. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Cyber Insurance: Mitigates digital risks, growing in 2020 with rising cybercrime. - Digital Economy: Cyber threats necessitated insurance coverage. - IRDAI: Regulated 2020 cyber insurance policies. - Key Takeaway: - Cyber insurance in 2020 covered restoration, extortion, and legal costs. - [2021-I] - Q129: In India, the central bank's function as the "lender of last resort" usually refers to which of the following? - Functions: 1. Lending to trade and industry bodies when they fail to borrow from other sources 2. Providing liquidity to the banks having a temporary crisis 3. Lending to governments to finance budgetary deficits - Options: (a) 1 & 2 (b) 2 only (c) 2 & 3 (d) 3 only - Answer: (b) 2 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - RBI’s lender of last resort function (2021) involves providing emergency liquidity to banks facing temporary crises (2, e.g., ₹2 lakh crore via LTRO in 2020–21). It doesn’t typically lend to trade/industry (1) or finance government deficits (3). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false (RBI lends to banks, not directly to industry). - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false (deficit financing is via bonds). - (d) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2021): Lender of last resort policy. - Economic Survey (2020–21): Banking liquidity measures. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Lender of Last Resort: RBI’s role in stabilizing banks during crises, critical in 2021 post-COVID. - Liquidity Adjustment Facility: Provided short-term liquidity (~₹15 lakh crore in 2021). - Shaktikanta Das: As RBI Governor, managed 2021 banking stability. - Key Takeaway: - RBI’s 2021 lender of last resort role focused on bank liquidity support. - Q130: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The Governor of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is appointed by the Central Government 2. Certain provisions in the Constitution of India give the Central Government the right to issue directions to the RBI in the public interest 3. Governor’s powers derive from the RBI Act (3). Section 7 of the RBI Act allows government directions (2), but no Constitutional provision exists for this. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false (no Constitutional provision). - (b) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI Act (1934): Governor’s appointment and powers. - Economic Survey (2020–21): RBI governance. - Related Concepts/Figures: - RBI Governance: Central Government appoints Governor, shaping 2021 monetary policy. - RBI Act, 1934: Defines RBI’s operational framework. - Shaktikanta Das: Appointed RBI Governor in 2018, led 2021 policies. - Key Takeaway: - RBI Governor’s 2021 role was defined by government appointment and RBI Act. - Q131: With reference to the casual workers employed in India, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. All casual workers are entitled for Employees Provident Fund Coverage 2. All casual workers are entitled for regular working hours and overtime payment 3. The government can by a notification specify that an establishment or industry shall pay wages only through its bank account - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (b) 2 & 3 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Casual workers get regular hours/overtime under labor laws (2, e.g., Minimum Wages Act, 1948). Government can mandate bank wage payments (3, Code on Wages, 2019). EPF coverage (1) applies only to establishments with 20+ employees, not all casual workers. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - Code on Wages (2019): Bank payment mandates. - EPF Act (1952): Coverage criteria. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Casual Workers: ~25% of India’s 2021 workforce, protected by labor laws. - Code on Wages, 2019: Ensures timely wage payments via banks. - Bhupender Yadav: As Labour Minister, oversaw 2021 labor reforms. - Key Takeaway: - 2021 labor laws protected casual workers’ wages and hours, not universal EPF. - Q132: Consider the following statements: Other things remaining unchanged, market demand for a good might increase if: - Factors: 1. Price of its substitute increases 2. Price of its complement increases 3. The good is an inferior good and income of the consumers increases 4. Its price falls - Options: (a) 1 & 4 only (b) 2, 3 & 4 (c) 1, 3 & 4 (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (a) 1 & 4 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Higher substitute prices (1) and lower own price (4) increase demand (e.g., demand curve shift, 2021). Complement price rise (2) reduces demand; inferior goods (3) see less demand with higher income. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statements 2 and 3 reduce demand. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 reduces demand. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 reduces demand. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2020–21): Demand dynamics. - Microeconomics principles: Substitute and inferior goods. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Demand Curve: Shifts right with substitute price rise or own price fall in 2021. - Substitute Goods: Increase demand when prices rise (e.g., tea vs. coffee). - Inferior Goods: Demand falls as income rises (e.g., low-quality goods). - Key Takeaway: - Substitute price rise and own price fall drove 2021 demand increases. - Q133: With reference to Urban Cooperative Banks in India, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. They are supervised and regulated by local boards set up by the State Governments 2. They can issue equity shares and preference shares 3. They were brought under the purview of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 through an Amendment in 1996 - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (b) 2 & 3 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - UCBs issue equity/preference shares (2) and were under Banking Regulation Act post-1996 (3, ~1,500 UCBs in 2021). RBI regulates UCBs, not State boards (1 false). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2021): UCB regulation. - Banking Regulation Act (1996 Amendment): UCB inclusion. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Urban Cooperative Banks: Serve urban credit needs, regulated by RBI in 2021. - Banking Regulation Act: Strengthened UCB oversight post-1996. - Shaktikanta Das: As RBI Governor, enhanced 2021 UCB reforms. - Key Takeaway: - UCBs in 2021 issued shares and were RBI-regulated under 1996 amendments. - Q134: Consider the following statements: The effect of devaluation of a currency is that it necessarily: - Effects: 1. Improves the trade balance - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 & 2 (c) 3 only (d) 1 & 3 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Devaluation (e.g., rupee in 1991) makes exports cheaper (1, ~$400 billion exports in 2021). It reduces foreign value of currency (2 false) and doesn’t always improve trade balance (3, depends on import elasticity). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is not guaranteed. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 3 is not guaranteed. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2021): Exchange rate policies. - Economic Survey (2020–21): Trade dynamics. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Devaluation: Lowers currency value, boosting 2021 export competitiveness. - Trade Balance: Affected by import/export elasticities, not always improved. - Marshall-Lerner Condition: Determines trade balance impact. - Key Takeaway: - Devaluation in 2021 reliably boosted export competitiveness. - Q135: Which one of the following effects of creation of black​ money in India has been the main cause of worry to the Government of India? - Options: (a) Diversion of resources to the purchase of real estate and investment in luxury housing (b) Investment in unproductive activities and purchase of precious stones, jewellery, gold etc. (c) Large donations to political parties and growth of regionalism (d) Loss of revenue to the State Exchequer due to tax​ evasion - Answer: (d) Loss of revenue to the State Exchequer due to tax​ evasion - Analysis: - Economic Context: - black​ money (e.g., ₹10 lakh crore estimated in 2021) primarily causes tax revenue loss (d, ~₹2 lakh crore annually), impacting fiscal capacity. Other effects are secondary. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Real estate is a symptom, not primary concern. - (b) Incorrect: Unproductive investments are less critical. - (c) Incorrect: Political donations are not the main issue. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (2020–21): tax​ evasion concerns. - Income Tax Department (2021): black​ money reports. - Related Concepts/Figures: - black​ money: Undermines fiscal revenue, critical in 2021 post-demonetization. - tax​ evasion: Reduced India’s tax-to-GDP ratio (~17% in 2021). - Nirmala Sitharaman: As Finance Minister, tackled 2021 black​ money issues. - Key Takeaway: - tax​ evasion from black​ money was India’s primary 2021 fiscal concern. - Q136: Which one of the following is likely to be one of the most inflationary in its effects? - Options: (a) Repayment of public debt (b) Borrowing from the public to finance a budget deficit (c) Borrowing from the banks to finance a budget deficit (d) Creation of new money to finance a budget deficit - Answer: (d) Creation of new money to finance a budget deficit - Analysis: - Economic Context: - New money creation (d, e.g., monetized deficit ~₹1 lakh crore in 2021) increases money supply, driving inflation (~6% CPI in 2021). Other options have less direct inflationary impact. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Debt repayment reduces money supply. - (b) Incorrect: Public borrowing redistributes existing money. - (c) Incorrect: Bank borrowing has limited money creation. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2021): Monetary policy and inflation. - Economic Survey (2020–21): Deficit financing effects. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Monetized Deficit: Increases money supply, fueling 2021 inflation. - Inflation: CPI-based, targeted at 4–6% by RBI in 2021. - Shaktikanta Das: As RBI Governor, managed 2021 inflation risks. - Key Takeaway: - New money creation in 2021 was highly inflationary. - [2022-I] - Q137: With reference to Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1.
