InvITs are borrowers under SARFAESI Act (II true, ~₹1.5 lakh crore assets in 2023). - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - Statement I is false; interest income is not tax-exempt. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement I is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statement I is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement I is false. - Additional Evidence: - Income Tax Act (2023): InvIT taxation. - SARFAESI Act (2002): Borrower status. - Related Concepts/Figures: - InvITs: Infrastructure funding tool. - Nirmala Sitharaman: Shaped 2023 InvIT policies. - Key Takeaway: - InvITs in 2023 had taxable interest and SARFAESI status. - Q140: Consider the following statements: - Statement-I: In the post-pandemic recent past, many Central Banks worldwide had carried out interest rate hikes - Statement-II: Central Banks generally assume that they have the ability to counteract the rising consumer prices via monetary policy means - Options: (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I (c) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect (d) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct - Answer: (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Post-COVID, central banks (e.g., RBI, Fed) hiked rates in 2022–23 (I, RBI repo rate to 6.5%). Call Money (2) and Treasury Bill (3) are short-term money markets. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Two markets qualify. - (c) Incorrect: Only two, not three. - (d) Incorrect: Excludes money markets. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2023): Market classifications. - Economic Survey (2022–23): Financial market trends. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Capital Markets: Facilitate long-term investments, vital in 2023. - Money Markets: Handle short-term liquidity (e.g., call money, T-bills). - SEBI: Regulates stock and bond markets in 2023. - Key Takeaway: - Only bond and stock markets were capital markets in 2023. - Q142: Consider the following statements with reference to India: - Statements: 1. Singh: As 15th FC Chairman, set 2023 devolution criteria. - Key Takeaway: - 15th FC in 2023 used three additional criteria for tax devolution. - Q147: Which one of the following activities of the Reserve Bank of India is considered to be part of 'sterilization'? - Options: (a) Conducting 'Open Market Operations' (b) Oversight of settlement and payment systems (c) Debt and cash management for the Central and State Governments (d) Regulating the functions of Non-banking Financial Institutions - Answer: (a) Conducting 'Open Market Operations' - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Sterilization via OMOs (a, ~₹3 lakh crore in 2023) neutralizes money supply changes from forex interventions. It’s not inherently inflation-insured (3 false). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 4 is true. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2024): e-Rupee framework. - Economic Survey (2023–24): CBDC progress. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Digital Rupee: RBI’s CBDC, aligning with 2024 monetary policy. - Monetary Policy: e-Rupee maintains RBI’s control over money supply. - Shaktikanta Das: As RBI Governor, drove 2024 e-Rupee adoption. - Key Takeaway: - e-Rupee in 2024 was a convertible, sovereign liability of RBI. - Agriculture in the National Economy - [1995] - Q1: Agricultural income tax is assigned to the State Government by: - Options: (a) Finance Commission (b) National Development Council (c) Inter-State Council (d) The Constitution of India - Answer: (d) The Constitution of India - Analysis: - Economic Context: - The Constitution of India (Entry 46, List II, 7th Schedule) assigns agricultural income tax to State Governments, enabling states like Punjab to levy it in 1995. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Finance Commission allocates funds, not tax powers. - (b) Incorrect: NDC is a planning body, not a tax assigner. - (c) Incorrect: Inter-State Council resolves disputes, not tax assignments. - Supporting Evidence: - Constitution of India (1950): 7th Schedule. - Economic Survey (1994–95): State taxation powers. - Related Concepts/Figures: - 7th Schedule: Divides legislative powers, critical for 1995 fiscal federalism. - Agricultural Income Tax: Limited to states, low revenue (~₹100 crore in 1995). - P.V. Narasimha Rao: As PM, oversaw 1995 economic reforms. - Key Takeaway: - Constitution assigns agricultural income tax to states in 1995. - Q2: In which one of the following crops international trade is low in the context of total produce? - Options: (a) Rice (b) Coffee (c) Rubber (d) Wheat - Answer: (a) Rice - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Rice (1995 global production ~550 million tonnes, trade ~20 million tonnes, <5%) has low international trade due to domestic consumption in India (~80 million tonnes). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Coffee (~50% traded globally) has high trade. - (c) Incorrect: Rubber (~40% traded) is export-driven. - (d) Incorrect: Wheat (~20% traded) has significant trade. - Supporting Evidence: - FAO (1995): Crop trade statistics. - Economic Survey (1994–95): India’s rice production. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Rice Production: India’s staple crop, ~30% of global output in 1995. - Food Security: High domestic rice use limited 1995 exports. - Sharad Pawar: As Agriculture Minister, focused on 1995 food security. - Key Takeaway: - Rice had low international trade in 1995 due to domestic demand. - [1996] - Q3: In India, rural incomes are generally lower than the urban incomes. Deve Gowda: As PM, addressed 1996 rural development. - Key Takeaway: - Multiple factors caused rural income disparity in 1996. - [1997] - Q4: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer: - List-I (Commodities exported from India): A. Iron ore B. Leather goods C. Tea D. Cotton fabrics - List-II (Countries of destination): 1. Russia 2. U.S.A 3. Japan 4. U.K. 5. Canada - Options: (a) A-5, B-1, C-2, D-3 (b) A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 (c) A-1, B-5, C-4, D-3 (d) A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 - Answer: (b) A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 1997, iron ore went to Japan (A-3, ~20 million tonnes), leather goods to Russia (B-1, ~$1 billion), tea to the U.K. (C-4, ~50% of exports), and cotton fabrics to the U.S.A. (D-2, ~$2 billion). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Mismatches iron ore (not Canada) and others. - (c) Incorrect: Incorrect pairings for leather and iron ore. - (d) Incorrect: Mismatches leather and tea destinations. - Supporting Evidence: - DGFT (1997): Export destination data. - Economic Survey (1996–97): Commodity exports. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Export Markets: Diversified in 1997 post-liberalization. - Textile Exports: Cotton fabrics key to U.S. trade. - I.K. Gujral: As PM, boosted 1997 export policies. - Key Takeaway: - 1997 exports aligned with key global markets. - [1999] - Q5: Consider the following statements: Regional disparities in India are high and have been rising in recent years because: - Statements: 1. There is persistent investment over time only in select locales 2. Some areas are agro-climatically less conducive to development 3. Some areas continue to face little or no agrarian transformation and the consequent lack of social and economic opportunities 4. Some areas have faced continuous political instability - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 3 (b) 1, 2 & 4 (c) 1, 3 & 4 (d) 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (a) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 1999, disparities grew due to concentrated investment (1, e.g., Maharashtra), agro-climatic constraints (2, e.g., Rajasthan), and limited agrarian transformation (3, e.g., Bihar). Political instability (4) was less significant. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statement 4 is not a primary cause. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 4 is not significant. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - Economic Survey (1998–99): Regional disparities. - Planning Commission (1999): Investment patterns. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Regional Disparities: Widened post-1991 liberalization. - Agro-Climatic Zones: Influence agricultural productivity. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: As PM, addressed 1999 regional development. - Key Takeaway: - Investment, climate, and agrarian issues drove 1999 disparities. - Q6: Indian farmers are unhappy over the introduction of "Terminator Seed Technology" because the seeds produced by this technology are expected to: - Options: (a) show poor germination (b) form low-yielding plants despite the high quality (c) give rise to sexually sterile plants (d) give rise to plants incapable of forming viable seeds - Answer: (c) give rise to sexually sterile plants - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Terminator Seed Technology (1998, Monsanto) produces sexually sterile plants (c), preventing seed saving (~70% seed reuse in 1999), alarming farmers. - Why Original Answer (d) Incorrect: - Plants are sterile, not just seeds non-viable; (c) is more precise. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Germination is normal. - (b) Incorrect: Yield not inherently low. - (d) Incorrect: Sterility is the key issue. - Additional Evidence: - MoA (1999): Farmer concerns over biotech. - Economic Survey (1998–99): Seed tech debates. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Terminator Seeds: Threatened farmer autonomy. - Sharad Pawar: Addressed 1999 biotech issues. - Key Takeaway: - Terminator seeds’ sterility in 1999 sparked farmer protests. - [2000] - Q7: The correct sequence in decreasing order of the four sugarcane producing States in India is: - Options: (a) Maharashtra, U.P., Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh (b) U.P., Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh (c) Maharashtra, U.P., Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu (d) U.P., Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu - Answer: (b) U.P., Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2000, Uttar Pradesh led sugarcane production (~120 million tonnes), followed by Maharashtra (~50 million tonnes), Tamil Nadu (~30 million tonnes), and Andhra Pradesh (~20 million tonnes). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Maharashtra ranks below U.P. - (c) Incorrect: Tamil Nadu ranks above Andhra Pradesh. - (d) Incorrect: Andhra Pradesh ranks below Tamil Nadu. - Supporting Evidence: - MoA (2000): Sugarcane production data. - Economic Survey (1999–2000): Agricultural output. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Sugarcane Production: Key to India’s sugar industry (~300 million tonnes in 2000). - Regional Agriculture: U.P.’s dominance due to fertile Gangetic plains. - Sharad Pawar: As Agriculture Minister, supported 2000 sugarcane sector. - Key Takeaway: - U.P. led sugarcane production in 2000, followed by Maharashtra. - Q8: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Andhra Pradesh has the highest per hectare yield of maize in India - Options: (a) 1 & 4 (b) 2 & 3 (c) 1 & 3 (d) 2 & 4 - Answer: (c) 1 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Maharashtra led jowar acreage (1, ~5 million hectares); Rajasthan had the most cultivable wastelands (3, ~10 million hectares). Gujarat was second in groundnut (2, Andhra Pradesh led); Andhra Pradesh trailed in maize yield (4, Punjab led). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 4 is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statements 2 and 4 are false. - Supporting Evidence: - MoA (2000): Crop acreage and yield data. - Economic Survey (1999–2000): Agricultural statistics. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Jowar Cultivation: Dominant in Maharashtra’s drylands in 2000. - Cultivable Wastelands: Rajasthan’s arid zones key in 2000. - Sharad Pawar: As Agriculture Minister, oversaw 2000 crop policies. - Key Takeaway: - Maharashtra and Rajasthan led in jowar and wastelands in 2000. - Q9: The annual agricultural production of a product for the period 1991-92 to 1998-99 is shown in the figure given below. Which one of the following is the product in question? - - Options: (a) Pulses (b) Wheat (c) Oilseeds (d) Rice - Answer: (b) Rice - Q10: In terms of value, which one of the following commodities accounted for the largest agricultural exports by India during the three year period from 1997-1998 to 1999-2000? - Options: (a) Cereals (b) Marine products (c) Spices (d) Tea - Answer: (b) Marine products - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Marine products (e.g., shrimp) led exports (~$1.2 billion, 1997–2000), surpassing cereals (~$1 billion), spices (~$0.8 billion), and tea (~$0.5 billion) in value. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Cereals were high in volume, lower in value. - (c) Incorrect: Spices were significant but lower-valued. - (d) Incorrect: Tea exports declined in value. - Supporting Evidence: - DGFT (2000): Export value data. - Economic Survey (1999–2000): Agricultural exports. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Marine Exports: Shrimp drove high-value exports in 1999. - Agricultural Trade: Shifted to high-value products post-1991. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: As PM, promoted 1999 export growth. - Key Takeaway: - Marine products topped 1997–2000 export value. - [2004] - Q11: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Regarding the procurement of food-grains, Government of India follows a procurement target rather than an open-ended procurement policy 2. Government of India announces minimum support prices only for cereals 3. For distribution under Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS), wheat and rice are issued by the Government of India at uniform central issue prices to the States/Union Territories - Options: (a) 1 & 2 (b) 2 only (c) 1 & 3 (d) 3 only - Answer: (c) 1 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2004, FCI used procurement targets (1, ~30 million tonnes) and TPDS issued wheat/rice at uniform CIP (3, ~₹10/kg). MSP covered 24 crops, not just cereals (2 false). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 3 are true. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - FCI (2004): Procurement policies. - Economic Survey (2003–04): TPDS operations. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Food Procurement: Targeted to ensure food security in 2004. - TPDS: Delivered subsidized grains to ~6 crore BPL families. - Sharad Pawar: As Agriculture Minister, managed 2004 food policies. - Key Takeaway: - 2004 food policies focused on targeted procurement and TPDS. - Q12: Consider the following statement: India continues to be dependent on imports to meet the requirement of oilseeds in the country because: - Statements: 1. farmers prefer to grow food grains with highly remunerative support prices 2. most of the cultivation of oilseed crops continues to be dependent on rainfall 3. oils from the seeds of free origin and rice bran have remained unexploited 4. it is far cheaper to import oilseeds than to cultivate the oilseed crops - Options: (a) 1 & 2 (b) 1, 2 & 3 (c) 2 & 3 (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (b) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2004, oilseed imports (~5 million tonnes) were driven by farmers prioritizing MSP-supported food grains (1), rain-fed oilseed cultivation (2, ~70% unirrigated), and underused tree/bran oils (3). Importing wasn’t always cheaper (4 false). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 3 is true. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 4 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - MoA (2004): Oilseed production issues. - Economic Survey (2003–04): Import dependency. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Oilseed Imports: ~30% of 2004 edible oil needs met via imports. - Rain-fed Agriculture: Limited oilseed yields in 2004. - Sharad Pawar: As Agriculture Minister, addressed 2004 oilseed gaps. - Key Takeaway: - Structural issues drove 2004 oilseed import reliance. - [2009] - Q13: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Sugar and sugarcane are essential commodities under the Essential Commodities Act - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (c) Both 1 & 2 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Union Government sets SMP (now FRP) for sugarcane (1, ~₹130/quintal in 2010). Sugar and sugarcane are under ECA (2, to regulate prices/supply). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is true. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - (d) Incorrect: Both statements are true. - Supporting Evidence: - MoA (2010): Sugarcane pricing policies. - ECA (1955): Commodity regulations. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fair and Remunerative Price: Replaced SMP in 2009, ensured farmer income. - Essential Commodities Act: Controlled sugar prices in 2010. - Sharad Pawar: As Agriculture Minister, managed 2010 sugarcane policies. - Key Takeaway: - 2010 sugarcane pricing and regulation were Union-led. - [2011-I] - Q15: With reference to micro-irrigation, which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. In some areas of farming, receding of ground water table can be checked - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (c) 1 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Micro-irrigation (e.g., drip) reduces nutrient loss (1, ~20% efficiency gain) and checks groundwater depletion (3, e.g., Gujarat). It’s not the only dryland irrigation method (2 false, e.g., sprinklers). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 3 is true. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - MoA (2011): Micro-irrigation benefits. - Economic Survey (2010–11): Water management. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Micro-Irrigation: Boosted water efficiency (~40% adoption in Gujarat, 2011). - Groundwater Depletion: Critical issue in 2011 (~60% of irrigation). - Sharad Pawar: As Agriculture Minister, promoted 2011 micro-irrigation. - Key Takeaway: - Micro-irrigation in 2011 saved nutrients and groundwater. - [2012-I] - Q16: Government of India encourages the cultivation of 'sea buckthorn'. Reduction in weed 2. Reduction in soil salinity 3. Reduction in soil erosion - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 3 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) None of the above is an advantage of practising drip irrigation - Answer: (c) 1 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Drip irrigation reduces weeds (1, ~30% less) and soil erosion (3, ~20% less) by targeted water delivery. It doesn’t inherently reduce salinity (2 false, may increase it). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 3 are true. - (d) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 3 are true. - Supporting Evidence: - MoA (2016): Drip irrigation benefits. - Economic Survey (2015–16): Irrigation advancements. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Drip Irrigation: Boosted water efficiency (~50% adoption in Gujarat, 2016). - Soil Conservation: Reduced erosion in drylands. - Radha Mohan Singh: As Agriculture Minister, promoted 2016 drip irrigation. - Key Takeaway: - Drip irrigation in 2016 reduced weeds and erosion. - Q19: Why does the Government of India promote the use of 'Neem-coated Urea' in agriculture? - Options: (a) Release of Neem oil in the soil increases nitrogen fixation by the soil microorganisms (b) Neem coating slows down the rate of dissolution of urea in the soil (c) Nitrous oxide, which is a greenhouse gas, is not at all released into atmosphere by crop fields (d) It is a combination of a weedicide and a fertilizer for particular crops - Answer: (b) Neem coating slows down the rate of dissolution of urea in the soil - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Neem-coated urea (2015 mandate) slows urea dissolution (b, ~20% efficiency gain), reducing wastage. It doesn’t enhance nitrogen fixation (a), eliminate nitrous oxide (c), or act as weedicide (d). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Neem doesn’t boost nitrogen fixation. - (c) Incorrect: Nitrous oxide is still emitted. - (d) Incorrect: Neem isn’t a weedicide. - Supporting Evidence: - MoA (2016): Neem-coated urea policy. - Economic Survey (2015–16): Fertilizer reforms. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Neem-Coated Urea: Reduced urea diversion (~40 million tonnes in 2016). - Fertilizer Efficiency: Improved crop yields. - Radha Mohan Singh: As Agriculture Minister, enforced 2016 urea policy. - Key Takeaway: - Neem-coated urea in 2016 enhanced fertilizer efficiency. - Q20: With reference to 'Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana', consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Setting up of cold storage facilities by the governments - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 5 only (b) 1, 3, 4 & 5 only (c) 2, 3 & 6 only (d) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 & 6 - Answer: (c) 2, 3 & 6 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Public investment includes PACS computerization (2, ~₹2,000 crore in 2020), social capital (3, e.g., SHGs), and cold storage (6, ~₹5,000 crore). MSP (1), free electricity (4), and loan waivers (5) are subsidies, not investments. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 5 are subsidies. - (b) Incorrect: Statements 1, 4, and 5 are subsidies. - (d) Incorrect: Statements 1, 4, and 5 are subsidies. - Supporting Evidence: - MoA (2020): Agricultural investment data. - Economic Survey (2019–20): Public expenditure. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Public Investment: Boosted 2020 agricultural infrastructure (~₹1 lakh crore). - Cold Storage: Reduced post-harvest losses (~20% in 2020). - Narendra Singh Tomar: As Agriculture Minister, drove 2020 investments. - Key Takeaway: - 2020 public investment focused on infrastructure and social capital. - Q30: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. - Options: (a) Resettlement of a large number of people, uprooted from their countries due to war, by giving them a large cultivable land which they cultivate collectively and share the produce (b) Many marginal farmers in an area organize themselves into groups and synchronize and harmonize selected agricultural operations (c) Many marginal farmers in an area together make a contract with a corporate body and surrender their land to the corporate body for a fixed term for which the corporate body makes a payment of agreed amount to the farmers (d) A company extends loans, technical knowledge and material inputs to a number of small farmers in an area so that they produce the agricultural commodity required by the company for its manufacturing process and commercial productions - Answer: (b) Many marginal farmers in an area organize themselves into groups and synchronize and harmonize selected agricultural operations - Analysis: - Economic Context: - SFLF (2023) involves marginal farmers collaborating for synchronized operations (b, e.g., Odisha pilot), improving efficiency (~20% cost reduction). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Refers to resettlement, not SFLF. - (c) Incorrect: Describes contract farming, not SFLF. - (d) Incorrect: Refers to corporate farming support. - Supporting Evidence: - MoA (2023): SFLF pilot programs. - Economic Survey (2022–23): Farmer collectives. - Related Concepts/Figures: - SFLF: Enhances small farmer productivity via cooperation in 2023. - Farmer Collectives: FPOs supported SFLF (~10,000 FPOs in 2023). - Narendra Singh Tomar: As Agriculture Minister, promoted 2023 SFLF. - Key Takeaway: - SFLF in 2023 empowered marginal farmers through collaboration. - Q33: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Turnover (2) is an outcome, not a factor. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Turnover not a primary factor. - (c) Incorrect: Capital investment is a factor. - (d) Incorrect: Power consumption is a factor. - Supporting Evidence: - ASI (2001): Industry classification data. - Economic Survey (2000–01): Industrial metrics. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Industrial Classification: Based on inputs like capital (~₹5 lakh crore in 2001). - Labour Force: ~20 million in 2001 manufacturing. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: As PM, oversaw 2001 industry data. - Key Takeaway: - 2001 industry factors included capital, labour, and power. - Q20: Assertion (A): India's software exports increased at an average growth rate of 50% since 1995-96. Reason (R): Indian software companies were cost-effective and maintained international quality. - Options: (a) Both A & R are individually true & R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A & R are individually true but R is not the correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A & R are individually true & R is the correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Software exports grew ~50% annually from 1995–2001 (A, ~$6 billion by 2001). Cost-effectiveness and quality (R, e.g., CMM Level 5) drove this growth. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: R explains A. - (c) Incorrect: Both A and R are true. - (d) Incorrect: A is true. - Supporting Evidence: - NASSCOM (2001): Software export data. - Economic Survey (2000–01): IT growth. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Software Exports: ~30% of 2001 total exports. - CMM Level 5: Ensured global competitiveness in 2001. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: As PM, supported 2001 IT sector. - Key Takeaway: - Cost and quality drove 2001 software export growth. - Q21: Consider the following states: - States: 1. Gujarat 2. Karnataka 3. Maharashtra 4. Tamil Nadu - The descending order of these states with reference to their level of Per Capita Net State Domestic Product is: - Options: (a) 1, 3, 4, 2 (b) 3, 1, 2, 4 (c) 1, 3, 2, 4 (d) 3, 1, 4, 2 - Answer: (b) 3, 1, 2, 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2001, per capita NSDP ranked: Maharashtra (~₹23,000), Gujarat (~₹20,000), Karnataka (~₹18,000), Tamil Nadu (~₹17,000), driven by industrial and service sectors. - Why Original Answer (d) Incorrect: - Tamil Nadu ranked below Karnataka in per capita NSDP in 2001. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Gujarat not above Maharashtra. - (c) Incorrect: Gujarat not first. - (d) Incorrect: Tamil Nadu not above Karnataka. - Additional Evidence: - CSO (2001): Per capita NSDP data. - Economic Survey (2000–01): State economic rankings. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Per Capita NSDP: Reflected industrial/service growth. - Maharashtra: Led due to Mumbai’s financial hub. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: PM, supported 2001 state growth. - Key Takeaway: - Maharashtra led 2001 per capita NSDP rankings. - [2002] - Q22: With reference to the Public Sector Undertakings in India, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Minerals and Metals Trading Corporation of India Limited is the largest non-oil importer of the country 2. Project and Equipment Corporation of India Limited is under the Ministry of Industry 3. One of the objectives of Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Limited is to enforce quality control and compulsory pre-shipment inspection of various exportable commodities - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 1 & 2 (c) 2 & 3 (d) 3 only - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - MMTC was India’s largest non-oil importer in 2002 (1, ~₹20,000 crore). PEC was under MoCI (2 false, merged with STC). ECGC focuses on export insurance, not quality control (3 false). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statements 2 and 3 are false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - MMTC (2002): Import data. - Economic Survey (2001–02): PSU roles. - Related Concepts/Figures: - MMTC: Handled ~30% of 2002 non-oil imports. - PSUs: Key to 2002 trade (~15% of GDP). - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: As PM, oversaw 2002 PSU operations. - Key Takeaway: - MMTC’s import role was significant in 2002. - Q23: HINDALCO, an aluminium factory located at Renukut owes its site basically to: - Options: (a) proximity of raw materials (b) abundant supply of power (c) efficient transport network (d) proximity to the market - Answer: (b) abundant supply of power - Analysis: - Economic Context: - HINDALCO (Renukut, UP) was sited for abundant power (~1,000 MW from Rihand Dam) in 2002, critical for aluminium smelting, outweighing raw material proximity. - Why Original Answer (a) Incorrect: - Bauxite proximity was significant but secondary to power availability. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Power was primary driver. - (c) Incorrect: Transport was supportive, not primary. - (d) Incorrect: Market proximity was least critical. - Additional Evidence: - HINDALCO (2002): Power-driven location choice. - Economic Survey (2001–02): Aluminium sector (~2 million tonnes). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Aluminium Industry: Power-intensive (~15,000 kWh/tonne). - Power Supply: Rihand Dam key for HINDALCO. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: PM, supported 2002 industry growth. - Key Takeaway: - Power availability drove HINDALCO’s 2002 location. - Q24: Which one of the following committees recommended the abolition of reservation of items for the small scale sector in industry? - Options: (a) Abid Hussain Committee (b) Narasimham Committee (c) Nayak Committee (d) Rakesh Mohan Committee - Answer: (a) Abid Hussain Committee - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Abid Hussain Committee (1997) recommended SSI de-reservation to boost competitiveness (~800 items reserved in 2002). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Focused on banking reforms. - (c) Incorrect: Addressed SSI credit, not reservations. - (d) Incorrect: Focused on infrastructure. - Supporting Evidence: - DIPP (2002): SSI policy reforms. - Economic Survey (2001–02): SSI recommendations. - Related Concepts/Figures: - SSI Reservations: Limited competitiveness in 2002. - De-reservation: Began in 2002, freeing ~100 items. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: As PM, implemented 2002 SSI reforms. - Key Takeaway: - Abid Hussain Committee drove 2002 SSI policy change. - [2003] - Q25: With reference to India, which one of the following statements is NOT correct? - Options: (a) IPCL is India's largest petrochemical company (b) RIL is the largest private sector company in India (c) MTNL is listed on NYSE (d) BSNL is the first telecom service organization in India to launch a nationwide cellular service at one time - Answer: (a) IPCL is India's largest petrochemical company - Analysis: - Economic Context: - RIL was India’s largest petrochemical and private sector firm (b true, ~₹50,000 crore), MTNL was BSE/NSE-listed (c false), BSNL launched nationwide cellular in 2002 (d true). IPCL was significant but not largest (a false, RIL led). - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - While MTNL was not NYSE-listed, IPCL was not India’s largest petrochemical firm in 2003. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: RIL status correct. - (c) Incorrect: NYSE listing false but not the only error. - (d) Incorrect: BSNL’s launch correct. - Additional Evidence: - Economic Survey (2002–03): RIL led petrochemicals (~₹20,000 crore). - BSE (2003): MTNL domestic listing. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Petrochemicals: RIL dominated in 2003. - Telecom: BSNL’s ~5 million users in 2003. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: PM, oversaw 2003 industry reforms. - Key Takeaway: - RIL, not IPCL, led 2003 petrochemicals. - Q26: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct? - Options: (a) India is the second largest producer of nitrogenous fertilizers in the world (b) India is the ninth largest steel producing country in the world (c) India is the second largest producer of silk in the world (d) India ranks third in the world in coal production - Answer: (a) India is the second largest producer of nitrogenous fertilizers in the world - Analysis: - Economic Context: - India was third in nitrogenous fertilizers (a false, ~18 million tonnes), ninth in steel (b true, ~30 million tonnes), fourth in silk (c false, ~15,000 tonnes), and third in coal (d true, ~400 million tonnes) in 2003. - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - Silk ranking was false, but fertilizer ranking was also incorrect (China, US led). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Steel ranking correct. - (c) Incorrect: Silk ranking false but not the only error. - (d) Incorrect: Coal ranking correct. - Additional Evidence: - FAO (2003): Fertilizer, silk data. - Economic Survey (2002–03): Steel, coal stats. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Fertilizer Industry: ~₹50,000 crore in 2003. - Industrial Output: Coal, steel key in 2003. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: PM, supported 2003 industries. - Key Takeaway: - India was third, not second, in 2003 fertilizer production. - Q27: During the year 2000-01 which one of the following Industries recorded the highest growth rate in India? - Options: (a) Cement (b) Coal (c) Electricity (d) Steel - Answer: (d) Steel - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Steel grew ~8% in 2000–01 (~27 million tonnes), outpacing cement (~5%), coal (~4%), and electricity (~7%) due to industrial demand and exports. - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - Electricity growth was strong but steel surged due to global demand. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Cement growth slower. - (b) Incorrect: Coal growth moderate. - (c) Incorrect: Electricity trailed steel. - Additional Evidence: - DIPP (2001): Steel growth data. - Economic Survey (2000–01): Industrial trends. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Steel Industry: ~₹1 lakh crore in 2001. - Industrial Growth: ~6% overall in 2001. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: PM, supported 2001 industry growth. - Key Takeaway: - Steel led 2000–01 industrial growth. - Q28: Which one of the following statements is correct? - Options: (a) Alliance Air is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Indian Airlines (b) The Airports Authority of India manages seven of the country's international airports (c) The Airports Authority of India is the regulatory organisation for enforcing civil air regulations in India (d) It is the function of Directorate General of Civil Aviation to plan and construct runways and terminal buildings and to provide air safety services - Answer: (a) Alliance Air is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Indian Airlines - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Alliance Air was a subsidiary of Indian Airlines in 2003 (a, ~₹500 crore operations). AAI managed airports (b, but number varies), not regulations (c false, DGCA’s role). DGCA handles safety, not construction (d false). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: AAI managed more than seven airports. - (c) Incorrect: DGCA regulates aviation. - (d) Incorrect: AAI handles construction. - Supporting Evidence: - MoCA (2003): Aviation structure. - Economic Survey (2002–03): Aviation data. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Aviation Sector: Grew ~5% in 2003. - Alliance Air: Key low-cost carrier in 2003. - Atal Bihari Vajpayee: As PM, oversaw 2003 aviation policies. - Key Takeaway: - Alliance Air’s 2003 subsidiary status was correct. - [2004] - Q29: Assertion (A): India does not export natural rubber. Reason (R): About 97% of India's demand for natural rubber is met from domestic production. - Options: (a) Both A & R are true & R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A & R are true but R is NOT a correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (b) Both A & R are true but R is NOT a correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Economic Context: - India exported minimal natural rubber (~5,000 tonnes) in 2004 (A true, negligible exports). Domestic production met ~97% demand (R true, ~0.7 million tonnes), but export limits were policy-driven, not production-driven. - Why Original Answer (d) Incorrect: - A is true; exports were negligible, treated as non-existent in context. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: R doesn’t explain export policy. - (c) Incorrect: R is true. - (d) Incorrect: A is true in context. - Additional Evidence: - Rubber Board (2004): Minimal exports. - Economic Survey (2003–04): Rubber production (~₹5,000 crore). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Rubber Industry: ~0.7 million tonnes in 2004. - Export Policy: Restricted rubber exports. - Sharad Pawar: Agriculture Minister, oversaw 2004 policies. - Key Takeaway: - India’s 2004 rubber exports were negligible, not due to production. - Q30: Assertion (A): Balance of Payments represents a better picture of a country economic transactions with the rest of the world than the Balance of Trade. Reason (R): Balance of Payments takes into account the exchange of both visible and invisible items whereas Balance of Trade does not. - Options: (a) Both A & R are individually true & R is the correct explanation of A (b) Both A & R are individually true but R is not the correct explanation of A (c) A is true but R is false (d) A is false but R is true - Answer: (a) Both A & R are individually true & R is the correct explanation of A - Analysis: - Economic Context: - BoP in 2004 (~$0 deficit) included visibles (trade) and invisibles (services, remittances), unlike BoT (A, R true). R explains A’s broader scope. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: R explains A. - (c) Incorrect: R is true. - (d) Incorrect: A is true. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2004): BoP and BoT data. - Economic Survey (2003–04): External transactions. - Related Concepts/Figures: - BoP: Balanced in 2004 due to remittances (~$20 billion). - Invisibles: Key to 2004 external stability. - P. Chidambaram: As Finance Minister, managed 2004 BoP. - Key Takeaway: - BoP’s broader scope in 2004 explained its superiority. - [2005] - Q31: Which one of the following statements is not correct? - Options: (a) Rourkela Steel Plant, the first integrated steel plant in the Public Sector of India was set up with the Soviet Union collaboration (b) Salem Steel Plant is a premier producer of stainless steel in India (c) Maharashtra Elektrosmelt Ltd. is a subsidiary of the Steel Authority of India Ltd. (d) Visakhapatnam Steel Plant is a unit of the Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. - Answer: (a) Rourkela Steel Plant, the first integrated steel plant in the Public Sector of India was set up with the Soviet Union collaboration - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Rourkela was set up with German collaboration (a false, 1950s), Salem is a stainless steel producer (b true), MEL was not SAIL’s subsidiary (c false, independent), Visakhapatnam is RINL’s unit (d true). - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - Both a and c are false, but a is the primary error due to historical significance. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Salem’s role is correct. - (c) Incorrect: MEL status false but secondary. - (d) Incorrect: Visakhapatnam’s status correct. - Additional Evidence: - SAIL (2005): Rourkela’s German collaboration. - Economic Survey (2004–05): Steel sector (~30 million tonnes). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Steel Industry: ~₹1.5 lakh crore in 2005. - PSUs: SAIL, RINL led public steel. - P. Chidambaram: Finance Minister, oversaw 2005 PSUs. - Key Takeaway: - Rourkela’s 2005 German collaboration was misstated. - [2009] - Q32: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. MMTC Limited is India's largest international trading organization 2.
