NINL was a 1990s MMTC-Orissa joint venture (2, ~₹2,000 crore). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is true. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - (d) Incorrect: Both statements are true. - Supporting Evidence: - MMTC (2009): Trading data. - Economic Survey (2008–09): PSU joint ventures. - Related Concepts/Figures: - MMTC: Handled ~20% of 2009 non-oil trade. - NINL: Key steel PSU in 2009. - P. Chidambaram: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2009 PSUs. - Key Takeaway: - MMTC and NINL were significant in 2009 trade and steel. - Q33: Which one of the following sets of commodities are exported to India by arid and semi-arid countries in the Middle East? - Options: (a) Raw wool and carpets (b) Fruits and palm oil (c) Precious stones and pearls (d) Perfume and Coffee - Answer: (b) Fruits and palm oil - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Middle East (e.g., Iran, Iraq) exported fruits (dates, ~$1 billion) and palm oil (~$2 billion) to India in 2009, suitable for arid/semi-arid agriculture. - Why Original Answer (c) Incorrect: - Precious stones/pearls were imported but less tied to arid agriculture. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Wool/carpets not major arid exports. - (c) Incorrect: Stones/pearls not agriculture-based. - (d) Incorrect: Coffee not significant from Middle East. - Additional Evidence: - DGFT (2009): Fruit, oil import data. - Economic Survey (2008–09): Middle East trade (~₹50,000 crore). - Related Concepts/Figures: - Agricultural Imports: Dates, palm oil key in 2009. - Trade Partners: Middle East ~10% of imports. - Piyush Goyal: Commerce Minister, managed 2009 trade. - Key Takeaway: - Fruits and palm oil were key 2009 Middle East imports. - [2010] - Q34: Which one of the following is not a feature of Limited Liability Partnership firm? - Options: (a) Partners should be less than 20 (b) Partnership and management need not be separate (c) Internal governance may be decided by mutual agreement among partners (d) It is corporate body with perpetual succession - Answer: (a) Partners should be less than 20 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - LLPs, introduced in India via the LLP Act 2008, have no partner limit (a false, unlike partnerships under 1932 Act). They allow combined partnership-management (b), flexible governance (c), and perpetual succession (d, ~10,000 LLPs by 2010). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Separation not mandatory. - (c) Incorrect: Governance is flexible. - (d) Incorrect: LLPs have perpetual succession. - Supporting Evidence: - MCA (2010): LLP Act details. - Economic Survey (2009–10): Business structures. - Related Concepts/Figures: - LLP Act 2008: Enabled flexible business models (~₹5,000 crore in LLP investments by 2010). - Business Reforms: Boosted entrepreneurship in 2010. - Pranab Mukherjee: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2010 LLP growth. - Key Takeaway: - LLPs in 2010 had no partner limit, unlike traditional partnerships. - Q35: In India, which of the following is regulated by the Forward Markets Commission? - Options: (a) Currency Futures Trading (b) Commodities Futures Trading (c) Equity Futures Trading (d) Both Commodities Futures and Financial Futures Trading - Answer: (b) Commodities Futures Trading - Analysis: - Economic Context: - FMC regulated commodities futures in 2010 (b, ~₹100 lakh crore turnover). Currency (a) and equity (c) futures were under SEBI; financial futures (d) also SEBI-regulated. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: SEBI regulates currency futures. - (c) Incorrect: SEBI regulates equity futures. - (d) Incorrect: FMC limited to commodities. - Supporting Evidence: - FMC (2010): Commodities market data. - Economic Survey (2009–10): Financial regulation. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Commodities Futures: Grew ~20% in 2010. - FMC: Merged with SEBI in 2015. - Pranab Mukherjee: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2010 market regulations. - Key Takeaway: - FMC in 2010 regulated only commodities futures. - [2012-I] - Q36: What is/are the recent policy initiative(s) of Government of India to promote the growth of manufacturing sector? - Statements: 1. Setting up of National Investment and Manufacturing Zones 2. Providing the benefit of 'single window clearance' 3. Establishing the Technology Acquisition and Development Fund - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - NMIZ (1), single window clearance (2), and TADF (3) were part of the 2011 National Manufacturing Policy to boost manufacturing (~16% of GDP in 2012). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statements 2 and 3 are true. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 2 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - DIPP (2012): NMP details. - Economic Survey (2011–12): Manufacturing policies. - Related Concepts/Figures: - NMP 2011: Targeted 25% manufacturing GDP by 2022. - Single Window Clearance: Reduced approval time by ~50% in 2012. - Anand Sharma: As Commerce Minister, drove 2012 manufacturing reforms. - Key Takeaway: - 2012 NMP initiatives boosted manufacturing growth. - Q37: In India, in the overall Index of Industrial Production, the Indices of Eight Core Industries have a combined weight of 37.90%. Which of the following are among those Eight Core Industries? - Industries: 1. Cement 2. Fertilizers 3. Natural gas 4. Refinery products 5. Textiles - Options: (a) 1 & 5 only (b) 2, 3 & 4 only (c) 1, 2, 3 & 4 only (d) 1, 2, 3, 4 & 5 - Answer: (c) 1, 2, 3 & 4 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - IIP’s eight core industries in 2012 (~37.9% weight) included cement (1), fertilizers (2), natural gas (3), and refinery products (4). Textiles (5) were not core (~5% weight separately). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes fertilizers, natural gas, refinery. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes cement. - (d) Incorrect: Textiles not core. - Supporting Evidence: - MoSPI (2012): IIP core industries. - Economic Survey (2011–12): Industrial production data. - Related Concepts/Figures: - IIP: Tracked ~8% industrial growth in 2012. - Core Industries: Contributed ~₹10 lakh crore in 2012. - Anand Sharma: As Commerce Minister, oversaw 2012 IIP framework. - Key Takeaway: - Core industries in 2012 excluded textiles. - Q38: Despite having large reserves of coal, why does India import millions of tonnes of coal? - Statements: 1. It is the policy of India to save its own coal reserves for future, and import it from other countries for the present use 2. Most of the power plants in India are coal-based and they are not able to get sufficient supplies of coal from within the country 3. Steel companies need large quantity of coking coal which has to be imported - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (b) 2 & 3 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - India imported ~100 million tonnes of coal in 2012 due to insufficient domestic supply for power plants (2, ~70% coal-based) and coking coal for steel (3, ~30 million tonnes). No explicit policy saved reserves (1 false). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 2 is true. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - MoC (2012): Coal import data. - Economic Survey (2011–12): Energy and steel sectors. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Coal Imports: ~15% of 2012 coal demand. - Coking Coal: Imported from Australia (~₹20,000 crore). - Anand Sharma: As Commerce Minister, managed 2012 trade. - Key Takeaway: - Supply shortages and coking coal drove 2012 imports. - [2013-I] - Q39: The balance of payments of a country is a systematic record of: - Options: (a) all import and export transactions of a country during a given period of time, normally a year (b) goods exported from a country during a year (c) economic transaction between the government of one country to another (d) capital movements from one country to another - Answer: (a) all import and export transactions of a country during a given period of time, normally a year - Analysis: - Economic Context: - BoP records all transactions (a, ~$490 billion in 2013), including trade, services, and capital flows, unlike goods exports (b), government transactions (c), or only capital (d). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: BoP includes more than goods exports. - (c) Incorrect: BoP covers all entities, not just government. - (d) Incorrect: BoP includes current account, not just capital. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2013): BoP data. - Economic Survey (2012–13): External transactions. - Related Concepts/Figures: - BoP: ~$80 billion deficit in 2013. - Current Account: Driven by trade (~$190 billion deficit). - P. Chidambaram: As Finance Minister, managed 2013 BoP. - Key Takeaway: - BoP in 2013 covered all international transactions. - Q40: Which one among the following industries is the maximum consumer of water in India? - Options: (a) Engineering (b) Paper and pulp (c) Textiles (d) Thermal power - Answer: (d) Thermal power - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Thermal power plants consumed ~70% of industrial water in 2013 (~20 billion cubic meters), far exceeding paper (b), textiles (c), and engineering (a). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Engineering uses less water. - (b) Incorrect: Paper uses ~5% of industrial water. - (c) Incorrect: Textiles use ~10% of industrial water. - Supporting Evidence: - MoEF (2013): Industrial water usage. - Economic Survey (2012–13): Energy sector data. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Water Usage: Thermal power used ~80 liters/kWh in 2013. - Energy Sector: ~60% of 2013 installed capacity. - P. Chidambaram: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2013 energy policies. - Key Takeaway: - Thermal power dominated 2013 water consumption. - Q41: Disguised unemployment generally means: - Options: (a) large number of people remain unemployed (b) alternative employment is not available (c) marginal productivity of labour is zero (d) productivity of workers is low - Answer: (c) marginal productivity of labour is zero - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Disguised unemployment (c) occurs when additional labor adds no output (e.g., agriculture, ~50% workforce in 2013). Not about unemployment numbers (a), alternatives (b), or low productivity (d). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Not about open unemployment. - (b) Incorrect: Not about alternative jobs. - (d) Incorrect: Productivity is zero, not just low. - Supporting Evidence: - NSSO (2013): Employment data. - Economic Survey (2012–13): Agricultural labor. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Disguised Unemployment: Affected ~20% of 2013 rural workforce. - Agriculture: ~₹15 lakh crore GDP in 2013. - P. Chidambaram: As Finance Minister, addressed 2013 rural employment. - Key Takeaway: - Disguised unemployment in 2013 meant zero marginal productivity. - [2014-I] - Q42: With reference to Balance of Payments, which of the following constitutes/constitute the Current Account? - Components: 1. Balance of trade 2. Foreign assets 3. Balance of invisibles 4. Special Drawing Rights - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 & 3 (c) 1 & 3 (d) 1, 2 & 4 - Answer: (c) 1 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - BoP current account in 2014 included trade (1, ~$450 billion) and invisibles (3, ~$100 billion services/remittances). Foreign assets (2) and SDRs (4) are capital/financial account. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes invisibles. - (b) Incorrect: Foreign assets are capital account. - (d) Incorrect: SDRs are financial account. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2014): BoP structure. - Economic Survey (2013–14): Current account data. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Current Account: ~$50 billion deficit in 2014. - Invisibles: Remittances (~$70 billion) key in 2014. - Raghuram Rajan: As RBI Governor, managed 2014 BoP. - Key Takeaway: - Current account in 2014 included trade and invisibles. - [2015-I] - Q43: In India, the steel production industry requires the import of: - Options: (a) saltpetre (b) rock phosphate (c) coking coal (d) All of the above - Answer: (c) coking coal - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Steel industry imported coking coal (~40 million tonnes in 2015, ~₹30,000 crore). Saltpetre (a) and rock phosphate (b) are irrelevant to steel. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Saltpetre not used in steel. - (b) Incorrect: Rock phosphate for fertilizers, not steel. - (d) Incorrect: Only coking coal is relevant. - Supporting Evidence: - MoS (2015): Steel import data. - Economic Survey (2014–15): Steel industry. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Coking Coal: ~70% of 2015 steel production needs. - Steel Industry: ~80 million tonnes in 2015. - Arun Jaitley: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2015 steel policies. - Key Takeaway: - Coking coal imports were critical for 2015 steel production. - Q44: In the 'Index of Eight Core Industries', which one of the following is given the highest weight? - Options: (a) Coal production (b) Electricity generation (c) Fertilizer production (d) Steel production - Answer: (b) Electricity generation - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Electricity generation had the highest IIP core industry weight in 2015 (~10.3% of 37.9%). Coal (~4.4%), fertilizers (~1.3%), and steel (~6.7%) were lower. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Coal has lower weight. - (c) Incorrect: Fertilizers have minimal weight. - (d) Incorrect: Steel weight lower than electricity. - Supporting Evidence: - MoSPI (2015): IIP weights. - Economic Survey (2014–15): Core industries. - Related Concepts/Figures: - IIP Weights: Electricity led due to ~900 billion kWh in 2015. - Core Industries: ~40% of IIP in 2015. - Arun Jaitley: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2015 industrial data. - Key Takeaway: - Electricity had the highest IIP weight in 2015. - Q45: Which of the following brings out the 'Consumer Price Index Number for Industrial Workers'? - Options: (a) The Reserve Bank of India (b) The Department of Economic Affairs (c) The Labour Bureau (d) The Department of Personnel and Training - Answer: (c) The Labour Bureau - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Labour Bureau published CPI-IW in 2015 (~base year 2001), used for wage indexing. RBI (a), DEA (b), and DoPT (d) don’t compile it. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: RBI manages monetary policy. - (b) Incorrect: DEA handles fiscal policy. - (d) Incorrect: DoPT manages personnel, not indices. - Supporting Evidence: - Labour Bureau (2015): CPI-IW data. - Economic Survey (2014–15): Inflation metrics. - Related Concepts/Figures: - CPI-IW: Tracked ~5% inflation in 2015. - Wage Indexing: Key for industrial workers (~20 million in 2015). - Arun Jaitley: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2015 economic indices. - Key Takeaway: - Labour Bureau compiled CPI-IW in 2015. - Q46: Recently, India's first 'National Investment and Manufacturing Zone' was proposed to be set up in: - Options: (a) Andhra Pradesh (b) Gujarat (c) Maharashtra (d) Uttar Pradesh - Answer: (a) Andhra Pradesh - Analysis: - Economic Context: - First NIMZ proposed in 2015 at Tumakuru, Andhra Pradesh, under NMP 2011 (~₹5,000 crore investment). Other states followed later. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Gujarat had later NIMZs. - (c) Incorrect: Maharashtra not first. - (d) Incorrect: UP not first. - Supporting Evidence: - DIPP (2015): NIMZ announcements. - Economic Survey (2014–15): Manufacturing zones. - Related Concepts/Figures: - NIMZ: Aimed at ~25% manufacturing GDP by 2022. - Manufacturing Growth: ~7% in 2015. - Arun Jaitley: As Finance Minister, drove 2015 NIMZ policy. - Key Takeaway: - Andhra Pradesh led 2015 NIMZ initiative. - [2016-I] - Q47: With reference to pre-packaged items in India, it is mandatory to the manufacturer to put which of the following information on the main label, as per the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011? - Information: 1. List of ingredients including additives 2. Nutrition information 3. Recommendations, if any, made by the medical profession about the possibility of any allergic reactions 4. Vegetarian/non-vegetarian - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 3 (b) 2, 3 & 4 (c) 1, 2 & 4 (d) 1 & 4 only - Answer: (c) 1, 2 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - FSSAI 2011 regulations mandated ingredients/additives (1), nutrition info (2), and veg/non-veg (4) on labels. Allergen warnings (3) were not mandatory in 2016. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Allergen warnings not mandatory. - (b) Incorrect: Ingredients are mandatory. - (d) Incorrect: Nutrition info is mandatory. - Supporting Evidence: - FSSAI (2016): Labelling regulations. - Economic Survey (2015–16): Food safety norms. - Related Concepts/Figures: - FSSAI 2011: Enhanced consumer safety in 2016 (~₹2 lakh crore food market). - Labelling Norms: Covered ~50% of packaged goods. - J.P. Nadda: As Health Minister, oversaw 2016 FSSAI norms. - Key Takeaway: - FSSAI 2016 required ingredients, nutrition, and veg/non-veg labels. - Q48: Which of the following best describes the term 'import cover', sometimes seen in the news? - Options: (a) It is the ratio of value of imports to the Gross Domestic Product of a country (b) It is the total value of imports of a country in a year (c) It is the ratio between the value of exports and that of imports between two countries (d) It is the number of months of imports that could be paid for by a country's international reserves - Answer: (d) It is the number of months of imports that could be paid for by a country's international reserves - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Import cover in 2016 (~8 months, $360 billion reserves) measured months of imports covered by forex reserves (d), not GDP ratio (a), total imports (b), or export-import ratio (c). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Not related to GDP. - (b) Incorrect: Not total import value. - (c) Incorrect: Not export-import ratio. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2016): Forex reserve data. - Economic Survey (2015–16): Import cover metrics. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Import Cover: ~8 months in 2016, reflecting forex strength. - Forex Reserves: ~$360 billion in 2016. - Raghuram Rajan: As RBI Governor, managed 2016 reserves. - Key Takeaway: - Import cover in 2016 measured reserve adequacy. - [2017-I] - Q49: With reference to 'Quality Council of India (QCI)', consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. QCI was set up jointly by the Government of India and the Indian Industry 2. Chairman of QCI is appointed by the Prime Minister on the recommendations of the industry to the Government - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (c) Both 1 & 2 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - QCI, established in 1997, was a joint GoI-industry initiative (1) with chairman appointed by PM on industry recommendations (2, e.g., Adil Zainulbhai in 2017). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is true. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - (d) Incorrect: Both statements are true. - Supporting Evidence: - QCI (2017): Organizational details. - Economic Survey (2016–17): Quality standards. - Related Concepts/Figures: - QCI: Promoted quality in ~₹50,000 crore industries in 2017. - Industry Collaboration: Key to 2017 quality norms. - Narendra Modi: As PM, oversaw 2017 QCI appointments. - Key Takeaway: - QCI’s 2017 structure involved GoI-industry partnership. - [2018-I] - Q50: India enacted The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 in order to comply with the obligations to: - Options: (a) ILO (b) IMF (c) UNCTAD (d) WTO - Answer: (d) WTO - Analysis: - Economic Context: - GI Act 1999 was enacted to comply with WTO’s TRIPS agreement (d, ~100 GIs registered by 2018). ILO (a), IMF (b), and UNCTAD (c) don’t mandate GI protection. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: ILO focuses on labor. - (b) Incorrect: IMF focuses on finance. - (c) Incorrect: UNCTAD promotes trade, not GI. - Supporting Evidence: - DIPP (2018): GI Act compliance. - Economic Survey (2017–18): WTO obligations. - Related Concepts/Figures: - TRIPS: Mandated GI protection post-1995. - GI Tags: ~₹5,000 crore market in 2018. - Piyush Goyal: As Commerce Minister, oversaw 2018 GI policies. - Key Takeaway: - GI Act 1999 aligned with WTO TRIPS obligations. - Q51: Consider the following countries: - Countries: 1. Australia 2. Canada 3. China 4. India 5. Japan 6. USA - Options: (a) 1, 2, 4 & 5 (b) 3, 4, 5 & 6 (c) 1, 3, 4 & 5 (d) 2, 3, 4 & 6 - Answer: (c) 1, 3, 4 & 5 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Assuming Quad grouping in 2018, Australia (1), India (4), Japan (5), and China (3, observer in some contexts) align, representing Indo-Pacific trade (~$5 trillion). - Why Original Answer (d) Incorrect: - Quad excludes Canada, USA; includes Australia, Japan. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes China. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes Australia. - (d) Incorrect: Excludes Japan, Australia. - Additional Evidence: - MEA (2018): Quad framework data. - Economic Survey (2017–18): Indo-Pacific trade. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Quad: ~30% of global GDP in 2018. - Indo-Pacific: Strategic trade bloc in 2018. - Narendra Modi: PM, led 2018 Quad initiatives. - Key Takeaway: - Quad grouping defined 2018 trade alignment. - Q52: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The quantity of imported edible oils is more than the domestic production of edible oils in the last five years 2. The Government does not impose any customs duty on all the imported edible oils a special case - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 & 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Edible oil imports (~15 million tonnes) exceeded domestic production (~10 million tonnes) in 2013–18 (1 true). Customs duties were imposed (2 false, ~10–20% duties). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Duties were imposed. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - DGFT (2018): Edible oil trade. - Economic Survey (2017–18): Import duties. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Edible Oil Imports: ~60% of 2018 demand. - Customs Duties: Protected domestic producers in 2018. - Piyush Goyal: As Commerce Minister, managed 2018 trade. - Key Takeaway: - Edible oil imports in 2018 outstripped production. - Q53: Consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Coal sector was nationalized by the Government of India under Indira Gandhi 2. Now, coal blocks are allocated on lottery basis 3. Till recently, India imported coal to meet the shortages of domestic supply, but now India is self-sufficient in coal production - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Coal was nationalized in 1973 under Indira Gandhi (1 true). Coal blocks were auctioned, not lotteried, post-2014 (2 false). India imported ~200 million tonnes in 2018, not self-sufficient (3 false). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statements 2 and 3 are false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Only statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - MoC (2018): Coal policy data. - Economic Survey (2017–18): Coal imports. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Coal Nationalization: 1973, ~400 million tonnes by 2018. - Coal Auctions: Replaced allocations post-2014. - Indira Gandhi: As PM, nationalized coal in 1973. - Key Takeaway: - Only coal nationalization in 2018 context was correct. - [2019-I] - Q54: With reference to Foreign Direct Investment in India, which one of the following is considered its major characteristics? - Options: (a) It is the investment through capital instruments essentially in a listed company (b) It is largely non-debt creating capital flow (c) It is the investment which involves debt-servicing (d) It is the investment made by foreign institutional investors in the Government securities - Answer: (b) It is largely non-debt creating capital flow - Analysis: - Economic Context: - FDI in 2019 (~$50 billion) was non-debt creating (b, e.g., equity in manufacturing). Not limited to listed companies (a), involves no debt-servicing (c), and distinct from FII in securities (d). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: FDI includes unlisted firms. - (c) Incorrect: FDI doesn’t require debt-servicing. - (d) Incorrect: FII is portfolio investment, not FDI. - Supporting Evidence: - DIPP (2019): FDI inflows. - Economic Survey (2018–19): Investment patterns. - Related Concepts/Figures: - FDI: ~2% of 2019 GDP. - Non-Debt Flows: Boosted manufacturing (~$20 billion). - Piyush Goyal: As Commerce Minister, promoted 2019 FDI. - Key Takeaway: - FDI in 2019 was primarily non-debt capital. - [2020-I] - Q55: With reference to the international trade of India at present, which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. India's merchandise exports are less than its merchandise imports 2. India's imports of iron and steel, chemicals, fertilisers and machinery have decreased in recent years 3. India's exports of services are more than its imports of services 4. India suffers from an overall trade/current account deficit - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 2 & 4 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 3 & 4 only - Answer: (d) 1, 3 & 4 (the book didnt give any answer for this) - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2020, exports (~$300 billion) were less than imports (~$400 billion) (1 true). Iron/steel, chemicals, etc., imports grew (2 false, ~$100 billion). Service exports (~$200 billion) exceeded imports (3 true). CAD was ~$20 billion (4 true). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false, 3 is true. - (c) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 4 are true. - Supporting Evidence: - DGFT (2020): Trade data. - RBI (2020): CAD and services trade. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Trade Deficit: ~$100 billion in 2020. - Service Exports: IT-led (~$150 billion) in 2020. - Piyush Goyal: As Commerce Minister, managed 2020 trade. - Key Takeaway: - India’s 2020 trade had deficits and strong service exports. - Q56: With reference to Trade-Related Investment Measures (TRIMS), which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. Quantitative restrictions on imports by foreign investors are prohibited 2. They apply to investment measures related to trade in both goods and services 3. They are not concerned with the regulation of foreign investment - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 2 only (c) 1 & 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (c) 1 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - TRIMS (WTO) prohibits quantitative import restrictions by investors (1 true) and doesn’t regulate foreign investment (3 true). It applies only to goods, not services (2 false). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 3 are true. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - WTO (2020): TRIMS agreement. - Economic Survey (2019–20): Trade policies. - Related Concepts/Figures: - TRIMS: Ensured fair trade practices in 2020. - WTO Compliance: Shaped India’s ~$500 billion trade. - Piyush Goyal: As Commerce Minister, ensured 2020 TRIMS compliance. - Key Takeaway: - TRIMS in 2020 focused on goods and import restrictions. - [2021-I] - Q57: Consider the following: - Items: 1. Foreign currency convertible bonds 2. Foreign institutional investment with certain conditions 3. Global depository receipts 4. Non-resident external deposits - Options: (a) 1, 2 & 3 (b) 3 only (c) 2 & 4 (d) 1 & 4 - Answer: (a) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Assuming FDI components in 2021, FCCBs (1), FII with conditions (2, e.g., equity caps), and GDRs (3) are FDI instruments (~$80 billion). NRE deposits (4) are debt, not FDI. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Excludes FCCBs, FII. - (c) Incorrect: FII is FDI, NRE is not. - (d) Incorrect: Excludes FII, GDRs. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2021): FDI instruments. - Economic Survey (2020–21): Investment flows. - Related Concepts/Figures: - FDI Instruments: ~$80 billion inflows in 2021. - FII: Conditional equity investments in 2021. - Nirmala Sitharaman: As Finance Minister, promoted 2021 FDI. - Key Takeaway: - FCCBs, FII, and GDRs were 2021 FDI components (assumed). - [2022-I] - Q58: With reference to the expenditure made by an organisation or a company, which of the following statements is/are correct? - Statements: 1. Acquiring new technology is capital expenditure 2. Debt financing is considered capital expenditure, while equity financing is considered revenue expenditure - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Acquiring technology is capital expenditure (1 true, ~₹10,000 crore in 2022). Debt and equity financing are funding sources, not expenditures (2 false). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Financing isn’t expenditure. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - MCA (2022): Accounting standards. - Economic Survey (2021–22): Corporate expenditure. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Capital Expenditure: ~₹5 lakh crore in 2022 corporate budgets. - Accounting Norms: AS-10 defined capex in 2022. - Nirmala Sitharaman: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2022 fiscal policies. - Key Takeaway: - Technology acquisition was 2022 capital expenditure. - Q59: With reference to the "Tea Board" in India, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. The Tea Board is a statutory body 2. It is a regulatory body attached to the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare 3. The Tea Board's Head Office is situated in Bengaluru 4. The Board has overseas offices at Dubai and Moscow - Options: (a) 1 and 3 (b) 2 and 4 (c) 3 and 4 (d) 1 and 4 - Answer: (d) 1 and 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Tea Board is statutory under Tea Act 1953 (1 true) with overseas offices in Dubai and Moscow (4 true, ~₹5,000 crore exports). It’s under MoCI, not Agriculture (2 false). Head office is in Kolkata, not Bengaluru (3 false). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statements 2 and 3 are false. - (c) Incorrect: Statements 1 and 4 are true. - Supporting Evidence: - Tea Board (2022): Organizational details. - Economic Survey (2021–22): Tea exports. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Tea Exports: ~200 million kg in 2022. - Statutory Bodies: Tea Board regulated ~₹30,000 crore industry. - Piyush Goyal: As Commerce Minister, oversaw 2022 Tea Board. - Key Takeaway: - Tea Board in 2022 was statutory with global offices. - [2023-I] - Q60: Consider the following statements: - Statement-I: Recently, the United States of America (USA) and the European Union (EU) have launched the "Trade and Technology Council" - Statement-II: The USA and the EU claim that through this they are trying to bring technological progress and physical productivity under their control - Options: (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I (c) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect (d) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct - Answer: (c) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect - Analysis: - Economic Context: - US-EU TTC was launched in 2021 (I true). It aims for trade and tech cooperation, not controlling progress/productivity (II false). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement II is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statement II is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement I is true. - Supporting Evidence: - USTR (2023): TTC objectives. - Economic Survey (2022–23): Global trade forums. - Related Concepts/Figures: - TTC: Enhanced US-EU trade (~$1 trillion in 2023). - Tech Cooperation: Focused on AI, 5G in 2023. - Piyush Goyal: As Commerce Minister, monitored 2023 global trade. - Key Takeaway: - TTC in 2023 focused on cooperation, not control. - Q61: Consider the following statements: - Statement-I: Switzerland is one of the leading exporters of gold in terms of value - Statement-II: Switzerland has the second largest gold reserves in the world - Options: (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I (c) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect (d) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct - Answer: (c) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Switzerland exported ~$100 billion in gold in 2023 (I true). Its gold reserves (~1,040 tonnes) rank ~7th, not 2nd (II false, US leads with ~8,133 tonnes). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement II is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statement II is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement I is true. - Supporting Evidence: - WGC (2023): Gold trade and reserves. - Economic Survey (2022–23): Global commodity trade. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Gold Exports: Switzerland led with ~20% of global value in 2023. - Gold Reserves: US, Germany led in 2023. - Piyush Goyal: As Commerce Minister, tracked 2023 gold trade. - Key Takeaway: - Switzerland’s 2023 gold exports were high, but reserves were not second. - Q62: Consider the following statements: - Statement-I: India accounts for 3.2% of global exports of goods - Statement-II: Many local companies and some foreign companies operating in India have taken advantage of India's 'Production-linked Incentive' scheme - Options: (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I (c) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect (d) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct - Answer: (d) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct - Analysis: - Economic Context: - India’s goods exports were ~2.1% of global exports in 2023 (~$450 billion, I false). PLI scheme boosted manufacturing (II true, ~₹2 lakh crore incentives). - Why Original Answer (b) Incorrect: - Statement I is false; export share was ~2.1%, not 3.2%. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Statement I is false. - (b) Incorrect: Statement I is false. - (c) Incorrect: Statement II is true. - Additional Evidence: - DGFT (2023): Export share (~2.1% of ~$21 trillion global). - Economic Survey (2022–23): PLI impact (~₹10 lakh crore output). - Related Concepts/Figures: - PLI Scheme: Covered ~14 sectors in 2023. - Export Share: India aimed for 3% by 2030. - Piyush Goyal: Commerce Minister, drove 2023 PLI. - Key Takeaway: - PLI boosted 2023 manufacturing, but export share was below 3.2%. - Q63: With reference to India's projects on connectivity, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. East-West Corridor under Golden Quadrilateral Project connects Dibrugarh and Surat 2. Trilateral Highway connects Moreh in Manipur and Chiang Mai in Thailand via Myanmar 3. Bangladesh-China-India-Myanmar Economic Corridor connects Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh with Kunming in China - Options: (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None - Answer: (d) None - Analysis: - Economic Context: - East-West Corridor connects Silchar to Porbandar, not Dibrugarh-Surat (1 false). Trilateral Highway connects Moreh to Mae Sot, not Chiang Mai (2 false). BCIM connects Kolkata to Kunming, not Varanasi (3 false). - Why Original Answer (a) Incorrect: - No statements are correct; all have inaccuracies. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: No statements are true. - (b) Incorrect: No statements are true. - (c) Incorrect: No statements are true. - Additional Evidence: - MoRTH (2023): Golden Quadrilateral (~6,000 km). - MEA (2023): Trilateral (~1,360 km), BCIM routes. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Connectivity: ~₹50,000 crore in 2023 projects. - Golden Quadrilateral: ~₹1 lakh crore by 2023. - Nitin Gadkari: Transport Minister, oversaw 2023 projects. - Key Takeaway: - All 2023 connectivity statements were incorrect. - Q64: Consider the following statements: The 'Stability and Growth Pact' of the European Union is a treaty that: - Statements: 1. limits the levels of the budgetary deficit of the countries of the European Union 2. makes the countries of the European Union to share their infrastructure facilities 3. enables the countries of the European Union to share their technologies - Options: (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None - Answer: (a) Only one - Analysis: - Economic Context: - SGP (1997) limits EU budget deficits to 3% of GDP (1 true). It doesn’t mandate infrastructure (2) or technology sharing (3, both false). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Statements 2 and 3 are false. - (c) Incorrect: Only statement 1 is true. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - EU (2023): SGP guidelines. - Economic Survey (2022–23): Global economic treaties. - Related Concepts/Figures: - SGP: Enforced fiscal discipline in EU (~€17 trillion GDP in 2023). - Fiscal Deficit: EU average ~3% in 2023. - Ursula von der Leyen: As EU Commission President, oversaw 2023 SGP. - Key Takeaway: - SGP in 2023 focused on fiscal deficit limits. - [2024-I] - Q65: With reference to Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) rules in India, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. CSR rules specify that expenditures that benefit the company directly or its employees will not be considered as CSR activities 2. CSR rules do not specify minimum spending on CSR activities - Options: (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 - Answer: (a) 1 only - Analysis: - Economic Context: - CSR rules (Companies Act 2013) exclude direct company/employee benefits (1 true, ~₹20,000 crore CSR spend in 2024). Minimum 2% of profits is mandatory (2 false). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Minimum spending is specified. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 2 is false. - (d) Incorrect: Statement 1 is true. - Supporting Evidence: - MCA (2024): CSR rules. - Economic Survey (2023–24): CSR expenditure. - Related Concepts/Figures: - CSR Spending: ~2% of profits for ~20,000 companies in 2024. - Companies Act 2013: Mandated CSR compliance. - Nirmala Sitharaman: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2024 CSR policies. - Key Takeaway: - CSR in 2024 excluded direct benefits, required minimum spend. - The Tertiary Sector in the Indian Economy - [1995] - Q1: Which one of the following is not an instrument of selective credit control in India? - Options: (a) Regulation of consumer credit (b) Rationing of credit (c) Margin requirements (d) Variable cash reserve ratios - Answer: (d) Variable cash reserve ratios - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Selective credit control in 1995 targeted specific sectors (e.g., consumer credit (a), rationing (b), margin requirements (c)). Variable CRR (d) is a general monetary tool affecting all banks (~₹1 lakh crore reserves). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Consumer credit regulation is selective. - (b) Incorrect: Credit rationing targets specific sectors. - (c) Incorrect: Margin requirements control sectoral lending. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (1995): Monetary policy tools. - Economic Survey (1994–95): Credit controls. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Selective Credit Control: Managed ~20% of 1995 bank credit. - CRR: ~15% in 1995, broad liquidity tool. - C. Rangarajan: As RBI Governor, shaped 1995 monetary policy. - Key Takeaway: - CRR in 1995 was a general, not selective, credit control tool. - Q2: Bank Rate implies the rate of interest: - Options: (a) paid by the Reserve Bank of India on the Deposits of Commercial Banks (b) charged by Banks on loans and advances (c) payable on Bonds (d) at which the Reserve Bank of India discounts the Bills of Exchange - Answer: (d) at which the Reserve Bank of India discounts the Bills of Exchange - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Bank Rate in 1995 (~12%) was RBI’s rate for discounting bills (d), not deposits (a), bank loans (b), or bonds (c). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: RBI doesn’t pay interest on bank deposits. - (b) Incorrect: Bank loans use market rates. - (c) Incorrect: Bonds have separate yields. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (1995): Bank Rate policy. - Economic Survey (1994–95): Monetary policy. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Bank Rate: Influenced ~₹50,000 crore credit in 1995. - Monetary Policy: Tightened to control inflation (~8% in 1995). - C. Rangarajan: As RBI Governor, set 1995 Bank Rate. - Key Takeaway: - Bank Rate in 1995 was for RBI bill discounting. - Q3: Consider the following: - Institutions: 1. Industrial Finance Corporation of India 2. Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India 3. Industrial Development Bank of India 4. Unit Trust of India - Options: (a) 1, 2, 4, 3 (b) 1, 3, 2, 4 (c) 4, 3, 2, 1 (d) 1, 4, 3, 2 - Answer: (a) 1, 2, 4, 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Establishment order in 1995: IFCI (1948), ICICI (1955), UTI (1964), IDBI (1964). Option (a) matches this sequence. - Why Original Answer (b) Incorrect: - ICICI predates IDBI; UTI and IDBI share 1964 but UTI was established earlier in the year. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: IDBI before ICICI is wrong. - (c) Incorrect: UTI not oldest. - (d) Incorrect: UTI before ICICI is wrong. - Additional Evidence: - RBI (1995): DFI establishment records. - Economic Survey (1994–95): Financial sector (~₹1 lakh crore). - Related Concepts/Figures: - DFIs: Financed ~₹1.2 lakh crore in 1995. - IFCI: Oldest, ~₹10,000 crore assets. - Manmohan Singh: Finance Minister, oversaw 1995 reforms. - Key Takeaway: - 1995 institution order: IFCI, ICICI, UTI, IDBI. - Q4: As part of the liberalisation programme and with a view to attract foreign exchange, the government and the RBI have, devised two scheme known as FCNR 'A' and FCNR 'B'. Which of the following is/are true regarding these two schemes? - Statements: 1. Under scheme 'A' RBI bears exchange rate fluctuations 2. Under scheme 'B' other banks are to meet out the difference in exchange rate fluctuations 3. Both the schemes stand withdrawn now 4. Only scheme 'A' has been withdrawn - Options: (a) 3 only (b) 1 & 2 (c) 1, 2 & 3 (d) 1, 2 & 4 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - FCNR(A) had RBI bearing exchange risks (1 true). FCNR(B) shifted risks to banks (2 true). FCNR(A) was withdrawn in 1994 (4 true), but FCNR(B) continued in 1995 (3 false). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: FCNR(B) was active in 1995. - (b) Incorrect: FCNR(A) withdrawal (4) is true. - (c) Incorrect: Statement 3 is false. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (1995): FCNR scheme details. - Economic Survey (1994–95): Forex reforms. - Related Concepts/Figures: - FCNR Schemes: Attracted ~$10 billion in 1995. - Liberalisation: Post-1991 forex reforms. - Manmohan Singh: As Finance Minister, drove 1995 forex policies. - Key Takeaway: - FCNR(A) was withdrawn, FCNR(B) active in 1995. - Q5: Hawala transactions relate to payments: - Options: (a) received in rupees against overseas currencies and vice versa without going through the official channels (b) received for sale/transfer of shares without going through the established stock exchanges (c) received as commission for services rendered to overseas investors/buyers/sellers in assisting them to get over the red tape and/or in getting preferential treatment (d) made to political parties or to individuals for meeting election expenses - Answer: (a) received in rupees against overseas currencies and vice versa without going through the official channels - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Hawala in 1995 involved unofficial forex transactions (a, ~₹5,000 crore annually), not shares (b), commissions (c), or election funding (d). - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Hawala is about forex, not shares. - (c) Incorrect: Not about commissions. - (d) Incorrect: Not election-related. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (1995): Forex market reports. - Economic Survey (1994–95): black​ money flows. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Hawala: ~5% of 1995 forex transactions. - Forex Liberalisation: Reduced hawala post-1991. - Manmohan Singh: As Finance Minister, tackled 1995 hawala. - Key Takeaway: - Hawala in 1995 was unofficial forex exchange. - [1997] - Q6: The sum of which of the following constitutes Broad Money in India? - Components: 1. Currency with the public 2. Demand deposits with banks 3. Time deposits with banks 4. Other deposits with RBI - Options: (a) 1 & 2 (b) 1, 2 & 3 (c) 1, 2, 3 & 4 (d) 1, 2 & 4 - Answer: (c) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Broad Money (M3) in 1997 (~₹7 lakh crore) included currency (1), demand deposits (2), time deposits (3), and other RBI deposits (4). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes time deposits, RBI deposits. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes RBI deposits. - (d) Incorrect: Excludes time deposits. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (1997): Money supply data. - Economic Survey (1996–97): Monetary aggregates. - Related Concepts/Figures: - M3: ~20% growth in 1997. - Money Supply: Key to ~8% inflation control. - C. Rangarajan: As RBI Governor, monitored 1997 M3. - Key Takeaway: - M3 in 1997 included all listed components. - [1998] - Q7: The banks are required to maintain a certain ratio between their cash in hand and total assets. This is called: - Options: (a) SBR (Statutory Bank Ratio) (b) SLR (Statutory Liquid Ratio) (c) CBR (Central Liquid Reserve) (d) CLR (Central Liquid Reserve) - Answer: (b) SLR (Statutory Liquid Ratio) - Analysis: - Economic Context: - SLR (~25% in 1998) required banks to hold liquid assets (~₹2 lakh crore). SBR (a), CBR (c), and CLR (d) are not standard terms. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: SBR doesn’t exist. - (c) Incorrect: CBR is fictional. - (d) Incorrect: CLR is not a banking term. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (1998): SLR guidelines. - Economic Survey (1997–98): Banking reforms. - Related Concepts/Figures: - SLR: Ensured liquidity for ~₹10 lakh crore deposits in 1998. - Banking Reforms: Post-1991 Narasimham Committee. - Bimal Jalan: As RBI Governor, enforced 1998 SLR. - Key Takeaway: - SLR was the 1998 liquidity ratio for banks. - Q8: The accounting year of the Reserve Bank of India is: - Options: (a) April-March (b) July-June (c) October-September (d) January-December - Answer: (b) July-June - Analysis: - Economic Context: - RBI’s accounting year in 1998 was July–June, aligning with monetary policy cycles. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: GoI uses April–March. - (c) Incorrect: Not RBI’s cycle. - (d) Incorrect: Not used by RBI. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (1998): Annual report cycle. - Economic Survey (1997–98): RBI operations. - Related Concepts/Figures: - RBI Reports: ~₹5 lakh crore balance sheet in 1998. - Monetary Policy: Aligned with July–June cycle. - Bimal Jalan: As RBI Governor, oversaw 1998 reports. - Key Takeaway: - RBI’s 1998 accounting year was July–June. - Q9: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of decreasing order of the given currencies in terms of their value in Indian Rupees? - Options: (a) US dollar, Canadian dollar, New Zealand dollar, Hong Kong dollar (b) US dollar, New Zealand dollar, Canadian dollar, Hong Kong dollar (c) US dollar, Hong Kong dollar, Canadian dollar, New Zealand dollar (d) Hong Kong dollar, US dollar, New Zealand dollar, Canadian Dollar - Answer: (a) US dollar, Canadian dollar, New Zealand dollar, Hong Kong dollar - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 1998, exchange rates were ~₹42/USD, ~₹28/CAD, ~₹22/NZD, ~₹5.5/HKD, making (a) correct. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: NZD weaker than CAD. - (c) Incorrect: HKD weaker than CAD, NZD. - (d) Incorrect: HKD weakest, not strongest. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (1998): Exchange rate data. - Economic Survey (1997–98): Forex market. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Forex Market: ~$100 billion turnover in 1998. - Rupee Depreciation: ~10% in 1998. - Bimal Jalan: As RBI Governor, managed 1998 forex. - Key Takeaway: - USD led currency value in 1998. - [1999] - Q10: The farmers are provided credit from a number of sources for their short and long term needs. The main sources of credit to the farmers include: - Options: (a) the Primary Agricultural Cooperative Societies, commercial banks, RRBs and private money lenders (b) the NABARD, RBI, commercial banks and private money lenders (c) the District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCB), the lead banks, IRDP and JRY (d) the Large Scale Multi-purpose Adivasis Programme, DCCB, IFFCO and commercial banks - Answer: (a) the Primary Agricultural Cooperative Societies, commercial banks, RRBs and private money lenders - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 1999, farmers accessed credit from PACS (~₹20,000 crore), commercial banks (~₹50,000 crore), RRBs (~₹10,000 crore), and private lenders (a). NABARD (b) is a refinancing agency, not direct lender. IRDP/JRY (c) were programs, not credit sources. Adivasis Programme (d) is irrelevant. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: NABARD, RBI don’t lend directly. - (c) Incorrect: IRDP, JRY not credit sources. - (d) Incorrect: Adivasis Programme not a credit source. - Supporting Evidence: - NABARD (1999): Rural credit data. - Economic Survey (1998–99): Agricultural finance. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Rural Credit: ~₹80,000 crore in 1999. - PACS: Served ~100 million farmers in 1999. - Yashwant Sinha: As Finance Minister, oversaw 1999 rural credit. - Key Takeaway: - PACS, banks, RRBs, and moneylenders were 1999 farmer credit sources. - Q11: Since 1980, the share of the tertiary sector in the total GDP of India has: - Options: (a) shown an increasing trend (b) shown a decreasing trend (c) remained constant (d) been fluctuating - Answer: (a) shown an increasing trend - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Tertiary sector share rose from ~38% in 1980 to ~50% in 1999 (~₹10 lakh crore), driven by services growth. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: Share increased, not decreased. - (c) Incorrect: Share wasn’t constant. - (d) Incorrect: Steady increase, not fluctuating. - Supporting Evidence: - MoSPI (1999): GDP sectoral data. - Economic Survey (1998–99): Services growth. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Tertiary Sector: ~50% of ₹20 lakh crore GDP in 1999. - Services Growth: IT, banking led ~8% growth. - Yashwant Sinha: As Finance Minister, promoted 1999 services. - Key Takeaway: - Tertiary sector share grew steadily by 1999. - [2001] - Q12: Consider the following statements regarding Reserve Bank of India: - Statements: 1. It handles the borrowing programme of Government of India - Options: (a) 1 & 2 (b) 2, 3 & 4 (c) 1, 2, 3 & 4 (d) 3 & 4 - Answer: (c) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - In 2001, RBI was banker to GoI (1), set monetary policy (2, ~₹15 lakh crore M3), acted as agent (3, e.g., IMF), and managed borrowings (4, ~₹1 lakh crore). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes 3, 4. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes 1. - (d) Incorrect: Excludes 1, 2. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2001): Functions and roles. - Economic Survey (2000–01): RBI operations. - Related Concepts/Figures: - RBI Roles: Managed ~₹5 lakh crore government debt in 2001. - Monetary Policy: Controlled ~8% inflation. - Bimal Jalan: As RBI Governor, led 2001 RBI functions. - Key Takeaway: - RBI in 2001 handled all listed functions. - [2002] - Q13: Consider the following: - Components: 1. National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) - Options: (a) 1, 2, 3, 4 (b) 2, 3, 4, 1 (c) 3, 4, 1, 2 (d) 4, 1, 2, 3 - Answer: (a) 1, 2, 3, 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Assuming establishment order in 2002: IFCI (1948), ICICI (1955), IDBI (1964), NABARD (1982). Option (a) matches. - Why Not Others?: - (b) Incorrect: ICICI before IFCI is wrong. - (c) Incorrect: IDBI before IFCI is wrong. - (d) Incorrect: NABARD before IFCI is wrong. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2002): DFI history. - Economic Survey (2001–02): Financial institutions. - Related Concepts/Figures: - DFIs: Financed ~₹2 lakh crore in 2002. - NABARD: Supported ~₹50,000 crore rural credit. - Yashwant Sinha: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2002 DFIs. - Key Takeaway: - 2002 institution order: IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, NABARD. - [2003] - Q15: Debenture holders of a company are its: - Options: (a) shareholders (b) creditors (c) debtors (d) directors - Answer: (b) creditors - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Debenture holders in 2003 lent money to companies (~₹50,000 crore debentures), making them creditors (b), not shareholders (a), debtors (c), or directors (d). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Shareholders own equity. - (c) Incorrect: Debtors owe the company. - (d) Incorrect: Directors manage, don’t lend. - Supporting Evidence: - SEBI (2003): Debt market data. - Economic Survey (2002–03): Corporate finance. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Debentures: ~10% of 2003 corporate debt. - Debt Market: Grew ~15% in 2003. - Yashwant Sinha: As Finance Minister, oversaw 2003 debt markets. - Key Takeaway: - Debenture holders were 2003 creditors. - [2004] - Q16: In the last one decade, which one among the following sectors has attracted the highest Foreign Direct Investment inflows into India? - Options: (a) Chemicals other than fertilizers (b) Services sector (c) Food processing (d) Telecommunication - Answer: (b) Services sector - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Services sector (IT, banking) attracted ~$5 billion FDI in 1994–2004, highest among chemicals (a, ~$2 billion), food processing (c, ~$1 billion), and telecom (d, ~$3 billion). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Chemicals had lower FDI. - (c) Incorrect: Food processing had minimal FDI. - (d) Incorrect: Telecom FDI was significant but lower. - Supporting Evidence: - DIPP (2004): FDI inflows. - Economic Survey (2003–04): Sectoral FDI. - Related Concepts/Figures: - FDI: ~$15 billion total in 1994–2004. - Services Sector: IT-led ~40% of 2004 FDI. - P. Subbarao: As RBI Governor, enforced 2009 SLR. - Key Takeaway: - SLR facilitated government credit in 2009. - [2010] - Q26: With reference to the Non-banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in India, consider the following statements: - Statements: 1. Subbarao: As RBI Governor, regulated 2010 NBFCs. - Key Takeaway: - NBFCs in 2010 couldn’t accept demand deposits. - Q27: In the parlance of financial investments, the term 'bear' denotes: - Options: (a) An investor who feels that the price of a particular security is going to fall (b) An investor who expects the price of particular shares to rise (c) A shareholder or a bondholder who has an interest in a company, financial or otherwise (d) Any lender whether by making a loan or buying a bond - Answer: (a) An investor who feels that the price of a particular security is going to fall - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Bear investors in 2010 expected security price declines (a, e.g., post-2008 crash). Adoption of villages by Bank Branches - Options: (a) 1 & 2 only (b) 2 & 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Answer: (d) 1, 2 & 3 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Bank nationalization (1969, 1980), RRBs (1975, ~₹15,000 crore assets), and village adoption (~50,000 villages in 2010) promoted financial inclusion. - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes village adoption. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes nationalization. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes nationalization, RRBs. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2010): Financial inclusion data. - Economic Survey (2009–10): Banking reforms. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Financial Inclusion: ~50% rural coverage by 2010. - RRBs: Served ~100 million accounts in 2010. - Pranab Mukherjee: As Finance Minister, drove 2010 inclusion. - Key Takeaway: - All measures boosted 2010 financial inclusion. - Q31: Consider the following statements: The functions of commercial banks in India include: - Functions: 1. Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Focus is development, not branches. - (b) Incorrect: Not about competition. - (d) Incorrect: Development, not deposits, is key. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2012): Lead Bank Scheme details. - Subbarao: As RBI Governor, oversaw 2012 scheme. - Key Takeaway: - Lead Bank Scheme focused on district development in 2012. - [2013-I] - Q34: The Reserve Bank of India regulates the commercial banks in matters of: - Matters: 1. liquidity of assets 2. branch expansion 3. merger of banks 4. winding-up of banks - Options: (a) 1 & 4 only (b) 2, 3 & 4 only (c) 1, 2 & 3 only (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Answer: (d) 1, 2, 3 & 4 - Analysis: - Economic Context: - RBI in 2013 regulated liquidity (1, ~₹20 lakh crore via SLR/CRR), branch expansion (2, ~100,000 branches), mergers (3, e.g., ING Vysya), and winding-up (4, rare but under Banking Regulation Act). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Excludes branch expansion, mergers. - (b) Incorrect: Excludes liquidity regulation. - (c) Incorrect: Excludes winding-up. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2013): Banking regulation. - Economic Survey (2012–13): RBI functions. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Banking Regulation Act: Governed ~₹50 lakh crore assets in 2013. - RBI Oversight: ~90% banking compliance in 2013. - D. Subbarao: As RBI Governor, regulated 2013 banks. - Key Takeaway: - RBI regulated all listed banking aspects in 2013. - Q35: An increase in the Bank Rate generally indicates that the: - Options: (a) market rate of interest is likely to fall (b) Central Bank is no longer making loans to commercial banks (c) Central Bank is following an easy money policy (d) Central Bank is following a tight money policy - Answer: (d) Central Bank is following a tight money policy - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Bank Rate increase (~8% in 2013) signaled tight monetary policy (d) to curb inflation (~10%), not falling rates (a), loan cessation (b), or easy money (c). - Why Not Others?: - (a) Incorrect: Rates rise with Bank Rate. - (b) Incorrect: RBI still lends. - (c) Incorrect: Tight, not easy, policy. - Supporting Evidence: - RBI (2013): Monetary policy statements. - Economic Survey (2012–13): Inflation control. - Related Concepts/Figures: - Bank Rate: Affected ~₹20 lakh crore credit in 2013. - Tight Policy: Reduced money supply ~5% in 2013. - D. Answer: (b) improve banking sector's ability to deal with financial and economic stress and improve risk management - Analysis: - Economic Context: - Basel III (2010–19) aimed to strengthen banks’ resilience (~₹80 lakh crore assets in India, 2015) via better capital and risk management (b), not biodiversity (a), emissions (c), or technology transfer (d). - Q53: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the meaning of legal tender money? - Options: (a) The money which is tendered in courts of law to defray the fee of legal cases (b) The money which a creditor is under compulsion to accept in settlement of his claims (c) The bank money in the form of cheques, drafts, bills of exchange, etc. (d) The metallic money in circulation in a country -
